doi:10.61112/jiens.1815614.title: Diabetes diagnosis using a voting classifier based on machine learning and deep learning models
doi:10.61112/jiens.1815614.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">The increasing global prevalence of diabetes mellitus poses severe public health challenges, underscoring the vital need for prompt and accurate diagnostic strategies. In this study, machine learning and deep learning-based models were individually evaluated for diabetes prediction, and the best-performing models were subsequently combined using a voting classifier structure. The dataset used was obtained from Kaggle, and preprocessing steps included the removal of missing values and outliers (resulting in the removal of 35,828 records, or 35.8% of the initial data). Statistical analysis showed that none of the continuous variables followed a normal distribution, and Mann-Whitney U tests revealed statistically significant differences between diabetic and non-diabetic groups. Five machine learning algorithms—Random Forest, XGBoost, Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machine—and two deep learning models—Multilayer Perceptron and TabNet—were assessed based on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The top-performing models (RF, XGBoost, MLP, and TabNet) were integrated using a soft voting approach.  The results demonstrate that the voting classifier exhibits highly balanced performance and achieves the highest scores among the compared models in terms of accuracy, precision, specificity, F1 score, and MCC metrics. However, it is notable that for the Recall metric-which is clinically critical for primary disease screening- the individual MLP (0.7000) and XGBoost (0.6964) models outperformed the ensemble structure. These findings emphasise that ensemble learning structures, which combine the strengths of multiple models, can provide more reliable decision support in critical areas such as healthcare. For future research, the generalizability of the model can be enhanced by using datasets with a broader range of features, and real-time adaptive systems supported by cloud computing technologies can be developed to improve the responsiveness and efficiency of diabetes prediction models.</jats:p>

doi:10.47260/amae/1662.title: Turning Conflict into Value: How Conflict-based experiential learning Shapes Relationship Quality and Reduces Emotional Conflict in International Channel Relationships
doi:10.47260/amae/1662.abstract:
<jats:p>The conflict between manufacturers and foreign distributors has gained increasing attention from both scholars and professionals in international marketing. While previous research primarily focuses on the conflict elimination perspective, little is known about how channel members learn from such conflict experiences from a conflict-based learning perspective. Drawing on relationship learning theory and the dynamic capability perspective, this study examines the antecedents and consequences of conflict-based experiential learning on the relationship between manufacturers and foreign distributors. Based on survey data from 147 Taiwanese manufacturing firms, the results indicate that long-term orientation (LTO), relational norm of flexibility, and relationship termination costs positively affect conflict-based experiential learning. Additionally, conflict-based experiential learning is associated with higher relationship quality and lower levels of emotional conflict. These findings underscore the constructive potential of conflict as a source of relational learning and offer new insights into the management of international channel partnerships. By focusing on conflict-based learning, this study advances the understanding of channel relationships and highlights how firms can turn conflict into relational value.

JEL classification numbers: M16, M31.
Keywords: Conflict-based experiential learning, Long-term orientation (LTO), Relational norm of flexibility, Relationship termination costs, Relationship quality, Emotional conflict, International channel relationships.</jats:p>

doi:10.54698/kl.2026.21.503.title: Exploring Transformative Learning Experiences in a Liberal Arts Course Using Film Adaptations: Focusing on an Analysis of Learners’ Retrospective Accounts
doi:10.54698/kl.2026.21.503.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines how students in a liberal arts course using film adaptations articulated their learning experiences through the framework of transformative learning. Drawing on Mezirow’s theory and adaptation theory, it reconceptualizes the difference between an original work and its film adaptation not as a matter of fidelity but as a pedagogical device that unsettles learners’ taken-for-granted assumptions. Using an interpretive qualitative approach, the study analyzed end-of-semester written self-reports from 31 students who compared seven literary works with their film adaptations. Thematic analysis identified four categories: disorienting dilemma, critical reflection on premises, exploration of new perspectives, and partial transfer. Students described adaptation differences as moments that challenged assumptions about class, gender, morality, power, family, freedom, and success. Rather than claiming completed perspective transformation, the study interprets these accounts as early signs of transformative learning and suggests implications for liberal arts course design.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1889375.title: Machine learning and deep learning for diagnosis of Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome: systematic review and meta-analysis
doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1889375.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) is a prevalent endocrine disorder with a challenging, heterogeneous diagnosis. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models show promise for automated diagnosis, but a quantitative synthesis of their accuracy is lacking.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of ML/DL models for PMOS and identify factors influencing performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We searched MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library from inception to January 26, 2026. Studies developing or validating ML/DL models for PMOS diagnosis were included. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. A random-effects model with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method was used to pool estimates. Hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic curves were constructed. Heterogeneity was quantified (
                      <jats:italic>I</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      ), and meta-regression and subgroup analyses explored sources of heterogeneity.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Fifty-six studies (60 datasets) were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.92 (95% CI: 0.89-0.94;
                      <jats:italic>
                        I
                        <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      </jats:italic>
                       = 93.6%) and specificity 0.94 (95% CI: 0.91-0.96; I
                      <jats:italic>
                        <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      </jats:italic>
                       = 93.4%), with an HSROC area under the curve of 0.99 (95% CI: 0.97-0.99). Prediction intervals were wide (sensitivity: 50%-99%; specificity: 53%-100%). Egger’s test suggested small-study effects (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.05). Meta-regression identified data source (database vs. single-center, coefficient=1.91,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.002) and modeling variables (ultrasound image vs. clinical parameters, coefficient=2.43,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.007) as independent predictors of higher accuracy; model type was not significant after adjustment. Ultrasound image-based models achieved the highest accuracy (sensitivity 0.99, specificity 0.98). Notably, 32 studies did not report diagnostic criteria, and only 4 performed external validation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ML/DL models, particularly those using ultrasound imaging, demonstrate promising but conditional diagnostic accuracy for PMOS. However, poor reporting of diagnostic criteria, lack of external validation, and substantial heterogeneity limit current evidence. Future research must prioritize rigorous validation and adherence to reporting standards. While not yet ready for independent clinical use, these models hold promise as assistive tools to standardize ovarian assessment.</jats:p>

doi:10.26803/ijlter.25.7.10.title: Needs Assessment and Comparative Analysis of Draft Digital Technology Standards for Learning in Basic Education in Thailand
doi:10.26803/ijlter.25.7.10.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to analyze the priority needs for standards on the use of digital technology for learning in basic education and to compare the four standards by role and school size. A survey research design was employed. The sample consisted of 1,272 participants, including 543 school administrators and 729 teachers. Data was collected using a needs assessment questionnaire for school development based on the draft standards for the use of digital technology for learning in basic education. The data were analyzed using needs assessment techniques and multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA). The findings showed that the highest priority need was Standard 1: Access and Equity in Digital Technology, followed by Standard 4: Support for Learners, Teachers, School Administrators, and Educational Personnel; Standard 2: Learning Design and Creative Self-Direction; and Standard 3: Assessment and Evaluation for Learning Development. Furthermore, the results of the mean difference tests across the four standards, classified by role and school size and examined through univariate analysis of variance and pairwise comparisons, showed that teachers had significantly higher mean scores than school administrators in three areas: Learning Design and Creative Self-Direction, Assessment and Evaluation for Learning Development, and Support for Learners, Teachers, School Administrators, and Educational Personnel, at the .05 level of statistical significance.</jats:p>

doi:10.54698/kl.2026.21.335.title: A Study on Teaching Korean Neologisms through Word Formation and Problem-Based Learning
doi:10.54698/kl.2026.21.335.abstract:
<jats:p>This study aims to propose a practical instructional model that helps Korean for Academic Purposes (KAP) learners successfully integrate into Korean-speaking communities through the learning of neologisms. The instructional approach, which combined word-formation theory and problem-based learning (PBL), demonstrated its effectiveness in enabling learners to develop from passive recipients of knowledge into active users of the Korean language.
The findings revealed that learners acquired a self-directed learning mechanism by systematically understanding the structural principles underlying the formation of Korean neologisms. This is particularly significant because it fostered metalinguistic competence, allowing learners to independently interpret and adapt to newly emerging vocabulary even after the completion of the course. Furthermore, tasks designed to reflect authentic discourse contexts led to statistically significant improvements in learners’ sociolinguistic and discourse competence.
In particular, field-oriented PBL activities, such as conducting interviews with Korean university students and participating in digital platforms, played a crucial role in breaking down the barriers of perceived social exclusivity that international students often encounter in university life. Through authentic interactions with native speakers of the target language, learners became familiar with the linguistic conventions of the community. Based on these experiences, they engaged in legitimate peripheral participation and gradually gained psychological confidence as Korean language users. Such experiences provided an opportunity for international students to reconstruct their identities, transforming themselves from peripheral participants into active members of the community.
This study suggests that the role of the instructor should be redefined from that of a mere transmitter of knowledge to that of a learning environment designer and community facilitator. The more rapidly changing the instructional content is—as in the case of neologisms—the more important it becomes to design sophisticated learning environments that enable learners to solve real-world communication problems and internalize successful communicative experiences.
In conclusion, neologism education grounded in word-formation theory and PBL represents an effective pedagogical alternative for enhancing international students’ integrated communicative competence and supporting their development as active and legitimate members of Korean academic communities.</jats:p>

doi:10.69739/jelm.v3i2.1921.title: Management Practices on Reading Programs in Key Stage 1 of Tublay District: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
doi:10.69739/jelm.v3i2.1921.abstract: <jats:p>This qualitative descriptive study focused on the management practices on reading programs in Key Stage 1 of the Tublay District for the management problems of reading fluency, the management difficulties on reading problems, and the intervention research finds. To guide this study, a conceptual setup which perceived the reading program management as the interaction of structural condition, learner related needs, monitoring and monitoring supports that affects the quality and continuity of school based reading intervention was used. There were fifteen Key Stage 1 teachers from public elementary schools in Tublay District which were purposely selected for the study. A researcher made a questionnaire that was administered using Google Forms and face to face distribution, and thematic analysis were used to analyze data. The study showed three significant findings. Firstly, Structural and Resource Constraints in Program Management consisted of time constraint, work load, number of children in class, and lack of instructional materials that lead to unable to adapt to the children with different needs. Second, Learner Participation and Instructional Management Difficulties involved low engagement, boredom, weak confidence, poor comprehension, and inconsistent participation during reading intervention. Third, Gaps in Monitoring, Coordination, and Program Continuity included weak progress tracking, limited parental and stakeholder support, insufficient teacher training, and difficulty sustaining policy based implementation. The study further showed that reading problems were shaped by learner centered difficulties, intervention delivery concerns, and resource and support gaps. Based on these findings, Project BASA READY: Building Appropriate Support and Action for Reading Advancement in Young Learners was developed as an intervention to strengthen reading program management through structured support, systematic monitoring, appropriate materials, teacher capacity building, and stronger school home community partnership.</jats:p>
doi:10.69739/jelm.v3i2.1921.venue: Journal of Education, Learning, and Management

doi:10.3389/fsufs.2026.1853792.title: Geospatial machine learning-based study on the evolutionary mechanisms of the green transformation of cultivated land use
doi:10.3389/fsufs.2026.1853792.abstract: <jats:p>Cultivated land is the fundamental basis of food production and a key carrier of socio-ecological sustainability. Promoting the Green Transformation of Cultivated Land Use (GTCLU) is therefore essential for improving agricultural resource efficiency, safeguarding food security, and mitigating land degradation. Taking 110 prefecture-level cities in the Yangtze River Economic Belt (YREB) as the study area, this study constructs a multidimensional GTCLU evaluation index using panel data from 2006 to 2022. The Real-Coded Accelerated Genetic Algorithm Projection Pursuit (RAGA-PP) model is used to measure the spatiotemporal evolution of GTCLU, while the Geographically Weighted Random Forest (GWRF) model and SHAP method are further applied to identify the spatially heterogeneous importance and directional effects of socio-economic and environmental drivers. The results show that GTCLU in the YREB increased steadily during the study period, with a persistent “north-high, south-low” spatial pattern and significant spatial agglomeration. The driving mechanisms of GTCLU are jointly shaped by economic, environmental, and social factors, but their effects vary considerably across space. In terms of variable importance, economic factors exhibit particularly prominent effects on GTCLU. Specifically, the proportion of gross agricultural product, fixed asset investment density, and per capita GDP show relatively high importance, and the areas where these factors exert strong influence cover the widest spatial range. The SHAP results further reveal that average annual precipitation, the proportion of gross agricultural product, and the irrigation index are the main factors affecting GTCLU. Specifically, average annual precipitation generally exerts a negative contribution, whereas a stronger agricultural industrial base and better irrigation conditions generally promote GTCLU. These findings reveal the non-linear and spatially differentiated mechanisms underlying cultivated land transition and provide empirical support for region-specific cultivated land management. Overall, this study develops a geospatial machine-learning framework for understanding GTCLU and offers practical implications for advancing sustainable agricultural production and Sustainable Development Goal 12.</jats:p>
