doi:10.1108/md-10-2025-3128.title: The post-crisis non-learning loop: failing to sustain crisis-induced learning
doi:10.1108/md-10-2025-3128.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper introduces the post-crisis non-learning loop (PCNL), a conceptual framework explaining how crisis-induced learning gradually decays after disruptions subside. The study argues that crises are not only sites of adaptation and experimentation, but also contexts in which psychological relief, cultural inertia, structural rigidity and organizational forgetting contribute to post-crisis regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A structured conceptual review informed by PRISMA principles was conducted to examine organizational learning, crisis management, resilience, organizational forgetting and post-crisis adaptation across studies published between 2008 and 2026. A thematic synthesis of the literature informed the development of the five-stage PCNL framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review indicates that crisis-induced adaptations frequently remain temporary and weakly institutionalized. As crisis conditions stabilize, psychological relief, cultural normalization, structural rigidity and unintentional forgetting interact to erode adaptive practices and reinforce regression toward familiar pre-crisis routines. The PCNL framework conceptualizes these dynamics as a cyclical process of post-crisis non-learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As a conceptual framework, the PCNL requires empirical testing across organizational contexts and crisis types. The study provides a foundation for future longitudinal and comparative research examining the sustainability of crisis-induced learning and the mechanisms underlying organizational regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework highlights the importance of institutionalizing adaptive practices beyond immediate crisis response. Embedding crisis-induced learning into governance systems, organizational memory structures and performance mechanisms may reduce vulnerability to post-crisis regression and forgetting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sustaining adaptive learning after crises may strengthen organizational resilience, accountability and long-term societal trust in institutions operating under conditions of uncertainty and disruption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study contributes to crisis-management and organizational-learning literature by integrating psychological, cultural, structural and forgetting mechanisms into a unified explanation of post-crisis learning decay. The PCNL framework foregrounds organizational forgetting as a central process shaping the erosion of crisis-induced adaptation over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1007/s10143-026-04422-7.title: The use of machine learning models for subdural hematoma detection: a single-arm meta-analysis
doi:10.1007/s10143-026-04422-7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Manual evaluation of non-contrast CT scans (NCTS) for detecting subdural hematoma (SDH) is time consuming, potentially inaccurate, and subjective to the expert analyzing them. In recent years, two deep learning (DL) algorithms have been popularly studied in this respect, namely convolutional neural networks (CNN) and U-Net architectures, the latter being a specialized type of CNN. We performed the first meta-analysis comparing various DL models for SDH detection. MEDLINE, Cochrane, Scopus, and Embase databases were searched from inception through December 2025. Studies evaluating ML model performance on an independent test dataset were included. The main outcome measures were sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio (DOR), accuracy, and precision of CNN, U-Net, and hybrid DL models. Univariate meta-regression analyses were performed. 30 testing datasets incorporating 67,266 NCTS were included. U-Net demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity (0.916;
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.04) and precision (0.983;
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.001) while high specificity, DOR, and accuracy values were consistently observed across all DL techniques. Internal testing (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.05) was a borderline significant predictor of high specificity while recent publication year (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.001), U-Net architecture (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.035), and 3D models (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.022) emerged as significant moderators of high precision. The U-Net architecture was also a borderline significant predictor of high DOR (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     = 0.049). While this single arm meta-analysis depicts potential superiority of U-Net models with respect to sensitivity and precision, these findings are based off only 4 pooled U-Net datasets in comparison to the 22 pooled for CNN architectures. Future well-powered studies evaluating the U-Net model are necessary to ensure a fair comparison of U-Net architectures to other DL designs before reaching to any definitive conclusions in this respect.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fmedt.2026.1902471.title: A comparative performance analysis of ensemble learning and regularized neural networks in cardiovascular risk prediction
doi:10.3389/fmedt.2026.1902471.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Heart disease classification using small structured clinical datasets requires evaluation procedures that account for sampling variability, model-selection bias, probability calibration, and clinically relevant operating characteristics. This study presents an internally validated comparison of classical classifiers, modern tree ensembles, and regularized artificial neural networks using a cleaned Cleveland heart disease dataset containing 303 observations, 13 predictors, and a binary outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Continuous variables were standardized, nominal variables were one-hot encoded, and all preprocessing transformations were fitted exclusively within training folds. Model performance was evaluated using five-fold outer cross-validation repeated five times, with inner stratified cross-validation for hyperparameter optimisation. Twelve models were assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values, F1-score, Matthew's correlation coefficient, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Brier score, and calibration measures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CatBoost achieved the highest mean ROC-AUC of 0.909 ± 0.041 and F1-score of 0.862 ± 0.041, while Logistic Regression achieved a comparable ROC-AUC of 0.906 ± 0.041. Random Forest obtained the highest mean PR-AUC of 0.916 ± 0.040. CatBoost did not significantly outperform Logistic Regression in ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, F1-score, or paired classification errors. Held-out permutation analysis identified the number of major vessels, thalassemia status, and chest-pain category as the most influential predictors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that no model family was universally superior and that a carefully regularized linear model remained competitive with substantially more complex approaches. These findings represent internal validation only and require confirmation using independent clinical cohorts before deployment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/978-1-83662-552-020261006.title: Finding and Using Funds of Anti-racist Education: A Research Study with Racially Diverse Teachers in the Rural Southwest of England
doi:10.1108/978-1-83662-552-020261006.abstract: <jats:p>Racism is an everyday reality for children and teachers from the Global Majority – a term used to describe people who are Black, Asian, Brown, dual-heritage, Indigenous to the Global South, or otherwise racialised as ‘minorities’ in predominantly white societies, despite representing most of the world's population. However, the voices of Global Majority teachers working in rural English schools are often absent from national conversations about Anti-racist Education (ARE) and the creation of training resources aimed at supporting educators. This co-authored chapter examines how reflective and dialogic activities with teachers living and working in a predominantly white rural area of southwest England can help teacher educators better understand how professional identities and pedagogical practices – formed during Initial Teacher Education and Training (ITET) – might adapt to the everyday realities of racism across English schools. This chapter draws on Malcolm's doctoral research, a participatory action research project informed by concepts from Critical Pedagogy and Critical Race Theory (CRT). Nine teachers, including Malcolm, took part in Funds of Identity (FoI)-informed activities designed to explore their relationships with Black British people, cultures, and experiences. We use reflections from two Global Majority participants to revisit Malcolm's analysis, highlighting two common themes evident across contributions. We discuss how teacher identity development within ITET can better embed ARE in rural settings by emphasising two new additional ‘funds’: (1) racial linguistic funds – how teachers can negotiate institutional hierarchies using empowering and critically relevant language; and (2) aspirational funds – how teachers can employ open, non-essentialising, and high educational aspirations in practice.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-83662-552-020261014.title: Becoming FEAR-less: Adventures in Heterotopic Affinity Space
doi:10.1108/978-1-83662-552-020261014.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter traces how doctoral research on heterotopic affinity spaces (HAS) evolved into the broader concept of FEAR-less learning: Learning in which Formal Environments and Academic Regulation are minimised to foster higher levels of agency, autonomy, and flow. Drawing on Foucault's heterotopia, Gee's affinity spaces, Papert's constructionism, and Freire's critical pedagogy, the study explored the Foundry at University of the West of England (UWE) Bristol, a purpose-built HAS used for game jams, where learners manipulated space, self-organised, engaged both deeply and boisterously to an extent uncommon in formal computer labs. Using a media-rich mini-ethnography, this chapter establishes how social connectedness and spatial otherness combine to shape behaviour, revealing two key contributions. First, how lateral moments (off-task, reflective, seemingly disruptive episodes) were integral in enabling learners to reset, recharge and return to flow states. Second, the Phases of HAS Engagement (PHASE) model demonstrated how learners oscillated between on-task and off-task modes, transitioning in and out of flow structured by individual and group lateral moments. These transitions were found to be adaptive rather than disruptive phenomena. The researcher argues that FEAR-less learning is both a conceptual lens and a practical design framework for innovative learning environments, demonstrating how heterotopic, high-agency affinity spaces can be translated into more generalisable educational settings. Recent implementations at one university in China illustrate this movement from one-off innovative space to institutional blueprint for active learning. This chapter concludes by reflecting on practitioner–researcher identity, showing how designing, studying, and iterating such spaces reshapes both theory and self-understanding within doctoral practice.</jats:p>

doi:10.4102/phcfm.v18i1.5246.title: A conducive clinical learning environment in primary care as a wicked problem: A scoping review of enablers, obstacles, and strategies
doi:10.4102/phcfm.v18i1.5246.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: The clinical learning environment (CLE) in primary care is increasingly recognised as critical to undergraduate medical education. However, its design and implementation are shaped by multiple interdependent factors, such as mentorship, autonomy, relationships and logistics, which make it a complex challenge.
Aim: This study aimed to map the literature on the contributing factors to conducive CLE for medical students in primary care settings, identify enablers and obstacles and strategies for improvement.
Setting: Primary care clinical learning environments, including community health centres, primary healthcare clinics, general practices, and district hospitals involved in undergraduate medical education.
Methods: A scoping review was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist. Four databases were searched with no language or date restrictions. Articles were screened independently by two reviewers. Data were charted using Gruppen’s conceptual framework and thematically synthesised.
Results: A total of 34 articles were included. Common enablers included effective mentorship, student autonomy, positive interpersonal relationships, organisational alignment and supportive infrastructure. Obstacles included inadequate space, transport constraints, authoritarian teaching styles and a lack of student agency. Few articles proposed solutions, and many challenges were systemic and persistent. The CLE in primary care emerged as a wicked problem – a complex, context-sensitive issue involving multiple stakeholders without a definitive solution.
Conclusion: A conducive CLE in primary care requires coordinated, multilevel strategies that address both human and structural domains. Isolated interventions are unlikely to produce lasting change.
Contribution: This review highlights the CLE in primary care as a wicked problem and provides a framework for developing systemic, adaptive responses to support medical education in diverse contexts.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/jsm-11-2025-0811.title: Verbal and nonverbal cues in influencer performance: a deep learning perspective on livestreaming e-commerce
doi:10.1108/jsm-11-2025-0811.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Grounded in the elaboration likelihood model (ELM), this study aims to examine how influencer performance shapes sales outcomes in livestreaming e-commerce through the concurrent activation of the central route (verbal cues) and peripheral route (nonverbal cues), and how these two routes interact to jointly determine sales effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using multimodal deep learning techniques, including computer vision and audio analysis, the authors analyzed 2,346 livestreaming videos to objectively extract nonverbal cues (beauty, smile and voice loudness) and manually coded verbal cues (product information), linking all measures to actual sales outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Verbal cues exert a positive linear effect on sales, while nonverbal cues exhibit inverted U-shaped relationships − moderate levels are most effective, with both under- and over-expression reducing sales. Critically, verbal cues systematically amplify these inverted U-shaped effects: higher product information intensifies both the positive and negative portions of the nonverbal cue curves, revealing that the central and peripheral routes operate not independently but interactively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Influencers should provide rich, informative product content while maintaining moderate levels of nonverbal expressiveness. Importantly, strong verbal delivery amplifies the consequences of nonverbal calibration − making script quality and expressive moderation complementary, not independent, levers for sales optimization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study makes two primary contributions. First, it extends ELM by reconceptualizing the central and peripheral routes as concurrently activated and mutually interactive in livestreaming contexts − moving beyond the traditional assumption of route exclusivity. Second, it introduces a scalable multimodal deep learning pipeline that enables simultaneous, objective measurement of verbal and nonverbal cues at scale, providing an empirical infrastructure for future research on influencer persuasion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fphy.2026.1866797.title: Post-quantum ready multimodal federated learning for adaptive threat defence
doi:10.3389/fphy.2026.1866797.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Federated learning (FL) is a key enabler for collaborative intelligence across distributed, privacy-sensitive critical infrastructures, but multimodal FL is constrained by data heterogeneity, modality misalignment, and insecure information fusion, limiting real-time threat detection under emerging post-quantum threats.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We propose PQ-FedCMCA, integrating soft cross-modal contrastive learning at the client level (adaptive scaling/relaxation for flexible many-to-many alignment) with a cross-attention-based global–local aggregation mechanism at the server level, plus knowledge distillation for generalisation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Experiments on benchmark datasets show PQ-FedCMCA outperforms state-of-the-art FL methods in cross-modal retrieval and classification tasks while enhancing post-quantum-aware privacy preservation and robustness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework advances trustworthy, privacy-preserving, post-quantum-aware AI for secure, adaptive threat detection in next-generation critical infrastructures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1861203.title: Perceived behavioral control, language mindsets, and self-determination theory: a structural analysis of learning Arabic as a second language
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1861203.abstract: <jats:p>Intensive L2 Arabic programs may place strong cognitive, emotional, and motivational demands on international students, yet limited research has examined how learners’ capability beliefs and language mindsets are related to motivation in this context. Most existing work has focused on English-dominant settings, while evidence from scholarship-based L2 Arabic programs in the Arabian Peninsula remains scarce. To address this gap, the present study tested 18 hypotheses and reports new findings from a larger funded project on learner psychology in L2 Arabic. The study examined how perceived behavioral control relates to fixed and growth language mindsets, and how these mindsets are associated with four Self-Determination Theory motivation types. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 181 multilingual international L2 Arabic learners enrolled in an intensive program at a Saudi public university, and the data were analyzed using generalized structured component analysis. The findings showed acceptable measurement quality and supported 10 of the 18 hypotheses. Perceived behavioral control was strongly associated with higher Growth Mindsets and lower Fixed Mindsets. Fixed Mindsets were linked only to External Regulation. Growth Mindsets were strongly associated with Intrinsic Motivation and Identified Regulation and were also positively associated, though more weakly, with Introjected Regulation and External Regulation. The strongest indirect associations between perceived behavioral control and the four motivational outcomes operated through Growth Mindsets. These findings suggest that L2 Arabic teachers, program leaders, and policy makers may strengthen motivation by supporting learners’ sense of control, offering scaffolded tasks and clear feedback, and fostering growth-oriented beliefs in demanding instructional settings.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1896094.title: The longitudinal relationship between foreign language learning anxiety and willingness to communicate in vocational English classrooms among Chinese students: the mediating roles of instrumental motivation and learning engagement
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1896094.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The willingness to communicate (WTC) in vocational English classrooms involves the combined roles of achievement emotions, future-oriented motivational beliefs, and classroom engagement. Drawing on control-value theory (CVT) and the L2 motivational self system (L2MSS), this study developed a three-wave longitudinal mediation model to examine the relationships among foreign language learning anxiety, instrumental motivation, learning engagement, and willingness to communicate (WTC) among Chinese non-English major vocational students. Participants (
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 232) from a vocational college completed three waves of surveys at the beginning, middle, and end of the semester. Foreign language learning anxiety was assessed using the 8-item S-FLCAS; instrumental motivation for vocational English was measured using an adapted version of the Instrumental Motivation subscale; learning engagement was tracked via the 9-item Language Classroom Engagement Scale; and WTC was evaluated using an adapted WTC in English scale. The longitudinal path analysis indicated that Time 1 foreign language learning anxiety was negatively associated with Time 3 WTC. Crucially, Time 2 instrumental motivation and Time 3 learning engagement each served as a significant mediator in this relationship, and sequentially formed a significant longitudinal chain mediation path. These findings indicate that initial anxiety is longitudinally related to subsequent differences in career-related instrumental motivation and classroom engagement, which are further associated with students’ willingness to communicate in vocational English classrooms. The findings highlight the importance of considering emotional experiences, vocational relevance, and classroom engagement when designing vocational English instruction.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.26689/jcer.v10i7.15739.title: Research on Teaching Reform and Optimization of University Fuel Cell Courses Integrated with Machine Learning
doi:10.26689/jcer.v10i7.15739.abstract: <jats:p>Driven by the global low-carbon energy transition and China’s dual-carbon strategy, fuel cell technology has become a core compulsory course for energy chemistry, new energy science and engineering, and other related majors in universities. This course features obvious interdisciplinary attributes covering electrochemistry, catalytic materials, fluid mechanics, and automatic control. However, microscopic reaction mechanisms and multiphysics coupling processes are invisible and abstract, bringing great learning difficulties to students. At present, domestic fuel cell teaching faces prominent bottlenecks including fragmented curriculum content, insufficient visual demonstration of microscopic mechanisms, high cost and safety risks of physical experiments, disconnection between teaching and industrial frontiers, and lack of intelligent technology integration. Traditional lecture-based teaching only focuses on theoretical knowledge indoctrination, failing to cultivate students’ data analysis, modeling optimization, and engineering innovation capabilities, which cannot meet the talent demand of intelligent upgrading of the fuel cell industry. Machine learning (ML) has outstanding advantages in nonlinear data fitting, performance prediction, multi-objective optimization, and microscopic mechanism inversion, which provides a new path for fuel cell curriculum reform. Targeting practical teaching pain points of energy majors, this paper summarizes five major teaching dilemmas of existing fuel cell courses, and explores multi-dimensional integration paths of ML and classroom teaching, virtual simulation experiments, project training, and university-enterprise collaborative education. Furthermore, this paper puts forward targeted reform strategies from four aspects: hierarchical knowledge system construction, inquiry-based teaching innovation, practical teaching system expansion, and teacher training and evaluation mechanism optimization. The research results integrate data-driven thinking and intelligent modeling methods into the whole teaching process, effectively solving the problems of abstract mechanism explanation, limited experimental conditions, and lagging frontier technology updates. It provides theoretical support and practical reference for intelligent curriculum reconstruction and innovative engineering talent cultivation of fuel cell courses under an emerging engineering education background.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/jocm-04-2025-0318.title: Knowledge-oriented leadership and team members’ change-oriented behavior: a social learning perspective
doi:10.1108/jocm-04-2025-0318.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As generative artificial intelligence reshapes knowledge work, knowledge workers – employees who create, share and utilize knowledge – are compelled to actively adapt to and drive these transformations. Knowledge-oriented leadership (KOL) can address their urgent needs for knowledge updating and skill upgrading, enabling them to adapt to and engage in organizational change. Given the importance of KOL, this study explores its relationship with team members’ change-oriented behavior, focusing on the mediating role of individual intellectual capital (the sum of work-related knowledge accumulated by employees) and the moderating role of task novelty in this relationship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted two studies to test our model. Study 1 (field study) collected data from 376 members in 76 teams in three waves, and Study 2 (scenario experiment) used data from 237 participants.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results show that (1) KOL is positively related to team members’ change-oriented behavior; (2) individual intellectual capital mediates the effect of KOL on team members’ change-oriented behavior; (3) task novelty positively moderates the relationship between KOL and individual intellectual capital and (4) task novelty positively moderates the indirect relationship between KOL and team members' change-oriented behavior through individual intellectual capital.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study situates KOL within the framework of organizational change, providing a knowledge-based explanation of how leadership influences team members’ change-oriented behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.65339/ijsair.v2.i3.850.title: Barriers and Challenges in Learning Basic English Competencies Among TESDA Adult Learners: A Phenomenological Study
doi:10.65339/ijsair.v2.i3.850.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the barriers and challenges encountered by TESDA adult learners in acquiring basic English competencies at the Masbate Institute of Fisheries and Technology (MIFT). Guided by the principles of adult learning and a phenomenological perspective, the study aimed to identify the barriers experienced by learners, describe their learning experiences, and determine the coping strategies they employed to overcome difficulties in learning English. A qualitative descriptive research design using a phenomenological approach was employed. Fifteen TESDA adult learners enrolled in Food and Beverage Services NC II, Trainers Methodology Level I, Housekeeping NC II, Events Management Services NC III, and the 3-Year Diploma Program in Hotel and Restaurant Operation and Management were purposively selected. Data were gathered through a validated semi-structured interview guide and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings revealed seven major barriers: limited vocabulary and difficulty understanding English, lack of confidence, difficulty in pronunciation, limited exposure and practice, difficulty understanding spoken English, anxiety and pressure during assessments, and environmental distractions. Learners’ experiences reflected both positive and negative dimensions of language learning, including skill development, learning through failures, emotional challenges, motivation to improve, appreciation of instructional support, and limitations in learning resources. To address these challenges, learners employed six coping strategies: self-practice and repetition, use of technology and online learning tools, observation and peer interaction, exposure to English media, self-motivation and confidence-building, and support from teachers, peers, and family. The study concluded that TESDA adult learners demonstrate resilience and adaptability despite linguistic, emotional, and environmental barriers. It recommended the implementation of an English Communication Enhancement Action Plan to strengthen learners’ confidence, vocabulary development, communication skills, and access to learning resources. The study aligns with SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by supporting inclusive language learning and workforce readiness. Its sustainability impact lies in strengthening educational, institutional, and socio-economic development through improved communication competencies among adult technical-vocational learners.</jats:p>
doi:10.65339/ijsair.v2.i3.850.venue: International Journal of Sustainability and Advanced Integrated Research

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1831252.title: Multimodal deep learning for prediction of postoperative recurrence in clear cell renal cell carcinoma: a clinical-radiologic-pathologic approach
doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1831252.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study intends to develop and validate a multiclass system that efficiently integrates complementary information from patients’ multimodal data (clinical, imaging, and pathological) to identify individuals at a high risk of 5-year postoperative recurrence among patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective multicenter study enrolled 270 clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) patients, allocating 215 (79.6%) for model development/validation and 55 (20.4%) to an independent test cohort. Patients were categorized into recurrence and non-recurrence groups based on whether tumor recurrence occurred within 5 years after surgery. The final included case in this cohort underwent surgery in July 2018. Single-modality models were created using radiomics, deep learning (ResNet34), and deep features-based radiomics. Subsequently, multi-modality models were constructed by combining the predicted probabilities from the single-modality models and transferring them to another classifier. All models was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 25 classification models were constructed. Notably, single-modality fusion models generally outperform their radiomics and deep learning-based radiomics (DL) counterparts. Among five single-modality fusion models, the Fused_Non-enhanced model demonstrates best predictive performance, achieving an AUROC value of 0.837 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.729-0.946). Similarly, multi-modality radiomics or DL models exhibit superior performance compared to single-modality counterparts. The multi-modality radiomics-DL model demonstrates the highest prediction performance, achieving an AUROC value of 0.967 (95% CI: 0.929-1.0) in the independent testing dataset.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The multi-modality radiomics-DL model demonstrates high accuracy in predicting the 5-year postoperative recurrence risk of clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.31538/tijie.v7i4.3207.title: Intellectual Degradation Amidst the Development of AI Technology: A Comparison Between AI Dependency Students and AI Assisted Learning Students
doi:10.31538/tijie.v7i4.3207.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to compare the trends in Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage patterns among students of the Islamic Religious Education (PAI) Study Program at Nahdlatul Ulama Islamic University, Jepara, namely AI Dependency and AI Assisted Learning. These trends are determined based on the patterns of AI use in academic activities, including the use of AI without editing, the use of AI in writing scientific articles without filtering, the use of AI as a framework for assignments, reference searches through AI, and information verification using official scientific sources. The study used a comparative quantitative approach with a survey design of 84 PAI students. Data were collected through an online questionnaire and analyzed descriptively-comparatively using frequency distribution and percentages. The results showed that 98.8% of respondents acknowledged that AI helped complete academic assignments and 95.2% felt an increase in learning efficiency. However, only 10.7% of respondents used AI completely without editing, while 81% stated that excessive use of AI has the potential to reduce critical thinking skills and academic integrity. In addition, 63.1% of respondents used AI to obtain initial references, while 79.8% continued to verify information through scientific indexing pages. These findings indicate that Islamic Religious Education students are more likely to adopt AI-assisted learning patterns than AI-dependency, utilizing AI as a learning support tool, not a substitute for thinking. This research underscores the importance of strengthening AI literacy and ethical guidelines for AI use in Islamic higher education.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fcimb.2026.1880496.title: Machine learning-based feature selection suggests circulating proteins as best at predicting and diagnosing tuberculosis in Mycobacterium tuberculosis-exposed rhesus macaques
doi:10.3389/fcimb.2026.1880496.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</jats:italic>
                    (Mtb), bacteria causing tuberculosis (TB), is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Even though billions of individuals have evidence of past or present Mtb infection and millions develop TB yearly, most individuals exposed to Mtb do not progress to TB (active disease) and successfully control (and perhaps eliminate) the infection. Factors determining the likelihood of TB progression of Mtb-exposed individuals remains poorly understood, however. Mtb-exposed non-human primates (NHPs) such as rhesus macaques (RMs) also exhibit variable likelihood of developing active disease. Previous analysis of Mtb-exposed RMs suggested that blood proteins such as C-reactive protein (CRP), albumin to globulin (A/G), and kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratios and blood leukocytes (e.g., neutrophil frequency) were best correlated with TB diagnosis. We extended this previous work by using several machine learning (ML) techniques to further quantify the relative contribution of 20 features (and their derivatives) to predict development or diagnosis of active disease in Mtb-exposed RMs. We found that independent of the specific ML technique (random forest, linear support vector machine, or logistic regression), CRP and A/G ratio values and lung CFU were most informative at discriminating between animals with active disease or no disease; furthermore, when excluding endpoint measurements (measurements done at necropsy), CRP.peak and A/G.bottom dramatically outperformed all other features at determining progression to active disease. Top 5 (when including all features) or top 2 (when excluding endpoint measurements) features together had nearly as high discriminatory power (AUC ≥0.98) as all 20+ features. Importantly, in our analysis, frequency of blood leukocytes (e.g., percent of neutrophils or lymphocytes) or their ratios (e.g., neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio) had relatively poorer predictive or diagnostic value (AUC&lt;0.8). Our results thus suggest that a combination of CRP and A/G ratio have a high power at predicting and/or diagnosing TB in Mtb-exposed RMs. Future studies will need to investigate if temporal changes in blood protein concentrations and leukocyte frequencies may further improve our ability to predict and/or diagnose TB in NHPs.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1108/jarhe-12-2025-1153.title: Fostering transversal competences in early architectural education: an active learning approach
doi:10.1108/jarhe-12-2025-1153.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the debate on integrating employability skills into university curricula. It examines early interventions for the development of Transversal Competencies (TC) in architecture education. It explores the extent to which an Active Learning Methodology (ALM)-based activity supports the development of four TC. It also derives methodological recommendations through critical reflection on teaching outcomes related to competence acquisition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study was conducted with first-year architecture students enrolled in two compulsory subjects. A blended model combining project-based and service-learning was implemented. Students created wayfinding infographics addressing real campus needs while integrating academic knowledge with professional and community contexts. A pre–post self-assessment of four employability-related competencies was analysed (n = 38) to identify significant changes and consistency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate a significant improvement in social responsibility, suggesting the potential of ALM to support the development of TCs in the early stages of higher education. Other competencies – self-motivation and self-awareness, problem-solving and quality orientation – showed more variable outcomes influenced by reflective learning challenges and certain methodological constraints. The study offers insights and recommendations to strengthen the understanding, development and assessment of TCs in early higher education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Grounded in the progressive nature of competence acquisition, this study is original for two reasons: empirical research on TCs development in architectural education remains scarce, and studies examining first-year interventions are rarer still. By analysing an early-stage, real-world ALM activity, it illustrates how introducing and scaffolding TCs from the outset can help strengthen the alignment between early-year learning and programme-wide competence development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/978-1-83662-552-0.title: Theoretical Perspectives on Learning and Teaching
doi:10.1108/978-1-83662-552-0.abstract:
<jats:p>Theoretical Perspectives on Learning and Teaching showcases the ways in which theories, from education and beyond, have been used by researchers who have recently completed their doctoral studies in education. The studies are contextualised across different UK education sectors from primary education to higher education.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Engaging with theory is one of the key criteria for assessing doctoral studies across disciplines. Research shows that recent doctoral graduates often struggle to transition from being researchers to publishing in academic books and journals. This collection, featuring chapters from thirteen recent education doctoral researchers, provides an opportunity for recent graduates to showcase how they engaged with theory in their doctoral studies. Each chapter highlights how different theories were applied or developed in their research across various educational sectors and explores how theory informed or was generated by their studies, utilizing diverse methods such as narrative inquiry, mixed methods research, creative methods, evaluation techniques, and ethnographic methods.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Readers who are doctoral researchers themselves and their supervisors will find the chapters stimulate thinking and discussion about the diverse range of theories that can be drawn upon to inform research at different stages of the study, from design to analysis. The focus on ‘lessons from doctoral studies’ will benefit readers who are postgraduate researchers and their supervisors, as well as the wider education research community.</jats:p>

doi:10.4324/9781003669326-5.title: Community-Based Learning in Urban Planning at a Minority-Serving Institution
doi:10.4324/9781003669326-5.abstract: Minority serving institutions often implement high-impact practices for improving students&s; academic achievements. One of those high-impact practices is experiential learning. Students succeed when they develop a connection with the topic that they are learning about through learning by doing. Community-based learning in urban planning education offers just that. Working with local communities helps students connect with what they are learning and what they will be practicing upon graduation. This chapter discusses six community-based learning projects implemented through the Community Design Program housed in the Urban Studies and Planning Department at California State University, Northridge, a minority serving institution. All six projects included college students, most of whom were Latinos, working with communities of predominantly Latino neighbourhoods of the northeast San Fernando Valley in Los Angeles. Students implemented community design techniques to work with community members mimicking professional urban planning practice, which gave community members a voice in the planning process.

doi:10.4324/9781003716518-21.title: A Theoretical Review of Identity Formation for Workplace Management under an Intelligent Tutoring System Learning Environment
doi:10.4324/9781003716518-21.abstract: The formation of students&s; identities within contemporary university settings presents a significant challenge that educators in higher education must address. Modern students seek to understand their sense of self before graduation, necessitating timely support throughout their academic journey. Consequently, effective management of the learning environment emerges as a critical factor that, when proficiently implemented, can facilitate this developmental process. The integration of artificial intelligence technologies enhances teaching management by enabling Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) to tailor the educational experience, thereby promoting the development of students&s; personal identities. A student&s;s identity is developed when both appropriate references and a conducive learning environment are present. Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) can facilitate students in actively shaping their own identity formation. This process is highly dynamic, involving continuous interactions among all relevant stakeholders daily. This chapter aims to enhance the theoretical understanding of the relationship between identity formation and learning in the context of encountering differences within an ITS environment, including the conflicts that may emerge. Such experiences encompass students&s; adaptation to new roles, the navigation of feelings of alienation from peers, and the management of life challenges encountered throughout this process. Prior studies have predominantly focused on the processes through which individuals engage in self-reflection concerning their identities and learning experiences. This chapter aims to explore the manner in which students and their peers manage vulnerabilities, foster resilience, and participate in collaborative learning within the context of ITS and the challenges inherent to these environments. Furthermore, it investigates potential avenues for future research by concentrating on the micro-communities that form around ITS, as well as examining how ITS can support and enhance students&s; comprehension of identity development.

doi:10.1080/15475441.2026.2709871.title: Conventional and alternative classifier selection in Mandarin-speaking children: the roles of typicality and input statistics
doi:10.1080/15475441.2026.2709871.abstract: In Mandarin, a classifier must be placed between a numeral and a noun, and classifiers encode semantic features. A noun category may take several classifiers, yet speakers typically use one classifier most frequently, which we call the category’s conventional classifier. Prototypical members have features that match the conventional classifier’s meaning, whereas less typical members may mismatch its meaning. We ask whether Mandarin-speaking children select conventional classifiers for these less typical members, and how input frequency and consistency of each classifier – noun pair interact with typicality to shape classifier selection. Eighty-six 5–7-year-old children produced numeral – classifier – noun phrases for 24 images (8 noun categories × 3 typicality conditions: prototypical, less typical, cross-category lookalike items). Conventional classifier use was highest for prototypical items, reduced for less typical items, and near floor for cross-category lookalikes. Frequency increased conventional classifier use for prototypical items, whereas consistency predicted conventional use for both prototypical and less typical items; when modeled together, consistency was a stronger predictor. Children’s non-conventional responses to less typical items were overwhelmingly the Mandarin general classifier (gè). Together, the findings support the conclusion that children integrate both item typicality and pairing statistics while balancing convention-following and semantic-adjustment strategies in classifier selection.

doi:10.18848/2327-7955/cgp/a363.title: The Mediating Effect of the Use of AI on the Influence of Work Stress on the Collegiate Work Dynamics of University Teachers
doi:10.18848/2327-7955/cgp/a363.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">This study examined the mediating effect of artificial intelligence’s (AI’s) use on the relationship between work stress and collegiate work among university professors. Using a cross-sectional quantitative design grounded in the transactional theory of stress and coping, 259 professors from six public and private Peruvian universities in the northern region were surveyed through the Artificial Intelligence Mediation Scale in Work Stress and Collegiate Work (EMIAETC). Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed to test mediation hypotheses. Results confirmed that work stress significantly increases AI adoption (β = 0.585, p < 0.001), which in turn substantially facilitates collegiate work (β = 0.634, p < 0.001). A complete mediation effect was identified (indirect effect: β = 0.371, p < 0.001), revealing that work stress does not directly influence professional collaboration (β = 0.127, p = 0.143) but operates indirectly through technological adoption. The model explained 49.6% of variance in collegiate work and 34.2% in AI use. The study concludes that AI functions as a compensatory mechanism that transforms stress impact on collaborative dynamics, suggesting that higher education institutions should prioritize strategic digital literacy training and AI infrastructure development to promote effective teacher collaboration in high-demand work contexts.</jats:p>

doi:10.1201/9781042003679-67.title: Adaptive MOS Enhancement VOIP Quality Monitoring Through Graph-Based Deep Learning Approaches
doi:10.1201/9781042003679-67.abstract: Maintaining the best possible user experience in Voice over IP (VOIP) systems requires precise real-time speech quality monitoring. Most traditional techniques for calculating Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) are based on pre-established network parameters such as packet loss, jitter, and delay, as well as rule-based models. Although these systems can perform basic assessments and start corrective actions, they cannot adapt to dynamic network topologies, user-specific audio conditions, and rapidly changing environments. This paper showcased a new deep learning framework that explains adaptive MOS prediction that is backed by PyTorch-built Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The system captures intricate relationships between network nodes, user behaviors, and environmental conditions by representing speech and network-related features in a graph-structured data. Tools like PESQ and POLQA, real VoIP call data labeled with MOS, are used to train the model in a controlled lab environment. With 0.19 Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and an R2 score of 0.88, it establishes that the GNN-based system overtakes other deep learning baselines and traditional models, providing accuracy in prediction. Additionally, the model accelerates continuous learning and real-time inference, allowing for proactive network optimization and customized quality corrections. For contemporary VOIP quality monitoring, this method provides a reliable, scalable, and creative solution.
