doi:10.1002/nop2.70718.title: Culturally Safe Nursing: Transformative Learning Experiences Through Critical Reflection Assessment
doi:10.1002/nop2.70718.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aim</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To explore the transformative learning experiences of postgraduate nursing students engaging in an Aboriginal culture and history module, through an analysis of a critical reflection assessment, in particular the student development of cultural awareness and culturally safe practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite mandated inclusion of Aboriginal cultural content in Australian nursing curricula, culturally unsafe practices and racism persist. Transformative learning, underpinned by critical reflection, can challenge fixed assumptions and promote cultural awareness and culturally safe care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative descriptive study using thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Written critical reflections from 15 consenting postgraduate nursing students who completed the Ngany Kalyakal Katatjiny Boordawan Module, which was developed to promote culturally safe care of Australian nurses, were analysed using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis and interpreted through Tsimane and Downing's conceptual model of transformative learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The three developed themes were: (1) Students' initial awareness and understanding of Aboriginal culture, history and health—revealing knowledge gaps and societal influences; (2) The learning experience—characterised by emotional responses, identification with Aboriginal experiences and critical re‐examination of traditional healthcare perspectives; and (3) Practice through a new lens—demonstrating conceptual shifts and intentions to apply culturally safe approaches in practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Critical reflection of culture and health learning activities can support transformative learning, challenge prior assumptions and facilitate the development of skills and attitudes aligned with culturally safe nursing practice. Careful planning of these learning activities is needed to manage student emotional discomfort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Impact</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings highlight the need for authentic, meaningful reflective activities and ongoing evaluation of cultural and health education across nursing curricula.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Implications for Nursing Practice</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings highlight the importance of integrating authentic, meaningful learning experiences into nursing curricula, including reflective assessment strategies that foster transformative learning and equip future nurses to provide culturally safe care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1061/9780784486962.059.title: Enabling Intelligent Collaboration in Architectural Programming: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework for Mega Transportation Projects
doi:10.1061/9780784486962.059.abstract: In mega transportation projects (MTPs), architectural programming serves as the starting point of the project lifecycle, and its quality directly influences subsequent stages of design, construction, and operation. However, architectural programming often faces challenges such as multi-stakeholder collaboration, multi-objective conflicts, and uncertainties in the external environment. This study proposes a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework, which integrates multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO), counterfactual regret minimization (CFR), and hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) to enhance intelligent collaborative decision-making during the architectural programming stage of MTPs. Using empirical data from the Shanghai East Railway Station project, a simulation environment is constructed to validate the framework’s feasibility and effectiveness in improving solution quality, decision-making efficiency, and conflict minimization. The study not only offers methodological support for the intelligent transformation of architectural programming but also provides a transferable technical pathway for multi-stakeholder collaboration optimization in complex systems.

doi:10.3390/educsci16091378.title: Learning Without Walls: A Systematic Review of Evaluation Approaches and Educational Outcomes in Chemistry and Science Field Trip Research
doi:10.3390/educsci16091378.abstract: <jats:p>Field trips in chemistry and science education provide students with opportunities to learn beyond the classroom walls. The aim of this systematic review was to identify the evaluation approaches used to investigate field trips in chemistry and science education and to examine them both quantitatively and qualitatively. The systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, with predefined eligibility criteria and reasons for exclusion reported in the PRISMA flow diagram. The results revealed a wide variety of evaluation approaches used to investigate outdoor field trips in chemistry and science education, including questionnaires, pre-tests/post-tests, interviews, drawings, mind maps, concept maps, discussions, notes, observations, videos and photographs, portfolios, journals and diaries, reports, student conversations, audio recordings, Q methodology, and other non-traditional approaches. Although outdoor science field trips are studied worldwide, research has predominantly focused on environmental education, while only a small number of studies have examined field trips in chemistry education.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/diagnostics16172744.title: Simultaneous Preoperative Prediction of Locally Advanced Breast Cancer, DCIS Component, and Multifocality Using Structured Mammographic Features and Gradient-Boosting Machine Learning
doi:10.3390/diagnostics16172744.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Accurate preoperative detection of locally advanced breast cancer is essential for neoadjuvant therapy planning. We developed and validated gradient-boosting models using structured BI-RADS mammographic features to simultaneously predict locally advanced breast cancer (LABC), DCIS component, and multifocality in a multi-center cohort. Methods: This retrospective study enrolled 2295 patients from three university-affiliated hospitals; features were coded according to BI-RADS. CatBoost and logistic regression models were built using stratified 60/20/20 splits, with performance assessed via bootstrap resampling, nested cross-validation, and sensitivity analyses. AUROC, AUPRC, Brier score, and calibration metrics assessed discrimination and clinical utility; a leakage audit and SHAP analysis supported interpretation. Results: CatBoost achieved an AUROC of 0.906 (95% CI: 0.876–0.932) for LABC. Because several top predictors overlap with the anatomical criteria defining this outcome, we repeated the analysis excluding them; the reduced model retained a mean AUROC of 0.739, indicating genuine predictive signal beyond the staging overlap. Net benefit was positive across all relevant thresholds, with calibration error of 0.053. DCIS prediction was highly accurate (AUROC 0.979; nested AUROC 0.9707), with no evidence of leakage. Multifocality prediction was more modest (AUROC 0.810), reflecting known limits of two-dimensional mammography. Sensitivity analyses confirmed stable performance across splits, training sizes, and class-weighting schemes. Conclusions: Structured mammographic features combined with gradient-boosting support clinically meaningful, though partly overlapping, risk stratification for LABC; once accounted for, the model still retains independent value. The DCIS model performed very well; multifocality prediction remains more limited, and external validation is needed before clinical use.</jats:p>

doi:10.1177/10775463261483243.title: Predictive rollout–guided constrained reinforcement learning for low-conservatism robust vibration control under parametric uncertainty
doi:10.1177/10775463261483243.abstract: <jats:p>Active vibration control of mechanical structures is unavoidably affected by bounded parametric uncertainty caused by varying payloads, aging, and modeling errors. Such uncertainty can degrade nominal vibration suppression and, more importantly, trigger violations of hard safety limits such as travel, deflection, and strain bounds. This study proposes a Predictive Rollout–Guided Constrained Reinforcement Learning framework (PECRL) for empirical robustness enhancement with reduced nominal conservatism under bounded parameter variations. The controller is trained in a nominal environment, while uncertainty-aware behavior is promoted through differentiable finite-horizon closed-loop rollouts evaluated at the vertices of an uncertainty set. The rollouts provide two complementary training signals: a smooth vertex-based surrogate of predicted hard-limit exceedance and an envelope-width penalty for reducing parameter-induced trajectory dispersion. These terms are incorporated into policy learning through multi-constraint primal–dual Lagrangian updates. PECRL is intended as an empirical robustness-enhancing framework rather than a formal worst-case safety certificate. Numerical validation is conducted on a Van der Pol oscillator, a quarter-car active suspension with hard travel limits, and an uncertain cantilever-beam benchmark with actuator saturation.</jats:p>

doi:10.59653/jemls.v4i03.2580.title: Methodological Organization of the Theoretical Anatomy Class: Proposal Informed by Teaching Practice in Health Sciences
doi:10.59653/jemls.v4i03.2580.abstract: <jats:p>The teaching of Anatomy in Health Sciences continues to face the challenge of moving beyond pedagogical models focused solely on isolated morphological description, which may limit knowledge integration and its application to clinical reasoning. This article proposes a methodological framework for structuring theoretical sessions in Human Anatomy II, oriented toward strengthening basic-clinical correlation and fostering meaningful learning. A qualitative approach with a reflective-interpretative design was adopted, drawing on Schön’s reflective practice model to analize teaching experiences and didactic materials used in medical education. The resulting framework organizes the class session into three pedagogical phases (introduction, development, and conclusions) integrating strategies for cognitive activation, active retrieval of information, cognitive load regulation, and early clinical integration. The findings suggest that this methodological structure enhances the integrated understanding of anatomical knowledge and strengthens the early development of clinical reasoning, constituting a reproducible pedagogical framework for competency-based education in Health Sciences.</jats:p>

doi:10.1201/9781042013234-10.title: Hybrid Deep Learning Framework Sustainable Environmental System
doi:10.1201/9781042013234-10.abstract: Accurate forecasting of solar irradiance plays a crucial role in optimizing the usage of solar energy and advancing sustainable energy practices. This comprehensive study explores a novel framework that improves forecasting accuracy by combining complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN), permutation entropy (PE), and a hybrid deep learning framework encompassing convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) units. In the proposed approach, CEEMDAN is utilized to decompose the irradiance into intrinsic mode functions (IMFs), effectively extracting both short-term variations and underlying trends. PE is subsequently employed to evaluate the complexity of these IMFs, allowing the generation of informative input features for prediction. The hybrid CNN-BiLSTM architecture is then adopted to collect spatial patterns and temporal dependencies within the processed data. An evaluation using solar irradiance data from the HI-SEAS open-source repository and a custom setup at NITK confirms the enhanced performance of the model with respect to conventional approaches that do not incorporate decomposition techniques. Furthermore, a comparison is conducted between the proposed hybrid framework and other decomposition techniques. The results obtained by the proposed architecture with HI-SEAS data have an MAE of 10.256 W/m 2 , an RMSE of 17.688 W/m 2 , and an R 2 score of 0.984 for one step ahead, which surpasses those of other models in terms of the error metrics.

doi:10.1080/2573234x.2026.2720241.title: Predicting user engagement across heterogeneous social media campaigns: a multiclass machine learning framework
doi:10.1080/2573234x.2026.2720241.abstract: Introduction Social media campaigns shape online communication across diverse contexts, yet most studies examine engagement within individual campaigns or specific domains. This study aims to identify engagement predictors that generalize across contexts and those that remain context dependent. Its novelty lies in evaluating engagement systematically across multiple campaigns and communication domains using a unified predictive framework.Methodology We model user engagement as a multiclass classification problem using more than 7.5 million tweets from twelve campaigns spanning social, political, technology, and sustainability domains. The framework incorporates user-profile characteristics, temporal features, sentiment, emotion, hashtags, mentions, URLs, and other tweet-level attributes. Five supervised machine learning algorithms are evaluated and compared across campaigns.Results Random Forest provides the most consistent predictive performance across campaign contexts. User-related features, particularly account reach and activity, consistently emerge as the strongest predictors of engagement. In contrast, the importance of temporal, sentiment, and content-related features varies across campaigns, highlighting the influence of communication context on engagement patterns.Practical implications The framework helps campaign managers distinguish broadly reliable engagement predictors from context-specific factors. These insights can support more informed audience targeting, content planning, and campaign management across diverse communication settings.

doi:10.1007/s13748-026-00473-5.title: Machine intelligence approaches for preventing adversarial malware attacks in intrusion detection systems: A systematic review
doi:10.1007/s13748-026-00473-5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In academia, the epistemology of Adversarial Malware Attacks (
                    <jats:bold>AMAs</jats:bold>
                    ) in the context of an Intrusion Detection System (
                    <jats:bold>IDS</jats:bold>
                    ) has not been fully grasped. Using Machine Intelligence (
                    <jats:bold>MI</jats:bold>
                    ), many attempts have been made to reproduce modeling techniques and methods within IDSs that can properly track, trace, and prevent AMAs from reappearing. However, there seems to be a lack of comprehensive and cohesive literature reviews in this area on which existing scholars can rely to pursue future research and broaden the field of Information Security and Networks (
                    <jats:bold>ISN</jats:bold>
                    ) research. Motivated by the absence of a universal IDSs framework,
                    <jats:italic>termed a ’one-stop shop,’</jats:italic>
                    this systematic review hopes to serve the research community by aligning thinking and firmly consolidating the historical knowledge and progress made in MI approaches, thereby providing a better understanding of AMAs, including their prevention and the implementation of viable and efficient IDSs. No other systematic review of this kind has yet been produced. Starting with nearly 1,000 papers and applying rigorous analysis, this study covers 132 research papers in multiple bibliographic databases since January 2020, highlighting studies on IDSs deployed for AMA detection and classification using MI learning techniques such as Machine Learning (
                    <jats:bold>ML</jats:bold>
                    ) and Deep Learning (
                    <jats:bold>DL</jats:bold>
                    ); methods involving feature extraction; studies discussing static, dynamic, memory, and hybrid feature analysis; and finally, studies providing experimental results and accuracy metrics from these IDSs. Throughout this comprehensive review, the emphasis is placed on highlighting the differences, strengths, and shortcomings from each MI-IDS approach, as well as providing discussions and suggestions for further exploration in future research. Following the PRISMA protocol, this systematic literature review (SLR) provides a rigorous, transparent, and reproducible foundation for knowledge by synthesizing all available evidence on IDSs over recent years.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1093/9780198995746.003.0005.title: Processing Information from the Public
doi:10.1093/9780198995746.003.0005.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter shows how the challenges of information volume and complexity are addressed through information processing, and develops a typology to understand the differences between distinct ways in which information can be processed. It shows how two dimensions characterizing policymakers’ desired information outputs—specificity and novelty—help us make sense of the different ways in which information from the public can be processed, and the varying requirements of that processing in terms of individual attention and domain-specific knowledge. The chapter reviews each of the resulting four types of information processing—aggregative, summarative, classificative, and generative—and illustrates them with examples drawn from a variety of settings around the world. It also shows how the same information inputs can be processed in different ways, the consequences of these choices for the costliness of information processing, and the potential for mismatch between the mode of processing employed and policymakers’ actual learning goals.</jats:p>

doi:10.57260/csdj.2026.284732.title: Attitude and Utilization of Generative AI as a Learning Tool among Pre-Service Mathematics Teachers
doi:10.57260/csdj.2026.284732.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the attitudes and utilization of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a learning tool among pre-service mathematics teachers. Employing a descriptive-correlational research design, data were collected from 71 respondents through a structured survey instrument to determine their perceptions of generative AI and the frequency of its use in learning mathematics. Findings revealed that respondents demonstrated a moderately positive attitude toward generative AI across cognitive, affective, and behavioral dimensions. In terms of utilization, participants commonly used generative AI tools for step-by-step explanations, clarification of mathematical concepts, and assistance in solving mathematical problems. However, integration of these tools into regular study routines remained limited. Correlation analysis showed a significant moderate positive relationship between attitudes and frequency of use, indicating that more favorable perceptions are associated with higher levels of engagement with generative AI in academic tasks. Respondents also perceived the curriculum as moderately supportive in developing competencies for effective AI utilization, particularly in enhancing problem-solving skills, critical thinking, and conceptual understanding. Nevertheless, some hesitation was noted in encouraging peer use, reflecting concerns about appropriate and responsible application. In general, the study highlights the need for structured integration of generative AI in mathematics education. It is recommended that teacher education institutions provide targeted training, clear guidelines, and pedagogical strategies to strengthen technological competence, critical thinking, and ethical use of AI. Future research may further examine its long-term effects on learning outcomes and professional readiness.</jats:p>

doi:10.18421/tem153-73.title: Integrating Teaching Factory Learning Management for Sustainable Entrepreneurial Competence Development
doi:10.18421/tem153-73.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to analyze the management of teaching factory (TeFa) learning in enhancing the entrepreneurial competence of Fashion Design students at SMK Negeri 3 Kendari. Using a descriptive qualitative approach, data were collected through observation, questionnaires, interviews, and documentation involving the vice principal for curriculum, head department, teachers, industry partners (DUDI), and grade XI students. The data were analyzed using the Likert scale with SPSS support and processed through the Sugiyono model, which includes data reduction, display, and verification, while validity was tested through technical and source triangulation. The results indicate that teaching factory learning management is generally in the good category. The planning component achieved an average score of 3.85, organizing 3.89, implementation 3.98, and evaluation 3.81. These findings suggest that effective teaching factory management covering planning, organization, implementation, and evaluation successfully bridges the gap between theoretical learning and industrial practice, thereby improving students’ entrepreneurial competence.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1898974.title: Investigation of factors affecting egg breakage resistance in laying hens using data mining and machine learning methods
doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1898974.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to evaluate the predictive performance of different machine learning algorithms and to identify the key factors influencing eggshell breaking resistance in laying hens.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three machine learning methods, C5.0 decision tree, Random Forest (RF), and Support Vector Regression (SVR), were applied to egg classification and prediction tasks. Eggshell strength (ER) was predicted using egg weight (EW), shell weight (SW), shell thickness (ST), and shape index (SI).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The C5.0 decision tree, trained on 464 eggs, achieved an overall classification accuracy of 65.1%, with a tendency to misclassify brown eggs as white, suggesting potential feature overlap or class imbalance. Among the regression models, RF outperformed SVR, yielding higher R
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      (0.852 vs. 0.553) and adjusted R
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      (0.835 vs. 0.548) values, along with lower error metrics (MSE, RMSE, and MAPE). In addition to superior predictive accuracy, the RF model provided insights into the relative importance of egg quality traits affecting eggshell breaking resistance.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, the findings indicate that ensemble-based machine learning methods are effective tools for both accurate prediction and identification of influential factors related to eggshell strength.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3390/su18178782.title: How Agricultural Cultural Heritage Tourism Promotes Cultural Learning for Sustainable Heritage Development: The Mediating Role of Cultural Identity and the Moderating Role of Income
doi:10.3390/su18178782.abstract: <jats:p>Whether agricultural cultural heritage (ACH) tourism supports sustainable heritage development depends partly on whether visits sustain the communication and internalization of heritage knowledge rather than merely produce favorable consumption evaluations. Drawing on experience economy theory, social identity theory, and tourism learning theory, this study constructs a mechanism model linking ACH experiences to tourists’ cultural learning. To reduce conceptual overlap, experience quality is defined as visitors’ perceived distinctiveness, novelty, and memorability of the visit, whereas perceived value is defined as a utilitarian assessment of gains relative to the money, time, and effort invested. ACH experience is therefore divided into three analytically distinct dimensions: experience quality, perceived value, and knowledge transfer. Cultural identity is introduced as a mediating variable and is understood as a layered psychological construct including cognitive recognition, affective attachment, and evaluative commitment. Income level is introduced as a moderating variable and is interpreted as a within-sample socioeconomic boundary condition after controlling for education and other demographic characteristics. In this study, sustainability is defined narrowly as the sociocultural continuity of ACH from the visitor side and is operationalized through perceived knowledge transfer, cultural identity, and self-reported cultural learning; income is used to examine whether this pathway differs across socioeconomic groups. Based on 430 valid questionnaires collected from visitors to ACH sites in Fujian Province, this cross-sectional study conducts empirical tests using structural equation modeling (SEM), Bootstrap mediation analysis, and hierarchical regression analysis. The results show that experience quality and knowledge transfer are positively associated with tourists’ cultural learning, with knowledge transfer showing the stronger association. Perceived value has no significant relationship with cultural learning, indicating that a consumption-level perception of value for money does not necessarily correspond to deeper cultural learning. Cultural identity fully mediates the statistical relationship between knowledge transfer and tourists’ cultural learning, revealing a dominant pathway linking knowledge transfer, cultural identity, and cultural learning. Income level positively moderates the relationship between cultural identity and tourists’ cultural learning. Because the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, these findings indicate theoretically consistent associations rather than definitive causal effects. The study contributes to sustainability research by offering a quantifiable visitor-side framework for monitoring knowledge communication, cultural connection, and learning-related outcomes. Repeated measurement of these indicators may support adaptive heritage management and inclusive cultural participation, but they should be combined with ecological, economic, and community-based indicators rather than treated as a complete sustainability index.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/make8090260.title: GRIMCELL: A Graph Neural Network to Predict the Impact of New Cells in Mobile Networks
doi:10.3390/make8090260.abstract: <jats:p>Network densification will play a vital role in next-generation cellular networks, as it addresses coverage and capacity issues in the radio access domain. However, new cell deployments can negatively impact neighbor cells, requiring careful planning. Unfortunately, the complexity of advanced radio resource management schemes implemented in Beyond 5G and future 6G networks makes it challenging to predict the impact of radio deployments in the existing cells accurately. This work presents GRIMCELL, a novel data-driven method to estimate the impact of radio deployments (i.e., new carriers, sectors, or sites) on cell performance. For this purpose, GRIMCELL combines radio planning, configuration management and performance management data gathered in commercial vendor equipment. The core of GRIMCELL is a proven message passing graph neural network (XENet) to forecast the performance of both new and existing cells after the deployment. Assessment over data from a commercial LTE-A Pro network has shown that GRIMCELL provides high accuracy and flexibility across diverse deployment scenarios.</jats:p>

doi:10.1093/9780198995746.003.0007.title: The Politics of Information Processing
doi:10.1093/9780198995746.003.0007.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter returns to questions of political incentives that shape how politicians design opportunities to learn from the public, how participants strategically engage with them, and the consequences that these may have. What does a better understanding of different types of information processing and their tradeoffs offer us in answering these questions? This chapter in particular focuses on the consequences of potential bias and manipulation, whether through unrepresentative participation, strategic participation, or by strategic policymakers. Importantly, filtering-based information processing is not so easily manipulated by biased samples of contributions, as the information outputs do not reflect every single value in the same way as does a numeric average. But filtering can be more easily biased at the processing stage, creating opportunities for policymakers with political goals to cherrypick contributions to suit their interests.</jats:p>

doi:10.1088/1361-6501/ae9977.title: Dynamic uncertainty evaluation of axial displacement of optical scanning coordinate measuring machine based on neural network
doi:10.1088/1361-6501/ae9977.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The inner-surface geometry of high-aspect-ratio microholes critically influences the cooling performance of turbine blades in aero-engines. Optical scanning coordinate measuring machines are widely used to inspect such microholes owing to their non-contact operation and high measurement efficiency. During scanning, the axial displacement along the hole axis functions as a key intermediate quantity for three-dimensional reconstruction. However, this displacement is influenced by servo tracking errors, microvibrations, and thermal drift, resulting in pronounced time-dependent behavior and dynamic uncertainty that conventional static uncertainty evaluation frameworks, such as the Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement, fail to capture adequately. To overcome this limitation, this paper proposes an image-sequence-based method for the dynamic uncertainty evaluation of axial displacement. Convolutional neural networks are used to obtain image features, while reference-frame-conditioned relative features and a gated recurrent unit are employed to model the temporal evolution of displacement. A heteroscedastic Gaussian regression framework is introduced to jointly estimate the displacement mean and its dynamic uncertainty, with Monte Carlo dropout applied to quantify predictive uncertainty. The proposed method operates without requiring additional hardware modifications and provides a reliable axial displacement prior for microhole point cloud registration and subsequent uncertainty propagation. Experimental results show that the predicted displacements generally follow the measured values, while the estimated uncertainty exhibits appropriate 95% confidence interval coverage and a strong correlation with residuals.</jats:p>

doi:10.1061/9780784486993.054.title: System Usability and Affective Assessment of a Virtual Learning Environment for Ergonomic Risk Identification and Exoskeleton Use in Construction Tasks
doi:10.1061/9780784486993.054.abstract: Exoskeletons have been regarded as a potential technology to mitigate ergonomic risks and MSDs. However, construction education that prepares the current and future workforce lacks the requisite tools to integrate this technology. Given this, this study evaluates the usability and affective impact of a Virtual Reality (VR) learning environment designed to teach construction students the recognition of ergonomic hazards and the use of exoskeletons. Twelve construction students used the VR learning environment and subsequently completed two standard evaluation instruments: the System Usability Scale (SUS) and the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM). The VR learning environment scored an average SUS score of 71.04 (SD = 18.99), indicating adequate usability, though improvements are still needed. An analysis of the SAM dimensions revealed higher scores for pleasure (M = 7.25, SD = 2.34) and Arousal (M = 7.17, SD = 1.75), which implies that users experienced the system as pleasant and exciting. Dominance scores (M = 6.58, SD = 2.11) indicated that users were generally in control throughout the interaction. Spearman correlation analysis revealed significant positive correlations for SUS scores and pleasure (ρ = 0.668, p = 0.018) and dominance (ρ = 0.742, p = 0.006), but no significant correlation was found for arousal. The findings indicate that the VR learning environment is both usable and emotionally engaging and holds promising prospects for its integration into construction education to promote ergonomic awareness and enable exoskeleton use.

doi:10.36728/iceete.v4i1.393.title: Apps Learning Lontara: Student Interest in Learning Lontara Script Based on Local Wisdom of Makassar Culture Irwan Aditia1*, Bahrur Rahman Hasba2, Dwi Astria3, Hasrianti4
doi:10.36728/iceete.v4i1.393.abstract: <jats:p>The Makassar ethnic group of South Sulawesi holds a rich cultural heritage, notably the Lontara script, which records traditional values, messages, and rituals. However, teaching of local languages, including Makassar Lontara, has become rare in elementary schools, and most Phase B students have limited familiarity with the script. This study aims to design Apps Learning Lontara, an Android-based application intended to increase Phase B students' interest in and understanding of the Lontara script rooted in local wisdom, and to empirically evaluate its effect on students' learning interest. The study combined a Research and Development (R&D) approach using the ADDIE model with a quasi-experimental one-group pretest-posttest field trial involving 30 Phase B students across three parallel classes and five class teachers at SD INPRES Parangrea. Learning-interest questionnaire data were analyzed descriptively and with a two-way (Time x Class) ANOVA. Findings indicate a statistically significant increase in students' learning interest scores after using the application, with no significant difference in the magnitude of improvement across the three classes, indicating a consistent effect. Teachers reported the application to be practical and engaging to use alongside conventional instruction. These results suggest that technology-based, culturally grounded learning media such as Apps Learning Lontara can serve as an effective alternative for revitalizing local-content education at the elementary level.</jats:p>

doi:10.47572/muskutd.1881577.title: Postoperative Complications in Older Adults After Local Surgical Procedures; Risk Factor Analysis and Comparison of Machine Learning Methods
doi:10.47572/muskutd.1881577.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Older adults frequently undergo excision of cutaneous lesions under local anesthesia and may be at increased risk of postoperative complications due to comorbid conditions and concomitant medications. This study aimed to identify predictors of postoperative complications in patients aged 65 years and older and to compare the predictive performance of logistic regression with machine-learning models. This retrospective study included 314 patients who underwent cutaneous lesion excision under local anesthesia. Demographic, clinical, and perioperative variables were collected and assessed using multivariable logistic regression. Decision tree, random forest, and gradient boosting models were developed using an 80/20 training–testing split. Missing data were imputed, and class imbalance was addressed using resampling techniques. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Postoperative complications occurred in 119 patients (37.9%). Patients with complications were older, had lower body mass index, and more frequently had diabetes, coronary artery disease, and antithrombotic therapy. Logistic regression identified low body mass index, diabetes, and coronary artery disease as independent predictors but demonstrated limited discriminatory ability. Among machine-learning models, the random forest achieved the best performance, with superior discrimination and calibration. Body mass index, perioperative blood pressure, age, and procedure duration were the most influential predictors. Postoperative complications are common among older adult patients undergoing cutaneous surgery under local anesthesia. Low body mass index, cardiometabolic comorbidities, perioperative hemodynamic factors, and operative duration are key determinants of risk. Machine-learning approaches, particularly random forest models, may improve perioperative risk stratification in this population.</jats:p>

doi:10.1080/03098265.2026.2722200.title: Comparing augmented and virtual reality modalities for learning about marine conservation in an undergraduate geography course
doi:10.1080/03098265.2026.2722200.abstract: Extended reality (XR) technologies like augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) have the potential to be effective classroom tools in geography courses, where students are routinely required to visualize and interpret spatially complex relationships. However, little is understood about how XR technologies differ in their impact on students’ learning achievement in both individual and systematic ways. In this study, we used a pretest-posttest design to compare differences in learning outcomes among three different gamified XR technologies (monoscopic AR, stereoscopic AR, and VR) and a traditional reading worksheet in an undergraduate geography classroom activity about marine conservation. We also tested whether learning outcomes were moderated by gender identity or recreational gaming habits. We found that students who used any type of XR learned more than students who used a traditional reading worksheet. Furthermore, we found that students who utilized VR had the highest post-test scores across all groups, and students who utilized stereoscopic AR had greater learning improvement compared to those who used monoscopic AR. However, we found no significant gender effects on learning achievement, nor significant relationships with recreational gaming habits. These findings suggest that XR technologies, particularly stereoscopic AR and VR, may be well suited for supporting spatial learning objectives in undergraduate geographic instruction.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10817409/v1.title: An annotated dataset of soybean root nodules for deep learning-based object detection
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10817409/v1.abstract: Technological advances have expanded the adoption of digital technologies in agriculture, helping to reduce labour effort, increase profitability, improve crop efficiency and productivity, enhance product quality, mitigate environmental impacts, and promote human health. This context also extends to soybean farming, a sector of major economic importance in Brazil. Most importantly, Brazil has the global leadership in soybean production with biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) replacing chemical fertilisers. The research and evaluation of BNF is limited by manual counting of nodules, a time-consuming procedure. This study presents SoyNodules, designed for the automatic identification of soybean nodules, consisting of a dataset of images. The dataset includes 1,701 images acquired under controlled conditions: 1,662 images of soybean roots with nodules and 39 images of isolated nodules without roots. A total of 49,210 nodule instances are manually annotated with bounding boxes. SoyNodules was designed to promote reuse and interoperability in alignment with the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) and to support the development, training, and evaluation of computer vision and deep learning methods for precision agriculture.

doi:10.1128/jmbe.00323-25.title: Harnessing AI and chatbots to develop an interactive learning activity: student perceptions and outcomes
doi:10.1128/jmbe.00323-25.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed various industries, and education is no exception. This paper details how AI can be utilized to support the development of an interactive, choose-your-own-adventure learning activity for pre-health students. With ChatGPT assistance, we identified and implemented the open-source platform Twine to create a branching, scenario-based activity focused on sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), allowing students to engage with clinical decision-making and apply course concepts. Additionally, ChatGPT’s natural language processing capabilities allowed educators to create a script-based learning experience informed by prior student feedback, providing students with immediate, targeted feedback and support. This study describes how AI was used to develop a novel learning activity that encourages student engagement and application of course concepts. Students who piloted this activity in an upper-division course reported the activity to be an effective and engaging learning experience that helped them apply course content to real-life scenarios. Importantly, the use of AI helped streamline the development of this activity, lowering barriers to creating complex educational activities that may otherwise be difficult to implement. Here, we demonstrate how AI can be leveraged to support the development of interactive, scenario-based learning activities and provide practical guidance for instructors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1080/00207217.2026.2724110.title: Design and fault classification of charge pump PLLs using statistical learning
doi:10.1080/00207217.2026.2724110.abstract: Phase-locked loops (PLLs) form an essential component of mixed-signal systems shared by communication and control systems as they commonly provide functionally related features such as frequency synthesis, phase alignment, and modulation/demodulation as well as numerous other uses. Because of their continued use in such applications, the demand for efficient methods of testing PLLs is becoming increasingly important both during prototype phase and in high volume manufacturing processes. All of these factors compound the effect of testing costs and complexity. A statistical learning-based fault diagnosis approach is proposed for charge pump (CP) PLLs, where Back Propagation Neural Network (BPNN) and Probabilistic Neural Network (PNN) are employed to distinguish different fault conditions . Simulation results indicate an overall 99.77% percent accuracy of fault classification as well as an average precision of 0.998, recall of 0.998, and F1 score of 0.998 for PLL fault classes indicating a high reliability of the proposed classification method. The results confirm that the developed PNN-based fault classification method is successful at classifying nonlinear patterns of fault characteristics as well as successfully accounting for variations in the input parameters to the CP PLL and to the PNN classifier. Since this proposed classification method for CP PLL faults is able to classify faults quickly, accurately, and automatically, it will improve the overall efficiency and reduce cost of testing PLL devices.

doi:10.1201/9781003688174-12.title: Deep Learning–based NLP Models for Decision Support in Defence Operations
doi:10.1201/9781003688174-12.abstract: The massive growth of digital communication in defence systems requires some intelligent mechanisms to find and remove toxic or malicious content of the internet. These conversations may compromise security, damage morale, erode trust, and enable adversarial propaganda which makes toxic content detection a mission-critical task. This study proposes a multi-layered toxic comment detection framework comprising Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), and Generative AI (GenAI). The approach combines traditional ML models for lightweight deployment with advanced DL architectures for deeper semantic analysis. GenAI is employed for synthetic data augmentation, generating realistic defence-specific toxic examples to handle data scarcity, improve class balance, and enhance resilience to evolving adversarial language. Jigsaw data set and Wikipedia Talk Pages are used for the evaluations of the study and a curated defence corpus showed the better results in terms of the precision, recall, F1-score, and robustness in toxicity. The designed system is securely integrated for defence communications and meets the standards of cyber-security which supports real-time inference and enables human oversight for the critical cases. The system is getting a scalable and robust solution to protect defence communication system for internal and external threads by integrating machine learning, deep learning and GenAI in a single architecture.

doi:10.59653/jemls.v4i02.2769.title: Development of Ecotheology-Based Islamic Animated Videos as a Learning Medium for Environmental Morals
doi:10.59653/jemls.v4i02.2769.abstract: <jats:p>This research is motivated by the low level of moral understanding of elementary school students, particularly regarding environmental awareness as part of the implementation of Islamic values in daily life. The development of educational technology has not been fully utilized to provide learning media that are interesting and relevant to the needs of students. Moral learning is still dominated by lecture methods and the use of textbooks, resulting in students being less enthusiastic and having difficulty understanding the relationship between Islamic teachings and the responsibility to protect the environment. In addition, research on the development of animated video media based on Islamic ecotheology at the elementary school level is still relatively limited. Therefore, this study aims to develop Islamic animated video media based on ecotheology to improve the moral understanding of elementary school students. The research method used is a quantitative paradigm with a Research and Development (R&D) approach using the ADDIE model which includes the stages of Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation. The study also used a simple experimental design in the form of a pretest and posttest to determine the effectiveness of the developed media. The research data sources consist of primary and secondary data. Primary data was obtained through observations, interviews, questionnaires, and tests with students, teachers, and media and material validators. Secondary data was obtained from books, journals, and supporting documents related to learning media, moral education, and the concept of Islamic ecotheology. Data analysis was conducted using descriptive quantitative techniques through percentage analysis and gain tests to determine the media's feasibility and effectiveness. The results indicate that the development of islamic animated videos based on ecotheology successfully increased students' motivation, participation, and engagement during the learning process. Teachers also gained practical experience in utilizing innovative learning media, making classroom instruction more effective and enjoyable. Therefore, this research contributed positively to improving the quality of Islamic Religious Education learning at Madrasah Ibtidaiyah Nurur Rahmah. Future programs are recommended to strengthen technology-based learning media, enhance teachers' professional competencies, and provide continuous mentoring to ensure the sustainability of the program's impact. The contribution of this research lies in its triadic integration—combining Islamic theology (ecotheology), animation media technology, and environmental moral education into a single, empirically tested learning medium. This study introduces a new framework: animated videos designed as instruments for instilling environmental morality rooted in Islamic spirituality. This addresses the growing demand for learning media that align with global responses to the ecological crisis.</jats:p>
doi:10.59653/jemls.v4i02.2769.venue: Journal of Education Method and Learning Strategy

doi:10.3390/fi18090455.title: FairAI: A Blockchain- and IPFS-Enabled Framework for Verifiable Ethical Federated Learning with Proof-Based Approval-Gated Aggregation
doi:10.3390/fi18090455.abstract: <jats:p>Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing raw training records, but it does not inherently provide verifiable model provenance, enforceable fairness policies, or auditable control over aggregation. This paper presents FairAI, a blockchain- and IPFS-enabled framework that treats each local model as a governed artifact linked to performance and group-fairness metrics, content identifiers, manifests, Groth16 evidence, and smart-contract decisions. Only models approved on-chain and subsequently retrieved and validated through their registered CIDs are eligible for aggregation. The primary real-data evaluation used the Adult and COMPAS datasets under IID and joint label/protected-group non-IID partitions, with ten paired seeds comparing standard FedAvg, post hoc fairness assessment, a pre-aggregation fairness policy gate, and FairFed. Under heterogeneous Adult data, the policy gate reduced the demographic-parity gap from 0.0273 to 0.0127, while accuracy decreased from 0.7740 to 0.7629. Under heterogeneous COMPAS data, the equalized-odds gap decreased from 0.2262 to 0.1226, while accuracy decreased from 0.6495 to 0.5809; the paired accuracy and equalized odds differences remained significant after Holm correction, with adjusted p-values of 0.0318 and 0.0491, respectively. Additional bounded experiments evaluated a small multilayer perceptron, policy threshold sensitivity, logical-client scaling, poisoning, coordinate-wise median aggregation, two native Kubo/IPFS peers, V2 Groth16 verification, and smart-contract overhead. Thirty valid V2 proofs were accepted, six inconsistent cases were rejected, and direct Solidity verification consumed 348,811 gas per measured transaction. A full-path false-metric experiment showed that the proof verifies threshold compliance and artifact binding for supplied values, but does not establish their correct derivation from private data. When an approved artifact became unavailable, FairAI cancelled the round before aggregation and published no global model.</jats:p>

doi:10.65820/2t6hr825.title: Development, Validity, and Effectiveness of an Ethnomathematics-Based Learning Medium Using Menara Kudus to Improve Fifth-Grade Students' Understanding of Quadrilateral Area
doi:10.65820/2t6hr825.abstract:
<jats:p>Purpose: This study aimed to develop and evaluate an ethnomathematics-based interactive learning medium using the Menara Kudus landmark to improve fifth-grade students' conceptual understanding of quadrilateral area, addressing the gap between technology-focused and culturally grounded approaches in mathematics instruction.
Methodology: A Research and Development (R&D) design based on the Borg and Gall model, as adapted by Sugiyono, was employed, encompassing needs analysis, product design, expert validation, revision, and field testing. Participants comprised 28 fifth-grade students (experimental group) and 27 students (control group) from two Madrasah Ibtidaiyah in Kudus. Data were gathered through observation, interviews, expert and student validation questionnaires, and a pre-test–post-test instrument, and were then analysed descriptively and using a gain-score comparison.
Results: The developed medium, comprising an interactive module, student worksheet, teaching materials, and a snake-and-ladder game, achieved high validity (91% material, 78% media, 90% language) and strong practicality (89% student response). The experimental group recorded a higher normalised gain (57%, moderate category) than the control group (43%), though this difference was descriptive rather than statistically confirmed.
Novelty and Contribution: Unlike prior studies that treat multimedia design and ethnomathematics separately, this research integrates both into a single validated instructional product centred on a specific local landmark, offering a replicable model for culturally embedded digital learning design.
Practical and Social Implications: The medium equips teachers with a ready-to-use, culturally contextualised tool for teaching geometry, while reinforcing local cultural identity and heritage awareness among students, supporting broader efforts to make mathematics education more meaningful, equitable, and contextually relevant.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/qrde-03-2026-0017.title: Understanding online faculty perceptions and design considerations regarding the principles of universal design for learning in online courses
doi:10.1108/qrde-03-2026-0017.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative case study aimed to explore faculty perceptions and design considerations regarding the application of Universal Design for Learning (UDL)principles to support diverse learning needs and student success.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five faculty members from a public urban research university were interviewed through semi-structured interviews. Participants also submitted online course artifacts for review to illustrate the implementation of UDL principles. Inductive thematic analysis was used to answer two research questions that guided this study: How do faculty apply UDL guidelines in their online course design? How do faculty perceive the challenges of incorporating UDL guidelines into the design of online courses?</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants discussed applying UDL strategies to their online course designs, including those related to structure and usability. Participants also shared challenges in applying UDL principles in online course design, including increasing engagement and a lack of institutional support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Future studies should examine the application of UDL principles from a student perspective to broaden the understanding of effective strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings have implications for online program administrators, online faculty, course designers, and developers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results of this study showed that engagement was the most frequently represented UDL principle. During the interviews, all participants shared their aspirations to increase engagement in their courses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study revealed key findings regarding the application of UDL standards to online faculty's design considerations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.65405/mnn0cy23.title: How Second Language Learning Reshapes the Brain: A Narrative Review of Neurolinguistic Evidence
doi:10.65405/mnn0cy23.abstract: <jats:p>Second language (L2) learning is a complicated process that can lead to significant changes in the brain’s function and structure. This research paper examines neurolinguistic evidence on how learning a second language reshapes the brain and identifies the major factors that influence language-related neuroplasticity. Drawing on findings from neuroimaging and cognitive neuroscience research, this review explores both structural and functional brain changes associated with second language learning; changes in grey matter, white matter connectivity, cortical organization, and neural efficiency are included. In addition, it explores the influence of age of acquisition, language proficiency, exposure, immersion, learning intensity, and individual differences as well. The review also discusses the cognitive benefits of bilingualism, particularly in executive functions, attention, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. It considers the implications of neurolinguistic evidence for English language teaching, emphasizing retrieval practice, spaced repetition, multimodal learning, meaningful interaction, feedback, and sustained exposure. The evidence suggests that L2 learning is a dynamic experience which can enhance lifelong neuroplasticity and cognitive adaptation, while also providing valuable insights for developing more effective, brain-informed language teaching practices.</jats:p>

doi:10.36728/iceete.v4i1.385.title: Design of a Web-Based 3D Learning Media for Three-Dimensional Geometry
doi:10.36728/iceete.v4i1.385.abstract: <jats:p>Three-dimensional geometry is a fundamental topic in senior high school mathematics that requires students to develop spatial visualization and conceptual understanding. However, conventional learning media often rely on static two-dimensional illustrations, making it difficult for students to comprehend the characteristics of three-dimensional objects and their mathematical relationships. This study aims to design Dimensia-3D, a web-based interactive learning media that supports the learning of three-dimensional geometry through interactive visualization and calculation simulation. The proposed learning media was designed using the Web Development Life Cycle (WDLC) methodology, with the research scope limited to the planning, analysis, and design phases. The analysis phase produced a set of functional and non-functional requirements that defined the learning and system functionalities, while the design phase resulted in a navigation flowchart, use case diagram, and low-fidelity wireframes describing the system architecture and user interaction. A key contribution of the proposed design is the integration of learning materials, interactive 3D visualization, and geometric calculation simulation within a single web-based interface covering seven geometric solids: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone, square pyramid, and triangular prism. The resulting design provides a structured and implementation-ready blueprint that can support the future development of interactive geometry learning media for senior high school students. Future research will focus on implementing the proposed system and evaluating its usability and educational effectiveness.</jats:p>

doi:10.1128/jmbe.00287-25.title: Connecting the dots: an active learning flashcard activity to teach soil microbiology through nutrient cycles
doi:10.1128/jmbe.00287-25.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>Understanding microbial roles in nutrient cycling is essential in environmental science and engineering education, yet students often struggle with these topics due to limited microbiology background and the abstract nature of microbial processes. To support deeper learning, I developed a flexible, low-cost classroom activity using narrative-style flashcards representing soil microorganisms for my Soil Science class on soil microbiology session. Rather than delivering nutrient cycles through direct instruction, I facilitated a student-centered session in which learners collaboratively mapped microbial transformations across the nitrogen, carbon, phosphorus, and sulfur cycles. Students first identified key nutrient forms and then used their flashcards to construct systems diagrams through guided reasoning, peer discussion, and instructor cues. The activity emphasized connections between microbial function, environmental context, and ecosystem outcomes, with applications to real-world systems such as wastewater treatment. Post-activity quiz results showed high content retention (average 9.5/10), and classroom observations indicated strong engagement and emerging systems thinking. This approach offers an accessible model for introducing microbiological concepts in interdisciplinary environmental curricula.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1093/9780198995746.003.0006.title: Delegating Information Processing
doi:10.1093/9780198995746.003.0006.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter focuses on how the costs of information processing are managed through some form of delegation, and the tradeoffs between different goals and values that result. The processing of information from the public can be delegated to expert intelligence, to collective intelligence, or to artificial intelligence, but each of these comes with downsides and limitations. For some types of information processing where domain-specific knowledge is needed, there is a trilemma between goals of efficiency, accuracy, and impartiality. At most two of these goals can be pursued, while any third must remain necessarily limited. This chapter also highlights the limitations of artificial intelligence, contrary to much recent optimism about its applications in participatory and deliberative institutions. As a way forward, it discusses the opportunities for hybrid approaches to information processing that involve some delegation to artificial intelligence while still involving human domain-specific knowledge.</jats:p>

doi:10.4324/9781003656012-7.title: Induction and Logic-Based Machine Learning
doi:10.4324/9781003656012-7.abstract: The aim of this chapter is to explore the two-way interaction between philosophical views of induction and the development of logic-based machine learning. We will begin by explaining some logic-based machine learning systems and showing how they were influenced by philosophical ideas about induction. Then we will consider how the striking results produced by some of these systems influenced the philosophical debates about induction, which we described in chapter 4 .

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10815711/v1.title: Machine Learning versus Deep Learning for Public Financial Report Classification and Popularity Prediction: A Feasibility Study on Ghana's Controller and Accountant-General's Department
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10815711/v1.abstract: Government agencies increasingly publish financial reports online, but small public-sector portals rarely have the labeled data needed to test automated classification tools. This study evaluates the feasibility of these tools using a corpus of 131 official reports from Ghana's Controller and Accountant-General's Department (CAGD). We compare classical machine learning models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting [XGBoost] with Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique [SMOTE]) and character-level deep learning models (bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory [LSTM] and Text Convolutional Neural Network [TextCNN]) across three tasks: category prediction, binary popularity classification, and log-download forecasting. Models were evaluated using a stratified 70/15/15 train, validation, and test split, randomized hyperparameter search, and a final fine-tuning phase. The fine-tuned XGBoost classifier achieved 1.00 accuracy on the five-class category task. Logistic Regression reached 0.75 accuracy (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve [ROC-AUC] of 0.80) on the binary popularity task, and Random Forest reached an R-squared of 0.85 on log downloads. An ablation study removing twenty-five keyword features dropped category accuracy from 1.00 to 0.80, a stable drop across five randomized data splits. This indicates keyword features inflated initial results, though remaining performance confirms the models learn non-tautological structure. This work serves as an honest feasibility check, showing that thorough feature ablation is essential before deploying these models on live government portals.
