doi:10.20944/preprints202609.1751.v1.title: Action-Unit-Constrained Graph Learning with Counterfactual Recourse for Auditable Facial Expression Recognition
doi:10.20944/preprints202609.1751.v1.abstract: <jats:p>Facial expression recognition (FER) systems often explain predictions with saliency maps that neither identify specific facial behaviour nor indicate how a decision could change. We present AU-GRACE, which couples an action-unit (AU) relation graph with an explicit AU bottleneck to provide counterfactual recourse as small sets of plausible AU edits. Facial Action Coding System (FACS)/EMFACS knowledge supplies reliability-gated soft constraints, allowing departures from prior edges weakly supported by data. The emotion head accesses the image through the AU vector and a norm-penalised residual, so AU edits intervene on the decision. An amortised solver generates edits in 6.4 ms. AU-GRACE achieves 96.78%, 69.19% and 94.92% accuracy on RAF-DB, AffectNet-7 and FERPlus, respectively, under the evaluation protocols defined by the dataset authors. Counterfactual validity is 94.8%, with 2.3 edited AUs and 86.4% plausibility. Agreement with six certified FACS coders reaches κ¯=0.71, close to their inter-coder agreement. The edits remain effective after rendering and re-classification by an independent model. These results show that competitive recognition accuracy can be combined with AU-level recourse through an explicit AU bottleneck.</jats:p>

doi:10.1002/berj.70281.title: Observed teacher collaboration indices: Professional learning impact, self‐efficacy and job satisfaction among lower and upper secondary teachers in <scp>TALIS</scp> 2024
doi:10.1002/berj.70281.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Teacher collaboration is widely promoted as a resource for professional learning, teacher efficacy and retention, but research and policy often treat collaboration as a single practice and use frequency as a proxy for professional value. This risks overlooking differences between routine exchange, coordination and deeper forms of collaborative inquiry. Using TALIS 2024 teacher data from eight education systems with both lower and upper secondary participation (
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 33,137), this study examines how two content‐defined observed practice indices—practice‐focused and exchange/coordination—are associated with perceived professional learning impact, teaching self‐efficacy and job satisfaction. Teacher‐weighted controlled path models with country fixed effects and school‐cluster robust standard errors were estimated. A formal within‐model contrast showed that the practice‐focused index had a larger standardised association with perceived professional learning impact than the exchange/coordination index. Professional learning impact was associated with teaching self‐efficacy, which was associated with both teaching‐profession and work‐environment satisfaction. Formal interaction tests found no statistically detectable ISCED 2/3 differences in the five core path coefficients or in the practice‐focused versus exchange/coordination coefficient gap. Country moderation was detected for the practice‐focused index association but not for the exchange/coordination index association. Because professional learning impact was a single self‐report item whose observability depended on questionnaire‐form allocation, participant‐specific non‐administration, routing and response, the results are interpreted as theory‐guided indirect associations rather than causal mediation. The findings suggest different associations for the two observed indices; weak measurement diagnostics preclude interpreting them as clearly separated collaboration types.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1017/aee.2026.10207.title: Reflective Environmental Pedagogy in Design Learning: Students’ Experiences in Türkiye
doi:10.1017/aee.2026.10207.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study examines how students in a faculty of architecture develop environmental awareness through sustained engagement with the multi-layered historic and ecological setting of a place. It explores how the city’s complex historical fabric functions as an active pedagogical agent, moving beyond abstract instruction towards a transformative relationship between the student and the environment. Learning is examined as an ontological bond in which the physical, social and cultural contexts of the site actively shape architectural perception and environmental awareness. Drawing on students’ reflections, the study investigates how direct engagement with a real-world setting supports the development of socio-ecological consciousness within the framework of place-based pedagogy. Data were collected through reflective interviews with graduates of Istanbul Technical University who voluntarily participated in design studies in Mardin. Both qualitative and quantitative data were obtained and analysed. The findings suggest that future pedagogical models could benefit from more sustained site-specific engagement, enabling the environment to function as a central catalyst in architectural learning processes.</jats:p>

doi:10.55713/jmmm.v37i1.2693.title: Intelligent material recognition from thermal signatures using hybrid deep learning frameworks
authors: Boddu L. V. Siva Rama KRISHNA
P. V. V. S. D. NAGENDRUDU
doi:10.55713/jmmm.v37i1.2693.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate material identification using thermal infrared signatures has significant implications for industrial inspection, autonomous systems, and non-contact diagnostics. In this study, we propose a physics-informed deep learning framework for intelligent material recognition based on transient thermal behavior. A large-scale dataset, ThermalMat-85K, comprising 85,000 long-wave infrared (LWIR) images across ten material classes, was constructed under controlled multi-angle, multi-distance, and multi-environment conditions. Each sample was validated through Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to ensure chemical and structural integrity prior to thermal acquisition. Seven deep learning architectures were systematically evaluated, including VGG-16, ResNet-50, MobileNet-V3, DenseNet-121, EfficientNet-B4, a CNN+LSTM temporal hybrid, and a proposed Hybrid Net integrating convolutional, transformer, and recurrent modules with cross-modal attention gating. EfficientNet-B4 achieved the highest Top-1 accuracy (93.1%) and macro F1-score (92.8%), demonstrating superior class-wise stability. Residual and dense connectivity architectures also exhibited strong performance, while lightweight and temporal hybrids revealed trade-offs between efficiency and discriminative power. Class-wise confusion analysis indicates that misclassification trends correlate strongly with thermophysical proximity, particularly thermal conductivity and emissivity overlap. These findings confirm that transient thermal decay dynamics encode physically meaningful features suitable for material discrimination. The results establish a robust benchmark for physics-informed thermal material recognition and provide guidance for selecting architectures based on deployment constraints and robustness requirements.</jats:p>
doi:10.55713/jmmm.v37i1.2693.venue: Journal of Metals, Materials and Minerals

doi:10.1145/3818305.3830258.title: Learning Based Parameter Estimation in Diffusion Models-An Identifiability Study
doi:10.1145/3818305.3830258.abstract: This work proposes a learning-based biosensing receiver (BSR) for estimating diffusion parameters in molecular communication (MC) systems. It is done from timely observations of concentration and first passage time signals (FPTD). CNN+LSTM and CNN+GRU sequence-to-vector models are used to estimate the diffusion coefficient and transmitter (TX)-BSR distance from analytically generated data. GRU achieves better performance, particularly for diffusion coefficient estimation. Results show that longer observation windows improve estimation accuracy because it captures both the early time exponential and late time scaling behavior, while parameter identifiability limits performance.

doi:10.1021/acs.jcim.6c01426.title: Multiscale Interpretable Deep-Learning Framework for the Identification and Visualization of Deformation Stages in Molecular Dynamics Trajectory
doi:10.1021/acs.jcim.6c01426.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Microscopic deformation stage recognition from molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories is crucial for understanding the evolution of material damage; however, traditional empirical analysis and black-box single deep-learning models lack both high-throughput spatiotemporal modeling and transparent physical interpretability. This work develops a multiscale interpretable deep-learning framework to automatically classify elastic, plastic, and fracture stages from uniaxial tensile MD trajectories and physically decode model decision logic. First, a 3D atomic trajectory is converted to 2D gray-scale image sequences; a CNN-LSTM hybrid architecture is built to jointly extract spatial atomic textures and long-time deformation dynamics, reaching 98.8% test accuracy and far surpassing spatial-only CNN baselines in both supervised classification and unsupervised clustering. More importantly, a hierarchical multiscale interpretability toolkit, including multilayer feature heatmaps, smoothed gradient saliency maps, gradient-weighted class activation maps, and regularized SHAP attribution, is integrated to quantify positive/negative feature contributions and localize model focus regions. The visualized attention zones perfectly match core physical fields (von Mises strain, atomic displacement, and nonaffine deformation), resolving the explainability gap of conventional MD data mining pipelines. This work establishes a generalizable, trustworthy AI paradigm that connects data-driven prediction to intrinsic microscale mechanical mechanisms for computational material research.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s41935-026-00581-2.title: AI-assisted age estimation from first molars: an integrated evaluation of regression, machine learning, and 1D-CNN models using CBCT-derived pulp-dentin index
doi:10.1186/s41935-026-00581-2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Accurate age estimation is crucial for forensic identification, and teeth serve as durable biological markers due to their post-mortem stability. While cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) enables precise three-dimensional assessment of age-related pulp changes, most existing studies rely on traditional regression models that do not adequately capture the non-linear complexity of dental aging. This study developed and compared a multi-model framework for adult age estimation using CBCT-derived pulp-dentin index (PDI) of first molars.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      PDI values of all four first molars from 2000 Sichuan Han adults (aged 18–65 years) showed strong negative correlations with chronological age (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = − 0.798 to − 0.866,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.05), with significant variations by sex and by maxillary versus mandibular position. The dataset was randomly partitioned into training, validation, and test sets (8:1:1 ratio). Machine learning (ML) models substantially outperformed traditional regression. Among all models, the Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model using tooth-specific PDI achieved the best overall performance, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 2.51 years and
                      <jats:italic>R²</jats:italic>
                      = 0.907. This represents a 51.4% reduction in prediction error compared to models using averaged PDI. The 1D-CNN model achieved an MAE of 4.24 years, outperforming the best traditional regression model.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The CBCT-derived first molar PDI is a reliable forensic age indicator. Utilising multi-tooth data significantly enhances accuracy, with the XGBoost model achieving the best predictive performance. The 1D-CNN offers a promising automated alternative that, with further optimization and larger datasets, may serve as a pragmatic tool for forensic practice, and this multi-model framework provides enhanced methodological rigour and flexibility for practical dental age assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1933259.title: Music performance anxiety, sleep problems, and disordered eating: the role of performance and learning self-efficacy
doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1933259.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Music students face chronic evaluative stress, increasing their vulnerability to sleep problems and disordered eating. Drawing on transdiagnostic and self-regulation frameworks, this study examined whether music performance anxiety (MPA) is associated with both outcomes and whether music performance and learning self-efficacy moderate these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional survey of 260 Chinese music students assessed music performance anxiety, sleep problems, disordered eating, and self-efficacy. Robust maximum likelihood structural equation modeling and Johnson–Neyman analyses were used, controlling body mass index, age, gender, and years of music study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Music performance anxiety correlated with disordered eating (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = .24,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt;.001) and sleep problems (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = .21,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt;.001). In the structural model, music performance anxiety was positively associated with disordered eating (
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                       = 0.25,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt;.01). For sleep problems, music performance self-efficacy showed a negative main effect (β = −0.41,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt;.001), whereas the direct effect of music performance anxiety was non-significant (β = 0.04,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &gt;.05). The interaction between music performance anxiety and music performance self-efficacy was negatively associated with sleep problems (β = −0.41,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt;.01). Johnson–Neyman analyses showed that music performance anxiety was associated with sleep problems only when music performance self-efficacy was &lt; 3.80 or &gt; 5.55.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Music performance anxiety is a transdiagnostic risk factor among music students, directly relating to disordered eating, while its link to sleep problems depends on domain-specific self-efficacy. Interventions may combine anxiety reduction with balanced self-efficacy support to improve recovery under performance pressure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10855765/v1.title: Integrating postharvest quality assessment and deep learning to identify the optimal harvest maturity stage of apricot fruit
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10855765/v1.abstract: Accurate determination of harvest maturity is essential for maintaining apricot fruit quality and maximizing postharvest storage potential. This study integrated postharvest quality assessment with deep learning to identify a favorable harvest maturity stage and develop a rapid, non-destructive image-based classification approach. Apricot fruits were harvested at five physiological maturity stages and stored at 6°C for 35 days, during which firmness, weight loss, total soluble solids, titratable acidity, pH, and color attributes (L*, C*, h°, and ΔE) were evaluated at weekly intervals. Fruits harvested at Stage 3 exhibited the most favorable overall postharvest performance, characterized by greater firmness retention, lower weight loss, and comparatively greater stability in soluble solids, acidity, pH, and color attributes. To facilitate rapid recognition of the maturity stages, a lightweight dual-path convolutional neural network incorporating regular and dilated convolutional branches was developed using 1,032 RGB images acquired under natural orchard conditions. On the independent test dataset, the model achieved weighted precision, recall, and F1-score values of 0.81, 0.78, and 0.79, respectively, with most misclassifications occurring between adjacent maturity stages. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating physiological quality assessment with deep learning to support rapid and non-destructive maturity-based harvest decisions in apricot. Further validation across cultivars, orchards, seasons, and field imaging conditions is required to establish the robustness and practical applicability of the proposed approach.

doi:10.59261/bustechno.v7i4.761.title: Tarsius Image-Source Classification Using VGG Feature Extraction and Machine Learning Classifiers
doi:10.59261/bustechno.v7i4.761.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Reliable classification of heterogeneous Tarsius imagery is relevant to digital wildlife-data management, yet real photographs and AI-generated images may share visual characteristics that complicate automated separation.
Objective: This study compares VGG-16, VGG-19, and InceptionV3 feature extraction combined with Logistic Regression and Neural Network classifiers for real, cartoon-style, and AI-generated Tarsius images.
Methods: A balanced dataset of 300 web-sourced images (100 per category) was processed in Orange Data Mining. Performance was evaluated using AUC, classification accuracy (CA), F1-score, precision, recall, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), confusion matrices, Multidimensional Scaling (MDS), and silhouette plots.
Results: Logistic Regression with VGG-19 produced the strongest reported combination (AUC = 0.997, CA = 0.967, F1 = 0.967, precision = 0.968, recall = 0.967, and MCC = 0.950), closely followed by VGG-16 with Logistic Regression. Cartoon-style images were generally the most distinguishable, whereas real and AI-generated images showed the greatest overlap. InceptionV3 produced clearer two-dimensional MDS separation but lower aggregate predictive performance than the VGG-based Logistic Regression configurations.
Conclusion: VGG-19 with Logistic Regression provides the most balanced performance for the available dataset. The findings demonstrate that predictive metrics and feature-space visualizations should be interpreted jointly and remain limited by the small, web-sourced dataset and incomplete provenance records.</jats:p>
doi:10.59261/bustechno.v7i4.761.venue: Journal of Business, Social and Technology

doi:10.1007/s10618-026-01267-y.title: When, how long and how much? Interpretable neural networks for time series regression by learning to mask and aggregate
doi:10.1007/s10618-026-01267-y.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Time series extrinsic regression (TSER) aims to predict a continuous target variable from an input time series. It arises in domains such as healthcare, finance, environmental monitoring, and engineering, where both accuracy and interpretability are essential. Despite strong predictive performance, state-of-the-art TSER models typically operate as black boxes, making it difficult to understand which temporal patterns drive their predictions. Post-hoc explanation methods attempt to address this issue but often produce coarse, noisy, or unstable explanations. Inherently interpretable approaches based on additive decompositions or concepts offer an alternative, yet they often require concept supervision, struggle to capture multivariate interactions, and lack expressiveness for complex temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we propose Mask-and-Aggregate Networks for Time Series (MAGNETS), an inherently interpretable neural architecture for TSER. MAGNETS learns a compact set of human-understandable concepts directly from data, without requiring concept annotations. Each concept corresponds to a learned, mask-based aggregation over selected input features, revealing both
                    <jats:italic>which</jats:italic>
                    features influence the prediction and
                    <jats:italic>when</jats:italic>
                    they matter. Predictions are expressed as transparent combinations of these concepts, yielding faithful, input-specific explanations by design. Experiments on synthetic and real-world univariate and multivariate TSER datasets show that MAGNETS achieves accuracy comparable to black-box models while substantially outperforming existing interpretable baselines, particularly on tasks involving multivariate feature interactions.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.68290/jodieg.v1i1.10.title: NEGOTIATING GENDER DISCOURSE IN COMMUNITY LEARNING SPACES: THE CASE OF SEKOLAH PEREMPUAN IN BALI
doi:10.68290/jodieg.v1i1.10.abstract: <jats:p>Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis bagaimana diskursus gender dinegosiasikan dalam ruang belajar komunitas melalui kegiatan Sekolah Perempuan Kartini di Desa Dauh Puri Kangin, Bali. Sekolah Perempuan merupakan inisiatif pemberdayaan perempuan berbasis komunitas yang dirancang untuk meningkatkan kesadaran gender, kapasitas kepemimpinan perempuan, serta partisipasi perempuan dalam kehidupan sosial masyarakat. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan metode studi kasus. Data dikumpulkan melalui wawancara mendalam dengan anggota Sekolah Perempuan Kartini, observasi partisipatif terhadap kegiatan pembelajaran komunitas, serta analisis dokumen kegiatan pemberdayaan perempuan yang dilaksanakan pada periode 2024–2026. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa Sekolah Perempuan Kartini berfungsi sebagai ruang dialog sosial yang memungkinkan perempuan untuk merefleksikan pengalaman hidup mereka dan memahami berbagai bentuk ketidaksetaraan gender dalam kehidupan sehari-hari. Namun demikian, proses pemberdayaan perempuan dalam komunitas tradisional masih menghadapi berbagai tantangan, terutama norma budaya patriarkal, pembagian peran domestik yang kuat, serta keterbatasan akses perempuan dalam ruang pengambilan keputusan komunitas. Penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa pemberdayaan perempuan dalam masyarakat tradisional berlangsung melalui proses negosiasi sosial yang bertahap. Keberadaan ruang belajar komunitas seperti Sekolah Perempuan memiliki peran penting dalam memperkuat kesadaran gender serta membuka ruang partisipasi perempuan dalam kehidupan sosial masyarakat.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s40662-026-00509-w.title: Preoperative predictive factors for opaque bubble layer formation and area during small-incision lenticule extraction: predictive models based on machine learning
doi:10.1186/s40662-026-00509-w.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aimed to develop exploratory machine learning (ML)-based predictive models for the occurrence and area of an opaque bubble layer (OBL) during small-incision lenticule extraction (SMILE) and identify associated preoperative and surgical-planning factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective study included 216 eyes (72 with an OBL, 144 controls) that underwent SMILE at the Zhongshan Ophthalmic Center between August 2024 and August 2025, which were matched 1:2 by age and sex. Comprehensive preoperative ocular examinations were performed using a Pentacam HR camera system and standard equipment. The OBL area was quantified from intraoperative videos using ImageJ software. Fifty-four preoperative and surgical features were used to develop the ML models: 15 classification algorithms for OBL occurrence, and 19 regression algorithms for the relative OBL area. Shapley additive explanations analysis was applied for model interpretability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Extra Trees model achieved optimal performance for predicting OBL occurrence (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve = 0.885, accuracy = 0.820). The top five key factors included femtosecond laser energy, intraocular pressure, residual stromal thickness, 10-mm corneal volume, and total astigmatism, all of which showed positive correlations. For OBL area prediction, the random forest regression model performed best in the test sets (mean absolute error = 2.89%, root mean square error = 3.37%). Corneal optical density (within the central 2-mm zone of the anterior 120-μm corneal layer) and age were negatively associated with OBL area, whereas keratoconus index showed the strongest positive association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The ML models showed exploratory predictive ability for OBL occurrence and area during SMILE using preoperative and surgical-planning parameters. External validation and recalibration in consecutive cohorts with a natural OBL prevalence are required before clinical use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.15294/upej.v15i1.42547.title: The Use of Problem Posing Type Post Solution Posing Model in The Development of Learning Materials to Improve Students' Problem Solving Skills
doi:10.15294/upej.v15i1.42547.abstract: <jats:p>Problem solving skills are one of the essential competencies possessed by a student. This study aims to develop learning material that can improve students' problem solving skills in the work and energy topic. The learning material was developed by following the problem-posing type post-solution posing principle. The development research method used is 4D (define, design, develop, and disseminate).  However, the development process in this study was limited to the development stage, including expert appraisal and developmental testing. The participants of the research were 43 senior high school students. The research instruments used were a questionnaire validity sheet, a practicality sheet, and a problem-solving test. The evaluation results of the learning material feasibility were considered very feasible based on the assessment of 12 experts, who were divided into three learning design experts, three linguists, three media experts, and three material experts. The tested learning material demonstrated preliminary effectiveness in improving students’ problem-solving skills, with an N-gain of 0.43 in the moderate category. The results of the practicality of the learning material on student responses obtained a score of 84.72% in the very good category, and based on the three responses from the physics teacher, obtained a score of 91.67% in the very good category. The results in this study can be used as a reference in developing learning material on other physics topics.</jats:p>

doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202662240.title: A machine-learning-driven dataset of 144,111 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon infrared spectra for interpreting aromatic infrared bands
doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202662240.abstract:
<jats:p>The interpretation of interstellar aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) relies on reference spectral libraries, but the chemical space covered by existing databases remains incomplete relative to the vast structural diversity of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) expected in the interstellar medium.
We present a large-scale, high-throughput PAH infrared (IR) spectral database that complements existing reference libraries by providing significantly more continuous coverage of the PAH chemical space for small to medium-sized PAHs.
We used a machine-learning double-harmonic (ML-DH) framework that integrates neural network force fields with electronic dipole models. This framework achieves quantum-chemical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. It has been validated against independent density functional theory calculations and benchmark spectral databases.
The resulting dataset comprises 144,111 IR spectra for 48,037 closed-shell, even-carbon benzenoid PAH structures across neutral, cationic, and anionic charge states, complete with per-spectrum uncertainty estimates.
The spectral library, optimized geometries, and model code are publicly available. They can be used to complement existing libraries for interpreting and modeling Space Telescope (JWST) AIB observations and those from future IR missions. James Webb</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s13394-026-00599-8.title: A systematic review of mathematics intervention approaches for primary school students who experience difficulties with learning mathematics
doi:10.1007/s13394-026-00599-8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mathematics interventions play a critical role in supporting primary school students who experience difficulties with learning mathematics but do not have a diagnosed disability. However, the intervention approaches used in schools vary considerably in their theoretical orientations, content focus, and instructional approaches, and research in this field is similarly diverse. This systematic review investigated the characteristics and instructional approaches of mathematics interventions for primary students. A comprehensive search of eight databases identified 1,321 studies published between 2000 and 2024, of which 38 met the inclusion criteria. Interventions were included if they involved small-group formats (fewer than seven students), were conducted outside the classroom, and targeted students identified as experiencing difficulties in learning mathematics. Data were extracted concerning intervention characteristics, mathematics content focus, delivery, and instructional strategies. Findings identified that most studies were conducted in the United States and were delivered by researchers or research assistants, with fewer interventions implemented by classroom teachers. The majority of interventions in the early years addressed the topics of number and operations. Fractions and word problems were prevalent topics in later primary years. Nine instructional strategies were examined for each intervention, with representations, computational fluency, and explicit instruction most frequently employed, and problem-solving employed least frequently. The findings indicate that existing mathematics interventions typically focus on a narrow curriculum. Valuable directions for future research include investigating the potential of interventions using broader and more connected mathematics topics, diversifying international research contexts, and prioritising teacher-led interventions in authentic school settings.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/eisfl-05-2026-0073.title: Sustainable curriculum design: a comparative analysis of curriculum design methodologies, SDG integration and sustainability competency frameworks in national curriculum policies
doi:10.1108/eisfl-05-2026-0073.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how curriculum design methodologies – specifically competency-based curriculum (CBC) design and backward design – are represented in relation to the integration of Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) and the framing of student sustainability competencies within national curriculum policy at the school level. It identifies structural patterns and divergences across four national education systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study adopts a qualitative comparative research design grounded in interpretivist philosophy and an inductive approach. A single researcher read the official national curriculum policy documents and Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) strategy papers from Japan, Finland, the USA and the United Kingdom in full and thematically interpreted them, informed by Constructive Alignment Theory (Biggs, 1996) and Transformational Learning Theory (Mezirow, 1991). Countries were selected to represent contrasting curriculum governance models, ranging from centralised to highly decentralised systems. The analysis focuses on three themes: curriculum design methodology, SDG integration and the framing of student sustainability competencies within policy documents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Competency-based curriculum design and backward design appear, within the documents reviewed, most closely aligned with sustainability goals, learning outcomes and assessment procedures. Japan and Finland, which have centralised national curricula, demonstrate the most consistent policy-level SDG integration and sustainability competency framing. Finland's phenomenon-based, student-centred approach appears associated with the most holistic competency framing across dimensions. The USA and the United Kingdom show more variable implementation, reflecting decentralised and semi-centralised governance, with competency development appearing more dependent on individual teachers and school agencies. These patterns reflect policy orientation rather than measured student outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study relies exclusively on policy-level document analysis and does not capture classroom-level enactment, teacher practice, or empirical student outcome data. All four countries represent developed, high-income education systems, limiting generalisability to developing-country contexts. Thematic analysis was conducted by a single researcher, with interpretation synthesised during writing rather than documented in a separate formal coding log, and no second coder was used, introducing researcher subjectivity as a limitation. Future research should adopt mixed methods, including teacher interviews, classroom observations and student assessments and extend the comparative scope to lower-income education systems and a broader range of stakeholders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Policymakers and curriculum designers should embed sustainability competencies as mandatory core learning objectives rather than as optional themes. Competency-based curriculum and backward design frameworks offer replicable models for aligning sustainability outcomes with teaching strategies and assessment. Countries with decentralised systems should consider stronger national coordination mechanisms to reduce inconsistency in SDG integration across schools and states. Teachers should be professionally supported to adopt project-based, activity-based and inquiry-driven pedagogies that actively develop student sustainability competencies at the school level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study makes an original contribution by examining the three-way relationship between curriculum design methodology, SDG integration and student sustainability competencies within a cross-national comparative framework at the school level. Unlike existing literature that focuses predominantly on higher education or single-country contexts, this research provides school-level, document-based evidence and identifies curriculum centralisation as a factor associated with more coherent policy-level ESD framing. The integration of constructive alignment theory and transformational learning theory within a comparative curriculum policy analysis framework offers a lens for future ESD research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1007/s11082-026-09132-4.title: Machine-learning-assisted loss prediction and analysis of photonic lantern MUX/DEMUX for SDM systems
doi:10.1007/s11082-026-09132-4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Photonic lanterns (PLs) are pivotal passive components for mode-division multiplexing (MDM) in space-division multiplexed (SDM) optical interconnects, enabling low-loss, adiabatic coupling between multiple single-mode and multimode fiber. However, their design relies on computationally intensive full-wave electromagnetic solvers, such as the finite-element method (FEM), beam propagation method (BPM), and finite-difference time-domain (FDTD), which hinder efficient multi-objective optimization across high-dimensional parameter spaces. To overcome this bottleneck, we propose an XGBoost-based supervised surrogate modeling framework for simultaneous prediction of insertion loss (IL), mode-dependent loss (MDL), and polarization-dependent loss (PDL), trained on a physics-validated 2,000-sample FEM dataset spanning seven multicore geometries across the full C-band (1530–1590 nm). The surrogate achieves
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$R^2> 0.98$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ,
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\textrm{RMSE} < 0.13\,\textrm{dB}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\textrm{MAE} < 0.075\,\textrm{dB}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    across all three targets, reducing per-design evaluation time from
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\sim 6.8\,\textrm{h}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    (FEM/BPM) to
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$<1\,\textrm{ms}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    —a speedup of
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\sim 2.45 \times 10^{7}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    —while maintaining sub-
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$0.1\,\textrm{dB}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    spectral stability across the full C-band. This capability enables rapid parametric sweeps of PL configurations in under
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$10\,\textrm{s}$$</jats:tex-math>

doi:10.59373/jelin.v3i2.369.title: The Effect of RME Instruction on Fourth-Grade Madrasah Ibtidaiyah Students’ Learning Outcomes in Plane Geometry
doi:10.59373/jelin.v3i2.369.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the effect of Realistic Mathematics Education (RME) on fourth-grade students’ learning outcomes in the perimeter and area of plane figures at MI Miftahul Ulum Pandanarum, Pacet, Mojokerto. The study employed a quantitative pre-experimental method using a one-group pretest-posttest design. The sample consisted of 28 students purposively selected from Class IV Al-Wahhab. The researchers collected data through essay tests, observations, interviews, and documentation. Experts validated the test instrument, and empirical testing showed that 12 of 15 items were valid. The instrument demonstrated acceptable reliability, with a Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient of 0.707. Descriptive analysis showed an increase in students’ mean scores from 60.25 on the pretest to 73.61 on the posttest, indicating improvement after implementing RME. Furthermore, the paired-sample t-test yielded a significance value of 0.000 (Sig. 2-tailed), indicating a statistically significant difference between students’ pretest and posttest scores. The normalized gain score was 0.4256 (42.56%), which was categorized as moderate. These findings suggest that implementing RME contributed positively to students’ learning outcomes in geometry. By connecting abstract mathematical concepts to meaningful, familiar real-life contexts, RME helped students understand perimeter and area more concretely and contextually. Therefore, RME can be considered an effective instructional approach for supporting elementary students’ understanding of plane geometry, although further studies using experimental designs with control groups are recommended to strengthen evidence of its effectiveness.</jats:p>

doi:10.61467/2007.1558.2027.v18i1.1516.title: Meteorological Time Series Interpolation: A Literature Review of Classical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Approaches
doi:10.61467/2007.1558.2027.v18i1.1516.abstract:
<jats:p>Meteorological time series are frequently affected by missing observations caused by sensor failures, communication problems, maintenance activities, or data acquisition errors. Subsequent analyses, including forecasting, climate monitoring, hydrological assessment, and environmental decision-making, may therefore be biased or weakened. In this review, interpolation methods for meteorological time series are reviewed, including classical, statistical, machine learning, and deep learning approaches. Emphasis is placed on the distinction between prediction and interpolation, since both tasks are often treated as equivalent. The literature is also organized according to reconstruction strategy, including recursive, bidirectional, probabilistic or generative, and hybrid or evolutionary approaches. Current challenges, evaluation practices, open gaps, and future trends for meteorological data reconstruction are discussed.
 
Spanish-language metadata / Metadatos en españolTítulo en español:Interpolación de series temporales meteorológicas: una revisión de la literatura sobre enfoques clásicos, de aprendizaje automático y aprendizaje profundo
Resumen:Las series temporales meteorológicas se ven afectadas con frecuencia por observaciones faltantes causadas por fallos de sensores, problemas de comunicación, actividades de mantenimiento o errores en la adquisición de datos. En consecuencia, los análisis posteriores, incluidos la predicción, la monitorización climática, la evaluación hidrológica y la toma de decisiones ambientales, pueden presentar sesgos o verse comprometidos.
En esta revisión se examinan los métodos de interpolación aplicados a series temporales meteorológicas, incluidos los enfoques clásicos, estadísticos, de aprendizaje automático y de aprendizaje profundo. Se hace especial hincapié en la distinción entre predicción e interpolación, dado que ambas tareas se tratan con frecuencia como equivalentes. La literatura también se organiza según la estrategia de reconstrucción empleada, incluidos los enfoques recursivos, bidireccionales, probabilísticos o generativos, e híbridos o evolutivos.
Asimismo, se analizan los desafíos actuales, las prácticas de evaluación, las brechas de investigación existentes y las tendencias futuras en la reconstrucción de datos meteorológicos.
Palabras Claves:Series temporales meteorológicas, interpolación, datos faltantes, imputación, redes neuronales, aprendizaje profundo, predicción de datos climáticos.

doi:10.1017/s026357472510297x.title: Transformer and self-supervised learning-based state-of-charge prediction method for lithium-ion batteries
doi:10.1017/s026357472510297x.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The state-of-charge (SOC) estimation of lithium-ion batteries is essential for the performance, safety, and longevity of electric vehicles. While traditional physics-based models face difficulties in predicting SOC under complex conditions, data-driven methods demand large volumes of labeled data, limiting their practical applicability. This paper introduces a Transformer-based SOC estimation method that incorporates a self-supervised learning framework. By combining a masking recovery mechanism with a self-attention mechanism, the approach effectively captures SOC’s long-term dependencies and identifies global patterns under complex operating conditions. Experimental results on the Nissan Leaf and University of Maryland datasets demonstrate significant performance improvements. Compared to traditional deep learning methods, this approach delivers higher prediction accuracy and robustness, offering an innovative solution for efficient SOC estimation in complicated environments.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922588.title: Capturing learning persistence through fractional dynamic modeling: evidence from secondary school students
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922588.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Student academic performance develops through cumulative learning experiences, yet conventional educational performance models generally assume that Educational support and learning behavior variables produce immediate effects. This study proposes a fractional dynamic framework to capture the persistence of learning and examine associations between educational support, learning behavior, and academic performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed micro-level data from 649 Portuguese secondary school students using a fractional-order educational performance model that incorporated educational memory through a fractional formulation. The analysis examined associations between school study support, paid academic assistance, family educational support, attendance behavior, and study time and final academic performance while controlling for academic history and socioeconomic characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed fractional model outperformed the benchmark specification by increasing the adjusted coefficient of determination from 0.849 to 0.886 and reducing the root mean square error from 1.04 to 0.87. The estimated fractional-order parameter (α = 0.83) indicated temporal dependence within the observed academic assessment structure. Family educational support and weekly study time were positively associated with academic performance, whereas student absences and previous academic failures were negatively associated with final achievement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that incorporating educational memory provides a useful representation of temporal dependence in student academic performance. The observed associations between educational support, learning behavior, and achievement provide descriptive evidence that may inform future longitudinal and intervention-based research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77409-z.title: Design of white circularly polarized luminescence with high glum across entire visible regions by dual-loop active learning
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77409-z.abstract: White circularly polarized luminescence (WCPL) materials have attracted increasing attention. However, achieving WCPL simultaneously with high color rendering index (CRI) value at ideal CIE coordinates and large dissymmetry factor (glum) across entire visible regions remains a significant challenging, due to the vast chemical design space and the inefficient experimental screening by human-driven intuition-based methods. Herein, we propose an AI-assisted interactive experiment–learning evolution strategy to accelerate the discovery of WCPL materials with optimal trade-offs, integrating model recommendation, experimental validations, and active learning in each iterative refinement cycle. A multi-objective optimization algorithm automatically guides the experimental design with a dual-loop active learning framework, one for maximizing CRI at ideal CIE coordinates, and the other for optimizing glum value across entire visible regions. High-performance WCPL materials with excellent |glum | (>1.5) range of 410 to 680 nm, high CRI ( > 90) at ideal CIE coordinates (0.33, 0.33) can simultaneously be achieved with limited experimental date. Moreover, this workflow also enables on-demand fabrication of high performance white circularly polarized organic light-emitting diodes as well as the user-specified correlated color temperature, facilitating their application in lighting and full-color 3D display. White circularly polarized luminescence materials are promising but combining favorable white-light colorimetric properties and strong chiroptical activities is difficult. Yang et al. adopted a dual-loop active learning strategy to realize high-performance materials and devices.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-72464-4.title: Dissociating subjective and objective cognitive flexibility in fibromyalgia using a novel partial-contingency reversal learning task
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-72464-4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cognitive dysfunction (“fibrofog”) is a common symptom of fibromyalgia (FM) that includes subjective mental haze and measurable cognitive difficulties. Prior work suggests that subjective complaints may dissociate from objective cognitive performance in FM, yet most studies assessed subjective and objective cognition in separate contexts and timescales. We tested subjective and objective cognitive flexibility within the same behavioral context using a novel partial-contingency probabilistic reversal-learning task. Specifically, 298 participants (169 FM; 129 healthy controls [HC]) completed an acquisition phase followed by a reversal phase, in which reward contingencies changed for one stimulus pair while remaining stable for another. Objective learning was quantified by choice accuracy, and subjective task knowledge by explicit reward probability estimates after each block. HC outperformed FM participants on objective choice accuracy while subjective reward-probability estimates showed differential patterns between groups. Furthermore, while in HC objective accuracy and subjective estimates were positively correlated, no such association emerged in FM, suggesting altered coupling between behavioral adaptation and explicit contingency awareness. Depressive symptoms and overall FM impact did not moderate the relationship between objective and subjective indices in FM. Together, findings reveal reduced cognitive flexibility and partial dissociation between objective learning processes and subjective representations of learned contingencies in FM.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-70743-8.title: Quantum game-theoretic reinforcement learning for autonomous vehicle navigation and communication in vehicular networks
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-70743-8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Autonomous vehicle (AV) navigation and communication in highly dynamic vehicular networks require fast decision-making, reliable coordination, and energy-efficient connectivity. However, traditional Reinforcement Learning (RL) and game-theoretic approaches often suffer from slow convergence and limited scalability in dense multi-agent environments. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel Quantum Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning (QGTRL) framework that integrates quantum-inspired policy encoding using Parameterized Quantum Circuits (PQCs) with game-theoretic multi-agent coordination. The proposed approach uses quantum superposition and complex probability amplitudes to enhance exploration efficiency and improve policy convergence stability. In addition, a communication-aware coordination mechanism is incorporated to support robust interaction in dynamic Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) and Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) environments. The QGTRL framework is benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods, including Deep Q-Network (DQN), Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG), Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) Deep Recurrent Q-Network (QLSTM-DRQN), and Quantum Deep Reinforcement Learning (QDRL), under realistic simulation conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that QGTRL improves path-planning accuracy by 18.7%, reduces communication latency by 15.3%, and decreases energy consumption by 22.4% compared to baseline models, while maintaining higher mission success rates in dense and high-mobility scenarios. Furthermore, the framework operates on quantum-inspired classical computation, eliminating the need for specialized quantum hardware and enabling practical deployment. These results highlight QGTRL as a scalable, efficient, and robust solution for next-generation cooperative autonomous vehicle systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.37012/jpkmht.v8i2.3790.title: Strengthening Literacy and Higher-Order Thinking Skills Among Elementary School Students Through the Implementation of Problem-Based Learning
doi:10.37012/jpkmht.v8i2.3790.abstract: <jats:p>This community service activity was motivated by the need to strengthen literacy and higher-order thinking skills in Indonesian language instruction for elementary school students. The activity aimed to improve the literacy and higher-order thinking skills of sixth-grade students at Krapyak Godean Public Elementary School in Sleman through the implementation of Problem-Based Learning (PBL). The activity involved 24 students and was carried out through the stages of preparation, problem-based learning implementation, mentoring, and evaluation. The activity was evaluated using a 20-question written test and classroom observations, employing instruments that had been validated by two experts. The success of the activity was analyzed descriptively based on students’ average scores and the percentage of learning objectives achieved. The evaluation results showed a consistent improvement in students’ abilities. The average score increased from 64.58 at the beginning of the study to 72.50 after the first phase and reached 80.21 in the subsequent phase. The percentage of students who met the learning objective criteria also increased from 20.83% at the beginning of the study to 54.17% and then to 79.17%. These results indicate that the implementation of PBL provides a learning experience that encourages student engagement in understanding problems, thinking critically and creatively, and collaborating in the Indonesian language learning process. This activity contributes to strengthening students’ literacy and higher-order thinking skills through meaningful, student-centered learning experiences.</jats:p>

doi:10.29140/tltl.2026.104438.title: University students’ readiness for ChatGPT-assisted English learning: an explanatory mixed-methods study
doi:10.29140/tltl.2026.104438.abstract: <jats:p>The growing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning has raised increasing interest in learners' readiness to engage with such tools effectively. However, existing research has largely focused on isolated constructs such as technology acceptance and AI literacy, providing limited insight into learners' overall preparedness in authentic learning contexts. This study therefore investigates university students' readiness for ChatGPT-assisted English learning from a multidimensional perspective. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed. Quantitative data were collected from 586 undergraduate students using the Learners’ Readiness for ChatGPT-Assisted English Learning (LRCEL) scale developed and validated by Luo and Zou (2024b), followed by semi-structured interviews with 12 participants to explain the quantitative findings. The results indicate that students demonstrated relatively high levels of operational readiness, particularly in perceived behavioral control, attitude, and enjoyment. However, readiness was not stable, as intention to use ChatGPT remained moderate and highly dependent on task conditions. In addition, a clear gap was identified between students’ ability to use ChatGPT and their capacity to critically evaluate its outputs. The findings further reveal that readiness is socially constructed, with peer networks playing a more influential role than teachers in shaping students’ engagement with ChatGPT. These findings suggest that learner readiness is dynamic, uneven, and context-dependent, highlighting the need to reconceptualize readiness beyond purely cognitive or technical dimensions in AI-assisted language learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11081248/v1.title: Structural and Evolutionary Predictors of VIM-2 Mutational Fitness Revealed by Leakage-Aware, Position-Aware Machine Learning
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11081248/v1.abstract: Deep mutational scanning (DMS) provides a powerful experimental framework for resolving the functional consequences of protein mutations at scale, but predictive modeling of DMS landscapes is vulnerable to overly optimistic evaluation when variants from the same sequence position are distributed across training and test sets. Here, we developed a leakage-aware, position-aware machine-learning framework to identify generalizable determinants of mutational fitness in the VIM-2 metallo-β-lactamase. We analyzed 5,016 mutations spanning 266 sequence positions and nine experimentally defined phenotypes under different antibiotic concentrations and temperatures. Mutation-level predictors integrated physicochemical remodeling, evolutionary substitution scores, local sequence context, hydrogen-bond capacity, side-chain properties, and structural descriptors, including solvent accessibility and distances to the metal site, active-site pocket, and structural loops. Two complementary architectures were evaluated: a 65-predictor model excluding sequence position and a 66-predictor model incorporating position. Final architecture selection was performed exclusively using pooled position-aware out-of-fold performance from five-fold nested outer-test evaluation, while conventional random-split evaluation was retained as a secondary benchmark. Position-aware predictive performance varied substantially across phenotypes (R² = 0.169–0.506), with the position-inclusive architecture selected for six of nine phenotypes. Structural features consistently represented the dominant predictive feature group across all nine phenotypes, while individual predictors such as solvent accessibility, BLOSUM62, and metal-site proximity provided complementary information. Robustness analysis supported stable outer-fold and leave-one-fold-out performance across all nine phenotypes. Together, these results show that VIM-2 mutational fitness is partially predictable from integrated structural, biochemical, and evolutionary information, while revealing phenotype- and fitness-range-dependent predictive performance and underscoring the importance of position-disjoint validation for assessing transferable genotype–phenotype relationships in DMS datasets.

doi:10.1017/aer.2026.10218.title: Learning-based artificial potential field guidance for hypersonic glide vehicle penetration
doi:10.1017/aer.2026.10218.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the penetration guidance problem for hypersonic glide vehicles in complex constrained environments and proposes a learning-based efficient evasion guidance framework. First, a baseline strategy for determining the vehicle’s reference heading in obstacle environments is designed using an artificial potential field method. This baseline algorithm mitigates the inherent contradictions arising from the direct integration of the artificial potential field into a penetration guidance framework. Second, the key sensitive parameter set affecting penetration performance is identified. Based on a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework combining the multi-head self-attention mechanism and twin-delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3), an online parameter optimiser dependent on time-series state data is designed. Meanwhile, to ensure the effectiveness of strategy learning for this optimiser and avoid sparse rewards, three reward function models are constructed to guarantee the stable convergence of the agent’s strategy learning. This optimiser generates real-time responses for evasion strategy adjustments according to environmental dynamics, thus avoiding the potential limitations of manual offline adjustments and the rigidity of online-loaded strategies. Finally, a series of ablation studies and comparative experiments are conducted. These experiments systematically verify the effectiveness and superior performance of the proposed strategy under both standard and disturbed environmental conditions.</jats:p>

doi:10.1137/25m1731885.title: Value-Aware Estimation of Diffusion Systems for Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Surrogate Loss and Financial Applications
doi:10.1137/25m1731885.abstract:
<jats:p>Abstract.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>We estimate diffusion systems modeled by SDEs to solve optimal control problems in a continuous-time model-based reinforcement learning framework. Instead of minimizing a statistical loss, we estimate models by reducing the mismatch between the model-based value process and empirical rewards under a given policy. Direct optimization of this loss is generally intractable due to the difficulty of computing the value function of the model. To overcome this challenge, we construct an emulator of the model-based value process, yielding a surrogate loss tractable for optimization even in high dimensions. We establish convergence of the surrogate minimizer to the original loss minimizer and quantify the error from time discretization. Applications to mean-variance portfolio selection and stock portfolio liquidation demonstrate that our approach substantially reduces decision bias and more accurately estimates weak signals from noisy environments than classical statistical methods. We also show that our model-based approach requires far fewer samples to reach comparable performance levels than model-free learning in an empirical study.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-243-620261003.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Loss of the ‘Writing Struggle’: Is Struggle Essential to Learning?
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-243-620261003.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) writing tools into educational settings presents a fundamental challenge to traditional pedagogical approaches in K-12 settings that value cognitive struggle as important to learning. Drawing on cognitive psychology’s desirable difficulties framework and constructivist learning theory, this chapter argues that the writing struggle, which encompasses ideational, compositional, revision and problem-solving challenges, develops critical thinking, metacognitive awareness and intellectual resilience that cannot be replicated through AI-generated content alone. Using a conceptual and scenario-based analytical approach, this chapter develops a structured framework to examine how different modes of AI integration affect cognitive engagement in writing tasks. Specifically, the analysis introduces a Cognitive Engagement Matrix that categorises AI use across stages of the writing process and levels of student effort. Further, through an analysis of three illustrative implementation scenarios (AI-Replacement, AI-Collaboration and AI-Scaffolding models) and synthesis of current neuroscientific research, this chapter proposes strategic frameworks for preserving productive cognitive challenges while using AI’s supportive capabilities. This chapter also develops potential implementation strategies as practical guidance for educators managing this technological transition. This chapter concludes that successful AI integration requires fundamental reconceptualisation of writing instruction, assessment practices and curriculum design to ensure that technological efficiency does not compromise the cognitive development that makes writing a uniquely powerful tool for intellectual growth.</jats:p>
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-243-620261003.venue: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Literacy Education

doi:10.1108/lht-05-2026-0146.title: From access to engagement: AI literacy, technological play and academic libraries as sociotechnical learning environments
doi:10.1108/lht-05-2026-0146.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how academic libraries can support AI literacy through technological play, informal learning, librarian mediation and technology-rich spaces. It argues that AI literacy is sociotechnical: access to tools is necessary but does not by itself produce meaningful participation. The study also considers how institutional resources, governance and professional authority shape who can develop, support and benefit from AI-related learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a qualitative critical interpretive design, the study analyzes library and information science scholarship, professional frameworks, and selected institutional and higher education documents published between 2010 and 2026. Critical discourse analysis identifies recurring narratives of innovation, access, experimentation and professional responsibility. A political-economy lens examines the material and organizational conditions including funding, staffing, infrastructure, professional development, workload and governance that enable or constrain participation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four interrelated patterns emerge. Academic libraries are framed as sites of technological promise and innovation; librarians mediate AI learning through instruction, consultation, ethical guidance and collaborative problem-solving; technology-rich environments can support exploratory and play-based engagement; and opportunities for participation are unevenly shaped by funding, staffing, infrastructure, professional development, governance and institutional authority. AI literacy therefore develops through the interaction of tools, spaces, labor, pedagogy, experimentation and institutional conditions rather than through access alone.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As a conceptual, document-based study, this research does not measure AI learning or library practice across a representative sample of institutions. Its findings are interpretive and should be tested through multi-site case studies, observations, interviews and comparative research across institution types. A systematic or scoping review is also needed to map the empirical evidence on AI literacy, technological play, library space, librarian labor and institutional conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Library leaders should complement AI-tool provision with sustained investment in staff expertise, protected professional-development time, accessible infrastructure, low-risk opportunities for experimentation, clear policy guidance and meaningful participation in campus AI governance. Makerspaces, learning commons, workshops, sandboxes, consultations and peer-learning opportunities can support critical engagement when they are paired with human guidance and institutional support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Equitable AI literacy requires more than nominal access to generative AI tools. Differences in institutional funding, staffing, expertise, time and decision-making authority can shape learners' opportunities to experiment, question AI outputs, receive support and develop informed judgment. Academic libraries can help reduce these inequities by creating inclusive conditions for critical participation, reflection, and informed non-use alongside skill development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study integrates AI literacy and Technological Play Theory with a sociotechnical and political-economy account of academic library space, librarian labor, institutional resources and governance. It distinguishes access from meaningful participation and frames academic libraries as environments where technological, human, spatial, and organizational capacities converge. This framework offers researchers and library leaders a more comprehensive way to evaluate AI-learning initiatives beyond counting usage of tools, licenses or workshops alone.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1515/dx-2026-0080.title: “Learning bystander activation”: resident-led diagnostic error case conferences and sustained reflective engagement among junior residents
doi:10.1515/dx-2026-0080.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0080_abs_001">
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Diagnostic errors are a major patient safety concern, particularly in emergency settings where junior residents frequently perform initial evaluations. Diagnostic error case conferences are used as educational interventions, but their impact on sustained learning behaviors remains unclear. This study examined whether participation in resident-led conferences is associated with changes in reflective and self-directed learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0080_abs_002">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This single-center mixed-methods study involved junior residents participating in weekly diagnostic error case conferences. Pre- and post-intervention surveys assessed awareness of diagnostic errors and cognitive biases, and engagement in reflective and self-directed learning. Quantitative data were analyzed using Fisher’s exact test, and qualitative responses were analyzed thematically.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0080_abs_003">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Recognition of diagnostic errors increased from 62.5 to 100 % (p=0.006), and awareness during emergency practice from 58.3 to 100 % (p=0.003). The proportion reviewing more than 70 % of their cases increased from 54.2 to 87.5 % (p=0.040). Qualitative analysis identified heightened diagnostic vigilance, emotional engagement, and environment-driven reflective pressure, even among residents not directly involved in the cases.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0080_abs_004">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Resident-led diagnostic error case conferences were associated with increased reflective engagement. We propose the concept of “learning bystander activation,” defined as the activation of reflective and self-directed learning behaviors through exposure to a shared learning environment, even without direct involvement in the clinical case.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1088/1402-4896/ae9e95.title: Prediction of sawtooth mode characteristic parameters in tokamaks based on machine learning and physical models
doi:10.1088/1402-4896/ae9e95.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sawtooth oscillation frequently occur in the core of tokamak plasmas. Predicting the occurrence of sawtooth modes in advance is beneficial for the operation and control of tokamak discharges. This paper employs the kinetic-magnetohydrodynamic hybrid simulation code M3D-K (Multi-level 3D Kinetic) for numerical simulations to construct a dataset correlating safety factor profiles with sawtooth oscillation amplitude, period, and growth rate. Three models—Random Forest (RF), K-nearest neighbors, and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)—are adopted to achieve predictions for sawtooth oscillations. Results show that all three models exhibit good predictive performance. In comprehensive comparison, the XGBoost model achieves predictions which best match the simulation data for period and growth rate, while the RF model shows more potential for amplitude prediction. Using these two selected models for data prediction, validation on 10 random sets of data shows the error between predicted and true growth rates is below 8%, and the relative errors for period and amplitude predictions are within 15%. This further confirms the reliability and accuracy of these models in predicting sawtooth oscillations. This study provides a rapid surrogate model which can be used in pre-experimental discharge parameter optimization, offering valuable references for experimental scenario design in tokamaks.</jats:p>

doi:10.54536/ajdsai.v2i2.7696.title: DenGuess: Design and Development of a Machine Learning Web-Based Application for Dengue Outbreak Prediction in City of Koronadal Using Random Forest Model Classifier
doi:10.54536/ajdsai.v2i2.7696.abstract: <jats:p>Dengue outbreaks remain a major public health problem in Koronadal City with limited technology for monitoring the disease. Health workers are often challenged in accessing and preventing outbreaks due to the lack of available tools. While Random Forest models have been shown to be useful for predicting dengue, their practical application remains still limited. In this study, the researchers developed a machine learning web application to predict dengue outbreaks for five (5) selected barangays in Koronadal weekly, using the epidemiological and meteorological data from 2020 to 2025. The model’s performance was measured using a) real-time simulation accuracy, b) precision, c) recall, and d) F1-scores, and the website was evaluated using the user interface and user experience. The findings demonstrate that the model provides balanced and satisfactory predictions, and the website scores high on all criteria, confirming the usability and reliability of the website. This system provides timely forecast information to support the decision-making process, create more awareness among the community and increase preparedness in the city. Researchers suggest further systematizing the UI and UX of the website and to integrate the system into the city’s public health infrastructure to improve data collection, validation, and engagement within the community.</jats:p>
