doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1937520.title: SSLVNet: an explainable multi-modal hybrid framework integrating self-supervised learning and vision transformers for multi-label classification of retinal diseases
doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1937520.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Retinal Diseases are the main reason for vision loss and blindness worldwide. Initial identification of retinal abnormalities is essential for avoiding severe retinal-related complications and improving patient results. Traditional retinal disease diagnosis mainly depends on manual checks of retinal fundus images, which are slow and highly dependent on medical expertise. Deep learning methods are used in retinal disease classification. Existing methods are primarily based on labelled image data and often do not fully utilize complementary clinical information. The proposed hybrid multi-model framework classifies retinal diseases from the available retinal fundus images.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SSLVNet combines a Self-Supervised Learning encoder, Lesion Attention, CNN, ViT, and a Simplified lesion Graph. Also, Grad- CAM provides visual elucidations of the model predictions. ODIR-5K dataset, which includes multiple ocular disease categories, is used.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results are promising, with an Exact Accuracy of 84.44%, a Hamming accuracy of 96.92%, and a Macro F1-Score of 90.36%. An ablation study was done to understand the contribution of individual components in the proposed framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results indicate that the proposed work can effectively support reliable and interpretable retinal disease classification in real-world healthcare applications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fbinf.2026.1891949.title: A machine learning framework for interpreting phylogenetic tree patterns in interkingdom horizontal gene transfer
doi:10.3389/fbinf.2026.1891949.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Horizontal gene transfer (HGT), the movement of genetic material between unrelated organisms, is widely recognized as an important driver of genome evolution in bacteria. In eukaryotes, however, the evolutionary impact of HGT remains debated. The identification of interkingdom HGT (iHGT) is especially challenging due to the lack of gold standard methods. While automated approaches for iHGT candidate detection exist, the interpretation of phylogenetic tree topologies into biologically meaningful evolutionary patterns has traditionally depended on expert manual inspection, a process that is subjective, difficult to reproduce, and not scalable to large datasets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We present a computational framework that formalizes phylogenetic tree interpretation as a supervised machine-learning problem. We define five recurrent phylogenetic patterns (iHGT, NoHGT, Limited donor evidence, Multiple major clades, and Patchy phylogeny) and developed a feature-extraction pipeline that captures taxonomic composition and phylogenetic topology through six biologically interpretable descriptors derived from unrooted gene trees. Several machine-learning algorithms were evaluated using repeated stratified cross-validation, and model interpretability was assessed through permutation importance, SHAP analysis, rule-based baselines, and feature ablation. Performance was further validated on simulated datasets, real biological iHGT candidates, and an independently annotated external dataset.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A Random Forest (RF) classifier achieved the best performance (AUC–ROC = 0.98; accuracy = 0.89). Topological distance and lineage-distribution features were identified as the strongest contributors to classification performance. Feature ablation and rule-based baseline comparisons demonstrated that model performance cannot be explained solely by explicit annotation rules and benefits from combining clade-composition and topology-based information. The RF classifier showed low misclassification rates on simulated and real biological datasets (7.8% and 10.43%, respectively), showed substantial agreement (69.4%) with an independently annotated external dataset, and consistently outperformed AVP (Alienness vs. Predictor), Alien Index, and HGT Index across all evaluated metrics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results support the use of machine learning for the automated, reproducible, and scalable classification of expert-defined phylogenetic patterns. The framework also highlights that some topologies commonly interpreted as evidence of iHGT may reflect alternative evolutionary processes, emphasizing the need for cautious and context-aware inference.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1080/13569775.2026.2731048.title: Limits of autocratic learning: institutional constraints on policy diffusion in Eurasian autocracies
doi:10.1080/13569775.2026.2731048.abstract: In the twenty-first century, several Eurasian autocracies have successfully reformed their institutions of governance and emerged as high-capacity regulatory states. Much of this transformation occurred through institutional diffusion and regulatory policy transfer. Eurasian autocracies have borrowed policies and institutions from democratic regimes, successfully adapting them to serve the autocrats’ benefit. But can we successfully identify which types of policies and institutions are likely to diffuse across regime types? Focusing on economic regulatory policies in Ukraine, Kazakhstan, and Russia, this paper investigates constraints on autocrats’ ability to improve institutional quality. I argue that the political strategies of regime survival affect the extent to which autocratic states can ‘borrow’ best practice policies and institutions from democratic regimes, leaving them with fewer institutional options for building effective states. By linking mechanisms of policy implementation to political strategies, this research explores the limits of policy diffusion and institutional borrowing in autocracies.

doi:10.53819/81018102t4416.title: Influence of Parental Provision of Learning Resources on Implementation of Competence-Based Education in Public Junior Schools in Langata Sub-County, Nairobi County, Kenya
doi:10.53819/81018102t4416.abstract:
<jats:p>This study examined the influence of parental engagement on the implementation of Competence-Based Education (CBE) in public junior schools in Langata Sub-County, Nairobi County, Kenya. Guided by five research questions, the study investigated parental provision of learning resources, participation in school-based platforms, engagement in learners' homework, challenges to engagement, and strategies for strengthening parental involvement. The study was anchored on Epstein's Theory of Overlapping Spheres of Influence and complemented by Fullan's Theory of Educational Change. A mixed methods approach, specifically a convergent parallel design, was adopted. The target population comprised 11 public junior schools, 11 Head Teachers, 275 teachers, and 5,500 parents. The sample consisted of 6 schools, 6 Head Teachers, 90 teachers, and 150 parents. Data were collected using structured questionnaires, semi-structured interview guides, focus group discussion guides, and document analysis. Validity was established through face, content, construct, and criterion validity, while reliability was confirmed using Cronbach's Alpha, with all subscales exceeding 0.70. Quantitative data were analysed using SPSS version 28, while qualitative data were analysed thematically using NVivo 14. Findings revealed that all three dimensions of parental engagement significantly influenced CBE implementation, with provision of learning resources being the strongest predictor (β = .312, p < .001), followed by school-based participation (β = .185, p = .017) and homework engagement (β = .168, p = .031). The regression model explained 28.7% of the variance in CBE implementation. A significant perception gap existed between teachers and parents, with parents reporting higher engagement levels than teachers perceived.  The study recommends a national framework for parental engagement, parent education, financial support for needy families, measures to address the digital divide, and integration of parental engagement into teacher training.
Keywords: Parental engagement, learning resources, Competence-Based Education, junior schools, digital divide, Kenya</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s12880-026-02825-y.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early determination of whether a patient with coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is in progression or remission stage is crucial for optimal clinical management, but currently there is no rapid and effective solution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A new 3D convolutional neural network coupled mixed convolution and attention mechanisms named COV-DSNet was proposed to analyze pulmonary computed tomography (CT) scans and clinical data screening from 578 COVID-19 patients, which made it capable for rapidly staging. Subsequently, the role of AI staging diagnosis in predicting disease exacerbation and infectivity was analyzed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      297 CT scans from 156 patients were included in the COV-DSNet analysis. Results showed that COV-DSNet achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.820 ± 0.030 (95% CI: 0.792–0.844). In a randomly assigned verification sets, COV-DSNet achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.864 (95% CI:0.750–0.947) with a sensitivity of 0.708 and a specificity of 0.921, which demonstrated higher specificity than manual reading under the pre-specified single-center scope and reader setting. COV-DSNet- derived stage diagnosis improved the clinical model only with APACHE II score and PaO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      /FiO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      for predicting severe progression within 7 days (AUC 0.978 vs. 0.908), demonstrated good calibration (bootstrap-corrected mean absolute error 0.047), also helped to avoid misjudgments about infectivity by Sars-cov-2 RT-PCR Ct value in part of COVID-19 patients.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The COV-DSNet system provides a rapid staging tool for COVID-19 patients in our single-center study, which may contribute to the selection of rational treatments. It also provides new ideas and solutions for early clinical management of other pneumonias.</jats:p>

doi:10.3846/jeelm.2026.28264.title: Geospatial and machine learning techniques for spatiotemporal analyses of urban dynamics in the Coimbatore city, South India
doi:10.3846/jeelm.2026.28264.abstract: <jats:p>Rapid urbanization has drastically changed the land use and environmental conditions in Indian cities and need to be monitored continuously for sustainable urban planning. The study used Landsat satellite images of the years 2001, 2013 and 2023 to examine the spatiotemporal urban dynamics of the Coimbatore city of South India. The impacts of urban sprawl on the environment were evaluated from Land Use/ Land Cover (LULC), Land Surface Temperature (LST) and spectral indices (NDVI, NDWI and NDBI). The built-up land increased by 1.21% (2001–2013) and 1.67% (2013–2023) and agricultural land decreased by 1.62% (2013–2023). The LULC classification had an Overall Accuracy of 95.76% with a Kappa coefficient of 0.95. The Kappa coefficient of 0.96 indicates that the ANN-CA model has high predictive reliability in predicting the LULC scenario in 2031. The results show that the continued expansion of cities leads to an increase in land surface temperature and a decrease in vegetation cover. This has major implications for sustainable urban development and contributes to SDG 11 and SDG 13.</jats:p>

doi:10.1088/1361-6501/aea4de.title: Single-frame fringe projection three-dimensional reconstruction by integrating phase priors and deep learning
doi:10.1088/1361-6501/aea4de.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Single-frame fringe projection three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction can avoid motion artifacts caused by multi-frame phase-shifting acquisition and is therefore important for high-speed dynamic measurement. However, a single periodic fringe image lacks direct absolute order information, so phase jumps and point-cloud outliers are likely to occur near edges and in low-modulation, occluded, or specular regions. This paper proposes a hybrid single-frame 3D reconstruction method that integrates a Gabor phase prior, fringe order prediction, phase residual compensation, and geometric reliability screening. During training, multi-frequency phase-shifting sequences are used to construct supervision for the absolute phase and fringe order. During inference, only one high-frequency fringe image is required. Physically meaningful prior features assist the network in recovering the absolute phase, which is then converted into a 3D point cloud through the calibrated camera–projector model. Experiments show that the proposed method substantially reduces period-level phase errors and 3D outliers compared with conventional single-frame analytical methods and end-to-end direct regression networks. It produces more continuous and stable reconstructions in reliable output regions, and standard geometric samples further demonstrate good measurement consistency. The main contribution is to unify the interpretability of classical phase analysis, the nonlinear representation ability of deep networks, and structured-light geometric constraints, providing a practical approach that balances accuracy and robustness for single-frame structured-light 3D reconstruction.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/ijlls-03-2026-0085.title: Revisiting direct proportion through lesson study
doi:10.1108/ijlls-03-2026-0085.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to explore how an experienced mathematics teacher restructured her pedagogical understanding of direct proportion through a dialogically mediated lesson study (LS) process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reports a qualitative case study conducted within an LS cycle. The participant was a secondary mathematics teacher with 21 years of experience. The process was facilitated by a mathematics teacher educator positioned as a Knowledgeable Other (KO) adopting a non-hierarchical stance. Data were collected through pre- and post-lesson reflective dialogues and analysed using the DLP–ILP framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings revealed a shift from routine-based descriptions toward interpretative and conceptually grounded pedagogical reasoning. The teacher developed a critical awareness of representation choices (e.g. decreasing patterns), conceptual boundaries and the nature of the constant of proportionality. These reflections informed the redesign of the subsequent lesson.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As the study relies on teacher discourse rather than direct student data, inferences about student learning remain indirect. Future research may integrate multiple data structures to link teacher learning with student outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings highlight the role of non-directive reflective dialogue and the mitigation of power distance in supporting teacher learning. These findings suggest that egalitarian facilitation can support meaningful pedagogical reframing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social implications – By foregrounding teacher voice and reflective dialogue, this study highlights the importance of creating professional learning environments grounded in trust, equality and collaborative inquiry. The findings suggest that when teachers are supported through non-hierarchical and dialogic structures such as Lesson Study, they become more responsive to student thinking and more attentive to conceptual depth. Such shifts may contribute to classroom cultures where questioning, multiple strategies and conceptual understanding are valued. In this sense, the study underscores the broader social value of dialogic professional communities in fostering more reflective, student-centred mathematics classrooms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study foregrounds teacher voice and conceptual reframing, contributing to the Lesson Study literature by showing how structured dialogue supported the shift from descriptive to interpretative pedagogical reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.61467/2007.1558.2027.v18i1.1532.title: Progressive Transfer Learning in Hybrid CNN-Transformer Architectures for Robust Diabetic Retinopathy Grading
doi:10.61467/2007.1558.2027.v18i1.1532.abstract:
<jats:p>Automated diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading requires both local feature extraction and global spatial reasoning. While Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers (ViTs) struggle individually with spatial context and data limitations respectively, we propose an optimized hybrid framework (ProGrad-DR) combining an InceptionV3 backbone with a ViT encoder. To mitigate ViT overfitting on imbalanced data, we introduce a Progressive Transfer Learning regime, pre-training on a binary task before transferring to 5-class grading, and utilizing algorithmic class-weighting instead of synthetic oversampling. Trained on a composite dataset (APTOS/MESSIDOR) and independently tested on IDRiD, our model achieved a State-of-the-Art Quadratic Weighted Kappa of 0.9048 and a Balanced Accuracy of 0.7534. Notably, Mild DR sensitivity reached 80.0% with 99.4% healthy specificity. This stable, generalizable methodology successfully yields a clinically safe automated triage tool for multi-class DR grading across diverse settings.
 
Spanish-language metadata / Metadatos en españolTítulo en español:Aprendizaje por transferencia progresiva en arquitecturas híbridas CNN-Transformer para una clasificación robusta de la retinopatía diabética
Resumen:La clasificación automatizada de la retinopatía diabética (RD) requiere tanto la extracción de características locales como el razonamiento espacial global. Mientras que las redes neuronales convolucionales (CNN) y los Transformers de visión (ViT) presentan, de forma individual, limitaciones relacionadas con el contexto espacial y la disponibilidad de datos, respectivamente, proponemos un marco híbrido optimizado (ProGrad-DR) que combina una arquitectura base InceptionV3 con un codificador ViT.
Para mitigar el sobreajuste del ViT en datos desbalanceados, introducimos un esquema de aprendizaje por transferencia progresiva, basado en un preentrenamiento mediante una tarea binaria antes de transferir el modelo a una clasificación de cinco clases, utilizando además una ponderación algorítmica de clases en lugar de sobremuestreo sintético. Entrenado con un conjunto de datos compuesto (APTOS/MESSIDOR) y evaluado de forma independiente con IDRiD, nuestro modelo alcanzó un coeficiente kappa ponderado cuadrático de 0.9048 y una exactitud balanceada de 0.7534. Cabe destacar que la sensibilidad para la RD leve alcanzó el 80.0 %, con una especificidad del 99.4 % para los casos sanos.
Esta metodología estable y generalizable permite obtener una herramienta de triaje automatizado clínicamente segura para la clasificación multiclase de la RD en diversos entornos.
Palabras Claves:Retinopatía diabética, clasificación de imágenes médicas, aprendizaje por transferencia progresiva, redes neuronales híbridas, aprendizaje profundo, Transformers de visión, inteligencia artificial en medicina, triaje automatizado.

doi:10.52716/jprs.v16i3.1075.title: Machine Learning and Flow Zone Indicator for Permeability Estimation in Uncored Intervals of a Southern Iraqi Oil Field
doi:10.52716/jprs.v16i3.1075.abstract: <jats:p>The precise estimation of permeability is a difficult task due to the nature of heterogeneous reservoirs. Attributable to the high costs of core sampling and the poor accuracy of the linear regression method, the Flow Zone Indicator (FZI) method is regarded as one of the most commonly used techniques in Iraqi fields in recent years to predict permeability. However, this method requires statistical or machine learning to predict FZI in uncored intervals. This study aims to identify the most suitable machine learning model for FZI prediction in uncored intervals using conventional well logs as input. Following this, the reservoir is divided into hydraulic flow units (HFUs) using unsupervised learning. Specifically, AutoGluon is used as an automated machine learning framework to find the best algorithm and optimal hyperparameters for FZI estimation. The k-means algorithm was employed to classify the reservoir into HFUs. This integrated approach was applied to a field case study in southern Iraq. The study utilized both core and log data from three wells. The results demonstrated that the neural network (NN) outperformed the other algorithms within the framework, achieving more than an R² of 90% and a root mean squared error (RMSE) of 1.69 on the test data, and more than an R² of 96% and an RMSE of 0.493 on the training data. By applying the derived correlations for each HFU, the permeability prediction achieved an R² of 85% and an RMSE of approximately 0.37. This demonstrates the effectiveness of the automated machine learning framework in improving FZI estimation and, consequently, permeability predictions.</jats:p>

doi:10.59373/jelin.v3i2.373.title: Psychological Challenges and Academic Success among Students from Broken Homes: The Contribution of Islamic Education
doi:10.59373/jelin.v3i2.373.abstract: <jats:p>The phenomenon of broken families resulting from parental separation or divorce has emerged as a serious concern due to its substantial influence on children’s psychological and educational development, particularly among students in primary and secondary schools. Students experiencing family disruption may face various emotional and psychological challenges, including anxiety, depression, diminished self-confidence, and reduced motivation to learn, all of which can negatively affect their academic performance. This study examines the psychological dynamics of students from broken home backgrounds and investigates the role of Islamic Education in providing intervention and support to facilitate their academic achievement. Employing a qualitative approach with a case study design, the findings reveal that students from broken families frequently encounter internal emotional conflicts that interfere with their concentration, classroom engagement, and learning processes. Nevertheless, the internalization of Islamic educational values, including tawakkal (reliance on God), patience, sincerity, and character formation through consistent religious practices, can contribute to strengthening students’ psychological resilience. Islamic Education therefore extends beyond the transmission of religious knowledge and serves as a spiritual and moral support system that enables students to respond to difficult family circumstances with greater emotional stability and inner peace. Furthermore, Islamic value-based learning can help students reinterpret their family experiences positively and transform adversity into motivation for academic improvement. Islamic Education teachers also serve as significant others by offering emotional support, moral direction, and encouragement, thereby helping students manage stress and maintain their commitment to educational goals. The study concludes that integrating psychological support with Islamic educational values is essential for mitigating the adverse effects of family disruption and fostering students’ resilience and academic success despite challenging family circumstances.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fsoil.2026.1937878.title: Machine learning-based prediction of soil aggregate stability for sustainable land management in the eastern Himalayan region of India
doi:10.3389/fsoil.2026.1937878.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Plot-scale rainfall-induced soil erosion data are scarce in the eastern Himalayas of  India. Soil aggregate stability (SAS), commonly quantified by mean weight diameter (MWD), is a key indicator of erosion susceptibility. As laboratory determination of MWD is labor-intensive, machine learning (ML)-based pedotransfer functions (PTFs) using readily measurable soil properties offer an efficient alternative.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In this study, 126 topsoil samples (0–15 cm depth) were collected from agricultural (n = 61) and forest (n = 65) lands in a sub-watershed of Sikkim, India, to develop and evaluate ML-based models for soil MWD prediction. Eleven soil physico-chemical parameters, i.e., ten ‘input’ (%Sand, %Silt, %Clay, %OC, BD, pH, Ca
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      , Mg
                      <jats:sup>2+</jats:sup>
                      , CO
                      <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                      <jats:sup>2−</jats:sup>
                      , and HCO
                      <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                      −), and one ‘target’ (MWD), estimated in the laboratory, were used in this study. Three supervised ML techniques, such as ANN, RF and SVM, along with empirical MLR, were used to predict soil MWD.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The mean BD, %OC and MWD of agricultural land were 1.25 g/cm
                      <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                      , 3.37% and 1.09 mm, respectively, whereas those of forest land were 1.17 g/cm
                      <jats:sup>3</jats:sup>
                      , 4.23% and 1.11 mm, respectively. The sand fraction was found more in agricultural land (61.34%), while the clay proportion was found more in forest land (30.11%). All three ML models performed better than MLR in predicting soil MWD. The RF model performed best for the agricultural land (R
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0.89, NSE = 0.89 for training; R
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0.66, NSE = 0.66 for testing), while the ANN model was found to be superior for the forest land (R
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0.92, NSE = 0.92 for training; R
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0.91, NSE = 0.91 for testing). The SVM model predicted soil MWD more accurately for the pooled dataset (R
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0.98, NSE = 0.98 for training; R
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      = 0.72, NSE = 0.72 for testing). No single technique is superior for all the land uses; however, the SVM model is either best or second best in all the cases. Therefore, the developed SVM-based SAS model can be employed to accurately predict soil MWD across the eastern Himalayan region and facilitate regional soil erosion investigations.
                    </jats:p>
