doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1936790.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Universal Design for Learning (UDL) has been widely promoted as a framework for supporting inclusive education by addressing learner diversity through flexible curriculum design, instructional practices, and assessment approaches. In 2015, Ghana adopted UDL in its policy on inclusive education to address the diverse educational needs of all children. Despite this policy focus, most research has centered on classroom teachers' implementation of UDL, with limited attention to how teacher educators understand UDL and perceive their preparedness to implement it.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To address these gaps in the literature, this study investigated teacher educators' perceptions and experiences of UDL, differences across demographic and professional characteristics, relationships among UDL understanding, preparedness, and institutional support, and the predictors of preparedness. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 156 teacher educators from three public colleges of education. Colleges were selected via convenience sampling across three regions in Ghana. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, one-way multivariate analysis of variance, Pearson product -moment correlation, and hierarchical multiple regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The participants demonstrated moderately positive levels of UDL understanding, preparedness, and perceived institutional support. Significant differences were identified across selected demographic and professional characteristics, including age, subject specialization, department, teaching level, teaching experience, and prior introduction to UDL. Understanding, preparedness, and institutional support were positively associated. Importantly, both general understanding and perceived institutional support significantly predicted preparedness, with institutional support emerging as the stronger predictor.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that strengthening UDL implementation requires attention to both teacher educators' individual capacity and the institutional conditions that enable practice. Sustained, practice-oriented professional learning, leadership support, collaborative opportunities, and explicit integration of UDL into institutional teaching and learning practices are therefore recommended to strengthen inclusive teacher preparation in Ghana.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10879351/v1.title: Integrative SMR and multi-model machine learning characterize FCER1A- and INSIG1-associated phenotypes in arterial aging-related disease
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10879351/v1.abstract: Background and aims : Global population aging has made age-related cardiovascular disease an urgent public health challenge, and inflammation is closely associated with arterial aging. This study aimed to identify inflammation-related molecular features associated with arterial aging-related disease using an integrative analytical framework. Methods : We integrated summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. SMR used FinnGen coronary artery disease GWAS and GTEx v8 whole-blood eQTL data. Models were evaluated in GEO transcriptomic datasets; single-cell and macrophage-state analyses resolved cell-type expression patterns. Expression was assessed in serially passaged human umbilical vein endothelial cells and naturally aged C57BL/6J mice. Drug-response prediction, docking, and molecular dynamics simulations prioritized candidate compounds and assessed modeled interactions. Results : FCER1A and INSIG1 were preferentially expressed in macrophage populations and varied across connected macrophage states and inferred trajectories in diseased vessels. Their expression was also increased during serial-passage-associated endothelial senescence and in aged mouse arterial tissue. Computational analyses prioritized dihydrorotenone and entospletinib and supported plausible modeled interactions with the corresponding protein structures. Conclusions : The integrative analysis prioritized FCER1A and INSIG1 as molecular features associated with arterial aging-related disease and provided cell-type localization and experimental expression evidence. These results set the stage for follow-up mechanistic and pharmacological investigations to dissect causal relationships and explore their therapeutic relevance.

doi:10.5201/ipol.2026.514.abstract: In this work, we study active learning techniques to highlight their strengths and limitations in the context of surrogate modeling.We implemented an iterative algorithm that uses active sampling methods to approximate known functions.Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of active learning in improving surrogate models by wisely selecting informative data points.Furthermore, we examine cases where active learning may face challenges, particularly when balancing exploration and exploitation.This study provides information on the improvement of the efficiency and accuracy of surrogate models in practical applications.

doi:10.5194/hess-30-5925-2026.title: Predicting streamflow drought in the conterminous United States using machine learning and a donor-gage approach, 1982–2020
doi:10.5194/hess-30-5925-2026.abstract: <jats:p>Drought is a highly consequential natural disaster that may likely increase in both severity and extent across the conterminous United States (CONUS). The mechanisms affecting the propagation of drought from the atmosphere to streamflow are complex and interactive, making the prediction of streamflow drought difficult with current modeling approaches. Machine learning is an emerging tool in the field of hydrology that may be well-suited to prediction of streamflow drought across large and topographically diverse areas. Here, we train and analyze 3198 random forest models at U.S. Geological Survey streamgages to understand common meteorological drivers of streamflow drought and to define physiographic characteristics of basins sensitive to these drivers. We also develop a novel dynamic regionalization approach using donor gages to predict daily streamflow drought at pseudo-ungaged locations. Our results show that teleconnections, temperature, evaporative demand, and snow–water equivalent are important drivers of streamflow drought in the West, Southwest, and Northern Rocky Mountains (Northern Rockies) regions of the United States, and precipitation and soil moisture are primary drivers of streamflow drought in the Northeast, Southeast, and the Northwest regions. Prediction using dynamic regionalization shows comparable performance to at-site models. This method may be applicable to other hydrologic prediction problems requiring transferability to ungaged locations.</jats:p>

doi:10.31098/jess.v4i2.4308.title: Language Learning Strategies as Predictors of Reading Comprehension Performance in English
doi:10.31098/jess.v4i2.4308.abstract: <jats:p>Reading is a crucial skill for school success because it allows students to access information and participate in class. However, there is a lack of local research showing which specific language learning strategies actually predict reading comprehension for Grade 9 students in the Philippines. To explore this, the study used a quantitative predictive design with 304 students from Biñan Integrated National High School. Data was collected using Oxford’s Strategy Inventory for Language Learning (SILL) survey and a standardized reading comprehension test drawn from DepEd Open Educational Resources (OER) and the Philippine Informal Reading Inventory (PHIL-IRI). This test assessed students' ability to understand texts at the literal, inferential, and critical levels. The findings revealed that students frequently used learning strategies, particularly metacognitive and social strategies. Despite this high usage, their overall reading comprehension stayed at a developing, "instructional" level. Students were best at finding direct facts but struggled with deeper analysis, such as drawing conclusions or evaluating meaning. The study also found that female students had higher reading comprehension scores and used cognitive, metacognitive, affective, and social strategies more than male students did. Most notably, the research showed that metacognitive, cognitive, memory, and social strategies positively predict reading comprehension performance, while affective and compensation strategies were negative predictors. This pattern suggests that affective and compensation strategies were linked to lower scores, likely because struggling readers use these coping methods more often when they experience difficulty. Overall, the study finds that active thinking and self-regulation are key to reading success. These insights provide teachers with practical ways to design targeted reading lessons that help high school students move beyond basic decoding and become independent readers.</jats:p>
doi:10.31098/jess.v4i2.4308.venue: Journal of Elementary and Secondary School

doi:10.1108/jarhe-01-2026-0167.title: From learning to leading: cognitive and motivational drivers of entrepreneurial orientation in higher education
doi:10.1108/jarhe-01-2026-0167.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As universities are increasingly expected to develop entrepreneurial graduates capable of addressing socio-economic challenges, entrepreneurial education has become a strategic priority. However, limited research has examined how teaching strategies and entrepreneurial motivation jointly influence entrepreneurial orientation and the mechanisms underlying these relationships. This study identifies and prioritizes entrepreneurial education teaching strategies and investigates their effects, alongside entrepreneurial motivation, on entrepreneurial orientation in Iranian comprehensive universities. It further examines the mediating role of entrepreneurial self-efficacy and the moderating role of social entrepreneurial capability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was adopted. In the qualitative phase, interviews with university professors were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify teaching strategies, followed by pairwise thematic comparison (PTC) to prioritize them. In the quantitative phase, student survey data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eight entrepreneurial education teaching strategies were identified, with “experiential learning” and “real-world application and innovation” receiving the highest priority. The findings show that teaching strategies and entrepreneurial motivation positively influence entrepreneurial self-efficacy and entrepreneurial orientation. Entrepreneurial self-efficacy partially mediates these relationships, while social entrepreneurial capability strengthens the effects of teaching strategies and entrepreneurial motivation on entrepreneurial self-efficacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances entrepreneurial education research by integrating pedagogical, motivational, cognitive, and contextual factors into a unified framework. By combining thematic analysis, PTC, and PLS-SEM, it provides empirical evidence on how teaching strategies and entrepreneurial motivation contribute to entrepreneurial orientation through self-efficacy and social entrepreneurial capability. The findings offer theoretical insights and practical guidance for designing entrepreneurial education programs that foster entrepreneurial competencies in higher education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1956924.title: Academic emotions, self-efficacy, and deep learning behaviors in online nursing education: a mediation analysis
doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1956924.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nutrition care for older adults women with gynecologic cancers is an emerging and clinically critical competency domain in nursing education. With the accelerated shift toward online learning, understanding the psychological mechanisms that drive deep learning behaviors in this specialty area is essential for curriculum design and educational quality improvement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine associations between academic emotions, academic self-efficacy, and deep learning behaviors in undergraduate nursing students participating in an online specialty nursing course, and to evaluate the mediating role of academic self-efficacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional survey was conducted from September 2023 to January 2024 among third- and fourth-year undergraduate nursing students at three universities located in eastern, central, and western China. Of 540 distributed questionnaires, 487 were returned and 461 valid responses were included. The Academic Emotions Questionnaire for Online Learning (AEQ-OL), Academic Self-Efficacy Scale for Nursing Students (ASES-NS), and Deep Learning Behavior Scale (DLBS) were administered electronically. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and bootstrap mediation analysis were performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 461 valid questionnaires were analyzed (effective response rate 94.7%). Positive academic emotions (mean 3.72 ± 0.61) were positively associated with academic self-efficacy (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      = 0.542,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.001) and deep learning behaviors (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      = 0.631,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.001). Academic self-efficacy was also positively associated with deep learning behaviors (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      = 0.587,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.001). In the positive-emotion model, the indirect effect through academic self-efficacy was significant (
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                      = 0.322, 95% bootstrap CI: 0.260–0.386), accounting for 50.6% of the total effect. In the negative-emotion model, the direct effect became non-significant after inclusion of academic self-efficacy, whereas the indirect effect remained significant.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Academic emotions were significantly associated with deep learning behaviors in this online nursing education context, and academic self-efficacy showed a significant mediating association. These findings support the educational relevance of emotionally supportive learning environments and strategies that strengthen students’ confidence, while causal and temporal relationships require confirmation in longitudinal or experimental studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1007/s11042-026-21936-w.title: Rock tomography image retrieval: a deep metric learning approach with N-pair loss

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Content-based image retrieval (CBIR) has become an essential tool in several industries, allowing images to be searched efficiently based on their properties. In the context of digital rock studies, a CBIR system assists, for example, in applications in the oil and gas industry, where the identification and categorization of different rock formations directly impact resource management and extraction. In this paper, we present a Deep Metric Learning (DML) approach using the N-pair Loss function in conjunction with an architecture composed of notable backbones from the literature. The experiments were conducted on two datasets, one consisting of carbonates and the other of sandstones. The result of the model trained with the DenseNet201 backbone reached
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\varvec{98.87 \pm 1.17\%}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    of F1-Score and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\varvec{98.83 \pm 1.22\%}$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>

doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2406.title: Before we automate WIL evaluation, we need to ask what we're actually measuring
doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2406.abstract: <jats:p>Community-engaged Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) is increasingly positioned as a mechanism for advancing graduate employability and social responsibility, yet the frameworks used to evaluate it remain anchored to countable proxies: employment rates, satisfaction scores, and placement completions. This provocation argues that these metrics are structurally misaligned with what WIL practitioners actually know about placement quality: knowledge that is relational, contextually rich, and routinely invisible in institutional reporting. As Generative AI enters WIL evaluation, this misalignment becomes urgent. Automating existing frameworks will not resolve their limitations, and risks further marginalising the evidence that most reliably signals whether community-engaged WIL is working. Drawing on research into practitioner agency in learning analytics, this provocation calls for evaluation frameworks that legitimise practitioner judgement, centre community partner perspectives, and deploy GenAI in service of relational knowledge rather than as a substitute for it. Effective WIL evaluation is not primarily a measurement problem, it is a question of whose evidence counts.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s11222-026-10972-z.title: Faster Hamiltonian Monte Carlo by learning leapfrog scale: an offline randomized solution
doi:10.1007/s11222-026-10972-z.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We introduce a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) methodology based on an offline empirical calibration of randomized leapfrog parameters. The approach, referred to as eHMC, where
                    <jats:italic>e</jats:italic>
                    stands for empirical, leverages importance sampling to construct an empirical distribution on discretization parameters, thereby eliminating the need for manual burn-in diagnostics and online adaptation. The proposal distribution used in the calibration stage is obtained via a Population Monte Carlo scheme with tempering and relies on flexible parametric variational families such as normalizing flows. Once the calibration stage complete, the resulting algorithm defines a homogeneous Markov chain via a mixture of HMC kernels with a fixed mixing distribution, and hence preserves the target distribution. Numerical experiments indicate that eHMC can achieve competitive or improved sampling efficiency compared to the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) in the case useful integration times can be summarized by the offline distribution. The comparison is assessed by standard efficiency metrics normalized by the number of leapfrog steps during the post-calibration sampling phase.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1177/03611981261485238.title: Spatial Analysis of Driving Under the Influence Origins in Seoul Using Geographically Weighted Machine Learning
doi:10.1177/03611981261485238.abstract: <jats:p>Driving under the influence (DUI) of alcohol remains a critical public safety concern, accounting for a significant proportion of road traffic injuries and fatalities. Although numerous predictive models have been developed to estimate DUI risk, many conventional approaches such as ordinary least squares (OLS), random forest (RF), and geographically weighted regression (GWR) are constrained by assumptions of spatial homogeneity, linearity, and multicollinearity. To overcome these constraints, this study applies a geographically weighted random forest (GW-RF) model to investigate the spatially varying determinants of DUI incidents in Seoul, South Korea. The analysis targets DUI occurrence density based on trip origin locations within each administrative neighborhood. Explanatory variables include the density of DUI offenses with or without crashes, alcohol-serving land use, transit accessibility, and demographic composition, reflecting environmental exposure and population characteristics. The results indicate that GW-RF achieves competitive predictive accuracy while more effectively accounting for spatial heterogeneity and reducing residual spatial autocorrelation compared with conventional models. Spatial cross-validation further confirms stable out-of-sample generalization across geographically separated partitions. The relative importance and marginal effects of key predictors, including the density of non-crash DUI offenses, alcohol-related crashes, and general food establishments, vary considerably across space. Partial dependence analyses reveal heterogeneous nonlinear effects, including threshold and saturation patterns. A spatiotemporal comparison reveals stronger nighttime clustering and increased influence of alcohol accessibility, indicating time-dependent variation in DUI risk mechanisms. These findings indicate that spatially adaptive machine learning offers an approach for capturing localized risk structures and supports the design of geographically targeted strategies for DUI prevention.</jats:p>

doi:10.67563/asesconf2026028k.title: MACHINE LEARNING-BASED PREDICTION OF CONCRETE COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH FOR STRUCTURAL ENGINEERING APPLICATIONS
doi:10.67563/asesconf2026028k.abstract: <jats:p>&lt;p&gt;The increasing availability of experimental data in civil engineering has created new opportunities for the application of artificial intelligence techniques in structural engineering research. Machine learning approaches provide powerful tools for identifying complex relationships between material composition and mechanical properties. In this study, data-driven methods are applied to investigate the prediction of concrete compressive strength using a publicly available experimental dataset. The considered parameters include the main components of concrete mixtures as well as the age of concrete specimens. The objective is to explore the capability of machine learning models to capture nonlinear relationships between mixture composition and the resulting compressive strength. The presented framework represents a preliminary step toward broader applications of artificial intelligence in structural engineering problems, including reinforced concrete elements such as beam&amp;ndash;column joints.&lt;/p&gt;</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10644971/v1.title: Effects of AI-Assisted Case Discussion and Virtual Patient Consultation on Medical Students' Learning Outcomes
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10644971/v1.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) holds broad application prospects in medical education; however, systematic empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness in facilitating case discussions and virtual patient consultation remains scarce. This study recruited undergraduate medical students and conducted experiments to examine the pedagogical effects of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation. Methods A total of 207 medical undergraduates participated in this study. Using the self-developed intelligent experimental platform, medical students engaged in AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation. Experiment 1 employed a single-factor, three-level between-subjects design to compare the effects of AI-assisted case discussion, peer case discussion, and a learning-only control condition on medical students' knowledge acquisition, intrinsic motivation, and interaction quality. Experiment 2 utilized a single-factor, four-level between-subjects design to examine the effects of virtual patient consultation and the sequencing of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation on medical students' knowledge acquisition, intrinsic motivation, and consultation process quality. The control group participants were the same individuals across both experiments. Results Results indicated that the AI-assisted case discussion group achieved significantly higher knowledge scores than the control group. The virtual consultation group, the consultation-then-discussion group, and the discussion-then-consultation group all outperformed the control group in knowledge acquisition. The discussion-then-consultation group demonstrated higher intrinsic motivation and consultation comprehensiveness, yet exhibited lower empathy than the consultation-then-discussion group. Conclusions These findings suggest that both AI-assisted case discussion and virtual patient consultation can effectively enhance medical students' knowledge acquisition, while different intervention sequences exert differential effects on intrinsic motivation, consultation comprehensiveness, and empathy. The results provide theoretical foundations and practical guidance for AI-empowered medical education.

doi:10.31098/jess.v4i2.4527.title: Navigating Science: Experiences and Coping Strategies of Grade 12 STEM Students in Laboratory Learning
doi:10.31098/jess.v4i2.4527.abstract: <jats:p>Laboratory learning is a fundamental component of STEM education, promoting scientific inquiry, hands-on learning, and the application of theoretical knowledge. However, existing studies have primarily focused on laboratory resources, instructional practices, and academic outcomes, offering limited insight into students' lived laboratory experiences and coping mechanisms. Thus, this study explored the experiences, engagement, and coping mechanisms of Grade 12 STEM students at Maria Asuncion Rodriguez Tiñga High School during laboratory activities. Using a phenomenological design, nine STEM students were selected through purposive sampling. Data were gathered through in-depth interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings showed that laboratory activities promoted hands-on learning, collaboration, and skill development. Nevertheless, limited resources, equipment shortages, and time constraints influenced students' experiences. Despite these challenges, students demonstrated resilience through support-seeking, self-regulation, and sustained motivation. The study extends Kolb’s Experiential Learning Theory and Lazarus and Folkman’s Psychological Stress and Coping Theory, explaining how laboratory experiences and adaptive coping jointly shape student engagement. Findings also support improved laboratory instruction and student support. To improve laboratory learning, teachers should undergo training on time-efficient and inquiry-based activities, implement structured group roles, and use low-cost materials. Resilience-building strategies may also be integrated. Future research may explore teachers’ perspectives and compare schools with varying laboratory resources to further understand laboratory learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2413.title: Community Engagement is optional until it isn’t: Rethinking postgraduate psychology placements
doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2413.abstract: <jats:p>Universities want placements filled, students want them completed, and community partners are left to reconcile a mismatch no one asked them to navigate. This practice-informed provocation draws on work-integrated learning (WIL) scholarship and my experience as placement coordinator to argue that community engagement is often raised as a value in psychology placements but insufficiently embedded in placement infrastructure. Community engagement may appear in program rationales and accreditation documents but rarely in the structural design of how placements are resourced and supported. In other words, there is a gap between what we say about community engagement and what we build into our placement systems (Jackson et al., 2017). Based on my experience, I argue that community partners are often positioned as hosts rather than co-designers of professional learning, left carrying substantial, under-recognised responsibility for student learning. Postgraduate psychology placements cannot be ethically scaled through transactional placement models. If universities want community partners to sustain student learning, they must resource relational co-design as core placement infrastructure, rather than treat it as optional engagement work.</jats:p>

doi:10.1515/mt-2026-0236.title: Machine vision-based surface defect testing of industrial materials using a lightweight multiscale attention fusion network
doi:10.1515/mt-2026-0236.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Surface defect detection is essential for maintaining quality in industrial products, but in real industrial applications it faces a dilemma among accuracy, processing speed, and model lightweight. To address this challenge, we propose a method named global attention mechanism for deeply separable YOLO (simply denoted as GMD-YOLO) network. It integrates global context and local information in a multi-scale attention fusion module to improve the recognition of small defects, and an enhanced depth separable convolution to reduce computational cost. The model is evaluated in three typical scenarios individually involving pavement, wood surface and steel surface defects. The accuracy, processing speed, and model lightweight are quantitatively analyzed using mean accuracy, frame rate, and floating-point operations, respectively. Results show that GMD-YOLO not only maintains real-time performance but also outperforms the common methods in the YOLO family in all three metrics. High-resolution thermograms reveal the robust decision basis of the model, and ablation experiments confirm the synergistic gain effect between the sub-modules.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10925657/v1.title: PE-Tab2Conv: Clinically structured convolutional representation learning for preeclampsia risk modelling from routine electronic health records
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10925657/v1.abstract: Background: Machine-learning decision support from routine electronic health records requires representations that handle class imbalance while retaining clinically interpretable structure. We developed PE-Tab2Conv, a clinically structured tabular-to-matrix representation for preeclampsia risk modelling. Methods: Encoded maternal variables were arranged in a fixed $4 \times 6$ matrix spanning baseline and socioeconomic characteristics, obstetric history, extended obstetric and family history, and comorbidities. A lightweight two-dimensional convolutional neural network produced 32-dimensional embeddings for downstream classifiers. Models were evaluated on a locked 2023 temporal cohort from RS Adhyatma ($n=531$), comparing a portable core feature space (17 predictors) with an extended space (21 predictors). Interpretability used SHapley Additive exPlanations and matrix-cell occlusion. A second hospital contributed 72 preeclampsia-positive records for positive-case transportability assessment. Results: In the extended setting, PE-Tab2Conv with logistic regression achieved an area under the precision--recall curve of 0.817 (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.922; Brier score 0.047), numerically above extended tabular XGBoost (0.800). The extended-to-core gain was primarily associated with historical predictors; prior preeclampsia had the largest cell-level occlusion effect ($\Delta\mathrm{AUPRC}=0.210$). External positive cases retained elevated model scores, but the absence of external controls precluded full external validation. Conclusions: PE-Tab2Conv offers a compact, traceable representation-learning method for health-informatics risk modelling and potential clinical decision-support development. Balanced multicentre validation is required before deployment.

doi:10.21009/jrpms.102.08.title: Pengaruh Problem-Based Learning Berbasis STEM terhadap Kemampuan Pemecahan Masalah Statistik Siswa SMP
doi:10.21009/jrpms.102.08.abstract: <jats:p>Pembelajaran statistika di SMP perlu memberi kesempatan kepada siswa untuk tidak hanya menyajikan data, tetapi juga menggunakan data tersebut untuk memahami persoalan, menentukan strategi, dan menarik kesimpulan. Penelitian ini menguji efektivitas Problem-Based Learning (PBL) berbasis STEM dalam meningkatkan kemampuan pemecahan masalah statistik siswa kelas VII. Sebanyak 51 siswa SMP IT Adzkia terlibat dalam desain kuasi eksperimen pretest–posttest control group, yang terdiri atas 25 siswa kelompok eksperimen dan 26 siswa kelompok kontrol. Pembelajaran berlangsung selama empat pertemuan pada materi Penyajian Data. Kemampuan siswa diukur menggunakan delapan soal uraian yang merepresentasikan empat tahapan Polya: memahami masalah, merencanakan strategi, melaksanakan strategi, serta memeriksa dan menafsirkan hasil. Perbedaan capaian akhir dianalisis melalui ANCOVA dengan skor pretest sebagai kovariat. Setelah kemampuan awal diperhitungkan, kelompok PBL berbasis STEM memperoleh capaian yang secara signifikan lebih tinggi dibandingkan kelompok pembelajaran reguler, F(1,48) = 152,462, p < 0,001, dengan partial eta squared 0,761. Rata-rata terkontrol kelompok eksperimen mencapai 77,58 dan kelompok kontrol 62,09. Analisis per tahap menunjukkan efek terbesar pada kemampuan memeriksa dan menafsirkan hasil, diikuti melaksanakan strategi, merencanakan strategi, dan memahami masalah. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa PBL berbasis STEM terutama memberi keuntungan pada proses penggunaan dan interpretasi data dalam penyelesaian masalah statistik.</jats:p>

doi:10.4208/jml.251216.title: Numerical Investigation of Sequence Modeling Theory using Controllable Memory Functions
doi:10.4208/jml.251216.abstract: <jats:p>The evolution of sequence modeling architectures, from recurrent neural networks and convolutional models to Transformers and structured state-space models, reflects ongoing efforts to address the diverse temporal dependencies inherent in sequential data. Despite this progress, systematically characterizing the strengths and limitations of these architectures remains a fundamental challenge. In this work, we propose a synthetic benchmarking framework to evaluate how effectively different sequence models capture distinct temporal structures. The core of this approach is to generate synthetic targets, each characterized by a parametric memory function $\rho(s, \alpha)$ and a controllable parameter $\alpha$ that determines the temporal strength. This setup allows us to produce a continuum of tasks that vary in temporal complexity, enabling fine-grained analysis of model behavior with respect to specific memory properties. We focus on four representative memory functions, each corresponding to a distinct class of temporal structures: exponential and polynomial functions for decay dynamics, impulse functions for long-range dependencies, and Airy functions for sparsity patterns. Experiments on several sequence modeling architectures confirm existing theoretical insights and reveal new findings regarding approximation capabilities, optimization dynamics, and architectural trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in advancing theoretical understanding and highlight the importance of using controllable targets with clearly defined structures for evaluating sequence modeling architectures.</jats:p>

doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2400.title: Work-Integrated Learning in the Centre for Research and Social Change at Anglicare Southern Queensland
doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2400.abstract: <jats:p>Anglicare Southern Queensland (Anglicare) is a not-for-profit organisation that delivers community and human services. With a long history of hosting applied student placements in aged care, social work and community services, mental health and wellbeing, youth support, and nursing and allied health, Anglicare has in recent times begun to expand our hosting of work-integrated learning (WIL) relating to research and evaluation, advocacy, and community outreach. Proceeding from the principle that different types of WIL are advantageous to social science and humanities students at all levels, we currently host a variety of industry research projects, student placements, and internships. These arrangements encompass everything from formal assessment to projects that are co-designed between student/s and supervisor/s. The benefits of hosting WIL include supporting the future careers of emerging professionals while simultaneously expanding our capacity in research, evaluation, and advocacy. As working with students who are new to a corporate workplace can also be time intensive, WIL programs need adequate university staffing to support students’ engagement with industry hosts and moderated timelines for assessment and reporting requirements. In this practitioner reflection, we discuss how Anglicare’s Centre for Research and Social Change establishes and manages community engaged WIL partnerships, welcoming undergraduate and postgraduate students in all areas of the social sciences and humanities.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1915056.title: Development and validation of an interpretable machine learning model for concurrent identification of kinesiophobia in older patients with coronary heart disease after percutaneous coronary intervention
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1915056.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Kinesiophobia reduces participation in cardiac rehabilitation and impairs exercise adherence among older patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). This study aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning (ML) model for identifying prevalent kinesiophobia in this population at the time of assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      From December 2024 to August 2025, 502 older patients with CHD who underwent PCI were recruited from three tertiary grade-A hospitals in Lanzhou, Gansu Province, China. After stratification by kinesiophobia status, participants were randomly assigned to a development set (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 352) and an internal validation set (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 150). A further 150 patients recruited from the same hospitals between September and October 2025 constituted a temporal validation cohort. Five candidate algorithms were evaluated: Random Forest (RF), Logistic Regression (LR), Decision Tree (DT), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Support Vector Machine (SVM). Model development was conducted using a rigorous nested cross-validation framework with a 10-fold outer loop and a 5-fold inner loop. Data preprocessing, feature selection, synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) resampling, and hyperparameter tuning were independently repeated within the corresponding training partitions. The final algorithm was selected based on predictions generated from inner cross-validation within the development set, jointly considering discrimination, overall prediction error, calibration, and clinical net benefit.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 15 predictors were identified, including the Barthel Index, avoidance, residence, fear of disease progression, clinical classification, confrontation, resignation, pain severity, educational level, smoking status, gender, depression, drinking status, exercise self-efficacy, and self-perceived burden. The mean outer-loop area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values for LR, DT, RF, SVM, and XGBoost were 0.884 ± 0.076, 0.795 ± 0.069, 0.876 ± 0.071, 0.879 ± 0.072, and 0.878 ± 0.072, respectively. XGBoost demonstrated the best overall performance. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.821 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.755–0.884] in the internal validation set and 0.981 (95% CI: 0.963–0.994) in the external validation set. The Brier scores were 0.170 and 0.062 in the internal and external validation sets, respectively. The corresponding calibration intercepts were 0.269 and 0.150, while the calibration slopes were 0.744 and 2.072, respectively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study developed an interpretable ML model for the concurrent identification of kinesiophobia in older patients with CHD after PCI. After further validation in broader populations, the model may support early identification and personalized cardiac rehabilitation management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10945655/v1.title: Validating Statistical Zonation for Groundwater Natural Background Levels Using an Integrated SOM-KNN Machine Learning Approach in a Heterogeneous Mountainous Terrain, North China
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10945655/v1.abstract: Determining reliable groundwater natural background levels (NBLs) in heterogeneous mountainous regions remains challenging because multiple flow domains (pore, fracture, and karst) generate complex hydrochemical patterns governed by recharge–flow–discharge processes. A critical yet unresolved question is whether predefined hydrogeological units are consistent with hydrologically controlled groundwater organization. In this study, we develop a process-informed framework that integrates unsupervised Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) and supervised K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and use this combined SOM–KNN approach as a diagnostic tool to evaluate whether statistical zonation reflects hydrologically meaningful groundwater organization and to quantify transitions between flow regimes. The framework is applied to a mountainous aquifer system in North China, where 480 groundwater samples were collected across six predefined units. The SOM analysis reveals a dominant mineralization gradient that reflects progressive groundwater evolution from recharge-dominated zones to flow and discharge zones, while trace elements exhibit localized signatures associated with lithological heterogeneity. Projection of hydrogeological unit labels onto the SOM topology demonstrates that most predefined units are consistent with the underlying hydrologically organized structure, while transitional zones emerge at unit boundaries. The KNN classification further quantifies inter-unit separability and identifies overlapping regions that correspond to hydrologically mixed flow regimes. These overlaps provide a quantitative basis for refining hydrogeological zonation and improving the delineation of NBLs. Cross-validation with conventional statistical approaches confirms the robustness of the identified outliers and transitional samples. Overall, the proposed framework moves beyond purely data-driven classification by explicitly linking hydrochemical patterns to hydrological processes and by providing a transferable approach for validating conceptual hydrogeological models. This contributes to more reliable NBL estimation and supports groundwater quality assessment in complex aquifer systems.

doi:10.1108/jwl-12-2025-0460.title: Replenishing the learner: the role of leader humor in providing the energy resources necessary for learning from failure
doi:10.1108/jwl-12-2025-0460.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While leader humor is widely acknowledged as an effective, resource-infusing communication tool, its role in facilitating learning from failure – a process that requires substantial resources – remains underexplored. Grounded in conservation of resources theory, this study aims to examine whether leader humor enhances employee energy at work, a pivotal resource, which in turn promotes learning from failure. Furthermore, this study posits learning goal orientation (LGO) as a key moderator that influences how energized employees allocate their resources.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using two-wave data from 345 Chinese employees, this study tested the hypotheses via hierarchical multiple regression and bootstrapping.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analysis of two-wave survey data based on 345 employees supports the hypothesized model: energy at work mediates the relationship between leader humor and learning from failure, and this indirect effect is stronger among employees with higher LGO.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances research on learning from failure by introducing a resource-dynamic perspective that complements existing cognitive models. The authors identify that leader humor replenishes the energy required for learning from failure, and introduce LGO as a key moderator explaining how individual goals determine whether replenished energy is invested in productive learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.6c03935.title: Machine Learning-Assisted Discrimination of Isobaric Histone Acetylations by Nanopore
doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.6c03935.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Histone acetylation, a post-translational modification, is associated with cancer progression, invasion, and metastasis, serving as a promising biomarker. The accurate discrimination of acetylation sites has strong potential for cancer diagnostics. Herein, we engineered an R220Q aerolysin nanopore to detect isobaric histone acetylations. By exposing the paired negative charge (D222) at the pore entrance, peptides with a higher positive charge density encounter a lower U* for pore entry and subsequent translocation. With the assistance of machine learning, we achieved direct discrimination of isobaric acetylations in histone peptides. Monoacetylated peptides H3K9ac and H3K14ac, as well as diacetylated peptides H3K4acK9ac and H3K4acK14ac were unambiguously identified in mixtures with identification accuracies of 99.4% and 98.8%, respectively. This work offers a label-free approach for analyzing acetylated biomarkers with potential applications in cancer detection and drug target development.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41746-026-03264-3.title: A spatially aware deep learning framework for multiscale cellular ecology profiling to predict 5-year recurrence in invasive lung adenocarcinoma
doi:10.1038/s41746-026-03264-3.abstract: Recurrence remains a major clinical challenge in surgically resected invasive lung adenocarcinoma (ILA), where existing staging and grading systems fail to capture the cellular complexity that underlies tumor aggressiveness. We present PathRosetta, an AI framework that models cellular ecology of tumor microenvironment (TME) from hematoxylin-and-eosin slides. Rather than treating slides as set of independent patches, PathRosetta represents individual cells within their local spatial neighborhoods and integrates this cellular context with tissue-level architecture to predict five-year recurrence. Across 430 patients (876 slides), PathRosetta reached an AUC of 0.78 ± 0.04 on the internal cohort, outperforming IASLC grading (0.71), AJCC staging (0.64), and competing AI models (0.62–0.72), and generalized to external TCGA (0.75), CPTAC (0.76), and WFBCCC (0.75) cohorts. It achieved a hazard ratio of 9.54 and a concordance index of 0.70 and remained independently prognostic after adjusting for other variables (adjusted HR:4.05, p < 0.001 ). Most notably, within clinically homogeneous AJCC Stage I patients, PathRosetta isolated a high-risk subgroup with markedly poorer outcomes (5-year RFS 46.7% vs. 84.7%; p < 0.001 ). Exploratory analysis further suggested morpho-spatial subgroups within individual cell types, motivating future molecular validation. By characterizing the spatial cellular ecology of the TME, PathRosetta delivers interpretable, generalizable recurrence prediction that complements existing clinical systems.

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920084.title: Technology-mediated Chinese learning beyond the classroom: the role of L2 resilience and L2 engagement
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1920084.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Out-of-class autonomous language learning is an important dimension of second language (L2) development, particularly in higher education contexts where learners are expected to regulate their own learning beyond formal instruction. In technology-mediated learning environments, this autonomy increasingly depends on learners' technology literacy (TL), understood not merely as the ability to operate digital tools but as a self-regulated capacity to select resources, evaluate information, solve learning problems, and sustain participation in digital learning contexts. In Chinese as a Second Language (CSL) learning, however, relatively little is known about CSL learners' TL in autonomous out-of-class learning or about the learner-side factors that may support this capacity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This mixed-methods study examined the current profile of TL among 327 international CSL learners in mainland China and investigated whether L2 resilience and L2 engagement predicted TL. Quantitative data were collected through questionnaire surveys and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, multiple regression, and robustness checks. Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews with six participants and analyzed thematically.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Learners reported a moderate level of TL. Both L2 resilience and L2 engagement significantly and positively predicted TL, with L2 engagement showing the stronger predictive effect. Interview findings further indicated that learners used technology to support examination preparation, maintain Chinese exposure, access authentic digital communities, and connect Chinese learning with academic, professional, and everyday life needs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that TL in out-of-class CSL learning is closely connected with learners' persistence, engagement, and self-regulated use of digital resources. The study offers implications for helping CSL learners select, combine, and sustain technology-mediated Chinese learning practices beyond the classroom.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/samamj-02-2026-0018.title: Work-related learning in the AI era: the influence of formal and informal learning on employee attitudes toward artificial intelligence
doi:10.1108/samamj-02-2026-0018.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Limited research has examined how employees’ broader participation in work-related learning relates to their attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI). This study aims to examine how formal and informal work-related learning predicts positive and negative attitudes toward AI and whether these relationships differ across traditional, remote and hybrid work settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A quantitative, survey-based design was used to collect data from 252 full-time employees in the USA working in traditional, remote and hybrid settings. Relationships were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, with multigroup analyses used to assess differences across work settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Formal work-related learning positively predicted both positive and negative attitudes toward AI. Informal work-related learning positively predicted positive attitudes toward AI, but was not significantly related to negative attitudes toward the technology. These relationships did not differ significantly across traditional, remote and hybrid work settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings demonstrate that employees’ broader engagement in work-related learning influences their perceptions of AI. Formal learning influences both favorable and unfavorable attitudes, which highlights the importance of developing employee capabilities while addressing concerns surrounding AI. Informal learning influences positive attitudes and may complement structured development through everyday workplace learning experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study extends organizational learning research into the context of workplace AI by examining whether employees’ broader engagement in formal and informal learning predicts both positive and negative attitudes toward AI. The inclusion of work setting further establishes whether these relationships differ across contemporary work environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/ils-04-2026-0146.title: Learning time privacy in early childhood: reciprocal mother–child learning of temporal boundaries
doi:10.1108/ils-04-2026-0146.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explores how time privacy is understood and negotiated in early childhood through a structured educational intervention. Framed within a learning sciences perspective, the study examines how children and mothers make sense of temporal boundaries through everyday interaction and reciprocal learning, thereby extending discussions of privacy beyond informational and spatial dimensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study employed a qualitative intervention design involving 19 children aged 48–72 months and their mothers. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews conducted before and after a structured educational intervention and were analyzed using thematic content analysis to explore participants’ evolving understandings of time privacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that children increasingly interpreted time privacy through familiar everyday experiences, including recognizing their own and others’ personal time within daily family routines. Mothers similarly described greater awareness of temporal boundaries and more intentional conversations about personal time in everyday life. Rather than indicating uniform behavioral change, the findings point to the gradual development of time privacy through reciprocal mother–child learning, everyday interaction, and shared meaning-making. The study also proposes the Time Privacy Learning Model in Early Childhood, which conceptualizes time privacy as a relational and learnable dimension of privacy literacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the learning sciences by conceptualizing time privacy as an emerging dimension of privacy literacy in early childhood. It extends existing privacy research by positioning temporal boundaries as a relational construct that develops through reciprocal mother–child interaction and everyday family experiences. The proposed conceptual model offers an interpretive framework for understanding how temporal awareness, relational awareness, and self-regulation may contribute to children’s developing understandings of time privacy. These findings provide practical implications for early childhood education and family-based learning in increasingly digitally mediated contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202659504.title: Unsupervised machine learning analysis of plasma wave turbulence statistics from Solar Orbiter RPW-TDS measurements
doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202659504.abstract: <jats:p>With the increasing amount of observational data and in situ measurements, the demand for automated processing and classification is also growing. Statistical methods and machine learning techniques are powerful tools for such tasks. In this paper, we consider measurements of electric fields obtained with the RPW-TDS instrument on board the Solar Orbiter spacecraft. We used a Pearson classification technique together with a residual neural network and unsupervised clustering to perform a primary sorting and analysis of data obtained between June 2020 and February 2026. We have developed a comprehensive software toolkit that enables the processing of typical-structured diagrams. We identify two characteristic types of β distributions, and we present the temporal distribution of their occurrence within different clusters  as a function of the distance to the Sun. The resulting clustering structure provides an initial organization of the dataset and highlights periods that may correspond to different conditions of the solar wind. The developed methodology and software package can be used to cluster signals of various natures.</jats:p>

doi:10.5194/nhess-26-4529-2026.title: Infra-Net: a robust parallel decision-making network for discriminating natural hazards and anthropogenic infrasound events via multi-view feature learning
doi:10.5194/nhess-26-4529-2026.abstract: <jats:p>The accurate classification of infrasound signals is a cornerstone of global geophysical monitoring, essential for both natural hazard early warning systems (e.g., volcanic eruptions, debris flows, and earthquakes) and the verification of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. However, the development of reliable automated systems is hindered by the inherent scarcity of representative event data, particularly for rare extreme events, as well as the presence of complex, non-stationary background interferences. To maximize the diagnostic value of limited geophysical datasets, this paper proposes Infra-Net, a novel parallel decision-making network driven by multi-view feature learning and a confidence-based fusion mechanism. We introduce a logarithmic wavelet scattering transform to produce robust, mathematically grounded feature representations. Unlike conventional methods that process scattering matrices holistically, our approach treats individual columns as independent feature vectors, providing multiple localized perspectives of the same acoustic event. Architecturally, Infra-Net utilizes a dual-branch structure to simultaneously capture multi-scale spatial features and discriminative temporal patterns. These parallel evaluations are synthesized through a custom confidence-based fusion module, which employs weighted averaging and an inner-product mechanism to ensure a stable and comprehensive final classification. Tested on both public infrasound datasets and real-world Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization (CTBTO)-measured data, Infra-Net achieved accuracies of 100 % and 82.07 %, respectively. These results demonstrate that Infra-Net offers a highly robust soft computing solution for enhancing Earth system monitoring and the reliable identification of natural hazards amidst anthropogenic noise.</jats:p>
doi:10.5194/nhess-26-4529-2026.venue: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1819272.title: Core practices as anchors for grounding teaching in research on learning and instruction
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1819272.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The concept of core practices has gained increasing prominence in teacher education, yet important conceptual questions remain unresolved. In particular, there is little agreement on what constitutes a core practice, what it means for core practices to be research-based, and how to embed them within broader teacher education curricula. This paper proposes a theoretical framework to answer these questions. Building on the defining features proposed in foundational work on core practices (e.g.,
                    <jats:xref>Grossman et al., 2009</jats:xref>
                    ), we argue that core practices are instructional activities enacted in social interaction, occupying a medium level of granularity between broad domains of practice and specific teaching behaviors. Elaborating on this conception, we argue that core practices may function psychologically as basic-level categories (
                    <jats:xref>Rosch, 1978</jats:xref>
                    ) which novice teachers developed during their long-time apprenticeship of observation at school. Core practices thus provide ideal anchor points around which teacher education can be organized. Using the core practices of explaining and modeling, we demonstrate how core practices can be grounded in evidence-based instructional principles derived from research on learning and instruction, exemplifying what it means for core practices to be research-based. To address how such research-based core practices can be situated within a broader vision of teacher education, we propose a three-part framework in which (a) core practices serve as anchors for introducing novices to evidence-based principles from research on learning and instruction; (b) core practices are situated within middle-range theories of learning and instruction, enabling novices to decide when and why to enact them and to orchestrate different core practices in ways that promote student learning; and (c) core practices are related to the most fundamental goals of teaching, such as, for example, supporting students’ individual knowledge construction, supporting students’ participation in disciplinary discourse, or supporting students’ identity development, enabling novice teachers to deeply understand the purposes of teaching and reflect on and develop their teaching accordingly. Taken together, conceptualizing core practices as basic-level categories, grounding them in research on learning and instruction, and using them as anchors within broader teacher education curricula provides a foundation for a research-based signature pedagogy for teacher education.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.67563/asesconf2026069h.title: COMPARISON AND TUNING OF MACHINE LEARNING MODELS FOR COLUMN WEB PANEL IN TRANSVERSE COMPRESSION
doi:10.67563/asesconf2026069h.abstract: <jats:p>&lt;p&gt;The component method enables efficient design of steel joints by decomposing them into individual components characterized by their resistance and stiffness. This paper presents a machine learning-based approach for resistance prediction of the column web panel in transverse compression, based on a numerical dataset generated using IDEA StatiCa Connection. Three machine learning models are investigated and compared: a deep neural network, Random Forest, and XGBoost. Particular attention is given to the influence of model tuning on predictive performance, where the deep neural network is tuned using a manual sensitivity-based procedure, while Random Forest and XGBoost are tuned using grid search. The results highlight differences in model behavior, sensitivity to tuning, and overall prediction accuracy. The study emphasizes the importance of appropriate model selection and tuning when applying machine learning models to resistance prediction problems in steel joint design.&lt;/p&gt;</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10935535/v1.title: Deep Learning in the Diagnosis of Choroidal Melanoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10935535/v1.abstract: Purpose: Uveal melanoma (UM), particularly its most common subtype, choroidal melanoma (CM), is the leading intraocular malignancy in adults. Early diagnosis is crucial for improved prognosis, but accurately identifying small or early lesions remains challenging due to limitations in imaging. Artificial intelligence, especially deep learning (DL), shows promise for enhancing diagnosis and risk assessment of choroidal lesions. This study summarized DL models' diagnostic performance, clinical usefulness, limitations, pooled estimates, and research needs for detecting CM. Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Databases searched included PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Embase up to August 3rd, 2026. Our analysis comprised research studies that used DL to diagnose CM among other conditions. Quality assessment was performed using the QUADAS-AI tool. Results: Ten studies met the inclusion criteria for the qualitative synthesis. Six of the ten studies were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled sensitivity was 0.92 (95% CI, 0.89–0.94). Individual study estimates of sensitivity ranged from 0.80 to 0.96. The pooled specificity was 0.97 (95% CI, 0.79–1.00). Across the included studies, individual specificity estimates ranged from 0.76 to 1.00. The leave-one-out sensitivity analysis showed that the pooled sensitivity and specificity estimates were consistent, regardless of which studies were excluded. Conclusion : Our study strongly supports the use of DL in diagnosing CM while highlighting areas for further research. These findings could guide future studies and clinical practices in diagnosing and managing CM.
