doi:10.3389/fped.2026.1969179.title: An interpretable machine-learning model identifies obesity-related metabolic complications in children attending a tertiary obesity clinic
doi:10.3389/fped.2026.1969179.abstract: <jats:p>Childhood obesity-related metabolic complications are common in Northwest China, yet region-specific evidence and risk-stratification tools are lacking. In a single-visit cross-sectional study of 131 children (3–18 years) with overweight or obesity attending a Gansu maternal and child-care hospital, obesity-related metabolic complications (ORMC) were present in 31.3% (dyslipidaemia 16.0%, hyperuricaemia 9.2%, elevated blood pressure 7.6%). An interpretable model combining LASSO-selected adiposity measures (body mass index, neck circumference, body fat percentage) with penalised logistic regression achieved moderate, internally cross-validated discrimination (AUC 0.72, 95% CI 0.62-0.82) that awaits external validation, comparable to a random forest (0.73). Screen time was the strongest modifiable behavioural correlate. Routine metabolic screening and simple body-composition measures should be embedded in paediatric obesity clinics, with screen-time reduction as a counselling priority.</jats:p>

doi:10.1096/fj.202602171rr.title: Integrative Multi‐Omics and Machine Learning Reveal Senescent Fibroblast‐Associated <scp>ADAMTS2</scp> as a Critical Indicator of Intestinal Inflammation in <scp>IBD</scp>
doi:10.1096/fj.202602171rr.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Although cellular senescence contributes to tissue dysfunction in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), the heterogeneity of senescence at the single‐cell resolution remains poorly defined. In this study, we systematically characterized the senescence landscape within the IBD microenvironment, with particular emphasis on fibroblast subpopulations and their systemic consequences. Single‐cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‐seq) dataset was applied to profile senescence‐associated feature heterogeneity. Fibroblasts were classified into high‐senescence (HS‐Fibro) and low‐senescence (LS‐Fibro) groups according to senescence scores. HS‐Fibro‐specific gene signatures were identified and functionally annotated. Intercellular communication networks were constructed using CellChat to delineate the HS‐Fibro interactome atlas, with emphasis on identifying cellular targets responsive to senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) signals. Integrated microarray datasets were employed to elucidate the systemic impact of HS‐Fibro in IBD. Through the integration of differential expression analysis, Weighted Gene Co‐expression Network Analysis (WGCNA), and an ensemble of 113 machine learning algorithms, seven hub genes implicated in IBD progression were systematically identified and prioritized. In the IBD microenvironment, fibroblasts exhibited enhanced senescence activity. HS‐Fibro displayed potent pro‐inflammatory properties and enhanced communicative capacity. IBD patients with high HS‐Fibro infiltration showed sustained immune‐inflammatory activity. Systematic bioinformatic analysis and immunohistochemistry validation identified ADAMTS2 as a robust diagnostic indicator for IBD, with substantially elevated expression in patients relative to controls. The human colon fibroblast cell line CCD‐18Co was treated with H
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    to establish a cellular senescence model, demonstrating marked upregulation of ADAMTS2, SASP markers, and fibrosis‐related genes. Moreover, siRNA‐mediated knockdown of ADAMTS2 resulted in obvious attenuation of these SASP and fibrosis‐associated genes.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1108/jwl-03-2026-0146.title: Entrepreneurial knowing under uncertainty: a communicative perspective on social and intellectual capital
doi:10.1108/jwl-03-2026-0146.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine how entrepreneurs in early-stage startups develop knowledge – referred to as entrepreneurial knowing – through communicative processes under conditions of uncertainty. It explores how interactions shape belief formation and belief testing and how social capital influences the development of intellectual capital.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a qualitative approach, 20 semi-structured interviews were conducted with early-stage entrepreneurs in the New York City metropolitan area. The data were analyzed to examine how uncertainty is interpreted, negotiated and enacted through communication during entrepreneurial knowing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four communicative mechanisms – market hybridity, identity complexity, disciplinary ambiguity and access constraints – shape entrepreneurial knowing in early-stage startups. These mechanisms create epistemic fragmentation, concentrate interpretive authority among founders and filter external feedback. Social capital functions as a communicative infrastructure that both enables and constrains intellectual capital development by shaping access to knowledge, trust and shared interpretation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reconceptualizes intellectual capital as an emergent outcome of entrepreneurial knowing and demonstrates how communication shapes knowledge development under uncertainty. By integrating entrepreneurial knowing, social capital and intellectual capital through a communicative perspective, it advances research on workplace learning in entrepreneurial contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1017/s2058631026101238.title: Socrates, Ovid, and Claude walk into a bar: using generative AI tools to support learning about the ancient Mediterranean
doi:10.1017/s2058631026101238.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In the Fall term of 2024, I taught a class on the ancient Mediterranean, with a focus on Plato, Ovid, and Roman satire. The goals of the class include exposure to epic, philosophy, and humour from antiquity; honing critical thinking skills; and consideration of how human nature has changed (or has not) over the millennia. To pull back the curtain surrounding generative AI tools, I required students to use Claude.ai on their essay assignments. Students critiqued the large language model (LLM)’s composition of essay questions, its judgement of virtue of fictional characters, and its gloss on Platonic idealism. I also required students to write about their experiences with Claude.ai at the end of term. This paper offers a case study of classroom use and my own explorations of this emerging technology. While instructors’ apprehension surrounding AI tools is justified, there is room for using LLMs to show students what the tools can and cannot do. As familiarity with these tools becomes a requirement for new graduates and rising professionals, we need not forget the lessons of antiquity. My investigations illustrate a challenge that humanity has always faced: we must learn how to confront the siren song of technology without it leading to our demise.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-71324-5.title: A novel deep learning-based approach for liver segmentation from 3D CT images using probabilistic shape guidance
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-71324-5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Accurate liver segmentation is essential for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems, yet it remains challenging due to anatomical variability, indistinct organ boundaries, and tissue intensity variations in both normal and pathological cases. To address these challenges, a deep learning-based framework is proposed for segmenting liver regions from 3D computed tomography (CT) volumes. Initially, this system creates a 3D probabilistic shape map to estimate the probability of each voxel being a liver voxel, utilizing a reference atlas dataset. To facilitate this, the atlas references are first aligned with the input CT volume via 3D affine registration, establishing a coarse but essential spatial correspondence. Following this alignment, the model adaptively matches each voxel in the input CT volume with cubic neighborhoods of varying sizes derived from the aligned liver atlas to compute the final shape map probabilities. Finally, a dual-path UX-Net (DPUX-Net) architecture is introduced which receives the original CT volume, combined with its corresponding probabilistic shape map, as input, and produces accurate and anatomically consistent liver segmentations. The efficacy of the proposed liver segmentation system is assessed on 120 CT volumes using multiple quantitative metrics, including the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), Jaccard index, absolute volume difference (AVD), and Hausdorff distance (HD), achieving scores of
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$93.19\%\pm 2.53\%$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ,
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$87.12\%\pm 4.42\%$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ,
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$4.53\pm 3.20$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , and
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$7.37\pm 5.19$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , respectively. The evaluation includes both hold-out test samples from the training dataset and entirely unseen external datasets, demonstrating the robustness and generalizability of the proposed framework. In comparison to the current state-of-the-art deep learning-based segmentation models, the proposed system surpasses them, highlighting its potential and reliability in precisely segmenting liver regions in CT volumes.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.63498/injelps108.title: Special education-related practices in regular Taiwanese schools through the lens of Filipino teachers
doi:10.63498/injelps108.abstract: Aim: This research explored special education related-practices that are implemented in regular schools of Taiwan as perceived by 30 Filipino Teachers working at regular public schools in Changhua County, Taiwan.It also examined the challenges they encountered in implementing and adapting to inclusive educational practices and served as a basis for developing a Cultural Adaptation Guide to support their teaching practices in inclusive classrooms. Methodology:The study employed a convergent parallel mixed-methods design.Quantitative data were collected from 30 Filipino teachers through a researcher-made survey questionnaire, while qualitative data were gathered through semi-structured interviews with 10 purposively selected participants.Results: The findings showed that all areas of special education-related practices, including instructional strategies, classroom management, assessment and progress monitoring, and collaboration and support systems, were highly implemented.However, Filipino teachers encountered significant challenges, particularly language and communication barriers, limited access to specialized training in special education, and difficulties in adapting to Taiwanese educational norms and culture.Conclusion: Despite Taiwan's established inclusive education framework, Filipino teachers' implementation of special education-related practices occurred alongside notable linguistic, cultural, and professional preparation challenges.The findings highlight the importance of strengthening teachers' adaptive resilience, cross-cultural communication, instructional adaptation, classroom management, and collaborative practices.The proposed Cultural Adaptation Guide may serve as a practical resource to support Filipino teachers in navigating inclusive classrooms and enhancing their capacity to address the needs of learners with disabilities in Taiwanese educational settings.

doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2403.title: From Community Engagement to Career Readiness: The Role of Micro-Credentials in Enhancing Graduate Employability
doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2403.abstract: <jats:p>This study explored undergraduate students’ and community partners’ perceptions of the value of micro-credentials within community-engaged Work-Integrated Learning (WIL) in technical education programs in South-East Nigeria. Guided by Experiential Learning Theory, Human Capital Theory, and Signaling Theory, the study adopted a mixed-methods exploratory design to examine how micro-credentials were perceived in relation to employability-related competencies, professional confidence, and career readiness. Quantitative data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to 412 undergraduate students enrolled in technical education programs incorporating community-engaged WIL, while qualitative data were generated through semi-structured interviews with 20 students and 12 community partners involved in WIL supervision and collaboration. Findings revealed generally positive student perceptions regarding the usefulness of micro-credentials for recognising competencies developed through experiential learning, strengthening confidence in communicating skills, and supporting preparedness for future employment. Qualitative findings further suggested that students viewed micro-credentials as useful for documenting technical and transferable competencies, encouraging reflective learning, and articulating skills gained through community-engaged experiences. Community partners similarly perceived micro-credentials as potentially valuable indicators of students’ preparedness and engagement within collaborative projects. However, participants identified institutional and contextual constraints, including limited awareness, inconsistent implementation, inadequate guidance, and weak digital infrastructure. The study suggests that micro-credentials may serve as useful mechanisms for recognising and communicating learning developed through community-engaged WIL while highlighting the need for stronger institutional support and clearer implementation strategies.</jats:p>
doi:10.21153/jtlge2026vol17no2art2403.venue: Journal of Teaching and Learning for Graduate Employability

doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1952855.title: Development and validation of an interpretable machine learning model for pulmonary heart disease in patients with pneumoconiosis
doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1952855.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Pneumoconiosis patients with pulmonary heart disease (PHD) face an elevated risk of mortality. Early identification of individuals at higher risk of PHD is important for timely risk stratification and clinical management. However, few risk-screening models have been specifically developed for pneumoconiosis in primary care settings, where access to advanced diagnostic resources may be limited. Therefore, this study developed and validated a machine learning model based on routinely available data to support early risk stratification and clinical decision-making in resource-limited environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A dual-design occupational pneumoconiosis cohort, comprising retrospective and prospective components, was established using occupational, epidemiological, and laboratory data obtained from electronic medical records and questionnaires. Key variables were selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression; five machine learning models were developed using five-fold cross-validation with grid search for hyperparameter tuning. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), F1 score, accuracy, precision-recall area under the curve (PR AUC), calibration metrics, and threshold analysis. The prospective cohort was used to evaluate the generalizability of the models. Model interpretability was assessed by Shapley additive explanations (SHAP).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following strict application of the inclusion and exclusion criteria, the retrospective cohort included 984 hospitalized patients (2012–2021), whereas the prospective cohort comprised 829 patients enrolled since 2021. LASSO identified 10 variables for model construction. All models demonstrated satisfactory discrimination, with logistic regression (LR) achieving an AUC of 0.816 in the external validation cohort. Lower BMI, albumin, and platelet large cell ratio (P-LCR), as well as higher red blood cell distribution width coefficient of variation (RDW-CV), older age, and stage III pneumoconiosis, were associated with higher predicted risk of PHD. The SHAP interaction network further indicated prominent statistical interaction patterns among hematological abnormalities, nutritional status, and disease severity, based on their joint contributions to model predictions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study indicates that machine learning models, particularly LR, may be useful for PHD risk screening and stratification among patients with pneumoconiosis. SHAP analysis identified clinically accessible variables that were important for model predictions, indicating a multidimensional pattern of associations across hematological, nutritional, and disease-severity domains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/tldr-04-2026-0031.title: Defining, measuring, and honoring assent: evidence from a community-based ABA clinic
doi:10.1108/tldr-04-2026-0031.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this practice-based research was to evaluate a systematic approach to measuring assent and responding to assent withdrawal in the context of applied behavior analytic services for autistic children. A second purpose of this research was to evaluate the effects of the assent measurement system and procedures on clinician behaviors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research was practice-based and was conducted in collaboration between a university and a local organization that provides services to children with autism. This research used a single-case research design, specifically a multiple-baseline design across three child participants and their service teams.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The authors’ findings serve as a proof-of-concept for the application of assent procedures within a clinical setting. They demonstrated that assent and withdrawal can be defined and measured, and withdrawal was consistently honored while having virtually no negative impacts on overall productivity or service delivery. The authors found that behavior technicians were able to consistently and reliably take data on assent and withdrawal behaviors, and these data indicated that assent was generally sustained at high levels for all participants. They also found that the participants emitted both withdrawal-disruptive and withdrawal-self-advocacy, although self-advocacy did not consistently displace disruptive forms of withdrawal.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Limitations included a data collection system that likely overestimated withdrawal and may have obscured meaningful patterns, and that the intervention did not produce a full shift from withdrawal -disruptive to -self-advocacy for all participants. Due to the small sample size and conducting the study at one clinic site, more research is needed to assess the generality of our findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study serves as a proof-of-concept demonstration of how to practically embed assent procedures into existing clinical practice to better support the ethical obligation to respect persons within the context of service delivery for children with autism. Further, this research contributes to more inclusive service delivery strategies for children with autism by building an initial evidence base for assent procedures within the context of clinical service delivery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite a growing conceptual literature base that recommends including assent procedures in service delivery, empirical demonstrations of assent practices within clinical service delivery remain absent. Our study provides one of the first data-based demonstrations of assent procedures embedded within applied behavior analysis-based service delivery grounded in the recommendations of prior conceptual work.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1088/2632-2153/aea5d6.title: QuantumCanvas: a multimodal benchmark for learning two-body quantum interactions
doi:10.1088/2632-2153/aea5d6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Most molecular and materials machine-learning models fit correlations across whole molecules or crystals rather than learning the quantum interactions between atomic pairs. Yet bonding, charge redistribution, orbital hybridization, and electronic coupling all emerge from these two-body interactions. We introduce
                    <jats:italic>QuantumCanvas</jats:italic>
                    , a multimodal benchmark that treats the two-body quantum system as the minimal, exhaustively enumerable unit of interatomic interaction. It covers 2850 element–element pairs, each at a single optimized geometry, and evaluates 17 benchmark target quantities spanning electronic, thermodynamic, dipole, and charge-derived each unique properties. Each pair is also represented by ten-channel images of orbital populations and charge- and dipole-derived fields that encode angular and electrostatic structure without explicit atomic coordinates. Benchmarking graph, vision, and fusion architectures on element-pair-disjoint splits reveals modality-specific inductive biases: graph encoders achieve the lowest MAE on most reported targets, while late fusion gives the lowest MAE for the reported Mermin free-energy label. Controls on the energy gap and dipole magnitude show that destroying the spatial layout of the images does not degrade accuracy and that a model fed the generating scalars directly outperforms both image variants: the rendering is an alternative encoding of the same scalars, not an independent signal. Pretraining on
                    <jats:italic>QuantumCanvas</jats:italic>
                    lowers mean test error in 11 of 16 encoder-target comparisons across
                    <jats:italic>QM9</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>MD17</jats:italic>
                    , and
                    <jats:italic>CrysMTM</jats:italic>
                    .
                    <jats:italic>QuantumCanvas</jats:italic>
                    thus provides a controlled, physically grounded testbed for studying which signals each modality captures, how they combine, and how they transfer across molecular, dynamical, and crystalline regimes.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag321.title: Deep learning without weight symmetry
doi:10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag321.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Backpropagation, a foundational algorithm for training artificial neural networks, predominates in contemporary deep learning. Although highly successful, it is widely considered biologically implausible, because it relies on precise symmetry between feedforward and feedback weights to accurately propagate gradient signals that assign credit. The so-called weight transport problem concerns how biological brains learn to align feedforward and feedback paths while avoiding the non-biological transport of feedforward weights into feedback weights. To address this, several credit assignment algorithms, such as feedback alignment and the Kolen-Pollack rule, have been proposed. While they can achieve the desired weight alignment, these algorithms imply that if a neuron sends a feedforward synapse to another neuron, it should also receive an identical or at least partially correlated feedback synapse from the latter neuron, thereby forming a bidirectional symmetric connection. However, experimental studies of cortical connectivity do not support the widespread prevalence of such symmetric connections, and in fact report many unidirectional connections, thus imposing a new biological constraint on credit assignment. We refer to the failure of existing algorithms to satisfy this constraint as the weight symmetry problem. To address this challenge of biological constraints on connectivity, we introduce the Product Feedback Alignment (PFA) algorithm. We demonstrate that PFA can eliminate explicit weight symmetry entirely while closely approximating backpropagation and achieving comparable performance in deep convolutional networks. Our results offer a novel approach to solve the longstanding problem of credit assignment in the brain, leading to more biologically plausible learning in deep networks compared to previous methods.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-9871169/v1.title: Explainable Dual-view Workflow Discovery for GenAI-supported Learning in Higher Education
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-9871169/v1.abstract: Generative AI tools are increasingly embedded into higher education, yet empirical evidence remains limited on how students organize AI interaction with reading, writing, annotation, and feedback uptake. This study introduces Explainable Dual-view Workflow Discovery, a learning analytics framework for identifying and interpreting student workflows in a GenAI-supported information problem-solving course. Using FLoRA Open Data IPS records from 278 students with complete log and outcome data, the framework constructed a sequence path view and a student profile view, then integrated both through Dual-view Workflow Consensus Embedding, DWCE. Model comparisons showed that latent sequence workflow clustering produced the clearest path taxonomy, with cosine silhouette of .552, while PCA-based student profiling produced interpretable mechanism profiles, with cosine silhouette of .348. The DWCE consensus solution yielded two balanced workflow clusters, with n = 145 and n = 133 and cosine silhouette of .517: a reading-chat exploratory workflow and an AI-integrated writing absorption workflow. Explainable analyses showed that essay action rate, write token rate, trace events, chat token rate, navigation rate, annotation rate, sequence length, and revision rate were the most outcome-relevant workflow features. Findings indicate that effective GenAI interaction is not explained by chat frequency alone. Educational value emerges when AI feedback is absorbed into writing growth, revision, and cross-resource regulation.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1934358.title: Applying the Rasch partial credit model to evaluate the school as a learning organization framework in special education contexts
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1934358.abstract: <jats:p>The School as a Learning Organization (SLO) framework supports continuous improvement and collaborative learning within educational institutions. However, psychometric evidence for SLO instruments in special education contexts remains limited. This study evaluated the psychometric properties of the OECD School as a Learning Organization instrument among 121 teachers from special schools in South Jakarta Region I, Indonesia, using the Rasch Partial Credit Model (PCM). The 76-item instrument represented seven SLO dimensions. Rasch analysis examined item fit, rating scale functioning, reliability, separation, dimensionality, Differential Item Functioning (DIF), and person-item targeting. The PCM was used as the primary analytical framework because it accommodates item-specific threshold structures for ordered polytomous response categories. Person and item real reliability were both .95, with real separation indices of 4.30 and 4.59, respectively. The primary dimension explained 49.9% of the variance, and nine items fell outside the adopted MNSQ criteria. The four-point scale generally demonstrated ordered functioning, although the lowest category was rarely endorsed. Following Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction, no statistically significant systematic gender DIF remained across the 76 items. Person-item targeting indicated that many items were relatively difficult for respondents, with limited coverage around the 0.0 to +2.0 logit region. These findings provide preliminary psychometric evidence for the expanded SLO instrument and support its potential use as a diagnostic measure in special education settings.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1916078.title: Bioecological correlates of learning outcomes: testing the moderating role of obesity in academic performance
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1916078.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the moderating role of obesity in adolescent academic performance using the Bioecological Model of Human Development as the theoretical framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data from 2,127 adolescent students in the PISA 2022 dataset were analyzed using multi-group path analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sixteen of the seventeen associations examined were of comparable magnitude in the two groups, and the joint test of all seventeen provided no evidence of moderation. Contrary to expectations, body image was negatively associated with achievement in both groups, meaning that adolescents more satisfied with their bodies performed less well. The association was more than twice as strong among obese adolescents, the only between-group difference observed, and it did not persist after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Psychosomatic symptoms also showed a positive relationship with achievement, contrary to what the literature reports, reaching significance among obese adolescents alone, while perceived school safety reached significance only among their non-obese peers; in neither case did the groups differ. Curiosity, emotional control, and perseverance were positively related to achievement in both groups, and social connections, cooperation, and school risk were negatively related.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings locate the difference associated with obesity in adolescents' body-related self-perception rather than in the relational or institutional resources available to them. Educational strategies that address weight-inclusive environments and bias training may therefore complement traditional health-focused interventions in supporting these students.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1931835.title: Associations between AI literacy and learning engagement in smart classrooms: the chain mediating roles of self-efficacy and learning satisfaction
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1931835.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>With the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education, smart classrooms have become an important component of higher education's digital transformation. College students' learning engagement is an important indicator for understanding learning experiences in smart classroom environments. However, as a key capability for adapting to AI-supported learning, the psychological pathways through which AI literacy is associated with learning engagement remain insufficiently understood. This study constructed a chain mediation model to examine the association between AI literacy and college students' learning engagement in smart classrooms, with self-efficacy and learning satisfaction as potential mediators.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study employed an exploratory cross-sectional design. A total of 2,751 valid questionnaires were collected from 75 colleges and universities in China using a convenience sampling method. Data were collected using the AI Literacy Scale, Learning Engagement Scale, Self-Efficacy Scale, and Learning Satisfaction Scale. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), correlation analysis, and a preliminary single-factor assessment of potential common method bias were conducted using SPSS 26 and AMOS 26. Percentile bootstrap analysis using 5,000 resamples in the PROCESS macro was conducted to test the chain mediating roles of self-efficacy and learning satisfaction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      (1) AI literacy was significantly and positively associated with learning engagement in smart classrooms (total effect,
                      <jats:italic>B</jats:italic>
                      = 0.899,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.001; direct effect after including the mediators,
                      <jats:italic>B</jats:italic>
                      = 0.304,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.001); (2) self-efficacy mediated the association between AI literacy and learning engagement [indirect effect = 0.084, 95% CI = (0.060, 0.108)]; (3) learning satisfaction mediated the association between AI literacy and learning engagement [indirect effect = 0.427, 95% CI = (0.380, 0.476)]; and (4) the serial indirect path through self-efficacy and learning satisfaction was significant [indirect effect = 0.085, 95% CI = (0.064, 0.108)]. The total indirect effect was B = 0.595 [95% CI = (0.544, 0.644)] and accounted for 66.185% of the total effect.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI literacy was directly associated with learning engagement and was also indirectly associated with learning engagement through self-efficacy and learning satisfaction. These findings provide preliminary cross-sectional evidence for understanding the cognitive–affective pathways linking AI literacy and learning engagement in smart classroom contexts. Rather than establishing causal effects, the study offers preliminary evidence that students' self-efficacy and learning satisfaction may be important psychological factors in AI-supported learning environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1177/10692509261477152.title: Rapid seismic vulnerability assessment using closed-form damage index equations obtained via explainable machine learning
doi:10.1177/10692509261477152.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In the early stages of seismic vulnerability assessment for a large number of structures, Seismic Damage Indices (SDIs) are computed to quantify the overall damage state. The Maximum Interstory Drift Ratio (MIDR) is widely employed, yet it is conventionally evaluated through computationally intensive nonlinear time history analyses (NTHAs). Machine Learning (ML) algorithms have been previously employed for this task, but their lack of interpretability limits their adoption into practice. This research effort aims to bridge this gap, by developing analytical equations to estimate MIDR, which approximate the behavior of a fully trained ML model. This task was carried out by employing the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) methodology, which is commonly utilized as a valid explainability tool. A
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Light Gradient Boosting Machine</jats:italic>
                    model was initially trained, which achieved very high accuracy. Subsequently, analytical terms were fitted to the SHAP values of each feature. The final equations, obtained via the so-called “SHAP additive property”, reached comparable high performance levels, with the underlying ML model. Furthermore, they correctly classified the damage state, especially for the “Heavy” and “Slight” damage classes. The overall results are promising, and they indicate the potential applicability of the proposed methodology in real life cases.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1088/2632-2153/aea2ef.title: Adaptive filtering on KPFM data: a deep neural network approach
doi:10.1088/2632-2153/aea2ef.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) measurements often exhibit widely varying signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) because of non-ideal acquisition conditions, especially in time-sensitive experiments. Although conventional filters can suppress noise, inappropriate parameter settings may distort quantitative surface-potential information, and manual tuning reduces reproducibility. In this study, we propose a self-supervised deep learning framework for automatic optimization of filter parameters for KPFM data. The framework combines a multi-layer perceptron that predicts global filter parameters from 22 image-level features and structural complexity information with a convolutional neural network that generates pixel-wise local parameter adjustments. The model was trained on 13 218 real-world KPFM images without requiring clean reference data and adaptively adjusted filtering strength according to the noise level of each image. Under high-noise conditions, it achieved effective noise reduction while preserving structural features, yielding an edge preservation index of 0.984. Under low-noise conditions, it minimized unnecessary alteration of the original data, with a peak SNR of 39.4 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.940. The framework was implemented for five classical filters, namely Wiener, Gaussian, mean, bilateral, and total variation filters, and provides an objective and reproducible alternative to expert-dependent manual parameter tuning for quantitative KPFM analysis.</jats:p>

doi:10.5256/f1000research.199249.r517905.title: Peer Review Report For: Calcyon: An AI-Based Chatbot Framework for Calculus Learning to Support Computational Thinking Skill and Self-Regulated Learning [version 1; peer review: 1 approved, 1 approved with reservations]
doi:10.5256/f1000research.199249.r517905.abstract: * Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into mathematics education has advanced rapidly, yet limited attention has been given to systematic AI based chatbot frameworks that integrate computational thinking (CT) and self regulated learning (SRL) scaffolding within university calculus. This study developed and validated Calcyon, an AI based chatbot framework designed to support differential calculus learning through coordinated CT and SRL scaffolding. Methods A Research and Development approach guided by the ADDIE model was employed. Expert validation (n = 3) was conducted across five quality dimensions using Aiken's V formula. A student pilot readability and feasibility test (n = 11) assessed practical usability across six dimensions. A design and development research approach guided by the ADDIE model was employed. Three experts evaluated the framework across five quality dimensions using a four point rating scale, with content validity assessed using Aiken's V. A formative pilot involving 11 undergraduate calculus students evaluated readability and feasibility across six dimensions. Results Expert validation indicated that Calcyon demonstrated strong validity across the evaluated content, instructional, technical, linguistic, and media design dimensions. Most validation items met the predefined validity criterion, while a small number were refined based on expert feedback. The student pilot further indicated good readability and feasibility, with responses showing consistently positive evaluations of the prototype. Conclusions Calcyon provides an empirically validated instructional design framework that combines AI mediated interaction with explicit CT and SRL scaffolding for university calculus. The findings support the framework's expert rated validity and preliminary readability and feasibility. Further experimental research is required to determine its effectiveness in improving CT, SRL, and calculus learning outcomes.

doi:10.4208/jml.260309.title: Error Bounds for Physics Informed Neural Networks in Generalized KdV Equations Placed on Unbounded Domains
doi:10.4208/jml.260309.abstract: <jats:p>In this paper we study a rigorous setting for the numerical approximation via deep neural networks of the generalized Korteweg-de Vries (gKdV) model in one dimension, for subcritical and critical nonlinearities, and assuming that the domain is the unbounded real line. The fact that the model is posed on the real line makes the problem difficult from the point of view of learning techniques, since the setting required to model gKdV is structured on intricate oscillatory estimates dating from Kato, Bourgain and Kenig, Ponce and Vega, among others. Therefore, a first task is to adapt the setting of these techniques to the deep learning setting. We shall use a battery of Kenig–Ponce–Vega suitable norms and Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to describe this approximative scheme, proving rigorous bounds on the approximation for each critical and subcritical gKdV model. We shall use these results to provide clear approximation results in the case of several gKdV nonlinear patterns such as solitons, multi-solitons, breathers, among other solutions.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fphys.2026.1855555.title: Explainable deep learning-based classification of Wolff-Parkinson-White electrocardiographic signals
doi:10.3389/fphys.2026.1855555.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is a cardiac electrophysiology (EP) disorder caused by the presence of an accessory pathway (AP) that bypasses the atrioventricular node, faster ventricular activation rate, and provides a substrate for atrio-ventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT). Accurate localization of the AP is critical for planning and guiding catheter ablation procedures. While traditional diagnostic tree (DT) methods and more recent machine learning (ML) approaches have been proposed to predict AP location from surface electrocardiogram (ECG), they are often constrained by limited anatomical localization resolution, poor interpretability, and the use of small clinical datasets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this preliminary patient-specific study, we present a Deep Learning (DL) model for the localization of single manifest APs across 24 cardiac regions, trained on a large, physiologically realistic database of synthetic ECGs generated using a personalized virtual heart model. We also integrate eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods, Guided Backpropagation, Grad-CAM, and Guided Grad-CAM, into the pipeline. This enables interpretation of DL decision-making and addresses one of the main barriers to clinical adoption: lack of transparency in ML predictions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On the considered single heart geometry, our model achieves a localization accuracy above 94% and an average F1 score over 93%. XAI outputs are physiologically validated against known depolarization patterns, and a novel index is introduced to identify the most informative ECG leads for AP localization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results highlight lead V2 as the most critical, followed by aVR, and aVL in the left ventricle (LV) and V1 in the right ventricle (RV). This work demonstrates the potential of combining cardiac digital twins with explainable DL to enable accurate, transparent, and noninvasive AP localization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fsufs.2026.1952456.title: Identifying drought-responsive candidate genes in root and shoot tissues of wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) through RNA sequencing, cluster analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and machine learning models
doi:10.3389/fsufs.2026.1952456.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Drought stress severely affects the growth, development, and yield formation of wheat. However, the differentiated regulatory mechanisms of wheat roots and shoots during drought adaptation remain to be further analyzed. Therefore, this study used RNA-seq datasets of roots and shoots from multiple wheat varieties, combined with differential expression analysis, Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis, clustering analysis, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and machine learning were used to characterize drought-responsive transcriptional changes. Differential expression analysis identified 90 and 3,991 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in roots under DS1 and DS2 respectively, compared with 34 and 1,940 DEGs in shoots. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that root DEGs were mainly involved in root growth, cell wall remodeling, water transport, and osmotic adjustment processes, whereas shoot DEGs are mainly enriched in processes related to stomatal regulation, photosynthesis, lipid metabolism, and oxidative stress responses. WGCNA identified 18 and 19 co-expression modules in roots and shoots, respectively, among which the yellow module was significantly correlated with the response to drought stress in root and shoot tissues. To further screen drought-responsive candidate genes from these modules, we compared multiple machine learning models. The XGBoost model achieved the highest and AUC in both roots and shoots. Combined with SHAP feature contribution analysis, 30 drought-responsive candidate genes with high discriminatory power were identified separately in roots and shoots. Analysis of
                    <jats:italic>cis</jats:italic>
                    -acting elements in candidate gene promoters revealed abundant drought- and stress-responsive elements, including MYB, G-box, ABRE, MYC, MBS, and LTR. MYB (183 in roots and 164 in shoots), G-box (168 and 98), and ABRE (148 and 86) were particularly abundant, and several candidate genes contained more than five ABRE copies in their promoters, suggesting potential involvement in ABA-mediated drought responses. This study reveals the different transcriptional response processes of wheat roots and shoots under drought stress, and identifies key co-expression modules and core candidate genes through WGCNA combined with XGBoost and SHAP analysis. These findings provide a basis for understanding organ-specific molecular responses to drought stress and offer potential targets for improving drought tolerance in wheat.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10766033/v1.title: Bayesian Concept Consolidation for Concept-Level Stability in Continual Learning
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10766033/v1.abstract: Continual learning methods commonly mitigate catastrophic forgetting by constraining parameter change (e.g., Elastic Weight Consolidation) or by rehearsing stored samples (replay). Neither approach directly measures or protects the semantic content encoded in a model's internal representations, leaving open the question of whether accuracy retention implies that a class's learned \emph{concept} remains stable. We propose Bayesian Concept Consolidation (BCC), a continual learning framework that introduces a concept-stability loss operating on a Bayesian concept bottleneck layer, together with a posterior-variance-derived adaptive weighting term and an uncertainty-prioritized replay buffer. To evaluate concept-level drift independently of task accuracy, we introduce the Knowledge Stability Index (KSI), defined as the cosine similarity between a class's concept representation at first acquisition and at a later evaluation point. On Split-MNIST (5 tasks, 2 classes each), a controlled ablation over 3 random seeds shows that concept-stability regularization improves KSI from $0.467\pm0.069$ (no concept loss) to $0.997\pm0.0004$ (full method) at statistically indistinguishable task accuracy ($94.3\%$--$94.7\%$ across conditions). Under the evaluated protocol, a diagonal-Fisher Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) baseline without replay collapses to near-chance accuracy ($19.6\%\pm0.1\%$), an outcome we trace to an early task-boundary gradient shock that outpaces Fisher-penalty accumulation; adding replay to EWC restores accuracy ($93.2\%\pm0.7\%$) but not concept stability (KSI $0.476\pm0.050$, statistically indistinguishable from replay alone), isolating concept-stability regularization -- rather than replay -- as the mechanism responsible for concept preservation. These results indicate that accuracy retention and semantic concept stability are dissociable quantities under the studied conditions, and that existing regularization and replay mechanisms address the former without necessarily addressing the latter.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10766033/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-9662686/v1.title: Nowcasting Italian Municipal Income with Nightlights: A Deep Learning Approach
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-9662686/v1.abstract: This paper assesses whether NASA Black Marble nightlight intensity can serve as an early indicator of annual taxable income at the Italian municipal level, where official data are released with a 12--18 month lag. Using a panel of 7{,}631 municipalities over 2012--2021, we compare four recurrent neural network architectures (LSTM, BiLSTM, GRU, Transformer) against six benchmarks: simple persistence, panel fixed effects, autoregressive distributed lag, and two spatial econometric specifications (SAR, Spatial Durbin) on a queen-contiguity matrix. Models are trained on 2012--2019 and evaluated out-of-sample on 2020--2021 with a cross-sectional Diebold--Mariano test. A single-layer GRU achieves a median forecast error of 1.07 million euros across the cross-section of municipalities --- approximately \((4%)\) of the median municipal IRPEF income of 29 million euros --- statistically dominating every benchmark (DM \((>4)\) against persistence, \((>40)\) against spatial linear models, all \((p<0.001)\)). Spatial models recover statistically significant spatial autocorrelation (\((\rho \approx 0.71)\)) and a meaningful nightlight spillover (\((\theta \approx 0.05)\)), but their forecasting gap with the GRU is virtually identical to that of spatially-naive linear specifications. We conclude that nightlights contain genuine predictive content for municipal income, but extracting it requires a model class flexible enough to capture cross-sectional heterogeneity and non-linearities that linear specifications, spatial or otherwise, cannot recover. JEL Classification: C45 , C53 , R12

doi:10.1002/for.70217.title: FPGA‐Based GRU Accelerator for Streaming Data Processing
doi:10.1002/for.70217.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In the evolving landscape of edge devices, unlocking artificial intelligence (AI) services via the cloud has consistently raised concerns related to energy consumption, latency, and privacy. Shifting these services locally onto edge devices powered by CPUs and GPUs have always been hindered by their limited storage and computational power. This intensifies the demand for custom‐designed AI accelerators. In this work, we propose an FPGA‐based AI accelerator capable of efficiently processing time‐series information. The proposed accelerator is built around a core algorithm modeled by a new variant of the standard gated‐recurrent unit (GRU), namely random gated‐recurrent unit (RGRU), thereby offering low latency, minimized resource utilization, and high performance compared to existing GRU accelerators. These improvements are achieved through parameter quantization, reduced computational overhead, and data localization, along with a 49 reduction in memory footprint compared to the standard GRU. The proposed design is evaluated on forecasting tasks using several standard benchmarks, including Yahoo Finance, Electricity Load, and Mackey–Glass, and demonstrates performance comparable to the standard GRU while requiring significantly fewer hardware resources.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-72881-5.title: Classification of real plastic waste using machine learning-assisted laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-72881-5.abstract: Plastic type classification using laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) was evaluated using actual waste samples under non-optimized experimental conditions designed to approximate laser-sample variability encountered in industrial operation. The study addresses challenges in plastic sorting crucial for enhancing recycling efficiency and mitigating $$\:{co}_{2}$$ emissions and environmental harm from plastic waste overflow. Held-out testing using physically separate real-waste specimens was performed using data from standard materials for modeling and data from real waste for the test. The target plastic types were polypropylene, polyethylene terephthalate, high-density polyethylene, and low-density polyethylene, which are major types of plastic waste. Plastic sorting was assisted by two machine-learning techniques: principal component analysis and k-nearest neighbors. Twenty-three pre-processes and seven variable selection methods were examined to enhance accuracy. The synergistic impact of preprocessing and variable selection was evident, elevating accuracy from 0.617 to 1.00. This study demonstrates the potential of machine learning-assisted LIBS for real plastic waste classification, emphasizing the importance of relevant wavelength selection.

doi:10.1007/s11165-026-10368-z.title: An Accelerated Longitudinal Design Study Examining Emotional Engagement toward Learning Science from Grades 3 through 12
doi:10.1007/s11165-026-10368-z.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As educators, we often see the enthusiasm for learning science in schools starting out strong in primary years and then fading as student progress into middle and secondary school. The motivation of this study is to offer a picture of how students’ emotional engagement in learning school science changes from Grades 3 to 12. This study applies an accelerated longitudinal design which collected data from 11 back-to-back cohorts of students from four US school districts. Each cohort was surveyed two times each school year, fall and spring, over two years in four waves of data collection. The sample includes more than 7000 participants. While a longitudinal study spanning this period of time would take nearly a decade to complete and pose significant data collection and data integrity challenges, the accelerated longitudinal design provides a simulation of longitudinal data in a two-year time span. The results show an unambiguous decline in emotional engagement which appears to begin in Grade 3 continuing to Grade 9 before flattening to ambivalent levels in Grade 10. These findings show that the decline happens both across and within each grade level. These results suggest that the decline is not just an artifact of science becoming more challenging in upper grade levels, but rather school science experiences may be having a negative impact within each school year.</jats:p>

doi:10.1088/3049-4761/aea29b.title: Hidden electrode subgroups revealed by independent analysis of charge and discharge formulas using Shapley behavioural spaces
doi:10.1088/3049-4761/aea29b.abstract: Battery electrode materials exist in distinct charged and discharged states described by different chemical formulas, yet most machine learning studies use a single formula as the compositional descriptor for a material. We apply Shapley behavioural spaces to the Mendeleev-encoded charge and discharge formulas of two battery data sets independently: a computational set of density functional theory-computed instances and an experimental set derived from the literature-compiled database. \revision{We use the kurtosis behavioural space, which decomposes the tail-weight of the elemental composition distribution via Shapley values, and subgroup identification that uses only chemical formula information; physicochemical properties are computed post-hoc to characterise the discovered classes. Every class we identify is carried by a single element, displaced either because that element is rare across the database or because a commoner element occurs at an unusual stoichiometric count, and several pairs of classes are separated by that count alone. In the computational data, the charge formula space resolves a praseodymium host family that is absent from the discharge space and is almost exclusively a divalent-ion host, while the discharge formula space resolves two rubidium host families, separated by whether the discharged phase carries one rubidium or two to three, and a germanium class whose discharged phases lie on or close to the computed convex hull. In the experimental data, a lithium titanate family and antimony iron phosphorus alloy anodes are visible only in charge space, while two niobium oxide classes, the Wadsley-Roth phases and lower-niobium materials, are visible only in discharge space. These findings demonstrate that the charge and discharge formulas encode different and complementary electrochemical information: treating them as interchangeable representations systematically conceals material classes whose identity is carried by one electrode state and not the other.

doi:10.1007/s00062-026-01726-5.title: Deep Learning-Based Image Reconstruction in Ultra-High-Resolution CT Venography for Improved Visualization of Cerebral Venous Drainage
doi:10.1007/s00062-026-01726-5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the diagnostic confidence and image quality of deep-learning-enhanced ultra-high-resolution CT venography (CTV) in venous neurovascular imaging, compared with hybrid iterative reconstruction of ultra-high-resolution CT datasets and normal-resolution CTV.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective, single-center study included 31 consecutive patients with suspected cerebral venous and dural sinus thrombosis who underwent CTV. CTV datasets were reconstructed using hybrid iterative reconstruction with (i) Normal-Resolution CTV (NR-CTV), (ii) an Ultra-High-Resolution CTV (UHR-CTV), and (iii) a deep learning algorithm specifically trained for neurovascular imaging, applied to the UHR-CTV datasets (DL-UHR-CTV). Quantitative analyses included signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and frequency power spectra (FPS). Qualitative evaluation of image quality, contrast, noise, artifacts, diagnostic confidence, and assessability of dural sinuses and intracranial veins was performed by three radiologists using a 4-point Likert scale. A descriptive analysis assessed concordant detection of venous pathologies across reconstructions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      SNR and CNR in DL-UHR-CTV were significantly higher than in UHR-CTV (SNR:
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.02; CNR:
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.01). NR-CTV and DL-UHR-CTV were similar. Compared to NR-CTV and UHR-CTV, DL-UHR-CTV showed a significantly lower FPS amplitude across wide frequency ranges. In qualitative analysis, DL-UHR-CTV outperformed UHR-CTV in all parameters (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001) except vessel contrast (

                    </jats:p>
