doi:10.61251/cej.v4i3.476.title: Peningkatan keaktifan belajar IPAS dengan model Discovery Learning berbantuan media puzzle di sekolah dasar
doi:10.61251/cej.v4i3.476.abstract:
<jats:p>Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan keaktifan belajar IPAS materi Sejarah Masyarakat di Lingkungan Tempat Tinggal melalui penerapan model Discovery Learning berbantuan media puzzle pada murid kelas III C SD Negeri Percobaan 4 Wates Tahun Ajaran 2025/2026. Penelitian ini merupakan Penelitian Tindakan Kelas (PTK) yang dilaksanakan dalam dua siklus dengan menggunakan model Kemmis dan McTaggart yang meliputi tahap perencanaan, pelaksanaan tindakan, observasi, dan refleksi. Subjek penelitian adalah murid kelas III C SD Negeri Percobaan 4 Wates. Teknik pengumpulan data yang digunakan meliputi observasi, wawancara, dan dokumentasi. Data keaktifan belajar dianalisis secara deskriptif kuantitatif berdasarkan hasil observasi selama proses pembelajaran. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa penerapan model Discovery Learning berbantuan media puzzle dapat meningkatkan keaktifan belajar IPAS murid. Rata-rata keaktifan belajar pada siklus I sebesar 63,45% dan meningkat menjadi 88,82% pada siklus II. Peningkatan tersebut menunjukkan bahwa penggunaan model Discovery Learning berbantuan media puzzle mampu menciptakan pembelajaran yang lebih aktif, menarik, dan melibatkan murid secara langsung dalam proses menemukan pengetahuan. Penelitian ini memberikan kontribusi terhadap pembelajaran IPAS di sekolah dasar melalui penerapan model pembelajaran dan media yang dapat mendorong keterlibatan aktif murid dalam memahami materi Sejarah Masyarakat Di Lingkungan Tempat Tinggal.
This study aimed to improve students' learning activity in IPAS on the topic of the History of Communities in Their Local Environment through the implementation of the Discovery Learning model assisted by puzzle media among third-grade students at SD Negeri Percobaan 4 Wates in the 2025/2026 academic year. This study employed Classroom Action Research conducted in two cycles using the Kemmis and McTaggart model, consisting of planning, action, observation, and reflection stages. The subjects of this study were third-grade students of class III C at SD Negeri Percobaan 4 Wates. Data were collected through observation, interviews, and documentation. Students' learning activity data were analyzed descriptively and quantitatively based on observations conducted during the learning process. The results showed that the implementation of the Discovery Learning model assisted by puzzle media improved students' learning activity in IPAS. The average learning activity increased from 63.45% in the first cycle to 88.82% in the second cycle. This improvement indicates that the use of Discovery Learning assisted by puzzle media can create a more active and engaging learning environment and encourage students to participate directly in the process of discovering knowledge. This study contributes to IPAS learning in elementary schools by providing an alternative learning model and learning media that encourage students' active involvement in understanding the history of communities in their local environment.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73268-2.title: Beyond transfer learning: a generative self-supervised framework for fMRI-based diagnosis on small and imbalanced datasets
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73268-2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Diagnosing neurological and psychiatric diseases (NeuroPsyD) from functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) using Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) is challenging, particularly when datasets are small and imbalanced, leading to severe overfitting, instability, and biased sensitivity–specificity trade-offs. Transfer Learning (TL), including supervised and self-supervised pre-training, can partially mitigate these challenges, but its effectiveness remains limited by domain shift, annotation bias, majority-class bias, and limited gains on very small datasets. To address these limitations, we propose a purely in-domain generative self-supervised framework that does not require external pre-training, called Boundary-aware Variational Autoencoder + Self-Supervised Mixup (BVAE+SSup-Mixup). The framework integrates SSup-Mixup for label-free representation learning, multivariate VAE-based minority-class oversampling, and boundary-aware synthetic sample selection, which retains informative generated samples near the decision boundary while reducing outliers and poorly positioned synthetic samples. The framework is evaluated on five fMRI-based NeuroPsyD diagnosis tasks covering extremely and moderately small, imbalanced datasets. Compared with supervised and self-supervised TL approaches and a state-of-the-art RHVAE-based generative baseline, BVAE+SSup-Mixup improved accuracy, F1-score, and AUC across most tasks, achieving accuracies of 87.7–95.0% and AUCs of 89.3–94.7%. It also produced a more balanced sensitivity–specificity profile, with both measures mostly above 85%. These balanced gains suggest that boundary-aware augmentation provides targeted minority-class evidence that TL may not fully exploit. These findings provide a proof of concept for a TL-competitive framework in severely data-limited and imbalanced medical imaging settings.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/dlo-07-2026-0413.title: Beyond technology: Institutional foundations for AI-driven personalised learning in higher education
doi:10.1108/dlo-07-2026-0413.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Successful AI-driven personalized learning depends as much on institutional conditions as it does on technology. Drawing on a sociotechnical systems perspective, this viewpoint explores the curriculum, governance and human capabilities needed for responsible and effective AI implementation in higher education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The article draws on findings from two complementary empirical studies on students’ motivation and staff perspectives, alongside broader research on personalized learning and intelligent tutoring, to examine AI-enabled personalized learning through a sociotechnical systems perspective.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI can build learner profiles and adapt content, pacing and feedback at scale, but its effectiveness depends on data quality and stops at the classroom door: socioeconomic status, family circumstances, and other off-platform pressures stay invisible to AI even though they are established drivers of attrition. Confidence, motivation and belonging stay central throughout, shaped by curriculum and educators as much as by any platform.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, the conclusions require validation across different institutional contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Universities should assess curriculum fit, strengthen governance, equitable access and AI literacy, and keep educators central when determining where and how AI-enabled personalization should be scaled.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This viewpoint reframes AI-enabled personalized learning as a discipline-sensitive institutional readiness problem, highlighting curriculum fit, AI literacy, algorithmic bias, equitable access, and the continuing importance of human care and judgment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
doi:10.1108/dlo-07-2026-0413.venue: Development and Learning in Organizations: An International Journal

doi:10.1108/lthe-03-2025-0017.title: Enhancing teacher self-efficacy to sustain inclusive education: restructuring teacher education
doi:10.1108/lthe-03-2025-0017.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research paper explores the relationship between teacher education and pre-service teacher (PT) and in-service teacher (IT) self-efficacy beliefs toward sustainable inclusive education. In line with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD)’s call for monitoring and evaluation, this study examines how current teacher training and education programs strengthen PT and IT self-efficacy beliefs to support inclusive practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research paper used a mixed-method approach to examine pre-service and in-service teachers' beliefs and self-efficacy regarding inclusive education. The study used the Beliefs about Learning and Teaching Questionnaire (BLTQ) and the Teacher Efficacy for Inclusive Practices (TEIP) scale to collect quantitative data from 56 graduate MA teachers, divided into pre-service and in-service categories and then conducted interviews with 14 participants.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study's findings revealed that PTs and ITs held more positive beliefs about flexible instruction, incremental views of ability and positive self-efficacy in instruction and collaboration. The findings suggested only small descriptive differences in instructional and self-efficacy beliefs between PTs and ITs and are therefore reported as exploratory patterns. Teacher interviews further emphasized the importance of mandating inclusion courses across all education specializations and running advanced specialized courses and workshops offered by inclusion specialists.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While this study investigated PTs’ and ITs’ self-efficacy beliefs toward inclusive education, the small sample size of graduate teachers limits the generalizability of the results. To address these limitations, future research studies with larger samples and balanced numbers of PTs and ITs could improve the reliability of group comparisons and strengthen generalizability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Primary priorities for policymakers and educators are to initiate critical reforms to teacher education and training programs, including (1) mandating introductory inclusion courses across all graduate education specializations, (2) conducting field trips to autism and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder centers and (3) providing access to specialized inclusion professionals, especially during the practicum.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlights the critical role of restructuring teacher education programs to strengthen pre-service and in-service teachers' self-efficacy in implementing inclusive education in the UAE and the broader GCC region. Improved teacher preparation can bridge the gap between ambitious national inclusive policies and classroom realities, fostering greater acceptance of diversity, stronger parent–school partnerships and long-term societal benefits. Ultimately, investing in teacher self-efficacy advances social justice and helps build tolerant, cohesive Gulf societies aligned with national visions for sustainable development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By integrating the United Nations Theoretical Framework of Inclusive Education (2016) with Bandura's self-efficacy theory (1977–1997), examining both PTs and ITs and using a mixed-methods approach that is not commonly used in this area, this research contributes to both global understanding and the local advancement of inclusive education in the UAE and the broader GCC region, calling for targeted reforms in teacher education structures and curriculum design to better align with national visions and the UN framework. It highlights the value of mastery and vicarious experiences in building positive beliefs while revealing persistent theory-practice gaps that resonate with broader calls to reform teacher education programs across the GCC and globally.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11169715/v1.title: Integrated Machine Learning and Structure-Based Computational Prioritization of KIF11 Inhibitor Candidates for CNS-Oriented Drug Discovery
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11169715/v1.abstract: Background Kinesin family member 11 (KIF11/Eg5) is an essential mitotic kinesin motor protein involved in bipolar spindle assembly and represents a target for antimitotic cancer drug discovery. Objective An integrated machine-learning and structure-based computational screening workflow was developed to prioritize potential KIF11 inhibitor candidates with predicted central nervous system (CNS) permeation potential. Methods A curated dataset of 831 unique wild-type KIF11 bioactivity records from ChEMBL was evaluated using ensemble QSAR models combining physicochemical descriptors and circular fingerprints (ECFP4). Model reliability was assessed using scaffold-aware cross-validation, nested outer-fold evaluation (R² = 0.5471), Y-randomization, applicability-domain analysis, and a locked external test set (n = 177). Top candidates were evaluated by molecular docking against human KIF11 (PDB ID: 2WOG), multi-parameter ADMET profiling, and supplementary solvent-relaxation analysis. Results Five structurally diverse candidates were prioritized. CHEMBL392148 showed the highest predicted potency (pIC₅₀ = 7.75), predicted interactions with Arg119 and Leu214, and a predicted blood–brain barrier permeability probability of 0.98. Structural-alert screening identified no PAINS, BRENK, or NIH alerts for CHEMBL392148; one BRENK alert was identified for CHEMBL383402. The short-timescale trajectory analysis is reported separately in the Supplementary Information. Conclusion The prioritized molecules provide rational computational starting points for subsequent biochemical inhibition and cell-based evaluation in CNS-oriented oncology models.

doi:10.1093/jas/skag272.319.title: 29. Introducing Data Science Concepts to Animal Science Graduate Students Through Application-based Learning.
doi:10.1093/jas/skag272.319.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and data science into biological research has created a growing need for computational literacy among graduate students in life science disciplines. However, many students’ entering biology-related graduate programs have limited formal training in programming, statistics, or machine learning, creating a significant barrier to engaging with modern data-driven research. The objective of this study was to evaluate baseline perceptions of AI and data science among animal science students prior to participating in a course introducing these concepts through application-based learning. A pre-course perception survey was administered to students enrolled in an introductory AI and data science course in animal science (n = 10). Survey questions used a 5-point Likert scale to assess prior programming experience, familiarity with AI concepts, attitudes toward AI applications in animal science and motivation to learn these skills. Students reported limited prior experience with programming languages (mean = 2.9 ± 1.45) and moderate use of AI tools in daily life (mean = 2.98 ± 1.32). Despite limited technical exposure, students indicated moderate understanding of basic AI and data science concepts (mean = 3.6 ± 0.70 and 3.6 ± 0.52, respectively). Participants expressed strong agreement that AI and data science can be effectively applied in animal science (mean = 3.9 ± 0.57) and that learning these skills would benefit their academic or professional development (mean = 4.0 ± 0.67). Students also expressed moderate motivation to learn AI applications in livestock systems (mean = 3.5 ± 1.08). While this project provides the current perceptions of students and their skill levels in AI and data science, a follow-up post survey to assess the effects of such a course, and combining it with a Mann-Whiteney U test will further inform the required pedagogical shifts. These preliminary findings highlight the value of interdisciplinary teaching approaches that integrate biological applications with computational methods (such as an AI in animal science course) and may inform curriculum design for graduate programs seeking to prepare life science students for increasingly data-intensive research environments.</jats:p>

doi:10.1201/9781042036325-25.title: Human Emotions in Machine-Mediated Work: A Review of Emotional Intelligence and Workplace Synergy
doi:10.1201/9781042036325-25.abstract: With the growing application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the organisational process of communication, coordination and decision-making, the present-day workplace is becoming increasingly focused on human feelings as individual interpretations, adaptations (and collaboration) with AI Systems shape performance outcomes and the quality of workplace interactions. Hence, this study investigates the role of emotional intelligence (EI) in facilitating effective synergy between humans and AI in the workplace. In this study, three key dimensions are identified where EI has an impact on machine-assisted work. The former, emotional coping is the step whereby employees use EI to control anxiety, uncertainty and resistance towards automation, algorithmic surveillance and job role changes. The second is the interpretive mediation which demonstrates how the emotionally intelligent workers put the AI generated results in context, refine and humanise the results which leads to more accurate interpretation and less communicative ambiguity. The third congruence, synergistic, demonstrates that AI supported communication practices can lead to building trust, enhance cooperative interaction and encouraging ethically sound and culturally responsive decision-making in AI enhanced teams. The results proved that EI is not only an individual skill, but also a relationship and organisational resource that determines the quality of AI interaction between people. Further, the study proposed to develop emotionally sustainable, resilient and collaborative human–AI ecosystems in the changing 21st century work environment.

doi:10.1007/s13313-026-01197-9.title: Diverse structural features and putative functional roles of early-stage Austropuccinia psidii effector proteins
doi:10.1007/s13313-026-01197-9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The fungus
                    <jats:italic>Austropuccinia psidii</jats:italic>
                    is an invasive pathogen of myrtaceous plants. During infection,
                    <jats:italic>A. psidii</jats:italic>
                    uses ‘effector’ proteins to manipulate various host plant cellular processes. Four effector proteins (AP1260, AP5292, AP10948, and AP143) have been identified as being important during the first 24 h of infection. However, there are no data on the molecular role these effectors play during infection. Here we report a bioinformatic analysis of these candidate effector proteins to generate experimental hypotheses. Successive genome improvements reveal that while AP5292 and AP143 remain conserved, AP1260 and especially AP10948 have expanded into highly divergent multi-haplotype families, with AP10948 now comprising 25 tandemly duplicated variants. Sequence homology searches show that all effectors exhibit low sequence homology across rust fungi and AP10948 appears to be unique to
                    <jats:italic>A. psidii</jats:italic>
                    . The effectors contain secretion signals, typical of effectors, and are predicted cytoplasmic effectors, functioning within the plant cell. Structural modelling predicts they contain regions of disorder, but all except AP10948 have folded regions. AP1260 shares weak structural similarity with
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                    -acetyl-
                    <jats:italic>D</jats:italic>
                    -glucosamine binding folds, and AP5292 with MAX/ToxB-like fungal effectors. AP10948 has no meaningful structural matches. AP143 has significant structural homology to kiwellins, papain inhibitors, expansins, and cellulose-binding domains, suggesting potential roles in cell-wall interaction or protease inhibition. Protein physicochemical properties of these effectors are reported, which are useful for future laboratory work. Insights from these bioinformatic analyses provide a basis for further biophysical research into their true roles and functions, clarifying how
                    <jats:italic>A. psidii</jats:italic>
                    can infect its wide host and geographical range.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fninf.2026.1930795.title: Window leakage in clinical EEG machine learning: matched subject-independent evaluation across ADHD and Parkinson cohorts
doi:10.3389/fninf.2026.1930795.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Windowed electroencephalography (EEG) pipelines can produce misleadingly high performance when segments from the same participant occur in both training and testing. We define this contamination as
                    <jats:italic>window leakage</jats:italic>
                    and test it in two clinically and technically distinct public cohorts: 121 children (61 attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [ADHD], 60 controls) and 149 adults (100 Parkinson's disease, 49 controls). Signals were harmonized to 18 common channels and 128 Hz. All primary models used stratified 8-fold participant-disjoint evaluation, 50%-overlapping windows, participant-level probability aggregation, and validation participants drawn exclusively from each outer-training fold. A deliberately contaminated Random Forest audit contrasted random-window and participant-disjoint splitting. Random-window balanced accuracy reached 95.59% in ADHD and 92.02% in Parkinson's, but fell to 60.98% and 56.17%, respectively, when participants were held out. Thus, the inflation replicated across disorders, ages, recording tasks, and acquisition systems. Under correct evaluation, CNN-LSTM achieved the highest ADHD subject-level balanced accuracy (73.21%), whereas EEGNet achieved the highest Parkinson's balanced accuracy (63.75%). No architecture comparison remained significant after Bonferroni correction. One-, 2-, 4-, and 8-s windows produced no consistent cross-cohort ranking. Removing ATCNN-SA components also yielded dataset-dependent changes, and no ablation difference was significant after correction. Participant-bootstrap intervals remained wide despite tens of thousands of windows, indicating that inferential precision was governed by participant count rather than segment count. Window-level random splits contaminate clinical EEG performance estimates and must not be used to claim generalization to unseen individuals. Participants should be separated before model fitting, results should be reported at subject level, and split, windowing, aggregation, and uncertainty procedures should be disclosed explicitly.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.68306/k3f6xq53.title: Enterprise Infrastructure Modernization beyond VMware: A Cost-Optimized Decision Framework for the Broadcom Era
doi:10.68306/k3f6xq53.abstract: <jats:p>Modernization in terms of enterprise infrastructure has become a more significant topic due to organizations review their virtualization schemes in changing VMware licensing and commercial status alongside the acquisition of Broadcom. This proposed research paper presents a cost-efficient decision model adopting the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) and Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) theories, to assess VMware continuation, alternative virtualization, and Private/HCI, Public Cloud, and Hybrid/CloudNative solutions. The framework takes into account the financial, technical, operational, and strategic criteria and is tested with representative enterprise cases, robustness and sensitivity analysis. Findings indicate that Public Cloud has the minimal fiveyear TCO, and least break even time, whereas Hybrid/Cloud-Native has the optimum score of 0.695 on the overall MCDA. Scenario analysis additionally illustrates that the best infrastructure decisions will depend on the enterprise characteristics and priorities. The sensitivity test suggests that rankings of the strategies are rather stable, with shifting migration-cost assumptions. The proposed framework offers enterprises with an organized and flexible tool of balancing the longterm cost-efficiency, technological viability, functional practicability, risk, and strategic adaptability.</jats:p>
doi:10.68306/k3f6xq53.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence and machine learning in Engineering

doi:10.15688/jvolsu2.2026.3.4.title: PROTOTYPE IN NEURAL MACHINE TRANSLATION OF PROMOTIONAL TEXTS: ALGORITHMIZATION OF THE SOURCE TEXT
doi:10.15688/jvolsu2.2026.3.4.abstract: <jats:p>The article examines the quality of neural machine translation of promotional texts in the context of digitalization and the active integration of artificial intelligence into multilingual communication. The authors state that source texts should be deliberately optimized for machine translation in order to enhance the quality of translations produced by large language models (LLMs). The empirical material comprises promotional content from the multilingual website of the Singapore-based company Linguise, which develops software solutions for connecting websites to neural machine translation systems, as well as the website of the German hospitality company Traumferienhäuser Schwarzwald – presented by Linguise as a successful case of multilingual logistics. The methodology combines contrastive and translatological analysis of source and target texts, aimed at identifying structural, grammatical, and lexical congruence, as well as typical transformations and translation techniques. The results prove that a high degree of predictability and adequacy in neural machine translation is achieved through the prototypization of the source text, including a modular text structure, a fixed sequence of functional blocks, syntactic simplicity, and terminological consistency. It affirms that texts oriented towards a universal international market and devoid of culturally marked and expressive vocabulary exhibit the greatest stability in automatic translation. Based on the analysis, an algorithm for creating an "ideal" promotional source text is proposed, contributing to improved quality of multilingual neural machine translation and a reduced need for post-editing.</jats:p>
doi:10.15688/jvolsu2.2026.3.4.venue: Vestnik Volgogradskogo gosudarstvennogo universiteta. Serija 2. Jazykoznanije

doi:10.67167/vertex.739.title: Inclusion or Isolation? Exploring the Learning Experiences of Students Exhibiting Neurodivergence In Mainstream Education”
doi:10.67167/vertex.739.abstract: <jats:p> This study explores the lived learning experiences of students exhibiting neurodivergence in mainstream education, focusing on whether inclusion fosters genuine belonging or results in isolation. Utilizing a qualitative phenomenological research design, the study was conducted at Don Jose Integrated High School with five purposively selected neurodivergent participants. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis to identify recurring patterns in their experiences reveal that neurodivergent students experience inclusion as complex, inconsistent, and highly dependent on instructional practices, peer relationships, and emotional factors. Participants reported challenges such as difficulty keeping up with fast-paced lessons, anxiety during participation, cognitive overload, and struggles with attention and task management. Despite these barriers, support from teachers and peers—such as clear explanations, visual aids, and collaborative learning—significantly enhanced their understanding and engagement. The study also highlights that students’ sense of belonging is conditional and fluctuates depending on their academic comprehension and social interactions. While inclusion is present in structure, it is not always fully realized in practice, often leading to feelings of partial inclusion or isolation. Neurodivergent students demonstrated adaptive coping strategies, including self-review, peer assistance, and repetition, to manage their challenges. Overall, the findings underscore the need for responsive, flexible, and inclusive teaching strategies that address diverse learning needs. The study recommends improving instructional clarity, pacing, and support systems to foster meaningful participation and a stronger sense of belonging among neurodivergent learners in mainstream classrooms. </jats:p>
doi:10.67167/vertex.739.venue: The International Review of Multidisciplinary Research

doi:10.33422/sshconference.v2i1.2003.title: Active Learning Strategies in Higher Education Evidence from the University of Vlora “Ismail Qemali”, Albania
doi:10.33422/sshconference.v2i1.2003.abstract: <jats:p>The transformation of pedagogical practice in higher education has become one of the most pressing imperatives of the twenty-first century, as universities worldwide are called upon to prepare graduates who are not only knowledgeable but also critical, adaptive, and collaborative. This paper examines the implementation and observed outcomes of active learning strategies within the context of Albanian higher education, drawing on empirical observations and reflective practice at the University of Vlora “Ismail Qemali”, an institution that has increasingly embraced pedagogical reform as part of its commitment to academic excellence and regional development. The study explores a range of student-centred methodologies, including problem-based learning, cooperative learning structures, and flipped classroom models, evaluating their effectiveness in enhancing student engagement, critical thinking, and learning outcomes at the undergraduate level. Grounded in constructivist learning theory and informed by current international research, the paper analyses how these approaches challenge the prevailing lecture-based tradition still dominant in many Albanian university classrooms. It further identifies key institutional enablers and barriers including faculty development, curriculum design, and assessment alignment that shape the success of pedagogical innovation in this specific socio-educational context. The findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting the value of active learning in diverse higher education settings and offer a contextually situated perspective from South-Eastern Europe. Practical recommendations are proposed for educators, department heads, and policy-makers seeking to advance student-centred teaching across Albanian universities.</jats:p>

doi:10.2118/232132-ms.title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Surface Equipment Requirements for Well Tie-In Operations
doi:10.2118/232132-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Well tie-in is a critical process for connecting new wells to the production system, maintaining flow assurance and system stability. The increasing complexity of reservoirs, surface facilities, and real-time operational constraints has made tie-in optimal planning more challenging. One primary step is to plan all surface equipment required for the tie-in, as missing any equipment will cascade into delays. This paper presents a novel machine learning (ML) engine that predicts all required surface equipment prior drilling. The paper discusses a pipeline of two ML models to predict the required tie-in surface equipment. The first model clusters existing wells into groups based on their geographical location and field characteristics using a technique called DBSCAN, which is a type of unsupervised learning that groups similar data points together. The second model is then trained using a classifier chain technique along with a classifier algorithm on these clustered wells to produce a multi-label prediction for the required equipment. To further improve the clustering accuracy, additional data dimensions were generated using Haversine distance technique and Cartesian map projection coordinates. The developed ML models were successfully integrated and used to predict the required surface equipment for well tie-in operations, including flowmeters, H2S detection systems, corrosion inhibition systems, and other essential components. Among all tested algorithms, Random Forest model delivered the highest performance, achieving an overall prediction accuracy of approximately 90%. The model consistently captured equipment patterns across diverse scenarios. Operational benefits were clearly observed. Automated early predictions helped avoid costly rework and unnecessary storage fees. Additionally, the automated prediction workflow reduced labor hours, minimizing manual analysis time and accelerating the tie-in preparation process. This paper presents a novel approach in expediting the well tie-in process by utilizing the pattern of clustering geospatial data in a model. The approach resulted in enhancing and expediting the well tie-in planning by predicting the appropriate surface equipment and reducing human input errors, which resulted in saving time and resources.</jats:p>

doi:10.55151/ijeedu.v8i3.517.title: Exploring Teachers’ Perceptions, Experiences and Needs for Augmented Reality-Based Mathematics Learning in Elementary Schools
doi:10.55151/ijeedu.v8i3.517.abstract: <jats:p>Augmented reality (AR) offers promising representational affordances for elementary mathematics, yet its classroom feasibility depends on teachers’ experience, technological conditions, and implementation support. This study examined teachers’ perceptions of AR, prior digital and AR experience, perceived barriers, mathematics-topic priorities, and requirements for prospective AR-based learning media. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted with 50 elementary-school teachers recruited purposively from 20 public and private schools. Data were collected using a validated questionnaire (S-CVI/Ave = 0.93; Cronbach’s Alpha = 0.79–0.84 for multi-item constructs) and analyzed using descriptive statistics and exploratory nonparametric tests with Holm adjustment. Teachers reported highly favorable perceptions across the four measured constructs (M = 4.59–4.75), although 62% had no prior AR experience and only 8% used AR often or very often. Three-dimensional geometry received the highest perceived need for AR visualization (M = 3.30, SD = 0.91). The most prominent barriers were limited technological devices and school infrastructure (both M = 4.00), while interactive content, ease of use, offline functionality, curriculum alignment, age-appropriate design, institutional support, and training emerged as key implementation requirements. Exploratory associations involving digital-technology use, prior AR experience, and perception scores did not remain statistically significant after Holm correction. These findings position AR adoption as a teacher-informed, needs-driven design problem and provide an empirical basis for prototype development, usability testing, and classroom feasibility evaluation rather than evidence of AR effectiveness or demonstrated implementation readiness.</jats:p>
doi:10.55151/ijeedu.v8i3.517.venue: International Journal of Environment, Engineering and Education

doi:10.53941/jmlis.2026.100020.title: Distributed Two-Stage Fixed-Time Optimization Algorithm for Formation Control of Multi-Agent System Based on Local Voting Event-Triggered Mechanism
doi:10.53941/jmlis.2026.100020.abstract: <jats:p>This article proposes a two-stage fixed-time distributed optimization algorithm based on a local voting event-triggered mechanism for continuous-time multiagent systems, which simultaneously guarantees fast convergence, high 3D formation precision, and communication efficiency. This algorithm consists of two stages: the gradient-driven stage ensures each agent quickly converges from the initial position to the local optimal solution, and the event-triggered consensus stage realizes coordinated formation and cuts down communication frequency. In this case, this algorithm avoids the insufficient convergence speed existing in single-stage counterparts. First, an exponential trajectory compensation term is introduced into the second stage, aiming to eliminate precision loss induced by spatial dimensional conversion in formation control. Second, a local voting-based event-triggered mechanism that adopts exponential decay thresholds and introduces neighbor state feedback is developed, under which an agent can only trigger communication when its local state error exceeds the threshold and at least one neighbor satisfies the same triggering condition. The designed cooperative triggering strategy eliminates isolated triggering and stale information utilization, which reduces controller updates and communication consumption. Furthermore, a timeout fallback module is embedded to avoid triggering deadlock caused by strict neighbor-consensus constraints, ensuring stable and reliable triggering performance. Third, theoretical analysis is demonstrated that the proposed algorithm achieves the fixed time convergence, while achieving optimal formation control for multi-agent systems. It is also strictly proven that the proposed event-triggered mechanism avoids Zeno behavior. Finally, numerical simulations verified the precise convergence of the proposed algorithm to the optimal value in 3D formation tasks.</jats:p>
doi:10.53941/jmlis.2026.100020.venue: Journal of Machine Learning and Information Security

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1963943.title: How teacher support, peer connection, and embodied meaning-making interact in drama-based social-emotional learning in higher education
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1963943.abstract: <jats:p>Drama-based social-emotional learning has gained increasing attention in higher education, yet participation in embodied activities does not in itself ensure sustained engagement or social-emotional development. Less is known about how teacher support, peer interaction, and embodied participation become interconnected in classroom practice, or about the conditions under which this process may be disrupted. This multisite interpretive qualitative study was conducted across four universities in eastern China. Data were generated through interviews with 24 students and eight teaching staff, supplemented by 24 reflective journals, 24 classroom observations, and 16 course documents. Reflexive thematic analysis produced three themes: participatory safety and bounded autonomy supported by teacher scaffolding; peer connection and group belonging developed through embodied collaboration; and emotional resonance and self-awareness emerging through embodied meaning-making. Safety, responsiveness, and a sense of meaning were associated with students’ willingness to participate, whereas unclear boundaries, limited peer responsiveness, and excessive emotional intensity were associated with reduced participation. The findings conceptualize drama-based social-emotional learning as interconnected classroom processes involving teacher scaffolding, peer connection, embodied participation, and reflective integration.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10987061/v1.title: Development of a Process-Based and Machine Learning Early Warning System for Malaria Transmission Dynamics under Multi-Scenario Climate Change: A Subnational Assessment of the North Bank Region of The Gambia
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10987061/v1.abstract: Background Malaria is a major health challenge in the West African Sahel, driven by variable hydroclimatic conditions. Traditional surveillance relies on retrospective clinical data, limiting proactive resource allocation. This study aims to: (1) quantify nonlinear biological and statistical lags through which meteorological factors influence malaria in the North Bank Region (NBR); (2) compare machine learning models with traditional biological models to identify the best early warning system; and (3) project malaria risk and economic impacts under climate change using the MPI-ESM1-2-HR and NCAR-CESM2 climate models across SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios to 2055. Methodology : Using an 11-year longitudinal database (2011–2021) comprising 132 consecutive months of clinical surveillance records from the National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP), this study integrated satellite-derived meteorological data (CHIRPS precipitation, MODIS land surface temperature, and relative humidity). I ran a process-based biological simulation with the Liverpool Malaria Model (LMM), mapped continuous relative risks with a Distributed Lag Non-linear Model (DLNM), and conducted an out-of-sample machine learning tournament (SVR, XGBoost, and Random Forest) within a strict 24-month pandemic-era validation window (2020–2021). Optimized models were projected across a cross-model matrix pairing MPI-ESM1-2-HR with NCAR-CESM2 climate surfaces under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios through 2055, and results were linked to a health-economic valuation matrix. Results The baseline Random Forest model demonstrated exceptional explanatory power, accounting for 95.56% of continuous transmission variability. Lagrangian feature mapping identified delayed, multi-month rainfall patterns as key drivers, with three-month-lagged rainfall (RFt3) showing the highest predictive importance at 24.66%. In validation, Random Forest was the top performer, limiting the average absolute error to 85.13 cases. Projections indicate that risks will expand nonlinearly across the inland savannah, with risk levels rising to 90.15% under the MPI-ESM1-2-HR model and 87.65% under the NCAR-CESM2 model under the extreme SSP5-8.5 scenario, effectively closing the historic protective gap near the estuarine coast. A cross-model comparison reveals that MPI-ESM1-2-HR offers a more geographically precise and physically constrained view of regional climate feedbacks than NCAR-CESM2, which tends to overestimate aridity during transitional decades. Economic analysis shows that interventions guided by this early warning system could prevent up to 42,100 cases and save approximately $189,450 USD in healthcare costs within the interior savannah by mid-century. Conclusion Shifting from reactive disease management to proactive, climate-informed targeting through robust tree-based machine-learning early-warning frameworks is a vital humanitarian and fiscal imperative for protecting vulnerable Sahelian communities from accelerating climate change, across multiple models.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10987061/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1833470.title: Absolute and lung volume-normalized deep learning-derived pulmonary vascular measures in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: distinct clinical associations and the role of lung volume in prognosis
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1833470.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) has an unpredictable course and poor outcome, and lung function-based risk stratification remains incomplete. Whether absolute and lung volume-normalized deep learning-derived CT pulmonary vascular measurements show distinct associations with disease severity and mortality in patients with IPF remains unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In this dual-center retrospective study, 118 adults with newly diagnosed IPF, including 57 from the Italian cohort and 61 from the French cohort, underwent baseline chest CT analyzed with a deep learning-based quantitative pipeline combining lung parenchyma (whole lung volume, WLV; fibrosis extent) and pulmonary vascular metrics (total blood volume, TBV; and derived BV
                      <jats:sub>5</jats:sub>
                      and BV
                      <jats:sub>&gt;10</jats:sub>
                      indices representing vessels with cross-sectional areas of &lt;5 mm² and &gt;10 mm²). Twenty subjects without lung disease served as a comparison group. Associations with fibrosis were assessed by Pearson correlation, mortality by multivariable Cox hazards models, and longitudinal lung function by linear mixed-effects models. Additional models examined the prognostic associations of vascular metrics after accounting for WLV.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Compared with controls, IPF patients had lower WLV and higher absolute TBV. Relative TBV (normalized to WLV) correlated strongly with fibrosis, while absolute TBV showed weaker associations. Relative vascular metrics inversely related to baseline lung function, whereas absolute TBV showed no significant association. Baseline TBV, BV
                      <jats:sub>5</jats:sub>
                      , and BV
                      <jats:sub>&gt;10</jats:sub>
                      did not predict forced vital capacity (FVC) or diffusing capacity of the lung for CO trajectories, but higher WLV predicted better FVC over time. Over a median 7.8-year follow-up, 72 deaths occurred. In multivariable models, higher absolute TBV, lower-lobe BV, BV
                      <jats:sub>5</jats:sub>
                      , BV
                      <jats:sub>&gt;10</jats:sub>
                      , and WLV, but not normalized TBV, were associated with reduced mortality after adjustment for established clinical variables. These findings suggest that preservation of lung volume and pulmonary vascular volume may be associated with improved survival. However, the associations of absolute vascular metrics with mortality were substantially attenuated after additional adjustment for WLV.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Normalized and absolute pulmonary vascular metrics capture different aspects of IPF, with normalized measures associated with fibrosis burden and functional impairment, while absolute vascular volumes were associated with mortality, although this association was substantially attenuated after accounting for WLV. Absolute vascular volume may therefore partly reflect preserved lung volume rather than an independent prognostic effect. Prospective validation is warranted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.58812/wsis.v4i09.3149.title: Inclusive Curriculum Management in Early Childhood Education to Realize Welcoming and Meaningful Learning
doi:10.58812/wsis.v4i09.3149.abstract: <jats:p>Early childhood education (PAUD) provides strategic services in improving the quality of child development. The implementation of inclusive curriculum management is one effort to realize fair, friendly, and meaningful learning for all students without discrimination. This article will present the concept, implementation, and objectives of inclusive education for early childhood to make learning more meaningful. This research uses a literature study method, data obtained through a review of various scientific sources, including books, national and international journal articles, and policy documents related to inclusive education and PAUD curriculum. The results of the study indicate that inclusive curriculum management includes four main functions: planning, organizing, implementing, and evaluating a curriculum that is flexibly designed according to the characteristics of students. To realize the implementation of inclusive education, it is supported by assessment, differentiated learning planning, and teacher resources. The implementation of inclusive curriculum management can increase children's participation in the learning process, optimize the development of all aspects of child development, and create a learning environment that respects diversity.</jats:p>

doi:10.1142/s0218126626300047.title: Advancements in Deep Learning for Automatic Moving Vehicle Detection in Intelligent Traffic Surveillance: A Comprehensive Review and Statistical Analysis
doi:10.1142/s0218126626300047.abstract: <jats:p>The traffic monitoring system plays an important role in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), representing a substantial investment by transportation agencies. It serves to gather and analyze traffic data, optimizing road usage, enhancing transportation safety and shaping future transportation strategies. Recent strides in MEMS, deep learning and wireless communication have spurred the development of innovative traffic monitoring systems. This paper investigates state-of-the-art schemes, focusing primarily on vehicle categorization, discussing their organization, research challenges, technical complexities, hardware/software frameworks, deployment insights and performance. Additionally, crucial open issues and future research avenues are explored, aiming to offer valuable insights to academia, industry and government entities for effectively choosing the technologies suited to the traffic monitoring needs.</jats:p>

                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.341,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.01); Learning engagement was significantly positively correlated with academic buoyancy (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.313,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>

(2) Physical education classroom environment was positively and significantly associated with female students’ academic buoyancy, with a direct association of 0.2525, accounting for 69.60% of the total effect. (3) In the relationship between physical education classroom environment and academic buoyancy, positive academic emotions and learning engagement showed both independent mediating effects and a chain mediating effect, with effect sizes accounting for 16.50, 10.70, and 3.20% of the total effect, respectively.

doi:10.2118/232034-ms.title: Machine Learning Application for Reciprocating Compressor Performance Prediction Under Varying Suction Pressures: A Case Study on Gas Pipeline Pump-Back Operations
doi:10.2118/232034-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>During gas pipeline maintenance, degassing is required to maintain operational safety and to support integrity and corrosion monitoring. Flaring is commonly used for this purpose, but it creates emissions and can trigger regulatory challenges. As an alternative, a skid-mounted reciprocating compressor can recover the gas and redirect it back into the pipeline. However, during pump-back operations the suction pressure often declines continuously. This causes compressor capacity and power demand to vary over time, which complicates scheduling and cost estimation. This study develops machine-learning fast proxy models to predict reciprocating compressor performance under variable suction pressures using a structured performance dataset generated with the Ariel Performance Program for a representative pump-back case. After cleaning and numeric consistency checks, the dataset contains 3111 operating points spanning 61 suction-pressure conditions (50 - 350 psig) and discharge pressures of ∼750 - 1000 psig, with flow ranging ∼0.4 - 3.0 MMSCFD and brake horsepower (BHP) ranging ∼82 - 223 BHP. Two independent machine learning models were trained, one for flow and one for BHP, using suction pressure, discharge pressure, and compressor speed (fixed at 1800 RPM for all cases) augmented with physics-informed features (ΔP, compression ratio, and ln(compression ratio)). Performance was assessed using grouped cross-validation by suction pressure and a low-suction holdout test (Ps &lt; 150 psig) to evaluate generalization in the most operationally challenging regime. Under grouped cross-validation, the best flow model (ridge regression) achieved RMSE 0.0247 MMSCFD and MAPE ∼0.75%, while the best power model (gradient boosting) achieved RMSE 2.49 BHP and MAPE ∼1.58%; however, errors increased under low-suction holdout conditions (flow MAPE ∼22%; BHP MAPE ∼30%), indicating that extrapolation below the sampled suction range, the situation faced when early-job data are used to forecast late-stage pump-back, is the dominant source of uncertainty and motivating improved low-suction data coverage and/or regime-specific modeling. Finally, integrating the flow proxy into an inventory-based blowdown simulation yielded time-to-empty estimates of ∼6.72 days (Pd ramp 1000 to 750 psig) and ∼6.82 days (Pd constant 1000 psig) for a 9 MMSCF inventory substantially longer than a simple constant-rate estimate. This enables planning-grade forecasting of pump-back duration and provides a machine learning driven workflow that supports scheduling, cost estimation, and emissions reduction; flaring the same 9 MMSCF of natural gas would produce on the order of ∼493 metric tons of CO2 based on representative heating value and standard combustion factors.</jats:p>

doi:10.2118/232058-ms.title: Machine Learning-Based Production Rate Forecasting from ESP Parameters with SHAP Explainable AI
doi:10.2118/232058-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrical submersible pump (ESP) wells often operate without continuous flow metering, forcing engineers to infer rate from sparse tests and noisy telemetry. This study builds a virtual flow metering workflow that predicts daily oil rate directly from ESP operating parameters and explains each prediction using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). A field dataset of 4,700 daily records was used with eight inputs spanning downhole pressures and temperatures, surface electrical measurements, fluid API gravity, and submergence. Three tree-ensemble regressors (ExtraTrees, XGBoost, and LightGBM) were trained and benchmarked using an 80/20 train-test split and 5-fold cross-validation. All models achieved strong generalization; the best model (ExtraTrees) reached R2 = 0.977 on the test set with AAPE = 1.55% (MSE = 5.4×103). Cross plots cluster tightly about the 45° line, and residuals are centered near zero, indicating minimal bias. SHAP analysis shows that intake temperature (Ti) and VSD output current are the dominant drivers of predicted rate: high Ti systematically reduces predicted production, while stronger electrical drive conditions increase it. The explanations are consistent with ESP physics and provide actionable diagnostics for operations. The results demonstrate that accurate, transparent rate forecasting can be achieved from routine ESP data, enabling practical real-time production surveillance and optimization.</jats:p>

doi:10.4038/atrsj.v6i1.70.title: Hybrid Rule-Based and Machine Learning Decision-Support Framework for Smart Paddy Farming
doi:10.4038/atrsj.v6i1.70.abstract: <jats:p>Paddy farming decisions are affected by changing weather conditions, water availability, soil conditions, and crop health, creating a need for decision-support approaches that combine agronomic knowledge with data-driven prediction. This research presents a hybrid rule-based and machine-learning decision-support solution for paddy management that combines interpretable agronomic rules and lightweight predictive models. The temporal alignment, interpolation, normalization, feature engineering, and crop-stage aggregation of weather and NDVI data were integrated and preprocessed. It is a rule-based engine with 63 expert rules that was fused with Decision Tree, Logistic Regression, and Random Forest models using a weighted decision-fusion mechanism. The hybrid model performed with 90% accuracy, 0.91 precision, 0.88 recall, and 0.89 F1-score, while the rule-based model had 72% accuracy, and the best standalone Random Forest model had 86% accuracy. The hybrid model also yielded the minimum RMSE of 7.6. The results of the simulation scenarios showed increases in yield of 3–17% and savings in irrigation-water use of 12.4%. There were 10 farmers and 2 agricultural officers who participated in the preliminary usability test and were scored from 4.0 to 4.8 out of 5. The key is an adaptive machine-learning prediction integrated with clear agronomic logic, in a lightweight advisory system. The yields and water-saving benefits, however, are simulated, and experimental testing on a wider range of locations and seasons will be needed to determine the full agronomic benefits.</jats:p>
doi:10.4038/atrsj.v6i1.70.venue: Journal of Agro-Technology and Rural Sciences

doi:10.1021/acs.jpclett.6c02477.title: Polyhedral-Cluster Machine Learning Potential for Efficient and Accurate Modeling of Complex Li-Ion Cathodes
doi:10.1021/acs.jpclett.6c02477.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Li-ion layered cathodes undergo complex structural evolution during delithiation, where local coordination changes, transition-metal migration, and oxygen-framework distortion are coupled across multiple length scales. Machine learning interatomic potentials can enable efficient atomic modeling of these processes, but conventional local descriptors often struggle to capture medium-range structural correlations without introducing redundant features. Here, a polyhedral-cluster potential (PCP) is proposed for Li–Mn–Ti–O cathode materials to combine short-range local coordination and medium-range oxygen-framework connectivity in a compact representation. SOAP descriptors encode the local environments within oxygen-centered polyhedra, while O–O-mediated cluster features describe interpolyhedral correlations. Compared with a conventional local potential, PCP improves DFT energy and force predictions for both ordered rocksalt-like and delithiated distorted structures, reducing the force MAE of the distorted structure from 101.22 to 41.99 meV Å–1. Descriptor analysis further shows that PCP decreases the feature number from 952 to 250 and lowers redundancy from 45.6% to 18.0%, while increasing the contribution of physically meaningful O–O correlations. Applications to equation-of-state (EOS) and Li-ion migration-path configurations demonstrate that PCP reproduces DFT energy trends under lattice strain and nonequilibrium defect environments. This work may provide a compact and interpretable descriptor framework for machine learning potentials of complex Li-ion cathode materials.</jats:p>
doi:10.1021/acs.jpclett.6c02477.venue: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters

doi:10.69900/ag.v6i5.634.title: Religious Moderation in Islamic Education Learning and Its Influence on Students’ Multicultural Attitudes in Multiethnic Areas
doi:10.69900/ag.v6i5.634.abstract: <jats:p>This article examines the relevance of religious moderation in Islamic Religious Education (PAI) learning to the formation of multicultural attitudes among students, particularly in multiethnic regions such as Balangan Regency, South Kalimantan. Using an integrative literature review approach, this study analyzes the relationship between the concept of religious moderation (tawassuth, tawazun, i'tidal, tasamuh) and the dimensions of multicultural attitudes as framed by James A. Banks. Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Theory is employed as a meta-theory to understand the position of PAI learning as an agent of value socialization within the school microsystem. Findings indicate that PAI learning that consistently and contextually integrates moderation values is both relevant and effective in building students' multicultural attitudes across cognitive, affective, and conative dimensions. PAI teachers who serve as role models (uswah hasanah) for inclusive values and employ dialogical and cooperative learning methods function as the most strategic transformative agents. The implications of this study affirm the necessity of reformulating PAI learning approaches from doctrinal transmission toward contextual and participatory value internalization, especially in regions with complex multiethnic compositions outside Java</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/lthe-12-2025-0098.title: Adopting applied experiential learning pedagogy in the Gulf region through evaluating 3D printing characteristics
doi:10.1108/lthe-12-2025-0098.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study is to explore how applied, project-based learning can deepen engineering students' understanding of additive manufacturing (AM) processes. This study investigates how infill structures and surface finishes affect material performance by guiding students through the design, printing and thermal evaluation of polylactic acid (PLA) samples. The goal is to illustrate how hands-on experimentation builds practical competence, supports critical thinking, and reinforces theoretical concepts related to heat transfer, sustainability and process capability. The work highlights experiential learning as an effective strategy for bridging classroom instruction with authentic engineering practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study applied an experiential learning methodology in which students progressed from computer-aided design (CAD) modeling to AM and thermal testing. PLA samples with varied infill structures and surface textures were printed using fused filament fabrication technology. Thermal conductivity was measured using the International Organization for Standardization (ISO)-aligned Transient Plane Source method, while process capability was evaluated through Cp and Cpk to assess dimensional consistency. The instructional design blended structured experimentation, collaborative problem-solving and guided reflection, enabling students to link theoretical instruction with practical engineering challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings indicate that students gained a clearer understanding of how design parameters influence thermal and manufacturing outcomes. Concentric and cross infill patterns showed strong process capability and predictable thermal behavior, while grid and line patterns provided better insulation due to internal voids. Rough surfaces exhibited higher thermal resistance than smooth prints. The hands-on testing reinforced how infill geometry, print settings and material response collectively affect print quality. Students demonstrated improved analytical reasoning, interpretation of Cp/Cpk results and recognition of the engineering trade-offs inherent in AM.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Because the project was designed as a course-based learning activity, the scope was intentionally narrow, with one polymer, one printer and a selected range of infill patterns and finishes. Environmental factors, mechanical behavior and long-term thermal stability were not explored. While these restrictions limit generalization, they reflect typical constraints of instructional laboratory settings. The implications point to the value of expanding future student-led investigations to multiple materials, environmental conditions and performance measures. The structured limitations also highlight how bounded experimental tasks can still produce meaningful learning gains and support iterative improvement in engineering pedagogy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work demonstrates that experiential laboratory activities can meaningfully enhance students' technical judgment and understanding of manufacturing variability. Incorporating 3D printing, thermal testing and statistical quality tools allows learners to practice industry-relevant skills while reinforcing conceptual knowledge in materials, heat transfer and process optimization. These insights can guide educators in designing hands-on modules that highlight sustainability considerations and encourage iterative problem-solving. Such activities provide a practical bridge between classroom instruction and professional engineering practice, improving students' readiness for work in AM and related fields.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study supports broader social goals by promoting sustainable thinking and technological literacy among future engineers. Through hands-on work with biodegradable materials and energy-aware printing strategies, students gain awareness of environmentally responsible manufacturing practices. The project also strengthens problem-solving, collaboration and data-driven decision-making skills that contribute to a more capable and adaptable workforce. The approach helps prepare graduates who are better equipped to address societal challenges related to resource efficiency, innovation and sustainable development through integrating experiential learning into higher education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The originality of this study lies in its interdisciplinary approach, combining AM, thermal science and statistical quality control within a student-centered learning environment. Few educational frameworks engage students in full-cycle experimentation from design and printing to thermal evaluation and process capability analysis. This work demonstrates how this approach enhances conceptual understanding while developing practical engineering skills. It offers educators a valuable model for embedding sustainability and real-world problem-solving into engineering courses, bridging academic learning with emerging industry needs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/ijebr-04-2026-0503.title: Jugaad as a decolonising cultural logic in entrepreneurship education: pluralising entrepreneurial learning in the United Arab Emirates
doi:10.1108/ijebr-04-2026-0503.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how Jugaad, a culturally-embedded South Asian entrepreneurial logic, remains meaningful beyond its place of origin and what its comparison with curriculum-mediated student reasoning reveals about pluralising entrepreneurship education (EE).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Qualitative data were collected from immigrant entrepreneurs who practice Jugaad and EE students enrolled in formal entrepreneurship education programs in the UAE. The analysis examines how practice-based Jugaadi reasoning differs from curriculum-mediated reasoning among entrepreneurship education students.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Jugaadi entrepreneurs drew on relational knowledge, contextual adaptation, cultural intuition and practical engagement, whereas students relied more heavily on structured models and formal analysis. The contrast identifies forms of entrepreneurial reasoning that planning-centred EE may under-recognise and reveals pedagogical possibilities for incorporating culturally-embedded knowledge into entrepreneurship learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>UAE-based qualitative sample may limit generalisability but provides grounds for research in diverse cultural and educational contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings offer educators four Jugaad-informed practices: designing with constraints, validating ideas through relationships, assessing contextual judgement and comparing planning-centred with improvisational approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher education institutions are encouraged to pluralise EE curricula by recognising culturally embedded ways of entrepreneurial knowing. The findings also support SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by strengthening youth enterprise development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study demonstrates how a culturally-embedded entrepreneurial logic can remain generative beyond its place of origin and become a pedagogical resource for pluralising EE. It conceptualises Jugaad as a distinctive way of entrepreneurial knowing and explains how comparing it with curriculum-mediated student reasoning can inform curriculum, teaching and assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
