doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1893983.title: A multimodal deep learning radiomics nomogram integrating clinicopathological features for predicting pathological complete response after neoadjuvant therapy in triple-negative breast cancer: a multicenter retrospective study
doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1893983.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Accurate noninvasive estimation of pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) may support multidisciplinary discussions, but multimodal MRI-ultrasound evidence remains limited. We developed and externally validated a clinicopathological deep learning radiomics nomogram and explored its potential auxiliary value in a strictly hypothetical post-hoc surgical-planning scenario.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>With institutional review-board approval and waived consent, this retrospective multicenter diagnostic accuracy study included 436 biopsy-proven TNBC patients who underwent NAT and surgery: Center 1 training cohort (n = 268) and internal validation cohort (n = 86), plus historical cases from cooperating Centers 2–3 for external validation (n = 82). pCR was defined as ypT0/is ypN0. Pretreatment dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI), diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)/apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) maps, T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), and B-mode ultrasound were analyzed. Intratumoral and 5-mm peritumoral ring radiomics features were extracted and selected by LASSO. DenseNet-121 extracted modality-specific deep features, fused using multi-head self-attention. Age, tumor size, Ki-67, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), cT/N stage, and histological grade were integrated with imaging scores in a logistic-regression nomogram. Parameters and thresholds were locked after Center 1 development and applied once to external data. No model output was used clinically. Feature standardization and ComBat harmonization parameters were strictly locked to the training cohort before application to validation data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>pCR occurred in 182/436 patients (41.7%). The nomogram achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.917 (95% CI, 0.881-0.947) in training, 0.883 (0.814-0.937) in internal validation, and 0.856 (0.773-0.921) in external validation, exceeding clinical (external AUC, 0.721), radiomics (0.786), and deep learning (0.819) models. External sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy at the locked threshold were 0.765, 0.813, and 0.793, respectively. Calibration was acceptable (slope, 0.93; intercept, −0.06; Brier score, 0.16). Decision curve analysis showed net benefit for thresholds of 0.20-0.70. Multi-threshold analysis revealed that a high-specificity threshold (0.65) yielded a positive predictive value of 0.85, potentially identifying a subset of patients with very high confidence of achieving pCR. Compared with the clinical model, external reclassification improved (continuous net reclassification improvement [NRI], 0.34; integrated discrimination improvement [IDI], 0.11; P = 0.003 and P = 0.008, respectively).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among the few multicenter TNBC studies combining MRI, ultrasound, intratumoral/peritumoral radiomics, and attention-based deep learning, this nomogram showed good retrospective accuracy for pCR prediction after NAT. The model is presented as an aid for pCR prediction and preoperative stratification rather than as direct support for surgical decision-making. Prospective validation and clinical-impact studies are required before implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73360-7.title: MLCL: LVLM-guided multi-level contrastive learning for fake news detection
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73360-7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The widespread dissemination of multi-modal disinformation on social media platforms poses a serious threat to public safety and social stability, elevating the need for automated detection of such content. Although existing studies have started to incorporate multimodal data, effectively modeling cross-modal interactions remains difficult, often leading to insufficient mining of information within individual modalities. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel LVLM-Guided multi-level contrastive learning network (MLCL). Within the textual modality, BERT and CLIP encoders extract features at varying granularities, while ResNet and CLIP encoders capture visual representations. Additionally, a Large Vision-Language Model is leveraged to derive text-based representations that reflect both local details and global contexts from images. We further introduce a multi-level alignment strategy: inside each modality, a normalized InfoNCE loss aligns features from the two encoders to reduce redundancy. Before cross-modal fusion, we jointly align the three modality-level features using both InfoNCE loss and batch-hard triplet loss, thereby explicitly modeling their consistency and relative distance. A modality-wise attention module is also incorporated to adaptively reweight and aggregate features. Experiments on two real-world datasets show that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving overall accuracy improvements of 2.2% on Weibo and 1.5% on Gossipcop. The source code is publicly available at
                    <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://github.com/Ylh-s/MLCL" ext-link-type="uri">https://github.com/Ylh-s/MLCL</jats:ext-link>
                    .
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fimmu.2026.1925067.title: Immune and inflammatory features associated with pyroptosis- and myocardial fibrosis-related genes in HFpEF: a machine learning study
doi:10.3389/fimmu.2026.1925067.abstract:

                    Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a heterogeneous syndrome marked by inflammation, immune dysregulation, and myocardial fibrosis. Whether pyroptosis intersects with fibrotic remodeling in HFpEF remains uncertain. Two murine cardiac transcriptomic datasets were integrated after batch correction and intersected with curated pyroptosis- and myocardial fibrosis-related gene sets. Functional enrichment, univariate logistic regression, support vector machine–recursive feature elimination (SVM-RFE), and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression were used for feature selection. Complete separation in the ordinary three-gene logistic fit prompted refitting with Firth bias-reduced logistic regression. Performance was assessed by apparent area under the curve (AUC), stratified bootstrap optimism correction, and repeated nested cross-validation; the panel was re-estimated in a human left-ventricular dataset for exploratory replication. Cell-type Identification by Estimating Relative Subsets of RNA Transcripts (CIBERSORT) estimated immune-cell fractions, and expression was examined in a high-fat diet (HFD)/N

                    -nitro-L-arginine methyl ester hydrochloride (L-NAME) murine model and whole blood from patients with HFpEF. Six candidates—
                    <jats:italic>Pparg</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>Ace2</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>Smad2</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>Lcn2</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>Ptpn11</jats:italic>
                    , and
                    <jats:italic>Sqstm1</jats:italic>
                    —were identified. Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes analyses linked them to SMAD binding, autolysosome/amphisome activity, cellular senescence, efferocytosis, and renin-angiotensin signaling. In the 45-sample discovery cohort, the fixed

                    -
                    <jats:italic>Ptpn11</jats:italic>
                    -
                    <jats:italic>Ace2</jats:italic>

Repeated nested cross-validation produced a mean out-of-fold AUC of 0.9286 (2.5%–97.5% percentile interval, 0.8726–0.9700), revealing additional feature-selection uncertainty. Re-estimation in the human dataset represented panel-level replication rather than validation of a locked cross-species model. No inferred immune-cell fraction differed between HFpEF and control after false-discovery-rate correction, although exploratory correlations were observed among deconvolved fractions and with

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02828.title: Predicting Chemical Stressor Effects on Conjugative Plasmid Transfer Rates Using Machine Learning
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02828.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chemical stressors in environmental and clinical settings can alter conjugative plasmid transfer, which is a key process driving antibiotic resistance dissemination. However, predicting these effects across chemically diverse compounds is challenging. Here, we compiled and curated data on the effect of chemical stressors on RP4 plasmid transfer, extracting compound identity, concentration, conjugation frequency, and experimental metadata from 73 in vitro studies. Chemicals were characterized by functional use categories and molecular descriptors, including physicochemical properties, MACCS keys, Morgan fingerprints, and extended descriptors from the OCHEM platform (AlvaDesc, Dragon 7, and 3D-shape descriptors). An exhaustive evaluation of 1022 feature set combinations across 3066 models showed that chemical concentration alone provides no meaningful predictive signal (Q2ext &lt;0), whereas integrating Morgan fingerprints substantially improves predictive performance. The best-performing model combined concentration, Morgan fingerprints, and experimental conditions using extreme gradient boosting (XGB), achieving Q2ext = 0.373 on a held-out compound-aware test set and a median Q2ext of 0.319 within the defined applicability domain across 20 independent splits. SHAP analysis revealed that Morgan fingerprints account for 69% of total predictive weight, with quaternary ammonium compounds and long-chain alkyl structures associated with inhibition of conjugation and sulfonamide and amine-containing compounds associated with promotion. These results demonstrate that chemical structural features provide critical information for predicting the chemical modulation of conjugative plasmid transfer. This work highlights that combining chemically informed descriptors with machine learning (ML) anticipates chemical contributions to antibiotic resistance dissemination, providing a scalable framework for the prioritization and risk assessment of chemicals.</jats:p>

doi:10.38124/ijisrt/26sep1075.title: Predicting Faults in Mechanical Systems Using Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning
doi:10.38124/ijisrt/26sep1075.abstract:
<jats:p>The occurrence of unexpected malfunctions of mechanical systems such as bearings, gearboxes, turbofan 
engines, and other rotating machinery is still the main cause of downtime, safety hazards, and maintenance cost 
throughout the manufacturing, energy, and transportation sectors. Recent technological advances in artificial intelligence 
(AI) and machine learning (ML) technology have transformed fault prediction from an entirely physics-based activity to a 
data-based activity, in which sensors, signal processing, and learning algorithms estimate the health state of a machine 
together. This paper provides a structured assessment and comparative synthesis of AI/ML fault-prediction literature. 
Nineteen peer-reviewed studies obtained from scholarly and web-based databases for the period 2011–2026 are reviewed. 
A review of the two main tasks: fault diagnosis – classification of fault type, location and severity – prognosis – prediction 
of remaining useful life, RUL. The evidence is structured into a six-stage pipeline – data acquisition, pre-processing, 
feature extraction, model training, output, maintenance decision. The analysis is conducted using various test rigs 
including the CWRU bearings as well as NASA C-MAPSS turbofan engines and gearbox. The results show that on these 
benchmarks, convolutional and recurrent deep architectures, attention-augmented LSTMs, and ensemble methods 
consistently outperform classical classifiers; root-mean-square errors (RMSE) on C-MAPSS RUL errors are about 12 
cycles and classification accuracies on CWRU exceed 98%. Simultaneously, the review also outlines a number of ongoing 
open challenges, like data scarcity, domain shift, class imbalance, limited interpretability, and overoptimistic evaluation, 
which must be overcome before lab results can become consistent with the reliable deployment in the industry. To 
conclude the paper suggests a standardized benchmarking of multi-fidelity methodologies and explainability-augmented 
models.</jats:p>
doi:10.38124/ijisrt/26sep1075.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology

doi:10.3390/jrfm19100757.title: Pooled Information and Model Flexibility: Decomposing Machine-Learning Gains in Corporate Budgeting and Forecasting
doi:10.3390/jrfm19100757.abstract: <jats:p>Corporate financial planning and analysis (FP&A) is being reorganised around machine learning, yet the supporting evidence consists largely of vendor case reports using undefined accuracy measures. This study decomposes the machine-learning advantage into components that prior work bundles together—information recency versus model re-estimation, and pooled estimation versus learner flexibility—measured on corporate income-statement data rather than retail or equity series. An open benchmark from SEC XBRL data covering 2599 non-financial US filers and 118,406 firm-quarters, from 2011 to 2025, evaluates five pre-registered hypotheses under rolling-origin validation with clustered inference. First, the advantage of continuous re-forecasting over annual budgeting derives from information recency rather than parameter updating: supplying current quarterly actuals to a model estimated once at fiscal year start recovers 27 to 58 percent of forecast error, whereas quarterly re-estimation produces no detectable improvement (p = 0.82), a result that holds across the COVID-19 and 2022 inflation regimes. Second, the advantage is an interaction rather than a main effect: a pooled linear model modestly outperforms a Theta benchmark, a flexible learner fitted per firm underperforms it, and a foundation model pooled across unrelated domains underperforms further; only pooling across comparable firms combined with a flexible learner realises the full gain. Third, model ranking reverses under asymmetric budget-variance cost.</jats:p>
doi:10.3390/jrfm19100757.venue: Journal of Risk and Financial Management

doi:10.1145/3829807.3829822.title: The Work to Make Assistance Work: Learning from Videos by Visually Impaired Content Creators
doi:10.1145/3829807.3829822.abstract: While multimodal AI holds strong potential to support the blind and visually impaired (BVI), current systems often fail to provide meaningful assistance. In this paper, we analyse online videos created by BVI content creators to understand how assistance unfolds in practice. Across two studies, we examine videos of BVI creators engaging with systems, peers, and BVI experts (such as surfer, soccer player) in everyday and challenging situations. We show how these actors both succeed and fail in shaping how BVI people project, coordinate, and interpret their worlds. Particularly, interactions among BVI experts revealed how effective assistance unfolds through back-and-forth interaction. From this, we characterise the concept of worldmaking, where assistance is centred on constructing a shared worksite of objects and actions. These findings highlight directions for designing multimodal AI systems that support worldmaking, enabling both AI and BVI people to make the world intelligible together.
doi:10.1145/3829807.3829822.venue: Proceedings of the 14th Nordic Conference on Human-Computer Interaction

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-74484-6.title: A support vector machine classifier of PM₂.₅-based air quality index categories from co-pollutants and meteorological variables in Ahvaz, Iran
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-74484-6.abstract: Ahvaz, in southwestern Iran, experiences some of the most severe particulate air pollution in the world, driven by Middle Eastern Dust events, industrial emissions, and traffic. Continuous monitoring of fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) is essential for public-health protection, yet PM₂.₅ monitors in the region frequently suffer outages and data gaps. This study evaluates whether the PM₂.₅-based Air Quality Index (AQI) category can be estimated from routinely measured co-pollutants (O₃, NO, NO₂, SO₂, CO, and PM₁₀) and meteorological variables (air temperature, dew point, relative humidity, wind speed, and wind direction), providing a surrogate risk label when direct PM₂.₅ measurements are unavailable. Hourly observations from the Naderi monitoring station in Ahvaz (October 2014 – July 2017) were aggregated into 3-hour intervals; each interval with at least two of three observed hourly PM₂.₅ values was labelled with one of six AQI categories using the U.S. EPA PM₂.₅ breakpoints in force during the study period, yielding 7,509 samples. A class-weighted radial-basis-function Support Vector Machine (SVM) was tuned by rolling-origin cross-validation within the training period (October 2014 – January 2017) and evaluated on a strictly held-out chronological test period (January – July 2017), alongside multinomial logistic regression, linear SVM, random forest, and gradient boosting baselines trained under identical protocols. On the unseen test period, the SVM achieved an exact-category accuracy of 0.633, macro-averaged F1 of 0.38, Cohen’s κ of 0.47, and quadratic-weighted κ of 0.61; 94.5% of predictions fell within one category of the truth, and misclassifications concentrated between adjacent categories. The random forest baseline performed best overall (accuracy 0.674; quadratic-weighted κ of 0.70; 97.7% within one category). Permutation importance and ablation experiments identified PM₁₀ as the dominant predictor: excluding it reduced SVM accuracy from 0.633 to 0.431, while PM₁₀ alone reached 0.523. Performance for the rare extreme categories (Very Unhealthy and Hazardous) remained limited and is reported transparently. At this station and over this period, co-pollutant and meteorological measurements—chiefly PM₁₀—can provide an operationally useful, near-real-time surrogate for the PM₂.₅ AQI category when the PM₂.₅ channel fails, while underscoring that such a surrogate cannot replace properly maintained PM₂.₅ instrumentation, particularly for extreme pollution episodes.

doi:10.30973/progmat/2026.18.1/2.title: Desinformacion y Alfabetización Mediática: Clasificación de Patrones de Confianza en Noticias entre Adolescentes mediante Machine Learning
doi:10.30973/progmat/2026.18.1/2.abstract: <jats:p>Este estudio examina la detección de noticias falsas entre adolescentes utilizando técnicas de Machine Learning. Se plantean dos preguntas fundamentales: cómo reaccionan los jóvenes ante la desinformación y qué nivel de confianza tienen en la veracidad de las noticias. A través de un análisis detallado con algoritmos de aprendizaje automático, como k-means, Decision Trees y Random Forest, se clasificaron las respuestas de los participantes, revelando patrones significativos en su confianza hacia los medios de comunicación. Los hallazgos sobre esta muestra indican que aproximadamente el 15% de los adolescentes no confían plenamente en las noticias y casi el 50% carece de habilidades para identificar información falsa. Esto resalta la necesidad urgente de implementar programas de alfabetización mediática que fortalezcan la capacidad crítica de los jóvenes para discernir la veracidad de la información en un entorno digital saturado de desinformación. Además, el estudio sugiere que futuras investigaciones deben explorar otros algoritmos de Machine Learning y evaluar el impacto de intervenciones educativas en la alfabetización mediática.</jats:p>

doi:10.1142/s0218625x26501131.title: Machine Learning-Based Modeling and Multi-Criteria Optimization of Wire-EDM Parameters
doi:10.1142/s0218625x26501131.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Wire-EDM (Wire Electrical Discharge Machining) plays a crucial role in the precision manufacturing of complex geometries, particularly for materials that are difficult to machine using conventional methods. Intelligent modeling and optimization of process parameters are required to improve performance, especially to maximize Material Removal Rate (MRR) and minimize kerf width. This study presents a machine learning (ML)-driven approach for predictive modeling and multi-objective optimization of Wire-EDM input settings. Using 31 experimental data points from existing literature, the influence of four important parameters i.e. V
                    <jats:sub>g</jats:sub>
                    (Average gap-voltage), W
                    <jats:sub>f</jats:sub>
                    (wire feed-rate), T
                    <jats:sub>on</jats:sub>
                    (pulse-on time) and T
                    <jats:sub>off</jats:sub>
                    (pulse-off time) on MRR and kerf width was systematically investigated. Three advanced regression techniques i.e. RFR (random forest regression), SVR (support vector regression), and GBR (gradient boosting regression) are utilized to capture the complex nonlinear relationships between inputs and outputs. Among these, the SVR model demonstrated superior performance, achieving a high R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    value of approximately 0.92, indicating strong predictive accuracy. To interpret the model and assess feature significance, SHAP analysis is conducted, identifying gap voltage as the most influential factor affecting both MRR and kerf width. The optimized parameters generated by the SVR model led to enhanced machining performance, aligning well with the experimental results. This research underscores the potential of tree-based ensemble learning techniques like gradient boosting and random forest regression in advancing Wire-EDM process optimization, offering a robust, intelligent framework compatible with the goals of smart manufacturing and Industry 4.0. The methodology sets a strong precedent for data-driven decision-making in precision machining.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1952443.title: An explainable and leakage-aware machine learning model for early risk stratification of radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer: development and single-center geographic external validation
doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1952443.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer (RAIR-DTC) poses a major therapeutic challenge, with loss of radioiodine avidity, limited treatment options, and worse outcomes. Current risk stratification systems were not designed to predict RAIR transformation before clinical refractoriness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This retrospective two-center study included a development cohort of 302 consecutive patients and an external validation cohort of 122. Candidate predictors were restricted to baseline demographic, clinicopathological, molecular, and biochemical variables available at or before first postoperative RAI administration; all post-treatment, response-related, and time-dependent variables were excluded
                      <jats:italic>a priori</jats:italic>
                      . Six machine-learning algorithms were developed with repeated cross-validation and compared by discrimination, probability accuracy, and clinical utility. Model interpretation used SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). External transportability was assessed by discrimination, calibration, decision-curve analysis, and validation of prespecified risk groups.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-six patients (15.2%) developed RAIR-DTC in the development cohort and 18 (14.8%) in the external cohort. Random forest was selected for the most favorable balance of cross-validated discrimination and probability accuracy, despite comparable external discrimination from XGBoost and the stacked ensemble. It achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.896 and Brier score of 0.078 in the internal test cohort, with robust external discrimination (AUC, 0.892; PR-AUC, 0.597; sensitivity, 0.778; specificity, 0.798). Raw external calibration was poor (calibration slope 0.304; observed-to-expected ratio 0.613), indicating that ranking was preserved whereas absolute risk estimates required local recalibration. SHAP analysis identified age ≥55 years, TERT promoter (TERTp) mutation, vascular invasion, initial stimulated thyroglobulin (sTg), and extrathyroidal extension (ETE) as the dominant contributors. Training-derived quantile cut points generated three-tier risk groups, identifying a low-risk subgroup with zero events in the external cohort and a low event rate (3.3%) in the internal test set, while enriching the high-risk subgroup to event rates of 75.0% and 37.2%, respectively, with 95% confidence intervals of 47.6%-92.7% and 23.0%-53.3%, respectively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An explainable, leakage-aware random forest based exclusively on routinely available baseline variables provided robust external discrimination and clinically meaningful early risk stratification for RAIR-DTC. Preserved discrimination did not guarantee transportable probability estimates, underscoring that external calibration and site-specific recalibration are essential prerequisites for responsible clinical deployment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956939.title: Generative AI in creative education: baseline-linked evidence on learning processes, artistic performance, and authorship
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956939.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping creative learning in higher education art courses, yet its educational value remains contested when creative support, output generation, authorship, and skill development become intertwined. This study investigates AI-supported creative learning in an undergraduate art course.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study used linked data from 133 students, including prior course performance, final creative-performance assessment, and post-project questionnaire responses. AI use was operationalized through two dimensions: assistive use for ideation, refinement, process management, and technique learning, and content-generative use involving AI contributions to creative output. The analysis combined baseline-adjusted outcome models, performance-change models, propensity-score adjustment, AI-use intensity comparisons, and robustness checks across alternative AI-use definitions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings show a clear process-outcome decoupling pattern. AI use was associated with stronger perceived support and skill transfer, while final artistic performance and baseline-to-final performance change showed no corresponding improvement. Content-generative AI use was associated with lower evaluated authorship, suggesting that AI-shaped artifacts may reduce the visibility of students' creative decision-making in final outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study contributes a differentiated account of AI in creative education and argues that responsible AI integration should focus on how students use, document, justify, and reflect on AI within the creative process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.31234/osf.io/hdjp3_v3.title: Multimodal Dynamics in Learning and Explaining Abstract and Concrete Concepts: A Triadic Interactive Task with Families
doi:10.31234/osf.io/hdjp3_v3.abstract: Studies have shown that learning abstract concepts (e.g., freedom compared to table) may be particularly challenging. To address concept learning, most studies use paradigms involving a single participant, such as lexical decision, match to sample, induction, and rating tasks. Here, we use an interactive task involving three family members—mother, father, and a 5-year-old child—and examine how concepts differing in abstractness are explained by the parents, either individually or together, and how the child learns and employs them. We investigate multimodal dynamics in interaction, studying gestures, movements of bodily parts, and movement coordination among interactors, in an effort to capture different embodied signatures characterizing concepts differing in abstractness. Results reveal that people gesture differently with abstract and concrete concepts, but in both cases tend to instantiate the conceptual referent, either metaphorically or iconically. Subtle differences in head movements and social touch suggest that people struggle more to understand the meanings of abstract concepts than concrete ones. Finally, with abstract concepts, coordination episodes are longer. Overall, the results provide support for the view that, with abstract concepts, people use more communicative signals and tend to converge more than with concrete concepts.

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1704-3.ch005.title: Forensic Geospatial Intelligence
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1704-3.ch005.abstract: <jats:p>The review followed the PRISMA 2020 framework. Literature searches were conducted across IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. From 120 candidate records identified through database searching, 64 studies met the predefined eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis, comprising 51 direct studies and 13 methodologically transferable studies. The findings indicate that supervised learning remains the dominant paradigm, with convolutional neural networks, Vision Transformers, and semantic segmentation architectures achieving strong performance in image classification, manipulation detection, object localisation, and land-cover mapping. Emerging data-efficient approaches, including self-supervised learning, transfer learning, and hybrid models, increasingly address limitations associated with scarce labelled data, domain shift, and heterogeneous imaging environments. This review contributes a unified comparative framework that bridges forensic and geospatial image analysis.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/ijlls-03-2026-0100.title: Fostering student data literacy through a community-based STEM project: a lesson study investigation
doi:10.1108/ijlls-03-2026-0100.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explores the potential of community-based STEM projects, supported by Lesson Study (LS) framework, to foster data literacy (DL) among elementary school students.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An LS team conducted two iterations centered on a community-based STEM project in which students designed flotation devices to address local flooding. Data sources included pre- and post-assessments, student surveys, video recordings of lessons and planning meetings. Quantitative data were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, while qualitative analysis of research lessons identified four types of learning opportunities. Student surveys were examined using descriptive statistics and qualitative approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although no statistically significant gains in DL knowledge were found, qualitative results indicated high student engagement and improved understanding of the DL process and its relevance to community issues. Classroom discourse revealed opportunities for students to formulate investigative questions, explore data through graphical representations and interpret results. Challenges included supporting students in posing meaningful statistical questions and analyzing relevant data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Embedding a DL lesson within an LS cycle and analyzing classroom discourse provides insight into how learning opportunities emerge through task design and targeted questioning. Limitations include limited capture of small group talk, partial assessment of DL, and the focus on a single project in one grade band.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study highlights the need for sustained integration of DL across multiple iSTEM cycles, clearer scaffolds for formulating statistical questions, and stronger synthesis routines to support coherence-building.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study offers empirical insights into how community-based STEM projects supported by LS can create meaningful opportunities for developing students' DL and inform the design of innovative, practice-based instruction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10345-0.title: The extended functional practical examination (EFPE): an innovative model for advancing assessment for learning in postgraduate medical education
doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10345-0.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Extended Functional Practical Exam (EFPE) is an innovative postgraduate assessment model designed to overcome the limitations of traditional single-point practical examinations by adopting a longitudinal, experiential, and institution-based approach. This study aimed to critically explore the implementation of EFPE across different medical schools and examine its perceived educational value, impact on learners and institutions, and areas for improvement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methodology</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A reflective qualitative study involving different medical schools was conducted. Three samples were included in the study: a convenience sample of the postgraduate students and a purposive, convenience sample of faculty members and medical school stakeholders. Insights from the three samples were collected through semi-structured interviews. All the interviews were audio recorded and transcribed verbatim and thematically analyzed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The thematic analysis of data from the three samples (S1, S2, and S3) under the classified themes revealed several themes and subthemes. The main themes included the format and differences from traditional exams, the exam’s impact, and challenges and areas for improvement. Participants appreciate the alignment of EFPE tasks with institutional needs and the positive role of feedback and mentorship. However, challenges such as stress, workload, resource demands, and issues with topic selection and clarity were noted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>EFPE is highly valued for its practical, structured, and process-focused approach, which leads to significant skill development and confidence building among postgraduate students. Suggestions from participants include extending the duration of the EFPE, involving students in topic selection, maintaining continuous feedback and mentorship, and ensuring tasks are relevant and sustainable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1145/3849812.title: SSRESF-OPT: A Sensitivity-Aware Framework for Single-Particle Radiation Effects Simulation and Optimization in SoC Platforms Using Machine Learning
doi:10.1145/3849812.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The increasing scale of System-on-Chip (SoC) architectures exacerbates the reliability risks of single-particle radiation effects, rendering traditional exhaustive gate-level fault injection prohibitively slow. To address this, we propose SSRESF-OPT, an end-to-end simulation and optimization framework combining accelerated dynamic fault injection with machine learning-driven prediction. The framework first introduces a cross-layer static binding mechanism to eliminate runtime string resolution, reducing per-injection simulation overhead to
                    <jats:inline-formula content-type="math/tex">
                      <jats:tex-math notation="TeX" version="MathJaX">\(\mathcal {O}(1) \)</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    complexity. Building on this optimized engine, an SVM-based classification pipeline, guided by structural clustering, accurately predicts the radiation vulnerability of unsimulated circuit nodes using netlist-derived features. To maximize resource efficiency, an OPT-based top-
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">k</jats:italic>
                    hardening strategy is then employed to prioritize critical architectural bottlenecks. Evaluations across 15 gate-level netlists, including massive AES subsystems and RISC-V PULP SoCs, demonstrate the framework’s efficacy. The model-assisted approach achieves an average end-to-end runtime speedup of 6.35 × over the highly optimized simulation baseline while maintaining a 94.58% prediction accuracy. Furthermore, hardening only the top 10% of ranked nodes reduces system Soft Error Rate (SER) by 85%, providing a fast and actionable methodology for radiation-hardened microprocessor design.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.29303/jppipa.v12i10.15853.title: Development of Comic-Assisted Interactive Media to Improve Learning Outcomes on Lithosphere Material in Grade X Geography: A Contribution to Quality Education (SDG 4)
doi:10.29303/jppipa.v12i10.15853.abstract: <jats:p>Lithosphere processes are difficult to observe directly, while teacher-centered instruction and static media limit students' conceptual understanding. This study developed comic-assisted interactive media for Grade X geography and evaluated its validity, practicality, and effectiveness. Research and development followed the ADDIE model. The product was created with Lumi Education as an H5P Interactive Book that integrated sequential comics, interactive videos, image hotspots, and quizzes with immediate feedback. Three experts assessed validity; one geography teacher and students evaluated practicality in small-group and whole-class trials; and 36 students participated in a one-group pretest-posttest evaluation. The media was highly valid for material (95.00%), media design (100.00%), and language (98.00%). Practicality was also high for the teacher (98.00%) and students in both the small-group and whole-class trials (97.00%). The mean score increased from 60.67 to 89.63; the Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated a significant paired difference (p < .001), and the mean normalized gain was 0.73 (high). These findings indicate that the media is valid, practical, and potentially effective for supporting visualization, self-assessment, and teacher-facilitated discussion of lithosphere concepts</jats:p>

doi:10.1515/cti-2026-0059.title: Systems thinking in sustainable chemistry education: connecting systems thinking with the open inquiry-based learning activity “Can CO <sub>2</sub> be good and bad?” for secondary chemistry education
doi:10.1515/cti-2026-0059.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Systems thinking (ST) is increasingly recognised as an important approach for addressing sustainability challenges, yet its integration into chemistry education remains limited. This article presents an open inquiry-based learning (IBL) environment that uses the socio-scientific context of carbon dioxide to foster systems-oriented reasoning. Students explore the guiding question “Can CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    be good and bad?”, develop and investigate their own research questions, and reflect on the multifaceted roles of carbon dioxide in environmental, industrial, and societal systems using two systems-oriented activities. Experiences from the implementation in nine secondary school classes show that 9th graders tend to rely on simplified and often one-sided interpretations of the role of carbon dioxide. However, participation in the activities and subsequent reflection supported more differentiated understandings that considered multiple perspectives, functions, and consequences of carbon dioxide. The experiences suggest that combining open IBL with explicit systems-oriented reflection can support the development of ST in chemistry education in different formats and contexts and provide a productive approach for addressing complex socio-scientific issues.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1142/s0218001426400719.title: SCRAMBLE: Safe Cooperative Risk-Aware Multi-Agent Belief Learning for Embodied Reinforcement Learning in Partially Observable Dynamic Environments
doi:10.1142/s0218001426400719.abstract: <jats:p>Safe decision-making in partially observable dynamic environments remains a fundamental challenge for multi-agent embodied reinforcement learning, where agents must cooperate with limited local observations while responding to evolving environmental changes and safety-critical interactions. Existing methods often emphasize coordination efficiency or reward maximization, but they are less effective at jointly handling latent state uncertainty, dynamic non-stationarity, and safety constraints in a unified learning framework. To address this issue, we propose SCRAMBLE, a safe cooperative reinforcement learning algorithm for multi-embodied agents operating in partially observable dynamic environments. SCRAMBLE combines cooperative belief modeling, risk-aware safety estimation, and constrained policy optimization to enable agents to infer hidden environmental dynamics, anticipate unsafe interactions, and adapt their joint behaviors under changing conditions. Specifically, the cooperative belief module fuses local observation histories and inter-agent information to construct a shared latent representation for decentralized decision-making. On top of this representation, a risk-aware safety estimator evaluates potential hazards caused by environmental variations and multi-agent interactions, allowing the policy to proactively avoid unsafe actions. Meanwhile, the constrained optimization mechanism improves task performance while maintaining safety compliance during learning and execution. Through this integrated design, SCRAMBLE enhances both cooperative robustness and safety adaptability in complex embodied scenarios. Experimental results in representative partially observable dynamic benchmark tasks show that SCRAMBLE consistently achieves superior performance in cumulative reward, safety satisfaction, and adaptation capability compared with existing baseline methods.</jats:p>
doi:10.1142/s0218001426400719.venue: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence

doi:10.4038/jmtr.v11i4.469.title: Machine learning-based adaptive learning systems in higher education: A systematic review of techniques, outcomes, and ethical implications for knowledge translation
doi:10.4038/jmtr.v11i4.469.abstract: <jats:p>Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have revolutionized the development of adaptive learning systems (ALS) that can personalize learning in higher education. A comprehensive and synthesized understanding of the most common ML techniques used, their reported effectiveness in improving educational outcomes, and the ethical challenges of their use in this context is needed. This systematic review synthesizes 19 peer-reviewed articles published from 2015-2025 to: (1) map and classify ML and AI techniques used in higher education adaptive learning systems; (2) assess evidence of impact on student academic performance, engagement and retention; (3) explore ethical issues such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, governance and transparency; and (4) recommend a knowledge translation approach to ethical implementation of AI-ALS within higher education settings. Following PRISMA 2020 Statement, searching in five digital databases (Google Scholar, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library), 19 articles were included, based on eligibility criteria, including systematic reviews, scoping reviews, empirical research and bibliometric analyses and prospective studies. The most commonly encountered ML techniques were collaborative filtering, Bayesian knowledge tracing, deep learning (LSTM and transformer-based models), reinforcement learning, NLP-based tools and learning style prediction algorithms. The studies reported significant gains in learning performance, engagement (15 - 30% improvement) and retention with AI-ALS. However, serious ethical questions were raised in most studies, such as algorithmic bias, lack of informed consent, black-box issues, and lack of institutional governance strategies, especially in under-resourced and Global South settings. ML-based ALS has great power to enhance higher education through personalized, data-driven learning. However, this potential must be realized in an ethical and equitable manner through strong governance, explainable AI, and multi-stakeholder accountability. A five-layer knowledge translation model is advocated.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73132-3.title: Explainable deep learning for SEM-based classification of six Sclerodermataceae taxa
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73132-3.abstract: Accurate identification of closely related fungal species remains challenging because of substantial morphological similarities and overlapping diagnostic characters. This study evaluated explainable deep learning approaches for the image-level classification of six predefined Sclerodermataceae taxa using scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of fungal spores An original dataset consisting of 961 SEM micrographs representing Scleroderma areolatum , S. cepa , S. bovista , S. polyrhizum , S. verrucosum , and Pisolithus arhizus was constructed under specimen-preparation protocol. Image preprocessing included grayscale conversion, brightness normalization, histogram equalization, and annotation removal. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and test subsets, and data augmentation was applied to improve model generalization. Nine pretrained convolutional neural network architectures, including ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, RegNet-Y8GF, ConvNeXt-Small, SENet-154, VGG-16, Inception-V3, Xception, and EfficientNet-B3, were comparatively evaluated using identical training conditions. Performance assessment was conducted using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, balanced accuracy, Cohen’s kappa, expected calibration error, and brier score. ResNet-50 achieved the highest classification performance with 99.48% accuracy, 99.49% precision, 99.48% recall, 99.48% F1-score, and 99.38% MCC, misclassifying only one test sample. Grad-CAM++ and occlusion sensitivity analyses suggested that model attention was predominantly associated with biologically relevant spore ornamentation regions. These findings support the applicability of SEM-based deep learning and qualitative XAI approaches for image-level classification among the six predefined Sclerodermataceae taxa examined under the present experimental conditions.

doi:10.1145/3821402.3830160.title: You Cannot Optimize Learning Like a Factory
doi:10.1145/3821402.3830160.abstract: Across contemporary educational systems, the language of efficiency, throughput, measurability, and process control increasingly shapes how teaching and learning are governed. This paper argues that such logic imports assumptions from industrial production into a domain that is fundamentally different in kind. Learning is not a linear transformation of input into output, nor is education a stable production process that can be optimized without loss. Rather, education is a socio-pedagogical ecosystem shaped by uncertainty, relationality, professional judgment, temporal depth, and human development.

doi:10.3390/electronics15194517.title: Federated and Differentially Private Learning for Root Cause Classification Across Heterogeneous Semiconductor Fabs
doi:10.3390/electronics15194517.abstract: <jats:p>Federated learning (FL) can train a shared model without pooling client records, but it does not by itself provide differential privacy (DP). We compare centralized training, local-only training, federated averaging (FedAvg), and client-level DP-FedAvg on a fully released synthetic benchmark of free-text root-cause-analysis (RCA) records from six simulated semiconductor fabs. The benchmark uses a fixed public vocabulary, 240 records per client, a 480-record in-distribution test set, a separately authored 480-record template-disjoint test set, and five training seeds. All methods receive 24 passes over their available training data. The reference classifier is an auditable multinomial softmax regression with 512 parameters. The DP mechanism assumes fixed-roster replace-one client adjacency, clips only private client updates, adds Gaussian noise calibrated to the sensitivity of the weighted aggregate, and composes twelve releases with Rényi DP. In-distribution accuracy was 53.94% [53.60, 54.27] (mean, 95% confidence interval) for local-only training, 74.71% [73.05, 76.37] for FedAvg, and 91.88% [90.62, 93.13] for centralized training. Template-disjoint accuracy was 19–24% for all three. DP-FedAvg reached 65.92% [61.40, 70.44] at ε≈204 and fell to chance level at ε≈3.6 (δ=10−5). These results characterize a controlled benchmark and do not establish applicability to real fabs.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/biomimetics11100701.title: A Dual-Stream Feature Learning Framework with Adaptive Bio-Inspired Protozoa–Starfish Optimization for Melanoma Classification
doi:10.3390/biomimetics11100701.abstract: <jats:p>Melanoma accounts for a small fraction of skin cancer cases but for the majority of skin-cancer-related deaths, making accurate early detection essential. Although deep learning-based dermoscopic image analysis has shown strong diagnostic potential, its performance depends strongly on training hyperparameters and loss-function weighting, which are commonly tuned manually or through computationally expensive grid search. To address this, Adaptive Combined Artificial Protozoa–Starfish Optimization (AC-APSO) is introduced as a bio-inspired hyperparameter optimization strategy that dynamically regulates the contributions of the Artificial Protozoa Optimizer (APO) and the Starfish Optimization Algorithm (SFOA) at each iteration according to population diversity, fitness improvement, and optimization progress. AC-APSO configures RM-LBAT-Net, a hybrid CNN–Transformer architecture that integrates Res2Net-50-based multi-scale feature extraction, MaxViT-Tiny-based global contextual learning, a Deformable Lesion Boundary Attention Module (DLBAM), and Cross-Scale Adaptive Semantic Fusion (CSASF). The optimized framework achieved an accuracy of 98.85%, with precision, recall, and F1-score of 98.70%, 99.00%, and 98.85%, respectively. Controlled ablation studies showed that each architectural component contributed under both fixed and optimized configurations and that adaptive coordination outperformed APO alone, SFOA alone, and a fixed-weight APO–SFOA combination. In a head-to-head comparison under an identical protocol, the framework outperformed contemporary architectures, including ConvNeXtV2-Tiny and Swin Transformer V2-Tiny. Five-fold cross-validation and external validation on the ISIC 2016 dataset (97.36% accuracy) further indicated stable performance and promising cross-dataset generalization.</jats:p>

doi:10.55606/jpmi.v5i3.7950.title: Penguatan Kompetensi Digital Pendidik Nonformal melalui Pelatihan Pengembangan Sumber Belajar Digital Berbasis Learning by Doing
doi:10.55606/jpmi.v5i3.7950.abstract: <jats:p>Limited skills among nonformal educators in developing digital technology-based learning resources remain a challenge in improving the quality of learning in equivalency education. This community engagement program aimed to improve nonformal educators’ knowledge and skills in designing, developing, and integrating digital learning resources through participatory training based on learning by doing. The program was conducted over two days at PKBM Bunda Samarinda and involved 40 nonformal educators from several community learning centers in Samarinda City. The activities consisted of needs identification, a pre-test, conceptual reinforcement, demonstration, hands-on practice, mentoring, product development, review and feedback, followed by a post-test and evaluation. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the Shapiro-Wilk test, and a paired-samples t-test. The results showed that the participants’ mean score increased from 60.78 on the pre-test to 85.25 on the post-test, representing an increase of 24.47 points. The paired-samples t-test indicated a statistically significant difference between the pre-test and post-test scores (t(39) = 53.056; p < 0.001). These findings indicate that participatory training based on learning by doing can support the improvement of nonformal educators’ ability to understand and develop digital learning resources. The findings recommend continued post-training mentoring and sustainable development of digital learning products to strengthen educators’ digital competence in nonformal education settings.</jats:p>

doi:10.56943/sujana.v5i4.1046.title: Teacher Performance in a Frontier Region: Principal Leadership, School Climate, and Organizational Culture in Paniai, Papua
doi:10.56943/sujana.v5i4.1046.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the effects of principal leadership, school climate, and organizational culture on teacher performance at state senior high schools in Paniai Regency, Papua Province. A quantitative approach with an ex post facto design was employed. The population consisted of 160 students at four state senior high schools, who provided their perceptions of principal leadership, school climate, organizational culture, and teacher performance. A sample of 62 respondents was determined using proportional stratified random sampling based on the Slovin formula. Data were collected through a Likert-scale questionnaire that had satisfied tests of validity and reliability, and were analyzed using simple and multiple linear regression. The results showed that principal leadership had a positive and significant effect on teacher performance, contributing 7.4 percent; school climate exerted the strongest effect, contributing 26.0 percent; and organizational culture had a positive and significant effect, contributing 8.4 percent. Collectively, the three variables exerted a positive and significant influence on teacher performance, accounting for 40.3 percent of the variance. These findings indicate that strengthening principal leadership, fostering a conducive school climate, and reinforcing organizational culture constitute important strategies for improving teacher performance, particularly in schools situated in geographically and socioculturally distinct regions such as Paniai Regency.</jats:p>

doi:10.18502/kss.v11i8.21703.title: An Overview of Entrepreneurial Resilience and Learning from Innovation Failure on Entrepreneurial Well-being within the Minangkabau Community: A Conceptual Paper
doi:10.18502/kss.v11i8.21703.abstract: <jats:p>This conceptual paper develops an integrative framework explaining how entrepreneurial resilience and learning from innovation failure shape entrepreneurial well-being within the Minangkabau cultural context. Using an integrative literature review, this study synthesizes theories of resilience, failure learning, and well-being and situates them in the matrilineal and migration-oriented merantau traditions of the Minangkabau society. The proposed model posits that resilience enables entrepreneurs to regulate emotions, adapt to uncertainty, and engage in constructive reflection after failure. Learning from innovation failure then mediates the pathway from resilience to enhanced entrepreneurial well-being, covering emotional, social, and spiritual dimensions. Minangkabau cultural values, such as communal obligations, social reputation, and adaptive wisdom– “Alam takambang jadi guru”– are proposed as contextual conditions that shape these relationships. The paper offers testable propositions and provides culturally grounded insights for future empirical studies.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73518-3.title: A hybrid machine learning framework integrating persian NLP for occupational risk classification in steel manufacturing
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73518-3.abstract: Human error remains a leading cause of occupational accidents in high-risk industries, yet traditional risk assessment methods often overlook valuable information embedded in unstructured textual data. This study develops and validates a hybrid machine learning framework combining structured risk data with Natural Language Processing (NLP) to improve hazard classification accuracy in industrial settings. Data were collected from 258 work activities across 16 operational units in a steel manufacturing facility over five months, yielding 3,110 validated risk scenarios. Hazard identification employed Job Safety Analysis (JSA), while quantitative risk evaluation used the William Fine method. The dataset comprised structured variables (severity, exposure, probability) and unstructured Persian-language text (hazard descriptions, locations, activities). Text preprocessing included tokenization, stopword removal, stemming, and lemmatization. Features were extracted using TF-IDF vectorization for all models. Random Over-Sampling (ROS) addressed class imbalance. Four traditional machine learning algorithms were evaluated: Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Support Vector Machine (SVM). On unbalanced data, SVM achieved the highest accuracy (93%), with F1-scores of 0.96, 0.83, and 0.92 for low, medium, and high-risk categories, respectively. After ROS balancing, performance showed practical improvements across most models, particularly for minority risk classes; however, the difference did not reach conventional statistical significance (p = 0.189), likely due to the small comparison sample (n = 3 models). SVM reached near-perfect classification, whereas KNN remained the weakest performer. The hybrid framework significantly outperforms traditional risk assessment methods by leveraging both structured data and unstructured textual information. The prevalence of low-risk scenarios (66.1%) suggests effective existing safety controls, while improved classification of medium and high-risk cases enables targeted interventions. This approach provides a foundation for real-time AI-driven safety monitoring systems in high-risk industrial sectors.

doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15009765/v1.title: Neural Kinetics: LEARNING KINETICS AS TRANSPORT IN COMPOSITIONAL SPACE
doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15009765/v1.abstract: <jats:p>Complex bio-derived and fossil mixtures contain thousands of molecules whose individual structures and reaction pathways cannot be fully resolved, making conventional mechanism-based kinetic modelling impractical. A reaction network detailed enough to describe every formula-level transformation would contain far more reactions and parameters than the available data can constrain. We propose to overcome this limitation by representing mixtures directly as abundance fields on a compositional grid indexed by molecular descriptors, specifically carbon number (#C) and double-bond equivalent (DBE), and by learning a time-conditioned, chemistry-informed operator that maps the initial composition to predict a later state. The evolution rates of the chemical space are learned by a two-dimensional Fourier neural operator (FNO) acting jointly on a set of heteroatom classes, with normalized time and compositional coordinates appended as input channels. Because experimental data are limited, we enlarge the training set with synthetic trajectories generated from the measured samples, pre-train on this ensemble, and then calibrate a small subset of parameters on the measured distributions. We tested the framework on a case of oxidation of a complex hydrocarbon mixture that is tracked by FTICR-MS over sixty seconds of reaction. On an independent sample the framework, that we named NeuralKinetics, reproduced the measured endpoint class composition within a mean absolute error of approximately one percent and arranged the heteroatom classes correctly on the compositional grid. The second test was an entirely different system: litter decomposition in a peatland warming experiment, also followed by FTICR-MS but over two years. The developed operator accurately predicted the endpoint class composition of the held-out sample proving that the framework is flexible enough to adapt to diverse reactive systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c10344.title: Accelerated Electrolyte Engineering by Deep Learning: A Quaternary Ammonium Additive Enables Ultra-Stable Zinc Anodes
doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c10344.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Currently, achieving long-cycling zinc anodes for aqueous zinc-ion energy storage devices remains a challenge owing to uncontrolled dendritic growth and concurrent hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Electrolyte engineering via molecular additives has emerged as an effective strategy for modulating zinc anode interfacial chemistry, but the vast structural space of candidate molecules renders conventional trial-and-error screening inefficient. Here, we present a deep learning (DL) framework for screening high-performance quaternary ammonium cation (QAC) additives for aqueous zinc electrolytes. We developed GATGLP, a graph attention network-based HOMO–LUMO gap (Gap) predictor, to address the data scarcity inherent in ionic molecular systems, which was first pretrained on a curated subset of the QM9 molecular data set and subsequently fine-tuned via transfer learning on a DFT-calculated QAC data set. Through a dual-descriptor screening strategy based on the predicted Gap and the octanol–water partition coefficient (XlogP), a validated library of 378 QAC compounds was ranked, and three candidates were selected for systematic electrochemical validation. Among them, n-octyltrimethylammonium bromide ([N8111]Br) showed a Zn//Zn cycling duration of more than 1800 h at 1 mA cm–2/1 mAh cm–2 and a cycling lifespan of approximately 180 h at 5 mA cm–2/5 mAh cm–2. Across the ZSO-Br, N6111 and N8111 electrolytes, which share the same bromide concentration, three quantities measured by different methods show the same ordering: the relative (002) diffraction proportion, the maximum −Z″ of the impedance arc, and the Zn//Cu sequence length increase from ZSO-Br to N6111 to N8111. The chronoamperometric transient does not follow this ordering, but N8111 is the only electrolyte in which the current magnitude decreases during the step. Taken together, these observations suggest that the selected organic cations may differ in their interfacial accumulation, which could redistribute the Zn deposition flux and contribute to flatter, more continuous deposits. This work combines DL-assisted molecular screening with experimental validation to identify QAC additives for aqueous zinc electrolytes.</jats:p>

doi:10.18502/kss.v11i7.21717.title: The Effectiveness of the Problem-based Learning Model to Improve Civic Skills in Civics Courses
doi:10.18502/kss.v11i7.21717.abstract: <jats:p>This study is a qualitative research that aims to analyze the effectiveness of the problem-based learning model in improving civic skills in civics courses. The participants comprised 19 students. The data were collected through interviews, observation, and documentation. The interview data were gathered using a structured guide. Observations were conducted to assess the effectiveness of the PBL model in enhancing students’ civic skills in civics courses. Documentation was obtained by reviewing the implementation of the civics course instruction in the UMS accounting study program, class in the odd semester of 2024/2025. Data analysis followed an interactive approach. The validity of the findings was ensured through triangulation: data source triangulation, method triangulation, and theory triangulation. The results indicate that the problem-based learning model to improve civic skills in civics courses was very effective, at 84%. The observed improvements in civic skills competencies in the classroom can be attributed to the development of the following skills: (1) critical and analytical thinking, (2) social and political participation, (3) problem-solving, (4) communication and collaboration, (5) social awareness and responsibility, (6) ethical decision-making, (7) legal literacy and human rights awareness, and (8) leadership and social responsibility. Based on these findings, it is recommended that teachers implement the problem-based learning model in civics courses to enhance students’ civic skills.</jats:p>

doi:10.3892/etm.2026.13320.title: Development and internal validation of explainable machine learning models for predicting failure of first ambulation within 12 h after cesarean delivery: A retrospective cohort study
doi:10.3892/etm.2026.13320.abstract: Early ambulation is a notable component of postoperative recovery after cesarean delivery, but some women fail to complete first ambulation within the early postoperative period because of pain, dizziness, orthostatic discomfort, residual lower limb numbness, nausea or vomiting, hypotension or poor activity tolerance.Early identification of women at high risk of ambulation failure may support timely and individualized nursing interventions.The present study aimed to develop and internally validate explainable machine learning models for predicting failure of first ambulation within 12 h after cesarean delivery using routinely collected obstetric perioperative nursing assessment data.The present single-center retrospective cohort study included relatively stable women who underwent cesarean delivery between January 2022 and December 2025 and were considered clinically eligible for early mobilization.The primary outcome was failure of first ambulation within 12 h after surgery, defined as no documented successful ambulation within 12 h or discontinuation of an ambulation attempt because of nursing-documented intolerance.Candidate predictors included demographic, obstetric, pregnancy-related, laboratory, anesthetic, surgical and early postoperative nursing assessment variables.Postoperative symptoms and vital signs were assessed within predefined early postoperative intervals, whereas first turning time was treated as a dynamically updated indicator that became available when the first spontaneous or assisted turning event was documented.The model was therefore interpreted as a dynamic early postoperative risk-assessment approach rather than a prediction model applied exclusively at a fixed 4-h time point.The final analytic dataset contained no item-level missing values; therefore, no imputation was performed.The cohort was randomly divided into training and internal validation cohorts at a ratio of 7:3.Logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and LightGBM models were developed and compared.Model performance was assessed using discrimination, classification metrics, calibration, Brier score and decision curve analysis.SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used to interpret the final model.A total of 1,486 women were included, and 326 women experienced failure of first ambulation within 12 h, with an incidence of 21.9%.The training and validation cohorts included 1,040 and 446 women, respectively.In the validation cohort, LightGBM achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.809 and a Brier score of 0.132, whereas XGBoost achieved an AUC of 0.805 and a Brier score of 0.134.The paired DeLong test showed no statistically significant difference between the validation AUCs of the two models (P= 0.647).XGBoost achieved higher sensitivity, negative predictive value and F1 score than LightGBM (0.714 vs. 0.653, 0.906 vs. 0.892 and 0.567 vs. 0.561, respectively).Because these metrics were particularly relevant to identifying high-risk women and minimizing missed high-risk cases, XGBoost was selected as the final model.Calibration curves showed acceptable agreement between predicted and observed risks, and decision curve analysis demonstrated net benefit across relevant doi:10.3390/jrfm19100759.title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Tokenomic Collapse Risk: Evidence from 155 Real-World Tokens and a Small Prospective Holdout
doi:10.3390/jrfm19100759.abstract: <jats:p>Can a token’s collapse be predicted from design parameters fixed at launch, before it has market history? We compile on-chain data for 155 tokens (79 survived, 76 collapsed) and benchmark seven classifiers under leave-one-out cross-validation. Random Forest attains the highest area under the curve (AUC; 0.909; nested cross-validation 0.906), though no pairwise test separates the leading models. The result is not a category prior: out-of-fold AUC stays high within categories (decentralized finance 0.943 on 64 tokens; layer-1/layer-2 0.923 on two collapsed tokens, hence unstable), and excluding the two categories whose labels are near-definitional costs 0.014. Leave-one-category-out validation yields a mean AUC of 0.764 but fails for memecoins (0.571), which bounds the claim. Using only four unambiguously pre-launch features costs 0.038; restricting to long-exposure tokens does not degrade the model (0.921). A 13-token prospective test under distributional shift, with three collapsed cases, is merely indicative. Shapley-value attributions, permutation importance, and Sobol sensitivity agree that inflation rate dominates; team allocation is second by the first two and by standardized logistic coefficients, whereas Sobol ranks whale concentration second. The Safe Operating Envelope, counterfactuals, and fragility screen are in-sample and illustrative. Collapse risk is substantially predictable from design parameters within the categories represented here.</jats:p>
