doi:10.1145/3776574.3840556.title: The Challenges of Human-Centered AI and Robotics: What We Want, Need, and are Getting From Human-Machine Interaction
doi:10.1145/3776574.3840556.abstract: Language-based AI is now ubiquitous, and user expectations for intelligent machines are scaling along with it: we expect machines to understand us, predict our needs and wants, do what we enjoy and prefer, and adapt as we change our moods and minds, learn, grow, and age. Physical AI, in the form of robotics, is the next major AI challenge, and it is not ready to leap into our daily lives yet. While massive investment is focused on functional behavior of humanoid robots (perceiving the world, moving around, and manipulating objects), human-robot interaction (HRI) is largely an afterthought, left for “later". This talk will discuss how bringing together robotics, AI, and machine learning for long-term user modeling, real-time multimodal behavioral signal processing, and affective computing is enabling machines to understand, interact, and adapt to users’ specific and ever-changing needs. We will overview methods and challenges of sparse and noisy heterogeneous, multi-modal, personal interaction data and of creating expressive agent and robot behavior toward understanding, coaching, motivating, and supporting a wide variety of user populations across the age span (infants, children, adults, elderly), ability span (typically developing, autism, anxiety, stroke, dementia), contexts (schools, therapy centers, homes), and deployment durations (from weeks to 6 months) through socially assistive robotics. We will discuss the challenges of understanding what we humans want from interactions with machines vs. what we need vs. what we are getting, and how those distinctions are shaping the future of not just AI and ML but society at large.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3840556.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.58764/j.im.2026.7.207.title: Transformasi Digital dalam Akuntansi Keuangan: Systematic Literature Review Menggunakan Pendekatan PRISMA
doi:10.58764/j.im.2026.7.207.abstract: <jats:p>Aim: This study aims to analyze the development of digital transformation in financial accounting, identify dominant technologies and research themes, and explore research gaps in the field of digital transformation in financial accounting. Method: This study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework. The data consist of scientific articles obtained from Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Emerald Insight, Google Scholar, and other scholarly sources. A total of 18 articles published between 2017 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed using content analysis with a thematic analysis approach. Results: The findings indicate that blockchain is the most dominant technology in the transformation of financial accounting due to its contribution to transparency, accountability, financial reporting quality, and fraud mitigation. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and automation also play important roles in improving the efficiency of accounting and auditing processes and supporting data-driven decision-making. However, existing research remains largely dominated by conceptual and literature-based studies, while empirical research examining the implementation of digital technologies in accounting practices remains relatively limited. Conclusion/Novelty/Implications: The novelty of this study lies in systematically mapping dominant technologies and research themes while identifying empirical research gaps. The findings imply that future research should integrate technology, governance, regulation, cybersecurity, and human resource competencies to support effective and sustainable digital transformation in financial accounting.</jats:p>
doi:10.58764/j.im.2026.7.207.venue: AL-IMAM: Journal on Islamic Studies, Civilization and Learning Societies

doi:10.1186/s40537-026-01579-2.title: Machine learning driven replication free storage optimization for wearable healthcare sensors
doi:10.1186/s40537-026-01579-2.abstract: Wearable sensors (WS) are becoming an important tool for detecting and monitoring physical changes in humans, which, together with improved diagnostic techniques and clinical procedures, represents an important development in the clinical field. The information obtained from these sensors is dynamic and dependent on human activities, making efficient storage crucial for subsequent analysis. However, if data quality management is not properly handled, strategic process failures can reach up to 40%. At the same time, scalability concerns can make it difficult to scale data processing without affecting consistency and security. Moreover, replicated entries in wearable sensors can be indexed at multiple points, increasing storage requirements. Another widespread problem that may affect the accuracy and reliability of data management systems is the absence of unique records. To address these problems, this work introduces Replication-Free Data Management (RDM) to ensure reliable data storage in healthcare systems. The proposed method is based on the Random Forest classification algorithm, which aims to differentiate between aggregation and classification instances. This approach helps minimize data loss caused by extended latency by categorizing activities and verifying their similarity. Conditional scheduling based on activity instances and scheduling slots is also used to distinguish similar sensor data from non-comparable data during storage access. Experimental results demonstrate that RDM supports different scheduling times while maintaining 0.0816 redundant data and 419.61 ms latency and supports different scheduling instances while maintaining 0.0831 redundant data and 426.58 ms latency. Furthermore, RDM achieves 92.28% storage utilization and 6.23% data loss for different classification instances, and 92.44% storage utilization and 6.28% data loss for different aggregation times. The proposed RDM achieves 97.12% performance and 98.43% efficiency ratios, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing data replication, data loss, and latency across various scheduling intervals and instances.

doi:10.35542/osf.io/yh5kb_v1.title: Lecture-Based versus Hands-On Learning Methods: A Review
doi:10.35542/osf.io/yh5kb_v1.abstract: This mini review compares lecture and instruction-based teaching, typical of traditional schools, with application-based learning using hands-on 3D materials and student-built models, as practised in Montessori schools. Meta-analyses, systematic reviews and randomized or lottery-based trials published mainly between 2006 and 2025 were reviewed. Passive lecture consistently underperforms active learning: in 225 university STEM studies, active learning raised scores by 0.47 SD and lecture students were 1.5 times more likely to fail. Yet structured, interactive explicit instruction is effective, and unguided discovery is weaker than explicit teaching. Montessori education shows modest, consistent advantages over conventional schooling, about 0.25 SD on academic and 0.33 SD on non-academic outcomes, with the strongest effects on executive function. A 2025 national trial of 588 children found higher reading, memory, executive function and social understanding by the end of kindergarten, and a French randomized trial found a delayed advantage in maths problem-solving. Concrete manipulatives and physical 3D models improve retention and spatial understanding, with smaller effects on transfer. Evidence is strongest for early childhood and weakest for secondary schools and non-Western settings. The findings favour a blended model: brief explicit teaching followed by guided work with physical models and student projects.

doi:10.59256/indjcst.20260503020.title: Hybrid Quantum–Classical Machine Learning for Sustainable Drug Discovery: Heat Capacity-Based Drug-Likeness Evaluation
doi:10.59256/indjcst.20260503020.abstract: <jats:p>Sustainable approaches to molecular analysis can support the development of computational methods for early stage drug discovery. This work explores whether combining quantum derived molecular representations with a classical regressor improves the prediction of heat capacity, and considers what that might mean for drug-likeness assessment. The QM9 molecular dataset is first prepared through numerical preprocessing, feature scaling, and dimensionality reduction, after which the resulting representations are encoded into a quantum circuit to produce quantum-derived features. These are combined with conventional molecular descriptors and fed into an XGBoost regressor to generate the final heat-capacity (Cv) predictions. To gauge whether this hybrid design offers any real advantage, its output is compared directly against a purely classical model, using R², MAE, and MSE as the basis for comparison. The hybrid configuration reaches an R² of approximately 0.947, versus roughly 0.923 for the classical model a gap that suggests quantum-derived representations can meaningfully sharpen prediction of this thermodynamic property, at least under the conditions tested here. Overall, the framework offers a computationally grounded approach that could support molecular screening and contribute to more sustainable early-stage drug-discovery strategies.</jats:p>
doi:10.59256/indjcst.20260503020.venue: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831233.title: SIGMA: Statistical Memory Head for Robust Class-Incremental Vision–Language Learning with CLIP
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831233.abstract: Class-incremental learning with vision–language models faces a fundamental tension: while CLIP provides strong zero-shot generalization, fine-tuning task-specific adapters induces representation drift and biases decision boundaries toward recent classes, leading to catastrophic forgetting. Freezing the CLIP backbone alleviates drift but does not resolve residual prediction bias, and existing adapter-based methods leave the stable raw CLIP feature space largely unexploited for logit recalibration. To address these limitations, we propose SIGMA (Statistical Inference Gaussian Memory Adaptation), a training-free inference module that accumulates per-class Gaussian statistics directly in the frozen CLIP feature space. SIGMA performs analytic discriminant classification to recalibrate predictions without using gradient updates, eliminating the overfitting risk inherent in adapter-based optimization. When integrated with lightweight adapters, SIGMA strikes an effective balance between short-term adaptation and long-term stability, addressing both representation drift and prediction bias within a unified inference-time framework. Experimental results on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and CUB-200 demonstrate consistent improvements compared to state-of-the-art continual learning methods.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831233.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831206.title: Affect-Aware Game Personalization with Reinforcement Learning: How to Improve Players' Engagement, Performance, and Emotions
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831206.abstract: Adaptive games are often evaluated through performance alone, even though gameplay experience also depends on players’ affective responses. We present an affect-aware game adaptation approach that combines a control loop architecture with tabular model-free reinforcement learning (MFRL) to adjust discrete game and user-interface parameters at runtime. The controller observes facial-expression categories together with gameplay variables, maps them to discrete states, and selects among interpretable adaptations. We integrated the proposed architecture and reward model into the CubeWars game. We evaluate the system in a within-subject study with 36 participants by comparing an adaptive RL-based version with a fixed baseline. The adaptive condition was associated with higher mean expression scores for happiness and surprise, while fear increased numerically but not significantly. Players showed better performance (i.e., reached higher levels and achieved more kills) under the adaptive condition. Post-experiment ratings further indicated favorable perceived personalization, usability, and enjoyment. This work introduces a reusable closed-loop architecture for affect-aware game adaptation and shows that lightweight, interpretable adaptations can improve player experience and performance.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831206.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.59256/indjcst.20260503018.title: Quantifying Evaluation Bias in Machine Learning Models for Concrete Compressive Strength: Mix-Level Replication in the Yeh Benchmark and Its Differential Effect on Model Comparison
doi:10.59256/indjcst.20260503018.abstract: <jats:p>The 1030-record dataset compiled by Yeh is the de facto benchmark of the concrete strength-prediction literature, and coefficients of determination reported on it routinely exceed 0.90. This study shows that part of that reported accuracy reflects the internal structure of the dataset rather than predictive capability. The 1030 records describe only 427 distinct mix proportions: one batch is cast and then tested at several curing ages, so that 76.1 per cent of records share their composition with at least one other record that differs only in age. Under the random partitioning used almost universally in this literature, models are therefore evaluated on mixes already seen during training. Five estimators spanning a range of flexibility are re-evaluated under random and mix-grouped five-fold cross-validation, each repeated ten times. The mix-grouped protocol lowers R² for every estimator, but unevenly: the reduction is negligible for ordinary least squares (0.002) and k-nearest neighbours (0.004) and material for support-vector regression (0.029), random forest (0.043) and gradient boosting (0.054). The apparent advantage of gradient boosting over least squares is consequently overstated by about 19 per cent. The penalty is concentrated in the sparsely sampled high-strength region (60 MPa and above), whose records are also the most heavily replicated; there, the root-mean-square error of the two tree ensembles rises by 42 and 44 per cent. A controlled experiment on synthetic data with a known generative law and a tunable per-mix batch effect confirms the mechanism: the gap is zero without a batch effect and grows monotonically with it. The study concludes that leakage-aware evaluation, rather than synthetic augmentation, is the appropriate corrective, and provides a single executable notebook that reproduces every result.</jats:p>
doi:10.59256/indjcst.20260503018.venue: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology

doi:10.61268/wwmhw250.title: A Review of Machine Learning Classifiers for Feature-Based Image Forgery Detection
doi:10.61268/wwmhw250.abstract: The increasing use of digital image manipulation and the generation of synthetic images has led to serious concerns regarding the authenticity and trustworthiness of images.The recent development of advanced generative models like Style-GAN, StyleGAN2, and diffusion models has the potential to generate very realistic synthetic images that are very difficult to distinguish from real images, thus leading to serious challenges in digital image forensics.This paper presents a comprehensive review of image forgery detection techniques with a primary focus on machine learning-based techniques.Various image forgery techniques, including traditional image forgery and AI-created synthetic images, are presented to understand their nature and challenges in image forgery detection.The paper presents a review of machine learning-based methods, popular datasets, and evaluation metrics for image forgery detection.Furthermore, the paper presents the challenges of existing methods, particularly their poor generalization capability for diffusion-based forgeries and the lack of representative benchmarks, and concludes with open challenges and future research avenues for developing generalized machine learning methods for authentic detection of image forgeries.

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831160.title: Using Machine Mental Imagery for Representing Common Ground in Situated Dialogue
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831160.abstract: Situated dialogue requires speakers to maintain a reliable representation of shared context rather than reasoning only over isolated utterances. Current conversational agents often struggle with this requirement, especially when the common ground must be preserved beyond the immediate context window. In such settings, fine-grained distinctions are frequently compressed into purely textual representations, leading to a critical failure mode we call representational blur, in which similar but distinct entities collapse into interchangeable descriptions. This semantic flattening creates an illusion of grounding, where agents appear locally coherent but fail to track shared context persistently over time. Inspired by the role of mental imagery in human reasoning, and based on the increased availability of multimodal models, we explore whether conversational agents can be given an analogous ability to construct some depictive intermediate representations during dialogue to address these limitations. Thus, we introduce an active visual scaffolding framework that incrementally converts dialogue state into a persistent visual history that can later be retrieved for grounded response generation. Evaluation on the IndiRef benchmark shows that incremental externalization itself improves over full-dialog reasoning, while visual scaffolding provides additional gains by reducing representational blur and enforcing concrete scene commitments. At the same time, textual representations remain advantageous for non-depictable information, and a hybrid multimodal setting yields the best overall performance. Together, these findings suggest that conversational agents benefit from an explicitly multimodal representation of common ground that integrates depictive and propositional information.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831160.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831191.title: Multimodal Anxiety Detection with Adaptive Hyperbolic Few-Shot Learning
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831191.abstract: Anxiety disorders impact millions globally, yet traditional diagnosis relies on clinical interviews, while machine learning models struggle with limited labeled data. In this work, we introduce the Hyperbolic Curvature Few-Shot Learning Network (HCFSLN), a novel framework for multimodal anxiety detection using speech, physiological signals, and video. Our approach leverages hyperbolic embeddings to better capture hierarchical structure in affective signals, along with cross-modal attention and adaptive gating to model interactions across modalities. We collect a multimodal dataset from 108 participants and evaluate HCFSLN under few-shot settings. Our results show that HCFSLN significantly improves robustness and generalization, achieving 88% accuracy and outperforming baselines by 14%. Audio achieves the best unimodal performance (0.88 on social anxiety dataset, 0.79 on our dataset in 1-shot); adding physiological signals improves accuracy by ∼ 3–5%, and tri-modal fusion reaches up to 0.86 (social anxiety dataset) and 0.83 (our dataset), while using all modalities slightly reduces performance (∼ 0.79, ∼ 0.75) due to noise. The adaptive gating mechanism provides interpretability by weighting modalities, consistently prioritizing audio and leveraging physiological signals, with t-SNE showing clearer class separation. Further analysis highlights complementary multimodal cues for anxiety detection. Our approach is effective in low-data settings. We release our dataset and code at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SIR-Lab/Multi-Modal-Anxiety-Dataset.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831191.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.62887/dataplus.004.02.00129.title: Patient feedback in digital primary care: A critical narrative review of measurement, organisational learning and trust
doi:10.62887/dataplus.004.02.00129.abstract: <jats:p>Digital primary care can collect patient experience close to the point of care, yet the presence of a survey does not ensure that the information changes services. This review examines how feedback moves from capture to interpretation, action and visible response. A critical narrative synthesis was developed from the literature assembled for a consultancy report on online general practice, supplemented by verification of selected primary publications and current English regulatory guidance. The source review searched Web of Science and Google Scholar for work on feedback, online consultations, service quality and digital trust, and identified 22 peer-reviewed articles. Evidence supports the practical value of multiple accessible feedback routes, measures that distinguish experience from outcomes, and staff processes for interpreting and acting on comments. Digital collection alone can amplify selection and access biases. Associations between patient experience and quality do not establish that feedback interventions cause clinical improvement. Trust is plausibly shaped by clear communication and visible response, but the proposed pathway has not been tested as a whole in private online primary care. A feedback system should specify ownership, escalation, patient involvement, privacy, and a closed loop in which actions are documented and communicated. Prospective evaluation should measure reach, representativeness, action completion, and patient experience alongside safety indicators.</jats:p>

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831162.title: Binaural Speech and Distribution Learning for Predicting Auditory Distance Perception in Audio Augmented Reality
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831162.abstract: This article presents the first experiments aimed at predicting the physical distance that listeners attribute to speakers rendered in Audio Augmented Reality - virtual immersive environments that engage hearing but not other senses. This problem is significant because physical distance between individuals is more than geometric information; it is a factor that both shapes and is shaped by the social relationship between speaker and listener. The primary challenge is that, in the absence of visual cues, people often struggle to localize sound sources accurately and, consequently, to determine the position of a speaker they cannot see. For this reason, the experiments adopt a distribution learning approach, predicting not a single position but a probability density function over the space of possible positions. This approach better reflects the variability in attributed positions observed across multiple listeners for a given speech stimulus. The experiments were conducted using a publicly available corpus of 360 spatially rendered speech stimuli from 120 speakers (60 women and 60 men). The results show that the perceived distance can be predicted with correlation up to 0.79 and Mean Absolute Error as low as 41 cm.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831162.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.1145/3776574.3832489.title: Multimodal Deep Learning for Context-Aware Engagement Estimation in Online Learning
doi:10.1145/3776574.3832489.abstract: Student engagement estimation is a key challenge in online education, where instructors have limited access to the behavioral cues available in traditional classrooms. This paper presents our approach to the Context-Aware Student Engagement Detection (CASED) Challenge, which aims to estimate continuous engagement from multimodal recordings of online lectures. We propose a novel multimodal architecture that integrates student and instructor behavioral cues with audio streams, lecture-slide context, and personality metadata. Our approach demonstrates strong predictive capabilities, achieving a Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 0.03 and a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.14. Ablation experiments show that contextual information improves engagement estimation compared with student-centered behavioral cues alone. Despite these architectural optimizations, evaluating the model on unseen data underscores the challenge of predicting engagement using only 10-second temporal windows. Additionally, the absence of data on the student’s workspace, including screen positioning and user perspective, limits the ability to predict complex behavioral dynamics, which is fundamental for engagement prediction.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3832489.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0001.title: An Integrated AI Platform for Accelerating Semiconductor Failure Analysis: Combining Similarity Search, Deep-Learning Image Retrieval, Automated Labeling, and Ontology-Guided Workflow Assistance
doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0001.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Semiconductor failure analysis (FA) requires rapid access to relevant historical cases, consistent failure labeling, image-based pattern recognition, and methodologically correct investigation planning. In practice, these tasks are often supported by disconnected tools, leading to workflow friction and delayed root-cause identification. This paper presents AiFAct, an integrated, on-premise AI platform that supports the FA workflow end-to-end through six coordinated capabilities: multi-criteria similarity search with pair-specific reranking feedback, ontology-based automatic label prediction, quiz-based human verification for continuous model refinement, on-premise large language model (LLM) support for structured summaries and next-step proposals, deep-embedding image similarity for microscopy retrieval, and process-ontology-constrained workflow guidance. Unlike point solutions, the platform is designed as a closed feedback system where analyst interactions continuously improve ranking, labeling, and recommendation quality during routine work. In production-scale deployment across multi-site FA data, core candidate retrieval and reranking remains sub-second for candidate pools above 50,000 jobs, and analyst-facing query responses are delivered in under five seconds. The key contribution is workflow-level orchestration and feedback coupling rather than a single new standalone model. This architecture improves analyst trust through transparent scoring, supports knowledge transfer across sites, and preserves data sovereignty via fully on-premise operation.</jats:p>
doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0001.venue: International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831164.title: Distilling the Noise: Value-Aware Contrastive Hypergraph Learning for Robust Multimodal Rumor Detection
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831164.abstract: The proliferation of multimodal misinformation on social media poses significant challenges for rumor detection. Existing approaches typically treat user comments as homogeneous auxiliary features for aggregation. However, this assumption overlooks the significant heterogeneity in comment quality, where high-value comments containing logical reasoning are often submerged by varying degrees of emotional noise or coordinated manipulation, thereby degrading detection performance. To address the underutilization of comment signals and the poor signal-to-noise ratio, this paper proposes a Multiview Hypergraph-based Multimodal Rumor Detection (MHMRD) framework. Specifically, the framework operates in two key phases. First, we introduce a Value-Aware Comment Discrimination Module, which leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct value-aware supervision, training a discriminator to suppress low-utility noise while amplifying credible evidence. Second, we construct a Multi-Scale Hypergraph Network encompassing micro-scale (intra-modal), meso-scale (comment interaction), and macro-scale (inter-post) views to capture high-order semantic correlations. Finally, these heterogeneous views are jointly optimized via a Dual Contrastive Learning strategy to achieve deep feature alignment. Extensive experiments on the Weibo and PHEME datasets demonstrate that MHMRD significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating its effectiveness and robustness in complex social contexts.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831164.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831192.title: Investigating Foundation Models, Disentanglement and Latent Alignment for Subject-Independent EEG Learning
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831192.abstract: Brain–Computer Interfaces (BCIs) require models that generalize across subjects, yet EEG signals exhibit strong inter-subject variability and non-stationarity, leading to performance degradation on unseen users. This limitation is particularly critical in interactive and multimodal systems, where reliable, calibration-free decoding is essential for real-time interaction, and even minor errors can directly affect user experience. To address this challenge, several paradigms have been explored: foundation models leverage large-scale pretraining, disentangled representation learning aims to separate subject, task, and noise factors, and alignment methods focus on reducing distribution shifts in the feature space. Despite their promise, a systematic comparison of these approaches is still lacking. In this work, we propose a modular framework for the unified evaluation of these paradigms in subject-independent learning. We conduct extensive experiments on Motor Imagery (MI) and Event-Related Potential (ERP) datasets, representative of interactive BCI scenarios spanning both oscillatory (MI) and event-related (ERP) paradigms, to analyze their relative effectiveness and practical trade-offs. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/phuselab/eeg_subj_indep_learning.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831192.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11018779/v1.title: Explainable machine learning estimates clinically significant prostate cancer risk in men with PSA 4–20 ng/mL
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11018779/v1.abstract: Men with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) values of 4–20 ng/mL often have overlapping risks of benign disease, clinically insignificant prostate cancer, and clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa). We retrospectively studied 859 men who underwent pathological evaluation; 76 had csPCa. Twelve prediction algorithms were assessed with 500 bootstrap resamples. In every resample, LASSO feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, and model fitting used only the bootstrap training sample, and performance was estimated from patient-level out-of-bag predictions. C5.0 had the highest AUROC point estimate (0.843, 95% CI 0.801–0.886), an AUPRC of 0.421, and a Brier score of 0.066. Calibration was broadly concordant at low-to-moderate predicted risks but uncertain in the sparse high-risk tail. At a 0.10 risk threshold, the model would avoid 544.8 biopsies per 1,000 men while missing 10.5 csPCa cases per 1,000. PSA-derived measures supplied most of the linear predictive signal, whereas the clearest additional gain arose with nonlinear integration. C5.0 may support pre-biopsy triage, but multicenter external validation, recalibration assessment, and prospective impact studies are required before clinical use.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11018779/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0075.title: Automation in Microwave-Induced Plasma Decapsulation Verification through Machine Learning
doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0075.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Microwave-induced plasma (MIP) decapsulation of microchips traditionally requires constant manual monitoring and verification to ensure an optimized process, a time-consuming task for researchers. This paper explores the feasibility of utilising an AI-driven approach to automate both the operation and verification of the MIP process. By leveraging machine learning trained on a dedicated image database, the AI successfully managed the etching cycles to automatically halt the process upon full die exposure. Furthermore, the system demonstrated the potential to identify the decapsulation states of unknown microchip not included in the original training set. These results suggest a significant opportunity to streamline industrial workflows through AI and expand automated failure analysis to more advanced microchip packaging.</jats:p>
doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0075.venue: International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis

doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0043.title: Deep Learning-Based ROI Alignment for Automated SEM Workflows
doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0043.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Over the past several years, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) based automated acquisition workflows have been widely used in semiconductor analysis to rapidly inspect fine patterns and defects in advanced memory and non-memory devices. In particular, during repetitive high-magnification imaging across multilayer structures, pattern alignment that stably maintains the region of interest (ROI) is a critical factor governing metrology reliability and throughput. However, most automated SEM workflows rely on rule-based methods such as intensity-profile peak finders or template matching, whose fixed configuration cannot accommodate the full diversity of imaging conditions. This imposes two coupled costs that grow as conditions diversify: the lower success rate forces repeated reacquisition that consumes instrument time, while restoring accuracy requires repeated manual re-tuning that consumes operator time. In this study, a deep learning ROI recognition framework based on a one-stage object detection model and a semantic segmentation model was evaluated within the Thermo Fisher iFast automation workflow for a NAND SEM workflow, and was compared with a conventional rule-based edge-finder baseline (intensity-profile peak detection) under the same Test-set and operational-specification conditions. The evaluation tasks consisted of (i) word-line (WL) nitride-layer-band alignment and (ii) channel-hole (CH) centering using adjacent word-line-cut patterns as recognition references. Approximately 200 SEM images were collected per task, and evaluation was performed on a fixed Test set of 30 images while varying training-set size (N_train) from 10 to 136 (step 10). On the 30-image Test set, both deep learning models substantially improved operational metrics over the edge-finder baseline (WL: success rate 74.8% → 98.1-99.4%, F1 72.5% → 98.7-99.7%; CH: success rate/F1 100%, FP/FN = 0). Together with single-image end-to-end inference latency below 20 ms for both models, these results confirm that both models provide alignment reliability and real-time feasibility sufficient for deployment in automation workflows.</jats:p>
doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0043.venue: International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831218.title: MapQA: A Map-Question-Answering Benchmark for Visual Language Model Reasoning
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831218.abstract: Maps are central to how humans make sense of the world, from navigation and environmental monitoring to military planning and historical interpretation. Yet despite rapid progress in large multimodal models (LMMs), these systems continue to struggle with interpreting maps – an essential skill for visual reasoning that goes beyond pattern recognition and text extraction. To further progress toward this capability, we introduce MapQA, the first large-scale benchmark specifically designed to evaluate LMMs on map understanding. MapQA contains over 9,700 carefully curated, open-ended question–answer pairs spanning diverse map types, each constructed to require reasoning directly from the map rather than relying on memorized world knowledge. Benchmark questions were generated through a scalable human-in-the-loop process to ensure quality, and evaluated using an LLM-as-a-judge protocol aligned with human judgments. Our experiments show that while humans answer over 91% of questions correctly, state-of-the-art proprietary models achieve barely a third of that performance, with open-source models below 30%. These findings highlight a substantial gap between human and machine map understanding, underscoring the need for benchmarks like MapQA to guide future progress in multimodal reasoning.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831218.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831224.title: Self-Supervised Dual-Stream Temporal Learning for Neonatal Pain Estimation
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831224.abstract: Neonatal pain estimation from video is clinically important but challenging due to limited labelled data and the reliance of existing automated methods on facial appearance alone. Current approaches use handcrafted features or single-frame deep representations, overlooking the temporal body dynamics (such as limb flexion, postural tension, and rhythmic movement) that clinicians routinely use alongside facial cues. We propose a self-supervised dual-stream temporal framework that combines facial and body information for framewise pain-score regression on APN-db. A face encoder is pretrained via contrastive learning on unlabelled neonatal video, producing domain-adapted features that substantially outperform generic pretrained representations. These frozen features, together with body-pose keypoints, are passed through separate temporal transformer encoders over short windows before learned gated fusion. This design captures body-pain dynamics that are invisible in single frames while leveraging unlabelled data to overcome the label-scarcity bottleneck. We evaluate under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation on two dataset splits and demonstrate substantial improvements over the prior APN-db benchmark, reducing mean absolute error by \(35\%\) on our primary split and \(25\%\) on a like-for-like reconstruction of the benchmark subset. A complementary experiment using a movement-derived target further validates that the dual-stream architecture effectively fuses body information when the prediction target depends on it.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831224.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0435.title: A Comparative Evaluation of Rule-Based and Deep Learning Approaches for SAM Inspection of QFN Packages
doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0435.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM) is increasingly employed in the up-screening of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) components for high-reliability applications, enabling detection of latent, field-failure-symptomatic, package-level defects beyond the reach of electrical test or visual inspection. As inspection volumes and acceptance stringency continue to grow, automated SAM image analysis is critical to sustaining throughput, consistency, and standards compliance. This work presents a comparative evaluation of two automated SAM inspection paradigms applied to Quad Flat No-Lead (QFN) packages: classical rule-based machine vision and supervised deep-learning inspection. Both approaches were assessed on identical top side and bottom side SAM datasets against industry-standard-informed customer requirements, using classification metrics and region-level spatial agreement relevant to quantitative accept/reject criteria. Deep learning models achieved strong classification performance for complex top side defect morphologies, while rule-based inspection demonstrated superior accuracy for bottom side die-attach voiding and perimeter delamination, where precise area-based thresholds govern acceptance. Limitations in region-level quantification, sensitivity to scan variability, and near-threshold classification were observed for the deep learning approach. These findings indicate that a hybrid strategy—combining deep learning for complex defect detection with rule-based analysis for standards-driven quantification—offers the most robust and defensible framework for automated SAM screening in high-reliability QFN up-screening workflows.</jats:p>
doi:10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2026p0435.venue: International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis

doi:10.1145/3776574.3828962.title: Multimodal detection and classification of humor in human-human and human-machine interactions
doi:10.1145/3776574.3828962.abstract: Humor is a fundamental of human communication. Integrating humor into human-computer interaction (HCI) is essential for developing conversational agents with a more natural and fluid communication. However, the computational recognition of humor remains a significant challenge due to its subjective. This PhD thesis focuses on the multimodal detection and classification of humor in informatics systems. This paper outlines a comprehensive research plan to investigate and model the mechanisms of humor detection. We first present the current state of the art in the field, followed by a discussion of our prior research and the preliminary results obtained thus far. Finally, we conclude by outlining the future perspectives and research directions to be explored.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3828962.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.1145/3776574.3832530.title: MULTIDATA: An Interactive Web Platform for Speech-Gesture Data Extraction and Visualization
doi:10.1145/3776574.3832530.abstract: Video collections contain rich evidence of multimodal interaction, but transforming audiovisual material into analyzable outputs often requires separate tools for transcription, acoustic analysis, pose extraction, annotation, and visualization. We present MULTIDATA, a free web-based platform that orchestrates speech and gesture processing in an interactive workflow. The demostration shows how a user can upload several short videos, generate time-stamped speech information, extract body keypoints, compute acoustic and prosodic measures, inspect time and frame indexed outputs, and export the files produced by the selected tools. The system integrates components such as whisperX for transcription and audio alignment, Speech Analysis and Praat for acoustic measurements, and OpenPose and MediaPipe for pose estimation. Its principal contribution is the web-based orchestration layer that makes multimodal processing accessible without requiring users to install heterogeneous tools, configure processing pipelines, or provide their own GPU hardware.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3832530.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.1145/3776574.3831212.title: Interoception-Inspired Emotion Estimation via Intrinsic Diffuseness-Guided Learning
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831212.abstract: Continuous emotion estimation from neurophysiological signals remains challenging due to multimodal heterogeneity, inter-individual variability, and the diffuse nature of emotional experience. Existing methods mainly emphasize signal-level fusion or label-level uncertainty modeling, while providing limited treatment of latent internal-state mechanisms underlying emotional feeling. We propose an interoception-inspired framework for continuous emotion estimation. The framework models emotional feeling through the Brain-inferred Body State, the Interoceptive Error, and their gain-modulated integration, and further introduces Emotional Diffuseness over continuous valence–arousal space to guide non-uniform supervision. Emotional Diffuseness is quantified from contextualized feeling expressions via a Bayesian embedding-to-affective projection, yielding a continuous diffuseness field over affective space. Experiments on the DEAP dataset under leave-one-subject-out evaluation show that the proposed method achieves effective continuous regression and competitive classification performance. Ablation results further confirm the contributions of both explicit interoceptive modeling and diffuseness-guided supervision. These suggest that organizing emotion estimation around internal-state mechanisms and affective diffuseness provides a promising direction for physiological emotion modeling.
doi:10.1145/3776574.3831212.venue: Proceedings of the 28th International Conference On Multimodal Interaction

doi:10.63498/injelps110.title: School administrators’ feedback styles and their relationship with teachers’ work motivation in public secondary schools in Ligao City, Albay
doi:10.63498/injelps110.abstract: Aim: This study examined school administrators' feedback styles and their relationship with public secondary school teachers' work motivation in Ligao City, Albay.It also identified teachers' challenges in receiving administrative feedback and used the combined findings to formulate an intervention for educational leadership and teacher professional development.Methodology: A concurrent-parallel mixed-methods design integrated a descriptive-correlational quantitative strand and a descriptive qualitative strand.The quantitative phase involved 251 teachers from 12 public secondary schools selected through proportionate random sampling, while 30 teachers participated in semi-structured interviews.Data were collected through a 40-item Feedback Style Questionnaire, a Teachers' Work Motivation Questionnaire adapted from the Work Tasks Motivation Scale for Teachers, and an expert-reviewed interview guide.Means, standard deviations, and Pearson's r were used for quantitative analysis, while thematic analysis was used for qualitative data.Results: All four feedback styles were very evident: result-oriented (M = 3.86), relational (M = 3.84), balanced (M = 3.64), and non-directive (M = 3.63).Overall work motivation was high (M = 5.94), with intrinsic motivation highest (M = 6.39) and extrinsic motivation lowest (M = 5.40).The overall relationship between feedback styles and work motivation was not statistically significant (r = .10,p = .11),although several relationships between specific feedback styles and motivational dimensions were significant.Eight qualitative themes described inconsistent feedback, faultfocused delivery, lack of specificity, public criticism, perceived bias, excessive monitoring, limited emotional support, and compliance emphasis over instructional support.Conclusion: Administrative feedback styles were significantly related to selected motivational dimensions but were not significantly related to overall work motivation.The findings support a developmental feedback approach that combines performance information with consistency, specificity, reflection, relational support, and instructional coaching.Project FEED-Motivate was proposed as an institution-level intervention.

doi:10.59256/indjcst.20260503021.title: Wheat Fungal Disease Detection Using a U-NET Deep Learning Model
doi:10.59256/indjcst.20260503021.abstract: <jats:p>world’s important cereal it often falls victim to diseases like Fusarium Head Blight (FHB) and rust. These diseases can seriously reduce wheat yields and threaten food supplies. Traditionally, identifying these diseases relies on experts carefully examining the plants by hand can be quite subjective. As a result, early and precise diagnosis is still difficult, hence the impetus for automated solutions. We suggest an automatic deep-learning solution for wheat disease segmentation and detection to overcome these issues. We utilize Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to obtain stable image-based classification and accurate symptom localization of the disease. In particular, EfficientNetB0 is used for disease classification because it is efficient and accurate, while a specially designed U-Net model is utilized for pixel-wise segmentation of infected areas. The experimental environment uses Kaggle's free GPU power for model training, OpenCV for image pre-processing, and TensorFlow/Keras for implementation. Significant hyperparameter optimization (tuning learning rates and batch sizes) is done to achieve optimal performance. In a series of experiments on a wheat disease image dataset, the suggested system.</jats:p>

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c04563.title: Niche Divergence-Based Identification of Microbial Indicators Tracking Cyanobacterial Bloom Succession: A Metagenomic and Machine Learning Framework
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c04563.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs) pose significant environmental and public health risks through toxin production, antibiotic resistance gene dissemination, and the disruption of biogeochemical cycles. Although extensive metagenomic investigations have explored microbial interactions between Cyanobacteria and coexisting members, the potential of incorporating functional indicators into early CyanoHAB monitoring systems remains underexplored. In this study, we employed metagenomic binning combined with machine learning approaches to analyze seasonal cyanobacterial succession and coexisting microbial communities across 19 sites in Erhai Lake across four seasons. We documented distinct niche shifts driven by the spatiotemporal heterogeneity in seasonal cyanobacterial succession alongside the formation of unique niches triggered by this asynchrony. Specialized microbial members (SN-MAGs) were identified as candidate bioindicators associated with early-stage cyanobacterial proliferation. Functional profiling showed r/K selection and metabolic adaptations in these SN-MAGs, including stress resistance and altered carbon metabolism, linked to cyanobacterial dynamics. Machine learning models leveraging these features were constructed and retrospectively evaluated. Cross-lake validation using an independent Lake Taihu dataset confirmed associations among these features and microbial community shifts preceding Microcystis proliferation. Our findings highlight the potential value of the dynamics of specific bacteria as a sensitive indicator of cyanobacterial dynamics. Moreover, we propose that these identified functional markers could potentially be developed into targeted molecular assays (e.g., qPCR assays), offering possible utility in predicting Microcystis population expansion.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73779-y.title: An adaptive federated few-shot learning method with intelligent device selection
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73779-y.abstract: Federated learning, which enables the training of intelligent models without transferring data and solely by relying on the computational capabilities of distributed devices, faces significant challenges in few-shot scenarios due to data heterogeneity, resource constraints, and slow convergence. The primary obstacle lies in the optimal selection of participating devices, as suboptimal choices can reduce model accuracy and substantially increase latency. In this study, we introduce AdaptFFSL-DS, an adaptive decision-making framework for Federated Few-Shot Learning. By integrating ResFed as the local model with an intelligent device-selection agent, this method first evaluates the system-level and statistical characteristics of each device and then selects an appropriate subset of devices for each learning round. Furthermore, by adaptively adjusting the number of local epochs, the framework maintains an effective balance between accuracy and latency. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach reduces the estimated aggregate device-latency by nearly one-third without a notable loss in accuracy and delivers up to 11.88% higher accuracy compared to intelligently tuned FedProx. Moreover, AdaptFFSL-DS remains robust under various forms of heterogeneity, shows low sensitivity to an increasing number of devices, and maintains its effectiveness even under limited-data conditions.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-72875-3.title: A machine learning framework for predicting potential urban cool island locations using Landsat 9 data: a case study of Oued Zenati, Algeria
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-72875-3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Urban heat stress is increasing in semi-arid Mediterranean towns, making the identification of Urban Cool Island (UCI) patterns essential for climate-resilient urban planning. This study developed an integrated remote sensing, GIS, and explainable machine-learning framework to map potential UCI locations in Oued Zenati, northeastern Algeria, using Landsat 9 imagery and geospatial environmental variables processed in Google Earth Engine. ArcGIS Desktop 10.8 was used for the final cartographic layout and map generation. Predictor variables included land surface temperature, albedo, elevation, slope, distance to roads, distance to rivers, and population density. Because field observations of UCIs were unavailable, proxy reference samples were generated from vegetation, moisture, and built-up indicators. Under the prevailing semi-arid conditions, NDWI values remained below − 0.06 across the study area, and all cool-zone reference samples were therefore derived from the vegetation criterion (NDVI ≥ 0.20). Four machine-learning algorithms (Random Forest, Gradient Tree Boosting, CART, and MaxEnt) were evaluated using a 70/30 training-testing split and independent validation. Gradient Tree Boosting achieved the highest discrimination ability (ROC-AUC = 0.916), whereas Random Forest provided the best threshold-dependent performance, with an accuracy of 0.900, Kappa of 0.800, Precision of 0.929, and F1-score of 0.897. Susceptibility maps showed that cooling potential is concentrated in vegetated and agricultural areas, while built-up and bare surfaces exhibit low cooling potential. SHAP analysis identified elevation as the most influential predictor, followed by slope, albedo, and land surface temperature, whereas distance to roads, distance to rivers, and population density exerted comparatively weaker effects. The proposed framework provides a robust, interpretable, and transferable approach for Urban Cool Island susceptibility mapping, supporting climate adaptation, green infrastructure planning, and sustainable urban development in semi-arid cities.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s41666-026-00255-7.title: Swarm Learning And Clinical Data: Evaluating The Benefit of a New Node For The Whole Network
doi:10.1007/s41666-026-00255-7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Digital technologies in healthcare have significantly enhanced clinical decision-making with complex data analysis. However, single clinical centers often lack sufficient data volume or diversity for effective modeling. Distributed learning solutions help to overcome these limitations, and in particular, Swarm Learning (SL) offers a privacy-preserving solution by allowing a decentralized and synchronized model training across multiple centers without direct data sharing. Swarm Learning’s inherent focus on data privacy makes it well-suited for distributed healthcare analysis. However, no studies have quantified the impact of an external individual center that wants to join the swarm network in terms of performance and fairness. In this paper, we propose an approach for evaluating the benefits from the point of view of both a new center and the existing swarm network, based on the amount of data introduced by the new center. We also present seven different Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) to measure the impact of the new center under different aspects related to the performance variation, model stability, fairness, and quality of the newly introduced data. We apply these indicators using real Intensive Care Unit (ICU) data from the
                    <jats:italic>MIMIC-III</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>MIMIC-IV</jats:italic>
                    datasets, and we analyze the impact of the new center based on different data distribution scenarios and different numbers of centers in the network.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s40948-026-01185-9.title: A machine-learning model for predicting sand production onset under true triaxial stresses based on CFD-DEM simulation dataset
doi:10.1007/s40948-026-01185-9.abstract: Predicting and managing sand production has become a critical research focus in geo-energy systems such as natural gas hydrates, petroleum extraction, geothermal energy, and underground hydrogen storage due to the safety risks associated with sand production during and after extraction processes. This work identifies the dependence of the critical drawdown pressure gradient of sand production on particle size distribution, true triaxial stresses, and slot width. Based on Particle Flow Code (PFC) software, a validated computational fluid dynamics and discrete element method (CFD-DEM) numerical model was applied for fluid-sand flow simulation behind the sand control equipment, e.g., slotted liner or wire-wrapped screen. A machine-learning model based on the CFD-DEM simulation dataset was developed using SPSS to predict the critical drawdown promptly. We found that some extreme values (D0, D10, and D100), the mid-value (D70) of particle size distribution, and the stress along the short axis of the slot are the key factors affecting the critical drawdown pressure gradient. Overall, the machine-learning model presented in this study offers a fast and reliable prediction of sand production. The model improves sand management and well productivity by allowing adjustments in wire spacing, slot width, and mechanical strength. It can also be easily installed on mobile devices and used at oil and gas development sites.
doi:10.1007/s40948-026-01185-9.venue: Geomechanics and Geophysics for Geo-Energy and Geo-Resources

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73768-1.title: Spectral index and machine learning-based evaluation of coastal urban thermal dynamics using google earth engine
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73768-1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This present study introduces a cloud-based geospatial and machine learning framework for assessing coastal urban heat island (UHI) dynamics in Thoothukudi coastal region, Southern India, using 12 seasonal Landsat composites (2010–2025) processed through Google Earth Engine (GEE). Seasonal classification followed Indian Meteorological Department definitions: Summer (March-June), Northeast Monsoon (October-November) and Winter (December-February). Multi-sensor Landsat Collection 2 Tier 1 Level-2 data included Landsat 5/7 (2010), Landsat 8 (2015) and Landsat 8/9 (2020, 2025). Land surface temperature (LST) was retrieved using USGS Collection 2 scale-factor protocol, capped to 0–65 °C to suppress cloud-contaminated pixels. UHI intensity (UHI = LST − P₂₅(LST)) and Urban Thermal Field Variance Index (UTFVI) were computed alongside four spectral indices (NDVI, NDBI, NDWI, NDMI). Summer was the hottest season in three of four observation years (mean LST: 38.69–48.67 °C). The 2020 Northeast Monsoon composite was excluded due to cloud contamination. Mean UHI intensity ranged from 2.03 to 5.17 °C. Pearson correlation confirmed NDBI as the strongest positive LST predictor (
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                     = 0.30–0.60), while NDMI mirrors this inversely. Random Forest and Gradient Tree Boosting models were trained on seven predictors using dual validation (70/30 split and 2 km spatial block cross-validation). Model performance yielded R² of 0.301–0.476 and RMSE of 2.74–6.23 °C with physically realistic values. GTB permutation feature importance identified NDBI and SWIR1 as dominant predictors. Ensemble scenario illustrations for 2030 and 2050, presented as linear extrapolations rather than climate-model forecasts, suggest sustained thermal stress in industrial and port zones with explicit uncertainty quantification (± 2.75 to ± 8.61 °C). The study demonstrates that rigorously validated Landsat time-series analysis provides actionable coastal urban thermal intelligence for heat adaptation planning aligned with SDGs 11, 13 and 3. The framework is applied here as the first four-epoch, IMD-season-resolved thermal characterisation of the Thoothukudi coast and the 2030 and 2050 outputs are intended to support the spatial targeting of persistent thermal hotspots rather than the prediction of absolute future temperatures.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.32628/cseit2612517.title: SkillSense: A Context-Aware Machine Learning Framework for Automated Skill Scoring in Resumes
doi:10.32628/cseit2612517.abstract: <jats:p>Keyword-based applicant tracking systems treat every mention of a skill as equal evidence of competence and therefore overlook qualified candidates whose resumes do not reproduce the exact phrasing of a job description. This paper presents SkillSense, a context-aware machine learning framework that extracts skills from resumes and scores their relevance to a target job role. The framework combines transformer-based named entity recognition for skill extraction, normalisation against the O*NET taxonomy, feature engineering that fuses TF-IDF vectors, 768-dimensional BERT embeddings and candidate metadata, and an attention-weighted scoring function that accounts for the priority of each requirement in the job description, the industry domain and the experience level. Six supervised classifiers (Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, XGBoost and a fine-tuned BERT classifier) were compared with five-fold stratified cross-validation on a curated dataset of 1,200 anonymised resumes and 350 job descriptions from five domains, of which 500 resume–job pairs were labelled by expert annotators. The BERT classifier performed best, reaching 95.1% accuracy, 0.942 precision, 0.929 recall and a 0.935 F1-score, while XGBoost was the strongest classical model at 93.4% accuracy. Context-aware weighting improved performance by 12–15% over context-agnostic baselines. SkillSense has been deployed as a three-tier web application that returns ranked candidates with a 0–100 score and a Recommended / Not-Recommended label, giving recruiters consistent, comparable and role-specific evidence for shortlisting.</jats:p>
doi:10.32628/cseit2612517.venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Computer Science, Engineering and Information Technology

doi:10.65021/mwsj.v2.i3.51.title: Predicting Electric Vehicle Adoption Intention Using Machine Learning: An AI-Driven Framework for Charging Infrastructure Planning in Karnataka, India
doi:10.65021/mwsj.v2.i3.51.abstract: <jats:p>Forecasting electric-vehicle (EV) demand is important for charging-infrastructure planning, but aggregate sales models offer limited insight into which consumers are considering a purchase. The study's methodological contribution is a reproducible, leakage-controlled workflow that applies machine-learning classifiers to primary survey data to predict individual purchase consideration in a secondary-city context, as a complement to aggregate forecasts. A convenience and snowball sample of 175 respondents was drawn from Mysuru and surrounding districts of Karnataka, India; the analysis used the 162 non-EV owners (117 Yes/Maybe; 45 No). Logistic regression and random forest classifiers were compared using stratified five-fold cross-validation. Random forest achieved pooled out-of-fold accuracy of 0.784 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.722–0.846) and ROC-AUC of 0.843 (95% CI: 0.784–0.898), compared with 0.735 and 0.823 for logistic regression; repeated cross-validation gave slightly lower but consistent estimates. Attitude-related measures ranked highest, but their importance is predictive, not causal. Because the sample is small and non-probabilistic, the findings are a methodological proof of concept that requires external validation, not a tool ready for planning use.</jats:p>

doi:10.1111/jvp.70112.title: From Drug Knowledge to Therapeutic Competence: Active Learning for Competency‐Based Veterinary Pharmacology Education
doi:10.1111/jvp.70112.abstract: Veterinary education has changed substantially over recent decades.Integrated curricula and competency-based veterinary education (CBVE et al. 2024) have prompted a transition from traditional didactic instruction to teaching focused on the development and assessment of clinical competencies.This is an important change that creates a particular challenge for pharmacology.Pharmacology is distributed across organ systems, species and stages of the curriculum; when it is integrated without deliberate design, the discipline can become fragmented, the education of its core concepts (Guilding et al. 2023) may be overlooked, and assessment may no longer incorporate meaningful pharmacological competence evaluation.The result is a risk that students learn lists of drugs without developing the reasoning required to select, prescribe and monitor treatment for patients.The eight contributions in this Special Issue offer practical responses to that challenge.Across different institutions, countries and learner groups, they show how pharmacology can be made visible within an integrated curriculum when competencies are mapped deliberately, learning is active and assessment reflects professional practice.Together, they support a central proposition: pharmacology should not be protected merely as a body of knowledge; it should be designed as a set of observable competences that underpin safe and evidence-informed therapeutic practice.
doi:10.1111/jvp.70112.venue: Journal of Veterinary Pharmacology and Therapeutics

doi:10.31235/osf.io/zy7ua_v1.title: Machine-Learning Geographic Sampling Frames Underrepresent People on the Move in Fragile Settings
doi:10.31235/osf.io/zy7ua_v1.abstract: Political science research often studies difficult-to-locate populations: internally displaced persons (IDPs), returnees, migrants, and others who move during war, disaster,or crisis. We compare machine-learning (ML)-generated building footprints against high-resolution satellite imagery for constructing sampling frames. In displacement-affected communities in Iraq, 15.5% of ML points were invalid or duplicated, and manual additions constituted 19% of the final hybrid frame. Manual additions reached10.2 percentage points more IDPs in rural communities and 10.1 more returnees in urban areas. We attribute differences to two mechanisms: temporary and informalshelters are harder for ML algorithms to detect, while post-bombardment reconstruction can create structures absent from the imagery underlying ML frames. ML-onlyframes produce systematic coverage error, and targeted satellite validation can reduce it.

doi:10.65881/creative.v1i4.205.title: Pemetaan learning agility siswa SMK sebagai fondasi menyiapkan generasi adaptif menghadapi dunia kerja
doi:10.65881/creative.v1i4.205.abstract:
<jats:p>Tujuan: untuk memetakan tingkat learning agility siswa SMK serta mengidentifikasi kecenderungannya berdasarkan gender, usia, dan jurusan sebagai dasar penyusunan rekomendasi penguatan kesiapan kerja siswa.
Metode: kegiatan pengabdian ini menggunakan pendekatan needs assessment melalui pemetaan psikologis terhadap 163 siswa kelas XII di sebuah SMK di Yogyakarta. Data dikumpulkan menggunakan skala learning agility 24 item dengan empat pilihan respons, kemudian dianalisis secara deskriptif untuk memperoleh profil dan kategorisasi learning agility. Analisis tambahan dilakukan untuk mengidentifikasi kecenderungan perbedaan berdasarkan gender, usia, dan jurusan.
Hasil: mayoritas siswa memiliki learning agility tinggi, tanpa perbedaan yang berarti berdasarkan gender, usia, dan jurusan. Temuan ini menjadi dasar rekomendasi penguatan learning agility melalui layanan BK, refleksi PKL, dan pembelajaran adaptif.
Kesimpulan: siswa memiliki modal learning agility yang baik sebagai fondasi kesiapan menghadapi dunia kerja. Hasil pemetaan dapat menjadi dasar bagi sekolah untuk merancang penguatan learning agility secara terarah dan berkelanjutan.
Kontribusi: menyediakan profil learning agility siswa sebagai dasar bagi sekolah dalam merancang program pendampingan dan penguatan kesiapan kerja yang berbasis kebutuhan.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s13148-026-02244-4.title: Liquid biopsy, cfDNA, and machine learning: an integrative approach to cardiovascular diseases
doi:10.1186/s13148-026-02244-4.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) and their complications remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide. However, obtaining diseased cardiovascular tissue is often invasive, costly, and clinically impractical, highlighting the need for noninvasive approaches that can capture dynamic pathological information. Cell-free DNA (cfDNA)-based liquid biopsy has emerged as a promising strategy for the diagnosis, monitoring, and risk assessment of CVDs. As cfDNA is released from injured, dying, or stressed cells, it carries multiple layers of biological information, including concentration changes, tissue-of-origin signatures, fragmentation patterns, nucleosome footprints, mitochondrial DNA signals, and epigenetic modifications. These signals can reflect global cellular injury, identify tissue origin, and indicate inflammatory or mitochondrial stress. Current cardiovascular evidence is unevenly distributed: donor-derived cfDNA has shown the strongest clinical relevance in heart transplant rejection surveillance; cfDNA concentration, cardiomyocyte-specific methylation, and fragmentomic features show promise in myocardial infarction, heart failure, and selected aortic diseases, whereas applications in hypertension, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, and cardiomyopathy remain exploratory. Among cfDNA features, methylation is especially informative because it provides stable tissue- and disease-associated signatures; however, methylation datasets are typically high-dimensional, sparse, and affected by low disease-derived cfDNA fractions. Machine learning may help address these challenges by selecting informative features, integrating methylation with fragmentomic and nucleosomal signals, and developing models for diagnosis, prognosis, tissue-of-origin inference, and longitudinal monitoring. In this review, we summarize the biological characteristics of cfDNA, evaluate its current applications in major CVDs, highlight how machine learning may improve cfDNA interpretation, and discuss key barriers to clinical translation.
