doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202660312.title: The NEMESIS general young stellar object catalogue. I. Supervised classification with deep learning methods
doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202660312.abstract:
<jats:p>In modern large-scale photometric surveys, young stellar objects (YSOs) are mostly identified by the infrared excess seen in their spectral energy distributions (SEDs). To this end, YSO identification and classification were mostly based on certain colours specific to a dataset, resulting in wavelength-specific methods and catalogues. However, a uniformly classified YSO catalogue can be constructed by using all available data and applying the same identification method to heterogeneous literature samples, thereby reducing systematic differences between catalogues and enabling more consistent studies of YSO populations and star formation.
Our primary goal is to develop a method that takes advantage of the heterogeneous data available in the VizieR database and to provide a tool that can be easily used to identify YSOs with a high accuracy. We also aim to create the largest homogeneous catalogue of YSOs to date.
We used the CDS VizieR and NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) databases to collect data for a large number of celestial objects of various types. The data collected include SEDs, photometric light curves, and direct imaging data, and they were used to build different image representations for our list of sources. These image representations were used to teach deep learning algorithms to differentiate between YSOs and all other types of sources. Established architectures from the library and custom-built convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were applied to create an ensemble of binary classifiers specialised in identifying YSOs against other types of astrophysical sources. PyTorch
The resulting method is able to automatically identify YSO candidates with an accuracy higher than 90%, while contamination is identified with an accuracy higher than 99%. We applied our classifier to numerous YSO catalogues from the literature to confirm the youth of the stars listed there and to create the largest catalogue of homogeneously identified potential YSOs ever, the NEMESIS General YSO (NGYSO) catalogue, which contains 274,408 unique high-reliability YSOs. Their positions on the colour-magnitude diagrams and their distribution relative to the local Galactic structures were also used to test their young nature.</jats:p>

doi:10.20319/ictel.2026.326327.title: ENCOURAGING ORAL ENGLISH IN NON-ENGLISH-SPEAKING CONTEXTS: PLAY-BASED STRATEGIES AND CLASSROOM CASES FROM EARLY EFL LEARNERS
doi:10.20319/ictel.2026.326327.abstract: <jats:p>In many non-English-speaking contexts, young learners are expected to speak English before they feel confident or emotionally ready. As a result, early English education often becomes stressful and accuracy-focused, which can reduce learners’ willingness to speak. This presentation explores practical ways to encourage oral English in EFL classrooms through play-based learning, without relying on early phonics instruction or formal academic structures. Based on classroom experiences from a private English academy in a non-English-speaking environment, this session shares case-based strategies used with early learners. The approach emphasizes emotional safety, meaningful interaction, and play as the foundation for oral output. Activities such as role play, storytelling, guided games, and interactive routines are used to create natural opportunities for learners to speak English voluntarily. Classroom observations indicate that when pressure is reduced and engagement is increased, learners begin to produce spontaneous oral English, even with limited vocabulary and without explicit phonics instruction at the early stages. These imperfect utterances are treated as part of natural language development rather than errors requiring immediate correction. This presentation highlights how play-based oral activities can support confidence, motivation, and willingness to communicate in EFL settings where exposure to English is limited. Participants will gain realistic, classroom-tested strategies that can be applied in non-English-speaking contexts to help young learners move from silence to speech in a low-stress learning environment.</jats:p>
doi:10.20319/ictel.2026.326327.venue: PUPIL: International Journal of Teaching, Education and Learning

doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1941799.title: Early prediction of gestational diabetes mellitus using deep learning applied to routinely collected clinical data
doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1941799.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prediction of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) in early pregnancy enables timely, targeted interventions to reduce risks for both the mother and fetus. We aimed to improve early GDM prediction and clinical risk stratification using a novel deep learning (DL) approach that transforms tabular clinical data into images using a genetic algorithm.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A dataset of 1,611 pregnancies was used. The dataset contained routinely collected early-pregnancy data, including clinical measurements, blood tests, and medical history. A novel method to transform tabular data into images was applied to enable the use of deep learning models for GDM prediction. A genetic algorithm optimized the spatial arrangement of variables during image generation by determining their spatial positions. Interpretability was assessed using gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) to identify variables the model preferentially attended to for positive and negative predictions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multiple model configurations were evaluated by varying the spatial arrangement of variables within the transformation. Prioritizing high sensitivity, one model achieved an accuracy of 0.86, sensitivity of 0.82, specificity of 0.87, and an AUC-ROC of 0.83. Another model achieved an accuracy of 0.79, sensitivity of 0.92, specificity of 0.77, and an AUC-ROC of 0.85. Compared with previously published machine learning models using the same dataset, our approach demonstrated improved performance. Our best models increased specificity by an average of 13.93 percentage points compared with traditional ML models at matched sensitivity levels, thereby reducing false-positive classifications that may lead to additional clinical evaluation. Grad-CAM analysis revealed that attention patterns of the model aligned with established clinical risk factors for GDM, with first trimester fasting glycemia and parity preferentially attended for positive predictions and maternal weight for negative predictions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study demonstrates that transforming tabular clinical data into image representations, optimized using a genetic algorithm, improves early GDM prediction. Representing tabular variables as images enables more effective application of DL models, which have demonstrated enhanced pattern recognition in image-based tasks compared with traditional machine learning methods. Performance improvements over state-of-the-art approaches were achieved. Accurate DL models can be developed using a limited number of input variables, supporting early identification of women at increased risk of GDM and facilitating timely clinical management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1932015.title: Optimizing multi-class intrusion detection in IIoT: advanced feature selection using grey wolf optimizer and machine learning classifiers
doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1932015.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid expansion of the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) has increased the cyberattack surface of industrial infrastructures, creating demand for intrusion detection systems (IDS) that combine predictive performance with deployment efficiency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study proposes a Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO)-guided fixed top-k feature-ranking framework for multi-class IIoT intrusion detection using candidate-dependent redundancy regularization, class-weighted learning, stratified cross-validation, repeated runs, and independent holdout evaluation. The framework was evaluated on the CIC IIoT Dataset 2025 and independently assessed on Edge-IIoTset as a secondary benchmark across six machine learning classifiers and several feature-selection baselines.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      On CIC IIoT Dataset 2025, Random Forest and Decision Tree achieved holdout Macro-F1 scores of 0.9389 and 0.9330, respectively, using only 10 selected features, representing an 85.92% reduction from the 71-feature model-input space. Repeated training-only comparisons showed significant overall differences among GWO, BA, LightGBM, and Boruta (Friedman
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                      ² = 16.920,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.000734; Kendall’s
                      <jats:italic>W</jats:italic>
                      = 0.564); GWO outperformed BA and LightGBM after Holm correction but did not differ significantly from Boruta. Ablation analysis further showed lower feature redundancy under adaptive regularization, although its predictive advantage was not statistically significant. Results on Edge-IIoTset showed that feature-selection effectiveness is dataset dependent.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Overall, the proposed framework provides a practical balance between predictive performance, feature compactness, and computational efficiency for resource-constrained IIoT intrusion detection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1007/s11251-026-09819-x.title: Deliberate erring improves scientific reasoning: Learning experimentation skills by intentionally designing invalid experiments
doi:10.1007/s11251-026-09819-x.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Mastering skills in designing valid, controlled experiments is foundational for scientific reasoning and inquiry. Whereas prevailing interventions to develop experimentation skills often induce cognitive conflict through comparing others’ invalid experiments with valid ones, this study tested the hypothesis that deliberately committing and correcting one’s own errors in invalid designs yields better learning and transfer than studying others’ errors. University students (
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 276) were instructed on experimental design principles (e.g., control of variables), then practiced applying them using one of three learning methods:
                    <jats:italic>derr-explain-fix</jats:italic>
                    (intentionally designing an invalid experiment then explaining and correcting one’s deliberate errors) or
                    <jats:italic>spot-explain-fix</jats:italic>
                    (spotting, explaining, and correcting others’ deliberate errors in invalid designs) or
                    <jats:italic>errorless practice</jats:italic>
                    (designing a valid experiment and explaining it). All students were then tested on their near and far transfer in designing an experiment that was structurally analogous to or more complex than the one during practice. They were also assessed on critiquing a given design’s validity, and their negative knowledge in anticipating problem-specific design errors. Both errorful learning methods outperformed errorless practice on the near transfer, design critique, and error anticipation tests. Crucially, the derr-explain-fix method improved near and far transfer more than the spot-explain-fix method, which did not yield better far transfer than errorless practice. Yet, students lacked metacognitive awareness of the benefits of deliberate erring and, more broadly, errorful learning. Overall, these findings demonstrate that intentionally designing and correcting one’s own invalid experiments during practice is an effective way to enhance learning and transfer of experimental design principles.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1080/10447318.2026.2734326.title: Understanding Practices, Device Ecologies, and Challenges in Video-Based Software Learning: An Empirical Study and Design Opportunities
doi:10.1080/10447318.2026.2734326.abstract: Video-based tutorials are a primary resource for learning feature-rich software, yet less is known about how learners coordinate tutorial viewing and software execution across device arrangements during authentic learning tasks. We conducted a mixed-methods study combining a survey of 87 learners with contextual inquiries involving eight participants. The survey characterized learning practices, device configurations, and frictions; the contextual inquiry analyzed pauses, rewinds, and task-blocking stuck moments as observable interaction breakdowns revealing underlying usability barriers. Findings show that frictions stem from insufficient input information, dense instructional pacing, preset or state mismatches, and missed or extra operations disrupting watch-and-do workflows. We identify design opportunities including input-action overlays, step-level segmentation, preset and state checkpoints, structured subgoal outlines, and coordination support across device ecologies. This work provides empirically grounded insights into situated video-based software learning and translates observed interaction breakdowns into actionable design implications.

doi:10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0710.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Air Quality Prediction, With Satellite and Weather Data
doi:10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0710.abstract: <jats:p>Air pollution is a major threat in current times and I consider PM2.5 as a pollutant because PM2.5 has negative impacts on human health. Hence PM2.5 prediction is crucial. The prediction of PM2.5 is a challenging task due to its non-linear relationship with various environmental factors and dust storm events. In this paper, we present a novel machine learning approach for predicting PM2.5 concentration in the Bhubaneswar region of Odisha. Using annotated data sets with corresponding meteorological parameters and satellite Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) we demonstrate our results. We have collected a total of 147 annotated data sets from 12 October 2025 to 28 June 2026. Along with PM2.5, we have collected ambient air temperature, relative humidity, atmospheric pressure, wind speed, wind direction, precipitation, and AOD 0.55 µm as input parameters for our models. We have implemented four machine learning regressors namely Linear Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting and XGBoost to predict PM2.5 concentrations. We perform experiments with two sets of input features consisting of only meteorological parameters and other consisting of meteorological parameters and AOD.For the purposes of evaluation, we calculate the Model Performance Statistics, including the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and finally, the R squared (R2). Additionally, we apply the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) method to explain our model, that is, to determine which variables influence the outcome. Gradient Boosting algorithm performed the best among all the models. Gradient Boosting when trained on the combined set of input parameters of meteorological data and AOD produced an R2 value of 0.79, an MAE of 11.52 µg/m3 and an RMSE of 15.78 µg/m3. We also observed that inclusion of AOD values improved performance of all the four models. This demonstrates that using combined sets of satellite and local data improves PM2.5 prediction accuracy. Similarly, the use of SHAP provided insights on the contribution of different parameters in the prediction process.</jats:p>
doi:10.47392/irjaeh.2026.0710.venue: International Research Journal on Advanced Engineering Hub (IRJAEH)

doi:10.3389/fimmu.2026.1937515.title: Identification of psoriasis-associated hub genes by integrated transcriptomics and machine learning
doi:10.3389/fimmu.2026.1937515.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    This study aims to systematically identify key hub genes in psoriasis pathogenesis through the integration of bioinformatics, machine learning and experimental validation methods. Four psoriasis microarray datasets were retrieved from the GEO database, with differentially expressed genes identified through comparative analysis. A dual machine learning approach screened core hub genes, whose expression levels and diagnostic efficacy were validated in an independent cohort. CIBERSORT was employed for immune cell infiltration analysis, whilst a multi-database approach constructed an mRNA-miRNA-lncRNA regulatory network. Molecular docking technology assessed interactions between the environmental pollutant bisphenol A, predicted drugs, and hub genes. Finally, an
                    <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                    psoriasis model was established by stimulating HaCaT cells with the M5 cytokine mixture, with hub gene expression validated via RT-qPCR. Results show that 77 co-differentially expressed genes were identified in psoriasis. Machine learning screened five key hub genes: CARHSP1, HPSE, PCLAF, SERPINB4, and SPRR2C. These were significantly upregulated in the validation cohort and demonstrated strong discriminative value for distinguishing psoriatic lesional skin from paired non-lesional skin, rather than serving as standalone diagnostic biomarkers for psoriasis. Immune cell infiltration analysis revealed extensive associations with immune subpopulations including T cells and macrophages. Molecular docking computationally predicted a potential binding interaction between the environmental pollutant BPA and the hub gene HPSE, which awaits future experimental validation. Concurrently, Genistein and HPSE were suggested a potential interaction that awaits functional validation.
                    <jats:italic>In vitro</jats:italic>
                    experiments confirmed significant upregulation of HPSE, PCLAF, and SPRR2C mRNA levels in M5-induced psoriasis cell models. HPSE emerged as a multifunctional core gene associated with immune dysregulation. Molecular docking additionally predicted a potential interaction between the environmental pollutant BPA and HPSE; however, this interaction remains a computational hypothesis requiring experimental validation.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.37394/23203.2026.21.30.title: Malware Detection by Machine Learning based on the LightGBM Model
doi:10.37394/23203.2026.21.30.abstract: <jats:p>Wannacry has grown to be considered one of the biggest threats affecting computer security over the past ten years, which has prompted continuous research on detection and mitigation techniques. The EMBER 2018 dataset, which contains sample WPE files categorized as harmless and harmful, is used to synthesize research findings and data in order to build an efficient machine learning model for malware identification. The pre-processed data is sent into a deep learning system for training. The machine learning model was built using dense and conventional dropout layers to reduce constraints on resources and generate quicker, accurate results. By evaluating the underlying API functionality that a file utilizes, we can determine if its behavior could be considered benign or malicious. LightGBM has been built utilizing over 1.55 million tagged example sets, each represented by 1,000 API-call-based attributes. Every model, including the Random Forest model, which displayed outstanding results with 99.49% reliability and fine-grained characteristics like precision and recall to lower mistakes, is assessed using conventional criteria for performance. The study idea is based on the implementation of contemporary standard machine learning models (such LightGBM) to guaranty the highest-level using malware identification accuracy and the usage of reputable software programs to extract standardized features from PE data files. The research also explores classification thresholds and performance optimization methods, aiming to provide a reliable and effective initial solution to the problem of static malware detection.</jats:p>
doi:10.37394/23203.2026.21.30.venue: WSEAS Transactions on Systems and Control

doi:10.66437/qjerp.v2i10.006.title: Interfaith Leaders of Mindanao: Challenges, Strategies, and Effects on the Learning Development of Students
doi:10.66437/qjerp.v2i10.006.abstract: <jats:p>This mixed-methods study examined the challenges encountered by interfaith leaders in Mindanao, the strategies they applied, and the effects of these factors on students’ learning development in selected private schools in Davao City and Cotabato City. The participants were 300 students and 30 school leaders selected through total enumeration. Quantitative data were gathered through adapted survey questionnaires and analyzed using means and regression analysis, while qualitative data from semi-structured interviews were examined through thematic analysis. The challenge dimensions were generally rated as moderate, with grand means ranging from 2.87 to 3.24; cultural awareness obtained 3.38 and was interpreted as not a challenge. School community engagement (M = 3.24) and school policies (M = 3.17) were often practiced, while students’ learning development was rated high (M = 3.20). In the combined regression model, challenges significantly predicted learning development (b = 1.15, t = 31.40, p < .001), whereas the aggregated strategies predictor did not (b = -0.02, t = -0.56, p = .57); the model explained 85% of the variance (R² = .85). In the separate strategy-factor model, however, school community engagement (b = .56, p < .001) and school policies (b = .11, p = .02) were significant, explaining 40% of the variance. Qualitative themes identified religion and culture misunderstandings, differing views about beliefs and practices, and silent division as challenges; safe spaces for dialogue, inclusivity and respect, and reflection as strategies; and openness to diversity, inclusive learning environments, and adaptive future leadership as effects. The findings informed an Interfaith Leadership Strategy Module comprising an interfaith dialogue guide, learning-development activities, and monitoring and evaluation tools.</jats:p>
doi:10.66437/qjerp.v2i10.006.venue: QualiSearch Journal of Educational Research and Practice

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-71965-6.title: SHAP-guided adaptive feature weighting for phishing URL detection with a federated learning extension
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-71965-6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Machine-learning phishing URL detectors routinely report accuracies above 97%, yet four weaknesses undermine these results: absent statistical testing, unfair latency benchmarking, uninterpretable predictions, and an inability to use data held privately across organisations. We address all four on the Hannousse-Yahiouche benchmark (11,430 URLs, 87 features). We introduce the SHAP-Guided Adaptive Feature Weighting (SAFW) layer, a trainable component initialised from XGBoost SHAP scores and evaluate seven architectures (including a DistilBERT reference case) with 10-fold cross-validation, twenty-one McNemar tests, five class-imbalance ratios, and CPU-only latency benchmarking. XGBoost dominates centralised training (97.00% accuracy, 0.79 ms latency); no statistically detectable difference was observed between SVM and BiLSTM (McNemar p = 0.469). Extending to a twenty-client federated setting (matching the N ≥ 20 convention in the federated-learning literature) under non-IID Dirichlet partitioning with a per-client sample guard, federated SAFW-Hybrid reaches 95.4% ± 0.5% over the final rounds on the same 80/20 split, showing no statistically detectable difference from its centralised counterpart (95.45%; McNemar p = 0.30; paired-difference 95% CI [− 1.05, + 0.22] pp against a ± 0.5 pp margin not formally equivalent, as the CI is not wholly contained within the margin). A naive federated XGBoost ensemble loses 4.2 points, but a purpose-built horizontal federated GBDT (cyclic federated XGBoost) recovers almost all of this (94.5–95.1%), matching federated SAFW-Hybrid within test-set noise. Excluding the two externally-sourced features (google_index, page_rank) leaves centralised and federated accuracy largely intact (within ~ 1% point) but sharply reduces class-imbalance robustness, with F1 at the most extreme ratio variying by 35.6% points depending on architecture. Cross-client analysis shows google_index remains highly stable across the twenty simulated clients under the evaluated non-IID FedAvg setting (mean weight 0.891, spread 0.0013) under a non-saturating initialisation, ruling out sigmoid saturation as the cause; because the clients are coupled through repeated FedAvg aggregation rather than trained in isolation, this stability is reported as a property of the evaluated setting rather than independent cross-client convergence. XGBoost therefore remains the accuracy leader in the centralised setting; no statistically detectable difference was observed between XGBoost and SAFW-Hybrid under the evaluated federated setting once aggregation is done properly; the federated value of SAFW-Hybrid is competitive accuracy combined with an interpretable, cross-client-stable per-feature weight vector that a tree ensemble cannot provide.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1950695.title: Beyond single scaffolding: a multidimensional scaffolding framework for flow-driven Game-Based Learning
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1950695.abstract: <jats:p>Meta-analytic evidence indicates Game-Based Learning (GBL) to be beneficial for enhancing learning motivation and promoting knowledge construction, with the design and provision of scaffolding within games playing a critical role in enhancing learning outcomes. How to simultaneously foster learners’ flow and learning remains a significant challenge in GBL scaffolding design; insufficient or inappropriate scaffolding may negatively impact both the gaming experience and learning outcomes. Recent meta-analyses have found that GBL has a moderate-to-large effect on cognitive outcomes, but the effect sizes show high heterogeneity. Furthermore, no significant improvement was observed in metacognitive outcomes. This imbalance may stem from the limitations of GBL research approaches that focus primarily on a single type of scaffolding. As GBL is a highly interactive and complex learning process, research on multidimensional scaffolding mechanisms has garnered increasing attention in recent years for its potential to enhance GBL effectiveness; however, there is currently a lack of systematic theoretical foundations and design guidelines. This study is a perspective article. Based on recent empirical research on GBL scaffolding, this study proposes a theoretical framework for Multidimensional Scaffolding in Game-Based Learning (MDS-GBL) in accordance with the characteristics of multidimensional forms of Flow Theory and the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) and presents a practical framework for scaffolding design and assessment. This study also draws on the results of recent empirical research on multidimensional scaffolding to support the proposed theoretical framework and presents three design principles for multidimensional scaffolding to serve as a reference for researchers and designers.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11131255/v1.title: Motor learning refines premotor cortical constraint during skilled forelimb behavior
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11131255/v1.abstract: Motor learning transforms variable actions into reliable skilled behavior, but how premotor cortex supports this transformation remains unclear. We longitudinally recorded bilateral local field potentials and single-unit activity from the rat rostral forelimb area while animals acquired a single-pellet retrieval task. Here, we show that improved skill was accompanied by reduced, rather than increased, task-related premotor recruitment. Despite this attenuation, firing remained dominated by suppression around pellet retrieval, and stronger pre-retrieval suppression was associated with greater odds of successful performance. Population neural state analysis further showed that successful actions were most strongly coupled to sustained pre-retrieval engagement early in learning, whereas later success occurred with less population-level engagement. These findings reveal premotor cortical constraint as a population-level process that is progressively refined as motor learning transforms variable actions into reliable skilled behavior.

doi:10.1186/s12982-026-03084-6.title: Integrating spatial analytics and explainable machine learning to analyse multi-pollutant mortality burdens in Africa
doi:10.1186/s12982-026-03084-6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Air pollution in Africa is a critical public health problem that has claimed many lives, especially in places where urbanisation and vehicle emissions are increasing. The present study used spatial analysis and a hybrid Genetic Algorithm–Machine Learning (GA–ML) approach to predict mortality rates, in a quest to minimise risks associated with this problem. The study employed varied datasets, in which SVR, Support Vector Regression-Generic Algorithm (SVR-GA), LightGBM, and LightGBM-GA were examined, using Egypt, Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa as a case study. In the spatial analysis, Nigeria and Egypt were identified as hotspots of mortality, whereas South Africa had moderate mortality rates. The SVR-GA algorithm registered superior results, producing an R
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    of 86.4%, MAE (0.034) and MSE (0.01), while the SVR had the second-best. SHAP analysis highlighted PM2.5 and CO as the dominant factors in building the models, highlighting the need for close monitoring of these pollutants. The model’s generalisation ability was improved by conducting the LOCO-CV and the country-wise validation processes. According to the results obtained, there is some level of positive spatial autocorrelation for deaths from air pollution, and hotspots and coldspots can be observed for the studied countries. Of all the tested models, SVR-GA performed the best, outperforming SVR, LightGBM, and LightGBM-GA. In terms of geographic validation, SVR-GA achieved the best results in predictive ability and stability across the countries studied, confirming its high generalisation ability. Using the Shapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) technique, it was established that PM₂.₅ and CO were the most crucial predictors of the models’ outputs. Moreover, the results were validated by the Taylor diagram and the Empirical Cumulative Distribution. In this way, the study contributes novel insights to environmental modelling through the integration of spatial statistics, advanced machine learning, metaheuristic optimisation, and a thorough evaluation. Furthermore, the hybrid GA-machine learning framework is a powerful and adaptable tool that can assist with data-driven environmental management and the realization of the Sustainable Development Goals relating to health, climate action, and sustainable urban development.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11222729/v1.title: When the customer is a machine: a systematic literature review and integrative framework of agentic commerce
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11222729/v1.abstract: Artificial intelligence agents now search, evaluate, negotiate, and pay on behalf of consumers, while firms deploy agents that create content, personalize offers, and complete transactions. Agentic commerce therefore weakens a foundational assumption of marketing thought and marketing measurement: that the recipient of marketing activity is a human being. The evidence is scattered across marketing, information systems, computer science, economics, and law, and it has a largely forgotten first act in the shopbot research of the late 1990s. Following the SPAR-4-SLR protocol with PRISMA 2020 reporting, we screen 5,157 records from Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCO Business Source and add verified snowballing to assemble 140 primary studies spanning 1994 to 2026. Each study is coded on influence direction, customer journey stage, delegation depth, method, and research wave. The synthesis yields an actor taxonomy with a five-level delegation ladder, an influence triad that separates marketing to, through, and by agents, an integrated account of trust and governance infrastructure, and a market-level analysis connecting both research waves. The Agentic Commerce Reference Framework consolidates this evidence into four auditable layers with explicit cross-layer dynamics, a ten-proposition research agenda, and five measurement instruments for analytics practice. A complete replication package accompanies the article.

doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c09413.title: Machine Learning-Based NOx Prediction and Combustion Optimization for a Coal-Fired Boiler: The Role of Feature Engineering
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c09413.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The choice between traditional machine learning and deep learning for industrial time series prediction remains unsettled, particularly when feature engineering is accounted for. Using 10,000 operational samples from a 660 MW coal-fired boiler, we systematically compare support vector machine (SVM), LSTM, XGBoost, Random Forest, and MLP for NOx emission prediction. Using a 139-dimensional representation comprising the current and first-to-fourth-order lagged values of 27 operational variables, together with four autoregressive NOx lag terms, SVM achieves RMSE = 10.124 mg/Nm3 and R2 = 0.934, outperforming LSTM (20.203, 0.738), XGBoost (12.405, 0.901), Random Forest (12.475, 0.900), and MLP (32.236, 0.332). A fair re-evaluation─training LSTM, Transformer, TCN, and BiLSTM on raw 20-step sequences without manual lag engineering─confirms that deep architectures remain less competitive than SVM with explicit feature engineering (best DL model: fair LSTM, RMSE = 18.541, R2 = 0.779). The HAC-adjusted Diebold–Mariano tests (all one-sided p &lt; 8.1 × 10–7), bootstrap confidence intervals, and Friedman–Nemenyi analysis provide convergent statistical evidence of SVM’s superiority. SHAP analysis identifies O2 as the dominant predictor (SHAP = 10.987), and time-series cross-validation confirms SVM’s robustness (mean RMSE = 6.062, std = 1.804). Single-objective differential evolution achieves a 21.16% NOx reduction at 600 MW load. A data-driven efficiency surrogate replaces hand-crafted formulas in multiobjective NSGA-II optimization, producing a scenario-dependent NOx-efficiency Pareto front whose sensitivity to coal calorific value is explicitly evaluated. These findings demonstrate that on industrial data sets of approximately 10,000 samples, domain-informed feature engineering can enable traditional methods to match or exceed deep learning at lower computational cost.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11233692/v1.title: GIS, Remote Sensing and Machine Learning Applications for Forest Fire Mapping, Susceptibility Assessment and Risk Analysis: A Systematic Review
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11233692/v1.abstract: Forest fires pose significant environmental and socioeconomic risks, increasing the need for reliable methods for spatial mapping, susceptibility assessment, and risk prediction. This systematic review synthesizes research on the application of remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and machine learning for forest fire mapping. A total of 202 articles were initially identified from five academic sources, of which 51 studies met the predefined inclusion criteria. The reviewed literature shows increasing research activity, with publications spanning 2021 to 2026. Asia accounted for the largest proportion of studies (62.7%, n=32), while Africa was represented by only four studies, indicating a geographical research gap. Among remote sensing datasets, MODIS was most frequently used (27 studies), followed by Sentinel-2 (14), while VIIRS and Landsat 8 were each used in six studies. Machine learning approaches dominated the analytical methods, with Random Forest being the most frequently applied model (28 studies), followed by XGBoost (20), Support Vector Machine (13), and Logistic Regression (12). Common predictor variables included temperature, precipitation, slope, aspect, elevation, distance to roads and settlements, land use/land cover, and vegetation indices. NDVI was the most frequently used spectral index, appearing in 43 studies. Key limitations included spatial resolution, data quality, data availability, and model performance. The review demonstrates a clear shift toward integrated GIS, remote sensing, and machine learning frameworks, including cloud-based platforms such as Google Earth Engine. Future research should prioritize improved spatial and temporal data resolution, broader geographical coverage, particularly in Africa, integration of multiple datasets and seasonal risk indices, advanced deep learning methods, continuous monitoring, and robust validation to reduce bias and improve model transferability. These advances can strengthen forest fire management and support evidence-based decision-making.

doi:10.1108/ijshe-11-2025-1497.title: Artificial intelligence use and personalized learning in higher education: pathways toward sustainable development goals and student mental health
doi:10.1108/ijshe-11-2025-1497.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence use (AIU) and personalized learning contribute to SDG-4 quality education (QE) and students’ mental health (MH) in higher education, and the study also investigates whether AIU statistically mediates the relationships between personalized learning and QE and MH.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 460 students at a Chinese university. The hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Open learning was positively associated with both queality education and mental health, information management was positively associated with mental health but not with quality education, and knowledge creation was positively associated with quality education but not with mental health. None of the three personalized-learning dimensions were significantly associated with artificial intelligence use. In turn, artificial intelligence use was positively associated with both quality education and mental health. Artificial intelligence use showed significant indirect effects only between open learning and quality education and between open learning and mental health. No significant indirect effects were found for information management and, knowledge creation. Because the study used cross-sectional self-reported data, these findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that higher education institutions consider creating open and knowledge-rich learning environments, integrating AI tools that provide adaptive support and strengthening students’ information management (IM) skills. These factors were positively associated with quality education and mental health. However, the results should be interpreted cautiously because the study does not establish causal relationships or directly measure institutional progress toward SDG-4.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines OL, IM and KC separately and tests their direct and indirect associations with QE and MH through AIU. The findings reveal dimension and outcome specific associations, with significant indirect effects only for the OL–QE and OL–MH relationships. Thus, AIU is not a common statistical pathway linking all personalized-learning dimensions with student outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1917386.title: A primary care-oriented framework for osteoporosis prediction: integrating multi-algorithm feature selection and machine learning model benchmarking
doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1917386.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Summary</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Large-scale screening and primary care diagnosis of osteoporosis are challenging due to the limited availability of dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Therefore, predictive models for osteoporosis that do not rely on bone mineral density measurements are essential. Using routine health examination data and applying a consensus feature selection strategy, we constructed machine learning (ML)-based models and compared their performance across multiple dimensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To develop a robust, low-cost, and interpretable framework for osteoporosis prediction based on readily available information, which can be easily integrated into electronic health systems to inform DXA referral in resource-limited settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Variables covered by the basic health examination package were obtained from participants who underwent health examinations between January 2024 and January 2025. We implemented a strategy in which only features selected by at least four out of the seven feature selection methods were retained. Six ML algorithms were employed to develop models, and their prediction performances were compared across discrimination, goodness-of-fit, and clinical utility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 2,260 participants were included, with an osteoporosis prevalence of 7.1%. Eight features: age, sex, body mass index, alkaline phosphatase, hematocrit, high-density lipoprotein, urea, and platelet count, were selected for model development. In the validation set, the random forest and artificial neural network (ANN) models demonstrated strongest screening performance, with AUCs of 0.895 (95% CI 0.867–0.923) and 0.890 (95% CI 0.862–0.919), respectively. The ANN model additionally exhibited superior calibration. Shapley additive explanations were applied to interpret the ANN model for osteoporosis prediction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study presents an easily integrable model for osteoporosis prediction based on routine health examination data. The ANN model provides robust prediction, offering a potential tool for pre-DXA triage and early identification of high-risk individuals in primary care and resource-limited settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1007/s10791-026-10631-x.title: Federated multi-agent deep reinforcement learning with digital twin-assisted cross-layer optimization for secure energy-aware massive MIMO-NOMA mobile edge computing systems
doi:10.1007/s10791-026-10631-x.abstract: The rapid growth of Mobile Edge Computing (MEC) and massive device connectivity in next-generation wireless networks has intensified the need for intelligent, secure, and energy-efficient resource management strategies. This paper proposes a novel Federated Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (FMADRL) framework integrated with Digital Twin (DT) - assisted Cross-Layer Optimization for secure and energy-aware Massive Multiple-Input Multiple-Output–Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (MIMO-NOMA) MEC systems. The introduction highlights the limitations of existing centralized approaches, which suffer from high latency, scalability constraints, and privacy risks due to extensive data sharing. Several critical issues are identified including inefficient power allocation, dynamic interference, heterogeneous user demands, and vulnerabilities in data transmission. To address these challenges, the proposed methodology employs Federated Learning (FL), enabling multiple distributed agents to collaboratively learn optimal policies without sharing raw data, thereby preserving privacy. A DT model is developed to replicate the real-time network environment, enabling predictive analysis and adaptive optimization. The multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework performs cross-layer optimization by jointly managing communication, computation, and security parameters, including task offloading, user clustering, and power control. The primary objective of this research is to enhance energy efficiency, reduce latency, improve spectral efficiency, and ensure secure communication in complex MEC-enabled networks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed FMADRL with digital-twin assistance significantly outperforms existing methods in energy savings, reduced delay, improved reliability, and robustness against security threats. This framework offers a scalable and efficient solution for future intelligent wireless communication systems.

doi:10.3389/fbioe.2026.1856872.title: An interpretable machine learning model for MRI-based morphological classification of lumbar disc herniation using functional biomechanical features
doi:10.3389/fbioe.2026.1856872.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lumbar disc herniation (LDH) is commonly assessed using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), although disc morphology does not necessarily correspond to pain intensity, functional impairment, neurological findings, or prognosis. This retrospective single-center exploratory study examined whether functional biomechanical indicators were associated with MRI-based morphological classification of LDH.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 58 patients were included, comprising 15 patients with disc bulging and 43 with disc protrusion or extrusion. Five predictors—lumbar extension, straight-leg-raising asymmetry, side-flexion asymmetry, gluteus medius asymmetry, and right Jiaji regional surface electromyography root mean square—were used to construct an interpretable L2-regularized logistic regression model. Model performance was evaluated using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times, with participant-level out-of-fold probabilities averaged across repetitions. Predictors were selected before cross-validation; therefore, the reported performance may include selection-induced optimism.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The model achieved a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve of 0.705 (95% confidence interval: 0.537–0.851), a precision-recall area under the curve of 0.844, and a Brier score of 0.218. At the exploratory Youden threshold of 0.566, balanced accuracy was 0.714, sensitivity was 0.628, specificity was 0.800, positive predictive value was 0.900, and negative predictive value was 0.429. A prespecified threshold of 0.500 yielded a balanced accuracy of 0.692, sensitivity of 0.651, and specificity of 0.733. Calibration was suboptimal, with an intercept of 0.999 and a slope of 0.752. In a separate exploratory bootstrap analysis, coefficient sign stability ranged from 97.0% to 99.9%, although the intervals remained wide.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest preliminary associations between selected functional biomechanical indicators and MRI-based disc morphology. Given the small and imbalanced sample, predictor-selection optimism, limited negative predictive performance, suboptimal calibration, and absence of external validation, the model should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than as a standalone clinical decision-support tool.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1930345.title: Interpretable machine learning prioritizes transcriptomic features associated with ferroptosis-mitochondrial permeability transition net activity states in cervical cancer
doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1930345.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated cervical carcinogenesis involves oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and altered non-apoptotic cell-death programs. Ferroptosis and mitochondrial permeability transition (MPT)-driven necrosis may share upstream stress-related transcriptional signals, but their joint pathway-state features in cervical cancer remain incompletely characterized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We constructed a directionality-aware net pathway activity framework using evidence-audited ferroptosis-promoting, ferroptosis-inhibitory, MPT-promoting, and MPT-inhibitory gene sets in 304 TCGA-CESC primary tumors. The score was benchmarked against ssGSEA, GSVA, and PLAGE and evaluated in controlled simulations. For feature prioritization, score-defining genes were excluded from predictors and Elastic Net feature selection, XGBoost tuning, and model fitting were performed strictly within repeated nested cross-validation. Outer-test SHAP, model-sensitivity analysis, and a 200-permutation complete-pipeline test were used for interpretation and robustness assessment. External validation used GSE138080, GSE63514, GSE223804, and GSE151666.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      CombinedNet showed moderate-to-high concordance with ssGSEA, GSVA, and PLAGE (Spearman rho = 0.735, 0.882, and 0.943, respectively), while 1,300 controlled simulations showed strong recovery of the latent promoter-minus-inhibitor balance across scenarios and effect sizes (mean rho = 0.944; mean sign-recovery accuracy = 0.902; mean standardized RMSE = 0.305). The leakage-resistant repeated nested-CV model yielded AUC = 0.780 (95% CI 0.766–0.795); a matched complete-pipeline permutation test gave empirical p = 0.005. Stability-weighted SHAP and perturbation prioritized
                      <jats:italic>CKMT1B</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic>KLK13</jats:italic>
                      , whereas
                      <jats:italic>GNA13</jats:italic>
                      ,
                      <jats:italic>PANX2</jats:italic>
                      , and all five sterol genes were not selected in any of 25 outer-fold models. The sterol genes retained modest score correlations but showed no model sensitivity. Across three lesion-progression cohorts, no pathway score remained associated with stage after FDR correction; in the cancer-only GSE151666 RNA-seq cohort, CombinedNet also showed no FIGO-stage trend.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This study supports directionality-aware transcriptomic scoring and a leakage-resistant feature-prioritization framework, but does not support
                      <jats:italic>GNA13</jats:italic>
                      /
                      <jats:italic>PANX2</jats:italic>
                      or cholesterol-biosynthesis signals as stable model drivers or the composite score as a validated lesion-stage biomarker. The findings remain hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1145/3776591.3832506.title: Continuous wrist kinematics carry lexical cues for temporal deixis
doi:10.1145/3776591.3832506.abstract: Human communication unfolds as a continuous multimodal stream in which speech, prosody, and gesture are tightly coordinated. Yet gesture is often analyzed as a sequence of discrete, manually segmented events, separated from lexical semantics. This study asks whether subtle continuous wrist movements co-ocurring with spoken temporal adverbs carry enough information to support above-chance discrimination among lexical categories without manual gesture annotation. Using a large aligned corpus of English television news, we extracted 13,061 clips containing the words yesterday, today, and tomorrow. After active-speaker verification, shot-change filtering, speaker masking, and pose-visibility checks, we represented each target token as an 80-frame wrist-trajectory sequence centered on the word midpoint. A bidirectional LSTM trained only on wrist kinematic features classified the three adverbs with 0.49 accuracy, above the 0.33 chance baseline and above a shuffled-label control. Binary tests showed a strong asymmetry: tomorrow was more discriminable than yesterday or today, reaching 0.697 accuracy in a one-versus-rest task. Feature ablations showed that performance dropped when the model was restricted to raw coordinates or to one hand, suggesting that the observed lexical cues are distributed across richer kinematic descriptors rather than raw wrist position alone. These preliminary results support a continuous, multi-flow account of multimodal interaction in which low-level bodily motion provides weak but measurable probabilistic cues associated with lexical meaning.

doi:10.3389/ffutr.2026.1972925.title: Semi-supervised zero-knowledge federated learning for intelligent transportation systems
doi:10.3389/ffutr.2026.1972925.abstract: <jats:p>Privacy-preserving machine learning in Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs) must address sensitive on-board data, limited ground-truth annotations, and verifiable model-update integrity. This paper proposes ZK-FL, a decentralized federated learning framework for Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) scene classification that combines semi-supervised pseudo-labeling, zk-SNARK-based update validation, and Hyperledger Besu blockchain auditability. Vehicles train local models, quantize the resulting updates, and generate zero-knowledge proofs demonstrating that distributed update probes satisfy a predefined norm-boundedness constraint. Road-Side Units (RSUs) verify the proofs before aggregation and anchor the corresponding audit metadata on-chain. The framework is evaluated on the BDD100K and Mapillary Vistas v2 datasets under multiple non-IID data distributions and five aggregation methods: FedAvg, Norm Clipping, Median, Trimmed Mean, and Krum. Since Mapillary Vistas does not provide scene-level annotations, two scene-label generation strategies, including a semi-supervised pseudo-labeling approach, are introduced. Experimental results demonstrate effective scene classification, verifiable update integrity, and practical proof-generation and verification, supporting the feasibility of privacy-preserving federated learning for ITS.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1965959.title: Is painless colonoscopy associated with trainee learning? A single-center study of insertion speed and adenoma detection curves in 1,769 procedures
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1965959.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To compare the learning curves of cecal intubation time and adenoma detection rate (ADR) between painless (sedated) and conventional (non-sedated) colonoscopy performed by trainees.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This single-center retrospective cohort comprised the first 1,769 colonoscopies performed by eight trainees without prior colonoscopy experience, grouped by sedation status into a conventional group (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 852) and a painless group (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 917). Mixed-effects models characterized the learning trajectories of cecal intubation time and ADR, and an extended model allowing a random case-order slope tested individual heterogeneity. The caseload to independent cecal intubation competency was estimated with a rolling 20-procedure success-rate threshold and Bernoulli cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Cecal intubation time was shorter in the painless group (median 6 vs. 10 min,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.001). The case-order × procedure-type interaction fell from −0.113/SD (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.001) in the random-intercept model to −0.027/SD (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.589) in the random-slope model and was not significant under an exact trainee-level permutation test (exact
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.23); the overall shortening of intubation time with painless colonoscopy was robust to all specifications. Sedation status, calendar era, and scope model were highly correlated at the trainee level (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.92), precluding separation of their independent effects. The overall ADR was 13.0% and declined early with experience (odds ratio 0.80/SD,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.002). Fewer procedures were required to reach independent cecal intubation competency in the painless group (rolling threshold 37 vs. 114; CUSUM 107 vs. 134); however, this difference could not be separated from calendar era and equipment upgrades.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intubation time was shorter overall under sedation, but the faster learning of the painless group vanished once individual heterogeneity was modeled, and ADR showed no robust improvement. Sedation, era, and equipment were confounded; no causal inference regarding the effect of sedation on learning can be drawn from these data, and prospective confirmation is required. Intubation speed alone should not serve as a benchmark of overall colonoscopy competence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1186/s12884-026-10029-z.title: Machine learning models to predict low birth weight in the Kenyan Coast
doi:10.1186/s12884-026-10029-z.abstract: Low birth weight (LBW, < 2500 g) is associated with poor outcomes across multiple domains of child development. Predicting high-risk pregnancies for LBW will therefore enable timely intervention. We aimed to develop and internally validate machine learning models to predict LBW in the Kenyan coast and determine the top predictors of LBW. We developed Machine Learning (ML) predictive models using data collected from pregnant women who delivered at Kilifi County Hospital between 2011 and 2019. Model training was conducted with logistic regression, random forest, extreme gradient boosting (Xgboost) and Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN). We used inverse probability of treatment weighting to adjust for potential confounding arising from differences in antenatal care (ANC) visits (> 4 vs. \(\:\le\:\) 4). Hyperparameter search done using 5-fold cross validation and guided using Bayesian optimization. Internal validation was done using a temporal split. Discrimination was assessed using area under the curve (AUC), calibration using calibration plots and overall performance with the Brier score. Approximately 17% of the 25,699 newborns included in the study had LBW. The TabPFN model showed an AUC of 0.693 (95% CI: 0.686–0.701), with performance comparable to logistic regression (AUC 0.688, 95% CI: 0.673–0.704). Across the four models, gestational age at first ANC, having a multiple pregnancy, mother’s age, history of high blood pressure during pregnancy and history of pregnancy complications were among the most common top predictors of LBW. Our findings indicate that logistic regression performed comparably to the best-performing ML models in predicting the risk of LBW. If effectively integrated into antenatal care workflows, these prediction models could enhance existing public health interventions by supporting risk stratification and targeted maternal care. However, further external and prospective validation, as well as cost-benefit analyses across diverse populations and settings, is needed before the models can be implemented in clinical practice.

doi:10.1186/s41747-026-00791-2.title: Radiomics machine learning models for lung cancer early diagnosis in heterogenous multicentre chest CT data: LIBRA study results
doi:10.1186/s41747-026-00791-2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We developed and validated radiomics models for lung cancer prediction in indeterminate pulmonary nodules that retain performance in heterogenous data from multiple centres.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The retrospective Lung Imaging Biobank for Radiomics and AI (LIBRA) study recruited 1,026 patients (2,071 computed tomography scans) with 5-to-30-mm lung nodules from seven UK hospitals (01/07/2020–30/09/2022). Benign and malignant nodules were segmented for feature extraction using PyRadiomics. Principal component analysis reduced feature dimensionality to twenty components. Logistic regression models using ComBat correction, fixed effects or random effects to mitigate for disparate data across study centres were compared. Models were fit to the whole dataset and evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. Internal-external validation assessed between-centre heterogeneity. Models were benchmarked against volume, Brock score and scrambled voxels. Calibration was assessed using calibration curves. Decision-curve analysis was used to assess net benefit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Between-centre discrimination variability was observed with an area under the curve (AUC) ranging 0.75–0.91. The mixed-effects model provided better discrimination over ComBat or fixed effects alone (AUC 0.91 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.90–0.93)
                      <jats:italic>versus</jats:italic>
                      0.75 (95% CI: 0.72–0.78) and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.86–0.90), respectively (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.0001 and 0.003, respectively) in cross-validation. Radiomics features retained significance in multivariable models including established clinical features. The final model was superior to models developed using volume alone, Brock score, and scrambled-voxels. The model was well calibrated (intercept -0.036, slope 0.89 with net benefit compared to volume or Brock score alone.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Radiomics models show between-centre heterogeneity, with resilience best achieved with mixed-effects models. The final model had high performance with net benefit over established risk models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Key Points</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:bold>
                        <jats:italic>Question</jats:italic>
                      </jats:bold>
                      Can heterogeneous data from multiple centres be used to predict lung nodule malignancy risk?
                    </jats:p>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:bold>
                        <jats:italic>Findings</jats:italic>
                      </jats:bold>
                      Radiomics cancer prediction models must account for heterogeneity to maintain performance between different centres. The mixed-effects model achieved AUC 0.91 (cross-validation) for cancer prediction.
                    </jats:p>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:bold>
                        <jats:italic>Relevance statement</jats:italic>
                      </jats:bold>
                      The model provided net benefit for nodule investigation over Brock score and volume alone and could assist in decision-making following prospective validation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.59944/postaxial.v4i2.1633.title: Managing Discipline as Professional Readiness in a SMK Kesehatan: A Qualitative Case Study of Character-Based Management
doi:10.59944/postaxial.v4i2.1633.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined how a health vocational school managed discipline as part of students’ character formation and professional readiness. A qualitative case study was conducted at SMK Kesehatan Tunas Madani in Sukabumi, West Java, Indonesia, from December 2025 to March 2026. Participants were purposively selected from the principal, vice principal for student affairs, character-development teacher, homeroom teachers, students, and parents. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, direct observations, and document review. Interactive analysis involved data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. Source and method triangulation and checks with key participants supported credibility. The findings showed that the school translated discipline, responsibility, and integrity into written rules, daily routines, classroom learning, and laboratory and teaching-factory practice. The alignment of written expectations, teacher monitoring, and vocational standard operating procedures produced a consistent behavioural message. Recognition and educational consequences were used to reinforce accountability. However, the evidence was stronger for observed compliance than for value internalisation or autonomous self-regulation. Implementation was also constrained by the absence of a counsellor with specialist training and discontinuity between routines at school and at home. Discipline in a health vocational school should therefore be managed as a context-specific professional practice, supported by fair response procedures, tiered counselling support, student reflection, and longitudinal behavioural evaluation. The study offers a bounded explanation of management mechanisms and does not establish causal improvement.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1914255.title: Temporal phase coverage and patient cohort size in deep learning-based cardiac cine computed tomography angiography segmentation
doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1914255.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Annotating all phases of cine computed tomography angiography (CTA) is burdensome. We evaluated how temporal phase coverage and patient cohort size affect deep learning-based cardiac segmentation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twelve 3D U-Net models were trained using a 110-patient single-phase CTA dataset or a 20-patient, 20-phase cine CTA dataset. Phase-coverage ablations used one, two, or 20 phases; patient-count ablations were performed within both datasets. One cine patient was used for validation and four independent patients were used for testing. Five cardiac structures were evaluated using Dice and the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95). Phase-wise and patient-level Dice consistency and structure-specific volumetric variability within and between subjects were assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Full cine training produced higher overall Dice (0.89 vs. 0.87) and lower overall HD95 (4.87 vs. 9.78 mm) than the single-phase reference (both
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.05). Right ventricular (RV) Dice was higher (0.91 vs. 0.84) and HD95 was lower (5.16 vs. 22.75 mm; both
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.05). The two-phase model achieved an overall Dice of 0.88 and an overall HD95 of 7.85 mm; neither metric differed significantly from the single-phase reference. HD95 generally increased with smaller cohorts, and both metrics deteriorated markedly in the five-patient configurations. Full cine training showed flatter phase-wise Dice profiles and lower across-phase variability. Between-subject volume differences exceeded phase-related within-subject differences for all structures (all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.05).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-cohort comparison, full cine training showed higher overall Dice, lower overall HD95, and greater phase-wise consistency than single-phase training. The evaluated two-phase configuration may inform annotation-efficient cine CTA dataset design, but broader validation is needed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1007/s44163-026-01886-w.title: Deep learning-based anxiety quantification assessment and emotional regulation recommendation generation model
doi:10.1007/s44163-026-01886-w.abstract: Accurately managing emotions and quantifying anxiety continue to be important challenges in affective computing and digital mental health, especially where continuous, objective, and personalized evaluation goes beyond self-reported anxiety. Current deep learning systems mainly have coarse emotion classification ability and have no built-in and interpretable regulation mechanisms. In order to overcome these limitations, the Deep Learning Based Anxiety Quantification and Emotional Regulation Recommendation Generation Model (DLAQ-ERRG) is proposed in this study. It comprises three key components: (i) a Neural Stochastic Differential Attention Encoder (NSDAE) for capturing the continuous-time affective dynamics and temporal uncertainty from multimodal wearable signals; (ii) a Hyperbolic Contrastive Affective Manifold Learner (HCAML) for learning a non-Euclidean space to embed latent emotional states while preserving the hierarchical structure of affective severity and boosting inter-subject separability; and (iii) a Hyperbolic Neural Symbolic Policy Generator (ER-NSPG) for generating constraint-consistent and uncertainty-aware emotional regulation recommendations. Experimental results under strict Leave-One-Subject-Out validation on the WESAD dataset show an improvement of 11.85% compared to the best baseline (CCC = 0.734) and the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.384 and the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.083, respectively. The overall anxiety prediction accuracy (AIPA) for affect-state classification is 87.3% for the model. Structured severity organization is confirmed by representation quality metrics: an Anxiety Severity Separation Score (ASS) of 0.726 and a Hyperbolic Clustering Quality Index (HCQI) of 0.681. The recommendation evaluation results in an Action Appropriateness Score (AAS) of 0.776, Recommendation Smoothness Score (RSS) of 0.764 and Emotion Regulation Diversity Score (RDS) of 0.701, all representing stable and tailored generation of interventions. The results illustrate the benefits of uncertainty-aware continuous estimation of anxiety-related arousal, improved structural representation, and interpretable support in regulating arousal within a single, uncertainty-aware framework.

doi:10.55241/spibio.v7i3.831.title: Development of an Augmented Reality Flipbook on Fern Morphology to Support Students’ Learning Interest
doi:10.55241/spibio.v7i3.831.abstract: <jats:p>Fern morphology is commonly taught using printed textbooks and static two-dimensional images, which limits students’ understanding of its three-dimensional structures, especially given the limited availability of real specimens in schools. The primary objective of this study was to develop a learning media utilizing Augmented Reality (AR) in a flipbook format focused on fern morphology, designed to support students’ learning interest in fern morphology. We employed a Research and Development (R&D) methodology guided by the ADDIE framework: analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation. This process produced FLORAVIA, an interactive AR-based flipbook that lets learners view realistic 3D models of fern structures on their smartphones. Participants consisted of one biology teacher and 35 eleventh-grade science students (Class XI IPA 1) at SMA Negeri 12 Surabaya. Data were collected through feedback questionnaires for the teacher and students, while media and subject-matter experts assessed the product using standardized validation sheets, and the data were analyzed descriptively to determine validity and practicality. FLORAVIA achieved a validity score of 85% from the subject-matter expert and 100% from the media expert, both categorized as valid. Furthermore, feedback from the student responses indicated that the media was categorized as practical to highly practical, with users praising its visual appeal, interactivity, and ease of navigation. These results indicate that the AR-based flipbook is a valid and practical resource for biology instruction. Its effect on students’ learning interest and conceptual understanding was not tested and should be examined in further experimental research.</jats:p>
