doi:10.3390/bioengineering13101168.title: BMA-Net: A Bilateral Attention Network with Retinal Domain Transfer-Learning for CIMT-Based Cardiovascular Risk Classification from Fundus Images
doi:10.3390/bioengineering13101168.abstract: <jats:p>Carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) is an established marker of subclinical atherosclerosis, but its reliance on ultrasound equipment and trained operators limits its suitability for large-scale screening. Retinal fundus photography may offer a more scalable approach to vascular assessment, as it contains retinal vascular features associated with systemic cardiovascular health and can be acquired quickly and non-invasively. This study proposes a two-stage transfer learning framework for CIMT-based cardiovascular risk classification. An attention-enhanced EfficientNet-B4 is first pretrained on the Asia Pacific Tele-Ophthalmology Society 2019 Blindness Detection dataset and subsequently transferred to a weight-sharing Siamese architecture to classify the China Fundus Carotid Intima-Media Thickness dataset. Across ten independent initializations, the proposed model achieved an average macro-F1 score of 77.81% and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 84.08% on the validation set and 78.29% and 85.22%, respectively, on the test set. It achieved overall higher point estimates for performance metrics than those previously reported for the Siamese ResNeXt baseline model with squeeze-and-excitation attention, and demonstrated a reduced disparity in class-wise performance. Grad-CAM analysis further revealed differences in the spatial activation patterns between models trained under different experimental configurations. Overall, these findings support the feasibility of fundus imaging as a scalable and non-invasive approach to CIMT-based cardiovascular risk assessment.</jats:p>

doi:10.4324/9781003654308-7.title: Navigating Conversations at End of Life
doi:10.4324/9781003654308-7.abstract: This chapter exposes the reader to the tough conversations that happen at the end of life. It ventures into more debated issues such as Medical Aid in Dying and recaps the surrounding legal debates of such movements. It returns to earlier topics surrounding the importance of language choice in clinical contexts by considering the entailments of terms like “physician-assisted suicide” and “medically assisted death.” The focus of the chapter allows for the exploration of the four pillars of bioethics: autonomy, beneficence, non-malificence, and justice. These concepts are part of every medical decision, but the risks of violating them are increased and scrutinized more fully during certain medical situations. Care, and communications about, the end of life is one such situation. The chapter looks at sentinel cases that have led to the current framework of end-of-life care. In a final communicative turn, the chapter interrogates how to talk about death in clinical settings. Many providers may employ well-established models for breaking bad news. Popular models for having tough healthcare conversations, like the SPIKES Model for Breaking Bad News, and subsequent related renditions, like the COMFORT model, will be offered, as will a conversation of their advantages and disadvantages.

doi:10.1108/jwl-04-2026-0203.title: Visible but learning-weak: trace visibility and within-phase distortions in digitally supported continuous improvement
doi:10.1108/jwl-04-2026-0203.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to explain why digitally supported continuous improvement can remain visibly active while becoming learning-weak in enacted practice under trace visibility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using a qualitative, mechanism-oriented cross-case analysis of eight external case accounts from industrial manufacturing settings of different organizational sizes, supplemented by one reflective practitioner account used solely as contextual contrast, the study reconstructs phase-internal profiles of learning conditions, trace cues, recurrent distortions and boundary conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Trace-producing improvement systems can sustain visible activity while enacted learning weakens under conditions of social exposure. The analysis identifies four corpus-grounded configurations: symbolic participation, scope retreat, parallel coordination channels and visibility without shared interpretation. Reporting drift is retained only as a bounded risk within the Value realization lens, while continuation without documented reconsideration is retained as a tentative risk pattern in the Renewal lens.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper offers a bounded mechanism-based explanation rather than prevalence estimates, outcome claims or intervention-effect evidence. It supports analytic generalization about learning-weak enactment under trace visibility without proposing a maturity model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rather than adding another list of workplace-learning antecedents, the paper specifies how durable, attributable and reviewable digital traces can redirect established learning conditions within CI phases and synthesizes this distinct mechanism space of within-phase learning weakness into a compact Mechanism Atlas.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.17345/ute.2026.4533.title: Los entornos personales de aprendizaje en formación profesional: una revisión de alcance
doi:10.17345/ute.2026.4533.abstract: <jats:p>Los entornos personales de aprendizaje (PLE) llevan cerca de dos décadas en la investigación educativa, pero su estudio en el contexto específico de la formación profesional (FP; Vocational Education and Training, VET) permanece disperso y sin una síntesis específica. Este trabajo presenta una revisión de alcance, cuyo informe se elaboró conforme a PRISMA-ScR, para mapear y sintetizar la evidencia sobre el uso de los PLE en contextos de FP/VET. La búsqueda cubrió Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC y Dialnet Plus, desde 2007 hasta marzo de 2026, fecha en que volvió a ejecutarse para comprobar la estabilidad de los resultados; no aparecieron registros nuevos que cumpliesen los criterios de elegibilidad. Tras un cribado en dos fases, se incluyeron 21 publicaciones. El análisis se organizó en torno a siete preguntas de investigación y nueve núcleos temáticos, combinando recuentos de frecuencias y síntesis narrativa cualitativa. Los resultados muestran una literatura escasa, concentrada entre 2013 y 2016 y configurada en gran medida por un grupo de proyectos europeos financiados sobre aprendizaje en microempresas. La FP reglada inicial está representada por solo tres publicaciones. La autonomía aparece frecuentemente condicionada por estructuras organizativas, mientras que la reflexión y el aprendizaje autorregulado responden a conceptualizaciones divergentes. La falta de tiempo aparece de forma recurrente entre las barreras identificadas. Se concluye que persisten lagunas relevantes en la FP reglada inicial y que los resultados de implementación se asocian recurrentemente con condiciones organizativas, institucionales y vinculadas al aprendiz, además del diseño de la herramienta tecnológica.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41524-026-02357-7.title: Fragment-based representation learning for polymers and heterogeneous formulations
doi:10.1038/s41524-026-02357-7.abstract: Real polymer systems include not only simple linear homopolymers, but also copolymers, branched architectures, crosslinked networks, and multicomponent formulations. Yet most polymer machine-learning models still rely on idealized repeat-unit representations. This mismatch limits not only the scope of polymer informatics, but also the development of foundation models for polymer systems. Here we investigate chemically meaningful fragments as a shared representation across small molecules, linear homopolymers, and component-defined polymer formulations. We develop CGMNet (Coarse-Grained Molecular Network), a framework that learns fragment-level representations from unlabeled small molecules through self-supervised pretraining and transfers them to downstream polymer property prediction. Using this framework, we show that fragment-based representations support strong predictive performance for small molecules, linear homopolymers, and component-defined polyester, epoxy-resin, and vitrimer formulations, while retaining interpretability through attribution to specific chemical motifs. Together, these results establish fragments as a practical representation interface for bridging small-molecule pretraining, linear-homopolymer benchmarks, and component-defined polymer formulations beyond a single-repeat-unit input.

doi:10.66074/t5v2w8x4y9.title: Pre-Service Teachers' Perceptions of the Internship Program and Its Contribution to Program Learning Outcomes
doi:10.66074/t5v2w8x4y9.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Teaching Internship (EDUC 401) provides pre-service teachers with experiential learning opportunities intended to support the attainment of program learning outcomes (PLOs). Examining students’ perceptions after completing their practicum provides evidence of the internship’s contribution to their academic and professional preparation. Objective: This study examined respondents’ perceptions of the Teaching Internship course (EDUC 401) and its contribution to the attainment of eight PLOs based on CHED Memorandum Order (CMO) No. 75, s. 2017. Methods: The study involved students who had completed their practicum during AY 2025–2026. Data were collected through a Google Forms survey administered from April to June 2026 following ethics clearance from the Bulacan State University Ethics Review Committee. Respondents voluntarily provided demographic information and rated the extent to which experiential learning contributed to each PLO. Proportions, means, and standard deviations were computed for the eight outcomes. Results: Overall perceptions were positive, with a mean rating of 4.091 (SD = 1.212) across the eight PLOs. Technology use in facilitating language learning and teaching received the highest rating (M = 4.242, SD = 1.226), while the remaining outcomes clustered closely around the overall mean. Most respondents agreed or strongly agreed that the internship contributed to the attainment of the desired learning competencies. Conclusion: The findings support the contribution of Teaching Internship to PLO attainment and provide evidence for continued attention to internship design, supervision, and curriculum alignment. The study recommends strengthening school-university partnerships, enhancing technology integration, and establishing systematic policies and practices for monitoring and documenting PLO attainment.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s11556-026-00443-9.title: Exercise prioritization in frailty: a pathophysiology-informed narrative review for rehabilitation in older adults
doi:10.1186/s11556-026-00443-9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Exercise and physical activity have become standard parts of frailty care, yet much of the literature treats frailty biology and exercise prescription as separate problems. Guidance is therefore less clear on which component should lead when weakness, breathlessness, gait instability, or post-acute deconditioning dominates the presentation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Main text</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We treat frailty as a multisystem state of reduced physiologic reserve and use this perspective to set rehabilitation priorities. Evidence from frailty-defined cohorts was preferred. Evidence from sarcopenia trials, broader exercise studies in older adults, and disease-specific cardiopulmonary or post-acute rehabilitation was included where relevant and explicitly identified as extrapolative. Progressive resistance training remains the core intervention when low force output, slow chair rise, or transfer difficulty most directly constrains function. Aerobic or cardiopulmonary training can take precedence when dyspnea, poor walking endurance, or orthostatic intolerance most constrains activity. Balance and motor-cognitive training are appropriate when unstable gait, turning difficulty, or dual-task breakdown limits participation. Because most frail older adults present with mixed deficits, multicomponent exercise serves as the default delivery framework. Low-load strengthening, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, digital tools, and mind–body exercise function as bridges or adjuncts. These priorities integrate physiological reasoning with indirect clinical evidence. Direct trials in frailty-defined populations should now test whether bottleneck-matched prescription improves outcomes compared with usual or non-matched exercise prescription.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Current evidence supports pathophysiology-informed exercise prioritization as a clinical framework. Formal validation as a treatment-matching algorithm remains the next research step. The practical task is to identify the dominant reserve-limiting bottleneck, begin at a tolerable dose, progress load and complexity according to explicit criteria, and distinguish direct frailty evidence from justified extrapolation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/mmms-05-2026-0173.title: Predicting and optimizing energy efficiency in buildings: a multi-output machine learning framework with explainability and constrained optimization
doi:10.1108/mmms-05-2026-0173.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nine multi-output regression models were compared for simultaneous HL and CL prediction, supplemented by domain-informed feature engineering, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP explainability), robustness testing and a calibrated physics baseline comparison. The best-performing model, Gradient Boosting (Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) = 0.95 kWh, R2 = 0.990), was used as a surrogate within a Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) multi-objective optimization framework to identify Pareto-optimal building designs minimizing total energy and peak load.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study presents an integrated machine learning framework for predicting, interpreting and optimizing the heating load (HL) and cooling load (CL) of residential buildings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>SHAP analysis revealed that overall height and relative compactness dominate both loads, while orientation has negligible influence. Partial dependence analysis uncovered nonlinear response patterns, and counterfactual scenario testing confirmed that the energy gap between single-story and two-story buildings remains constant regardless of glazing level, establishing height as the primary design lever. The NSGA-II optimization identified designs achieving total energy as low as 17.06 kWh.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework bridges prediction and actionable design guidance for energy-efficient buildings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work is a novel optimization of energy in a building using nine models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10555-6.title: Faculty priorities for lecture, flipped classroom, and problem-based learning in anesthesiology education: a fuzzy AHP–SAW multi-criteria decision analysis
doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10555-6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Selecting an appropriate teaching method is critical in anesthesia education, where learners must develop rapid decision-making, teamwork, and problem-solving skills. This study used a multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) to prioritize lecture, flipped classroom (FC), and problem-based learning (PBL) from faculty perspectives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional MCDA study included faculty members from five Iranian Universities of medical sciences with ≥ 3 years of teaching experience and prior use of lecture, FC, and PBL. Evaluation criteria were identified through a scoping review of studies published from 2011 to 2025 and refined by an expert panel. A researcher-made instrument comprising seven domains and 25 items underwent face and content validation. Five experts completed pairwise comparisons, which were analyzed using fuzzy analytic hierarchy process (FAHP), and 15 faculty raters evaluated the teaching methods for simple additive weighting (SAW). Time limitation and need for technology were treated as cost criteria. Robustness was examined through sensitivity analyses of all seven domain weights, rater-specific rankings, and 10,000 bootstrap resamples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Quality (0.2987), perceived effectiveness (0.2292), and interaction (0.1795) received the highest weights. PBL ranked first (0.9701), followed by FC (0.9148) and lecture (0.6068). PBL produced the largest weighted contributions in quality, interaction, perceived effectiveness, and performance; FC had the largest contribution in flexibility, whereas lecture had the largest contribution in availability. The ranking remained unchanged across all specified domain-weight scenarios. Concordance among rater-specific rankings was high (Kendall’s W = 0.804;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), and PBL retained first position in 99.99% of bootstrap resamples.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This faculty-based MCDA provides a context-specific decision-support framework for selecting teaching strategies in anesthesiology education. The findings support consideration of active-learning approaches alongside local educational priorities, available resources, and implementation conditions, while prospective studies should evaluate learner outcomes and clinical competence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.61227/33xaew35.title: Managing for Learning: Head Teachers' Communication, Leadership, and Labour Relations in Ubungo Public Primary Schools, Tanzania
doi:10.61227/33xaew35.abstract: <jats:p>Effective headship coordinates instruction, people, trust, and organizational conditions, yet evidence from Tanzanian public primary schools remains limited. This study examined the perceived influence of head teachers' managerial practices on teaching and learning in Ubungo District. Its main objective was to assess how communication, leadership, and labour relations jointly support classroom work. A mixed-methods approach and convergent parallel descriptive design were employed. The sample comprised 179 respondents: 170 teachers and nine head teachers. Schools and teachers were selected randomly, while head teachers were purposively selected. Structured questionnaires, semi-structured interviews, and documentary review generated data. After official access and informed consent, both strands were collected concurrently and integrated during interpretation. Frequencies and percentages summarized questionnaires, while interview and documentary evidence were analysed thematically. Objective-based instrument development, expert review, piloting, standardized questioning, and triangulation supported validity, reliability, and credibility; the achieved reliability coefficient was not reported. Confidentiality, voluntary participation, withdrawal rights, and academic-only data use were observed. Findings showed strongest approval for instructional supervision (71.7%), participation in decision-making (70.6%), teamwork (68.2%), and professional-development support (67.7%). Weaker areas included clear communication of school goals (43.5% positive), fair conflict management (41.2%), fairness in leadership (47.1%), and a supportive working environment (47.7%). </jats:p>

doi:10.24127/jasei.v1i2.13335.title: PROTOTYPE OF AN ARDUINO UNO-BASED INFRARED SENSOR SYSTEM FOR AUTOMATIC AVERAGE SPEED MEASUREMENT IN UNIFORM LINEAR MOTION EXPERIMENTS TO SUPPORT PHYSICS LEARNING
doi:10.24127/jasei.v1i2.13335.abstract: <jats:p>Uniform linear motion practicum still uses many manual measurements which have the potential to cause human error in time recording and speed determination. This research aims to develop a prototype of an automatic speed measurement system based on infrared (IR) sensors and Arduino Uno as a supporting instrument for physics experiments. The research uses the Research and Development (R&D) method with the ADDIE model which includes analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation. The prototype integrates two IR sensors, an Arduino Uno, and an LCD to record travel time and automatically calculate average speeds at a nominal distance of 0.10 m. Tests on 12 mass conditions of 50–220 g resulted in a travel time of 8.171–1.063 s and an average speed of 0.01224–0.09407 m/s. The entire speed value generated by the system was consistent with the recalculation (v=d/∆t) up to the three-decimal rounding limit, with a maximum absolute difference of about 0.000457 m/s. These findings show that the automation functions of time recording and speed calculation have been running consistently. Validation of accuracy and repeatability still requires repeated measurements under identical conditions and comparison with independent reference instruments. This prototype has the potential to support more measurable, transparent, and technology-based physics experiments.</jats:p>

doi:10.4324/9781003713463-19.title: From Human Bias to Machine Signal
doi:10.4324/9781003713463-19.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technology has reshaped how investors access information and make decisions, with social media emerging as a key driver of market sentiment. This chapter explores the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI), social media sentiment, and behavioural bias mitigation in the Islamic capital market (ICM). Evidence shows that social media significantly affects stock prices, trading volume, and volatility, often amplifying biases such as overconfidence, herding, anchoring, and emotional decision-making. AI serves as a decision-support tool in areas including market analysis, risk management, compliance monitoring, algorithmic trading, and robo-advisory services. In the ICM, AI enhances Shariah compliance through automated screening and portfolio monitoring aligned with Islamic principles. It also mitigates biases by converting unstructured sentiment into actionable signals. Nonetheless, adoption remains constrained by Shariah uncertainty, regulatory gaps, technical limitations, governance issues, and cybersecurity risks.

doi:10.68217/pr0x6441.title: Integrating hybrid machine learning and Bayesian inference for predictive risk management in business organizations
doi:10.68217/pr0x6441.abstract: <jats:p>Business organizations increasingly use predictive analytics to identify emerging operational, financial, and strategic risks, yet predictions alone do not establish how uncertainty should be represented or translated into risk decisions. This conceptual article develops an integrated framework linking hybrid machine learning, Bayesian inference, and organizational risk management. Drawing on an integrative synthesis of research in enterprise risk management, probabilistic machine learning, Bayesian decision theory, organizational information processing, and dynamic capabilities, it distinguishes three mechanisms, namely predictive signal extraction, evidence-based belief updating, and loss-sensitive decision support. It specifies two alternative architectures, one placing Bayesian estimation within the predictive model and one using a conventional model output as evidence through a conditional evidence model estimated on held-out or cross-fitted predictions, and treats Bayesian dependency graphs as a structure compatible with either rather than a third option. The article separates probability calibration from likelihood estimation, states when overlapping prior and evidence information can be combined without double counting, and explains how data quality, prior elicitation, monitoring, managerial comprehension, and governance condition the usefulness of the resulting risk information. Six conditional propositions link these mechanisms to risk information quality, adaptive assessment, and decision quality. The framework explains when integrated systems may support risk management without assuming that Bayesian inference improves accuracy, calibration, or interpretability. A research agenda identifies matched benchmarks, comprehension-based decision experiments, and longitudinal organizational studies.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s42484-026-00457-7.title: Quantum convolutional neural networks for jet images classification
doi:10.1007/s42484-026-00457-7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Recently, interest in quantum computing has significantly increased, driven by its potential advantages over classical techniques. Quantum machine learning (QML) exemplifies one of the important quantum computing applications that are expected to surpass classical machine learning in a wide range of instances. This paper addresses the performance of QML in the context of high-energy physics (HEP). As an example, we focus on the top-quark tagging, for which classical convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been effective but fall short in accuracy when dealing with highly energetic jet images. In this paper, we use a quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN) for this task and compare its performance with CNN using a classical noiseless simulator. We compare various setups for the QCNN, varying the convolutional circuit, type of encoding, loss function, and batch sizes. For every quantum setup, we design a similar setup to the corresponding classical model for a fair comparison. Our results indicate that, using a classical simulator, QCNN with proper setups tend to perform better than their CNN counterparts, especially when the convolution block has a lower number of parameters. For the higher parameter regime, the QCNN circuit was adjusted according to the dimensional expressivity analysis (DEA) to lower the parameter count while preserving its optimal structure. The DEA circuit demonstrated improved results over the comparable classical CNN model.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/ils-01-2026-0006.title: Applying a humanistic data science framework to curricular development and implementation: a forensic analysis of synergies and tensions across layers in middle school social studies
doi:10.1108/ils-01-2026-0006.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As data science education becomes more common in K-12 education, there is a need to teach students about the technical, sociopolitical, and ethical dimensions of data. The authors restrospectively apply a humanistic stance toward data science education to investigate middle school students’ engagements with data across the personal, cultural, and sociopolitical layers. The purpose of this article is to develop theory and knowledge toward sustainable data literacy education that foreground Indigenous perspectives in U.S. social studies curricula. To that end, the research questions focus on multiple stakeholders (e.g., students, teacher, Indigenous communities).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on a rich corpus of qualitative data, including reflective interviews with the students and teacher and student work, a forensic analysis of the designed and enacted curriculum was conducted, unpacking the personal, cultural, and sociopolitical layers of data, paying particular attention to synergies or tensions between the layers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal synergies between layers that foregrounded student agency and emphasized Indigenous perspectives alongside tensions between layers that disrupted student sensemaking and supported a deficit perspective of Indigenous communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study extends prior work on data science education in social studies by operationalizing three layers of a humanistic stance toward data science to analyze students’ interactions across layers of data science in the unit, drawing attention to the implications of taken-for-granted tools of classroom data science and power structures and positioning within and outside of the classroom.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.38124/ijisrt/26sep1357.title: Challenges and Solutions in the Implementation of Student-Centered Learning in Afghanistan
doi:10.38124/ijisrt/26sep1357.abstract: <jats:p>In Afghanistan, the concept of Student-Centered Learning (SCL) is a relatively new and progressive educational approach, first introduced in 2001 to improve the quality of education. Between 2010 and 2016, the Ministry of Higher Education of Afghanistan developed official policies for SCL implementation and launched teacher training programs. This pedagogical approach emphasizes students’ active participation, independent and critical thinking, practical skills, and social responsibility. Its goal is to transform students from passive recipients of information into active participants in the learning process. This review article, alongside global experiences, assesses the feasibility, challenges, and opportunities of implementing SCL under Afghanistan’s unique conditions. Findings reveal that the lack of professional capacity among teachers, limited teaching resources and technology, students’ low academic levels, the absence of a reading culture, language barriers, and negative social and economic conditions pose serious obstacles to SCL implementation. Based on existing research, reports, and evidence, this article presents several scholarly and practical recommendations to address these challenges, including the implementation of systematic teacher training programs, expansion of resources and facilities, curriculum revision, reforms in monitoring and evaluation, language support, and strengthening international collaborations. A detailed table at the end of the article links each challenge with corresponding solutions and scholarly references, providing a comprehensive and practical framework for policymakers, faculty, and researchers. This article highlights the urgent need for fundamental reform in Afghanistan’s higher education system and underscores the importance of shifting from traditional methods to the implementation of student-centered learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fcvm.2026.1969401.title: A screening method for aortic valve disease based on spectral analysis of a single-channel electrocardiogram using machine learning algorithms
doi:10.3389/fcvm.2026.1969401.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Given the high prevalence of aortic heart disease and the importance of early diagnosis, there is a need to develop a simple screening method to identify significant aortic heart disease based on available biosignals, one of which is a single-channel electrocardiogram (ECG).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aim</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aimed to develop a machine learning algorithm for analyzing single-channel electrocardiograms to identify patients with moderate to severe aortic stenosis and regurgitation, as well as significant aortic valve disease.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Patients (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 2,503) underwent echocardiographic examination and single-channel I-lead ECG recording using a portable electrocardiograph. Moderate to severe aortic stenosis on echocardiography was present in 62 (2.4%) patients, and moderate to severe aortic regurgitation was present in 157 (6.3%). Single-channel ECG analysis was performed using advanced signal processing and machine learning techniques.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Both models were evaluated under an identical 10-fold group cross-validation framework. For detecting moderate or severe aortic stenosis, diagnostic accuracy was 0.650 (Se 57.9%, Sp 65.0%) for Balanced Random Forest and 0.662 (Se 46.4%, Sp 66.5%) for XGBoost. For moderate or severe aortic regurgitation, accuracy was 0.726 (Se 60.5%, Sp 73.3%) for Balanced Random Forest and 0.712 (Se 61.7%, Sp 71.9%) for XGBoost. For significant aortic valve disease, accuracy was 0.724 (Se 61.1%, Sp 73.4%) for Balanced Random Forest and 0.691 (Se 67.8%, Sp 69.2%) for XGBoost.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate good diagnostic accuracy and potential applicability for screening for significant aortic heart disease using single-channel ECG parameters analyzed with modern signal processing and machine learning techniques.</jats:p>

doi:10.53941/mm.2026.100007.title: Dynamic Machine Learning for the Oxygen Evolution Reaction: From Static Catalyst Screening to Working-State Trajectory Learning
doi:10.53941/mm.2026.100007.abstract: <jats:p>Efficient water electrolysis is limited not only by the sluggish kinetics of the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), but also by the dynamic reconstruction and degradation of catalysts under operating bias. Machine learning (ML) has accelerated OER catalyst screening by linking precursor composition, structural descriptors and adsorption energetics to endpoint activity, yet static endpoint models cannot determine when a working interface forms, how reaction pathways redistribute, or where stability costs accumulate during operation. This Review does not treat catalyst reconstruction or ML-assisted operando analysis as new concepts; instead, it formalizes their intersection as a supervised trajectory-learning problem. We define dynamic OER ML operationally as learning in which ordered operating history enters the prediction and the target contains at least one time-resolved state, transition event, pathway redistribution, degradation event or transfer trajectory. The field is organized around three learning targets: active-interface formation from precursors, coupled evolution of OER mechanisms and degradation routes, and transfer of material behavior across pH, electrolyte, potential program, transport and device boundaries. Static ML is repositioned as a source of precursor priors, whereas dynamic ML must learn state transitions, rates, latent working states, uncertainty and protocol-dependent transfer from time-resolved evidence. We further provide operational routes from raw operando signals to quantitative labels, target-specific evaluation metrics, baseline comparisons and leakage-safe validation rules. By shifting OER learning from material-endpoint ranking to material-condition-trajectory prediction, dynamic ML can support the prediction, preservation and control of real catalyst working states.</jats:p>

doi:10.4324/9781003654308-6.title: Delivering Care in the Digital Age
doi:10.4324/9781003654308-6.abstract: The rise of computers and technology, and the most recent iteration of which is artificial intelligence, has profoundly affected medical care, similar to their impacts on other fields. While more information can be stored, accessing, filtering, and making sense of that information is still a challenge in medicine. This chapter looks at how electronic medical records, in their attempts to capture every piece of information, can actually reduce the quality of care through information and warning fatigue. Key words and phrases can signal doubt to future providers reading a note, while inaccurate information that is never updated can worsen medical outcomes. The plethora of information available online can also increase patient autonomy but, in combination with the burgeoning consumer model of medicine, can cause various types of pragmatic difficulties. The chapter concludes on a hopeful note about how artificial intelligence models can aid providers in addressing some of the above challenges.

doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10504-3.title: Integrating generative AI into cognitive apprenticeship–based problem-based learning in biochemistry: a quasi-experimental study
doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10504-3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Problem-Based Learning (PBL) is extensively employed in medical education to promote advanced cognitive skills. At the foundational level of medical education, novice learners frequently encounter difficulties in forming cohesive knowledge structures due to an excessive cognitive load. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for learning support, yet its pedagogical role and integration mechanisms in medical education remain insufficiently explored.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study developed an AI-supported problem-based learning model grounded in the cognitive apprenticeship framework (AI-CAS-PBL). Using the “Lipid Metabolism” unit in a biochemistry course, a quasi-experimental design was used to compare AI-CAS-PBL with conventional PBL and lecture-based learning (LBL). The same instructor taught all three groups. Learning objectives, core content, scheduled contact time, case materials, and research outcome assessment procedures were standardized across groups, whereas instructional approaches, learning support, and out-of-class activities differed.The AI learning agent was developed on the Coze platform and powered by the Doubao 1.5 Pro 32 K large language model. Learning outcomes included lipid metabolism knowledge and case-based clinical reasoning. Technology acceptance, perceived cognitive workload measured using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), self-efficacy, and cognitive apprenticeship experience were also assessed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Students in the AI-CAS-PBL group achieved significantly higher post-test lipid metabolism knowledge and clinical application analysis scores than both the conventional PBL and LBL groups (all
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.05). Students reported high perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of the AI learning agent. Compared with the conventional PBL group, students in the AI-CAS-PBL group reported lower perceived cognitive workload and higher self-efficacy.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The AI-CAS-PBL group demonstrated higher post-intervention lipid metabolism knowledge and case-based clinical reasoning scores than the conventional PBL and LBL groups. Compared with conventional PBL, students in the AI-CAS-PBL group reported lower perceived cognitive workload and higher self-efficacy. These findings are consistent with the possibility that AI-supported questioning and instructor modeling may provide complementary forms of instructional support. However, because the interaction between AI and instructor scaffolding was not directly examined, the proposed dual-scaffolding framework should be regarded as a theoretically informed interpretation rather than a confirmed causal pathway. The model represents a promising approach to human–AI collaborative teaching that warrants further evaluation in larger, multicenter, and multi-class studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/ijshe-11-2025-1467.title: Bridging instructional design and technology adoption: the mediating role of student preference in metaverse-based English learning
doi:10.1108/ijshe-11-2025-1467.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine how student-perceived technology, content and pedagogy design influence vocational students’ intention to use metaverse-based English learning platforms and assess the mediating role of student preference.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A survey of 374 students from five vocational colleges was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling to examine the direct and indirect relationships among metaverse Technology (MTE), Content Design (CDE), Pedagogy Design (PDE), student Preference (STP) and intention to use (ITU).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CDE and PDE directly predicted ITU (β = 0.237 and β = 0.239, respectively), whereas MTE influenced ITU primarily through the STP. STP was the strongest predictor of ITU (β = 0.451) and significantly mediated all the instructional design dimensions. The model explained 54.4% of the variance in ITU (R2 = 0.544), indicating a strong explanatory power.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study offers a learner-centered account of metaverse adoption by integrating student-perceived technology, content and pedagogy with student preference as a mediating mechanism. The findings suggest that vocational colleges should prioritize authentic occupational content, coherent pedagogy, teacher preparation, accessible implementation, staged scaling and evaluation beyond adoption intention. Its sustainability contribution is deliberately bounded: through an sustainable development goal(s) (SDG) 4 lens, the study identifies instructional quality and learner acceptability as conditions relevant to responsible digital implementation, while recognizing that equity, accessibility, learning outcomes, institutional capacity, governance and long-term viability require additional evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1186/s13040-026-00609-2.title: An evolutionary guided framework for robust latent representation learning in gastrointestinal endoscopy images: EvoLatent-FS
doi:10.1186/s13040-026-00609-2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Learning robust and discriminative representations from gastrointestinal endoscopy images remains challenging due to high visual variability, subtle pathological differences, and pronounced class imbalance. While variational autoencoders (VAEs) have shown promise for unsupervised and semi-supervised representation learning, directly constructing latent spaces from high-dimensional deep features often leads to redundant and clinically irrelevant representations. In this study, we introduce a deep feature learning approach that is called EvoLatent-FS, led by evolution, that directly optimizes feature representations before latent modeling. The suggested method incorporates an intermediary evolutionary optimization stage that refines deep feature representations prior to variational encoding, in contrast to current approaches that either perform feature selection after representation learning or apply latent learning directly to raw deep features. This architecture preserves diagnostically relevant patterns while suppressing superfluous visual input, allowing the learning of more structured and discriminative latent spaces. The three primary parts of the framework are latent representation learning using a variational autoencoder, population-based evolutionary feature optimization via binary feature masking, and deep feature extraction using a convolutional backbone. The suggested method creates a unique representation learning pipeline that is suited to the difficulties of gastrointestinal endoscopic imaging by separating feature optimization from latent modeling and putting it directly before variational encoding. The suggested framework produces more compact latent representations and better downstream classification performance than traditional pipelines that directly apply latent modeling to unoptimized deep features, according to extensive experiments carried out on labeled gastrointestinal endoscopy image datasets. These findings demonstrate the efficacy of evolutionary-guided pre-latent feature optimization as a novel and principled approach to medical image representation learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s10163-026-02748-4.title: Real-time classification of waste polyethylene using terahertz and raman spectroscopy integrated machine learning
doi:10.1007/s10163-026-02748-4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Efficient polymer classification is vital to recycling, yet conventional methods often struggle to distinguish plastics within the same class because of their similar thermophysical properties. This study presents an in-operation machine-learning (ML) approach combining terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS) and Raman spectroscopy for rapid classification of industrial polyethylene (PE)-rich waste feedstocks. Spectral data from six industry-provided PE-rich materials with differences in additives and physical form were collected to build a dual-modality spectral library. Principal component analysis (PCA) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA) were applied for dimensionality reduction, and the resulting features were used to train polymer-classification models. The combined THz–Raman PCA model achieved 94.44% accuracy, while the same approach with individual THz and Raman-only modes achieved 89.26 and 87.41% accuracy, respectively. Adding LDA after PCA overgeneralized the small dataset, reducing combined and THz-only accuracy by up to 3.14% while improving Raman-only accuracy by 1.85%. The results demonstrate the feasibility and complementary value of integrating surface-sensitive Raman information with bulk-sensitive THz features for distinguishing compositionally similar PE-rich waste feedstocks. The complete process takes approximately 33 s: 30 s for THz, 3 s for Raman, and 0.0014 s for model inference, supporting rapid feedstock screening and quality control.</jats:p>

doi:10.5815/ijisa.2026.05.05.title: Hybrid Hierarchical Path Planning and Adaptive Tracking Control for Autonomous Vehicles via HDBHP Optimization and Reinforcement Learning
doi:10.5815/ijisa.2026.05.05.abstract: <jats:p>The new hierarchical path planning and tracking control model for autonomous vehicles utilizes hybrid optimization techniques, an adaptive potential field approach, and reinforcement learning to achieve safe, efficient, and adaptive path planning of the vehicles. Initially, a dynamic environment is generated to process path planning and traffic control with obstacles. The global path is computed using the Hybrid Dung Beetle and Hippopotamus Optimization (HDBHP) algorithm for minimum path distance, minimum obstacles, and minimum energy. This path is smoothed using Robust Locally Weighted Regression with Curvature Smoothing (RLWR-CS) to fulfill the vehicle kinematic constraints and obtain smoothness. For real-time local modulation, the Tent Map-Artificial Potential Field (TM-APF) approach is used, which is sensitive to obstacles and uses a chaotic path to plan for a better response. Control is done through Goal-Conditional Q-learning (GCQL) and Prioritized Q-learning (PQL), where decision-making is made with specific goals and prioritized experience replay. An integrated reward function ensures that the path is accurate, safe, fast, and comfortable for the passengers and ensures that the vehicle adapts to the roads from the start to the destination. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves improved Cumulative Rewards of 171.704 at episode 968 and 196.141 at episode 9,251. Also, the presented approach has a lower execution time of 1.65 seconds and outperforms existing approaches such as Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Deep Q-Networks (DQN), and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC).</jats:p>

doi:10.68404/ijce.v2i1.29.title: DESIGN OF A WEB-BASED LEARNING PROTOTYPE INTEGRATING MULTIMEDIA CONTENT, INTERACTIVE ASSESSMENT, AND PROGRESS TRACKING
doi:10.68404/ijce.v2i1.29.abstract: <jats:p>Web-based learning environments increasingly combine multimedia resources, assessment tools, and progress information, but the coexistence of these features does not ensure a coherent learning workflow. This study develops a design specification for a web-based learning prototype integrating multimedia content, interactive assessment, and activity-based progress tracking. The reported work covers requirements analysis, traceability mapping, a three-layer architecture, a logical data model, an access-and-learning workflow, and four interface views within a staged Waterfall-oriented design process. Progress is defined through explicit activity-completion states rather than inferred from resource access or assessment scores. A prospective evaluation protocol separates functional verification, media-expert appraisal, subject-matter review, and intended-user feedback. The design is positioned against recent evidence on multimedia learning, online assessment, learning analytics, and LMS development. The available evidence supports the internal coherence and traceability of the proposed design but does not establish operational reliability, usability, learning gains, or engagement effects. The study therefore contributes a bounded integration design and an auditable evaluation framework for subsequent implementation and empirical testing.</jats:p>

doi:10.51878/educational.v6i4.15826.title: UPAYA MENINGKATKAN HASIL BELAJAR SISWA MENGGUNAKAN MODEL COOPERATIVE LEARNING TIPE STAD MATA PELAJARAN BAHASA INDONESIA
doi:10.51878/educational.v6i4.15826.abstract:
<jats:p>Indonesian language instruction in primary education is frequently dominated by conventional lecture methods that restrict peer collaboration, leaving students' reading comprehension and language competencies underdeveloped. The lack of structured cooperative learning frameworks that cultivate individual accountability within team tasks remains a major cause of suboptimal academic performance. This study aims to enhance fifth-grade elementary students' Indonesian language learning outcomes by applying the Student Teams Achievement Division (STAD) cooperative learning model at SD Swasta Anastasia. This study utilized Classroom Action Research (CAR) conducted across two cycles, each encompassing planning, acting, observing, and reflecting phases. The research participants comprised all 29 fifth-grade students selected through total sampling. Data were accumulated through teacher and student observation checklists, cognitive achievement tests, and documentation procedures validated by educational experts. The findings demonstrated that implementing the STAD cooperative learning model substantially augmented students' learning engagement and academic achievement. The class mean score rose from 64.31 in the baseline assessment to 74.48 in Cycle I, ultimately reaching 87.59 in Cycle II. Classical learning mastery escalated markedly from 44.83% prior to intervention to 72.41% in Cycle I, and peaked at 93.10% in Cycle II, comfortably surpassing the set success benchmark of 85%. Consequently, the STAD cooperative learning model is verified to be effective in elevating elementary students' Indonesian language learning outcomes.
ABSTRAK
Pembelajaran Bahasa Indonesia di sekolah dasar masih sering didominasi oleh metode ceramah konvensional yang membatasi interaksi antarsiswa, sehingga pemahaman materi teks dan keterampilan berbahasa belum berkembang optimal. Keterbatasan eksplorasi model pembelajaran kooperatif terstruktur yang menekankan tanggung jawab individu dalam kelompok menjadi faktor utama rendahnya ketuntasan belajar siswa. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan hasil belajar Bahasa Indonesia siswa kelas V melalui penerapan model Cooperative Learning tipe Student Teams Achievement Division (STAD) di SD Swasta Anastasia. Jenis penelitian yang digunakan adalah Penelitian Tindakan Kelas (PTK) yang dilaksanakan dalam dua siklus, di mana setiap siklus mencakup tahap perencanaan, pelaksanaan tindakan, observasi, dan refleksi. Subjek penelitian melibatkan seluruh siswa kelas V SD Swasta Anastasia yang berjumlah 29 orang dan dipilih menggunakan teknik total sampling. Teknik pengumpulan data dilakukan melalui observasi aktivitas guru dan siswa, tes hasil belajar kognitif, serta studi dokumentasi yang telah divalidasi oleh ahli. Hasil penelitian membuktikan bahwa penerapan model Cooperative Learning tipe STAD efektif meningkatkan keaktifan dan hasil belajar siswa secara berkelanjutan. Nilai rata-rata kelas meningkat dari 64,31 pada tes awal menjadi 74,48 pada Siklus I, dan mencapai puncaknya sebesar 87,59 pada Siklus II. Persentase ketuntasan belajar klasikal siswa melonjak drastis dari 44,83% sebelum perlakuan menjadi 72,41% pada Siklus I, hingga akhirnya mencapai 93,10% pada Siklus II, melampaui indikator keberhasilan yang ditetapkan sebesar 85%. Dengan demikian, model pembelajaran kooperatif tipe STAD terbukti efektif dalam meningkatkan hasil belajar Bahasa Indonesia siswa sekolah dasar.
 
 </jats:p>

doi:10.54254/2753-7064/2026.ba37500.title: Research on the Knowledge Reproduction Mechanism of Bullet Comment Interaction in the Bilibili Learning Zone from the Perspective of Mediatization Theory
doi:10.54254/2753-7064/2026.ba37500.abstract: <jats:p>Gen Z students are now turning to Bilibili's Learning Zone as a regular part of their self-study routines, yet the exact role of digital media in this shift is still not well understood. Bullet comments, once seen mainly as a quick way to vent or react emotionally, have clearly grown into something more: a key media practice where users actively take part in reproducing knowledge. Drawing on mediatization theory, this paper looks closely at how these bullet-comment interactions actually work on Bilibili. It asks a simple but important question: how do bullet comments—shaped by the platform's technical setup and the video content itself—help users rework, fix, and add to existing knowledge? The study identifies three main mechanisms behind this process. First, users correct factual errors and fill in missing details. Second, they expand on abstract concepts by adding real-world context and personal experience. Third, over time, high-quality comments are upvoted and pinned, gradually turning into a structured layer of shared knowledge attached to the video. Through these real-time commenting practices, users and creators end up co-producing a kind of "symbiotic text." This directly challenges the old, centralized model of knowledge production in traditional education, and instead supports a more decentralized, collaborative style of informal learning. Existing survey data and typical cases confirm that this bullet-comment-driven knowledge reproduction is not just an occasional habit, but a widespread practice. By applying mediatization theory to this specific context, the research expands its use in the field of educational communication, and also offers practical ideas for improving online learning platforms and building a learning-oriented society. That said, the study does have some clear limitations—most notably its focus on top-tier creators and its confinement to a single platform. Future research could address these gaps by carrying out cross-platform comparisons and conducting longitudinal tracking studies to better understand how media technologies continue to shape online education.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1974520.title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation through a systematic review
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1974520.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s10915-026-03496-1.title: Using Machine Learning to Design Time Step Size Controllers for Stable Time Integrators
doi:10.1007/s10915-026-03496-1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We present a new method for developing time step controllers based on a technique from the field of machine learning. This method is applicable to stable time integrators that have an embedded scheme, i.e., that provide a local error estimate similar to Runge–Kutta pairs. To design good time step size controllers using these error estimates, we propose to use Bayesian optimization. In particular, we design a novel objective function that captures important properties such as tolerance convergence and computational stability. We apply our new approach to several modified Patankar–Runge–Kutta (MPRK) schemes and a Rosenbrock-type scheme, equipping them with controllers based on digital signal processing which extend classical PI and PID controllers. We demonstrate that the optimization process yields controllers that are at least as good as the best controllers chosen from a wide range of suggestions available for classical explicit and implicit time integration methods by providing work-precision diagrams for a variety of ordinary and partial differential equations.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s12912-026-05469-z.title: Clinical nurses’ readiness for interprofessional learning in the hospital-wide bed-sharing model and its associated factors: a cross-sectional study
doi:10.1186/s12912-026-05469-z.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>With the expansion of the “hospital-wide bed-sharing (HWBS)” model, clinical nurses face multiple challenges in cross-departmental collaboration scenarios, particularly in adapting to their evolving roles. Investigating the current state of readiness for interprofessional learning (RIPL) and its influencing factors is a critical starting point for optimising collaboration processes and ensuring patient safety. This study aimed to determine the RIPL of clinical nurses in a HWBS model and the associated influencing factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional study was conducted using convenience sampling among 718 clinical nurses at a single tertiary hospital in Jiangsu Province, China, from June to August 2025. A self-developed demographic questionnaire and validated scales, including the readiness for interprofessional learning scale, a psychological capital scale for nurses, and a perceived organisational support scale, were administered.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The mean RIPL score was 80.26 ± 11.49. Hierarchical multiple regression analysis revealed that experience with mentoring interns (
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                       = 0.096,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), psychological capital (PsyCap;
                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                       = 0.499,

doi:10.1007/s44290-026-00641-5.title: Machine learning prediction of strain dependent soil damping improves seismic analysis of bridge foundations
doi:10.1007/s44290-026-00641-5.abstract: Conventional empirical soil damping models often neglect strain-dependent, site-specific variability in heterogeneous alluvial deposits (sands, silts, gravels), leading to uncertainty in seismic bridge foundation design. This study develops a Random Forest (RF) model to predict strain-dependent damping from routine geotechnical parameters (SPT-N₆₀, D₅₀, uniformity coefficient, curvature coefficient, fines content, and plasticity index) and integrates it into nonlinear soil-pile-structure interaction (SPSI) simulations. A physics-informed dataset of 2,340 soil-layer records from ten bridge foundation sites was compiled and used for model training and validation. The RF model achieves cross-validation R² = 0.88, RMSE = 0.52%, and MAE = 0.35%, outperforming XGBoost (R² = 0.85) and ANN (R² = 0.81). Feature importance analysis identifies shear strain amplitude as the dominant predictor (42%), followed by SPT-N₆₀ (18%) and fines content (12%), consistent with established soil dynamics theory. Compared to conventional empirical damping assumptions (Seed & Idriss, 1970; Vucetic & Dobry, 1991), ML-based damping reduces prediction error in pile bending moment from 26% to 6% (20% points) and lateral displacement from 29% to 8% (21% points). The proposed framework enables site-specific seismic performance assessment of bridge foundations in heterogeneous alluvial deposits using only routine geotechnical investigation data, without requiring specialized dynamic laboratory testing.

doi:10.7748/ldp.29.5.5.s1.title: ‘Systemic failures’ across specialist services for service users managing diabetes
doi:10.7748/ldp.29.5.5.s1.abstract: Safety concerns have been raised about people with learning disabilities who self-administer insulin. The Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) has published a report – Insulin: supporting safe self-administration for patients in the community with a learning disability – and found ‘systemic failures across specialist services, device design and staff knowledge’.

doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c08242.title: <tt>pdb2reaction</tt> : End-to-End Reaction-Path Elucidation from PDB Structures Using Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c08242.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Elucidating enzymatic reaction mechanisms requires a sequence of computational tasks comprising active-site extraction, minimum-energy-path search, transition-state (TS) refinement, intrinsic reaction coordinate (IRC) validation, and quasi-rigid-rotor harmonic-oscillator (QRRHO) thermochemistry─stages typically connected by ad hoc scripting and per-system tuning. We present pdb2reaction, an open-source Python command-line toolkit that automates this entire pipeline directly from a user-curated PDB using a single machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) backend. A GPU-accelerated pysisyphus fork is bundled to perform the Hessian-based heavy computations─Hessian, IRC, and vibrational analysis─on the same CUDA device as the MLIP for the default backend, minimizing data transfer overhead. This toolkit also implements a bond-change-driven recursive path-search algorithm, which recovered the two-step reaction mechanism of the geranyl pyrophosphate C6-methyltransferase BezA─an SN2-like methyl transfer followed by glutamate-mediated deprotonation via a cationic intermediate─locating both transition states and the intermediate itself without a user-supplied intermediate geometry: from a reactant-state active-site cluster and a minimal scan list, and independently from the reactant and product structures alone. On a benchmark of 23 reaction steps across six enzymes, the broadest-coverage backend, UMA-m-1.1, reproduced the literature mechanism for 19 steps, each with a single imaginary frequency at the transition state. For BezA, all five backends recovered the same two-step pathway and the same rate-limiting step. pdb2reaction enables rapid PDB-to-mechanism elucidation on a single GPU, providing a high-throughput complement to higher-cost DFT-based cluster-model calculations and full enzyme–solvent QM/MM calculations.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-75037-7.title: An integrated framework for explainable and uncertainty-aware software defect prediction with adaptive risk scoring and multi-task deep residual learning
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-75037-7.abstract: Software defect prediction (SDP) is a challenging problem in SQA, the majority of the approaches that have been proposed so far focus on this problem as a binary classification problem, without taking into account the risk associated with each defective module. This paper introduces an integrated framework of adaptive risk scoring, Multi-Task deep residual learning with gated feature attention, Monte Carlo Dropout uncertainty quantification, and SHAP-based explainability that is applied simultaneously towards both defect detection and risk classification. This is due to a data-d Single-Task riven parameter λ optimized via a Spearman correlation used to calculate the risk score and SMOTETomek resampling and focal loss to address severe class imbalance. A defect detection ROC-AUC of 0.9581, F1-score of 0.5928, and recall of 0.7616 is achieved by the proposed model on the pc5 dataset; while a macro F1-score of 0.98 and accuracy of 0.99 are achieved by the proposed model on the risk classification task, in which the three risk classes are model-derived prioritisation tiers rather than independently validated defect-severity labels. Monte Carlo Dropout also identifies 25.2% of modules as high uncertainty candidates for manual review, while feature attribution shows that cyclomatic density, comment percentage and global data density are the most important features affecting defect risk.

doi:10.5815/ijisa.2026.05.08.title: A Novel Deep Learning Framework for Customer Segmentation and Satisfaction Analysis in Tourism using Multimodal User-generated Content
doi:10.5815/ijisa.2026.05.08.abstract: <jats:p>The tourism industry has experienced substantial growth in recent years, propelled by the evolving customer preferences and pervasive influence of social media platforms. To gain a competitive advantage, it is imperative to develop innovative approaches that enable the delivery of personalized services and a deeper understanding of customer satisfaction. By leveraging user-generated content, firms can better understand dynamic customer trends and optimize their marketing strategies accordingly. However, our research aims to develop a novel customer segmentation framework using advanced deep learning techniques to analyze user-generated content within the rapidly growing tourism industry. The methodology employs a novel hybrid deep learning approach that integrates Sentence-BERT for contextualized embeddings and a GRU-based Autoencoder for feature reduction in an adaptive manner. This process is followed by k-means clustering, which segments customers using both multi-criteria ratings and online reviews to provide a holistic understanding of customer experiences. The proposed framework's effectiveness is compared with multiple state-of-the-art models using robust evaluation metrics such as the silhouette coefficient and the Davies–Bouldin index. The study’s findings highlight that the proposed model classifies customers into four distinct segments, and the statistical test performed shows the significance of our result. The research study contributes to the advancement of user-generated content based market segmentation in the tourism industry by unifying textual and numerical feedback into a single analytical framework. The findings offer valuable insights for tourism businesses seeking to enhance customer satisfaction through personalized service strategies and data-driven decision-making.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11283628/v1.title: Forecasting the Digital Divide: A Comparative Machine Learning Study of ICT Access Trajectories
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11283628/v1.abstract: Digital connectivity is an important dimension of digital inclusion, but connectivity should not be treated as equivalent to digital skills, quality of use, downstream benefits, or cybersecurity-governance capacity. This study constructs a composite Connectivity Index from Internet use, mobile subscriptions, fixed broadband subscriptions, and electricity access and evaluates its short-term predictability using persistence and multivariate supervised models. World Bank World Development Indicators are used after a reporting-coverage filter. The baseline index assigns weights of 0.40, 0.20, 0.20, and 0.20, respectively. Because these weights are theory-informed rather than estimated from data, alternative weighting schemes are evaluated as robustness checks. In the final rerun, the index is available for 2002-2024, while the lagged modeling sample covers 2004-2024 and contains 3,732 country-year observations from 196 countries. On the common test set of 537 observations, linear regression has the lowest RMSE (4.300), followed by random forest (4.353), XGBoost (4.454), and naive persistence (4.582). Thus, the final run supports a modest predictive improvement from multivariate regression over persistence, but not a general machine-learning advantage. The attempted ARIMA and Holt/ETS benchmarks produced zero valid test observations in the supplied rerun and are therefore not used for substantive model-ranking claims. Weight sensitivity shows that the index is highly correlated with the baseline specification, but country-level changes are non-negligible and predictive performance varies across weighting schemes. For Kazakhstan, long-horizon analysis is presented as scenario extrapolation rather than a point forecast, with 2049 scenario values of 96.72 for a recent-trend linear path, 77.35 for a full-history logistic path, and 77.70 for an accelerated pre-2018 logistic calibration. These values are relative index positions, not percentages of connected people or measures of digital-system scale. The study does not estimate cybersecurity-governance capacity or a causal connectivity-cyber-risk relationship; connectivity trajectories are interpreted only as planning inputs for stress-testing digital-service and cybersecurity requirements.

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1924421.title: Playful and physically active mathematics learning in primary education: an exploratory comparison of pupils in schools with and without the darts math program
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1924421.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The aim of this study was to compare mathematical performance and cognitive abilities among third- and fourth-grade pupils attending schools with established use of the Darts Math Program (DMP) and pupils attending schools following the general mathematics program (GP).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This cross-sectional, non-randomized comparative study included 124 pupils from four primary schools in Northern Hungary (DMP:
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 70; GP:
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 54). Schools were purposively selected, and DMP exposure was determined by pre-existing school-level implementation. Curriculum-aligned mathematics assessments and selected tasks from the Gyarmathy Cognitive Profile Test were administered. Group comparisons used independent-samples Student's t-tests or Welch's
                      <jats:italic>t</jats:italic>
                      -tests, as appropriate, with effect-size estimates and 95% confidence intervals, Holm correction applied separately within the mathematics and cognitive outcome families, and general linear models examining grade and group × grade effects. Sensitivity analysis indicated that, with 80% statistical power, the available sample was sufficient to detect effects of approximately d = 0.51 or larger.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Before correction for multiple comparisons, the DMP group achieved higher scores in algebra (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = .031, d = 0.40), spatial perception (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = .031, d = 0.39), and cognitive total score (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = .030, d = 0.38). None of the mathematics or cognitive group differences remained statistically significant after Holm correction within their respective outcome families. General linear models accounting for grade reproduced the same exploratory pattern, and no grou
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       × grade interaction was statistically significant.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings do not provide confirmatory evidence of systematic differences associated with DMP participation. Instead, they reveal small-to-moderate, domain-specific patterns that may provide a basis for hypotheses to be tested in adequately powered longitudinal or experimental studies. Because the observed effect sizes were smaller than the detectable effect indicated by the sensitivity analysis (d = 0.51), the non-significant findings should not be interpreted as evidence for the absence of smaller effects. Although school-level DMP exposure is confounded with teacher and school context and therefore precludes causal inference, the observed domain-specific patterns identify potentially useful directions for more rigorous future research on playful and physically active mathematics learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
