doi:10.31294/informatika.v13i2.13512.title: <b>Sentiment Analysis of Indonesian Mobile Banking Reviews on Google Play Store in 2025: A Comparison of Machine Learning Algorithms</b>
doi:10.31294/informatika.v13i2.13512.abstract: <jats:p>Mobile banking applications generate large volumes of user reviews that can be used to evaluate digital banking service quality. This study analyzes sentiment in Indonesian mobile banking reviews on the Google Play Store in 2025 and compares the performance of Naive Bayes (NB), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Random Forest (RF). A total of 270,977 reviews were collected from five applications, namely BRImo, Livin’ by Mandiri, myBCA, BYOND by BSI, and wondr by BNI. The data were processed through text cleaning, case folding, tokenization, word normalization, stopword removal, and negation retention. Sentiment labels were generated automatically using the InSet Lexicon and validated on 450 stratified review samples. The validation results showed moderate agreement between automatic and manual labels, with an accuracy of 0.6111, macro-F1 score of 0.5384, and Cohen’s Kappa of 0.4167. Review texts were represented using TF-IDF with unigram and bigram features, and model performance was evaluated across six stratified data-splitting scenarios using accuracy, macro precision, macro recall, macro-F1, confusion matrix, and macro ROC-AUC. The results show that RF in Scenario 6 achieved the best performance, with an accuracy of 0.9524, macro-F1 score of 0.8498, and macro ROC-AUC of 0.9798. Dominant-term analysis indicates recurring complaints related to login failures, transaction errors, system disruptions, and application updates. This study contributes a cross-application comparison of machine learning algorithms for Indonesian mobile banking sentiment analysis and provides practical insights for improving service reliability. However, the findings should be interpreted within the limitation of automatic lexicon-based labeling, particularly for neutral and context-dependent reviews. </jats:p>

doi:10.47764/2026.e08.1994.title: Inteligência Artificial (IA) no processo de ensino-aprendizagem da matemática
doi:10.47764/2026.e08.1994.abstract: <jats:p>Have you ever used AI in your math classes, and/or school and academic activities? It is known that AI in Education has emerged as a driving factor in transforming thoughts. The objective is to identify whether AI has influenced the teaching and learning processes of mathematics in basic education, based on statements from teachers in the Brazilian public education network. A qualitative case study research is presented, with exploratory purposes, aiming to gain knowledge about the use of AI in school and academic activities. It was identified in the data analysis that the teachers responding to the electronic questionnaire were unaware of AI and its contributions to teaching. But it is clear that they are curious about the topic, and refer to AI, but commonly, as a “simulator of human intelligence”. Thus, it is concluded that the discussion on the topic is relevant, and webinars, workshops and thematic mini-courses are proposed, elucidating the importance of a fruitful debate around ethical reflections that highlight the potential use of AI in school and academic spaces.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s12906-026-05632-8.title: A system pharmacology framework to explore the therapeutic mechanism of Bushen-Yizhi formula against Alzheimer’s disease via integrating UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS, network analysis, machine learning and experimental validation
doi:10.1186/s12906-026-05632-8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is an incurable neurodegenerative disease, and Bushen-Yizhi formula (BSYZ) has shown clinical potential for AD treatment, yet its bioactive components and pharmacological mechanisms remain unproven. To explore the therapeutic mechanism of BSYZ against AD-like cognitive impairment, a systems pharmacology framework was established via the integration of UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS, network analysis, machine learning and experimental validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chemical composition of BSYZ was characterized by UPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS. A scopolamine (SCOP)-induced mouse model of AD-like cognitive impairment was used to evaluate neuroprotective effects via behavioral, histopathological, and biochemical assays. AD-associated targets were identified by differential expression analysis and WGCNA. Core targets were screened using 127 machine learning models with SHAP interpretation and validated by RT-qPCR. Stage-stratified transcriptomic analysis assessed gene expression across AD stages. Molecular docking and 100-ns MD simulations explored binding of core components to targets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One hundred five compounds were identified from BSYZ. In SCOP-treated mice, BSYZ ameliorated cognitive deficits, oxidative stress, cholinergic dysfunction, and neuroinflammation. Bioinformatics uncovered 81 potential AD targets, from which seven core genes (HIPK2, CXCR4, CCKBR, PTPN13, SFN, ALB, ALDH1A1) were refined. RT-qPCR confirmed differential mRNA expression, and stage-stratified analysis revealed dynamic changes during AD progression. Molecular docking and MD suggested that isoquercitrin and epicatechin gallate bind to CXCR4 and CCKBR, providing computational evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings support the multi-component, multi-target neuroprotective effects of BSYZ against AD-like cognitive impairment, providing a basis for further preclinical development and mechanistic investigation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1093/her/cyag032.title: Effectiveness and retention of learning the use of an automated external defibrillator in adolescents: a comparative analysis of three teaching methods
doi:10.1093/her/cyag032.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study compared the effectiveness of three teaching methods (traditional, video-based, and augmented reality training) on the acquisition, performance quality, and retention of automated external defibrillator skills in secondary school students. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with post-intervention measurements and a 3-month follow-up. 193 untrained students (aged 13–15) were divided into three intervention groups (traditional training group, video training group, and augmented reality training group). Skills were individually assessed using a simulation manikin immediately post-intervention and at a 3-month follow-up, measuring shock effectiveness, safety, quality, and time. Immediately after training, all methods achieved high rates of effective and safe shocks, though performance quality was superior in the digitally supported groups. At 3 months, the augmented reality training group maintained a 100% effective shock rate, whereas the traditional training group showed a significant decrease. While execution times were similar initially, differences emerged during follow-up. In conclusion, although all methodologies are effective for initial skill acquisition, digital resource-based training promotes higher execution quality and superior long-term retention, strongly supporting their implementation in educational contexts.</jats:p>

doi:10.20319/ictel.2026.336337.title: SEMANTIC AMBIGUITY IN ENGLISH VOCABULARY AND ITS IMPACT ON LEARNING COMPUTER SCIENCE CONCEPTS: A BLOOM’S TAXONOMY APPROACH
doi:10.20319/ictel.2026.336337.abstract: <jats:p>Semantic ambiguity presents a significant challenge for English-as-a-Second-Language (ESL) students studying Computer Science (CS) in English-medium contexts. Many common English words, such as stack, queue, port, thread, and class, acquire specialized meanings in CS that diverge sharply from their everyday usage, creating cognitive interference that can hinder conceptual understanding and the application of CS principles. This phenomenological study investigates how seven Year 13 ESL learners enrolled in the Cambridge 9618 A Level Computer Science syllabus experience, interpret, and resolve ambiguity within CS vocabulary. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and student reflections, and analysed thematically. Three key themes emerged: (1) cognitive dissonance triggered by competing everyday and technical meanings, (2) learner-driven strategies including visualization, analogy, and scaffolded explanation, to reconcile semantic conflict, and (3) the role of instruction grounded in Bloom’s Taxonomy in promoting conceptual clarity, retention, and higher-order thinking. Findings indicate that semantic ambiguity affects learners across all cognitive levels, from basic recall to advanced abstraction. The study proposes a taxonomy-based instructional toolkit that emphasizes explicit contrastive teaching, multimodal scaffolding, and analogy-supported explanations. Implications for pedagogy, curriculum design, and vocabulary support in ESL-STEM learning environments are discussed.</jats:p>
doi:10.20319/ictel.2026.336337.venue: PUPIL: International Journal of Teaching, Education and Learning

doi:10.1002/jcal.70352.title: Ethical Generative <scp>AI</scp> Use in Higher Education: An Action Research Study Using the Think Aloud Method
doi:10.1002/jcal.70352.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, it presents significant challenges related to ethical use, academic integrity and students' potential over‐reliance on AI‐generated outputs. The Think Aloud method offers a pedagogical approach for making students' reasoning visible as they interact with generative AI tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This mixed‐methods action research study explored the role of the Think Aloud method as a pedagogical intervention in supporting students' metacognitive awareness and ethical engagement with generative AI tools in a first‐year entrepreneurship course.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected through reflective journals, classroom observations and a post‐intervention survey. The study involved 44 first‐year undergraduate students, with 38 students completing the post‐intervention survey. Qualitative data were analysed thematically, while survey responses were examined using descriptive statistics and an exploratory correlation analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings suggested that Think Aloud supported students' emerging awareness of prompt construction, verification practices and ethical decision‐making when using generative AI. However, students' critical evaluation of AI‐generated content often remained at a surface level, particularly among students requiring additional support. The study indicates that Think Aloud can make students' AI‐related reasoning more visible and can support more intentional engagement with generative AI, but it should not be viewed as a stand‐alone solution. Rather, it appears most effective when embedded within a broader pedagogical framework that includes AI literacy, prompt engineering, verification strategies and evaluative judgement. The study contributes classroom‐based evidence on process‐oriented approaches to ethical generative AI use in higher education and highlights the need for sustained instructional scaffolding to support deeper critical engagement with AI tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1038/s41746-026-03387-7.title: Early prediction of prolonged ICU stay in sepsis patients using an explainable hybrid deep learning model
doi:10.1038/s41746-026-03387-7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sepsis remains a leading cause of intensive care unit (ICU) admission and is frequently associated with prolonged ICU stay, which contributes to increased morbidity, healthcare utilization, and strain on critical care resources. Despite widespread use, existing clinical severity scores inadequately capture the individual risk of prolonged ICU stay in sepsis. We developed a hybrid deep learning (FT-TabNet) model with an adaptive gated fusion framework to predict prolonged ICU stay (>4 days) using 17 routinely collected Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-based features available within the first 24 hours of ICU admission. Model development and internal validation were performed using the MIMIC-IV dataset, with external validation conducted in a single-center cohort from Chungbuk National University Hospital (CBNUH) and Chungnam National University Hospital (CNUH), South Korea. The hybrid model showed strong discriminative performance in internal validation, achieving an AUROC of 0.848, and consistent performance across the external validation cohort, with modest variability, achieving an AUROC of 0.823 in the CBNUH and 0.781 in the CNUH cohort. SHAP-based explainability enabled transparent, patient-level interpretation of key contributors to prolonged ICU stay risk. These findings suggest that an explainable hybrid deep learning approach can help clinicians to identify patients at risk of prolonged ICU stay early in sepsis, using routine clinical data to support clinical decision-making and ICU resource allocation.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8735-2.ch002.title: AI-Driven Digital Assessment and Intelligent Feedback Systems for Personalized Learning Enhancement
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8735-2.ch002.abstract: <jats:p>The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) in educational assessment is revolutionizing the conventional assessment process to make it more dynamic, adaptive, and personalized. The present chapter discusses the application of AI in digital assessment in the context of personalized learning, utilizing theoretical foundations from educational psychology, cognitive sciences, and machine learning. Various models such as intelligent tutoring systems, automatic essay grading, knowledge tracing, and affective computing are discussed in detail. Comparative analyses of the different technologies, platforms, modes of feedback, and ethical considerations are also highlighted. Although empirical studies have proven the efficacy of AI-powered assessment, this chapter also highlights the need for transparency, equity, proper data management, and human supervision.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8735-2.ch002.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1363-2.ch004.title: Federated Learning and Blockchain Integration for Privacy-Preserving Smart Classrooms
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1363-2.ch004.abstract: <jats:p>The development of smart classroom technology hastened the implementation of data-driven and personalized learning systems, with the significant concern of data privacy, security, and trust. In this chapter, the author introduces a combined system of Federated Learning (FL) and blockchain to implement decentralized and privacy-sensitive smart classrooms. FL enables distributed nodes to collaboratively train models without exchanging raw student data, which is guaranteed to preserve the privacy of student data. Blockchain improves the reliability of the system by offering a secure, transparent and non-tamperable model updating and interaction validation. The paper contains a conceptual model, methodology, and case-based analysis with the evidence of privacy, accuracy, and scalability of the system improvement. The framework suggested will facilitate safe, effective and reliable learning ecosystems of the next generation smart learning classrooms.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1363-2.ch004.venue: Integrating Blockchain, Federated Learning, and Metaverse Ecosystems Into Decentralized Classrooms

doi:10.1108/eisfl-07-2026-0115.title: The donkey and the algorithm: cultivating judgement infrastructure for AI literacy in higher education
doi:10.1108/eisfl-07-2026-0115.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper reframes artificial intelligence (AI) literacy in higher education as a problem of judgement formation rather than tool fluency alone. It asks how students can be supported not only to use generative AI, but also to evaluate, limit, disclose or refuse its use responsibly under conditions of uncertainty.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper develops a conceptual and pedagogical argument through engagement with AI literacy scholarship, evaluative judgement, information judgement and educational theory. Rhetorical literacy, informal logic and argumentation, and ethical reasoning/phronesis are used as a pragmatic framework for analysing the judgement capacities required for meaningful AI engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper proposes a judgement-infrastructure account of AI literacy. It argues that student suspicion, selective use, uncritical reliance and refusal can be read as sites where judgement is practised, bypassed or left unarticulated. The Judgement-Infrastructure Gap Model is offered as a diagnostic heuristic for examining where judgement is supported or neglected across curricula, assessment, institutional policy and technological platforms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As a conceptual paper, the argument and model require empirical and design-based testing. Future research should examine how students justify AI use, limited use, disclosure and refusal across disciplines, and how programme-level scaffolding, assessment design, institutional policy and technological platforms support evaluative judgement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI literacy initiatives should include assessable activities that make reasoning visible, such as claim-evidence mapping, annotated AI outputs, oral defences, AI-free checkpoints, ethical decision logs and justified decisions about AI use, limitation, disclosure or refusal. These practices should be supported at programme and institutional levels rather than placed only on individual teachers or students.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper contributes a judgement-infrastructure account of AI literacy that treats both use and non-use as teachable and assessable forms of evaluative judgement. It extends existing AI literacy frameworks by linking student suspicion, refusal, assessment design, programme-level scaffolding and educational ecosystem conditions to responsible AI engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11137088/v1.title: Intelligent Test Case Scheduling Using Multi-Criteria Decision Making for Human–Machine Interface Testing​
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11137088/v1.abstract: Factory testing of industrial human–machine interface (HMI) system is typically conducted under stringent constraints: a fixed and non-extendable time budget, limited test resources, and zero tolerance for undetected critical failures. Under these conditions, the order and selection of test cases constitute a quality-risk decision rather than a mere efficiency concern. In practice, however, test case selection relies largely on engineers' experience and ad-hoc checklists, resulting in inconsistent coverage, inefficient resource use, and poor reproducibility across releases. To address this gap, we propose a Time-Weighted Utility Scoring Model (TWUSM) for automated test case prioritization and selection. The model evaluates each test case along three dimensions (risk impact on system safety, functional importance, and testing cost) and combines them into a single utility score that is updated with historical execution feedback. Test cases are then assigned to priority tiers: those above a predefined threshold are deterministically included as mandatory tests, while the remainder are admitted by probabilistic sampling with probability proportional to their normalized scores. This hybrid scheme enforces quality first by guaranteeing complete verification of critical functionalities, and then, subject to this constraint, maximizes fault detection per unit of testing time. Evaluated on an industrial HMI system, TWUSM achieves 100% detection of critical failures and an APFD of 0.9987. Compared with full test-suite execution (425.9 s), it reduces testing time to 174.9 s (− 58.9%) without any loss of failure coverage. The results show that utility-based prioritization can provide a reproducible, resource-aware basis for inspection planning in safety-critical industrial software, assuring product quality while substantially reducing test duration.

doi:10.1080/26889277.2026.2747483.title: Non-Destructive Imaging and Structural Techniques for Reliability Assessment of Power Electronic Modules: A Literature Review of Conventional, Automated and Machine Learning-Based Approaches
doi:10.1080/26889277.2026.2747483.abstract: The rapid expansion of electrified transport, renewable energy systems and high-efficiency industrial power converters relies on the robustness of power electronic modules and multi-chip packaging architectures. As module power densities rise and operating environments become more extreme, reliability becomes a key determinant of system lifetime, safety and cost. Thermo-mechanical degradation mechanisms such as die-attach delamination, bond-wire lift-off often initiate within material layers, making non-destructive testing (NDT) essential for quality and health monitoring. This literature review assesses state-of-the-art non-destructive imaging modalities for power electronic modules, with primary focus on IGBT packaging architectures. It covers X-ray imaging, scanning acoustic microscopy (SAM), optical metrology and infrared thermography. Rather than treating these modalities in isolation, it evaluates their compatibility, limits and fault-oriented application ranges. Emphasis is placed on the industry transition from manual evaluation to automated, machine learning-driven workflows for defect segmentation, void quantification and multimodal data fusion. It concludes by outlining industrial best practices, software and hardware bottlenecks and directions for embedding machine learning into autonomous packaging inspection. No single NDT technique provides complete assessment of module health, necessitating the complementary use of multiple modalities. Automation and machine-learning approaches improve defect detection but reamin dependant on physics-based measurements, high-quality data and application-specific workflows.

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1961926.title: Explainable machine learning for preoperative prediction of acute kidney injury after intertrochanteric fracture surgery in older adults
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1961926.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an important postoperative complication in older patients undergoing surgery for intertrochanteric femoral fracture. This study aimed to develop and internally evaluate an explainable model for preoperative AKI risk assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective study included 616 patients aged ≥60 years, including 54 (8.8%) who developed postoperative AKI. Candidate predictors were processed and selected using development-cohort data, and seven machine-learning algorithms were compared. Model performance was assessed across 100 repeated stratified 70/30 partitions and by 500-repetition model-specific and complete-pipeline bootstrap analyses. Calibration, decision-curve analysis, and SHAP were used to evaluate and interpret the selected model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The reported Naive Bayes model comprised baseline serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, chloride, uric acid, and chronic kidney disease or renal insufficiency. Across 100 repeated partitions, its mean validation AUC was 0.7231 (SD, 0.0260). The optimism-corrected AUC was 0.8004 for the fixed five-predictor Naive Bayes specification and 0.756 when the complete development pipeline was repeated; the latter analysis yielded a corrected Brier score of 0.084, calibration intercept of 0.02, and calibration slope of 1.70. In the original algorithm-comparison cohort, the observed AUC was 0.795 (95% CI, 0.698–0.892). When the first serum creatinine measurement obtained after admission was used as the alternative reference value, the number of AKI events decreased from 54 to 43 and the validation AUC was 0.706 (95% CI, 0.586–0.826).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The model showed moderate internal discrimination across repeated partitions. Model-specific and complete-pipeline bootstrap analyses provided complementary estimates of internal optimism. The model may complement routine preoperative renal assessment while its calibration and transportability are evaluated in additional cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.56201/ijcsmt.vol.11.no7.2025.pg25.title: Deep Learning-Based Detection of Malicious Nodes in PoS Permissionless Blockchains
doi:10.56201/ijcsmt.vol.11.no7.2025.pg25.abstract:
<jats:p>Identifying malevolent nodes on blockchain networks is essential for preserving the integrity
and safeguarding the security of decentralized systems. By utilizing advanced algorithms and
analysis approaches, such as machine learning and deep learning models, it is possible to
identify abnormal behaviours that suggest hostile intent. Through the analysis of transaction
patterns, node behaviour, and network interactions, these detection techniques may accurately
distinguish between legal nodes and those involved in malicious activities like as double
spending, Sybil attacks, or denial-of-service operations. By taking a proactive approach,
potential threats can be effectively mitigated, which in turn promotes confidence and reliability
in the blockchain ecosystem. This ultimately leads to widespread acceptance and scaling of the
technology. This paper Provides a detailed explanation of the methodology used to enhance
blockchain security by identifying and addressing rogue nodes. The analysis commenced with
an exploratory examination of the data, which allowed for a comprehensive grasp of the
numerical and categorical characteristics of the dataset. Afterwards, the Multi-Layer
Perceptron (MLP) method was utilized, showcasing exceptional performance with an accuracy
of around 98% for both the training and validation datasets. In addition, the model
demonstrated minimum loss values, at 0.06%, which suggests strong learning and
generalization ability. The results emphasize the effectiveness of deep learning methods in
strengthening blockchain networks against hostile actions, therefore guaranteeing their
integrity and dependability.</jats:p>

doi:10.1137/25m181088x.title: Learning Barycenters from Signature Matrices
doi:10.1137/25m181088x.abstract:
<jats:p>Abstract.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The expected signature of a family of paths need not be a signature of a path itself. Motivated by this, we consider the notion of a Lie group barycenter introduced by Buser and Karcher to propose a barycenter on path signatures. We show that every element of the free nilpotent Lie group is a barycenter of a group sample, where all but one sample element can be fixed arbitrarily. In the case of piecewise linear paths, we study the problem of recovering an underlying path corresponding to the barycenter of signatures. We determine the minimal number of segments required to learn from signature matrices, providing explicit transformations to the associated congruence normal forms.</jats:p>

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh3246.title: Machine learning–assisted directed evolution of plant Rubisco
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh3246.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (Rubisco) is foundational to life on Earth, catalyzing carbon dioxide (CO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) fixation to generate biomass. However, Rubisco is a slow and inefficient enzyme that has proven challenging to engineer. We applied the structure-informed machine learning (ML) model ESM-IF1 to identify plausible amino acid sites in the large subunit of
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Nicotiana tabacum</jats:italic>
                    Rubisco to target for directed evolution. ML-assisted library design followed by selection in Rubisco-dependent
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Escherichia coli</jats:italic>
                    identified multiple enriched variants displaying improved catalytic efficiency. Several improved variants carried amino acid changes not found in the evolutionary lineage of plants, despite being assembly competent in plant chloroplasts, demonstrating that ML-assisted protein design can explore functional sequence space beyond what is observed from natural sequence diversity. Most prominently, the T391I substitution improved carboxylation rate by 29% and aerobic carboxylation efficiency by 43%. Our findings illustrate the utility of ML-assisted evolution for engineering Rubisco with improved carboxylation efficiency and potential for enhancing crop productivity.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aea1557.title: AIMNet2-rxn: A machine-learned potential for generalized reaction modeling on a millions-of-pathways scale
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aea1557.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Mechanistic modeling of chemical transformations offers a compelling basis for understanding reactivity and allows for prediction of reaction outcomes before attempting experiments. Despite progress in machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), we demonstrate that available models lack the accuracy for diverse reaction modeling. With this motivation, we developed a general MLIP for mechanistic modeling of closed-shell carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen reactions, AIMNet2-rxn, using a dataset of ∼4.7 × 10
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    range-separated density functional theory calculations. AIMNet2-rxn enables reaction modeling ∼10
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    faster than the reference quantum mechanical (QM) methods while substantially outperforming graph-based ML, reaffirming the value using three-dimensional chemical information for training. On a test suite of well-known reaction mechanisms—such as amide formation, proton transfers, and pericyclics—AIMNet2-rxn yields 1 to 2 kilocalories per mole accuracy across reaction coordinates without retraining or system-specific fine-tuning. To exploit graphics processing unit parallelism and AIMNet2-rxn efficiency, we introduce a batched nudged elastic band procedure that readily achieves minimum energy pathway search on a millions-of-reactions scale. To demonstrate complex reaction characterization, the thermodynamics of an 11-step pathway producing hydroxymethylfurfural, the experimentally observed major product of glucose pyrolysis, is evaluated. Overall, the accuracy and efficiency afforded by AIMNet2-rxn create opportunities in high-throughput reaction discovery and deep reaction network analysis that would be infeasible with QM methods.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1108/lfet-05-2026-0066.title: Temporal epistemology in the age of AI: learning, knowing and the reorganization of chronological structure
doi:10.1108/lfet-05-2026-0066.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper argues that generative artificial intelligence (AI) has forced a reckoning with a long-standing inadequacy in the temporal assumptions that have structured educational thought since the Enlightenment. It introduces post-linear epistemology as a framework for understanding how knowledge functions when learning is no longer adequately modelled as movement through a temporal sequence and develops concrete implications for curriculum design, assessment and teacher practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper is conceptual. It synthesizes scholarship on complexity in education, non-linear learning, technological acceleration, futures studies and critical artificial intelligence in education and uses this synthesis to specify the conditions under which a post-linear account of educational knowledge becomes necessary.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper identifies three interrelated shifts that, on this account, characterize the post-linear condition and are proposed here as claims for further examination rather than as established findings. First, chronologically ordered curriculum sequences are argued to be no longer adequate as the default architecture of educational design – though not as the only legitimate one. Second, cumulative derivation is argued to be increasingly displaced, in AI-mediated contexts, by probabilistic and relational forms of knowledge production. Third, temporal literacy – the capacity to identify when information was produced, how it has drifted and what time-frame it presupposes – is proposed as a distinct educational capacity, with three specifiable components, that these conditions make newly necessary.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper is conceptual, not empirical. The claims about how recursive AI use affects student work and about whether temporal literacy can actually be taught and measured are presented as hypotheses for design-based research, not as findings. The framework is meant to make those questions easier to investigate, not to answer them.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three changes follow. Curriculum design should look at which prerequisite sequences are actually necessary and which are inherited habit. Pedagogy should teach temporal literacy directly, using provenance critique, drift mapping and positioning essays, instead of treating it as a by-product of other work. Assessment should measure how students locate and situate knowledge, not just what they can reproduce.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-generated text routinely blends sources from different periods into a single fluent voice. That makes the question of whose perspectives get amplified, and whose get smoothed away, a public concern rather than a specialist one. Temporal literacy is one of the capacities through which an ordinary reader can interrogate AI-mediated text for what it has left out.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Other accounts of non-linear learning (complexity theory, connectivism, postdigital thought) already cover much of what AI intensifies. None of them was built for one specific thing: AI generation flattens the temporal markers that normally tell sources apart. This paper picks out that specific feature, names the literacy needed to read against it and turns the conceptual claim into concrete recommendations for curriculum, assessment and teacher practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.47852/bonviewjcce62027832.title: Enhancing Molecularly Imprinted Polymer Development with Machine Learning Techniques
doi:10.47852/bonviewjcce62027832.abstract:
<jats:p>Molecular imprinted polymers (MIPs) have various applications such as chemical sensing and drug delivery systems because they can selectively attach molecules that fit the template. The imprinting factor (IF) is used to assess the degree of contact between the binding sites on MIPs and target molecules, enabling quantification of the binding affinity for MIPs. The machine learning (ML) prediction was carried out in association with a study conducted with 5-fluorouracil, which is a chemotherapy drug used to fight cancer. ML techniques, including K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forest, XGBoost, Decision Tree, Lasso, and Ridge Regressions, were used to predict IF values for MIP. The dataset includes 214 observations consisting of various template molecules, functional monomers, and crosslinkers. The performance of the model was evaluated and compared using root mean squared error (RMSE) values, mean absolute error (MAE), and R 2 . The Random Forest shows good performance with moderate RMSE (3.54), low MAE (2.19), and R 2 = 0.55, indicating acceptable error and moderate variance. A Streamlit-based web interface was developed for visualization of polymer interactions and usability of the models by researchers with similar interests. These results imply that with improved and more extensive data, we have the potential to achieve higher IF prediction accuracy with ML models. The limitations of conventional MIPs make experimental estimation of binding affinity challenging due to cost and time constraints; therefore, this study employs ML as a pre-screening tool for prediction.

doi:10.1088/1674-1056/aeb246.title: Amorphous TiO <sub>2</sub> from a statistical view based on molecular dynamics using machine learning interatomic potentials
doi:10.1088/1674-1056/aeb246.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We use molecular dynamics with a machine-learning interatomic potential based on the higher-order equivariant message-passing atomic cluster expansion (MACE) framework to construct an ensemble of 100 amorphous TiO
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    configurations. The final structures are subject to variable-cell relaxations using density functional theory calculations, where PBEsol functional is adopted as it reproduces the experimental densities for all the three crystalline phases, namely, rutile, anatase and brookite. The mean density is calculated to be 3.94 g cm
                    <jats:sup>-3</jats:sup>
                    . While the ensemble is dominated by 6-coordinated Ti and 3-coordinated O, the corresponding percentage is 57.4% and 66.8% only. There exist 28.9% of 5-coordinated Ti, 12.1% 7-coordinated Ti, 21.4% 2-coordinated 21.4% O and 11.8% 4-coordinated O. Using hybrid HSE06 functional with the exact-exchange fraction (α) set to 0.18, the ensemble average yields a band gap of 3.44 ± 0.12 eV for the amorphous phase, which is greater than those of the three crystalline phases obtained using the same computational framework, namely, variable-cell relaxation using PBEsol and band gap calculation using HSE06 (α=0.18). Analysis of the density of states suggests that the band-gap widening in the amorphous phase is associated with the narrowed Ti 3
                    <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>
                    band. It is potentially useful to adopt the protocol in this work to study the effect of amorphization on the electronic structures of other semiconductors.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s11671-026-04960-5.title: Machine learning analysis for the thermophoretic particle deposition in casson nanofluid with porous medium and heat generation
doi:10.1186/s11671-026-04960-5.abstract: The aim of this work is to evaluate the impacts of heat generation on the radiative flow of Casson nanofluid over a sheet under LTNE circumstances while microbes are present, utilizing machine learning techniques based on the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm. A simple method for moving tiny particles across a temperature gradient is thermophoretic particle deposition, which is essential for electrical and aerosol solution engineering. The energy equations are derived from the local thermal non-equilibrium to determine the unique thermal profiles of the solid and liquid phases. The current model, which combines the Levenberg-Marquardt method with AI-NN (artificial intelligence neural networks), offers a more complex computational solution than standard numerical methods. The proposed model has broad uses in environmental research, and industrial fluid dynamics. By optimizing microorganisms in MHD Casson nanofluid flow with thermophoretic particle deposition, the model improves pollutant removal by bio-convection, leading to better wastewater treatment. It helps in the growth of more efficient bioreactors for microbial fuel cells and pharmaceutical medication delivery systems. Furthermore, nanofluid-based heat transfers and advanced biotechnology applications gain from the capacity to precisely predict and control microbe behaviour in complex fluid environments through the use of ANNs (artificial neural networks). The concentration profile decreases as the thermophoretic parameter values rise.

doi:10.67207/mrj.2026.15.13.title: THE ROLE OF CONTEXTUAL LEARNING VS. WORD LISTS IN TEACHING ACADEMIC VOCABULARY TO ESL STUDENTS
doi:10.67207/mrj.2026.15.13.abstract:
<jats:p>This study compared contextual learning versus traditional word list memorization for teaching academic vocabulary to ESL learners. While word lists remain common in pedagogy, they often result in superficial understanding and limited application. Contextual learning through meaningful academic texts was hypothesized to promote deeper engagement, better retention, and more effective vocabulary integration. 
A quasi-experimental design with pre-test/post-test measures involved 40 intermediate ESL learners randomly assigned to two groups (n=20 each). Group A received instruction via word lists with example sentences, while Group B learned the same vocabulary through content-rich reading passages. Both groups were assessed on receptive and productive vocabulary knowledge immediately post-instruction and after one week. Participants also completed feedback questionnaires and interviews.  
Results showed the contextual learning group achieved significantly higher improvements in vocabulary recognition (M=8.7, SD=1.1) and production (M=7.9, SD=1.4) compared to the word list group (recognition: M=7.1, SD=1.3; production: M=5.6, SD=1.7). Independent samples t-tests confirmed statistical significance (recognition: t (38) =3.91, p<.01; production: t (38) =4.12, p<.001). Qualitative analysis revealed contextual learning participants found instruction more engaging and beneficial for retention. These findings support transitioning toward contextually enriched vocabulary instruction in ESL education, recommending reading-based tasks to enhance both receptive and productive vocabulary acquisition. </jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s00423-026-04335-5.title: Clarifying statistical comparisons and procedural change in the TAPP learning curve
doi:10.1007/s00423-026-04335-5.abstract: To clarify the interpretation of chronological changes reported in a recent study of laparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal (TAPP) inguinal hernia repair. We reconstructed selected contingency tables using only aggregate counts reported in the published article. These calculations do not reproduce the original patient-level analysis. We also considered how concurrent changes in operative practice may contribute to the interpretation of decreasing operative time. For complications occurring in 8, 4, and 2 of 42 patients across the three phases, the published counts yield an overall Pearson chi-square p = 0.105 and a two-sided Fisher–Freeman–Halton exact p = 0.135, whereas the article reports p = 0.048. An ordered trend remains detectable ( p = 0.038), consistent with a temporal decline in complications. Operative time also decreased substantially across phases. Concurrent reduction in mesh fixation may have contributed to, but does not negate, this improvement. The published aggregate data warrant clarification of the statistical procedure underlying the reported overall comparison. Distinguishing overall group differences from ordered temporal trends and considering concurrent procedural adaptation may refine interpretation of the observed learning process.

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73227-x.title: KT-CBHNET: a spatio-temporal deep learning framework for interpretable ECG signal classification for cardiovascular disease prediction
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73227-x.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals are non-stationary and exhibit complex temporal dependencies, making automated analysis challenging. Current deep learning methods tend to either extract spatial or temporal features separately, which do not provide a complete signal representation. In this paper, we propose KT-CBHNET, an interpretable spatio-temporal deep learning framework that combines staged reuse of learned ECG representations with CNN-based morphological feature extraction and BiLSTM-based temporal modeling for cardiovascular disease classification. This model combines a 1D CNN to extract local morphological features, with a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) network to capture long-range temporal dynamics.An in-domain transfer-learning strategy initializes the hybrid architecture using CNN representations pretrained on PTB-XL, followed by joint optimization of the transferred CNN and newly introduced BiLSTM layers. To achieve interpretability, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is used to indicate the clinically relevant waveform portions that impact the classification decisions, showing that the model’s focus is on clinically relevant portions. The results show that the accuracy of the proposed model (KT-CBHNET) is 94.61% on the PTB-XL dataset, the precision is 91.4%, the recall is 97.79%, the F1 score is 94.49%, and the AUC is 98.02%, which indicates that the model is accurate and interpretable for the ECG signal classification problem.

doi:10.1080/03067319.2026.2742467.title: Explainable machine learning for predicting microplastic burden in commercially important freshwater fish and assessing dietary exposure
doi:10.1080/03067319.2026.2742467.abstract: Microplastic (MP) contamination in commercially important freshwater fish represents an emerging concern for aquatic ecosystem integrity and human food safety. This study presents an interpretable machine learning framework for predicting and assessing MP accumulation in European sea bass (Dicentrarchus labrax), Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), bighead carp (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis) and crucian carp (Carassius auratus) collected from four retail markets in Yichang City, Hubei Province, China. A total of 480 fish specimens generated 980 analytical records following gastrointestinal tract (GIT) extraction by alkaline digestion using 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH). Recovered MPs were characterised using attenuated total reflectance Fourier-transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDS). Six supervised regression algorithms, namely XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Regression (SVR) and Artificial Neural Network (ANN), were evaluated using an 80:20 stratified training–testing split (784/196 records). XGBoost achieved the highest predictive performance (R2 = 0.96, RMSE = 0.48 MPs kg−1) and was selected as the optimal model. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified fish weight, total length, market of origin and species as the principal predictors of MP burden. Polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE) and polystyrene (PS) predominated, with fibres representing the dominant morphology. Estimated dietary exposure reached approximately 4,650 particles year−1 for adult males, while 32% of fish exceeded 0.04 MPs g−1 wet weight. Because MPs were measured exclusively in GIT tissue, this estimate represents a conservative upper-bound approximation of dietary exposure.
doi:10.1080/03067319.2026.2742467.venue: International Journal of Environmental Analytical Chemistry

doi:10.59261/inkubis.v8i3.417.title: From Human Judgment to Machine Learning: A Philosophical Study of Knowledge Creation in Modern Accounting
doi:10.59261/inkubis.v8i3.417.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning into accounting and auditing has transformed the creation, validation, and application of professional knowledge, raising questions about the legitimacy of algorithmic knowledge in accounting practice.
Objective: This study examines the epistemological shift from human judgment to algorithmic knowledge in the implementation of Financial Accounting Standards (Standar Akuntansi Keuangan [SAK]) and Quality Management Systems (Sistem Manajemen Mutu [SMM]).
Methods: This study employs a qualitative-interpretive approach through conceptual analysis and an examination of practitioners’ perspectives on the reliability, transparency, explainability, and trustworthiness of AI-assisted decision-making.
Results: The results of the study show that AI can improve efficiency, predictive accuracy, and analytical capabilities in modern accounting practices but, at the same time, poses epistemological challenges in the form of limited algorithmic transparency, limited explainability, and the potential erosion of auditors’ professional skepticism. Although the conceptual analysis indicates that AI can positively affect efficiency and predictive accuracy, it also raises epistemic challenges related to transparency, accountability, and the preservation of professional skepticism. The shift from judgment-based knowledge to data-driven inferential knowledge has transformed the traditional epistemic authority held by accountants and auditors. The application of SAK and SMM in the accounting profession has implications for defining professional responsibilities in maintaining the quality of financial reporting and audit processes.
Conclusion: This study proposes a human–machine epistemic partnership, in which AI functions as an analytical augmentation tool while accountants and auditors remain the primary epistemic authorities.</jats:p>

The framework should therefore be regarded as a property-dependent composition-only benchmark rather than as a generally reliable predictive tool for all three dielectric properties. doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1958746.title: Educational outcomes of CDIO-guided progressive case-based learning and gamification in undergraduate critical care nursing: an exploratory two-class quasi-experimental study
doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1958746.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study compared educational outcomes between nursing students receiving a CDIO-guided case-based and gamified teaching program and those receiving conventional teaching.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This two-class quasi-experimental study included 140 nursing students from two classes between March and June 2025. Classes were assigned by lottery to the intervention (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 65) or control (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 75) group. The intervention integrated progressive cases, microlectures, teamwork, board games, and escape-room simulation, whereas the control received traditional lectures and Small Private Online Course self-study. Self-directed learning, critical thinking, and learning engagement were assessed before and after the course. Post-course outcomes included theoretical performance, cardiopulmonary resuscitation performance, course performance, and teaching evaluation. Analysis of covariance, Welch’s t tests, and Holm correction were applied.

doi:10.14445/23488360/ijme-v13i9p101.title: Thermal Error Prediction of a Three-Axis CNC Machine Tool using an Artificial Neural Network with Optimized Hidden-Neuron Architecture
doi:10.14445/23488360/ijme-v13i9p101.abstract: <jats:p>Thermal errors are one of the major factors that affect the positioning accuracy of CNC machine tools and hence the quality of the manufactured products. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have been extensively used for modeling the thermal errors, but the impact of hidden-layer architecture on the prediction accuracy remains insufficiently explored. In this study, a Neuron-Optimized Artificial Neural Network (NO-ANN) model is proposed for predicting the thermal positioning errors of a three-axis CNC machine tool. The effect of the hidden-layer neuron configuration was systematically examined to determine the optimal configuration to capture the nonlinear relationship between the thermal variations and positioning errors. The model performance was assessed by Coefficient of Determination (R2), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). The optimized architecture of 11 hidden neurons demonstrated the highest overall performance, with an R2 value of 0.998, RMSE of 1.3247 μm, and MAE of 0.6539 μm, and the model showed high accuracy in both training and testing sets, indicating its robustness and generalization ability. Compared with previously reported thermal error prediction models, the proposed NO-ANN achieved comparable or superior predictive accuracy while requiring only 11 hidden neurons, indicating reduced model complexity and improved computational efficiency. The results indicate that the systematic optimization of hidden-layer neurons can significantly improve the accuracy of thermal error prediction of ANNs, which can be used to effectively compensate for the thermal error in intelligent CNC machining systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.53850/joltida.1893531.title: Exploring Vocational School Students' Conceptualizations of Artificial Intelligence Through Metaphors
doi:10.53850/joltida.1893531.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Artificial intelligence (AI) encompasses systems engineered to execute cognitive functions, including perception, reasoning, and decision-making. Advancements in big data and deep learning have facilitated the proliferation of AI in sectors such as healthcare, education, manufacturing, and transportation, concurrently prompting discussions on ethical and safety concerns. AI enhances education by facilitating personalized and data-informed learning via adaptive platforms, automated assessments, and virtual assistants. This study examined vocational school students' perceptions of AI using metaphors, which elucidate abstract concepts and uncover cognitive patterns. A qualitative, phenomenological approach was employed to collect data from 198 students through an online survey utilizing the prompt “AI is like… because…”. The analysis adhered to systematic metaphor procedures, and expert review validated a high degree of reliability. The results revealed 82 distinct metaphors that represent diverse perspectives. The recurrent use of metaphors such as “human,” “human brain,” “assistant,” and “facilitation” suggests that students perceive AI as possessing human-like qualities and as a supportive entity. Alternative metaphors characterize AI as technological instruments (robots, machines, programs) or repositories of information (libraries, web browsers). In addition to the beneficial aspects of assistance and facilitation, apprehensions regarding the risks and uncontrollability of AI have arisen. In conclusion, vocational students view AI as a practical, human-like tool that improves life, while also recognizing the uncertainties associated with the technology. The findings highlight the dual aspects of AI perceptions in educational settings, merging optimism with caution.</jats:p>
doi:10.53850/joltida.1893531.venue: Journal of Learning and Teaching in Digital Age

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1363-2.ch005.title: Blockchain Federated Learning Architecture
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1363-2.ch005.abstract: <jats:p>Customizing education technology with data-driven AI undermines student privacy. Centralized analytics risk illegal data access, single points of failure, and loss of institutional sovereignty. BFL-EdArch, a four-layer blockchain-enabled federated learning architecture, enables privacy-preserving collaborative intelligence in decentralized classrooms. Model aggregation runs off-chain for low latency and cost, while verification, reputation, and incentives are selectively anchored on a permissioned blockchain, resolving the privacy-transparency trade-off. Shapley value incentives, differential privacy, and zero-knowledge proofs mitigate model poisoning, free-riding, and inference attacks. Architectural details, pseudocode, and use cases (cross-institutional dropout prediction and personalized learning pathways) show BFL-EdArch can match centralized accuracy while guaranteeing privacy, auditable trust, and sustainable incentives. The chapter ends with a deployment checklist, risk assessment, and research agenda on federated learning and learner-centric governance.</jats:p>

doi:10.30935/cedtech/19552.title: ICT use intensity and perceived learning support: A decoupling in Spanish compulsory education
doi:10.30935/cedtech/19552.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">The integration of information and communication technologies (ICT) into compulsory education raises the question of whether more intensive technology use translates into a more favorable appraisal of its contribution to learning. This study analyzed the relationship between ICT use intensity and a set of objective and perceptual indicators in 1,969 primary (n = 868) and lower secondary students (n = 1,101) from several Spanish autonomous communities. A cross-sectional, non-experimental quantitative design was applied, analyzing a composite use intensity index through Chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests with effect sizes and through ordinal logistic regression models controlling educational stage and gender. Use intensity showed large associations with objective indicators of technology use and consistent differences by educational stage and school year, whereas gender exerted only a marginal influence. No association was found between use intensity and the perception that technology supports learning, even after adjusting for these covariates, whereas small positive associations emerged with specific indicators of decision-making capacity and desired learning. Primary students, despite less intensive use, appraised the educational usefulness of technology more favorably than secondary students. The findings support a decoupling between use intensity and perceived educational value and underline the relevance of pedagogical mediation over mere technological exposure.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpls.2026.1970840.title: Fine-tuning improves deep learning-based digital phenotyping of lettuce genetic resources
doi:10.3389/fpls.2026.1970840.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Morphological characterization of agricultural genetic resources relies largely on visual assessment by experts, and applying the same criteria repeatedly to large collections is labor-intensive. Image-based deep learning can support this process, but systematic evidence on training strategies suited to genebank trait data remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study targeted six morphological traits of lettuce genetic resources characterized according to the test guidelines of the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV). Using genebank images accumulated from 2012 to 2025, six convolutional neural networks were trained with three training strategies under identical conditions, and their performance was compared.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fine-tuning achieved the highest mean macro F1-score in 35 of the 36 backbone–trait combinations and significantly outperformed training from scratch and feature extraction, whereas no single backbone was superior across all traits. Misclassifications were concentrated in morphologically adjacent classes rather than randomly distributed, and for the ordinal traits, errors spanning two or more class levels were rare.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These patterns suggest that the remaining classification difficulty was associated in part with the morphological continuity between neighboring classes. The attainable performance also differed among traits, distinguishing traits for which the training strategy alone achieved relatively high performance from those for which it did not. These results provide empirical evidence for selecting training strategies and for determining the role of model-assisted characterization on a trait-by-trait basis in genebanks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.36548/jtcsst.2026.4.001.title: Janus: Dual-Sided Communication and Privacy Optimization for Federated Learning in Autonomous Vehicles
doi:10.36548/jtcsst.2026.4.001.abstract: <jats:p>Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across autonomous vehicles (AVs) without sharing raw driving data, but excessive uplink/downlink communication over bandwidth-constrained vehicular-to-everything links and privacy leakage through gradient inversion attacks limit its deployment. This paper proposes Janus, a unified FL framework combining adaptive Top-K gradient compression with error feedback on the uplink, genuine additive homomorphic encryption (HE, not a noise-based proxy) for secure aggregation, and compressed global-model broadcasting on the downlink. On real KITTI object-detection labels with 20 non-IID clients, Janus matches FedAvg/FedProx/QSGD accuracy (95.34% ± 0.01% vs. 95.35% ± 0.03%, 3 seeds) while cutting combined communication by 61.8%; the same saving (61.0%) is independently reproduced on CIFAR-10. A real Paillier HE implementation is verified exact (error below 10⁻⁶), and a genuine gradient-inversion attack (Deep Leakage from Gradients) shows raw gradients are reconstructed almost perfectly (relative error 0.0026) versus 0.0775 for Janus's compressed updates, with HE removing the attack surface entirely. The same communication saving is further reproduced on real KITTI camera images with a CNN roughly 24x larger than the tabular model and on a multimodal model fusing real camera and LiDAR features, alongside additional baselines (FedPAQ, DP-FedAvg), membership-inference and model-poisoning attacks, Markov-chain mobility, simulated network latency (61.9% reduction), an energy proxy (45.1% reduction), and a formal convergence analysis. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first vehicular-FL evaluation combining joint uplink-downlink compression with genuine HE-based privacy, validated through real cryptography, real privacy attacks, statistical testing, cross-dataset and cross-modality generalisation, and a convergence guarantee.</jats:p>

doi:10.67547/fanistiqbollari.2026.636.abstract: <jats:p>The article analyzes practical strategies for designing individual educational trajectories based on artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. The study draws on a comparative examination of the world’s leading adaptive learning platforms - Squirrel AI in China, ALEKS in the United States, and Khanmigo within Khan Academy. The aim of the article is to systematize four core strategies for AI-based design of individual educational trajectories (diagnostics- centered, knowledge-map-based, hybrid human-AI, and continuous-monitoring strategies) and to substantiate their effectiveness through international statistical evidence. The study applies comparative analysis, case study and statistical analysis methods. The findings show that AI-based strategies can raise course completion rates by up to 70%, test scores by up to 54%, while improving attendance and reducing dropout rates. The article concludes with a five-stage strategic design model adapted to the conditions of the Uzbek education system.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/lfet-04-2026-0057.title: Advancing high-stakes workforce training and learning with emerging digital twin technologies
doi:10.1108/lfet-04-2026-0057.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research aims to map the global landscape of digital twins (DTs) in high-stakes training. It identifies a potential gap where technical development appears to outpace instructional integration and outlines directions for future academic inquiry.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The researchers conducted a bibliometric analysis. The data set includes 611 peer-reviewed documents from the Scopus database. The study uses VOSviewer for visual mapping. Techniques include co-authorship, citation analysis, bibliographic coupling and keyword co-occurrence mapping. These methods visualize the intellectual topography and thematic clusters of the field.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis identifies five dominant clusters: algorithmic core, socio-technical frontier, precision validation, industrial backbone and human interface. Human-centric nodes remain comparatively peripheral to dense technical clusters. These peripheral nodes include concepts such as perception, training and competency. The digital architecture of DTs appears to be advancing rapidly, while standardized pedagogical frameworks for workforce productivity remain fragmented in the literature.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study relies solely on the Scopus database and English-language publications. Future research should further examine instructional fidelity and explainable AI to better understand the relationship between technical simulation and human cognitive load.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Human resource development practitioners may consider competency-based training models that integrate real-time DT data. The findings also suggest potential for DTs to evolve as adaptive instructional agents that could support the identification and development of individual skill gaps.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study maps the evolving DT research landscape, highlighting key themes and the emerging need for greater integration of technical and pedagogical dimensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.58s.115.title: Facial Expression Recognition In Low Light And Occluded Environment Using Machine Learning Approaches
doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.58s.115.abstract: Facial Expression Recognition (FER) is important in the context of intelligent systems to recognize human emotions, and has been applied across human-computer interaction, healthcare monitoring, surveillance, and driver assistance systems.Although considerable improvements have been made in recent years, performance of FER systems significantly decreases in the real-life situation, especially when using low-light scenarios and face obfuscation.These influences decrease the visibility of features, distort facial information and cause unfinished or unreliable representation, which decreases recognition accuracy.This review is a narrative synthesis of machine learning and deep learning methods to FER in such a challenging environment.It discusses methods of enhancement, occlusion-sensitive models as well as stateof-the-art architectures, such as attention systems and transformer frameworks.It is seen that the joint enhancementrecognition models can be more effective in restoring the semantically meaningful features when the light is low, and attention and transformer-based models are more efficient in coping with the occlusion through focusing on informative areas of the faces.Nevertheless, one of the main drawbacks of the current studies is the absence of cohesive datasets and benchmarks that can cover both the low-light and occlusion conditions at the same time.The review adds a hierarchical taxonomy of the current methodologies and indicates a way forward in future research to create robust and practical systems of FER.

doi:10.65726/ijrsat.2026.v26.i10.01.title: Deep Learning-Based Detection and Localization of Forged Caste Certificates Using Convolutional Neural Networks and Gradient-Weighted Class Activation Mapping
authors: Subramani, Muralidhara B L, Suresh R C
doi:10.65726/ijrsat.2026.v26.i10.01.abstract: <jats:p>Government-issued caste certificates serve as a gateway to constitutional benefits reserved for socially and economically disadvantaged communities in India. Growing misuse of image manipulation tools to fabricate such documents has created an urgent need for reliable automated verification mechanisms. This study introduces a deep-learning solution, referred to as LOCATE, that performs both classification and spatial fault-finding on suspect certificates. A four-layer Convolutional Neural Network trained on a purpose-built collection of 1,000 Karnataka state certificates (500 genuine, 500 manipulated) first separates authentic documents from tampered ones. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping then pinpoints the exact region within a flagged document that triggered the forgery verdict, giving human reviewers a clear visual basis for their decisions. At operating threshold τ = 0.7, the system attains 98% overall accuracy, 100% precision, 96% recall, and an F1-score of 0.98, while preserving 100% specificity. These results surpass all comparable prior approaches and demonstrate that the framework is ready for real-world administrative deployment.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1363-2.ch007.title: AI-Driven Student Performance Prediction in Next-Gen Decentralized Learning
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-1363-2.ch007.abstract: <jats:p>Decentralized learning ecosystems powered by blockchain, federated machine learning, and immersive metaverse environments are fundamentally reshaping educational data architecture and student engagement paradigms. This chapter presents a comprehensive investigation into AI-driven student performance prediction within these next-generation infrastructures, advancing a Privacy-Preserving Federated Prediction (P2FP) framework that integrates gradient-boosted ensemble models, on-chain credentialing, and cross-institutional federated aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate superior predictive accuracy and robust privacy guarantees over centralized baselines. Seven global case studies — spanning the USA, India, China, Japan, Russia, UK, and Australia — illustrate diverse deployment contexts. Advantages, systemic challenges, and a forward-looking research agenda are critically examined.</jats:p>
