doi:10.62805/cid2026.cid110.title: Identificación de Dificultades de Aprendizaje en Álgebra Lineal mediante Modelos Predictivos de Machine Learning
doi:10.62805/cid2026.cid110.abstract: <jats:p>Las dificultades que enfrentan los estudiantes universitarios en asignaturas como Álgebra Lineal suelen pasar desapercibidas hasta que los rezagos ya son difíciles de revertir. Este trabajo propone una alternativa basada en modelos de Aprendizaje Automático para detectar de forma temprana esas dificultades, tomando como población de estudio a cien estudiantes de segundo semestre de educación superior que cursaban simultáneamente varias asignaturas de ciencias exactas. Con el fin de aprovechar la información escrita generada durante el curso, se recopilaron respuestas y comentarios académicos de los participantes, los cuales fueron transformados en representaciones numéricas mediante la técnica de Frecuencia de Término-Frecuencia Inversa de Documento. Sobre esa base, se entrenaron y compararon dos clasificadores supervisados: Máquinas de Vectores de Soporte y Naive Bayes, orientados a distinguir entre estudiantes con y sin dificultades de aprendizaje. Ambos algoritmos alcanzaron niveles de desempeño satisfactorios, aunque las Máquinas de Vectores de Soporte mostraron ventajas claras en precisión y en la identificación de los casos más críticos. Estos hallazgos permiten concluir que incorporar herramientas de este tipo en los entornos educativos universitarios no solo es viable, sino que puede transformar la manera en que los docentes detectan y atienden las necesidades de sus estudiantes. Actuar con antelación, antes de que las dificultades se profundicen, representa un avance concreto hacia una educación más atenta, personalizada y sustentada en evidencia.</jats:p>
doi:10.62805/cid2026.cid110.venue: CIENCIA, INGENIERÍA Y DESARROLLO TEC LERDO

doi:10.67693/bjcr-lcekl6um.title: Comparative Analysis of CNN And SVM Machine Learning Technique for Maize Leaf Disease Detection
doi:10.67693/bjcr-lcekl6um.abstract: Maize (Zea mays L.) is one of the most crucial staple crops in the world and has high susceptibility to foliar diseases like Northern Leaf Blight, Common Rust and Gray Leaf Spot that may lower the yield by as much as 40 per cent unless controlled immediately.Manual-based disease-detection methods are tedious, arbitrary and poorly sensitive to disease outbreaks, especially in resource strained agricultural environments.Another possible solution is the machine-learning methods that have a potential to automatize the diagnosis of the maize leaf diseases by using image analysis and, thus, increase diagnostic quality.The present paper made a comparative assessment of two machine-learning-based language models including the Convolutional Neural Network and Support Vector Machines in identifying maize leaf disease automatically.The standard performance indicators were used to evaluate the models and they were precision, recall, F1-score, and accuracy.According to experimental results, the CNN has a better performance of an accuracy of 95.8, macro-and weighted-average precision of 0.958-0.959,a recall of 0.958, and F1-score of 0.958, compared to the SVM which has an accuracy of 93.5 and F1-score of 0.934.The constant superiority of the CNN proves the efficiency of the learning of discriminative spatial and texture features directly in the raw images.Furthermore, the results are consistent with the available literature on plant disease detection that documents high CNN accuracy that is usually 2-6% kernel points higher than that of SVM.

doi:10.3390/biomimetics11100722.title: β-PruNet: An Explainable, PSO-Optimized Degree-Centrality-Pruned Regularized Extreme Learning Machine for Lightweight Household Appliance Recognition
doi:10.3390/biomimetics11100722.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate recognition of individual appliances from their own power consumption profiles underpins non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM), yet deep learning models often incur high computational overhead and lack operational interpretability. This study proposes a new explainable and lightweight model named β-PruNet to recognize household appliances using daily power consumption signals. The task addressed here is appliance classification from submetered profiles rather than disaggregation of an aggregate household signal, so the model is positioned as the recognition stage of a NILM pipeline. Each 24 h signal (86,400 samples) is transformed into a 720-bin ordinal pattern (OP) distribution, and the distribution is summarized by 27 statistical and spectral descriptors over 48 sliding windows. A compact class-weighted convolutional neural network extracts 128 embedding features. Drawing inspiration from collective swarm intelligence and biological synaptic pruning, a particle swarm optimization (PSO)-tuned regularized extreme learning machine (R-ELM) classifier with beta-weight centrality pruning conducts classification via a diverse softmax ensemble. On an imbalanced 18-class benchmark containing 916 daily appliance profiles, β-PruNet achieved 98.9% classification accuracy and a 97.6% macro F1-score while pruning 87.3% of hidden neurons (from 1500 to 191) without accuracy loss. Post hoc explainability analyses using SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM confirmed that the pruning criterion strongly correlates with Shapley feature attribution (r = 0.974). These findings indicate that integrating symbolic dynamics with bio-inspired pruning delivers a computationally efficient, highly accurate, and transparent solution suitable for edge-oriented energy management systems. The theoretical contribution is that the magnitude of a hidden unit’s learned output weights provides a usable ranking signal at no additional computational cost beyond the closed-form solution already obtained. The practical contribution is that this signal allows the classifier head to be compressed by 87.3% without a measurable loss in accuracy.</jats:p>

arxiv:2610.13834.title: On the Design Space of Continuous Diffusion Language Models
arxiv:2610.13834.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) promise to bring the benefits of continuous flow modelling to language, including accelerated sampling and controllable generation. The field has grown rapidly, and the capabilities of CDLMs have begun to rival those of discrete diffusion. Yet, unlike for continuous modalities such as images or videos, our grasp of the levers that matter when training CDLMs remains limited. In this work, we focus on two of these levers, namely self-conditioning and embedding geometry, and shed light on some of the mechanisms behind them, which in turn suggest cheaper and more effective designs. We begin by showing that self-conditioning corrects a train/inference mismatch by exposing the model to inference-like states that are otherwise rare during training. These gains can be recovered without an extra forward pass by a two-level interpolant, coined $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, which improves TinyGSM accuracy more than threefold. Self-conditioning also aids in recognising tokens dominated by large-norm Gaussians$\unicode{x2013}$an issue known as token identifiability. To address it directly, we introduce discrete reveals to $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, yielding $\mathrm{SemiCat}$, which achieves discrete diffusion-level performance on TinyGSM, reaching $49.94\%$ with standard training hyperparameters and a tuned sampler. At the $1.7$B scale, $\mathrm{SemiCat}$ outperforms discrete diffusion on four of six likelihood-based evaluations, and surpasses one-hot flows on unconditional generation. On embedded spaces, we find that cross-entropy drives embeddings towards a geometry whose decoding error rate closely matches the one-hot one. We briefly explore a range of further options, such as hybrid corruption processes and noise schedules, including asynchronous ones. We believe this exploration can help the community better understand and advance the design space of CDLMs.

arxiv:2610.13778.title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
arxiv:2610.13778.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low-precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher-precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by $1.20$--$1.47\times$ over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about $1.8\times$ the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on the two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.

arxiv:2610.13767.title: DualQuant: Dual-scale Calibration-free Weight-and-Activation Quantization for LLMs
arxiv:2610.13767.abstract: Low-bit inference on accelerators with native 4-bit support requires quantizing both weights and activations to realize the full throughput gains these formats provide. While post-training weight quantization has been extensively studied, activation quantization remains considerably more challenging and typically requires calibration data. In this work, we introduce DUALQUANT, a dual-scale, calibration-free post-training quantization framework that directly minimizes the weight-reconstruction Mean Squared Error (MSE) and, as an immediate by-product, yields per-channel activation rescalings prior to activation quantization. Our key observation is that the scaling factors obtained by minimizing weight-reconstruction error provide effective activation rescalings, enabling competitive activation quantization without calibration data. We formulate DUALQUANT as a non-differentiable weight-reconstruction problem and develop an efficient solver based on variable splitting and block coordinate descent, where each subproblem admits a closed-form update. DUALQUANT provides a unified algorithm supporting a wide range of formats, including the full MX family and NVFP4. To our knowledge, DUALQUANT is the first dual-scaling method to formally support MX and NV block formats. Across Llama and Qwen models evaluated on WikiText-2, C4, and zero-shot downstream tasks, DUALQUANT matches or exceeds the accuracy of calibration-based SmoothQuant across most models and formats, and substantially outperforms calibration-free baselines, with large gains for MX and NV block formats. We validate these gains with a real packed W4A4 inference path for Llama-3.1-8B on an RTX 4090. The resulting implementation closely matches the accuracy of fake quantization while delivering up to 2.61x memory reduction and up to 2.46x throughput speedup over BF16.

arxiv:2610.13407.title: Accelerating Linear Bandits with Persistent Candidate Sets
arxiv:2610.13407.abstract: Exhaustive optimistic scoring can make action selection costly in linear bandits with a large fixed set of $K$ actions, requiring $\mathcal{O}(K)$ score evaluations per round. We introduce Persistent Candidate LinUCB (\textsc{PC-LinUCB}), which maintains $k$ active actions and samples $q$ challengers uniformly from the remaining $K-k$ actions at each round. By scoring only these $k+q$ candidates, \textsc{PC-LinUCB} reduces the number of score evaluations per round to $\mathcal{O}(k+q)$. We establish problem-independent and problem-dependent high-probability regret bounds consisting of a standard linear-bandit learning term and an additive discovery cost of order $\mathcal{O}\left((K-k)\log(K-k)/q\right)$ at fixed confidence. Notably, this additional cost does not grow with the horizon. For fixed gaps and sufficiently long horizons, we establish an $Ω\left((K-k)/q\right)$ regret lower bound under uniform challenger sampling, showing that partial candidate access itself imposes an unavoidable regret cost. Experiments show that \textsc{PC-LinUCB} substantially accelerates LinUCB while maintaining comparable regret, and that the persistent candidate mechanism can extend beyond LinUCB.

arxiv:2610.13382.title: BLOKS: Scaling Kernel Solvers with Sketched Block Preconditioning
arxiv:2610.13382.abstract: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a theoretically sound algorithm for nonparametric learning, which is also often used to investigate properties of deep learning. However, the exact KRR formulation incurs time and memory costs preventing applicability to large datasets, motivating the development of approximate solvers. These algorithms rely on (i) iterative methods, to avoid the computational burden of direct solutions; (ii) sketching or batching, to reduce the problem size; and (iii) preconditioning, to accelerate convergence. While crucial for fast convergence, preconditioning incurs memory costs that can be managed by lowering the number of free parameters of the model, potentially at the expense of expressivity and hence accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose BLOKS, a Conjugate Gradient-based solver for Nyström-sketched KRR built around a novel preconditioner that combines a block Jacobi approximation with sketching. The BLOKS preconditioner has memory cost independent of both the dataset size and the number of parameters, allowing scaling to large models. We provide a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation and show that BLOKS achieves excellent accuracy while retaining favorable time/memory complexity. Indeed, on standard large-scale datasets used to benchmark kernel solvers, BLOKS achieves comparable or better performances than state-of-the-art methods.

arxiv:2610.13292.title: Recovering Irreducible Three-Body Interactions with Lagrangian Neural Networks
arxiv:2610.13292.abstract: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn mechanical systems from trajectory data by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving the dynamics through the Euler-Lagrange equations, biasing the model toward motion that respects the variational structure of mechanics. The interactions studied so far have been pairwise-additive, leaving open whether LNNs can recover an irreducible many-body interaction from motion alone. We address this using the Axilrod-Teller triple-dipole interaction, the leading three-body dispersion term, whose dependence on the collective geometry of three particles cannot be represented by any sum of pairwise terms. We prescribe the kinetic energy exactly and learn only the potential, as a function of interparticle distances and angles. Combined with a signal-aware sampling strategy that concentrates training data where the three-body signal is strongest while preserving broad coverage of configuration space, this recovers the interaction from accelerations alone. The learned potential reproduces the radial scaling, angular dependence, and characteristic sign reversal of the Axilrod-Teller interaction, and generates stable trajectories. Embedding it within a pairwise Lennard-Jones potential lets us examine its observability: the three-body term is recovered once its dynamical signature exceeds the residual modeling error, which it does cleanly at amplified coupling but not at the coupling of a real noble gas, bracketing the transition between the two. Finally, symbolic regression on the trained potential, with no assumed functional form, returns the Axilrod-Teller expression with angular numerator, radial law, and coupling constant intact. An LNN with domain-specific structure can thus recover an irreducible three-body interaction from trajectories as a closed-form law, pointing toward learning interaction laws whose structure is not known a priori.

arxiv:2610.13234.title: Learning Schwarzschild Geodesic Motion with Lagrangian Neural Networks
arxiv:2610.13234.abstract: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn dynamics from trajectory data by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving accelerations through the Euler--Lagrange equation, providing a variational inductive bias that improves physical consistency over purely data-driven models. LNNs have recently been extended to general relativistic settings, leaving Schwarzschild geodesics as an open challenge. Training on complex relativistic systems is hindered by the diversity of the dynamics, as well as numerical instabilities and the difficulty of adequately sampling physically relevant, diverse orbital regimes. We introduce two coordinated improvements: a decoupled position--velocity normalization scheme that independently rescales each coordinate and its time derivatives, reweighting acceleration targets to balance contributions across all channels; and an energy-constrained log-uniformly sampled dataset generation strategy informed by the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) structure. With these improvements, our model accurately reproduces perihelion precession and relativistic time dilation, conserves energy and angular momentum to within a few percent even after completing multiple orbits around the central mass and predicts orbital trajectories across eight orbital scenarios in close, medium, and far-field regimes. These results establish that LNNs, augmented with physically motivated normalization and sampling, can reliably learn geodesic dynamics in curved spacetime. Our work also represents the first successful training of LNNs on Schwarzschild geodesics and offers a promising direction for data-driven modeling of complex relativistic systems.

arxiv:2610.13208.title: How Much Computation Does Every Forecast Need? Structured Block Skipping in Two Time-Series Foundation Models
arxiv:2610.13208.abstract: Time-series foundation models use the same network depth for every input, although forecasting windows differ in structure and difficulty. We test whether whole Transformer blocks can be removed at inference time in two pretrained models: Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM 2.5. Our bypasses avoid the original block computation and preserve the dense model exactly when all blocks are enabled. Masks are selected only on calibration windows and evaluated on 1,088 held-out windows from ETTh1, Traffic, Weather, and Exchange. At moderate sparsity, Chronos-Bolt with 7/11 candidate blocks and TimesFM with 16/20 blocks show little change in mean relative forecasting quality across datasets while reducing median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% and 13.4%. More aggressive TimesFM skipping accelerates inference further but substantially harms Traffic and Weather. Across both models, different equal-budget masks win on different windows, and a retrospective oracle significantly improves over the best static mask on every dataset. However, dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently, and Chronos representations do not support reliable unseen-domain routing. These results establish cross-architecture structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity, but not a deployable dynamic inference method.

arxiv:2610.13194.title: JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
arxiv:2610.13194.abstract: Long-horizon autonomous research has shown promise in accelerating scientific progress through sustained cycles of hypothesis generation, implementation, and validation. However, this Generate-Execute-Feedback paradigm relies on reactive trial-and-error, where costly and time-consuming executions introduce severe feedback delays, throttling evolutionary progress under explosively expanding search space. To address this challenge, we propose JANUS, a framework that unifies future outcomes forecasting and past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. Within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates while world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, then accordingly selects, refines, or prunes branches prior to execution. After receiving ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for research agent, exploration-strategy skills for world model, and their coordination protocols. This mechanism enables continual co-evolution: the research agent sharpens candidate generation while the world model refines its predictive judgment over extended horizons. Extensive evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks demonstrate that JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving both higher evolving efficiency and ceiling.

arxiv:2610.13035.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
arxiv:2610.13035.abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.

arxiv:2610.12970.title: Minions: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices
arxiv:2610.12970.abstract: The increasing demand for GPU-accelerated machine learning inference has exposed limitations in centralized GPU infrastructures, including high cost, limited elasticity, and long wait times under resource constraints. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon-based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Minions enables teams to leverage existing hardware without requiring additional GPU procurement. The system provides flexible GPU inference task execution, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilization. Our experience shows that idle macOS devices can be transformed into a practical distributed GPU inference platform in environments where centralized GPU resources are constrained.

arxiv:2610.12933.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
arxiv:2610.12933.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.

arxiv:2610.12820.title: Inverse Synthesis of Shock Time Series from Shock Response Spectra Using Ensembles of Conditional Variational Autoencoders
arxiv:2610.12820.abstract: The shock response spectrum (SRS) characterizes the peak responses of single-degree-of-freedom systems to transient acceleration. Because the mapping from an acceleration time series (waveform) to its SRS is many-to-one, inverse synthesis seeks candidate waveforms consistent with a prescribed spectrum. We extend an earlier conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) framework with a recurrent decoder that predicts multiscale wavelet coefficients and reconstructs waveforms through an inverse discrete wavelet transform. Individual models exhibit limited variability under latent sampling, motivating an ensemble of independently trained models spanning different mother wavelets and decomposition levels. Each member produces a separate candidate waveform for the same target SRS. Evaluation on four held-out benchmark datasets shows lower mean and median spectral errors for the illustrated wavelet model than for the earlier direct time-domain CVAE and a sum-of-decayed-sinusoids (SDS) baseline. A conditioning study examines frequency-grid and encoding choices. Comparisons with published inverse-SRS methods demonstrate superior performance across four holdout benchmark datasets (two operational shock datasets, one earthquake dataset, and one synthetic shock dataset) and competitive performance on synthetic targets reported by Brake. Single-model inference requires approximately 0.1-0.6 ms per waveform during batched inference compared with 5-8 s for SDS, excluding offline training. This low inference cost enables rapid generation of distinct SRS-compatible candidate waveforms across the ensemble, although their physical suitability requires assessment beyond spectral agreement.

arxiv:2610.12776.title: Coordinate-Free Automatic Differentiation
arxiv:2610.12776.abstract: Automatic differentiation (AD) is a cornerstone of modern machine learning. Since all AD frameworks implicitly fix a basis of Euclidean space to define gradients and Jacobians, they natively process mathematical objects that are arrays of a fixed set of coordinates. This makes it awkward to express objects such as rotations, volume forms, and curvatures that arise, for example, in applications of AI to science. Bespoke workarounds lack reusability. We show that (i) a single, basis-independent derivative operator can represent many geometric differential operations, and (ii) this operator can be expressed entirely in terms of existing AD primitives. This reusable transformation can be composed with JAX batching, compilation, and hardware acceleration. Geometry enters as algebraic data. We experimentally demonstrate its reuse across different manifold operators, its composition through a spacetime inverse-problem pipeline, and its use in optimization over different rotor subgroups.

arxiv:2610.12754.title: NV-Tesseract-AD: Curriculum-Enhanced Conditional Diffusion for Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection
arxiv:2610.12754.abstract: We propose NV-Tesseract-AD, a curriculum learning-enhanced conditional diffusion framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection. Our central hypothesis is that reconstruction difficulty can be explicitly structured along two complementary axes, masking severity and diffusion noise level, and that training from easier to harder tasks along both axes simultaneously stabilizes optimization and improves residual discriminability. We integrate a Transformer-based diffusion backbone with a three-stage dual curriculum over masking ratios and diffusion timesteps, retaining anomalous samples throughout training and relying on structured corruption to drive self-supervised representation learning. We evaluate NV-Tesseract-AD under two regimes: in-distribution training on the TSB-UAD-M corpus and strict zero-shot transfer to ten EasyTSAD benchmark families without per-dataset tuning. The dual-axis curriculum produces masking-invariant reconstruction, confirmed by a near-zero loss gap between complementary masking strategies within the first training stage, and yields an approximately 3.7-fold improvement in F1 and a 56 percent reduction in MSE relative to a non-curriculum baseline. Zero-shot performance reaches F1 = 0.984 on NAB and F1 = 0.948 on NormA. Weaker results on heterogeneous families are traced to unsupervised threshold calibration rather than reconstruction quality, identifying calibration as the dominant remaining detection bottleneck. Accelerated inference via DPM-Solver++ reduces sampling cost by a factor of 3.5 to 5.7 at the dataset level but couples to thresholding behavior, establishing that the sampler and threshold must be validated jointly. Together, these findings demonstrate that aligning diffusion denoising difficulty with curriculum learning principles provides a principled and practical approach for robust anomaly detection in complex multivariate time series.

arxiv:2610.12566.title: Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Post-Training
arxiv:2610.12566.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a memory-efficient alternative to backpropagation for fine-tuning large language models. However, existing ZO methods typically sample training examples uniformly, overlooking their evolving importance and leaving avoidable estimation variance. To address this limitation, we propose Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization (SAZO), which learns sample importance online and adaptively allocates queries to accelerate convergence. SAZO extracts gradient-norm information from existing directional differences to estimate sample importance without access to true gradients. Furthermore, to track evolving importance from sparse minibatch feedback, SAZO maintains per-example exponential moving averages that aggregate observations across updates. The method requires no additional model evaluations and only $O(N)$ additional scalar state compared with MeZO. We prove that SAZO asymptotically matches the leading convergence term of the minimum-variance sampling oracle, and achieves a strictly faster convergence rate than standard methods. Extensive experiments across four model families demonstrate improved average downstream performance and up to $6\times$ faster convergence to the same training loss in terms of query count.

arxiv:2610.12530.title: CacheScope: Exact-Compute Allocation for Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration
arxiv:2610.12530.abstract: Training-free feature reuse accelerates diffusion transformer inference by replacing full denoising computation at selected steps with cached approximations. Existing methods mainly improve the reconstruction of skipped features, but we find that once a stable first-order reconstructor is used, increasing reconstruction complexity brings limited gains, whereas the placement of exact-computation steps has a much larger effect on fidelity. More importantly, absolute shallow-probe variation is jointly affected by input-trajectory displacement and network response strength, and therefore does not directly reflect cache risk. We address this confounding by normalizing probe-output variation with the corresponding input displacement, yielding a directional gain per unit trajectory movement. Based on this signal, we propose CacheScope, which identifies high-risk reuse steps online and selectively falls back to full denoising computation while leaving the underlying cache reconstructor unchanged. CacheScope requires no additional training, gradients, auxiliary networks, or prompt-specific offline schedule optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, and Open-Sora 1.2, CacheScope achieves up to 3.57x acceleration and reduces median LPIPS by up to 70.1% over the strongest probe-based baseline.

arxiv:2610.12494.title: Algebraic Integer Quantization for Machine Learning Applications
arxiv:2610.12494.abstract: In this article, we propose algebraic integer number formats (AINF) as a framework for highly configurable and accurate compressed computation. A key property of AINF is its straightforward reduction to purely integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations. We develop a matrix multiplication engine that exploits this property, obtaining performance within a predictable factor of the most efficient numerical counterparts on modern hardware accelerators. Another key advantage of AIQ is the freedom to select algebraic integers tailored to the numerical characteristics of a given use case, offering optimization opportunities that are fundamentally unavailable in floating-point or fixed-point formats. Motivated by these properties, we introduce algebraic integer quantization (AIQ), a lossy compression format for large language model (LLM) inference, and provide results demonstrating that AIQ achieves competitive accuracy compared to the industry-standard MX format across a diverse set of models and benchmarks at equivalent bit-per-parameter budgets. The experiments presented in this article employ algebraic integers of degree two (quadratic integers); generalizations to higher-order and, in particular, multidimensional algebraic integers promise even greater computational advantages and remain a promising direction for future work.

arxiv:2610.13437.title: Local Diagnostics of Learned Event Representations for Anomaly Detection at the HL-LHC
arxiv:2610.13437.abstract: Anomaly detection, the identification of collision events that deviate from Standard Model expectations, is one of the most promising model-agnostic strategies for new-physics searches at the Large Hadron Collider. Searching for rare events in learned low-dimensional representations removes the need to commit to hand-crafted observables a priori, but sacrifices the immediate physical interpretation those observables provide. For anomaly detection to enter a discovery pipeline, flagged events must therefore be diagnosed locally, both to distinguish potential new physics from mismodeling or detector effects and to identify observables for targeted follow-up searches. We evaluate supervised and self-supervised neural embedding strategies on COLLIDE-2V, a 750-million-event dataset simulated under realistic High-Luminosity LHC conditions, using the reconstruction error of an autoencoder trained in the learned latent space as the anomaly score. Across the configurations and benchmark signals considered, supervised objectives, which exploit simulation process labels during training, generally outperform their self-supervised counterparts and, in their best configurations, improve on an autoencoder trained directly on kinematic features, raising the signal efficiency at 10% background acceptance on all held-out processes. We further introduce a local diagnostic pipeline that fits a Gaussian Mixture Model to the SM latent space, profiles each component through high-level observables without process labels, localizes the flagged events, and ranks observables by their local discriminating power. The ranking recovers the defining kinematics of the held-out processes, while correlating the anomaly score with the same observables quantifies how closely the score tracks them, revealing cases where the most discriminating observable is not the one the score follows most closely.

arxiv:2610.13494.title: Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits
arxiv:2610.13494.abstract: Existing LLM-based agent approaches for long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single-session execution lengthens, the agent's reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long-horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. These findings suggest that their benefits may not persist across versions, which motivates a workflow-level approach in which agents build on one another's work across sessions. We model these alternating agent sessions as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP) and establish sufficient conditions for alternation to exceed single-agent reference limits, derive an explicit experiment-budget bound, and characterize when session caps preserve this advantage. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which alternates two agents on a shared workspace, limits each session to at most k experiments and resets the context between sessions, without additional task-specific harness or prior knowledge supplements. Across 75 Kaggle tasks in MLE-bench, HMA reaches a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 8.0 points with a quarter of its time budget. Moreover, among six configurations spanning five heterogeneous agent pairs, HMA improves any-medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.4 points on average, demonstrating cross-pair generality. A supplementary case on kernel optimization reaches 878 cycles, within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader, demonstrating applicability beyond MLE.

doi:10.68296/ijvast20260073.title: TINYML’S HIDDEN FOOTPRINT: LIFECYCLE ENERGY USE, EMBODIED EMISSIONS, AND DISPOSAL PATHWAYS OF ULTRA-LOW-POWER ON-DEVICE AI — A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW
doi:10.68296/ijvast20260073.abstract: Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) is increasingly deployed on constrained devices to provide local intelligence with lowlatencyand reduced communication demand. However, the environmental sustainability of these systems cannot be determined frominferenceenergy alone because significant burdens may arise during model development, hardware production, maintenance, and end of life. Thisreview examines the hidden environmental footprint of TinyML from a cradle to grave perspective, integrating computational, hardware, communication, lifetime, and end of life dimensions. The review prioritizes empirical evidence and examines energy use across model training, optimization, deployment, sensing, preprocessing, inference, standby operation, wireless communication, firmware updates, battery replacement, recycling, and disposal. Attention is given to embodied energy and carbon from semiconductors, neural accelerators, sensors, printed circuit boards, power management components, batteries, enclosures, and transportation. The evidence indicates that TinyML can reduce operational energy by enabling local inference and minimizing transmission of raw data, while model compression, quantization, pruning, efficient memory use, event driven computation, and hardware acceleration can also reduce computational demand. Nevertheless, these gains do not necessarily translate into lower lifecycle environmental impact. Manufacturing burdens may becomerelatively dominant in highly efficient, intermittently operated, short lived, or low carbon powered systems, whereas operational andcommunication energy can become more important under intensive sensing, frequent transmission, extended duty cycles, and carbonintensive electricity supplies. Device lifetime is a critical determinant because longer service can distribute embodied impacts across moreuseful service, while premature replacement, sensor degradation, battery renewal, and repeated hardware turnover increase resource useand waste generation. Fleet scale further amplifies cumulative impacts through device proliferation, maintenance, updates, and disposal. The review identifies inconsistent system boundaries, functional units, measurement practices, and limited TinyML specific lifecycleinventories as major barriers to comparison. It highlights the need for harmonized lifecycle reporting, field based energy measurements, material inventories, regional assessment, and experimentally validated circular hardware strategies. Overall, sustainable TinyMLrequirescoordinated hardware, software, energy, and environmental design in which efficiency, longevity, repairability, modularity, reuse, refurbishment, and material recovery are considered alongside inference performance. Therefore, the review reframes TinyMLsustainability from minimizing inference energy to minimizing total environmental impact across the lifecycle

hash:f19e06d19672.title: Modelling of Pile-Up Effects in Ultra Fast Simulation Based on Flow Matching for LHC and HL-LHC
hash:f19e06d19672.abstract: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has recently concluded its Run 3 data-taking campaign, and in the coming years, the accelerator complex will undergo a major upgrade towards the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) era. The HL-LHC project aims to enhance the LHC's performance to maximize its discovery potential beyond 2030. The primary objective is to increase the integrated luminosity by a factor of 10 relative to the original design value. Since luminosity is proportional to the number of collisions, higher luminosity enables experiments to accumulate much larger datasets. This facilitates the study of known mechanisms, such as the Higgs boson, with unprecedented precision, and the observation of rare phenomena that may emerge at these energy scales. However, looking ahead to the HL-LHC era, unprecedented computational demands will challenge computer-based simulations in High Energy Physics, driven primarily by pile-up. With an expected average of up to 200 simultaneous interactions per bunch crossing, event reconstruction will become more complex. Simulating every particle produced in these complex environments using the traditional Geant4-based Full Simulation (FullSim) is computationally unsustainable, typically requiring O(30-60 s) per event in Run $3$, scaling up to several minutes at HL-LHC. Consequently, simulation represents a major bottleneck in the CMS analysis workflow. Alternative simulation frameworks have been developed to mitigate this issue. FastSim, for instance, replaces heavy Geant4 material interactions with simplified analytical parameterizations, reducing the simulation time by an order of magnitude (O(5 s)). However, it still requires the execution of standard Particle Flow reconstruction algorithms to produce the final analysis datasets, leaving a significant computational bottleneck in the workflow. To address this, the CMS group in Pisa developed FlashSim, an end-to-end Deep Learning-based fast simulation software that bypasses the Geant4 detector simulation and traditional reconstruction. By directly mapping generator-level particles to reconstructed physics objects in the compact NanoAOD format, FlashSim achieves a generation speed orders of magnitude faster than the full simulation chain (O(ms)). Because FlashSim relies on learning the gen-to-reco mapping, a fundamental challenge arises with fake objects, reconstructed components that do not have a generator-level counterpart from which to start. While this issue affects the reconstruction of all physics objects (including electrons, muons, taus, and photons), this thesis focuses specifically on the generative modelling of fake jets, which originate from pile-up interactions or random calorimeter noise, rather than from a genuine hard-scattered parton, and therefore represent a limitation of the gen-to-reco approach. The primary goal of this thesis is to address this limitation, improving the generative model used to simulate fake jets within the FlashSim framework. To evaluate the improved generative models, we validated FlashSim within the Run 3 environment, as part of an ongoing analysis of the Vector Boson Fusion (VBF) channel of the Higgs boson decay into two muons (H to mumu). This specific channel is of profound interest for both Run 3 and the upcoming HL-LHC, as its experimental sensitivity currently lies around the 5-sigma observation threshold. Despite its rarity, with a branching ratio of only BR(H to mumu) = 2.2 10^{-4}, this channel provides a direct probe of the Higgs interaction with second-generation fermions. However, this same rarity means that an enormous number of simulated events is required to accurately estimate the background in the signal region, and the signal itself is challenging to isolate, dominated by the Drell-Yan background. By rapidly generating massive simulated samples, FlashSim modelled this dominant background, populating the signal-enriched regions of the phase space. The thesis is composed of 7 chapters organized into three parts. Part I introduces the physical and technical context: Chapter 1 provides an overview of the LHC and the CMS experiment, while Chapter 2 reviews the Higgs mechanism and its main production and decay channels. Part II focuses on simulation and the machine learning tools that form the basis of this work. After Chapter 3 discusses current approaches to event simulation and their associated computational costs, Chapter 4 offers a comprehensive introduction to neural networks before focusing deeply on Continuous Normalizing Flows and Flow Matching. This chapter details how Flow Matching learns a continuous transformation to capture complex multidimensional phase spaces, framing the training process as a stable regression task. Part III presents the original contributions of this research. Chapter 5 describes the fake jet simulation module, detailing how the generation is decoupled into three sequential stages: predicting the total multiplicity, generating the joint distribution of the kinematic variables to preserve physical correlations within the event, and reconstructing all remaining jet features. The chapter also outlines how optimization resolved initial mismodelling issues, enabling the network to learn implicit constraints like the angular separation between jets. Furthermore, it explores the physical characterization of fake jets, highlighting their correlation to the total event energy scale. Finally, Chapter 6 demonstrates the application to the VBF H to mumu physics analysis, and Chapter 7 outlines the conclusions and future work.

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261003.title: Language Awareness, Language Ideologies, Language Attitudes, etc.: Different Names for Similar Phenomena?
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261003.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter begins by explaining why Language Awareness (LA) research has become particularly important for its author, not least because of his many years of professional activity in the languages department of a business university. In the following theoretical section, he compares the concept of LA with similar notions from the immediate and wider research context. In doing so, he argues for a broad interpretation of LA and for its status as a central notion in Applied Linguistics generally. At the same time, the LA concept shows similarities with ideas discussed in other applied linguistic (sub-)disciplines and research communities, especially those concerned with Language Attitudes, Language Ideologies, and Folk Linguistics. These similarities, however, seem to be acknowledged seldom by representatives of the various approaches. It is therefore argued that a larger research project should compare and contrast all of them with a view to clarifying their respective objects and the terminology they employ.</jats:p>

doi:10.58578/mikailalsys.v4i3.12081.title: Implementation of the Structured Debate Learning Model to Improve Learning Outcomes in Pancasila Education on the Topic of "the Territory of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia" at UPT SMP Negeri 3 Semanding
doi:10.58578/mikailalsys.v4i3.12081.abstract: <jats:p>Low initial learning mastery highlighted the need for more active instruction in Pancasila Education at UPT SMP Negeri 3 Semanding. This study examined changes in learning outcomes following the implementation of structured debate on the territory of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia (NKRI), with students divided into affirmative and opposing groups. A mixed-methods classroom action research design was conducted over two cycles involving 26 seventh-grade students in Class VII-C. Data were collected through observations, questionnaires/tests, and interviews and analyzed descriptively using quantitative and qualitative techniques. At baseline, two students (8%) met the minimum mastery criterion (KKM = 70), and the class mean score was 55. In Cycle I, mastery increased to 16 students (62%), with a mean score of 71. In Cycle II, mastery remained at 16 students (62%), while the mean score was 69. Qualitative findings indicated a progression from basic conceptual understanding toward analysis involving higher-order thinking skills, accompanied by greater self-confidence and stronger argumentation skills. These findings indicate that mastery gains relative to baseline were maintained across the two cycles, alongside qualitative improvements in students’ thinking and participation. The study provides contextual evidence for constructivist, debate-based civic pedagogy and practical insights for teachers seeking to strengthen analytical thinking, confidence, and argumentation through structured classroom debate.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s12186-026-09399-4.title: Training Methods in Higher Education and the Workplace: A Systematic Literature Review
doi:10.1007/s12186-026-09399-4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The growing use of technology-supported training has increased the need to examine training methods in higher education and workplace settings more thoroughly. Although the literature includes many studies that report a growing use of technology-supported training, such as simulation-based and immersive approaches, it still presents important gaps because it remains fragmented. Many studies focus on isolated training methods, specific sectors, or single outcomes, which limits a broader understanding of how training has been designed, evaluated, and measured across different contexts. To address this gap, this systematic literature review analyzes research published between 2019 and 2024 on training methods in higher education and the workplace. Following the PRISMA framework, this review of the literature analyzes 36 articles to examine how training methods, learning theories, and evaluation practices are reported and combined in both higher education and workplace settings. The analysis suggests that constructivist, cognitivist, and behaviorist perspectives have commonly guided training design approaches, with limited hybridization across them, while assessment practices have varied across contexts and include different research methods and structured evaluation models. In addition, outcome measures have mainly focused on learning, performance, and skill development, while fewer studies have examined long-term impact. The findings highlight that these elements are not consistently aligned across studies. Therefore, from a technology and design education perspective, this review identifies patterns, implications for instructional design, variations, and gaps, providing a clearer account of how training has supported knowledge in action and the integration of theory and practice, providing an integrated overview of how training methods have been designed and evaluated across technology-supported higher education and workplace settings.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261007.title: Learning Environments in Flux: Designing Through User Engagement
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261007.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter delves into the design of innovative learning environments underpinned by an iterative user engagement process, positioning the designer in the role of both facilitator and interpreter – balancing conceptual visions with the lived realities of educators and students. Addressing pedagogical needs for flexibility, the design research centres around allowing affordances for learning in a diverse range of modes. Cutting across various scales, the physical and social scale of the learning environment, the pedagogical scale of the learning activity and the time scale of an academic calendar, this chapter highlights the importance of treating user engagement as a core input to the design process, informing spatial strategies that allow learning environments to evolve, expand and shrink according to the users’ needs. Drawing from observations, participatory design workshops and key interviews, the design research uncovers latent needs and identifies nuances across multiple modes of teaching and learning. Ultimately, the chapter makes the case for embedding user engagement into the culture of designing for learning environments, advocating for an iterative process to ensure the learning environment can evolve alongside its users in a manner that is not just innovative, but also deeply relevant and responsive to the users they serve.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261011.title: Autobiographical Research and Identity: A Model for Methodological Innovation
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261011.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter examines the scholarly contributions of Professor Claudia Finkbeiner and their influence on contemporary understandings of identity, language awareness, cultural awareness, social justice, and intercultural communication, with particular reference to her work at the University of Calgary’s Werklund School of Education. It highlights Finkbeiner’s advocacy for culturally relevant education (CRE), an approach that emphasizes empowering learners by connecting pedagogy to their linguistic and cultural contexts. Central to this discussion is Finkbeiner’s ABCs Model for Cultural Communication, an autobiographical framework grounded in the principle of “know thyself, know others,” which supports identity formation and confidence-building among both learners and educators. The chapter also situates this work within ongoing collaborative research, including joint engagement in the Literacy Research Association (LRA), where efforts have focused on advancing knowledge in multilingualism, language and cultural awareness, digital learning environments, second language reading processes, and literacy development. The chapter contributes to broader discussions of methodological innovation in teacher education, demonstrating how autobiographical and intercultural approaches can deepen understanding of identity and enhance pedagogical practice in increasingly diverse educational contexts.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-303-720261003.title: Fostering School Relationships in Urban Schools to Cultivate Risk-Taking and Rigour in Learning
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-303-720261003.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this chapter, we explore how fostering meaningful relationships in urban school settings cultivates academic risk-taking and rigour, ultimately supporting student success and well-being. Grounded in relational pedagogy and informed by contemporary research, the chapter outlines three essential relationship domains: student-to-student, student-to-teacher, and student-to-school community. Through these lenses, we demonstrate how trust, collaboration, and belonging foster environments where students feel safe to take intellectual risks, learn from failure, and strive toward academic and personal growth. Practical strategies such as collaborative learning, personalized feedback, scaffolded inquiry, and inclusive recognition practices are explored. Emphasis is placed on ‘failing forward’ as a mindset that encourages students to view mistakes as opportunities rather than obstacles. A case study, the Hallway of Heroes project, illustrates how authentic school–community partnerships affirm student identity, raise academic expectations, and promote civic engagement. The chapter also includes discussion and practice questions designed to help educators examine their current practices and implement relational strategies in their classrooms. Ultimately, we argue that investing in robust relational ecosystems is critical for cultivating equity, resilience, and rigour. By centring relationships, urban educators can create inclusive, high-trust environments where students feel empowered to take risks, grow through challenges, and reach their full potential.</jats:p>

doi:10.1215/9781478062868-004.title: Trauma | Somatics
doi:10.1215/9781478062868-004.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores approaches to trauma studies that move in the direction of antiracism and political somatics, including through practice. Structured in the form of a reading list, or bibliographic altar, which is an important genre for both “self-help” and “study,” the chapter develops an idiosyncratic and queer bibliography, which includes Bessel van der Kolk, Resmaa Menakem, Staci Haines, Kai Cheng Thom, and Alison Bechdel, as well as accounts of practice in courses in embodied social justice and politicized somatics.</jats:p>

doi:10.1002/smtd.71113.title: Unveiling Hidden Patterns in Electrode‐Electrolyte Interphase Chemistry and Architecture Through Machine Learning‐Assisted Mass Spectrometry Analysis
doi:10.1002/smtd.71113.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrode‐electrolyte interphases (EEIs) govern battery performance, yet the interplay between their chemical composition and spatial organization remains challenging to resolve. Time‐of‐flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF‐SIMS) provides rich 3D chemical depth profiles of these interfaces, yet conventional analyses simplify the complexity by collapsing the data into 1D depth profiles or 2D maps, obscuring critical spatial features. Here, we apply a machine‐learning‐based approach directly to 3D TOF‐SIMS depth profiles, leveraging their full spatial and chemical richness to investigate the interphase structure and chemistry more comprehensively than conventional analyses. Principal component analysis (PCA) identifies fragments that dominate chemical heterogeneity across the EEI, reveals correlated and anticorrelated spatial distributions, and enables direct comparison of average interphase chemistry and chemical variability. Building on this, t‐distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t‐SNE) and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) resolve stratified structures and fine‐scale spatial interphase variations. Finally, applying PCA to fragment‐specific thickness maps enables comparison of interphase thickness heterogeneity and identifies the chemical species responsible for local thickness variations. Together, the approach creates a generalized framework for extracting chemically and spatially meaningful information from complex TOF‐SIMS datasets, linking interphase chemistry to electrochemical behavior and guiding the design of uniform interphases for advanced battery systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10867402/v1.title: Post-hoc reliability assessment and visual explanation for deep learning-based oral mucosal lesion detection
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10867402/v1.abstract: Background Modern deep learning detectors for oral mucosal lesions produce class predictions and softmax confidence scores, but neither reveals which learned visual patterns supported the prediction nor whether it can be trusted. We developed a post-hoc method that, without modifying an already-trained YOLO detector, makes the basis of each prediction explicit through embedding-space analysis and provides a training-distribution-aware estimate of its reliability. Methods A YOLOv11 detector was trained on 3104 intraoral photographs covering oral lichen planus (OLP), proliferative verrucous leukoplakia (PVL)/leukoplakia and oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), supplemented with 464 healthy mucosa images. For every detection, a feature embedding was extracted from the deepest backbone layer, projected to a 2-D manifold using supervised neighborhood component analysis (NCA) and unsupervised uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), and scored against per-class kernel density estimates fitted on correctly predicted training samples. Density scores were compared with softmax confidence using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and nearest-neighbor retrieval in the embedding space provided visual explanations of individual predictions. Results Per-class detection F1-scores were 0.88 (OLP), 0.76 (PVL/Leukoplakia), 0.73 (OSCC) and 0.93 (healthy mucosa). Density-based ROC area-under-the-curve (AUC) values ranged from 0.92 to 0.95 across the four classes, with NCA slightly outperforming UMAP. The density score consistently identified low-confidence predictions that softmax did not flag, and the nearest-neighbor mosaic produced visually interpretable explanations of individual predictions. Conclusions Embedding-space density on a frozen YOLO detector provides an interpretable, post-hoc reliability measure for oral mucosal lesion detection. Combined with nearest-neighbor visual retrieval, it complements softmax confidence and supports post-hoc clinical audit without retraining.

doi:10.5539/hes.v16n4p473.title: Learning Management to Promote Future Skills for Student Teachers: A Case Study of Social Studies Student Teachers at Songkhla Rajabhat University, Thailand
doi:10.5539/hes.v16n4p473.abstract: <jats:p>This mixed-methods case study examined instructional management and future-skill needs in higher-education social studies teacher preparation, developed community-based learning activities for the Social Studies Pedagogy course, and examined changes in six future-skill domains among student teachers. The participants were 30 third-year Social Studies student teachers enrolled at Songkhla Rajabhat University in the first semester of the 2025 academic year. Qualitative data were obtained from curriculum and document analysis, expert interviews, observations, and reflections; quantitative data were obtained from achievement measures, activity and lesson-plan evaluations, and pre- and post-intervention assessments of future skills. The six domains identified and used consistently throughout the study were digital skills, lifelong learning skills, social skills, creativity and innovation skills, flexibility and adaptability skills, and critical thinking skills. The community-based lesson plans achieved an efficiency index of 88.25/88.75. Learning-achievement scores increased from M = 14.23 (SD = 1.41) to M = 18.07 (SD = 1.28), t(29) = 17.84, p &lt; .001, Cohen&#39;s dz = 3.26. Descriptively, the overall future-skill mean increased from 4.701 (SD = 0.702) before the intervention to 5.225 (SD = 0.549) after the intervention. Because the study used one intact cohort without a control group, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of change within this course context rather than as proof of causal effectiveness. The study contributes a contextually grounded model for connecting community-based social studies learning with future-skill development in teacher education.</jats:p>

doi:10.1117/1.jrs.20.044501.title: Few-shot class-incremental SAR target recognition via multi-task representation learning network with structural knowledge distillation
doi:10.1117/1.jrs.20.044501.abstract: <jats:p>In recent years, significant progress has been made in class-incremental synthetic aperture radar (SAR) automatic target recognition (ATR). However, existing methods heavily rely on large-scale labeled data, which is impractical for real-world incremental scenarios where new classes emerge with limited samples. This scarcity of new-class data brings about dual challenges during class incremental learning: catastrophic forgetting of old classes and severe overfitting of new classes. To tackle these challenges, we propose a few-shot class-incremental ATR method called multi-task representation learning network with structural knowledge distillation, which effectively balances the dilemma of stability and plasticity of the model. Concretely, we develop a multi-task representation learning network to learn class-agnostic representation and strengthen the class decision boundaries under the paradigm of self-supervised learning and supervised learning at base sessions, which is very beneficial for the recognition model to generalize to new classes while maintaining the separation of the base classes. To alleviate the problem of catastrophic forgetting on old classes during class-incremental learning, we present a structural knowledge distillation-based knowledge recall strategy, which leverages the angular invariance among different features to constrain the drift of the intra-class structural relationship before and after the incremental update of the recognition model. Evaluation experiments on three publicly available SAR datasets illustrate that the proposed method is competitive with many state-of-the-art methods.</jats:p>

doi:10.53299/jppi.v6i4.5330.title: Faktor-Faktor yang Memengaruhi Niat Siswa Mengadopsi Game-Based Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
doi:10.53299/jppi.v6i4.5330.abstract: <jats:p>Game-Based Learning (GBL) adalah pendekatan pembelajaran berbasis permainan yang menghibur dan melibatkan peserta didik sekolah menengah. Namun, adopsi GBL masih diperdebatkan secara akademis dan memerlukan penyelidikan lebih lanjut. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis faktor-faktor yang memengaruhi niat siswa untuk mengadopsi GBL. Studi ini menggunakan Systematic Literature Review (SLR) dengan panduan PRISMA terhadap 20 artikel ilmiah terkemuka dari Google Scholar dan Scopus yang diterbitkan pada rentang tahun 2021 hingga 2026. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa faktor utama yang memengaruhi niat adopsi GBL dan keterlibatan siswa meliputi persepsi kegunaan dan kemudahan penggunaan (Technology Acceptance Model), penurunan kecemasan belajar (Learning Anxiety), interaksi guru-siswa, serta dukungan teknis dan kesiapan institusional sekolah. Temuan ini memberi panduan bagi pendidik untuk membangun ekosistem GBL yang inklusif dan berkelanjutan, serta menjadi acuan sekolah dalam mengadopsi teknologi pendidikan baru. Untuk penelitian yang akan datang, direkomendasikan penggunaan pendekatan longitudinal guna menguji retensi pengetahuan jangka panjang dan daya ingat siswa terhadap mekanika game. Selain itu, penelitian selanjutnya perlu memperluas pengujian model adopsi ini pada konteks sekolah dengan keterbatasan sarana infrastruktur serta penerapannya pada kurikulum digital lainnya.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s40536-026-00324-8.title: Latent variable or achievement-tailored composite?: The home resources for learning (HRL) index in TIMSS and PIRLS
doi:10.1186/s40536-026-00324-8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Background variables in international large-scale assessments are often combined into indices for statistical analyses. Using the Home Resources for Learning (HRL) index as an example, we draw from the Cowan et al. (2012) report on socio-economic status (SES) to consider parallel ways of defining HRL composites, and show how the choice among alternatives has the potential to affect estimation of cross-country HRL–achievement relationships. Prior studies have emphasized HRL indicator variables as reflective indicators of a latent HRL construct, and address cross-country measurement differences through latent variable partial-invariance models [e.g., Wendt et al. (2017); Jusufi et al. (2026)]. However, the latent variable logic commonly applied to constructs like HRL and the accompanying perspectives of measurement invariance that ensure can be questioned (Welzel and Inglehart, 2016). In this paper, rather than adopting a strong stand regarding which approach is best, we explore empirically the implications of adopting latent variable weights as opposed to achievement-tailored weights as a basis for improving cross-country comparability in HRL. Our empirical analyses using structural equation modeling demonstrate disproportionality between latent variable HRL indicator loadings and the corresponding predictive effects of the HRL indicator variables on achievement, suggesting a potential for differences between latent variable versus achievement-tailored composite approaches. Overall, parent–reported books in the home predicts achievement more strongly, and parental occupation less strongly, than is implied by their respective loadings on an HRL latent variable. While overall the implications of these effects appear small, they impact the estimated strength of HRL-achievement relationships in certain individual countries (systems).</jats:p>
