doi:10.14445/22315381/ijett-v74i9p107.title: Reinforcement-Learning based Self-Healing Banking Transaction System against Malware Attacks in IoT Networks
doi:10.14445/22315381/ijett-v74i9p107.abstract: <jats:p>The IoT technology that was at the height of popularity in the banking industry has resulted, improved real-time transaction processing, enhancing the availability of smart financial products and services, and the automated payment systems are more feasible than the traditional banking IoT security models. However, these implementations often fail to detect newly developed "zero-day” malware applications. In contrast, the proposed design for this research is based on developing a Reinforcement Learning (RL) system for banking IoT networks. As compared to traditional Intrusion Detection Systems, which send an alert and/or block the offending actions, the RL-based systems described herein treat the network as a continuous agent-environment dynamic loop that autonomously configures the network, including real-time/configurable routing protocol and resource allocation, in order to preserve transaction integrity during active malware propagation. The proposed research presents a banking transaction processing system that employs RL technology to identify, mitigate, and recover from malware-related events and intrusions in IoT-enab led financial networks by using real-time virus/abnormality detection via a deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) controller. The deep RL controller models the overall context of network security in accordance with the principles of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). The RL agent creates an effective mitigation strategy by detecting and isolating weak nodes, blocking harmful traffic, redirecting ways to conduct transactions, re-verifying identities safely, and reinstating service to the customer. The growing acceptance of Web of Things, or IoT, technologies in monetary infrastructures will enhance operational efficacy; however, it will also create new risks associated with connecting the banking industry to the Internet. Currently, the majority of malware detection systems based on machine learning and security products do not have any self-healing mechanisms for systems to recover from interruptions. This paper presents a new framework called the Reinforcement Learning-based Self-Healing Banking Transaction (RL-SHBT), which uses hybrid malware detection and enables flexible responses to attacks as well as automated methods for recovering from these attacks. The IoT banking environment has been modelled as a system based on Markov, where the use of a Deep Network with a set of flexible rewards will allow the DQN to learn the most effective response methods. This RL-based security model differs from existing models for the protection of IoT devices in that it utilizes transaction-sensitive state modelling and an adaptable reward system that encourages a balance between security and performance. The results of the experiments showed that this model has a detection accuracy of 99.02% (95% confidence interval: ±0.41%), a false positive rate of 1.12%, an average recovery time of 4.8 seconds, and a self-healing success rate of 97.8%. The research shows that an adaptive reward system with reinforcement learning speeds up the rate of learning by 34% compared to a fixed reward system. The results also indicate that reinforcement-learning-driven autonomous recovery greatly enhances cyber resilience and continuity of transactions within IoT-based financial systems. Machine learning and malware detection techniques have been designed to detect malicious network activities.</jats:p>
doi:10.14445/22315381/ijett-v74i9p107.venue: International Journal of Engineering Trends and Technology

doi:10.51601/ijersc.v7i5.1098.title: The Role of Teachers Using the Ki Hadjar Dewantara Approach in Implementing Student-Centered Learning: A Study at MAN 2 Model Medan
doi:10.51601/ijersc.v7i5.1098.abstract: <jats:p>Education not only aims to impart knowledge, but also to develop students' potential, character, independence, and social skills. One approach that supports this goal is Student-Centered Learning (SCL), which places students as the main subjects in the learning process. This approach has a strong connection with Ki Hadjar Dewantara's thinking regarding education as a process of guiding children according to their nature and potential. This article aims to describe the implementation of SCL, analyze the role of teachers, and examine its relevance to the principles of Ing Ngarsa Sung Tuladha, Ing Madya Mangun Karsa, and Tut Wuri Handayani. This study uses a qualitative descriptive approach through observation, interviews, and documentation at MAN 2 Model Medan. The results of the study indicate that teachers act as facilitators, guides, motivators, role models, and companions. Teachers provide space for students to ask questions, discuss, express opinions, explore information, solve problems, and develop their potential independently. The application of Ki Hadjar Dewantara's principles has proven relevant to the needs of students in the digital era, as long as the freedom to learn is accompanied by direction, responsibility, and character building.</jats:p>
doi:10.51601/ijersc.v7i5.1098.venue: International Journal of Educational Research & Social Sciences

doi:10.1021/acs.energyfuels.6c03787.title: Explainable Machine Learning Combined with Feature Selection and Bayesian Optimization for Predicting Rare Earth Elements and Yttrium in Coal: A Case Study of China’s Five Major Coal-Bearing Regions
doi:10.1021/acs.energyfuels.6c03787.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Determining the concentrations of rare earth elements and yttrium (REY) in coal is essential for evaluating coal-hosted critical metal resources and understanding their geochemical controls. However, conventional laboratory analyses are costly, time-consuming, and spatially sparse, limiting regional-scale assessment. In this study, we compiled 527 coal samples from 30 coalfields across China’s five major coal-bearing regions and developed an explainable machine learning framework for REY prediction. Unlike previous site-specific models, this framework integrates feature selection, Bayesian optimization, and SHAP interpretation for REY prediction at a broad regional scale. After data preprocessing, multicollinearity diagnosis, and correlation-based feature selection, 16 predictors were retained for model construction. Four ensemble regression models, including Random Forest (RF), Extra Trees (ET), CatBoost (CAT), and Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT), were optimized using Bayesian hyperparameter search and 5-fold cross-validation. The ET model achieved the best test-set performance among the four ensemble models, with RMSE = 39.962, MAE = 29.669, and R2 = 0.716, although predictions for highly enriched samples remained uncertain because of the long-tailed REY distribution. SHAP analysis identified Ga as the most influential predictor, followed by geological age and P2O5, suggesting that clay-related terrigenous input, stratigraphic context, and minor phosphate-associated phases may jointly influence model-predicted REY enrichment. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework can serve as an effective prescreening tool to prioritize coal samples for detailed REY analysis, while independent validation is recommended for high-value target areas.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/fire9100445.title: Near-Real-Time Wildfire Segmentation and Brightness Temperature Estimation from Geostationary Satellite Imagery Using Deep Learning
doi:10.3390/fire9100445.abstract: <jats:p>Near-real-time wildfire monitoring is essential for situational awareness and emergency response. The Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite (GOES) observes at 2 km every 5 min, whereas the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) observes at 375 m twice daily, leaving neither sensor able to track rapidly evolving fires in fine spatial detail. This study introduces a two-step deep learning approach that statistically infers VIIRS-like sub-pixel fire segmentation and brightness temperature (BT) from GOES imagery. The dataset comprises 257 U.S. wildfires within preselected regions of interest, pairing multi-spectral GOES imagery with VIIRS-derived references in four classes (Non-Fire, Small, Medium, and Large) defined by the number of fire pixels. Against an autoencoder-based baseline, the proposed method raises average precision from 0.105 to 0.368 and reduces the fire region BT root mean square error by 72.1% from 81.33 K to 22.69 K. Omission error rates fall from 9.41% to 1.96% for Medium fires and remain at zero for Large fires, whereas Small fires, 37% of the test set, remain at 39.91%. The false positive rate on Non-Fire images falls from 66.86% to 8.48%, near the operational GOES product’s 6.36% with lower omission (31.40% versus 40.35%). Inference completes within 5 min of observation for a monitored region.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261001.title: Introduction to Language, Culture and Literacy in Foreign Language Learning
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261001.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The present volume examines the dynamic interplay and interconnected roles of language, culture, and literacy in foreign language education. This introductory chapter defines these three core constructs, explains their relevance to foreign language learning and teaching and provides a comprehensive overview of the volume’s structure and chapters. Overall, this collection features diverse international and interdisciplinary perspectives from scholars in language education, linguistics, literacy studies, and subject didactics across various countries and pedagogical settings. The Language section addresses academic registers, language awareness, plurilingual competence, and technology-enhanced teaching, including the role of artificial intelligence. The Culture section explores pedagogical approaches to cultural understanding and communication, emphasizing autobiographical reflection and intercultural cooperation. Finally, the Literacy section focuses on reading development, digital literacies, as well as multimodal feedback literacies. Collectively, the contributions combine theoretical approaches, empirical insights, and innovative practices, while emphasizing critical, holistic, and multidisciplinary perspectives that are key to transformative pedagogies in a globally interconnected world. To this end, the chapter concludes by sketching specific avenues for future research and teaching practice in the field of foreign language education.</jats:p>

doi:10.1215/9781478062868-003.title: Disability | Madness
doi:10.1215/9781478062868-003.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter starts with the question of whether to claim tendencies to anxiety and depression as a disability. Rather than trying to settle definitively on an answer, the chapter focuses on learning from disability studies and mad studies not only by reading in the field but also by reporting on experiences in the classroom and in university administration. The chapter considers disability studies in relation to affect studies understood not just as a field but also as a resource for survival.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11310221/v1.title: Empirical Modeling and Machine Learning Prediction of Operational Electrical Load, Power Quality, and Carbon Emissions in a Korean Steel Manufacturing Plant
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11310221/v1.abstract: The electrical load of steel processing plants is set by induction motors, drives and transformers whose behaviour changes with operating regime. We analysed 35,040 fifteen-minute meter records (2018) from a Korean steel plant. A path model with day-block bootstrapping related tariff-period regime to reactive energy, power factor and active energy. Multilayer perceptrons (MLP) and random forests were tested as non-linear benchmarks against linear regression and a seasonal-naive forecast. Simulations evaluated power-factor correction, idle-load reduction, load shifting and grid decarbonisation under Scope 2 accounting. Maximum-load periods drew 8.1 times the energy of light-load periods. Power factor fell from about 91% at high load to 54% at idle; one-third of the energy differential co-varied with reactive energy. A schedule-only MLP reached a test R² of 0.72 (naive forecast: 0.32). In-plant measures abated 1.7% of 440 tCO₂/yr. Shifting peak energy to night raised emissions whenever night-time marginal emissions exceeded daytime ones. Moving evening load into midday solar hours instead cut emissions by 8–25 tCO₂/yr under the solar-rich grid profile.

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10932103/v1.title: Comprehension of Health Apps' Retention Rates Employing the Means of Machine Learning Models
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10932103/v1.abstract: Background: Health apps for multiple purposes have been widely adopted as the global health burden has increased. With an increase of their popularity, the economic significance of the health app market has become substantial. However, health apps continue to face the challenge of low user retention rates, which hinders their sustainable development and requires urgent attention. Therefore, this study develops solutions to this situation, identifying the determinants of retention and building a machine learning model to help predict the retention rate of health apps. Methods: In this study, three machine learning models were constructed based on linear regression, gradient boosting and XGBoost. Data preprocessing included checking missing values, encoding categorical variables, feature scal ing, and feature engineering. Model performance was evaluated using R2, MAE, MSE, RMSE, and Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient. Feature importance was analysed using Pareto diagrams, partial dependence plots, and ablation studies. Results: The results indicate that linear regression fails to capture nonlinear user psychological interactions and yields weak fitting results; XGBoost outperforms the other models via second-order optimization and regularization, with superior rank preservation critical for ordinal 1–5 rating data. It achieves the highest R2 and Spearman’s ρ, confirming that usability and medical communication are core retention drivers. Conclusion: This study provides possible prediction models for the retention rates of health apps, which developers can use as diagnostic tools to evaluate and optimize their app design for long-term user engagement. Trial Registration: Not applicable.

doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-0.title: Design for Learning
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-0.abstract:
<jats:p>Around the world, schools are investing billions in the design and construction of learning environments that reflect contemporary developments in educational and architectural thinking. Yet the knowledge that informs these investments, spanning across research, policy, and industry practice, often remains fragmented. Insights from across these spheres are frequently developed and applied in isolation, limiting our collective capacity to understand how learning environments shape student experience and outcomes.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Designing for Learning addresses this disconnect by foregrounding the interdisciplinary relationships between research, policy, and industry. Bringing together perspectives from educational research, design practice, systems policy, and professional expertise, the book positions learning environments as the product of dynamic interactions across these domains. The chapters illustrate how research evidence, regulatory frameworks, and industry innovation intersect to influence the planning, design, and enactment of educational spaces.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Through a rich combination of empirical research, policy analysis, and real-world case studies, Designing for Learning offers a comprehensive framework for creating inclusive, effective, and future-oriented learning environments. It explores how flexible spatial design, pedagogical intent, policy settings, and design practices can be aligned to support diverse learner needs.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>By making explicit the contributions and interdependencies of research, policy, and industry, this volume demonstrates how interdisciplinary collaboration can lead to more coherent, responsive, and impactful learning environments. It is an essential resource for educators, researchers, policymakers, designers, and industry professionals seeking to move beyond siloed approaches and toward integrated solutions that are not only functional but also transformative, inspiring, and inclusive.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/ijccsm-09-2025-0332.title: Unlocking wind energy potential in data-scarce regions: a deep learning framework for strategic climate action in Vietnam’s Central Highlands
doi:10.1108/ijccsm-09-2025-0332.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As Vietnam accelerates its transition toward a sustainable energy future under ambitious national strategies like the Power Development Plan VIII (PDP8), a critical barrier persists: the lack of high-fidelity resource maps for strategic planning. This is particularly acute in data-scarce regions with high potential, such as Vietnam’s Central Highlands. This study aims to address this strategic gap by developing and validating a robust deep learning framework to produce an enhanced and detailed high-resolution wind energy map for this region, providing a conservative proof-of-concept for regional energy planning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework integrates coarse-resolution daily wind speed data from an ensemble of 11 global climate models with long-term observational records (1985–2023) from a sparse network of meteorological stations. To preserve synoptic extremes critical for wind power, the downscaling was conducted at a daily temporal resolution. A suite of advanced machine learning and deep learning models were systematically trained. To address the limitations of spatial interpolation in complex terrain, the downscaled 10 m wind speeds were extrapolated to a 149 m commercial hub-height using a terrain-aware power law, integrating high-resolution surface roughness data. A technical potential map (GWh/km²/year) was then generated by combining the turbine power curve (Enercon E-101) with a GIS-based availability index (AI), factoring in constraints such as elevation, slope, land cover and urban buffers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deep learning architectures, particularly the convolutional neural network and XGBoost, significantly outperformed traditional models, achieving R-Pearson correlation coefficients exceeding 0.85 on daily predictions. Validation against ERA5 reanalysis data demonstrated that our ML-downscaled outputs substantially reduced severe negative biases present in ERA5 over complex terrain. The framework generated one of the most detailed wind energy maps for the region, identifying specific “hotspots” capable of generating significant yields (&gt;6.0 GWh/km²/year) while strictly masking physically constrained zones. Projections under future shared socioeconomic pathways indicate that this wind resource potential is expected to remain robust.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study could provide a powerful, replicable methodological blueprint for de-risking renewable energy investment in data-scarce regions. By embedding high-resolution spatial covariates (DEM, roughness) into the vertical extrapolation rather than relying solely on 2D interpolation, it delivers an early, scientifically rigorous tool to guide national energy policy, optimize land-use planning and accelerate the sustainable expansion of wind energy for other regions in the country and abroad.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
doi:10.1108/ijccsm-09-2025-0332.venue: International Journal of Climate Change Strategies and Management

doi:10.20885/ijcer.vol10.iss2.art11.title: Development of the Baamboozle Game-Based Interactive Learning Module on Acids and Bases
doi:10.20885/ijcer.vol10.iss2.art11.abstract: <jats:p>This study was motivated by the need for more interactive teaching materials to help students understand acid-base concepts. The aim of this research is to produce an interactive learning module based on the Baamboozle game on acid-base material. This study employed a research and development (R&D) methodology based on the ADDIE model, with implementation limited to the development stage. Data were collected through a teacher needs analysis questionnaire, validation forms for subject matter experts and media experts, and response questionnaires for teachers and students. The needs analysis questionnaire used the Guttman scale, while the validation forms and response questionnaires used the Likert scale. The data were analyzed using quantitative descriptive methods by calculating the percentage of scores to determine the product’s level of suitability and practicality. The results of the study indicate that the developed module received a feasibility rating of 89.17% from media experts and 87.03% from content experts, both categorized as “highly feasible.” The practicality test results showed a rating of 89.3% from teachers and 93.2% from students, categorized as “highly practical.” Thus, the Baamboozle game-based interactive learning module on acid-base material is deemed highly feasible and highly practical for use in chemistry instruction. The novelty of this research lies in integrating the Baamboozle game into an interactive learning module that is systematically designed and tailored to the stages of presenting acid-base material, so that the game activity doesn’t stand alone, but becomes part of the learning process within the module. Further research is recommended to test the module’s effectiveness on student learning outcomes.</jats:p>
doi:10.20885/ijcer.vol10.iss2.art11.venue: IJCER (International Journal of Chemistry Education Research)

doi:10.20885/ijcer.vol10.iss2.art4.title: Facilitating Deep Learning Characteristics through Problem-Based Learning and PhET Simulation in Molecular Geometry
doi:10.20885/ijcer.vol10.iss2.art4.abstract: <jats:p>Chemistry concepts related to molecular structure are challenging to learn due to their abstract nature, the necessity for multiple representations, and the demand for three-dimensional spatial visualization skills. This study examines the implementation of Problem-Based Learning (PBL) supported by PhET Simulation, an interactive virtual tool that enables students to visualize and explore molecular structures and chemical concepts. The objective is to promote deep learning through meaningful, joyful, and mindful learning experiences. An embedded mixed-methods approach with a one-group pretest–posttest design was utilized. The sample consisted of 36 grade X students from SMA Negeri 3 Palopo, selected via random sampling. Research instruments included a conceptual understanding test, a joyful learning questionnaire, an observation sheet, and a PBL-based Student Worksheet (LKPD). Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively using N-Gain, with hypothesis testing conducted via the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test for meaningful learning and a paired-samples t-test for joyful learning. Qualitative data from student observations and reflections were analyzed thematically. The results showed a significant increase in meaningful learning (N-Gain = 0.554, moderate category) and joyful learning (N-Gain = 0.576, moderate category). Observations and thematic analysis further indicated that mindful learning developed to a high degree (80.5%), as evidenced by metacognitive awareness, conceptual reflection, monitoring of understanding, and scientific argumentation during problem solving. These findings indicate that integrating PBL and PhET Simulation enhances conceptual understanding and fosters a meaningful, enjoyable, and reflective learning experience, thereby supporting the development of deep learning characteristics.</jats:p>
doi:10.20885/ijcer.vol10.iss2.art4.venue: IJCER (International Journal of Chemistry Education Research)

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11317441/v1.title: Stepwise Composition of Heuristic Components for Offline Strip Packing: A Controlled Study of Batch Reinforcement Learning
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11317441/v1.abstract: Learning to select heuristic components during construction offers flexibility, but its value beyond static diversity is unclear. We study batch reinforcement learning for stepwise composition in offline two-dimensional strip packing. A controller selects item-selection/placement-rule pairs in a shared skyline engine via tree-based fitted Q iteration and a dense reward aligned with height before postprocessing. Evaluation uses family holdout on 224 development instancesand 160 new same-generator test instances. On the 104-instance classical subset, adding the learned constructor to TWBF-18 and BBF-288 reduces mean gap by 0.305/0.163 points (paired 95% intervals exclude zero). Gains persist across four training seeds and the final set. The raw learned constructor trails the best train-selected fixed configuration. Development-set controls support state-dependent decisions; exploratory final-set controls do not confirm an advantage over anopen-loop stage policy. A 12-configuration train-selected static portfolio reacheslower mean gap at about one tenth of the augmented BBF-288 portfolio’s CPUcost. At its CPU budget, random-swap local search outperforms the constructorand both augmented portfolios. Capping native threads cuts measured inferenceCPU by 94.6%. The findings establish modest portfolio complementarity and itslimits against static portfolios and budgeted search.

doi:10.1201/9781042035762-106.title: Methodology Review: Intrusion Detection in Cybersecurity: A Study on Explainable Graphical Reinforcement Learning
doi:10.1201/9781042035762-106.abstract: This paper provides a structured methodological review of intrusion detection systems (IDS) in the field of cybersecurity, with particular attention to Explainable Graph-Structured Reinforcement Learning (XGRL). Instead of presenting experimental evaluations, the study concentrates on analyzing design principles and methodological frameworks that influence IDS effectiveness, scalability, and resilience to zero-day and polymorphic attacks. The progression from traditional signature-based systems and classical machine learning techniques to deep learning approaches is examined, leading to recent graph-based and reinforcement learning–driven solutions. The role of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in capturing relational and topological characteristics of network traffic is discussed alongside reinforcement learning methods that support adaptive and sequential security decision-making. Special emphasis is placed on explainability mechanisms that enhance model transparency, analyst confidence, and regulatory alignment. The review identifies methodological trade-offs involving detection accuracy, computational cost, scalability, and interpretability. Challenges related to real-time operation, encrypted traffic, and system complexity are also analyzed. The paper concludes by outlining future research opportunities, including efficient explainable architectures, continual learning strategies, and federated graph-based reinforcement learning frameworks for scalable and privacy-aware IDS implementations.

doi:10.14445/22315381/ijett-v74i9p120.title: NeuroEarlyAI: An Explainable Deep Learning Framework with EarlyDetectNet for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection and Classification using MRI Scans
doi:10.14445/22315381/ijett-v74i9p120.abstract: <jats:p>Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is an ageing and progressive neurodegenerative disease, and one of the most prevalent dementias that affects millions of patients worldwide, including millions of people in Europe, and is a public health priority. Early and right diagnosis is of paramount importance for early therapeutic intervention as well as retardation of the disease. The visual search for small changes in the brain is rather time-consuming and subjective. For comparison, we chose two traditional diagnostic procedures: clinical evaluation and manual MRI analysis, where the clinical evaluation is more appropriate for the intended user in healthcare centres. The automatic detection of AD using recent advancements in deep learning are yet to lack a few drawbacks, such as class imbalance, overfitting and generalisation issue on external datasets, low transparency in the decision-making of the deep learning model, which makes it difficult for clinical applications. To fill this gap, in this paper, we propose NeuroEarlyAI, an end-to-end learning framework with EarlyDetectNet, a new model for early and interpretable detection of AD from the structural MRI scans. The framework also consists of sophisticated pre-processing strategies (denoising, data augmentation and skull stripping) to enhance the quality and diversity of the data. EarlyDetectNet has an attention mechanism which highlights clinically relevant anatomical regions. As a contrast, the visual and feature-wise explanation modules are based on the Grad-CAM and SHAP techniques, respectively, which project the model prediction onto the visual and feature-wise explanations. Extensive tests are performed on two publicly available datasets: Alzheimer's MRI Dataset and OASIS-1 dataset. The proposed system demonstrated improvements over the state of the art on reaching accuracy for binary and multi-class classification in a cross-dataset setting, with 96.7% and 93.8% accuracy, respectively. These results show the promise of the applications and broader use of NeuroEarlyAI, a tool that could help to diagnose AD earlier for better patient care.</jats:p>
doi:10.14445/22315381/ijett-v74i9p120.venue: International Journal of Engineering Trends and Technology

doi:10.5256/f1000research.210886.r528475.title: Peer Review Report For: Design and expert validation of the OEPR learning model for sea turtle conservation educational tourism in Pacitan, Indonesia [version 1; peer review: 2 approved]
doi:10.5256/f1000research.210886.r528475.abstract: Background Sea turtle conservation sites can function as authentic learning environments, but educational visits frequently remain informal, knowledge-centred, and disconnected from sustained participation. This study developed and established the initial content validity of an experiential learning model for conservation-based educational tourism at Taman Beach, Pacitan, Indonesia. Methods An educational research-and-development study combined a preliminary needs assessment, document and literature analysis, field observation, stakeholder interviews, model design, and expert validation. Qualitative evidence was organised into six design needs. The resulting Orientation–Exploration–Practice–Reflection (OEPR) model was reviewed independently by experts in education, environmental education, and sea turtle conservation using five-point instruments covering syntax, social system, reaction principles, support system, model effects, model handbook, and facilitator guide. Scores were summarised as percentages, while written comments were analysed thematically and converted into revision decisions. Results The needs assessment identified fragmented visit sequences, mainly lecture-based interpretation, limited media, weak community coordination, no structured learner assessment, and no systematic follow-up. Eleven years of monitoring records contained 14,441 eggs and 11,892 hatchlings; annual hatching proportions varied substantially, reinforcing the need to connect education with authentic monitoring data. Expert validity was 98.33% for education, 96.94% for environmental education, and 98.24% for conservation. Reviewers retained the four-stage syntax but strengthened sense of place, inquiry, social–ecological analysis, authentic practice, standard operating procedures, safety, scaffolding, reflection, and action planning. Conclusions OEPR offers a coherent, place-based structure for transforming a conservation visit into an experiential and reflective learning cycle. The evidence supports content validity and readiness for feasibility and pilot testing, but not yet effectiveness. Subsequent studies should evaluate implementation fidelity, learner outcomes, and ecological safeguards with larger participant samples.

doi:10.3389/fpls.2026.1953590.title: Multi-source temporal fusion and multi-station learning for early warning of diamondback moth infestation in Brassica crops
doi:10.3389/fpls.2026.1953590.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Meteorological variability influences diamondback moth (DBM;
                      <jats:italic>Plutella xylostella</jats:italic>
                      ) infestation and the resulting damage to
                      <jats:italic>Brassica</jats:italic>
                      crops. Accurate multi-horizon forecasting requires models that preserve short-lived meteorological exposures while integrating thermal timing, spatial dependence, and recent infestation dynamics within a transparent framework.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Temporal–Geospatial Pest Network (TG-PestNet) forecasts the weekly percentage of inspected plants classified as DBM-infested 1 to 4 weeks ahead at four Guangdong stations, from origin-time information only. It preserves hourly exposure, encodes lookback weeks on a thermal-time axis, couples stations through a wind-informed graph, and protects infestation history in a gated anchor. Evaluation used 344 synchronized weeks, 66 later test origins, 13 history-only comparators, retraining ablations, matched-width controls, and input-matched generic encoders.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results and discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TG-PestNet achieved the lowest observed root-mean-square error, mean absolute error, and mean absolute percentage error in all 12 station–metric combinations, with mean reductions of 5.9%–13.0%. Year-ahead forecasts outperformed persistence in all four test years. Removing the history anchor increased error by 14.3% and remained significant after multiplicity correction, demonstrating its central contribution to forecast accuracy. Meteorological information provided complementary predictive value: its occlusion increased the error by 9.3%, and retraining without it increased the macro RMSE by 3.6%. TG-PestNet also substantially outperformed the two input-matched generic encoders, whose errors were approximately one quarter higher. These results establish TG-PestNet as an accurate, reproducible and auditable framework for multi-station pest forecasting, with component-level analyses that identify the dominant contribution of recent infestation history and characterize the predictive roles of high-resolution meteorology and structured spatial information.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fcomp.2026.1889642.title: A hybrid deep Kronecker and BN-eLU-AlexNet framework for early prediction of learner outcomes in e-learning platforms
doi:10.3389/fcomp.2026.1889642.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early prediction of learner outcomes in online learning environments can support timely academic intervention and learner support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study proposes DKBNE-AlexNet, a hybrid architecture combining a Deep Kronecker Network branch, a feature-token batch-normalized eLU AlexNet-inspired branch, gated residual fusion, and a wide linear residual path. Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, 24,153 enrolments from 22 module presentations and 22,234 learners were analyzed. Eighty-four predictors were constructed from learner characteristics, course design, and engagement during the first 25% of each presentation. The target was the weighted mean of tutor-marked and computer-marked assessment scores. Models were evaluated using five-fold cross-validation grouped by module presentation and repeated three times.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      DKBNE-AlexNet achieved an MAE of 11.424 (95% group-bootstrap CI 10.389-12.560), RMSE of 14.843, and
                      <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      of 0.117. Random Forest and LightGBM achieved slightly lower MAEs of 10.916 and 10.918, respectively, but the presentation-level difference between DKBNE-AlexNet and Random Forest was not statistically significant (Wilcoxon
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.388; Holm-adjusted
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 1.000). Distinct learning materials accessed and active learning days were among the strongest predictive contributors.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DKBNE-AlexNet provides a competitive and stable framework for early learner-outcome prediction, while strong tree-based models remain important baselines. The framework is best interpreted as an early-warning learning-analytics tool rather than a direct measure of teacher effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

It reaffirms the book’s goal of connecting affect studies to otherwise ways of knowing/feeling and being/doing in the world that can be found in many lineages and traditions.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261005.title: An Explanation of the Terms “Bildung” and “Erziehung” for the English-Speaking Reader
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261005.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The German terms “Bildung” and “Erziehung” are hardly translatable and are therefore occasionally used internationally as loanwords. This chapter explains their differential meanings in a brief manner to an international readership. In doing so, a distinction is made between formal scientific definitions and supplementary connotative meanings in the conversational language coined by different language cultures. Furthermore, broad and narrow sense definitions are being compared. Definitional features of “Bildung” and “Erziehung” as well as of the English term “education” which shape different variants of their concepts are explained and selected conceptualizations are suggested and justified for active and passive usage. Some of the considerations might be found useful to foster a thorough understanding and careful handling of the English term “education” as well.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10455330/v1.title: Design of an Adaptive Digital Intervention System for Preventing and Controlling Social Media Addiction in Adolescents: A Personalized Strategy Optimization Method Integrating NLP Sentiment Analysis and Reinforcement Learning
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10455330/v1.abstract: Adolescent social media addiction requires adaptive intervention strategies capable of addressing individual behavioral differences. This study proposes an adaptive digital intervention system that integrates natural language processing (NLP)-based emotion analysis with constraint-based reinforcement learning for personalized strategy optimization. The proposed framework extracts emotional tendencies from online text, constructs dynamic risk representations with a temporal decay mechanism to distinguish short-term variations from long-term risk accumulation, and employs a multi-dimensional reward function with prioritized experience replay to optimize intervention decisions according to individual risk states. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed system reduces overall risk by 32.1%, achieves a user acceptance rate of 82.4% (92.3% among low-risk users), decreases risk scores in high-risk individuals by 0.32, and reduces usage time by 20.1%. Compared with fixed-rule strategies and conventional reinforcement learning approaches, the proposed method achieves superior intervention performance. The results demonstrate that the integration of emotion-aware modeling and adaptive reinforcement learning can improve the effectiveness and personalization of digital intervention strategies. This work provides a computational framework for developing scalable and individualized approaches to behavioral risk management in digital environments.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10455330/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11312403/v1.title: Improving Fraud Detection Accuracy Through Data Preprocessing and Decision Tree Machine Learning
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11312403/v1.abstract: Digital payments have grown rapidly, and with them the scale and cost of financial fraud. Detection systems in use today still raise many false alarms, struggle with newly emerging fraud patterns, and are hampered by noisy, severely imbalanced transaction data. This paper investigates how far careful data preprocessing can improve the performance of a single, interpretable Decision Tree classifier. Using the public European credit-card dataset (284,807 transactions, of which fewer than 0.2% are fraudulent), the study applies duplicate removal, scaling, a stratified 70/30 split, feature selection, and SMOTE oversampling restricted to the training data. The trained tree (maximum depth 10) was evaluated on an untouched test set that keeps the original class distribution. It reached an accuracy of 0.9897, precision of 0.1152, recall of 0.7746, F1-score of 0.2005, and ROC-AUC of 0.8291, detecting 110 of 142 fraudulent transactions. The results show that a preprocessed Decision Tree can recover most fraud cases at low computational cost and with fully inspectable decision rules, although its low precision means the operating threshold must be tuned to the cost of false alarms.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11312403/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.59698/kognisi.v4i1.646.title: Game-Based Learning Model Assisted by Board Game Media to Improve Problem-Solving Skills of Elementary School Students
doi:10.59698/kognisi.v4i1.646.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to determine the effect of the game-based learning (GBL) model assisted by board game media on the mathematical problem-solving abilities of fifth-grade students at SD Al-Azhar 2 Bandar Lampung. This research is motivated by the still low mathematical problem-solving skills of students and the need for a more concrete, interactive, and enjoyable learning model. The method used is quantitative with a quasi-experimental approach through a pretest-posttest control group design. The research sample consisted of 55 students divided into an experimental class (28 students) who received the GBL model treatment assisted by board games, and a control class (27 students) who received a problem-based learning model treatment. Data were collected through an essay test on problem-solving skills that had been tested for validity, reliability, difficulty level, and discrimination power, and then analyzed using the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, the test Levene's homogeneity test and hypothesis testing with an Independent Sample T-Test were conducted. The analysis results showed that the data from both groups were normally distributed and homogeneous, while the hypothesis test obtained a t-value of -6.541 with a significance of <0.001 (<0.05), so H₀ was rejected and H₁ accepted. The average posttest score of the experimental class was 78.12, higher than the control class which scored 77.66. Therefore, it can be concluded that the GBL learning model assisted by board game media significantly affects the mathematical problem-solving skills of fifth-grade elementary school students, making it a viable alternative as an innovative mathematics learning model at the elementary level.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fbinf.2026.1745381.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research aimed to identify novel oxidative stress (OS)–related biomarkers and develop predictive models for the early detection of pediatric sepsis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five open-access datasets from the gene expression omnibus database were analyzed, which included peripheral whole blood samples from children with sepsis and healthy controls. Using bioinformatics approaches, we identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) associated with OS. We then combined weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and multiple machine learning algorithms (ML) to identify seven candidate genes, constructed a protein–protein interaction (PPI) network to screen six hub genes, and evaluated their correlations with the immune microenvironment. We subsequently evaluated the diagnostic performance of the hub genes using training datasets (GSE26440 and GSE26378) and validation datasets (GSE13904, GSE8121, and GSE9692). Moreover, molecular docking analysis revealed interactions between hub gene–encoded proteins and small-molecule compounds, which helps predict drug sensitivity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study identified 36 differentially expressed oxidative stress-related genes (OSRGs). Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses highlighted these genes’ roles in regulating inflammatory responses and reactive oxygen species metabolism. Seven candidate genes were identified using machine learning algorithms. Subsequently, through protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis, six hub genes, namely, GADD45A, HP, MAPK14, PGD, RETN, and S100A9, were identified as having significant diagnostic potential. Immune cell deconvolution analysis of peripheral blood transcriptomes suggested that hub genes related to oxidative stress may be linked to alterations in the composition of peripheral blood immune cells. The diagnostic performance of the six hub genes was validated with area under the curve (AUC) values between 0.908 and 0.982, showing their promising diagnostic performance. Additionally, molecular docking analysis suggested that small molecules Doxycycline, Ralimetinib mesylate, Tasquinimod might interact with the identified hub genes, which opens up new treatment options.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our research not only reveals potential diagnostic biomarkers of pediatric sepsis but also sets the stage for future studies. These studies aim to translate our findings into clinical practice, enabling earlier and more accurate diagnoses as well as targeted therapies to improve outcomes for children.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.56201/ijcsmt.vol.11.no9.2025.pg22.title: A Survey of Object Detection and Classification in Video Using Deep Learning Approaches
doi:10.56201/ijcsmt.vol.11.no9.2025.pg22.abstract:
<jats:p>Object detection and classification in videos has emerged as a core challenge in computer vision,
with applications spanning autonomous driving, surveillance, healthcare, robotics, and human–
computer interaction. Unlike still-image object detection, video-based detection requires handling
additional complexities such as temporal coherence, motion blur, occlusion, and real-time
constraints. Traditional approaches relying on handcrafted features and background subtraction
have given way to deep learning-based methods, particularly convolutional neural networks
(CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), transformers, and one-stage detectors such as the You
Only Look Once (YOLO) family. This paper provides a comprehensive review of object detection
in videos, surveying the evolution of methods from early handcrafted approaches to recent deep
architectures. We examine popular models, datasets, and benchmarks, with an emphasis on
accuracy–speed trade-offs and the unique challenges of real-world deployment. A comparative
analysis of state-of-the-art methods highlights trends and gaps, including the struggle with small
object detection, domain adaptation, and efficient training on large-scale datasets. Finally, we
outline promising future directions such as transformer-based detection, self-supervised learning,
multimodal video understanding, and edge-device optimization. This survey aims to serve as both
an introductory resource and a roadmap for advancing video-based object detection research.</jats:p>
doi:10.56201/ijcsmt.vol.11.no9.2025.pg22.venue: International Journal of Computer Science and Mathematical Theory

doi:10.1002/jso.70422.title: Machine Learning‐Based Recurrence and Survival Prediction in a Large Institutional Upper Extremity Soft Tissue Sarcoma Cohort
doi:10.1002/jso.70422.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Upper extremity soft tissue sarcomas (UE STS) present unique management challenges; existing prognostic nomograms were developed from mixed anatomic cohorts. This study develops anatomically specific machine learning (ML) models to predict UE‐STS outcomes and benchmarks them against established tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Time‐to‐event models for local recurrence (LR), distant metastasis (DM), and overall survival (OS) were developed in 188 patients treated at a single sarcoma center, treating death as a competing risk. Five survival algorithms were compared within a nested cross‐validation framework. Discrimination was benchmarked against the Sarculator, PERSARC, and MSKCC nomograms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Five‐year event rates were 24% (LR), 20% (DM), and 13% (death) over a median follow‐up of 3.9 years. Best‐performing models achieved competing‐risks concordance indices of 0.79 (LR), 0.67 (DM), and 0.75 (OS). Parsimonious models performed comparably. Discrimination was similar to Sarculator and PERSARC and higher than the MSKCC nomogram for LR (C‐index 0.90 vs. 0.68). Predicted‐risk groups separated clearly on cumulative‐incidence and survival curves (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results demonstrate the feasibility and potential value of anatomy‐specific, time‐to‐event risk modeling in UE STS, achieving discrimination comparable to established nomograms despite a smaller cohort. Multicenter cohorts and multidimensional data may strengthen future efforts. External validation is warranted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261003.title: Education Meets Architecture: An Interdisciplinary Approach
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261003.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter outlines the interplay between education and learning environments as a central requirement for a sustainable design of school buildings and future-oriented pedagogy. It shows the opportunities that lie in this interplay and how the learning environment can support and promote an inclusive 21st century education. Four projects of the Montag Stiftung Jugend und Gesellschaft are used to illustrate innovative solutions in the field of educational architecture that help schools in Germany respond to current challenges.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The Montag Stiftung Jugend und Gesellschaft (Montag Foundation for Youth and Society) is an independent non-profit foundation belonging to the Montag Foundations group in Bonn. Its projects are committed to creating an everyday world with equal opportunities that offers children and young people the best possible development and educational opportunities. For nearly 20 years, the Montag Stiftung Jugend und Gesellschaft has been advocating for a new mindset and new practices in school design in Germany. Working together with experts from education, architecture, planning and administration, it is developing fundamentals, guidelines and concepts – and is striving to implement them in practice. The aim is to create sustainable school buildings that support high-quality and future orientated education for all.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261011.title: Organizational Strategies for Learning Space Innovation: A Case Study From Oregon Tech, United States
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261011.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Transitioning from traditional lecture-based classrooms to contemporary active-learning environments presents significant challenges for educational institutions worldwide. Although active learning has gained widespread recognition over recent decades for its positive effects on student engagement and achievement, successful implementation requires more than simply introducing new spaces and technologies. Emerging research underscores that the effective integration and expansion of active-learning environments depend on a multifaceted set of conditions. These include strong institutional leadership and advocacy, inclusive stakeholder collaboration, sustainable financial strategies, deliberate spatial and pedagogical design, cultural adaptation, and alignment with broader institutional missions and strategic priorities.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This is the story of how Oregon Tech, a polytechnic university located in the western United States, strategically leveraged these organizational elements—while fostering collaboration between academia and industry—to design a cutting-edge facility with innovative learning spaces that advance its educational mission. The project’s success not only enhanced student learning but also inspired further investment in the ongoing transformation of the campus.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fbinf.2026.1925964.title: Machine learning-based identification of CXCL13 and CXCL10 as key biomarkers in rheumatoid arthritis
doi:10.3389/fbinf.2026.1925964.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is one of the autoimmune diseases that involve joint damage and synovial membrane inflammation. There have been many attempts to examine the utility of biomarkers in the diagnosis of RA, but there is no clinically accepted biomarker for the diagnosis of RA due to its heterogeneity. Thus, in this study, we tried to find RA biomarkers using machine learning and bioinformatics approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Three corresponding gene expression datasets (GSE55457, GSE12021, and GSE77298) were downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Batch effect correction was carried out using the
                      <jats:italic>ComBat</jats:italic>
                      function of the
                      <jats:italic>sva</jats:italic>
                      package in R. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) compared to controls were identified using
                      <jats:italic>limma</jats:italic>
                      . To identify the biological functions and pathways of DEGs, Gene Ontology, KEGG, and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) were conducted. The protein–protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed in Cytoscape using the STRING database. Genes identified through PPI analysis and further filtered by LASSO and SVM-RFE regressions were considered as diagnostic biomarkers. Additional analysis of hub genes was conducted using the GSE89408 dataset. CIBERSORTx was used to evaluate the immune cell infiltration in RA.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 440 DEGs were selected, including 197 downregulated and 243 upregulated genes. The DEGs were involved in biological processes and pathways associated with the immune system and were suggested by functional enrichment analysis. GSEA enriched in cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction, hematopoietic cell lineage, primary immunodeficiency, and RA pathways. The hub genes
                      <jats:italic>CXCL13</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic>CXCL10</jats:italic>
                      were chosen with the help of a machine learning algorithm. An external independent validation of the hub genes was conducted. In addition, ROC analysis showed a good diagnostic value of the two genes. The analysis of immune cell infiltration showed
                      <jats:italic>CXCL13</jats:italic>
                      was associated with multiple immune-cell populations, including plasma cells, T-cell subsets, and M1 macrophages, whereas
                      <jats:italic>CXCL10</jats:italic>
                      showed significant associations with M1 macrophages, plasma cells, and selected T-cell subsets. Correlation analysis showed a high correlation between chemokines CXCL13 and CXCL10 and many infiltrated immune cells.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The present study indicates the potential usefulness of
                      <jats:italic>CXCL13</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic>CXCL10</jats:italic>
                      genes as diagnostic biomarkers in RA. Synovial inflammation in RA is associated with the coordinated action of many genes involved in the recruitment of various immune cells to the inflammatory site. Although the term chemokines were used to designate them, these genes are the genes encoding molecules associated with the migration of particular immune cell types, and CXCR5 and CXCR3 may be considered the potential targets for future research.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21275/sr26827162518.title: An Integrated MLOps Framework for Developing, Tracking, and Deploying Ensemble Learning Models for Lower Limb Motion Classification
doi:10.21275/sr26827162518.abstract: Wearable inertial sensing has become an effective approach for lower limb motion classification, yet many existing studies primarily emphasize classification accuracy while providing limited support for reproducible model development, experiment tracking, and deployment. This paper presents a reproducible Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) framework for lower limb motion classification using biomechanically meaningful lower-limb joint-angle features obtained from wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) measurements. The framework processes hip, knee, and ankle joint-angle signals, performs sliding-window feature extraction using statistical, derivative based, and frequency-domain descriptors, and trains multiple supervised machine learning models, including XGBoost, Extra Trees, CatBoost, Ridge Classifier, and Histogram Gradient Boosting. The complete machine learning lifecycle is integrated using Git for version control, MLflow for experiment tracking, Docker for reproducible containerized deployment, and Streamlit for interactive inference and visualization. The framework was evaluated using Xsens Awinda data collected from five subjects performing six lower limb activities, namely Walking, Sitting, Standing, Stairs, SlopeUp, and SlopeDown, with 1,617 feature windows used for the reported test evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that the Extra Trees classifier achieved the highest performance, with an accuracy of 99.59 percent and a Macro F1-score of 0.9939, outperforming the other evaluated machine learning models. The proposed framework enables reproducible model training, artifact management, deployment, and interactive inference within a unified workflow while improving the interpretability of activity recognition through joint angle-based biomechanical feature representation. The proposed MLOps framework provides a practical and scalable solution for developing reproducible wearable sensing applications and offers a foundation for future real-time, multimodal, and edge deployable lower limb motion analysis systems.

doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261012.title: Forward Thinking: Setting an Agenda for Collaboration
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261012.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter supports a holistic and nuanced approach to understanding school learning environments, arguing that the provision of transformational, innovative learning spaces requires the synchronization of research, policy, practice, design and implementation elements.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Acknowledging that our current approaches to education, both pedagogically and in physical form, developed from a very focused and successful response to industrial era demands, this chapter highlights the emerging global challenges society now faces and how the traditional education forms mostly fail to respond to the pace, scale and complexity of societal change. It recognizes the heritage and value of traditional pedagogical constructs and teaching spaces, while arguing that these must be incorporated within far more sophisticated, trans-disciplinary enabled, learning landscapes to meet the needs of contemporary teaching and learning.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In closing all the authors’ contributions to this book, 10 key lessons are advanced for setting the path to a better education framework and to delivering transformational learning landscapes that will be successful, impactful and sustainable.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261012.title: A Dialogical Adventure in Foreign Language Education: ABCs of Cultural Understanding and Communication
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261012.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The debates on educational responses to globalization and immigration are significant and timely, addressing critical challenges faced by diverse societies in an increasingly globalized world. These discussions explore how education systems can adapt to shifting demographics, cultural integration, and the demands of a globalized economy. This chapter investigates the effectiveness of a pedagogical approach called the ABCs of Cultural Understanding and Communication in fostering intercultural awareness among foreign language learners. The chapter examines the ABCs approach, which utilizes autobiographies, biographies, and cross-cultural analysis to encourage learners to reflect on their own lives and develop empathy for others. The author conducted a case study involving Irish and German students learning each other’s languages through an online platform, analyzing how the ABCs approach influenced their perceptions of themselves and others. The research found that the ABCs approach can be effective in promoting cultural awareness, challenging stereotypes, and enhancing communication skills within a cross-cultural exchange, ultimately contributing to the development of global citizenship in students. This chapter is based on a doctoral dissertation. Notably, in 2017 Mary Masterton developed a holistic intercultural communication competence approach out of this study, expanding its implications for fostering empathy, understanding, and collaboration in diverse settings. Through structured activities and reflective practices, learners gained the ability to critically examine the role of culture in shaping thought processes and behaviors. This introspection and engagement with diverse perspectives fostered a deeper appreciation for cultural diversity, promoting empathy and intercultural understanding among participants. The study emphasizes the transformative power of guided reflection and dialog in breaking down cultural barriers and enhancing collaborative relationships in global contexts.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-331-020261010.title: Teaching and Learning in Higher Education With Implications for Student Veterans
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-331-020261010.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter explores the unique challenges faced by veterans as they transition from military service to higher education. The authors discuss the psychological, social, and academic barriers encountered, such as professional uncertainty, social isolation, and adapting from a regimented military environment to the less structured civilian academic world. Using personal narratives and theoretical frameworks like Schlossberg’s Transition Theory, the chapter highlights the difficulties veterans experience, including managing post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), financial constraints, and the cultural disconnect in classrooms. The authors advocate for institutional support systems tailored to veterans, including counseling, peer networks, and faculty engagement, to facilitate smoother transitions. By addressing these challenges, the chapter provides actionable recommendations to enhance the academic success and well-being of student veterans as they navigate higher education.</jats:p>

doi:10.51574/kognitif.v6i4.5916.title: Analysis of Students' Mathematical Thinking Skills in Trigonometry Learning through a Digital Worksheet Assisted by Virtual Reality
doi:10.51574/kognitif.v6i4.5916.abstract: <jats:p>Mathematical thinking skills are skills that students need to master, particularly in trigonometry. This study aims to analyze and describe students’ mathematical thinking skills in trigonometry learning through Digital Worksheet assisted by Virtual Reality. The method used was qualitative descriptive. The research subjects consisted of 32 tenth-grade students at SMA N 1 Belitang. The research procedure consisted of three stages: preparation, implementation, and the final stage. Data were collected through Digital Worksheet assisted by Virtual Reality, written tests, and interviews. Data analysis was conducted in three stages: data reduction, grouping the data based on four indicators of mathematical thinking skills, and presenting the data based on the Digital Worksheet assisted by Virtual Reality, written tests, and interviews, followed by drawing conclusions. The results of using a Digital Worksheet assisted by Virtual Reality in the specializing activity showed that students were able to identify and explain known and requested information. In the generalizing activity, students were able to transform contextual situations into right triangles. In the conjecturing activity, students were able to make conjectures about the appropriate trigonometric ratios to solve problems. In the convincing activity, students were able to prove their conjectures through calculations and draw conclusions. Based on the written test results and interviews, 14 students with very good skills were able to accurately meet all four indicators of mathematical thinking, 17 students with good skills were able to meet all four indicators although still some errors caused by rushing and a lack of attention to detail, and 1 student with fairly good skills was better able to demonstrate the specializing indicator but still experienced difficulties with the generalizing, conjecturing, and convincing indicators. The results of this study indicate that Digital Worksheet assisted by Virtual Reality in trigonometry learning to support students’ mathematical thinking skills.</jats:p>
doi:10.51574/kognitif.v6i4.5916.venue: Kognitif: Jurnal Riset HOTS Pendidikan Matematika

doi:10.3389/fmolb.2026.1958127.title: Explainable machine learning integrating CT-derived intratumoral heterogeneity for histological subtype prediction in pure ground-glass lung adenocarcinoma: multicenter validation and transcriptomic characterization
doi:10.3389/fmolb.2026.1958127.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Preoperative differentiation of lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma from other histological subtypes in lung adenocarcinoma presenting as pure ground-glass nodules remains challenging. We evaluated whether a CT-derived intratumoral heterogeneity score provides complementary predictive and biological information beyond routine clinical and CT features.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective multicenter study included 533 patients, divided into a training cohort (n = 373) and a held-out validation cohort (n = 160). Twelve supervised algorithms were compared exclusively within the training cohort using stratified five-fold cross-validation and grid-search optimization; predictors, hyperparameters, and the decision threshold were locked before the held-out cohort was evaluated once. Incremental value of the ITH score and leave-one-center-out internal–external validation were additionally assessed. Segmentation reproducibility was evaluated in 100 lesions. An independent radiogenomic cohort of 43 pathological Tis/T1 lung adenocarcinomas was analyzed by differential-expression and Hallmark gene-set enrichment analyses after median ITH-score stratification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>XGBoost achieved the highest training-set cross-validation AUC (0.908 ± 0.021) and was selected before held-out evaluation. In the validation cohort, the AUC was 0.919 (95% CI, 0.870–0.968), with accuracy 0.850, precision 0.857, sensitivity 0.545, specificity 0.966, and Brier score 0.098. Adding the ITH score to clinical and CT features increased AUC from 0.867 to 0.919 (ΔAUC = 0.052; DeLong P = 0.012), increased PR-AUC from 0.731 to 0.824, and reduced Brier score from 0.126 to 0.098. Leave-one-center-out AUCs ranged from 0.824 to 0.882. The ITH score showed good-to-excellent repeat-segmentation reproducibility. In the radiogenomic cohort, a high ITH score was associated with coordinated enrichment of G2M checkpoint (NES = 1.86, FDR &lt;0.001), E2F targets (NES = 1.86, FDR &lt;0.001), and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (NES = 1.55, FDR = 0.001).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CT-derived ITH provided incremental information for histological subtype prediction and was associated with proliferation-, cell-cycle-, and EMT-related transcriptional programs. The moderate sensitivity at the prespecified operating point and the retrospective design warrant prospective external validation before clinical implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1017/jme.2026.10286.title: The Legal Epidemiology Learning Cohort: Reflections and Spotlights After a Decade of Practice-Based Legal Epidemiology Training
doi:10.1017/jme.2026.10286.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    For years, in response to demand from the field, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Office of Public Health Law Services (OPHLS) has partnered with outside organizations, including Temple University’s Center for Public Health Law Research and ChangeLab Solutions, to operate the Legal Epidemiology Learning Cohort (Learning Cohort). This year-long opportunity offers training and mentorship to health department practitioners and others from public health-adjacent settings on the practical steps of legal epidemiology, which includes collecting, mapping, and evaluating legal texts. Participants work in transdisciplinary teams to design and carry out the
                    <jats:italic>foundational</jats:italic>
                    work for completing projects on research questions relevant to local public health challenges. Throughout 2023, ChangeLab Solutions and OPHLS coordinated training sessions and provided technical assistance to seven Learning Cohort teams across the country. This paper provides an overview of the Learning Cohort’s background, approach, and lessons learned. It also spotlights three recent Learning Cohort teams who describe the projects they completed and the benefits and challenges they found in learning foundational legal epidemiology methods for their public health work. Featured projects demonstrate how legal epidemiology can be used to examine topics like water safety, Tribal access to public health data, and the intersection of state and local law.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1201/9781042035762-92.title: Deep Learning Approaches for Automated Depression Detection: A Comprehensive Review
doi:10.1201/9781042035762-92.abstract: This paper demonstrates an EEG-based machine learning system of automated depression detection using the publicly available dataset of BRMH EEG data. The information is in the form of multi-channel power spectral density and coherence of different psychiatric disorders, mood disorders, anxiety, schizophrenia, and healthy controls. Numerous preprocessing and feature standardization and Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) were used to deal with missing data and the issue of class imbalance. Three classifiers were developed and tested K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Random Forest (RF); they were trained and tested on ten-fold stratified cross-validations using weighted accuracy, precision, recall and F1-scores. Of these, the Random Forest model performed best of all with an average accuracy of 92.6 with and without showing its ability to predict nonlinear EEG features relationship. KNN attained moderate outcomes, and SVM failed because of the dimension of data. The results point to the practicability of EEG biomarkers and ensemble learning in the exact and non- invasive detection of depression that would be used in the future in the development of deep learning and multimodal fusion to support clinical decisions.
