doi:10.38124/ijisrt/26sep1379.title: Internal Quality Assurance Mechanisms for Teaching and Learning, Research, and Community Engagement in Higher Education: A Critical Examination
doi:10.38124/ijisrt/26sep1379.abstract: <jats:p>This paper critically examines the internal quality assurance (IQA) mechanisms that higher education institutions use to govern teaching and learning, research, and community engagement. Drawing on a documentary analysis of peerreviewed scholarly literature, it identifies and evaluates key IQA instruments: student evaluation of teaching, peer observation of teaching, programme and departmental reviews, performance appraisals, internal quality assurance cells, research ethics committees, research output assessments, and community partnership frameworks. The analysis reveals a persistent tension between the developmental and accountability-oriented functions of IQA. Teaching-focused instruments are frequently co-opted for administrative surveillance rather than pedagogical improvement; research quality assurance remains heavily output-driven, with limited attention to process integrity; and community engagement, though increasingly recognised as a core mission, lacks robust internal metrics for assessing impact and reciprocity. The paper argues for an integrated, culture-based approach to IQA that aligns quality mechanisms with institutional mission, fosters professional trust, and positions internal quality assurance as a catalyst for transformation rather than mere compliance. Recommendations include strengthening formative feedback loops, decoupling evaluative metrics from punitive administrative decisions, and developing context-sensitive indicators for community engagement.</jats:p>
doi:10.38124/ijisrt/26sep1379.venue: International Journal of Innovative Science and Research Technology

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-1.title: Foreign Language Learning
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-1.abstract:
<jats:p>Foreign Language Learning: The Role of Language, Culture, and Literacy sheds light on the intricate and dynamic interplay between language learning, cultural understanding, and literacy development. Written by distinguished international contributors, this book offers a comprehensive exploration of key topics and innovative practices in foreign language education. Split into three sections, the intersectionality of language, culture, and literacy is brought to light in a holistic manner.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In the language section, the chapters delve into areas such as language awareness, technology-enhanced teaching and assessment as well as plurilingual testing. The culture section addresses the topics of identity, intercultural collaborative learning and autobiographical methods for fostering cultural understanding. Finally, in the literacy section, the contributors discuss the development of reading skills, digital literacies and feedback literacies. Altogether, the book combines theoretical reflections, empirical insights, innovative teaching practices and emerging technologies to create engaging and effective learning environments and will be useful to academics and practitioners alike.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This publication honors the intellectual curiosity and transformative pedagogy of Professor Dr. Claudia Finkbeiner as well as the enduring contributions she has made to the field. It serves as a valuable resource for educators, researchers, and language enthusiasts, providing a holistic understanding of foreign language education in a globalized world.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261009.title: Promoting Plurilingual and Intercultural Knowledge Using Educational Escape Rooms in French Lessons: An Intervention Study on the Use of Digital Learning Environments
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261009.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Plurilingual approaches are officially part of the curriculum for foreign languages and are also required by the Council of Europe. Although these official guidelines do exist, they are often not implemented by foreign language teachers. This also applies to digital tools: even though digital tools are quite common now, most of them do not integrate plurilingual approaches but instead teach languages through a monolingual lens, i.e. one other language only. This chapter focuses on a case study of educational escape games located in French cities, analyzing the digital aspects, the plurilingual approaches and the enjoyability (fun factor) regarding students’ progress in French. Moreover, it examines whether they themselves find the plurilingual approaches helpful during their learning process. The digital educational escape games are immersive and do not only contain plurilingual approaches but also intercultural aspects. The students in the case study that took place in Germany gave their feedback via a multiple-choice questionnaire in a pre-post design. The survey included 77 language learners aged between 13 and 17 in five different learning groups. The results show a positive correlation between the use of the escape rooms and the perception of the plurilingual tasks as well as between the use of the escape rooms and the perception of intercultural and immersive learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.15832/ankutbd.1883925.title: Design and Control of an Intelligent Mobile Gardening Robot Supported by Deep Learning-Based Image Processing
doi:10.15832/ankutbd.1883925.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">In this study, the design and control of a mobile gardening robot based on image processing and artificial intelligence were implemented. The system, running on Raspberry Pi 4B, can distinguish different plant species and weeds using a YOLOv5-based object detection and classification model; it performs tasks such as cutting weeds, watering useful plants, and moving autonomously while avoiding obstacles. Experiments conducted in a pot environment demonstrated that the robot can successfully perform plant detection, classification, and maintenance functions. With these features, the developed robot offers a low-cost and sustainable solution for small and medium-scale agricultural businesses. The mobile gardening robot designed within the scope of the study was experimentally tested for image processing-based plant recognition, autonomous plant orientation, plant cutting, and watering operations for different scenarios. When the results obtained were examined, it was seen that the developed deep learning-based plant detection model achieved an 82% mAP@50 success rate, while the plant classification model achieved a 92.9% mAP@50 success rate.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.2015631.title: Editorial: Learning on the edge: EdTech in conflict-affected and fragile regions
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.2015631.abstract: The aim of this special issue is to explore how students and educators sustain learning in the face of crisis, and how educational technology (EdTech) can support, enable, or, at times, distract from that process. We take a deliberately broad view of EdTech. Bozkurt et al. (2026) define EdTech as "a field of inquiry and practice, encompasses the research, understanding, design, orchestration, and evaluation of entangled human-technological systems-spanning analog, digital, organizational, social, and agentic dimensions-through which learning and meaning making are enabled, mediated, supported, and transformed" (p. 192). In this framing, EdTech is not reducible to devices or platforms; it also encompasses the human systems, tools, and techniques through which people acquire skills, make meaning, and adapt to changing circumstances.Through our work with colleagues and students around the world, we have become acutely aware of how armed conflicts, climate change, environmental disasters, health crises, and political upheaval can abruptly disrupt access to formal and non-formal education. Re-reading the accepted papers in this special issue while writing this editorial was, at times, an emotional experience. What emerges repeatedly is the creativity, endurance, and commitment of students and educators, and the importance of allowing participants' voices to resonate through the studies themselves. Collectively, the contributions show that continuing one's education within conflict-affected and fragile regions can be an act of resilience and hope, as well as a means of sustaining cultural and linguistic identity and psychological wellbeing. As George et al. (2026) write, being a student in an armed conflict requires intention and dedication. Although online learning in crisis conditions can become an additional source of stress, it is also a critical source of educational continuity (Khasawneh, 2026).The ten papers in this issue span a diverse range of geographic contexts, with two studies each conducted in Pakistan and the Philippines, and one study each from Lebanon, Colombia, Algeria, Somalia, Sudan and Palestine. Methodologically, the collection is equally varied, drawing on qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods approaches, including experimental, survey-based, case study, interview, ethnographic, phenomenological, and thematic-analysis designs. Sample sizes range from five to 3,430 participants, reflecting both the breadth of the questions posed and the very different conditions under which the studies were undertaken.Across the ten papers, five directly address how students and instructors cope with, adapt to, and continue educational activity during armed conflict in Sudan, Colombia, Gaza, and Lebanon. Four offer insights into education for disaster preparation and management in Pakistan, Algeria, and the Philippines. The collection also includes a sustained reflection on educational leadership during the COVID-19 crisis in 2020 and the forced pivot to remote learning in Pakistan, alongside a study of how young people can be better supported to find employment amid limited formal employment services in Somalia. Across these different contexts, a consistent message emerges: locally grounded solutions are essential in responding to deeply contextual and affective challenges, chiming with previous research (e.g., Park, Freeman & Middleton, 2019;Smith et al., 2024).Many contributors to this special issue highlight the relative scarcity of research conducted in regions that are remote, fragile, and/or experiencing crisis. Much of the existing evidence base has been generated within comparatively stable economic, environmental, and political settings. The closer we attend to each local context, the more apparent it becomes that assumptions embedded in Western, Global North models and frameworks may be inappropriate, or at best only partially useful, when transferred elsewhere. One of the contributors, Adnan ( 2026), writes about "the systematic misalignment of dominant global EdTech paradigms with the conditions of education systems in the Global South [in which there is] exclusion, staggering inequality, inadvertent harm, and the elevation of learning models that put machines and profit before people" (p. 9). The implication running through this collection is clear: responses must be grounded in geographic, environmental, cultural, linguistic, political, and socio-economic realities rather than imposed independently of them.Recurring themes across the collection include the need for leadership models tailored to local contexts, cultural competence in EdTech implementation, and close attention to structural inequality. The studies identify systemic inequities, power outages, and inadequate infrastructure, including unreliable access to the Internet, hardware, software and learning resources. In Gaza, the destruction of universities and loss of faculty also require students to adapt to volunteer faculty from outside the immediate context and to diverse teaching approaches (Khasawneh, 2026). These examples underline a central point: access to technology alone is insufficient unless the wider educational, institutional, and social conditions required for meaningful participation are also sustained.Context is not simply background in these studies; it actively shapes what education, technology, and resilience can mean in practice. Across the papers, community influences the uptake of technology, the use of media, and the functioning of institutions such as schools. Physical space also remains significant, even when EdTech is central to educational continuity. Such spaces are symbolic as well as functional, carrying meanings connected to identity and belonging (Mateus, 2026). A school that once represented social encounter, continuity, and safety can become a site of danger during armed conflict. War can undermine educators' and learners' mental health and contribute to academic underachievement and financial stress (Kharroubi, 2026). Displacement can further intensify problems of access, affordability, and poor living and study conditions. The significance of physical space therefore cannot be overstated; a participant in Kharroubi's (2026) study commented that a return to the classroom would provide a sense of normalcy.Recent tragedy in Nepal has again drawn attention to the speed and scale of risks associated with climate change. Alongside ongoing armed conflicts and wider global economic and political uncertainty, these conditions raise further concerns about displacement, migration, and associated violence. Educational institutions and services therefore need to plan proactively for emergency response, flexible and adaptable learning environments, crisis-assistance programmes, and mental-health support (Kharroubi, 2026). Khasawneh (2026) recommends creating supportive, equitable, and forgiving environments. Novel approaches to sustaining engagement through gamification (Jan et al., 2026) and possibly GenAI (Othman, et al., 2026), the integration of media and educational systems (Touati, 2026), enhanced leadership (Jemsy, 2026), and careful instructional design (Mutya, 2026) can all contribute to disaster preparedness and educational continuity in societies experiencing crisis or its aftermath.Taken together, the papers in this special issue resist the idea that EdTech itself produces resilience. Rather, its value depends on how technologies are embedded within relationships, institutions, communities, physical spaces, and locally meaningful practices. The central lesson is therefore not the need for a universal technological solution to crisis, but for educational responses that are flexible, humane, contextually grounded, and capable of sustaining learning when familiar systems are disrupted.

doi:10.3726/b23712.title: L'impatto del MALL (Mobile Assisted Language Learning) nell'insegnamento delle lingue straniere
doi:10.3726/b23712.abstract: <jats:p>Negli ultimi anni la pervasività delle tecnologie mobili ha ridefinito pratiche comunicative e processi di apprendimento, richiedendo una revisione critica dei modelli didattici tradizionali. Il presente volume offre un’analisi approfondita del Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL), esaminandone le potenzialità nei contesti di istruzione superiore. Attraverso un solido quadro teorico e l’esplorazione delle metodologie emergenti, il testo evidenzia come i dispositivi mobili favoriscano il coinvolgimento, la personalizzazione e l’autonomia dell’apprendente. Particolare attenzione è dedicata alle implicazioni pedagogiche della gamification e alle sfide connesse alla sua applicazione. Il volume si propone come strumento rigoroso per docenti, ricercatori e formatori impegnati nello studio dell’innovazione digitale nella didattica linguistica.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261009.title: From Disciplines to Ecosystems: Reimagining Learning Through Transdisciplinary Practice
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-896-020261009.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter explores how transdisciplinary learning reshapes the learner experience through the case of Learnlife in Barcelona. It examines how young people engage with real-world, purpose-driven challenges through pathways that transcend disciplinary boundaries and how such learning demands environments that function as ecosystems rather than classrooms. Drawing from earlier research on vision-led educational change (Harris, 2018) and the Learnlife Learning Paradigm, this chapter argues that space, culture and pedagogy must be deliberately integrated to support transdisciplinary practice.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Transdisciplinarity at Learnlife is not merely a fusion of subjects; it represents an ecological way of thinking and doing, where disciplines become resources and meaning is co-constructed through authentic work. Learners begin by developing foundations within domains before navigating self-chosen pathways and synthesising multiple knowledge areas into projects that hold personal and societal relevance.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This chapter demonstrates that learning environments – acoustic conditions, spatial rhythms, transparency, access to professional-grade studios and the presence of multi-modal zones – are not ancillary but central to transdisciplinary capability. The Learnlife hubs in Barcelona illustrate how environments designed as ecosystems foster agency, creativity, wellbeing and collaborative knowledge-building. These insights offer a potential model for how schools might transition from industrial-era structures toward human-centred, adaptive environments suited to an increasingly complex global landscape.</jats:p>

doi:10.1215/9781478062868-001.title: Grappling with a “Mental Health Crisis”
doi:10.1215/9781478062868-001.abstract: <jats:p>The introduction presents the book’s central questions about how to understand and address a so-called mental health crisis that is the product of systemic conditions. It introduces a theory of grappling as a practice of holding contradictions and explores the use of keywords and writing practice as affective methods. It discusses the book’s critical lineages, including the central influence of Black feminisms.</jats:p>

doi:10.2118/234493-ms.title: Enhancing Lithological Interpretation: An Integrated Machine Learning Approach for Automated Log Classification in Volcanic Geothermal Reservoirs, Japan
doi:10.2118/234493-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Japan's volcanic geothermal reservoirs present significant subsurface characterization challenges due to complex lithological heterogeneity, extensive faulting, and fracture-controlled permeability. Conventional lithological evaluation often relies on adequate wireline and logging-while-drilling (LWD) measurements, drilling cuttings and expert borehole image interpretation. However, the logging variety is often limited, and drilling cuttings recovery is frequently poor or absent within productive geothermal feed zones because of severe mud losses. As a result, critical information is unavailable where accurate reservoir characterization is most needed.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>This study presents an integrated machine learning workflow for automated lithofacies classification using borehole image data. The methodology combines unsupervised and supervised learning within a two-stage framework. In the first stage, key geological attributes, including high-frequency resistivity, boundary dip trend, and fracture density, are extracted from borehole images and used as inputs to an Index Probabilized Self-Organized Mapping (IPSOM) workflow (Leon et al., 2015). The resulting clusters are calibrated using geological interpretation and drilling cuttings information to establish lithofacies classes. In the second stage, these calibrated lithofacies labels are used to train a supervised deep learning model that directly predicts lithofacies from borehole images.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In this study, the IPSOM workflow successfully differentiated major volcanic lithofacies, including fractured andesite tuff and highly fractured dacite tuff intervals. The supervised model achieved a validation F1 score of 79%, demonstrating its ability to learn lithofacies characteristics from borehole image data. Application to blind test intervals showed promising performance in identifying highly fractured dacite tuff associated with permeable fluid-flow pathways. By integrating geological expertise with machine learning, the workflow reduced interpretation time from approximately one month to 4–6 hours while maintaining geological consistency. The methodology provides a scalable framework for rapid lithofacies characterization and supports more efficient geothermal reservoir evaluation and development.</jats:p>

doi:10.15832/ankutbd.1837705.title: A Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Framework for Paddy Leaf Disease Detection Using an Enhanced Pretrained Novel EfficientNet-Lite4 Model
doi:10.15832/ankutbd.1837705.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">The correct and prompt detection of leaf diseases in paddy crops remains essential for protecting agricultural output and yield stability and reducing major losses that occur during severe disease outbreaks. The widespread use of conventional centralized machine learning techniques becomes impractical for real-world agricultural applications, as their effectiveness diminishes under three main conditions: data privacy limitations, delayed transmission of information, along with reduced performance accuracy from non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data properties across different agro-climatic regions. This research develops a decentralized diagnostic system which combines Federated Learning with an Enhanced Pretrained Novel EfficientNet-Lite4 model designed for paddy leaf disease classification. The Paddy Doctor dataset served as training material for the system which contained 16,225 RGB images that classified 12 disease types alongside healthy categories. The proposed model reached 98.7% classification accuracy and 98.5% precision and 98.6% F1-score while maintaining a final loss of 0.21 after 100 communication rounds. The system underwent field testing which demonstrated its ability to generate accurate diagnostic results in real time in various working conditions. The study demonstrates how privacy preserving AI-based paddy disease management works in practice and recommends local agricultural institutions to build decentralized learning systems. The suggested system will give farmers direct access to field level decision support and facilitate the creation of sustainable digital pest management systems required to ensure food supply.</jats:p>

doi:10.17977/2502-471x.2986.title: FMEA Reveals PPE Noncompliance as the Priority Grinding Machine Accident Risk in an Indonesian Vocational School Workshop
doi:10.17977/2502-471x.2986.abstract: <jats:p>Occupational Safety and Health (OSH) in vocational school workshops represents an urgent priority given that students interact directly with high-risk equipment such as grinding machines, yet often demonstrate low compliance with safety protocols. This research aims to identify failure modes on grinding machines in SMKN 1 Jenangan workshop and formulate evidence-based risk control recommendations. A quantitative descriptive approach using Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) was employed, involving 10 purposively selected respondents (practical instructors and technicians). The research instrument was validated using Content Validity Index (CVI) by three experts in occupational safety and mechanical engineering. Results identified 15 failure modes with CVI = 1.0 (perfect validity). Risk Priority Number analysis revealed a positive risk distribution: 13 modes fell into low-risk category (RPN ≤ 50), 2 modes into medium-risk category (RPN 50-100) including non-compliance with protective gloves (RPN 58.21) and safety glasses (RPN 50.51), and no modes reached high-risk category (RPN ≥ 100). Critical finding demonstrates that the greatest risks originated from human behavioral factors, specifically non-compliance with Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) usage, rather than machine technical components. Risk control recommendations focus on three pillars: (1) intensifying direct supervision of students, (2) implementing continuous safety education programs with positive reinforcement, and (3) transforming safety culture in the workshop. This research contributes empirical evidence on risk profiles in vocational school workshops and emphasizes the importance of behavior-based interventions rather than technical improvements in enhancing occupational safety in vocational education settings.</jats:p>
doi:10.17977/2502-471x.2986.venue: Jurnal Pendidikan: Teori, Penelitian, dan Pengembangan

doi:10.36713/epra31732.title: DIALOGICAL APPROACH: INTELLECTUAL INTERACTION OF LITERACY IN TEACHING AND LEARNING WITH A COHESIVE STANDARD OF EDUCATION
doi:10.36713/epra31732.abstract: <jats:p>This paper introduces the Dialogic Education Theory, a transformative framework inspired by Mikhail Bakhtin’s dialogism, designed to reimagine education as a vibrant, inclusive process of co-creating knowledge. Rooted in the belief that every student’s voice matters, the theory promotes classrooms where diverse perspectives drive learning through dialogue. It offers a practical model that weaves dialogic principles into pedagogy, curriculum, assessment, and peer evaluation, fostering critical thinking, empathy, and cultural understanding. By celebrating diversity as a strength, the framework supports multicultural and equitable education, empowering teachers and students as partners in a shared journey. The paper explores the theory’s conceptual foundations, practical applications, strengths, and challenges, positioning it as a powerful tool for 21st-century classrooms that prepare students to thrive in a connected, diverse world. In this article, my contribution is to develop a new structure of the Dialogical Approach with a cohesive standard in education in teaching and learning through the implementation in a more effective way, where intellectual interaction will enlighten the students' efficacy. My restructuring of the dialogical approach added new ideas with peer evaluation, which encloses intellectual interaction through dialogue from both ends of teaching and learning. I added a positive approach, creativity analysis, perpetual instruction, and authentic exposition to improve the dialogical approach with parent involvement. My exploration includes a new concept with peer observation and peer assistance, where multicultural and multi-ethnographic essence will get equal emphasis to ensure the involvement of all students of all nations.</jats:p>

doi:10.37128/2520-6168-2026-3-9.title: IMPROVEMENT OF THE DESIGN OF A HIGH-SPEED SHEEP SHEARING MACHINE
doi:10.37128/2520-6168-2026-3-9.abstract:
<jats:p>This study presents a comprehensive substantiation of the rational design parameters of the pressure mechanism, lever system, and eccentric drive of a high-speed sheep shearing machine. The analysis was performed considering the kinematic, dynamic, and operational characteristics of shearing devices operating under increased oscillatory and impact loads. Particular attention was paid to optimizing the geometric parameters and relative arrangement of the mechanism components to improve reliability, reduce vibration, and ensure the stability of the sheep shearing process.
The kinematic analysis of the working elements made it possible to establish the relationships between the parameters of the eccentric mechanism, the oscillation amplitude of the cutter block, and the magnitude of the contact forces in the cutting zone. Rational relationships between the geometric and force parameters were determined to reduce energy losses, minimize component wear, and improve wool cutting efficiency.
It was established that deviations of the oscillation centers of the pressure rod and the lever from their optimal positions lead to additional dynamic loads, misalignment of the cutter assembly, and non-uniform distribution of contact pressure. These factors adversely affect shearing quality and reduce the service life of the machine components.
To eliminate these drawbacks, it is proposed to improve the manufacturing accuracy requirements for shearing head housings by introducing positional tolerances for the relative locations of the holes accommodating the lever oscillation center and the pressure mechanism. Ensuring the coaxial alignment of these elements minimizes misalignment and improves the operational performance of the shearing machine.
The obtained results provide a foundation for the further implementation of mechatronic control systems, sensor-based monitoring, and robotic technologies in sheep shearing. The integration of vibration, load, and temperature sensors enables adaptive real-time control of the machine operating modes, thereby enhancing operational reliability, efficiency, and equipment durability.</jats:p>

doi:10.53850/joltida.1895088.title: Developing and Examining the Responsible AI Use Knowledge Scale (RAUKS): Initial Evidence of a Three-Factor Structure among College Students in Teacher Education
doi:10.53850/joltida.1895088.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in online and blended higher education, pressing assumptions about authorship, academic integrity, and transparency are being re-examined, raising urgent questions for the transformation of the teaching and learning environment. While existing studies document students’ attitudes toward AI and general AI literacy, fewer instruments assess students’ self-reported understanding of responsible academic AI use. This study reports the development and preliminary validation of the Responsible AI Use Knowledge Scale (RAUKS) for college students in teacher education. Guided conceptually by the 6Cs approach as an item-development heuristic, an initial 46-item pool was administered to 410 undergraduate students. Exploratory structural equation modeling (ESEM) supported a refined 24-item instrument with a three-factor structure: Ethical Normative Knowledge (ENK), Critical Corrective Knowledge (CCK), and Procedural Disclosure Knowledge (PDK). The three-factor solution explained 61.67% of the total variance and demonstrated excellent model fit (χ² (230) = 364, p &lt; .001, RMSEA = .038, SRMR = .033, CFI = .999, TLI = .999). Internal consistency reliability was strong across factors (ω = .97 for ENK, .84 for CCK, and .81 for PDK). The results provide initial evidence that responsible AI use perceived knowledge is multidimensional, comprising integrity-related expectations, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and disclosure procedures. RAUKS contributes a knowledge-focused self-report assessment tool offering practical utility for diagnosing student preparedness, informing instructional design, and supporting integrity-oriented AI policies. Further cross-validation across institutions, programs, and modalities is recommended.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11236085/v1.title: Task-Based Learning in Education (1976-2025): A Bibliometric Analysis of Publication Trends, Citation Impact, Collaboration and Research Themes
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11236085/v1.abstract: Task-based learning (TBL) has developed across diverse educational contexts, although its research base remains strongly associated with language education. This bibliometric study analysed 1,055 Scopus-indexed publications from 1976–2025 using BiblioSpy to examine publication trends, citation impact, collaboration patterns, and major research themes. The dataset accumulated 19,783 citations and showed an annual publication growth rate of 10.15%, with output reaching 114 publications in 2025. China, the United States, and the United Kingdom were the leading country contributors, while collaboration patterns reflected expanding international participation in TBL research. Keyword and thematic analyses identified sustained attention to language learning, communication, task complexity, technology-mediated instruction, and broader pedagogical applications. Overall, TBL scholarship has expanded considerably in volume, influence, and thematic scope, while opportunities remain to strengthen research across disciplines, educational levels, contexts, and learning outcomes beyond its established language-education tradition.

doi:10.1108/aaouj-05-2026-0090.title: Predicting student success in open and distance learning: a comparative evaluation of machine learning models
doi:10.1108/aaouj-05-2026-0090.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study compares Logistic Regression, linear Support Vector Machine, Random Forest and Histogram Gradient Boosting for predicting four student outcomes in open and distance learning (ODL) from the first four weeks of study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, the analysis included 27,535 registrations from 24,841 students. Day-28 predictors comprised static characteristics, raw virtual learning environment (VLE) activity and engagement-focused behavioral features. Class-weighted models were evaluated using nested stratified group cross-validation, with student records grouped across partitions. The macro-averaged F1 score (macro-F1) was the primary metric.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>With engagement-focused features, the linear support vector machine yielded the highest macro-F1 (0.406) and 47.6% accuracy, followed closely by Random Forest (0.404) and Histogram Gradient Boosting (0.402). Engineered behavioral features improved macro-F1 by 0.014 over raw VLE activity, with a 95% confidence interval of [0.009, 0.019]. A secondary assessment-informed model reached a macro-F1 of 0.434, whereas excluding sensitive demographic attributes did not clearly reduce performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research contributes to ODL through a fixed early window, student-grouped validation and theory-aligned behavioral feature engineering. It supports timely learner review while treating VLE traces as partial rather than comprehensive indicators of engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11314841/v1.title: Rhythms of the Mind: The Physics of Sound, Neural Entrainment, and Sensorimotor Learning in Music—Implications for Cognitive Function, Psychological Well-Being, and Inner Peace
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11314841/v1.abstract: Music brings together physical sound, auditory perception, cognitive processing, motor coordination, emotional regulation, and subjective experience. Learning and practising music require the continuous integration of acoustic information, attention, memory, temporal prediction, movement, and feedback. This conceptual integrative review examines how the physics of sound and the neuroscience of rhythmic processing can inform the study of musical learning, sensorimotor integration, psychological well-being, and inner peace. It discusses acoustic frequency, period, wavelength, superposition, rhythm, and timing accuracy alongside auditory–motor coupling, neural entrainment, executive functions, and emotional regulation. Published evidence suggests that musical training can benefit selected auditory and closely related processing skills, while findings concerning far transfer to general cognition and stress recovery are more variable. The article distinguishes active musical learning from passive listening and professionally guided music therapy, and it avoids treating mechanical resonance as equivalent to neural entrainment or assuming that particular frequencies automatically produce healing. A physics-informed conceptual framework is proposed in which measurable acoustic features and structured practice may influence task-specific perceptual and motor learning, while emotional and well-being outcomes are shaped by personal preference, social context, and individual differences. Because no original participant data were collected, the results represent a qualitative synthesis of published evidence rather than new experimental findings. The article concludes that music offers a valuable interdisciplinary context for investigating the connections between physical sound, learning, coordinated action, and subjective well-being, while emphasizing the need for transparent methods and empirical testing.

doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1967799.title: Exploring nursing students’ experiences of using generative AI for emotional intelligence learning: a qualitative study
doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1967799.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Emotional intelligence is a core competency for nursing students; however, traditional nursing education faces challenges in fostering emotional intelligence, including curricular imbalances, limited teaching methods, and delayed assessment and feedback. The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new possibilities for addressing the above issues; however, existing research has not yet thoroughly explored how nursing students learn emotional intelligence through GenAI or their experiences in this process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the Teaching Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, and using Goleman’s five-dimensional model of emotional intelligence as a reference, this study explores the experiences of undergraduate nursing students in using generative artificial intelligence for emotional intelligence learning, as well as the factors that facilitate this process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study employed a qualitative descriptive research design and Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA). Using purposive sampling, 19 undergraduate nursing students (from freshman to senior year) were selected for one-on-one semi-structured in-depth interviews. All participants had experience using GenAI tools (such as DeepSeek and Doubao) for communication practice, case discussions, or sentiment analysis. The interview data were analyzed using the RTA six-stage process, with NVivo 12.0 software used to assist with data management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We identified and synthesized 238 initial codes into three core themes. Theme 1, “From Efficiency-Driven to Precise Empathy,” presents the differing descriptions of empathy-related experiences among students in different grade levels: lower-grade students more frequently reported efficiency-driven usage experiences; some middle-grade students described difficulties caused by technical barriers; and upper-grade students more often described the recognition of patients’ emotions in conjunction with clinical experience. Theme 2, “From Mimicking AI to Autonomous Expression,” focuses on students’ reported experiences related to social skills, including direct application, recognition and adjustment, autonomous expression, and the simulation gap that persisted throughout the process. Theme 3, “From Technical Frustration to Mental Rehearsal,” integrates experiences related to self-management, self-awareness, and self-motivation. The three themes correspond to different dimensions of emotional intelligence, with students in different grade levels reporting distinct experiential characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nursing undergraduates in different grades exhibit distinct experiential characteristics when using generative artificial intelligence to learn about emotional intelligence. Students’ reports repeatedly highlighted moderate tension around technological motivation, the ability to critically integrate technology, and the perceived value of technological friction. Based on these exploratory findings, we propose several preliminary educational implications—including grade-level-specific support, curriculum exploration, and education in critical technological literacy and ethics—for consideration in future research and practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.15832/ankutbd.1898342.title: Early Detection of Apple Scab in Orchards and Mildew in Vineyards Using A Novel Deep Learning Model and Multispectral Imagery
doi:10.15832/ankutbd.1898342.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Agricultural diseases are a significant problem for growers as they cause substantial damage to fruits and leaves, leading to yield losses. Therefore, developing systems for early detection of plant diseases is a crucial issue. In this study, a new deep learning-based hybrid model is presented for the detection and segmentation of plant diseases, specifically apple scab disease in apple orchards and mildew disease in vineyards. Multispectral imagery data collected in agricultural areas of Tekirdag province in Turkey via drones between May 2023 and December 2024 were used in developing the early disease detection system. The datasets contain 3625 images of apple orchards and 5625 images of vineyards. DJI Phantom 4 Multispectral drone, equipped with five spectral bands (Blue, Green, Red, Red Edge, and Near Infrared), was utilized to capture both spectral richness and temporal progression. This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture developed specifically for time series-based disease detection and segmentation using multispectral drone imagery. Changes in plants over time provide important information about the occurrence of plant diseases. For this reason, time series were used in this study to extract features from the changes in plants over time. The proposed model architecture was specifically designed to leverage time series information, enabling robust tracking of crop health changes over time. The model trained with the dataset collected for apple diseases achieved an average Intersection Over Unit (IoU) value of 82.05%, while the model trained with the dataset collected for vineyard diseases reached an IoU value of 79.67%. The findings highlight the effectiveness of integrating drone-acquired multispectral time-series data with advanced deep learning models for scalable, accurate, and timely plant disease detection in precision agriculture.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261019.title: Mutual Learning and Reading Comprehension in a Highly Diverse Setting
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261019.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mutual Learning is understood as a reciprocal process in which knowledge is co-constructed through joint engagement. This chapter investigates how learners mutually construct knowledge through peer scaffolding during text based reading tasks. Four research questions guide the analysis, focusing on the occurrence, patterns, and learning potential of peer scaffolding interactions, as well as the influence of learner pair composition. Peer scaffolding occurred in all pairs, despite generally low to medium language proficiency. Its quality varied substantially, with the most productive scaffolding emerging in pairs showing balanced engagement and strong mutuality. Bidirectional scaffolding provided favorable conditions for mutual learning and knowledge convergence, whereas passive or unequal engagement hindered these processes. The findings highlight the importance of preparing learners with strategies that support mutual learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261014.title: Cross-Language Awareness to Improve Understanding of Reading Challenges in Spanish-Speaking Students Immersed in English Classrooms
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261014.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Language awareness refers to explicit knowledge about language, as well as conscious perception and sensitivity in language learning, language teaching and language use. At the same time, the focus of research on language awareness has evolved from English as a native language to multilingualism. In that vein, more publications comparing different settings and languages and addressing teachers’ language awareness are needed. This chapter identifies potential linguistic challenges faced by Spanish-dominant students when they are learning to read, or continuing their reading development, in English-only classrooms. To support students with a strong Spanish base who are developing reading abilities in English, teachers need cross-language awareness, including an understanding of how prior language experiences impact linguistic schemata, as well as knowledge of potential challenges and suitable teaching approaches. This chapter reviews linguistic dimensions of Spanish and English relevant to reading acquisition in English, focusing on issues that may be particularly challenging for students who appear to be struggling.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-331-020261004.title: An Analysis of Military and Higher Education Learning Environments
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-331-020261004.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter employs an asset-based approach to examine the learning environments within the US military and higher education systems, highlighting their similarities and differences to provide deeper insight into veterans’ transitions to civilian life. In addition to the distinct cultures of these settings, the chapter explores the organizational diversity within the military and its influence on training and educational experiences. It also assesses the historical and current potential for reciprocity between military and civilian learning environments, uncovering mutual benefits for both. Furthermore, the chapter investigates the support systems available to veterans during their transitions, focusing on the implications for both military and higher education institutions. The discussion emphasizes the critical need for collaboration between military and civilian education systems to enrich the learning experiences of veterans and other adult learners.</jats:p>

doi:10.1215/9781478062868-002.title: Care
doi:10.1215/9781478062868-002.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter engages with recent work on care, including debates about the concept of self-care catalyzed by the wide circulation of Audre Lorde’s comments about “caring for myself.” Despite feminist critiques of care, it has also been taken up anew by feminist and queer scholars using it as an umbrella to propose alternatives to business as usual in activism and in the academy. The chapter reads Lorde on trusting feelings to develop theories and practices of self-care that insist on forms of sensory knowledge so often dismissed in academic scholarship and institutions. The chapter resituates care in relation to femme facilitation as theorized and practiced by activists Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha and adrienne maree brown, for whom care takes the form of strategies for organizing groups that make plenty of room for feelings, including negative ones.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/manm-01-2026-0004.title: From literacy to action: econometric and machine learning evidence on digital financial behaviour in India
doi:10.1108/manm-01-2026-0004.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines the impact of digital financial literacy (DFL) on digital financial practices (DFP) in India by combining causal inference and machine learning approaches. It investigates whether higher DFL translates into greater engagement with digital financial services and whether this effect varies by gender.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using primary survey data from 1,215 adults, the study applies covariate-adjusted ordinary least squares (OLS), propensity score matching (PSM) and overlap weighting to estimate the effect of DFL on DFP. Gender heterogeneity is analysed through interaction models and stratified matching. A Random Forest model is used to assess predictive importance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Results consistently show that higher DFL is associated with significantly greater DFP across all estimators, with effect sizes ranging from 0.86 to 1.41 (p &lt; 0.001). The effect is stronger among women, indicating a potential equalising role of literacy in digital finance adoption. Machine learning results further identify DFL as the most important predictor of DFP, explaining a substantial share of variation in outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation, and findings are specific to the Indian context. Future research can extend this work using longitudinal data and comparative frameworks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings highlight the need to shift from infrastructure-led to capability-driven financial inclusion strategies. Targeted DFL interventions, particularly for women and low-income groups, can improve adoption, trust and responsible use of digital financial services.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study integrates causal inference and machine learning to provide robust evidence on the role of DFL in shaping digital financial behaviour, offering both methodological and policy-relevant insights for advancing digital financial inclusion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.70148/rise.v3i6.1.title: Beyond Technocentrism in AI-Supported Special Education: The PAISEN Model of Teacher-Mediated Inclusive Learning
doi:10.70148/rise.v3i6.1.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) offers new possibilities for inclusive teaching and learning for students with special educational needs (SEN), yet AI-in-SEN research remains largely technocentric, often describing system capabilities without explaining how outputs become pedagogically meaningful. This conceptual paper develops the PAISEN Model (Pedagogical Artificial Intelligence for Special Education Needs) through an integrative synthesis of AI in education, inclusive pedagogy, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and assistive technology. The model proposes a non-deterministic sequence in which AI Teaching Support Systems provide data and adaptive affordances, Teacher Pedagogical Mediation interprets and contextualises them, and an Inclusive Learning Environment translates decisions into accessible participation opportunities. SEN learning outcomes are treated as proposed consequences rather than established effects. Teacher AI competency, institutional support, digital infrastructure, and learner characteristics function as boundary conditions, while an adaptive feedback loop links learner evidence to teacher reflection and instructional adjustment. The novelty of PAISEN lies in making teacher judgement the central explanatory mechanism and separating technology, pedagogical processes, learning conditions and moderators. Theoretically, it bridges AIED and inclusive education; pedagogically, it clarifies differentiated and UDL-aligned AI use without replacing teacher agency; practically, it provides a testable structure for implementation and evaluation. The proposed relationships require empirical validation in authentic SEN settings.</jats:p>
doi:10.70148/rise.v3i6.1.venue: Journal of Research, Innovation, and Strategies for Education (RISE)

doi:10.3389/fcvm.2026.1867707.title: A clinical-deep learning model for prolonged length of stay following endovascular aortic repair
doi:10.3389/fcvm.2026.1867707.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prolonged length of stay (PLOS) after endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is associated with increased complications, resource burden, and patient distress. Early identification of high-risk patients remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and externally validate a predictive model integrating clinical variables and three-dimensional deep learning (3D-DL) features from preoperative computed tomography angiography (CTA) to predict PLOS after EVAR.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 788 patients with AAA who underwent elective EVAR were enrolled from two hospitals. The internal training cohort consisted of 556 patients, and the external validation cohort included 232 patients. PLOS was defined as a LOS above the 75th percentile of the distribution. A clinical nomogram was developed using LASSO regression followed by multivariate logistic regression. Deep learning (DL) features were extracted from manually segmented computed tomography angiography (CTA) images using a 3D ResNet200 network, and LASSO regression was applied to select the most informative features. An ensemble model integrating the clinical predictors and the selected DL features was constructed. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration plots, and decision curve analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LASSO combined with multivariate logistic regression identified five independent clinical predictors: age, hemoglobin, albumin, maximum aneurysm diameter, and diabetes. The clinical model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.917 in the internal cohort and 0.944 in the external cohort. From the 3D ResNet200 network, 32 DL features were extracted. LASSO regression further selected two of these features. The ensemble predictive model, which integrated the clinical predictors and DL features, demonstrated improved discrimination, with an AUC of 0.971 in the internal cohort and 0.958 in the external cohort. Internal validation with 1,000 bootstrap resamples yielded optimism-corrected AUCs of 0.911 for the clinical model and 0.966 for the ensemble model. Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent model performance across age and diabetes strata, while performance in the female subgroup warrants further evaluation in larger cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study developed an ensemble predictive model to predict PLOS following EVAR. The model demonstrated excellent discrimination and provided significant prognostic value beyond clinical variables alone. This nomogram may serve as a preoperative tool for risk stratification and resource planning in this population. Future studies should focus on prospective validation and clinical integration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.56201/ijcsmt.vol.11.no9.2025.pg10.title: Machine Learning Based Predictive Market for Sales Forecasting
doi:10.56201/ijcsmt.vol.11.no9.2025.pg10.abstract:
<jats:p>Sales forecasting remains a cornerstone of effective retail management, guiding supply chain
optimization, inventory planning, and revenue strategies. Traditional forecasting models often fall
short in capturing the complexity of consumer behavior, seasonal fluctuations, and branch-level
variations, resulting in inefficiencies that affect profitability and customer satisfaction. To address
these challenges, this project explores the application of supervised machine learning techniques
for supermarket sales forecasting across multiple timeframes and outlets, with the goal of enabling
medium- to large-scale retailers to improve decision-making and operational efficiency. The
research followed a structured methodology in line with the project’s objectives. First, relevant
datasets were collected, cleaned, and preprocessed, ensuring removal of inconsistencies,
treatment of missing values, and preparation of training and testing subsets. Second, statistical
methods and feature-importance techniques were applied to engineer and select key variables
influencing sales, including temporal, promotional, and branch-specific factors. Third, supervised
machine learning models were selected, tuned, and evaluated, with attention given to their
suitability for different sales forecasting tasks. Finally, a prototype system was developed to
simulate the training and testing of these models, enabling scenario-based forecasting and
practical demonstration of outcomes. The prototype integrates predictive analytics into a userfriendly framework, allowing managers to visualize sales patterns, anticipate demand fluctuations,
and adjust supply chain strategies accordingly. Beyond improving forecast reliability, the system
contributes to reduced stockouts, minimized overproduction, and better alignment of resources
with demand. Future extensions will consider expanding the dataset across sectors, integrating
ensemble deep learning models, and deploying the prototype as a scalable decision support tool
for real-time retail intelligence.</jats:p>
doi:10.56201/ijcsmt.vol.11.no9.2025.pg10.venue: International Journal of Computer Science and Mathematical Theory

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261017.title: Awareness of Disciplinary Literacy and Academic Language Practice
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261017.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter is based on classroom experience, was written along the lines of an opinion paper, and addresses the complex nature of literacy. Limitations are acknowledged upfront: samples of qualitative data illustrate instances of awareness of academic language use; however, the objective is not to formulate generalizable explanations for the progressive development of disciplinary literacy. In fact, the main goals in this text are: (a) to highlight the relevance of the point of view of the learner and the first-person nature of language awareness (LA); (b) to revisit the notion of discourse community and discuss intricacies in the continual process of becoming (recognized as) especially literate. In pursuing these goals, the notion of LA is reviewed to support the claims and classroom procedures advanced in the chapter, then the topics of disciplinary literacy and discourse communities are analyzed and contrasted with excerpts of learners’ responses to specific tasks. Despite the focus on highly specific contexts for teaching academic English to speakers of other languages, the ideas and data in the chapter may help reframe lesson plans and stimulate classroom-based research involving professionals and scholars in the making.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261008.title: From Global Competence to Plurilingual Assessment: A Pilot Study
doi:10.1108/978-1-80686-855-120261008.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter presents three specific tasks that were designed in the context of a pilot study aimed to develop a plurilingual test. The tasks are based on three specific scales included in the Companion Volume of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages by the Council of Europe. They involve three particular skills connected with the notion of plurilingual competence: plurilingual comprehension, plurilingual production, and cross-linguistic mediation. The chapter includes a description of the rationale and design of each of the tasks as well as some comments on the outcome of their piloting.</jats:p>

doi:10.1215/9781478062868-005.title: Breath
doi:10.1215/9781478062868-005.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter weaves together descriptions of breath practice, including kundalini yoga and meditation practices developed by Rev. angel Kyodo williams and Alexis Pauline Gumbs, continuing the book’s trajectory of acknowledging the significance of Black feminisms.</jats:p>

doi:10.1215/9781478062868.title: Learning from the High Priestess
doi:10.1215/9781478062868.abstract: <jats:p>In Learning from the High Priestess, Ann Cvetkovich integrates theory and somatic practice to assemble a survival guide for artists, academics, and activists in search of new strategies for social justice in times of trouble. Building on her previous work on why feelings matter to political action and intellectual inquiry, Cvetkovich shows how experiments in writing can be a form of affective and somatic practice. She uses four key themes–care, disability and madness, trauma and somatics, and breath–as launch points for reframing discourses of mental health in the direction of practices for decolonizing bodyminds and for the sensory experience of freedom. Engaging with writer-practitioners from Alexis Pauline Gumbs and Alison Bechdel to Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samarasinha, Staci Haines, and Kai Cheng Thom, with particular emphasis on Black feminisms, Cvetkovich places femme care and embodied practice at the center of movements for social transformation.</jats:p>

doi:10.69739/jelm.v3i2.2474.title: The Hidden Curriculum of Generative AI: Institutional AI Policies and the Potential for Student Inequality
doi:10.69739/jelm.v3i2.2474.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, prompting institutions to develop policies governing its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Although existing discussions have emphasized academic integrity, assessment practices, and technological access, less attention has been given to the knowledge and competencies students may need to interpret and comply with institutional AI policies. This study examines how institutional GenAI policies establish explicit and implicit expectations for students and identifies potential pathways through which policy-navigation demands may contribute to educational inequality. Using comparative qualitative content analysis, publicly available policies and guidance documents from 20 purposively selected higher education institutions across the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and South Africa were examined. The analysis considered policy permissiveness, disclosure requirements, instructor discretion, student responsibilities, AI-literacy guidance, accessibility, equity, and implicit navigation demands. Findings indicate that acceptable AI use is frequently determined at the course, instructor, or assessment level, requiring students to interpret context-specific rules, understand disclosure requirements, verify AI-generated outputs, and reconcile varying instructor expectations. However, explicit consideration of differences in technological access, language, accessibility, and institutional knowledge was less consistently evident across the reviewed documents. Drawing on hidden-curriculum and digital-inequality perspectives, the study identifies AI policy-navigation burdens and proposes the concept of a potential policy-navigation divide. While the findings do not establish unequal student experiences or educational outcomes, they highlight institutional conditions through which inequalities could emerge. The study recommends clearer policy communication, transparent assessment-specific expectations, accessible AI-literacy support, and greater attention to equity in institutional AI governance.</jats:p>
doi:10.69739/jelm.v3i2.2474.venue: Journal of Education, Learning, and Management

doi:10.2118/234452-ms.title: Geological Concept-Driven Intervention in Machine Learning for Foraminiferal Reservoir Property Modeling
doi:10.2118/234452-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Machine learning has increasingly been applied in geomodelling to extract spatial relationships from well and seismic data and to support reservoir characterization. This study evaluates a geology-guided machine-learning approach for porosity modeling in the DA Field, a foraminiferal carbonate gas reservoir in the Madura Strait PSC. The objective is to test whether seismic-derived attributes, well-log porosity, and rock-type constraints can be integrated in a transferable workflow that preserves geological realism while improving modeling turnaround time.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The DA Field reservoir was characterized using rock types defined from facies distribution and hydrocarbon flow capacity. Seismic attributes, including acoustic impedance, amplitude, RMS amplitude, and instantaneous phase, were resampled into the structural grid and used as predictor variables. The modeling framework combines supervised learning with spatial prior information so that property estimation is not controlled by seismic attributes alone, but is also evaluated against geological concepts and blind-well validation.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>When the model relied mainly on seismic attribute inputs, the resulting porosity distribution generated 12–13% lower resource estimates than the existing conventional model. The discrepancy was traced to the acoustic impedance volume, which had been generated before the development drilling campaign and therefore did not fully represent the updated rock-type understanding. A subsequent scenario incorporated the rock-type model as a geological constraint rather than as a deterministic output template. This revised approach reduced the volumetric difference to 0.008% relative to the conventional model, shortened the modeling turnaround substantially, and retained a blind-well correlation of approximately 62–63%.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The implementation of machine learning with a domain-guided geological intervention capability enables the integration of depositional constraints, represented here by the rock type model. This approach demonstrates that newly available data can be directly used as input for model updates without repeating full variogram and geostatistical modeling routines, significantly reducing computational turnaround time. This workflow can be adapted to other reservoirs where seismic attributes, well control, and conceptual geological models need to be reconciled.</jats:p>

doi:10.53299/jppi.v6i4.5416.title: Pengembangan E-Book Mpa.a sama Berbasis Deep Learning untuk Meningkatkan Student Well Being Siswa Sekolah Dasar
doi:10.53299/jppi.v6i4.5416.abstract: <jats:p>Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengembangkan E-Book Mpa.a Sama berbasis deep learning sebagai bahan ajar digital yang mengintegrasikan kearifan lokal untuk meningkatkan student well-being siswa sekolah dasar. Penelitian menggunakan metode Research and Development (R&D) dengan model ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, dan Evaluation). Subjek penelitian melibatkan 30 siswa dengan teknik Purposive Sampling SDN Ncera, guru, kepala sekolah, serta ahli materi, bahasa, dan media. Data dikumpulkan melalui observasi, wawancara, lembar validasi ahli, angket respons guru dan siswa, tes pretest-posttest, serta skala student well-being, kemudian dianalisis secara deskriptif kualitatif dan kuantitatif. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa E-Book Mpa.a Sama dinyatakan sangat layak berdasarkan validasi ahli materi (95%), ahli bahasa (95,7%), dan ahli media (92,5%). Hasil belajar siswa meningkat dari rata-rata 71,33 (pretest) menjadi 82,33 (posttest), sedangkan respons guru berada pada kategori baik (rata-rata 3,20). Skala student well-being menunjukkan kategori sangat sesuai (rata-rata 3,27), dengan aspek emosional memperoleh skor tertinggi (4,00) dan aspek fisik memperoleh skor terendah (2,00). Temuan ini membuktikan bahwa integrasi teknologi digital, kearifan lokal, dan prinsip mindful, meaningful, serta joyful learning mampu meningkatkan keterlibatan, interaksi sosial, dan kenyamanan belajar siswa. Penelitian selanjutnya disarankan untuk memperluas cakupan subjek pada jenjang dan lokasi yang lebih beragam, menguji efektivitas produk melalui desain eksperimen dengan kelompok kontrol, serta mengembangkan strategi pendukung yang secara khusus menyasar aspek kesejahteraan fisik siswa agar dampak E-Book Mpa.a Sama terhadap student well-being dapat lebih optimal dan menyeluruh.</jats:p>

doi:10.17605/osf.io/fxsak.title: Deployment Readiness of TinyML and Edge AI for Precision Apiculture: A Systematic Review and Evidence Map
doi:10.17605/osf.io/fxsak.abstract: This systematic review and evidence map will assess how far TinyML and edge-AI systems for managed honey-bee (Apis mellifera) hive monitoring have progressed from offline algorithm development to physical on-device inference and validation under realistic apiary conditions. Deployment readiness is operationalised along two ordinal axes. The first is a computing-deployment taxonomy (C0-C4), ranging from offline, cloud, workstation, or otherwise non-target-device evaluation (C0) to physical inference on MCU-class hardware (C4). Intermediate categories distinguish claims of edge suitability from demonstrated local inference, including gateways, conventional local computers, single-board computers, and edge accelerators. The second is a validation taxonomy (V0-V4), ranging from benchmark or laboratory evaluation to sustained validation in operating apiaries. Full definitions and decision rules are specified in the registered protocol. Studies will be characterised by sensing modality, application, machine-learning or computational method, hardware platform, dataset, deployment characteristics, validation setting, and reported performance. Relevant acoustic, visual, environmental, chemical, and multimodal hive-monitoring studies will be considered according to the predefined eligibility criteria. Six primary bibliographic sources will be searched from database inception to the production-search date: Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, IEEE Xplore, the ACM Guide to Computing Literature, PubMed, and CAB Abstracts. Supplementary identification methods include backward and forward citation searching and predefined targeted discovery approaches described in the protocol. English-language full texts are required for inclusion; potentially eligible non-English records encountered during screening will be logged explicitly rather than silently removed. Database-specific search strategies were developed and validated before registration using a predefined 15-study sentinel set spanning relevant sensing, modelling, and deployment characteristics. Validation was assessed against the subset of sentinel studies indexed by each database. Pilot searches were conducted only for syntax development, query refinement, and sentinel validation; pilot records and pilot result counts will not enter screening, synthesis, or PRISMA reporting. Following registration, the frozen database-specific strategies will be rerun as production searches. Only records retrieved through the production searches and predefined supplementary identification methods will proceed to deduplication, screening, extraction, synthesis, and PRISMA accounting. Title/abstract screening will be conducted by the lead reviewer, with a predefined independent sample assessed by the second reviewer and inter-reviewer agreement evaluated according to the protocol. Potentially eligible full texts will undergo independent second-reviewer assessment, with disagreements resolved using the predefined reconciliation and escalation procedure. Data extraction and quality assessment will follow the verification procedures specified in the protocol. Synthesis will be descriptive and will include a C0-C4 × V0-V4 evidence map, cross-tabulations by sensing modality, application, and hardware class, deployment-evidence summaries, and reporting-completeness measures. No statistical meta-analysis is planned because substantial methodological, task, dataset, hardware, and validation heterogeneity is expected. Reporting will follow PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S principles. The review aims to quantify the extent of operational edge and TinyML deployment in precision apiculture, distinguish deployment claims from demonstrated physical inference and field validation, and identify the reporting practices required for deployment claims to be independently assessed. The observed density and distribution of evidence across deployment and validation levels will be reported irrespective of the pattern identified.

doi:10.5281/zenodo.22898176.title: Real-Time Multi-Modal 3D Perception and Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) Sensor Fusion for Autonomous Robotics: Empirical Benchmarking of LiDAR-Camera Deep Architectures on Embedded Edge Compute Substrates (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, Xavier, and Xavier NX)
doi:10.5281/zenodo.22898176.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), self-driving vehicles, and industrial automated guided vehicles (AGVs) operating in dynamic, unconstrained physical environments demand real-time, highly accurate, and robust 3D perception. While unimodal sensory perception—relying solely on dense RGB cameras or sparse Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds—suffers from severe environmental failure modes (such as camera degradation in zero-lux nighttime illumination or lens flare, and LiDAR point cloud attenuation during adverse rain, fog, and snow), modern sensor fusion architectures synthesize complementary multi-modal geometric and semantic streams into a unified Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) representation space. However, deploying compute-intensive multi-view camera transformations (e.g., Lift-Splat-Shoot / LSS, cross-view deformable attention) alongside 3D sparse voxel convolutions onto embedded edge hardware introduces critical execution bottlenecks governed by memory bandwidth limits, shared unified memory contention, and stringent latency budgets (<=50 ms) mandated by ISO 26262 Automotive Safety Integrity Level D (ASIL-D) functional safety standards. To resolve these architectural and microarchitectural challenges, this paper presents an exhaustive empirical benchmark evaluating contemporary multi-modal 3D perception paradigms across three prominent embedded robotic edge computing substrates: the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin 64GB (Ampere microarchitecture, 275 TOPS INT8, 204.8 GB/s unified bandwidth), the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier 32GB (Volta microarchitecture, 32 TOPS INT8, 137 GB/s bandwidth), and the power-constrained NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX 16GB (21 TOPS, 51.2 GB/s bandwidth), referenced against a high-end datacenter baseline (NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Lovelace 48GB). We systematically profile four representative fusion paradigms—Point-Level Fusion (PointPainting), Feature-Level BEV Fusion (BEVFusion), Temporal Query-Based Fusion (BEVFormer), and Late Decision-Level Tracking—across the nuScenes 1,000-scene dataset and challenging adverse weather edge cases. Our empirical findings establish that: • State-of-the-Art Detection Accuracy: Unified BEV Feature Fusion (BEVFusion) achieves a superior NuScenes Detection Score (NDS = 0.714) and mean Average Precision (mAP = 0.685), outperforming best-in-class camera-only architectures (NDS = 0.542) by 17.2 percentage points and unimodal LiDAR baselines (NDS = 0.648) by 6.6 percentage points. • Real-Time Edge Throughput: With TensorRT INT8 post-training quantization and kernel fusion of the LSS view transformation stage, BEVFusion attains an inference latency of 24.6 ms (40.6 FPS) on Jetson AGX Orin at 50W power consumption, operating comfortably within real-time robotic control loop tolerances (<=50 ms). • Adverse Weather & Sensor Degradation Robustness: Under severe simulated sensor degradation (50% camera occlusion or dense rainfall point attenuation), BEV multi-modal fusion retains >88% of nominal 3D detection precision, whereas unimodal camera and LiDAR pipelines collapse by 54% and 41% respectively. • Thermodynamic and Energy Efficiency: Offloading 3D backbone operations to Deep Learning Accelerators (NVDLA 2.0) reduces GPU active power draw by 34%, yielding an exceptional operational efficiency of 1.20 Joules per perceptual frame and sustained operation in thermal chambers up to +55°C. Finally, we formulate an open-source ROS 2 zero-copy integration pipeline, an ASIL-D fail-safe reconfiguration state machine, and an actionable hardware deployment matrix to accelerate real-world deployment of edge-native autonomous robotics.

doi:10.1145/3805696.3846050.title: Learning Subject Tags from Incomplete Labels: A Recall-Oriented VLM Pipeline for Historical Photographs
doi:10.1145/3805696.3846050.abstract: Assigning subject tags to photographs is essential for access and discovery in digital libraries, yet doing it by hand does not scale. Vision–language models (VLMs) are a powerful and increasingly popular tool for such tasks, but prompting them to generate open-vocabulary subject tags directly yields unsatisfactory results. Fine-tuning is the natural remedy, and here a second challenge arises: human-curated tags are an imperfect supervision signal: many true tags are missing, and the recorded ones appear in an arbitrary order. To address these challenges and improve the recall of meaningful tags, we propose a VLM fine-tuning pipeline for subject tagging of U.S. historical photographs. The pipeline begins with LoRA supervised fine-tuning. To counter the arbitrary tag order, we introduce an order-invariant training scheme that shuffles the target tags per example. To further raise recall, we continue training with reinforcement learning, specifically Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), under a recall-oriented reward. Finally, we apply a test-time scaling technique, self-consistency, to push performance further at inference. Evaluated on a ground truth rebuilt from the Digital Public Library of America, the combined techniques improve Recall@10 by + 0.51 (a ∼ 10 × gain) over the off-the-shelf VLM and by + 0.13 (\(+29\%\) relative) over plain LoRA fine-tuning.
