doi:10.1108/resep-05-2026-0015.title: From ambiguity to ownership: a reflective practitioner inquiry into team coaching in a global experiential learning environment
doi:10.1108/resep-05-2026-0015.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper examines how team coaching supported a student team in learning to organise itself under conditions of ambiguity, enabling collective ownership and shared leadership to emerge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper adopts a reflective practitioner inquiry to examine coaching practice within a single team participating in the Global Business Challenge (GBC). Reflection was informed by programme artefacts generated through routine educational practice, including coaching session transcripts, client interactions, student reflections and other contemporaneous materials. An iterative, interpretive analysis developed a five-phase process-oriented account of how collective ownership and shared leadership emerged as the team learnt to organise itself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings reveal a developmental trajectory from initial ambiguity and dependence toward increasing collective ownership and shared leadership. Team coaching did not resolve ambiguity but sustained it as a condition for learning, prompting the team to develop its own ways of organising.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper develops a process-oriented, practice-based account of how coaching supported teams to organise themselves under conditions of ambiguity, enabling collective ownership and shared leadership to emerge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1142/s0218625x26501209.title: Self-Supervised Contrastive Learning with Dynamic Cost-Sensitive Random Forest for Intelligent Fault Diagnosis of Diesel Engines
doi:10.1142/s0218625x26501209.abstract: <jats:p>Reliable identification of incipient degradation is critical to the durability and functional integrity of diesel engines. However, diagnosis is challenged by scarce degradation labels, severe class imbalance, and heterogeneous multi-source monitoring data. This study proposes a selfsupervised contrastive learning with dynamic cost-sensitive random forest (SSCL-DCSRF) framework for intelligent fault diagnosis with a focus on wear- and lubrication-related degradation states. Rather than directly measuring surface morphology, roughness, residual stress, or wear loss, the proposed method identifies operating states associated with surface-related degradation from multi-source monitoring data. A physically consistent view-generation strategy preserves operating-condition semantics and cross-variable relationships, enabling robust representation learning from unlabeled data. A dynamic cost-sensitive random forest then integrates class frequency, feature-space dispersion, and prediction uncertainty to improve the recognition of minority and difficult-to-classify states. Experiments on a multi-source diesel-engine fault dataset demonstrate that SSCL-DCSRF outperforms representative machine-learning methods in class-balanced diagnostic performance, with enhanced sensitivity to early wear and lubrication-related degradation. The proposed framework provides an effective data-driven approach for indirect identification of operating states related to surface degradation and integrity-oriented maintenance of critical tribological interfaces.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11058145/v1.title: Automated Spiral-Arm Pitch-Angle Estimation in Galaxy Images Using Deep Learning
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11058145/v1.abstract: Spiral-arm pitch angle is a compact quantitative descriptor of spiral-galaxy structure and is related to galaxy morphology, kinematics, and central mass concentration. Its large-scale use is nevertheless limited by the scarcity of homogeneous numerical labels and by the sensitivity of conventional measurements to deprojection, noise, dust, and arm fragmentation. We present an end-to-end deep-learning pipeline for continuous pitch-angle estimation from galaxy images. A parametric three-dimensional generator produces spiral galaxies with exact pitch-angle labels and controlled variations in arm number, viewing inclination, dust content, and flocculence. Images are processed by automatic disc deprojection followed by spatial-frequency enhancement using unsharp masking, contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalisation, and Fourier-domain filtering. A MobileNetV2 backbone pretrained on ImageNet is then adapted in two stages for regression. On 2,200 synthetic test images spanning pitch angles of 5°-35°, the full pipeline achieved a mean absolute error of 1.01° and a root mean square error of 1.34°. External validation on 65 Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxies with literature pitch-angle measurements reduced the mean absolute error from 7.07° without the full preprocessing pipeline to 5.83°, while the root mean square error decreased from 10.42° to 7.61°. The results show that geometry-aware preprocessing substantially improves synthetic-to-real transfer, although residual compression of the predicted pitch-angle range indicates that a larger real labelled sample and explicit treatment of bars and non-logarithmic arms remain necessary.

doi:10.1108/ijlls-01-2026-0029.title: Learning from student-led interdisciplinary projects: a lesson study–informed practice-based inquiry into mentorship, failure and motivation
doi:10.1108/ijlls-01-2026-0029.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reports a practice-based inquiry into student-led interdisciplinary projects in secondary computer science education, using a lesson study (LS)–informed practitioner inquiry stance to examine how teacher mentoring sustains student agency and motivation when experimental outcomes are unsuccessful.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study draws on a structured LS process conducted across one academic year by four subject teachers. Three cycles combined in-class diagnostic observation, joint observation of extracurricular project sessions and end-of-year synthesis. Five data streams were analysed through a three-pass iterative interpretive process with cross-source triangulation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The focal case showed different patterns of student reasoning from the technically successful comparison case when mentoring reframed experimental failure as an epistemological resource. Motivation was sustained through autonomy, disciplinary relatedness and personal meaning rather than outcome validation. Competition outcomes provided external corroboration. After non-qualification for a national final, focal-case students independently diagnosed a robotics competence gap and developed a new project, providing evidence of self-directed learning agency following sustained LS-informed mentoring.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four mentoring principles are proposed: agency-focused observation, failure-reframing language, affirmation of personal meaning and structured LS reflection on mentoring decisions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study extends LS to long-term mentoring contexts, reframes experimental failure as a productive site of teacher learning and identifies self-directed learning agency as a documentable mentoring outcome under uncertainty.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
doi:10.1108/ijlls-01-2026-0029.venue: International Journal for Lesson & Learning Studies

doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1980930.title: Machine learning-based prediction of HCV-related cirrhosis and the exploratory analysis of drug use influence
doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1980930.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection easily progresses to liver cirrhosis, and drug users represent a special high-risk population with accelerated liver damage and insufficient early screening strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to develop a machine learning model for identifying HCV-related cirrhosis, with stratified analysis between drug-using and non-drug-using subgroups. We enrolled patients with chronic HCV infection and collected blood routine, liver function, lymphocyte subsets, and drug use data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Among the seven models compared, the XGBoost model achieved the best performance, with an AUC of 0.86 on the test set. Stratified analysis showed significantly better predictive performance in drug users (AUC = 0.87) than in non-drug users (AUC = 0.72,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.05). Drug use did not independently improve model performance and showed significant interactions with only a limited number of key features (e.g., ADA). SHAP and decision curve analysis validated the model’s reliability and clinical benefit, especially in drug users.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The XGBoost model enables noninvasive and accurate cirrhosis prediction and is suitable for early screening in high-risk drug-using populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1680/jmacr.26.00138.title: Integrated experimental and machine learning study on sustainable concrete incorporating fly ash and eco-sand
doi:10.1680/jmacr.26.00138.abstract: <jats:p>The construction industry faces increasing pressure to reduce carbon dioxide emissions and minimise dependence on conventional cement and natural fine aggregates, motivating the development of sustainable concretes incorporating industrial by-products. In this study, the combined use of fly ash (FA) and eco-sand (ES) as partial replacements for cement (0–25%) and fine aggregate (0–20%) was evaluated across 26 concrete mix designs. Experimental assessments included mechanical, durability and microstructural characterisation through tests for workability, strength, water absorption, porosity and acid resistance, along with scanning electron microscopy/energy-dispersive spectroscopy analysis. The results showed that the mix with 15% FA and 10% ES achieved the highest compressive strength of 39.1 MPa, representing a 10.8% improvement over the control mix. The mix with 20% FA and 15% ES exhibited enhanced durability with reduced porosity (6.5%), water absorption (1.42%) and acid-induced mass loss. To extend the experimental investigation and enable predictive performance assessment, machine learning models (including support vector regression with radial basis function (SVR-RBF), bagging SVR and Gaussian process regression) were developed using a 70:30 training–testing split and leave-one-out cross-validation. SVR-RBF achieved the highest predictive accuracy (coefficient of determination of 0.9801 and root mean squared error of 0.349 MPa), although interpretation should consider the limited dataset size (n = 26). Shapley additive explanations analysis identified ES content and bulk density as dominant predictors, and a graphical user interface was developed for real-time prediction.</jats:p>

doi:10.1088/3049-477x/aea330.title: Advancing knotted protein design with ESM3: guided generation and topological insights
doi:10.1088/3049-477x/aea330.abstract: Abstract Multimodal protein language models have transformed protein design, yet their capacity to capture complex topological features remains poorly understood. We use knotted proteins, rare structures in which the backbone forms a nontrivial topological knot, as a test case to probe this capacity using ESM3, a generative protein language model. Topology-aware guided decoding strongly enriches ESM3 outputs for knotted topologies, producing structures classified as knotted at an 89% success rate (95% CI: 81– 94%), compared to ~0.5% for unguided diffusion-based approaches. A confidence analysis shows that freshly generated artificial knots have lower ESM3 pLDDT and pTM than real knotted proteins evaluated under the same pipeline, motivating a cautious interpretation of generated examples as model samples pending independent validation. In contrast, the robustness analyses on real knotted proteins are high-confidence: on average 84% of the protein sequence must be altered before the knot breaks, and the loss follows a sharp threshold rather than gradual degradation. Strikingly, structural drift accumulates well before topological disruption, suggesting that topology is more robust than specific three-dimensional arrangement. These findings position knotted proteins as a useful probe of how generative protein models represent rare, global structural features.

doi:10.1111/ssm.70069.title: Mathematical Anticipation and Representational Coordination Within Van Hiele Levels: Evidence From Pre‐Service Teachers Learning Linear Equations
doi:10.1111/ssm.70069.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This research examines how pre‐service mathematics teachers coordinate algebraic and graphical representations when solving linear‐equation problems. Particular attention is given to mathematical anticipation, including predictions, intermediate results, and verification as participants move between representations. A qualitative interpretive design was used with 126 pre‐service mathematics teachers working in 15 heterogeneous groups. Each group included participants representing the five van Hiele levels of geometric thinking: visualization, analysis, informal deduction, deduction, and rigor. Written and graphical solution artifacts from all groups were examined, and retrospective interviews were used to clarify participants' reasoning. Three representative cases were selected to capture distinctive patterns in the artifacts. The analysis identified three patterns of reasoning: separation of algebraic and graphical representations, emerging but incomplete coordination, and integrated coordination supported by prediction and verification. Across the cases, mathematical anticipation ranged from limited expectations to predictions that guided subsequent actions and were checked against information from other representations. The results indicate that spatial reasoning in linear‐equation problem solving involves more than producing or interpreting graphs. It also involves coordinating representations and using anticipation to guide and evaluate mathematical reasoning. The study provides a process‐oriented account of reasoning within heterogeneous groups organized according to participants' van Hiele levels.</jats:p>

doi:10.1142/s0218194026500786.title: A Hybrid Temporal Deep Learning Framework for Real-Time Depression Detection on Social Media
doi:10.1142/s0218194026500786.abstract: <jats:p>Depression is one of the most common mental health problems, as it influences mood, cognition, and quality of life. Social media offers an abundance of user-generated content that can be utilized to detect and track depressive tendencies at early stages. Conventional methods cannot always work to capture very complex temporal variations and other hidden contextual indicators within the unstructured social media data. To overcome these drawbacks, this research proposed the Neuro Thought Weave Mindstream Predictor (NTwMP), an atomistic hybrid temporal deep learning (DL) model that combines both long-term and short-term temporal modeling with a ThoughtWeave Attention mechanism. The NTwMP enables categorization of multi-level severity, abrupt deviation detection, and understandable predictions, which are useful in preventing mental health interventions. The model handles dynamic social media feeds in real-time with sliding time windows, which does not require retraining. Accuracy is 98.33%, which is considerably higher than that of existing DL methods. Other measures such as precision, recall, and F1-score also show excellent reliability and consistency. The main advantages are scalability, reproducibility, interpretability, and applicability in real-time, which makes it a strong and viable instrument to monitor depression trends and assist clinicians, caregivers, and automated systems in making timely decisions and taking early action.</jats:p>
doi:10.1142/s0218194026500786.venue: International Journal of Software Engineering and Knowledge Engineering

doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02059-5.title: Joint optimization framework for robot dance motion generation, aesthetic evaluation, and dynamic balance control based on conditional gans and safe deep reinforcement learning
doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02059-5.abstract: Artificial intelligence and intelligent algorithms provide effective technical support for generating complex robotic dance motions and maintaining stable execution under dynamic constraints. To address the separation among motion synthesis, aesthetic evaluation, and balance control in existing robot dance systems, this study proposes a joint optimization framework that integrates a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN), multimodal aesthetic scoring, and safe Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). A temporal motion representation model is first constructed to encode joint angles, angular velocities, center-of-mass trajectories, rhythm labels, and style conditions. The cGAN generates style-consistent dance sequences through content encoding, style embedding, and sequence decoding, while a mechanical safety filter constrains joint angles, torque limits, self-collision, and support-region feasibility. A multimodal aesthetic evaluation model is then developed by fusing visual posture features, motion smoothness, spatial symmetry, and acoustic rhythm features. Human expert ratings are introduced to calibrate the automated aesthetic score and validate its objectivity. At the control level, a PPO-based policy is trained with ZMP constraints, joint-limit penalties, energy penalties, and safety-priority reward weighting. All baseline models, including LSTM-GAN, Transformer-GAN, MotionGAN, PID, DDPG, PPO, and TD3, are trained under identical data partitions and evaluation protocols. Experimental results show that the proposed framework reduces FID to 24.8, improves style recognition accuracy to 91.7%, increases aesthetic-score correlation with expert ratings to 0.86, and lowers the fall rate to 1.2%. Ablation and robustness tests further confirm the contribution of style transfer, multimodal feature fusion, PPO control, and ZMP-based safety constraints under external disturbances, sensor noise, uneven ground, and high-complexity dance motions.

doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c04842.title: Neural Constrained Charge Equilibration for Extracting Charge Transport Parameters from Machine Learned Interatomic Potentials
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c04842.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) continue to gain popularity as efficient tools for predicting energies and forces for atomic structures at an accuracy comparable to quantum chemistry. However, there are limited trained MLIPs for certain important applications such as in charge transport. Accelerating and automating the determination of parameters for such applications can be of critical importance in the rapid discovery of materials such as organic electronics (e.g., OLEDs). This work develops and introduces neural constrained charge equilibriation (NcQEq) and applies the technique to AimNet2 and OrbMol-V2. The new method enables extracting information about the diabatic states and thereby charge transport parameters. The approach is demonstrated on model systems against constrained density functional theory charge transport and then tested on intramolecular hole transport properties for polyethylene. This work demonstrates that the NcQeq approach is compatible with the charge equilibration schemes for AimNet2 and the latent charge predictions of OrbMol-V2. After calibration to reference data, the method enables estimation of the electronic coupling, reorganization energy, and the free energy difference.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch005.title: Transformational, Instructional, and Adaptive Leadership in Learning Organizations
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch005.abstract: <jats:p>In the contemporary knowledge driven economy, organizations are increasingly required to evolve into dynamic learning systems capable of responding to rapid technological, social, and economic changes. The concept of the learning organization emphasizes continuous knowledge creation, collaboration, and adaptive capacity as essential for sustained performance (Peter M. Senge, 1990). This chapter examines the integrative role of transformational, instructional, and adaptive leadership in shaping sustainable learning cultures within organizations. Moving beyond traditional hierarchical leadership paradigms, leadership is conceptualized as a catalytic force that fosters innovation, continuous improvement, and collective capacity building (James MacGregor Burns, 1978; Bernard M. Bass, 1985).</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch005.venue: Shaping Learning Cultures Through Effective Leadership

doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8352-1.ch014.title: Adaptive Learning Analytics Architecture for Inclusive and Sustainable Universities
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8352-1.ch014.abstract: <jats:p>The accelerated development of the metaverse has turned the virtual worlds into immersive socio-digital worlds in which the dynamics of the human interaction are closer to the real world. Nevertheless, the lack of emotional intelligence in the existing systems prevents their capacity to facilitate the meaningful and context-sensitive interaction. The given paper suggests the paradigm of Affective Metaverse Computing, which incorporates the multimodal emotion intelligence into human-centered virtual interaction systems. Using the recent technologies of affective computing, deep learning, and multimodal data fusion, the framework proposed will allow recognizing, interpreting, and responding to the emotions of the user in real-time using visual, auditory, textual, and physiological data.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8352-1.ch014.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10542-x.title: Free movement of dentists and life-long learning requirements within the countries of the European Economic Area: a scoping review of existing insights and future considerations
doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10542-x.abstract: The free movement of dentists within the European Economic Area (EEA) is facilitated by the mutual recognition of professional qualifications under European Union legislation. However, continuing professional development (CPD) regulations vary considerably across Member States. This scoping review maps the literature on the challenges and implications of EEA-qualified dentists within the countries of the EEA in relation to the variations in life-long learning and CPD in those countries. Following JBI methodological guidance and the PRISMA-ScR framework, a systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus was conducted. English and Dutch sources published between 2000 and 2025 that explored postgraduate dental education, specifically CPD of EEA-qualified dentists in the EEA and the UK, were considered eligible. Following independent screening and data extraction, the findings were mapped and analysed using basic qualitative content analysis. Twenty-seven sources, published between 2002 and 2024, were included, and eight overarching themes were identified. Migration is driven by complex push factors (e.g. poor working conditions) and pull factors (e.g. higher remuneration). While mobility addresses workforce shortages in destination countries, it risks exacerbating health inequalities in source countries. Furthermore, substantial variations in regulatory structures, undergraduate curricula, and CPD requirements across Europe pose major challenges to the professional integration of migrant dentists and the maintenance of uniform patient safety standards. The literature addressing the implications of variations in CPD requirements across Europe for migrant dentists appears to be limited. The benefits of a mobile dental workforce may be enhanced through greater harmonisation of educational standards and CPD requirements across Europe. Robust, data-driven workforce planning, alongside targeted support programmes, may help facilitate the effective integration of migrant dentists and contribute to safeguarding public health.

doi:10.51287/cttle20264.title: Translators’ language competence in technology-mediated contexts: Building on past conceptualizations and charting future directions
doi:10.51287/cttle20264.abstract:
<jats:p>Language competence is the driving force behind and the basis for advanced translation competence, yet rapid technological change requires it to be reconsidered in light of current professional realities. Against this backdrop, the article discusses the past and present conceptualizations, definitions, and changing manifestations of translators' language competence, with particular emphasis on technology-mediated contexts, including revision, machine translation post-editing, AI-supported translation, and potential future developments. It argues that communicative language competence remains foundational, while the competences needed to analyse, explain, evaluate and manage linguistic problems in human and technology-generated texts are becoming particularly salient. Among these, diagnostic competence, conceptualised as a part of a broader analytical competence, assumes particular importance. On this basis, the article proposes a tentative, technology-neutral definition of translators’ language competence and identifies directions for future research.

Keywords: translators’ language competence, communicative language competence, analytical competence, diagnostic competence, technology-mediated translation contexts</jats:p>
doi:10.51287/cttle20264.venue: Current Trends in Translation Teaching and Learning E

doi:10.1002/sce.70108.title: Assessments as Sites for Teacher Sensemaking About Epistemic Learning Goals in Science
doi:10.1002/sce.70108.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Recent science education reforms aim to broaden allowable ways of knowing and learning in science classes. Doing so requires that we attend to and work to shift messages about useful ways to know and learn (i.e., epistemological messages) embedded in course designs and enactments. Since high‐stakes assessments (i.e., tests and exams) are especially consequential sources of epistemological messages for students, useful alterations to course messaging landscapes should attend to alignment between assessment‐embedded messages and instructors' epistemic learning goals. Here, we consider how reflexive dialog around articulating and communicating epistemic learning goals might support such alignment. We analyzed data from eight semistructured interviews and other instances of reflexive dialog with a high school teacher partner, along with classroom artifacts, collected over a 2‐year period. Our analysis illustrates how iterative, scaffolded sensemaking mediated the refinement of this teacher's epistemic learning goals and co‐occurred with principled changes in how he assessed and supported students’ progress toward these goals. Specifically, engaging in reflexive dialog about epistemic learning goals—particularly in relation to summative assessments—created opportunities for the teacher to make sense of new curricular materials, his own values and goals for students, and contextual factors shaping his practice. Addressing epistemic incongruencies in this way narrowed the gap the teacher perceived between his values and his practice, and was accompanied by meaningful adaptations to both curriculum and instruction. This study underscores high‐stakes assessments as a critical context, warranting greater attention from both teachers and researchers.</jats:p>

doi:10.32478/fzz92g91.title: Problem-Based Learning Dan Hasil Belajar Pendidikan Agama Islam: Bukti Dari SMP Islam Almaarif 01 Singosari
doi:10.32478/fzz92g91.abstract: <jats:p>Studies on Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) in Indonesia are dominated by classroom action research and qualitative designs, so the contribution of PBL implementation to learning outcomes in schools where it is applied only partially has rarely been measured. This study aims to determine the effect of PBL implementation on students' IRE learning outcomes at SMP Islam Almaarif 01 Singosari, Malang. The study used a quantitative ex post facto design. Data were collected from 50 eighth-grade students through a Likert-scale questionnaire and documentation, and analysed with validity, reliability, normality, and linearity tests, followed by simple linear regression using SPSS 25. All items were valid (r-count > r-table = 0.279); reliability was moderate for the PBL variable (α = 0.577) and acceptable for learning outcomes (α = 0.642). The residuals were normally distributed (sig. = 0.200) and the relationship was linear (deviation from linearity sig. = 0.808). PBL had a positive and significant effect on learning outcomes (F = 32.564; t = 5.707; p < 0.001), with the regression equation Y = 12.995 + 0.680X and R² = 0.404. PBL implementation thus explains 40.4% of the variation in students' IRE learning outcomes, indicating that even partial implementation contributes substantially and that its effect would likely be stronger with fuller implementation.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch006.title: Transformational Leadership and the Development of Learning Cultures for Organizational Excellence and Sustainable Performance
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch006.abstract: <jats:p>The modern world is increasingly unstable, requiring organizations to continuously learn, adapt, and innovate to remain successful. This chapter highlights the role of transformational leadership in building strong learning cultures that support long-term success and sustainability. Transformational leaders inspire and motivate employees, fostering trust, psychological safety, and curiosity. Such environments encourage knowledge sharing, learning from mistakes, and innovation. The chapter explains how learning cultures enhance employee performance, creativity, and organizational resilience. It also examines how leadership behaviors influence learning processes, leading to organizational excellence. Practical strategies and future research directions are discussed to help organizations develop effective learning environments. Overall, the chapter emphasizes that organizations led by transformational leaders are better equipped to face challenges and achieve sustainable growth.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch006.venue: Shaping Learning Cultures Through Effective Leadership

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch012.title: Linking Learning Culture to Organizational Performance, Competitiveness, and Sustainability
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch012.abstract: <jats:p>Organizations striving for excellence must embed learning cultures that systematically link knowledge creation, sharing, and application to measurable outcomes. This chapter examines how organizational learning culture drives performance, competitiveness, and sustainability by synthesizing thirty contemporary empirical studies. It integrates transformational leadership, dynamic capabilities, knowledge management, and digital transformation as pivotal mediating and enabling mechanisms. Theoretical foundations from Watkins and Marsick's (2023) learning organization model are revisited alongside evolving constructs such as organizational resilience, ESG strategy, and ambidextrous innovation. The chapter presents a conceptual framework connecting learning culture antecedents to multi-dimensional performance outcomes. Practical implications are offered for organizational leaders seeking to leverage learning culture as a strategic asset, alongside directions for future research.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch012.venue: Shaping Learning Cultures Through Effective Leadership

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11327494/v1.title: Comparing the Effectiveness of AI-Powered 3D Virtual Environments vs. Traditional Instruction in Vocational Education: An Empirical Study of Learning Outcomes, Efficiency, and Equity Across Two National VET Systems
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11327494/v1.abstract: Vocational education and training systems worldwide face persistent challenges in providing students with sufficient opportunities to practice practical skills before entering the workplace. AI-powered 3D virtual environments offer a potential solution, yet empirical evidence comparing their effectiveness to traditional instruction remains limited, particularly across different national VET systems. This study addresses this gap through a mixed-methods design combining a quasi-experimental comparison with qualitative interviews. A total of 214 vocational students across three fields electrical power, health work, and building decoration in Norway and China were assigned to either an AI-powered 3D virtual environment condition or a traditional instruction condition. Quantitative results show that students in the AI condition achieved significantly higher skill attainment (d = 0.62), reached competency 24% faster, and demonstrated stronger knowledge retention at four-week follow-up. Effects were strongest for procedural and safety-critical tasks. The AI condition also showed an equalizing effect, with students in the lowest pre-test quartile gaining disproportionately more, reducing the performance gap that persisted under traditional instruction. Qualitative analysis of 24 interviews found that personalized feedback and safe practice led to efficiency gains and that removing material and geographical barriers led to equity gains. Challenges for teachers included initial cognitive overload and concerns that excessive regulation of behavior could limit professional agency. The findings suggest that AI-powered 3D virtual environments can improve learning outcomes, efficiency and equity in VET, but that their effectiveness is contingent upon pedagogical design, field-specific demands and institutional context.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11327494/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.3390/en19204830.title: Physics-Guided Machine Learning for Joint Fault Diagnosis in Inverter-Fed Induction Motor Drives
doi:10.3390/en19204830.abstract: <jats:p>In intelligent electric vehicle (EV) traction drives, pulse-width modulation and field-oriented control (FOC) introduce broadband harmonics and non-stationary start-up transients. These dynamics obscure incipient inter-turn stator faults (ITSF), particularly when inverter switch failures and measurement interference co-occur. To meet the low-latency requirements of on-board vehicle control units (VCUs), this paper proposes a data-centric, physics-guided diagnosis pipeline. Relying exclusively on current measurements, the framework jointly detects and localises ITSF (1–3% severity), open-circuit IGBT faults, and additive white Gaussian noise (5–20 dB SNR). A compact 27-dimensional feature vector is constructed by fusing db4 discrete wavelet transform sub-band energies, residualised negative-sequence phasors, αβ hodograph descriptors, and harmonic energy ratios. This targeted extraction empowers an ensemble of bagged decision trees to perform lightweight classification suitable for embedded edge hardware. In a simulation-based evaluation across four scenarios (transient and steady state, with and without AWGN), the pipeline achieves cross-validated accuracies of 91.63–98.97% and hold-out test accuracies of 93.13–98.75%. Unlike traditional threshold detectors that conflate inverter or sensing artefacts with ITSF, this approach achieves subsystem-level localisation across motor, inverter, and sensing hardware, providing the reliable condition monitoring required for cyber–physical EV digital twins.</jats:p>

doi:10.1515/iral-2026-0234.title: Professional learning communities as catalysts for writing teacher feedback literacy: a case study of two EFL secondary schools
doi:10.1515/iral-2026-0234.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Despite growing recognition of the importance of feedback literacy, limited attention has been paid to how teachers engage in professional learning to enhance their writing teacher feedback literacy (WTFL). To address this gap, this qualitative case study investigated the development of WTFL among teachers in two school-based professional learning communities (PLCs). Data were collected over one academic year from multiple sources, including interviews with four focal teachers, recordings of PLC meetings, classroom observations and documents, and student writing samples. Findings reveal that through participation in the PLCs, teachers expanded knowledge of feedback, reoriented values toward student agency, and strengthened abilities through practice innovation. Additionally, variations in WTFL development were shaped by individual, structural, and institutional factors. By uncovering the mechanisms through which PLCs foster WTFL and demonstrating their varied impact, this study advances understanding of the under-explored construct of WTFL, providing useful implications for classroom feedback practices and teacher education.</jats:p>
doi:10.1515/iral-2026-0234.venue: International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching

doi:10.1007/s10669-026-10149-z.title: Regenerative hospitality model using tourist municipalities using web scraping and unsupervised machine learning
doi:10.1007/s10669-026-10149-z.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Based on the research question: How can the regenerative hospitality actions undertaken by municipalities listed on the tourism map be classified? This study proposes a classification model for regenerative hospitality in Brazilian tourist municipalities. To achieve this aim, the study adopted a municipal-level adaptation of the regenerative dimensions proposed by Inversini et al. (2023), followed by the adapted model. Data were collected using natural language processing techniques, supported by a Python-based web‑scraping system that extracted text from municipal webpages listed on the National Confederation of Municipalities tourism map. The system gathered data, computed cosine similarity, vectorised the text, and compared the results against entries stored in a MySQL database, according to the dimensions of the regenerative hospitality model. The system obtained approximately 14,000 records and aggregated them by municipality, federative unit, and dimension. The dataset was then subjected to exploratory factor analysis using the principal components method with varimax rotation, which yielded two dimensions—socio‑environmental regeneration (X‑axis) and regenerative co‑creation (Y‑axis)—that explained 68% of the variance. K-means clustering was then applied, and the Elbow method indicated a three‑cluster solution: Cluster 1—Connectivity and Ideation, Cluster 2—Expanded Regenerative Core, and Cluster 3—Initial Base (Regeneration). The proposed framework offers three contributions. Theoretically, it tests the boundary conditions under which a firm-level regenerative hospitality model can be adapted to a territorial governance unit. Methodologically, it demonstrates a reproducible, partially validated NLP pipeline for classifying public-sector managers. Practically, it gives public managers and researchers a tool to assess, compare, and prioritise regenerative action across municipalities.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956107.title: Technology-mediated feedback in instrumental music practice, performance, and learning: a systematic review of feedback architectures, performance outcomes, and effect-size feasibility
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1956107.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Technology-mediated feedback can support instrumental music performance during practice, but such gains do not necessarily indicate durable learning. This systematic review examined feedback architecture (information type, modality, timing, performance target, and function), performance outcomes, assessment conditions, and quantitative-synthesis feasibility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Scopus, Répertoire International de Littérature Musicale (RILM) Abstracts of Music Literature, Web of Science Core Collection, APA PsycINFO, and ERIC were searched in May 2026 for empirical studies published since 2000 involving instrumental music learners across expertise levels. Quantitative and mixed-methods designs with learner-level performance data were eligible. Appraisal used the 2018 Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Findings were mapped and tabulated by design, comparator, feedback characteristics, and outcome domain, with reporting guided by Synthesis Without Meta-analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 1,689 records, 29 were retained in the record ledger; 27 formed the systematic-synthesis set and 26 the descriptive synthesis set. Learners ranged from novices to advanced musicians, principally in piano and bowed-string tasks. Among these 26 records, 21 included visual feedback and 18 delivered feedback concurrently. Movement, posture, or technique and rhythm or timing each accounted for 9 of 43 performance outcomes. Three reports described later-session retention and two tested different pieces; assessment conditions did not consistently establish performance without feedback. Appraisal identified unclear allocation, assessor blinding, and measurement safeguards. Of seven reports examined quantitatively, two yielded standardized group differences favoring technology-supported instructional packages, and two yielded paired differences representing a feedback-format comparison and uncontrolled pre-post change. Three lacked sufficient numerical information. Heterogeneous designs and outcomes precluded pooling or technology rankings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Interpretation is limited by incomplete reporting, single-reviewer extraction with partial independent verification, and incomplete coverage of conference and gray literature. Organizing the identified evidence by feedback architecture connects the information provided with the performance processes targeted across technologies. The synthesis highlights alignment among feedback architecture, performance targets, outcome measures, and assessment conditions as a basis for distinguishing immediate performance from durable learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Systematic review registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:ext-link>https://doi.org/10.37766/inplasy2026.7.0069</jats:ext-link>
                      , identifier INPLASY202670069 (retrospectively registered).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.63808/iod.v2i4.400.title: AI Adoption Intensity and SME Innovation: A Configurational Perspective Based on Organizational Readiness and Learning Capability
doi:10.63808/iod.v2i4.400.abstract: <jats:p>This paper explores the configurations through which AI adoption intensity acts as a catalyst for innovation performance in SMEs. Based on configurational theory, a theoretical framework integrating AI adoption intensity, organizational readiness (IT infrastructure readiness, resource readiness, and culture readiness) and organizational learning capabilities (knowledge acquisition capability, knowledge integration and application capability) is developed. The findings of the fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis based on survey data collected from 196 SMEs in China indicate that none of the individual conditions is a necessary condition for achieving high levels of innovation performance. Three sufficient configurations are identified with a solution consistency score of 0.847 and a coverage score of 0.631. AI adoption intensity serves as a central condition in two configurations and a peripheral condition in one configuration, suggesting that its configurational role is context-dependent rather than uniform.</jats:p>

doi:10.1080/14790718.2026.2745152.title: Content teachers’ perceptions of science learning through CLIL: a perspective on cognitive complexity and cognitive load
doi:10.1080/14790718.2026.2745152.abstract: An understanding of the limitations of human cognitive architecture and of Cognitive Load Theory is essential for CLIL teachers to successfully manage the cognitive and linguistic challenges that arise from content-language integration. Given the limited research on the dual-layered complexity of CLIL, this study aims to explore whether—and under what conditions—cognitively demanding science subjects, such as mathematics, physics, and chemistry, can be effectively learned through CLIL from the perspective of secondary education specialist teachers. In this exploratory qualitative study, the analysis of CLIL teachers’ responses to open-ended questions revealed that learners experienced a considerable cognitive load when assimilating scientific knowledge due to its abstract nature and subject-specific demands. Although most content teachers supported the feasibility and appropriateness of teaching and learning science through CLIL, they also recognised that learners struggle to grasp complex and abstract scientific concepts and topics. The results support the view that when scientific knowledge is too cognitively demanding, CLIL learners may even experience cognitive overload. Despite these challenges, the main finding emerging from this study suggests that science learning through CLIL is feasible, provided that cognitive load is strategically managed through appropriate pedagogical design, particularly via translanguaging pedagogy and multimodal scaffolding.

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch013.title: Quantifying Learning Cultures for Organizational Excellence
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch013.abstract: <jats:p>In this chapter, it is proposed to develop a novel framework for quantifying learning cultures with integration of mathematical modeling and artificial intelligence. The aim of learning culture is to present it as a measurable organizational phenomenon based on characteristics such as leadership, engagement, knowledge flow and innovation. By developing A Learning Culture Index (LCI), systematic and quantitative evaluation of learning environments are provided. The theoretical framework integrates aspects of organizational learning and computational methods as models of organizational performance and learning culture. This framework is strengthened by the use of artificial intelligence technologies and their predictive, diagnostic, and optimization functionalities. The suggested approach provides a scalable, data-based system for evaluating, monitoring and enhancing learning culture and helps to sustain and enhance organizational excellence, innovation and adaptability and sustainable development.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch013.venue: Shaping Learning Cultures Through Effective Leadership

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch009.title: Building a Learning Culture for Organizational Excellence
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch009.abstract: <jats:p>The strategic value that introduces organizational flexibility, innovation and long-term performance to the highly dynamic business environments is learning culture. This chapter analyzes the theories, models and practices of nurturing a learning culture that embraces the daily acquisition of knowledge, skills acquisition and sharing of knowledge into organizational processes. The presence of the accent on the alignment of learning efforts with the organization objectives and learning objectives, the encouragement of learning collaboration, and the emphasis on the psychological safety to trigger experimentation and positive feedback is pointed out. The chapter ruminates on the mechanisms that include mentoring, coaching, digital learning platform, and performance support system that will be able to foster the skills of the work force and leadership. According to case studies, learning cultures have been effectively embraced in the various industries with evident productivity, innovation, employee engagement and strategic agility effects.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch009.venue: Shaping Learning Cultures Through Effective Leadership

doi:10.1145/3805696.3847299.title: Explaining the Performance Plateau in Machine Learning-based Juvenile Recidivism Prediction on PACT dataset
doi:10.1145/3805696.3847299.abstract: Predicting whether a juvenile will reoffend is an important problem in juvenile justice. The Positive Achievement Change Tool (PACT) is commonly used to assess juvenile risk and needs, but machine learning models based on PACT data often achieve Receiver Operating Characteristic - Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) values of only about 0.61–0.72. This paper investigates whether this performance plateau is caused by the machine learning pipeline or by limitations in the information available in the PACT assessment. We compared several machine learning algorithms and encoding strategies, expanded the feature set using Risk-Need-Responsivity (RNR) theory, and added county-level socioeconomic and community variables. We also used SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to examine which features contributed most to prediction. The results showed that changing algorithms, encoding strategies, and PACT feature sets produced only small changes in ROC-AUC. Adding county-level information resulted in a small but consistent improvement across repeated evaluations. SHAP analysis showed that attitudes/skills and criminal history were among the most important feature groups, while the overall PACT intake risk score contributed little once the individual assessment items were included. These results suggest that the prediction ceiling is mainly related to limitations in the information available at intake rather than the choice of machine learning method.
doi:10.1145/3805696.3847299.venue: Proceedings of the 26th ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries

doi:10.62159/jpi.v6i3.2952.title: Visual Attention Dynamics in Children with Special Needs During Eye-Tracking-Based Adaptive Learning Game Sessions in Pontianak, Indonesia
doi:10.62159/jpi.v6i3.2952.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Children with special needs (CSN), particularly those with attention disorders and autism spectrum conditions, may experience difficulty sustaining visual attention consistently. Eye-tracking technology allows visual attention to be measured objectively through eye-movement characteristics. Integrating eye tracking with an adaptive learning game has the potential to produce visual stimulation that is more responsive to individual user characteristics.
Objective: This study aimed to analyze changes in visual-attention indicators of children with special needs across three measurement sessions using an eye-tracking-based adaptive learning game.
Methods: This study used a quantitative approach with a one-group repeated-measures design. Sixteen children with special needs receiving services at the Disability Services and Assessment Center (LDAC) of Pontianak City served as subjects. Each participant underwent three measurement sessions on different days using an adaptive learning game system integrated with an eye tracker. The visual-attention indicators analyzed were mean fixation duration, saccade count, mean saccade distance, and gaze transition rate. Descriptive analysis was performed by calculating means and standard deviations. Differences across the three measurements were analyzed using the Friedman test, given the repeated-measures design on the same subjects. Post hoc analysis was conducted using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Bonferroni correction.
Results: Mean fixation duration increased from 494.50 ± 75.72 ms at the first measurement to 541.10 ± 108.74 ms and 564.87 ± 136.77 ms at the second and third measurements, but the difference across measurements was not significant (p = 0.087). Saccade count showed a significant change (p = 0.002), with the mean rising from 129.81 ± 83.31 to 223.25 ± 99.93, then decreasing to 147.69 ± 79.84. Gaze transition rate also showed a significant difference (p = 0.003), from 7.58 ± 2.66 times/second to 13.68 ± 5.56 times/second and then 9.18 ± 3.72 times/second. Mean saccade distance showed no significant difference (p = 0.087), changing from 273.03 ± 46.66 pixels, decreasing to 242.06 ± 32.52 pixels, and increasing again to 257.24 ± 42.13 pixels.
Conclusion: The eye-tracking-based adaptive learning game was associated with changes in eye-movement dynamics, particularly saccade count and gaze transition rate, across three measurement sessions. However, these changes did not follow a linear improvement pattern across all indicators. The results indicate an active oculomotor exploration phase at the second session followed by stabilization at the third session, a pattern relevant for the design of intervention sessions for children with special needs.</jats:p>

doi:10.3991/ijet.v21i04.62579.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Personalized Learning on Korean Language Performance
doi:10.3991/ijet.v21i04.62579.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming foreign language learning from traditional knowledge transmission into a data-driven adaptive learning process. Grounded in Personalized Learning Theory and technology-enhanced learning (TEL), this study examines the impact of AI application on Korean language learning performance (KAP) from the perspective of technological mediation and further explores the mediating role of intelligent recommendation systems (IRSs). Using questionnaire and academic performance data from 850 undergraduate students majoring in the Korean language, the study employs multiple regression and mediation analysis to test the proposed relationships. The results indicate that AI application significantly improves KAP (β = 4.684, p < 0.01) and exerts a significant partial mediating effect through IRSs. Specifically, AI application significantly increases the utilization of IRSs (β = 3.127, p < 0.01), while IRSs further enhance learning performance (β = 2.827, p < 0.01). Marginal effect analysis further reveals that the positive effect of AI is strongest at moderate usage levels, whereas excessive AI use leads to diminishing marginal returns. The findings demonstrate that AI not only directly improves learning outcomes through real-time feedback, speech recognition, and personalized learning support, but also promotes resource allocation optimization and dynamic learning path adjustment through AI-driven adaptive learning mechanisms. This study extends the mechanism-oriented explanation of AI-assisted language learning within the context of Korean language education and provides theoretical and practical implications for the development of intelligent and personalized Korean language learning platforms in higher education.</jats:p>
doi:10.3991/ijet.v21i04.62579.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
