doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch002.title: Integrating Learning Theories for Dynamic Learning Environments
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch002.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines major learning theories that have influenced contemporary education, including Behaviourism, Cognitivism, Constructivism, Humanism, Social Learning Theory, Experiential Learning Theory, and Transformative Learning Theory. The chapter argues that no single theory can adequately address the complexity of modern educational environments and proposes an integrated perspective for understanding learning. It analyzes the assumptions, strengths, limitations, and educational implications of each theory and explores their contributions to learner engagement, critical thinking, collaboration, personal development, and lifelong learning. The chapter also examines the relationship between learning theories and assessment practices, educational equity, and the growing role of artificial intelligence in teaching and learning. Through comparative analysis and practical applications, the chapter presents an integrated framework for designing dynamic, inclusive, and transformative learning environments that support both academic achievement and holistic learner development.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-0353-4.ch002.venue: Shaping Learning Cultures Through Effective Leadership

doi:10.3389/fphy.2026.1953430.title: A hierarchical evolutionary deep reinforcement learning algorithm for influence maximization in multilayer hypergraphs
doi:10.3389/fphy.2026.1953430.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Multilayer hypergraphs provide a unified representation of influence diffusion in complex networks by coupling relation layers through shared entities and encoding higher-order group interactions as hyperedges. Existing influence maximization (IM) methods have been extensively studied on ordinary graphs and single-layer hypergraphs, yet they leave two structural limitations unresolved. Single-layer methods cannot represent the propagation of an entity across multiple relation semantics, whereas most multilayer methods still use pairwise edges as their basic diffusion units and therefore omit hyperedge-induced group interactions. We address seed selection under the joint effects of multilayer coupling and higher-order influence by introducing Multi-Layer Hypergraph Linear Threshold with Cross-layer Thresholding (MLH-LT-CT). The model combines a dual-threshold intralayer mechanism for hyperedges and nodes with a
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="m1">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mi>δ</mml:mi>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    -threshold rule that couples entity states across relation layers. We extend the non-submodularity result for the single-layer hypergraph linear threshold (LT) model to the multilayer setting and show that cross-layer thresholding can further modify the marginal-gain structure induced by intralayer higher-order coordination. Consequently, the classical
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" id="m2">
                        <mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo>
                          <mml:mrow>
                            <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                            <mml:mo>−</mml:mo>
                            <mml:mn>1</mml:mn>
                            <mml:mo>/</mml:mo>
                            <mml:mi>e</mml:mi>
                          </mml:mrow>
                          <mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo>
                        </mml:mrow>
                      </mml:math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    guarantee for submodular greedy maximization does not directly apply. To optimize this non-submodular objective, we propose Hierarchical Influence Via Evolution (HIVE), which integrates population-level global search by differential evolution, adaptive seed-selection guidance from a deep Q-network, and topology-guided local refinement. We also establish an incremental-propagation equivalence theorem from the extensivity, idempotence, and monotonicity of the propagation closure. The theorem establishes equality of the final diffusion state obtained by incremental updates and full recomputation; it is not itself a running-time guarantee. Across 11 synthetic and real multilayer hypergraph datasets, HIVE strictly outperformed MA-IM on eight datasets. The ablation and sensitivity analyses further assess the contributions of evolutionary search, reinforcement-learning guidance, and topology-guided refinement; additional threshold scans characterize the transition between saturated, discriminative, and propagation-suppressed regimes; the correctness of incremental state reuse is established theoretically. These results support explicit cross-layer threshold modeling and hierarchical optimization as a coherent approach to non-submodular influence maximization in multilayer higher-order diffusion systems.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1142/s0218001426400744.title: Recognition of Cognitive Intervention Effects and Modeling of Learning Behavior Patterns in Second Language Acquisition Using a Multimodal Intervention-Aware Temporal Graph Network
doi:10.1142/s0218001426400744.abstract: <jats:p>To distinguish between “text improvement” and “cognitive gain” in generative-AI-assisted second language learning, this study proposes a Multimodal Intervention-Aware Temporal Graph Network (MITG-Net). The method integrates human-AI dialogue, revision trajectories, behavioral logs, and learner attributes. Through intervention-conditioned dynamic weighting and heterogeneous temporal graph modeling, it captures the relationships among prompts, feedback, revisions, and transfer, and jointly performs intervention-effect recognition and learning-behavior-pattern discovery. Experiments were conducted on 744 learning sessions collected from 186 undergraduates at three universities. MITG-Net achieved a Macro-F1 of 0.816 and a weighted Kappa of 0.854, outperforming the strongest baseline, HGT, by 3.4 percentage points in Macro-F1. Removing behavioral logs and revision trajectories reduced Macro-F1 by 0.054 and 0.045, respectively. The model identified five behavior patterns. Among them, the strategy-transfer application pattern achieved an average effect level of 2.78 and a transfer score of 0.82, substantially higher than the 1.36 and 0.31 obtained by the AI-dominated direct-adoption pattern. These results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively recognize cognitive intervention effects and provide interpretable evidence for personalized support in second language learning.</jats:p>
doi:10.1142/s0218001426400744.venue: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence

doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02310-z.title: A comprehensive review and bibliometric analysis of deep learning applications in plant disease detection
doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02310-z.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Agriculture is a major component of many countries’ economies worldwide, especially in developing nations. The major challenge farmers face is the rapid spread of plant diseases, which often goes unnoticed and causes major yield and economic losses. Traditional methods such as human inspection and laboratory testing are often time-consuming, inaccurate, labor-intensive, and unsuitable for large-scale farming. To overcome these challenges, advanced technologies like Machine learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) have emerged in recent times, providing early and accurate detection of plant diseases. This paper focuses on recent advances in applying deep learning techniques, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), to detect plant diseases. Across 1081 publications from 2014 to 2024, studies show that CNNs are well suited to extracting and analyzing features from plant images and clearly distinguishing healthy from diseased specimens. The models discussed in the surveyed literature generally report performance in terms of key parameters such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, which this review compiles and discusses rather than benchmarking through new experiments. The results show high accuracy and strong potential for real-world agricultural applications. The bibliometric analysis reveals growing interest and collaborative efforts in the research domain, especially among institutions specializing in artificial intelligence and agriculture. Moreover, the results support the practical application of deep learning in agriculture for plant health monitoring and highlight the importance of comprehensive studies in solving agricultural problems. The study provides a foundation for further innovations in automated plant disease detection and supports the transition to smart farming solutions.</jats:p>

doi:10.1145/3805696.3847136.title: Longitudinal Study of Web Page Lifespans and Evolution via Wayback Machine Sampling
doi:10.1145/3805696.3847136.abstract: To quantify web page longevity, our study samples from the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine to curate the NYPW Sample, comprising 27.3 million HTML URLs spanning 26 years of web history (1996–2021). Our empirical findings indicate an average web page lifespan of 5.0 years (median 2.3 years), with a substantial disparity between root URLs (median 8.8 years) and deep links (median 1.3 years). Traditional quantitative analyses of webpage longevity generally consider a URL as a static identifier, which may not capture the complex lifecycles in which underlying content, ownership, or semantic purpose changes while a link remains active. To address this limitation, we proposed the Multi-Resident URL framework, which models six distinct lifecycle phases and formally separates structural URL stability from evolving content identity. Furthermore, our redirection analysis demonstrates the fragility of relocated content, revealing that only 50% of redirecting URIs resolve to active pages and illustrating how redirection shapes domain states and creates sink URIs. Through an integrated analysis of web resource survival, temporal stability, URL lifecycle evolution, and redirection behavior, we aim to improve the accuracy of web-archive studies, reduce reliance on detailed memento analysis, advance archiving practices, and deepen understanding of long-term web content persistence.
doi:10.1145/3805696.3847136.venue: Proceedings of the 26th ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries

doi:10.54254/2755-2721/2026.37598.title: Deep Learning-Based Calligraphic Aesthetic Assessment Guided by Gestalt Psychological Features
doi:10.54254/2755-2721/2026.37598.abstract: <jats:p>Calligraphic aesthetic assessment requires the information about local stroke appearance and the spatial organization of the complete character. This paper develops a supervised regression method that combines twelve Gestalt-inspired geometric descriptors with a ResNet50 image encoder. The descriptors quantify the visual balance, ink distribution, reflected structure, projection rhythm, and distance-transform smoothness. Two feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) modules convert these measurements into channel-wise scales and shifts for intermediate convolutional features. A direct-concatenation control supplies the same descriptors to the regression head. This design allows explicit geometric information to interact with the learned visual representations during score prediction. In the ResNet50 experiment, intermediate FiLM achieves PCC 0.7067 and MAE 1.3554, compared with 0.6958 and 1.3793 for image-only regression. In whole-work assessment, combining local window-score statistics with global layout descriptors achieves PCC 0.6323. These results support descriptor-guided regression at the character level and the combination of local appearance with global composition for whole-work assessment.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10949679/v1.title: AFB-MAC: A Fuzzy-Bandit Reinforcement Learning Framework for Adaptive MAC Protocol Selection in Dynamic Wireless Sensor Networks
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10949679/v1.abstract: The structural weakness of classical design for Medium Access Control (MAC) is that a single fixed protocol (contention-based, schedule-based, or hybrid) is not efficient in all operating regimes in Dynamic Wireless Sensor Networks (DWSNs), which are networks where node mobility, duty-cycled sleep, spatially and temporally varying traffic, fluctuating interference change operating regime at runtime. Current adaptive techniques adjust the parameters of a protocol or employ a fixed heuristic to select the protocol to switch to, and adapt slowly, suffer from oscillations under noisy state estimates, and are not globally applicable across a wide range of deployments. AFB-MAC Selection is an Adaptive Fuzzy-Bandit MAC Selection framework in which each node deploys a lightweight self-learning agent that (i) estimates the residual energy, traffic intensity, channel occupancy from local observations, and mobility class from the channel's defined mobility model, (ii) transforms these noisy estimates into smooth suitability scores for the candidate MAC protocols using a fuzzy inference layer, and (iii) fuses these scores with an Upper-Confidence-Bound contextual-bandit learner refined by a Q-learning credit-assignment step to select and switch at runtime the active MAC protocol. The fuzzy layer is used to reduce the selection oscillation when there is measurement noise, and the bandit-Q hybrid ensures that the agent keeps exploring the network rather than getting stuck on an initial estimate. The performance of AFB-MAC is compared to five baselines: S-MAC, T-MAC, X-MAC, a reinforcement-learning MAC selector (SOMAC-style), and an ML-based adaptive MAC (ML-MAC), on networks of 50–300 nodes and traffic loads of 1–12 packets/s/node in a discrete-event simulation. The results demonstrate that AFB-MAC can achieve a packet delivery ratio up to 9.4 percentage points higher than S-MAC and 2.1 points higher than the best learning-based baseline under high load, reduce the energy consumption per node by 34–57% when compared to the classical protocols, decrease the end-to-end delay up to 46% at high topology dynamicity, and enhance the half-node-death lifetime of the network by approximately 60% compared to S-MAC. The results show that the proposed fuzzy and bandit reinforcement learning based self-adaptive MAC operation is a suitable approach with low overhead in the highly dynamic WSN deployment.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10949679/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.1186/s43897-026-00251-w.title: Machine learning-guided leaf margin classification and discovery that BcPHB promoter selection rewires a BcPHB–BcLMI1 module to shape leaf margins in Brassica campestris
doi:10.1186/s43897-026-00251-w.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The morphological diversification of leaf margins reflects the evolutionary reshaping of conserved developmental programs. However, fully deciphering the underlying molecular basis remains challenging due to difficulties in phenotype quantification and the incomplete characterization of complex regulatory networks. In this study, we established a computer-vision framework to decode leaf lobe trait and identified the HD-ZIP III factor
                    <jats:italic>PHABULOSA</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    ), combining genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and selective sweep analysis in
                    <jats:italic>Brassica campestris</jats:italic>
                    . We found that promoter variation defines two major haplotypes,
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>HapI</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>HapII</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    , driving divergent expression levels associated with entire and lobed leaves. Functionally,
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    knockdown lines (
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>ami</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    ) exhibited lobed margins, whereas complementation of lobed accessions with the
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>HapI</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    promoter partially restored the entire-leaf phenotype. Similarly, overexpression of
                    <jats:italic>LATE MERISTEM IDENTITY 1</jats:italic>
                    (
                    <jats:italic>BcLMI1</jats:italic>
                    ), a conserved regulator of leaf lobation, phenocopied the
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>ami</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    lines. Mechanistically,
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>BcLMI1</jats:italic>
                    form a reciprocal negative feedback loop that stabilizes margin patterning. Furthermore, domestication-driven selection of
                    <jats:italic>BcPHB</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>
                      <jats:italic>HapI</jats:italic>
                    </jats:sup>
                    facilitated the transition from ancestral lobed leaves to cultivated entire forms. This study reveals a pivotal developmental module and illustrates how regulatory evolution drives morphological diversification in crops.

doi:10.58830/ozgur.pub1473.c5893.title: Digitalization in Education, E-Learning, and Learning Analytics: Theoretical Perspectives
doi:10.58830/ozgur.pub1473.c5893.abstract:
<jats:p>The increasing digitalization of education has expanded the use of e-learning environments, learning analytics, and data-driven interventions; however, the theoretical assumptions underlying these technologies are not always explicitly incorporated into their design. This chapter examines the relationship between educational theory, digital learning environments, and learning analytics through a selective narrative synthesis of foundational and contemporary literature. It discusses constructivism, sociocultural theory, cognitive load theory, self-determination theory, blended learning, behaviorism, and process-oriented learning analytics frameworks, emphasizing how different theoretical perspectives shape the conceptualization of knowledge, learning activities, motivation, measurement, and intervention.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>The analysis further addresses personalization and adaptivity, digital inequality, algorithmic bias, and ethical considerations associated with educational data use. Two institutional cases, Purdue University's Course Signals and The Open University's OU Analyze, are examined to illustrate the practical consequences of different approaches to theoretical grounding, causal inference, implementation, and pedagogical intervention. The chapter argues that the central challenge in educational technology is not the absence of theory but its limited operationalization as a design constraint. Effective educational technologies therefore require theoretical commitments to influence what systems measure, how they interpret learner data, what interventions they recommend, and how their educational impact is evaluated. The chapter concludes that prediction accuracy and technological sophistication alone are insufficient; theory-informed design, contextualized pedagogical intervention, ethical safeguards, educator involvement, and evaluation based on meaningful learning outcomes are essential for sustainable and responsible digital education.</jats:p>
doi:10.58830/ozgur.pub1473.c5893.venue: Algorithmic Transformation: Technological, Managerial, Social, and Economic Dimensions of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization

doi:10.1186/s12872-026-06751-3.title: Risk prediction and probabilistic inference of carotid atherosclerosis based on machine learning algorithms and Bayesian network analysis
doi:10.1186/s12872-026-06751-3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Carotid atherosclerosis, an important subclinical manifestation of vascular injury, is closely associated with stroke, cardiovascular events, and systemic atherosclerotic burden. This study aimed to identify stable predictive factors for carotid atherosclerosis, characterize the interrelationships among these factors, and quantify their probabilistic impact on carotid atherosclerosis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 22,012 participants who underwent carotid ultrasound examinations at the Health Management Center of a tertiary hospital in Lanzhou, Northwest China, between 2023 and 2024 were included. Carotid atherosclerosis was defined as the presence of carotid plaques detected by ultrasonography. The dataset was randomly divided into training and testing sets at a ratio of 7:3. Five machine learning models were developed: LASSO-regularized logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, decision tree, and CatBoost. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, precision-recall curves, and decision curve analysis. Variables consistently identified by the best-performing models were used to construct a Bayesian network. Network structure was learned using the Maximum-Minimum Hill-Climbing algorithm, and conditional probabilities were calculated to quantify changes in the posterior probability of carotid atherosclerosis under different risk-factor patterns.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 22,012 participants, 8,987 (40.8%) were classified as having carotid atherosclerosis, while 13,025 (59.2%) were classified as having no carotid atherosclerosis. Among the five models, LASSO and CatBoost showed the best discrimination, each achieving an AUC of 0.803. LASSO provided higher sensitivity and more balanced classification performance, whereas CatBoost achieved the best overall accuracy, calibration, specificity, and positive predictive value. The two models identified 10 common predictors for Bayesian network construction. The final network contained seven nodes and 14 edges, with carotid atherosclerosis related conditional dependencies mainly involving older age, male sex, overweight, dyslipidemia, and elevated fasting blood glucose. The highest posterior probability of carotid atherosclerosis, 78.3%, was observed in individuals aged ≥ 60 years who were overweight and had elevated triglycerides and fasting blood glucose. Age and fasting blood glucose emerged as the most prominent nodes: age ≥ 60 years produced the largest increase from the prior probability, while elevated fasting blood glucose was consistently associated with higher carotid atherosclerosis probability across combinations with and without age. Gender-stratified analyses showed acceptable performance in both sexes, although discrimination and calibration were weaker in women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared with conventional risk prediction alone, this integrated prediction-inference framework may improve identification of individuals at high risk of carotid atherosclerosis while enhancing clinical interpretability. However, prospective studies and external validation in independent populations are required before clinical application.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.47941/japsy.4035.title: Effect of Blended Learning Strategy on Learning Motivation of Early Childhood Education Pupils in Katsina State, Nigeria
doi:10.47941/japsy.4035.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose: This study examined the effect of a blended learning strategy on the learning motivation of Early Childhood Education (ECE) pupils in Katsina State, Nigeria. Methodology: The research utilized a pre-test, post-test, non-randomized control group quasi-experimental design involving 188 ECE pupils (105 males, 83 females) selected through multi-stage sampling from public primary schools in Dutsin-Ma Zonal Education Quality Assurance (ZEQA). The experimental group (n=96) received six weeks of literacy and numeracy instruction via a WhatsApp-mediated flipped classroom model, while the control group (n=92) was taught using conventional face-to-face instruction. Data were collected using the Adapted Motivational Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (AMSLQ) and analyzed using paired-sample t-tests, independent-sample t-tests, and Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) in SPSS at an α=.05 significance level. Findings: Findings revealed a statistically significant increase in pupils' motivation scores within the experimental group following the intervention (t(95)=-19.41,p<.001). Furthermore, ANCOVA results demonstrated that after controlling for pre-test motivation scores, pupils taught using the blended learning strategy exhibited significantly higher post-test motivation scores than those taught using conventional methods (F(1,185)=7.490,p=.007). Additionally, no statistically significant difference was observed in post-test motivation scores between male (M=2.80,SD=0.47) and female (M=2.66,SD=0.42) pupils in the experimental group (t(94)=1.52,p=.373), indicating gender neutrality. The study concludes that blended learning is a superior and gender-inclusive pedagogical approach for boosting pupil engagement in ECE settings. Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: The study extends Self‑Determination Theory by showing that WhatsApp‑mediated flipped instruction fosters autonomy and competence among young learners in resource‑limited settings. It urges policymakers to adopt low‑bandwidth mobile tools in ECE curricula and offers educators a scalable, gender‑neutral blended model enhancing early literacy and numeracy motivation without widening gender gaps.</jats:p>

doi:10.1145/3805696.3846026.title: Supporting Information-Need Expression with Icons and Text: An Exploratory Study with Adults with Learning Disabilities
doi:10.1145/3805696.3846026.abstract: Access to digital information depends on a user’s ability to express an information need before a retrieval or answer system can respond. Text-centred query interfaces can make this entry point difficult for adults with learning disabilities when interaction depends on spelling, lexical recall, and abstract keyword construction. We combined community fieldwork with an exploratory study of an icon-supported multimodal query interface paired with a generative answer backend. Fieldwork observations informed design requirements for recognition-based input, visual composition, guided suggestions, and simplified interaction. Seven adults completed two structured activities under instruction-defined icon and text conditions within the same multimodal system, followed by a self-directed free-choice task. Screen and session recordings were analysed to trace query trajectories, assistance, input-resource crossovers, response outcomes, and observable evidence that participants followed the responses. Retrospective ratings of the two structured conditions and synchronised physiological traces provided secondary descriptive context. The observed patterns did not indicate a single best input resource. Most participants selected icon input for the self-directed task, but responses addressing the intended need were observed with both input resources. A crossover from text to icon input was also observed during query repair, while icon input sometimes introduced ambiguity and required assistance. We contribute a traceable account linking field observations to interface design and derive implications for inclusive digital-library query interfaces: providing multiple input resources, supporting movement between them, and making the system’s interpretation of a query visible to users. Given the small sample, fixed condition order, and use of generated rather than collection-retrieved answers, the findings should be treated as exploratory design evidence.
doi:10.1145/3805696.3846026.venue: Proceedings of the 26th ACM/IEEE Joint Conference on Digital Libraries

doi:10.1071/wf26142.title: Machine learning assessment of climate-driven variability in European forest fire burnt areas
doi:10.1071/wf26142.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite intensifying fire-conducive weather, European burnt forest areas show a contradictory trend, suggesting moderation by fire management systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aims</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We tested whether climate variables remain dominant drivers of burnt forest area variability across Europe, and whether machine learning models can robustly predict fire outcomes despite fire management changes over recent decades.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed forest fire data from 22 European countries (1990–2024) from United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) greenhouse gas reports, developing ensemble machine learning models using fire weather indices, dead fuel moisture, soil moisture and country as a categorical variable representing country-specific factors, including differences in fire management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Key results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The ensemble model explained 79 and 80% of variance in the calibration and verification datasets. Despite generally increasing fire-conducive weather, 20 of 22 countries showed stable or declining burnt areas; however, a pan-European break-point around the year 2014 indicates a reversal from declining to an increasing trend.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Climate-based models remain robust predictors of fire outcomes. European fire management appears to have successfully decoupled outcomes from climate pressure, but future climate change may challenge this effectiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adaptive management strategies and proactive knowledge transfer from Mediterranean to Boreal regions are crucial in the face of progressing climate change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fbioe.2026.1912951.title: A bimodal deep learning framework for cerebral perfusion assessment using synchronous ECG and near-field coupled CBF signals
doi:10.3389/fbioe.2026.1912951.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate real-time assessment of cerebral blood flow (CBF) is crucial for optimizing treatment decisions and improving prognostic outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke (AIS). In this study, leveraging the advantage of near-field coupling (NFC) technology in capturing blood flow information from intracranial vessels of different sizes, and in combination with synchronous ECG signals reflecting cardiac rhythm fluctuations, we propose a bimodal deep learning framework to characterize cerebral perfusion-related state changes under postural tilt using synchronous ECG and NFC-based CBF (NFC-CBF) signals. The framework consists of a Multi-Scale Feature Extractor (MSFE) and a Depthwise-Separable Cross-Attention Fusion (DSCAF) module, which work collaboratively to achieve hierarchical temporal representation learning and cross-modal fusion of ECG and NFC-CBF signals. Using synchronous ECG and NFC-CBF data collected from young and middle-aged healthy volunteers, we evaluated the proposed framework in binary and four-class classification tasks to assess its feasibility for cerebral perfusion-related state classification. The results show that NFC-CBF signals can capture CBF changes before and after tilt. Synchronous monitoring of ECG and NFC-CBF provided complementary information on cardiac rhythm and cerebral perfusion-related dynamics. The proposed framework outperforms Bimodal Feature Fusion, ResNet-SE-LSTM, and Cross-Transformer Network in terms of accuracy, F1-score, specificity, precision, and recall, achieving accuracies of 95.95% ± 1.54% and 79.29% ± 2.12% in the binary posture classification and four-class age–posture classification tasks, respectively. Ablation experiments indicate that bimodal modeling provided additional discriminative information compared with single-modality inputs, particularly for the four-class task involving both posture and age. The classification performance achieved after incorporating the DSCAF module is superior to that of other conventional feature fusion strategies. These findings support the feasibility of bimodal ECG and NFC-CBF modeling for cerebral perfusion-related state classification under postural perturbation, while further validation in larger, more diverse, and demographically balanced cohorts, including both patient and non-patient populations, is required before its clinical applicability can be established.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/diseases14100377.title: Prognostic Modeling of 1-Year Survival in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Methods with Class Balancing
doi:10.3390/diseases14100377.abstract: <jats:p>Objective: To develop and comparatively evaluate machine learning models for predicting 1-year survival in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients, focusing on the prognostic interplay between chronic liver diseases and diabetes aligned with the EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines (2018), and to assess the impact of class balancing via Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) on model performance. Methods: Retrospective analysis was performed on the UCI HCC Survival Dataset (N = 165). Following median/mode imputation of ~10% missing values, four classifiers were evaluated: Logistic Regression (LR), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Gradient Boosting (GB), and Random Forest (RF), each trained with and without SMOTE oversampling (eight variants total). Models were trained on 16 EASL-aligned clinical and biochemical features using a stratified 80/20 train/test split (training N = 132, held-out test N = 33). Performance was evaluated via accuracy, AUC-ROC (with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals across 1000 iterations), precision, recall, and macro F1-score. Stratified 5-fold cross-validation and multiple imputation sensitivity analyses (MissForest, KNN, MICE, complete-case) were conducted. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) was applied to the top-performing model to provide patient-level interpretability. Results: Diabetes was present in 33.9% of patients (56/165; 28/102 survivors [27.5%] vs. 28/63 non-survivors [44.4%]). Diabetes was significantly associated with 1-year mortality in univariate analysis (χ2 = 5.02, p = 0.025) but not after multivariable adjustment (aOR = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.21–1.22, p = 0.129). GB + SMOTE achieved the highest discriminative ability (AUC-ROC: 0.727, 95% CI: 0.552–0.886), while LR + SMOTE yielded the highest overall accuracy (72.7%) and macro F1-score (0.723). Without SMOTE, all models exhibited poor minority-class detection (non-survival F1 range: 0.300–0.615). SMOTE markedly improved non-survival recall across LR (0.231 to 0.769) and GB (61.5% to 69.2%). Stratified 5-fold CV AUC on the training set was highest for RF (0.779 ± 0.100), followed by GB (0.744 ± 0.065). TreeSHAP analysis identified ECOG performance status (mean |SHAP| = 1.284) and ALT (1.060) as the most influential predictors; diabetes ranked 15th (mean |SHAP| = 0.014), consistent with minimal independent predictive contribution. Conclusions: Gradient boosting and regularized linear regression combined with SMOTE class balancing provide competitive, well-calibrated, and transparent risk stratification on small, imbalanced tabular HCC datasets, offering an exploratory proof-of-concept for personalized prognostic modeling that requires external validation.</jats:p>

doi:10.3991/ijet.v21i04.62480.title: An Explainable Early Warning System for Student Academic Risk Prediction Based on Time-Windowing and SHAP
doi:10.3991/ijet.v21i04.62480.abstract: <jats:p>High dropout rates in online learning remain a persistent challenge, while many early warning systems (EWS) provide risk scores without explaining what instructors should do next. This study proposes an explainable EWS that integrates XGBoost with SHAP under a strict 30-day time-windowing protocol on the OULAD dataset, enhanced with five behavior-pattern features. The 30-day window is validated through a 14/30/60-day ablation, with PR-AUC reported to address class imbalance and robustness tested on the KDD Cup 2015 MOOC dataset. To preserve prospective prediction, OULAD records from students who had already withdrawn before the prediction-window endpoint were excluded. On OULAD Day-30, XGBoost achieved the strongest ranking and F1 performance under student-grouped cross-validation, with AUC 0.7865, PR-AUC 0.7652, and F1 0.6745. Day-14 reduced AUC to 0.7353 due to sparse early assignment submissions, whereas Day-60 improved AUC to 0.8154 but reduced intervention time. On KDD Cup 2015, XGBoost achieved AUC 0.8639 and PR-AUC 0.9498 under username-grouped cross-validation. SHAP identified first-assignment score, assignment lead time, active days, and selected academic-background features as key risk drivers, supporting targeted interventions rather than generic risk alerts.</jats:p>
doi:10.3991/ijet.v21i04.62480.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)

doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202662195.title: A deep learning approach to member identification and mass estimation in galaxy clusters
doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202662195.abstract:
<jats:p>Accurate dynamical mass estimates of galaxy clusters are essential for studies of cluster formation and evolution and for cosmological applications. However, interloper galaxies, which are not gravitationally bound to the cluster but are incorrectly identified as members, can bias dynamical mass measurements and increase their uncertainties.
We developed a probabilistic deep-learning framework for cluster member identification and dynamical mass estimation and tested the sensitivity of the inferred masses to cluster miscentring and radially dependent incompleteness in controlled mock experiments.
We used mock galaxy cluster catalogues to train a two-stage model. In this model, a long short-term memory (LSTM) network assigns membership probabilities to galaxies arranged by projected phase-space proximity. These probabilities are then used to construct membership-weighted projected phase-space density maps, from which a Bayesian neural network (BNN) infers cluster masses and predictive uncertainties.
The LSTM membership probabilities are well calibrated and form an isoprobability envelope in the projected phase space, with the łangle p_ ̊m mem ̊angle=0.5 contour broadly tracing the empirical member--interloper transition. Applying a threshold of p_ th =0.5 provides a good balance between member completeness and purity, with high completeness within R_ proj <r_ 200 . Membership weighting lowers the residual scatter of the fiducial BNN mass estimator, mathrm BNN _ 2D ^ Mem , to σ_ε=0.120, a 19.5% reduction relative to the unweighted baseline, although the predictive uncertainties are not uniformly calibrated across the BNN models. Using the brightest cluster galaxy rather than the gravitational centre lowers the median inferred mass by up to 47.6%, with larger reductions at larger centring offsets. By contrast, removing 40% of eligible non-central galaxies within r_200 lowers it by 6.1% relative to complete catalogues.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1913614.title: Technology-enhanced and AI-supported instruction: a meta-analysis of student learning outcomes with implications for writing development
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1913614.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has introduced new paradigms for teaching, learning, and assessment, especially in the development of students’ writing performance. This meta-analysis examines the effectiveness of blended, technology-enhanced, and AI-supported instructional interventions on student learning outcomes. Eleven studies representing 477 participants across primary, secondary, and higher-education settings were synthesized. The included studies represented heterogeneous educational contexts and assessed outcomes such as academic achievement, literacy, vocabulary and language learning, digital literacy, and motivation. Accordingly, the pooled effect represents an overall effect on student learning outcomes rather than a writing-proficiency-specific effect. Studies were identified through ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar and represented 477 participants across elementary, secondary, and higher-education settings and diverse disciplinary contexts. The results revealed a large and statistically significant pooled effect size [Hedges’ g = 0.89, 95% CI (0.76, 1.10)], showing that students who participated in technology-enhanced instructional interventions outperformed those receiving traditional instruction. Exploratory moderator analyses showed differences according to educational level, intervention duration, and technology type, with primary and secondary students, medium-length interventions (4–8 weeks), and interactive tools showing the strongest effects. The findings show the potential of thoughtfully integrated digital and AI-supported tools to enhance teaching and learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.7717/peerj-cs.4117.title: Towards efficient student performance prediction with tabular prior-data fitted network: a small-sample learning approach in data-scarce scenarios
doi:10.7717/peerj-cs.4117.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate prediction of student academic performance is crucial for enhancing educational outcomes and enabling personalized learning interventions. However, the limited availability of labeled data in many practical educational settings poses significant challenges for conventional machine learning models, which often require large datasets to achieve satisfactory performance and are prone to overfitting. To address this issue, we propose a novel small-sample learning framework based on the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN). By integrating a Transformer based architecture with Bayesian inference, TabPFN effectively leverages meta-learned priors to perform high-quality predictions without task-specific finetuning. We evaluated the approach on the Mathematics and Portuguese subsets of the UCI Student Performance dataset and on a pooled Combined dataset under small-sample conditions. Experimental results indicate that TabPFN achieved generally strong and competitive performance across the three datasets, with accuracies of 92.36%, 95.49%, and 94.29%, respectively. However, its advantage varied across datasets and metrics, and the results should be interpreted cautiously where confidence intervals overlapped with strong baseline models. Additionally, we employ Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) to interpret model decisions, identifying key influencing factors such as prior grades (G1, G2) and prior educational experience. The findings indicate that TabPFN constitutes a promising and effective solution for educational prediction in data scarce scenarios but also provides actionable insights for instructional design and student support.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8352-1.ch013.title: Designing AI-Enabled Enterprise Architecture to Support Online Problem-Based Learning in Undergraduate Studies
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8352-1.ch013.abstract: <jats:p>This study proposes an intelligent Online Problem-Based Learning (OPBL) enterprise architecture, a systems-based framework explaining how OPBL operates effectively in undergraduate finance education. Using a mixed-methods design integrating questionnaires, interviews, and reflections, the research demonstrates that OPBL effectiveness emerges from the coordinated interaction of cognitive scaffolding, social collaboration, process-visible assessment, digital mediation, and governance safeguards rather than from isolated instructional techniques. Findings show that structured workflows, continuous feedback, facilitator presence, and intentional community design reduce cognitive load, enhance engagement, and support the development of employability skills such as problem-solving, critical thinking, and leadership. The chapter further argues that OPBL should be implemented as an enterprise learning architecture aligned with institutional quality frameworks and ethical governance, preparing finance graduates for digitally mediated and AI-enabled professional environments.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8352-1.ch013.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1922098.title: Machine learning-based prediction model for hypoalbuminemia in ICU patients with venous thromboembolism and acute kidney injury
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1922098.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hypoalbuminemia is a prevalent and critical complication among intensive care unit (ICU) patients with venous thromboembolism (VTE) and acute kidney injury (AKI), significantly associated with increased mortality and prolonged hospitalization. However, reliable tools for early prediction of hypoalbuminemia in this high-risk population remain limited. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning-based prediction model for hypoalbuminemia in ICU patients with coexisting VTE and AKI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In this retrospective study, data from 585 ICU patients with VTE and AKI were analyzed. Patients were divided into a training cohort (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 409) and a validation cohort (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 176). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression with standardization was applied for feature selection. Five machine learning models-logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), and support vector machine (SVM)-were developed and evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Decision curve analysis (DCA), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and feature importance were performed for the optimal model. The performance of the best machine learning model was compared with conventional ICU severity scores (APSIII, LODs, and OASIS).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The standardized LASSO regression identified ten optimal predictors: creatinine (cr), age, tumor/cancer, body mass index (BMI), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), urine output, D-dimer (D_D), Charlson comorbidity index, anticoagulant use, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT). Among the five models, XGBoost achieved the best predictive performance with a validation AUC of 0.882 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.832–0.924], followed by RF (AUC = 0.878), LightGBM (AUC = 0.870), LR (AUC = 0.838), and SVM (AUC = 0.662). The 5-fold cross-validation AUC for XGBoost was 0.901 ± 0.042, with minimal overfitting (CV-test difference = −0.019). Decision curve analysis demonstrated favorable clinical net benefit of the XGBoost model across a wide range of threshold probabilities. SHAP analysis and feature importance consistently identified urine output, age, LDL, BMI, and D-dimer as the top contributors. Compared with conventional ICU severity scores, the XGBoost model significantly outperformed APSIII (AUC = 0.661), LODs (AUC = 0.652), and OASIS (AUC = 0.647). The logistic regression-based nomogram achieved a C-index of 0.838, providing a user-friendly bedside tool for clinicians.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The machine learning-based XGBoost model, incorporating ten readily available clinical variables, demonstrated excellent predictive performance for hypoalbuminemia in ICU patients with VTE and AKI. This model offers a practical and interpretable tool for early risk stratification and may guide proactive nutritional and therapeutic interventions in this vulnerable population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1922481.title: Development and multicenter validation of a machine learning model for predicting in-hospital postoperative cardiac arrest in elderly surgical patients: the critical role of intraoperative hemodynamic disturbances and blood transfusion
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1922481.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is a rare but life-threatening complication in elderly surgical patients. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning model for predicting IHCA and to identify key perioperative risk factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients aged ≥65 years who underwent non-cardiac surgery at six tertiary hospitals between January 2020 and January 2025. Clinical, laboratory, and perioperative variables were collected. Five machine learning algorithms, including Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), and K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN), were developed and compared. Model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, calibration, decision curve analysis, cross-validation, and external validation. SHAP analysis was applied to interpret the optimal model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among the five models, XGBoost demonstrated the best predictive performance, with AUCs of 0.967 and 0.960 in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. It also achieved the lowest Brier score and the highest clinical net benefit. External validation confirmed excellent discrimination (AUC=0.971) and calibration. SHAP analysis identified advanced age, intraoperative tachycardia, intraoperative hypotension, intraoperative blood transfusion, intraoperative hypoxemia, elevated postoperative neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, B-type natriuretic peptide, lactate, and D-dimer levels as the most important predictors of IHCA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An interpretable XGBoost-based model demonstrated excellent performance for predicting postoperative cardiac arrest in elderly patients. The identified risk factors reflected perioperative vulnerability, intraoperative hemodynamic instability, and postoperative physiological deterioration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

arxiv:2610.17241.title: Anomaly Detection in Bunch Oscillations for Early Warning of Sudden Beam Loss at SuperKEKB
arxiv:2610.17241.abstract: Sudden beam loss (SBL) events at the SuperKEKB collider result in the loss of a large fraction of the stored beam within just a few revolutions, on a timescale comparable to or shorter than the 20-30 μs latency of the existing abort system. Such events have damaged collimators and threaten Belle II subdetectors. Bunch Oscillation Recorders (BORs) capture transverse bunch positions at each revolution, which often show sizable oscillations that precede significant beam current loss. We test whether these precursors can be detected earlier than a charge-based reference that mimics the existing abort sensors. We apply several oscillation-based anomaly detection algorithms to 208 SBL events recorded in the low-energy ring during the 2024 run period, ranging from simple rolling statistics to machine learning models trained to forecast bunch oscillation. On 173 events not used for training or calibration, the best-balanced model (DeepLSTM) triggers before the charge-based reference in 86-90% of events across five training seeds, with a mean lead time of 25-30 μs. The only trigger classified as a false alarm fires on an oscillation that begins about 60 turns before the abort and persists until the beam is lost, making it more likely an early precursor than a spurious trigger. These results establish bunch oscillations as a viable early abort trigger and motivate a shadow-mode deployment to measure the false-alarm rate in continuous operation.

arxiv:2610.14537.title: Learn the Dynamics, Enforce the Physics: Generative Latent Operators for High-Dimensional Beam Evolution
arxiv:2610.14537.abstract: Particle-in-cell (PIC) simulation is indispensable for modeling beam dynamics in particle accelerators, but its computational cost limits many-query workflows, such as configuration exploration, virtual diagnostics, and controller design. We introduce GLOBE, a physics-constrained Generative Latent Operator for Beam Evolution, modeling the nonlinear, control-dependent, multiscale evolution of 3D beam--field dynamics covering $10^7$ spatial cells. GLOBE compresses beam--field states into a compact latent space and factors their evolution into two components. A control-conditioned neural operator learns the dominant dynamics, while an amplitude-normalized generative model captures the residual distribution, recovering fine-scale structures and conditional variations. GLOBE enforces field constraints by regime-specific, parameter-free operators: a Poisson solve reconstructs the electric field in the electrostatic regime, and a spectral projection imposes Gauss's law and a divergence-free magnetic field in the electromagnetic regime. On two high-resolution 3D particle-accelerator benchmarks, bunched-beam transport and plasma-wakefield acceleration, GLOBE lowers relative-$L_2$ error by 9\% and 13\%, low-frequency spectral error by 69\% and 51\%, and mid-frequency spectral error by 54\% and 20\% relative to the strongest baseline (DPOT), satisfies field constraints, and reduces hours of PIC simulation to a minute per rollout.

arxiv:2610.14824.title: Multi-Objective Design of C-Shaped Targets for Energy--Divergence Control in Laser-Driven Proton Acceleration
arxiv:2610.14824.abstract: We optimize the energy-divergence trade-off of laser-driven protons from a C-shaped target using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations and constrained multi-objective Bayesian optimization. Five geometry and focusing parameters are varied to maximize proton cutoff energy and minimize the RMS divergence of forward protons with E_k >= 5 MeV under a proton-only conversion-efficiency constraint of eta_H >= 9%. Of 82 designs, 60 are feasible and 15 Pareto-optimal. The Max-Energy and Min-Divergence endpoints yield 28.64 MeV at 52.51 degrees and 11.47 MeV at 11.13 degrees, respectively; a representative compromise yields 21.44 MeV at 38.44 degrees. Matched-stage diagnostics link these regimes to optical-field buildup, electron energization, charge separation, and outer-sheath organization. Numerical tests support the principal trends. Reflection timing does not support a monotonic trapping-duration law, and the charge-sheath relation remains non-local. These results establish a design-resolved route to controlling proton energy and angular quality.

arxiv:2610.18804.title: Registration is a Representation Problem: Solving Whole-Body PET/CT Registration
arxiv:2610.18804.abstract: Raw image intensities are a poor surrogate for similarity across images in correspondence problems. Further, while auxiliary segmentation labels can provide semantic identification and improve matching, they can assign only coarse identities to fine-grained anatomy and often cover only a subset of structures, particularly in whole-body settings. We present an approach that instead establishes correspondence using complementary representations of anatomy and demonstrate its utility for longitudinal whole-body PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg Challenge. Our 3D foundation model, anatomix, is used to derive fine-grained, per-voxel semantic representations that are consistent across volumes, and we further employ off-the-shelf segmentation models to obtain coarse anatomical identities. Together, these representations drive a GPU-accelerated iterative registration solver (FireANTs) in a hybrid multistage framework: the first stage estimates alignment from dense multi-channel features, after which a second refines the deformation using both anatomix- and segmentation-based losses. Lastly, because registration should not introduce non-biological tumor volume changes across time, we develop lesion-specific component-wise volume preservation schemes. Without any task-specific training, our system won first place in the PSMAReg Challenge leaderboard. Code and interactive visualizations are available at http://www.neeldey.com/reps-for-reg.

arxiv:2610.18735.title: SP$^2$ec: Adaptive Self-Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
arxiv:2610.18735.abstract: Speculative Decoding (SD) has demonstrated its efficacy in accelerating large language model inference, but for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), the diverse input modalities make it difficult for a small trained drafter to achieve consistently high throughput. Self-speculative decoding reuses parts of the target model as a drafter which retains the multi-modal capability of the VLMs, yet its efficiency depends on choosing a suitable draft configuration for each prompt. We propose Single-Peak SPeculative decoding (SP$^2$ec), a training-free bandit algorithm that adapts the draft configuration during generation. SP$^2$ec exploits the single-peak throughput pattern observed in existing self-speculative methods, including SWIFT, KnapSpec, SpecVLM, and our simple cosSim. Our algorithmic design explicitly minimizes a novel notion of wall-time regret for each given query, corresponding to the empirical wall-time latency. Theoretical guarantees on the wall-time regret show that SP$^2$ec can exploit the optimal draft configuration, with negligible exploration cost. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B across visual and textual tasks show consistent improvements of up to 11\% over the original self-speculative methods, demonstrating the wide applicability of the proposed SP$^2$ec algorithm.

arxiv:2610.18730.title: Learning When to Transfer: Reinforcement Learning for Carbon-Footprint Modeling in New Manufacturing Domains
arxiv:2610.18730.abstract: Manufacturers often need to characterize a new material, process, or product before enough operating data are available to train reliable predictive models for this new, target domain. Existing manufacturing operations contain potentially useful knowledge to accelerate this characterization, but indiscriminate reuse of data from existing source domains can cause negative transfer in learning of the new, target domain when the manufacturing domains differ sufficiently. This work proposes a reinforcement-learning method for selective knowledge transfer, where its reward scores each opportunity to transfer against supervised alternatives, so negative transfer is avoided and controlled during forward prediction instead of being diagnosed afterwards. Given limited data from a new target domain, the learned policy chooses among predictors based on individual source operations, subsets of the sources, or the supervised alternatives: fully pooled sources, or target data alone. A validation gate deploys the transferred prediction only when it improves upon the supervised alternatives. The method is designed for learning variables supporting carbon accounting, as well as performance and quality outcomes. We demonstrate the approach by quantifying the embodied greenhouse-gas emissions of parts produced via material-extrusion additive manufacturing, using data from 729 experiments spanning five materials: ABS, PETG, TPU, PLA, and recycled PLA. The response combines measured fabrication electricity with polymer-specific cradle-to-gate production factors, while 22 material, process, and toolpath features characterize each experiment. In leave-one-material-out evaluation, this method achieves a mean test RMSE of 5.2 g CO2e per part, 20.00% lower than target-only training (32.5% lower when only 5-10% of the target training data are available) and 10.30% lower than indiscriminate source-target pooling.

arxiv:2610.18683.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
arxiv:2610.18683.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9\% and 94.3\% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7\% and 70.8\% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.

arxiv:2610.18635.title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
arxiv:2610.18635.abstract:
The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming.
  In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics.
  We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.

arxiv:2610.18596.title: ACCRUE: Continual Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Robot Foundation Models
arxiv:2610.18596.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves robot foundation models (RFMs) beyond their demonstrations, but real-world deployment demands more: learning new tasks efficiently while retaining previously acquired behaviors. Existing continual RL methods on top of VLAs mitigate forgetting but rely on on-policy updates with limited forward transfer, whereas off-policy methods improve single-task sample efficiency without addressing learner persistence across tasks. We propose ACCRUE, a continual off-policy RL framework that carries lightweight actor and critic networks across tasks, allowing each stage to reuse behavioral and value knowledge acquired through prior RL. The inherited critic adapts only on current-task transitions and guides current-task actor learning, while prior behavior is preserved by distilling the actor toward cached targets on a small number of retained episodes. Fixed visual features keep the inherited learner and its replay compatible with base-policy updates. Across contact-rich assembly sequences in simulation and on real-robot hardware, ACCRUE accelerates subsequent-task learning with near-zero forgetting and significantly reduces real-robot training time by 31.0\% to 68.5\%.

arxiv:2610.18456.title: Learning Perturbation-Specific Representations through Conditional Energy Prior for Cellular Response Prediction
arxiv:2610.18456.abstract: AI-based cellular perturbation prediction is essential to accelerate drug discovery and therapeutic identification. However, perturbation-specific signals are generally obscured by cellular complexity, making it difficult for existing methods to correctly capture perturbation effects. To address this problem, we propose PerturbEnergy, which introduces a conditional energy-based prior over perturbation representations. It assigns lower energy (higher probability) to representations compatible with the given perturbation and higher energy to others, thereby explicitly tilting the latent space toward perturbation-preferred regions. Besides, PerturbEnergy can be integrated into autoencoder architectures as we find its Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is equivalent to the ELBO of the complete autoencoder. We further prove that optimizing PerturbEnergy increases the lower bound on the conditional mutual information between representation and perturbation. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our PerturbEnergy: it improves perturbation recognition especially in latent space with improvement of up to 83.2\%; It also achieves state-of-the-art performance for predicting top-50/100/200 differentially expressed gene(DEG) response and remaining competitive on highly variable gene(HVG) prediction. The code is provided: https://github.com/BlueWhaleLab/PerturbEnergy

arxiv:2610.18393.title: LunaTP: Enabling Efficient and Scalable Tensor Product for Equivariant MLIPs
arxiv:2610.18393.abstract: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.

arxiv:2610.18314.title: Complex materials engineering via Provenance Action Graphs: potential, structure and demonstration
arxiv:2610.18314.abstract: This work discusses and tests the potential of reaction graphs for material synthesis, in which events consist of reaction steps (actions) and their outputs (observations). The importance comes from the requirement to synthesize technologically useful materials, especially those that are kinetically stabilized. Often, it is a science that follows years of trial and error, culminating in (published) successful recipes, but is truly driven by far more (unpublished) failures. The entry into the era of AI provides an opportunity to use learning algorithms to encode rules from multi-dimensional synthesis pathways, regardless of their technological usefulness, and to decode both forward prediction and inverse learning modes. The main incentive is to accelerate material discovery by generating a global knowledge base that can be shared among data agents and contributed to by them. We will focus on several scenarios in the common synthesis process during solid-state synthesis, primarily because these reactions are kinetic in nature and require closer monitoring and control of the reaction history.

arxiv:2610.18130.title: Distance Prediction for Quantum Codes
arxiv:2610.18130.abstract: The distance of a quantum code is a fundamental metric that dictates its error-correction capability. While quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) families such as Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes offer a promising pathway to low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing, computing their distance is challenging. Current exact solvers and even search heuristics that provide a distance upper bound suffer from severe computational bottlenecks, restricting the discovery of optimal codes. In this paper, we construct a dataset of BB codes with corresponding distance upper bounds obtained through high-budget heuristic searches. We introduce BB-Net, an attention-based neural network architecture for predicting the distance of BB codes. It achieves 96.39% accuracy on the reference distances in the test set, compared with 94.86% for state-of-the-art heuristics with a budget of up to $10^{4}$ times more computational runtime. On a subset with certified exact distances, BB-Net achieves 98.94%. By relieving the distance-calculation bottleneck, BB-Net enables faster screening of large code spaces, particularly in ML-driven search pipelines, and thereby can accelerate the discovery of novel quantum error-correcting codes, an important capability for advancing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Our code is publicly available: https://github.com/NadavSc/BBNet

arxiv:2610.17956.title: Learning Distributions from Samples and Qualities
arxiv:2610.17956.abstract: We study parameter estimation when each sample from a continuous parametric distribution is accompanied by a binary quality label governed by the same unknown parameter. By imposing hard feasibility constraints, deterministic labels can accelerate estimation from the classical $n^{-1/2}$ rate of smooth quality-aware M-estimators to $n^{-1}$. Combining PAC guarantees with local error-to-parameter conversions, we establish this rate for both identifiable and finitely ambiguous quality classifiers, with likelihood information resolving the latter ambiguity. When the quality model is known only up to an additive constant, we construct threshold-free pairwise preferences from oppositely labeled samples and retain the accelerated rate despite the unknown threshold. We further show that pointwise qualities and pairwise preferences are incomparable: either can be strictly more informative than the other. Our assumptions hold for Gaussian, Laplace, and exponential families under thresholded log-likelihood rewards. Finally, a minimax lower bound establishes the optimal $n^{-1}$ dependence on sample size, up to logarithmic and dimension-dependent factors, while experiments confirm the benefits of constraint-based estimation.

arxiv:2610.17914.title: LinMorph: Learning to Morph Weights for Efficient Video DiT Linearization
arxiv:2610.17914.abstract: Post-hoc linearization is an attractive way to accelerate pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers (Video DiTs), yet existing methods largely treat the quality loss induced by attention replacement as a recovery problem. We show that a more fundamental bottleneck lies upstream: \emph{initialization}. Random initialization discards pretrained knowledge, whereas manual weight reuse transfers it through rigid and incomplete source--target correspondences. We introduce \textbf{LinMorph}, which recasts Video DiT linearization as a learnable softmax-to-linear weight transformation problem. Instead of copying predefined counterparts, LinMorph learns a cross-parameter morphism that lets each target Gated DeltaNet (GDN) parameter draw jointly from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including for parameters with no direct softmax counterpart. A single morphism is shared across layers and learned through local teacher alignment, while producing layer-specific initializations from their respective pretrained weights. The resulting weights are then materialized as independent GDN modules for progressive distillation and joint recovery.Since the morphism operates in weight space rather than token space, it can be learned on short, low-resolution clips and directly reused at larger video scales. Across pretrained Video DiTs, LinMorph enables markedly faster recovery and better final generation quality than random initialization and heuristic weight reuse. Results show that efficient linearization depends not only on how a converted model is recovered, but critically on how pretrained knowledge is transferred before recovery. Project page: https://lonelyling.github.io/LinMorph.

arxiv:2610.17734.title: Explore with Memory, Learn without It: In-Context Exploration and Self-Distillation for LLM Reasoning
arxiv:2610.17734.abstract: Exploration bounds learning efficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Current methods explore mostly through independent sampling, without fully using the information gathered along the way, such as known wrong answers and environment feedback. We propose LEAF, which injects a dynamic, problem-specific memory into the context before every rollout. The memory contains the most recent response, its reward, and other environment feedback. It is updated after every verifier call. We decouple policy updates from rollouts and update the policy through self-distillation. On four benchmarks and two open models, LEAF accelerates exploration by about 4x compared with a random sampling baseline. On unseen test sets, it improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.59 and 1.83 percentage points on the two models, while using less compute than any RL baseline. These results highlight the potential of LEAF in improving both exploration and learning efficiency. Code is available at: https://github.com/on1262/LEAF

arxiv:2610.17637.title: Mixed Precision Scaling Laws for Quantized Pretraining
arxiv:2610.17637.abstract: Since scaling laws were introduced for modern LLMs (Kaplan et al., 2020), several works have extended them to account for quantization, tracking the emerging low-precision data types supported on AI accelerators. We develop a more accurate scaling law for quantized pretraining with mixed precision across the forward and backward passes, grounded in optimization theory and validated empirically. Our formulation separates the effects of quantization on model capacity and on optimization efficiency, and explicitly models the persistent optimization error from forward and backward quantization identified through convergence analysis. To select the regimes for fitting and evaluating our law, we first decompose existing 4-bit training recipes into their forward and backward components, isolating those that most affect loss. Our Qwen3 experiments under selected 4-bit regimes, together with published Llama-style experiments, show that our law predicts loss with up to $11\times$ lower MSE than existing laws as model size and token count scale. Finally, we extend our law to layer-wise mixed precision and identify the optimal quantized-pretraining recipe, i.e., model size, training tokens, and per-layer forward/backward precision, under a hardware-aware compute budget. Unlike prior precision scaling laws, our law predicts that the optimal precision increases with the compute budget.

arxiv:2610.17528.title: ATTUNE: Agentic Throughput Tuning for LLM Training
arxiv:2610.17528.abstract: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's.
