doi:10.3389/fsysb.2026.1905585.title: ELM-CLAIM: a claim-calibration framework for adaptive, memory-like, learning-like, and goal-directed claims in engineered living materials
doi:10.3389/fsysb.2026.1905585.abstract: <jats:p>Engineered Living Materials (ELMs) combine living cells with matrices, interfaces, environmental fields, and sometimes electronic or computational controllers. Their multicomponent architecture creates an attribution problem: the same observed output may reflect passive material physics, active cellular regulation, interface or morphological change, environmental gradients, controller adaptation, or coupled-system dynamics. This article proposes ELM-CLAIM (Engineered Living Materials—Controls for Learning, Adaptation, Intelligence, and Memory), an author-proposed claim-calibration and reporting framework for matching adaptive vocabulary to measurable state variables, temporal criteria, attribution targets, and evidence classes. The framework classifies specific behaviors from passive responsiveness (L0) through active responsiveness (L1), adaptation (L2), memory-like behavior (L3), learning-like behavior (L4), and autonomous goal-directedness (L5). It also provides an evidence-tiered claim-to-control matrix, proportional substitution rules for experimentally intractable controls, component- and controller-level attribution logic, model-transparency requirements, and a reviewer-oriented reporting checklist. Essential entries denote evidential functions rather than a single mandatory assay, allowing justified orthogonal controls while requiring claims to be lowered when major alternatives remain unresolved. Published cases are used illustratively to stress-test interpretability rather than to validate the framework statistically. ELM-CLAIM calibrates language; it does not by itself validate an experiment, define cognition, or constitute a community standard. Community testing, inter-reviewer reliability assessment, and prospective experimental use remain necessary next steps.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1959885.title: Development and multi-database validation of machine learning models for 28-day mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and pulmonary hypertension
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1959885.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early mortality prediction in critically ill patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) coexisting pulmonary hypertension (PH) remains challenging, particularly because prediction models developed in intensive care unit (ICU) database may not perform consistently across other healthcare systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective multicenter study employed two large-scale databases to establish and validate ML models for predicting early mortality in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The MIMIC-IV database served as the model-development cohort (2555 patients), with external validation conducted on eICU CRD (292 patients) database. Six ML algorithms were adopted: Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Artificial Neural Network (ANN).</jats:p>
                    <jats:p>The baseline variables were screened to identify potential predictors via least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (Lasso) regression. Model interpretability was evaluated via SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The overall cohort consisted of 2,847 ICU patients with COPD and PH. Twelve consistently crucial clinical features were identified, including acute kidney injury, pneumonia, age, weight, heart rate, red blood cell distribution width (RDW), white blood cell (WBC), anion gap, chloride, creatinine, base excess, potential of hydrogen (pH). The Random Forest algorithm achieved the optimal performance, with a training Area Under Curve (AUC) of 0.938, internal validation AUC of 0.748, and eICU CRD external validation AUC of 0.800. SHAP analysis indicated that acute kidney injury was the most influential predictor, followed by base excess and RDW. Additionally, a web tool was developed in this study to facilitate the application of early death risk prediction in clinical practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is the multi-database validation of ML models for early mortality prediction in ICU patients with COPD and PH. The Random Forest model integrated with SHAP interpretability offers a reliable tool for clinical decision-making support, with consistent validity verified across two databases, including our internal validation cohort. This work provides a decision support tool to assist in identifying high-risk individuals within this complex comorbid population, and establishes a foundation for future studies with a more dynamic and personalized prognostic approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1051/swsc/2026036.title: Reproduction of substorm auroral currents in the ionosphere using a machine-learning-based emulator and SuperDARN data assimilation
doi:10.1051/swsc/2026036.abstract: <jats:p>Auroral electrojet dynamics during isolated substorms are reproduced using a machine-learning-based emulator with SuperDARN data assimilation. Representing such short-timescale variability is important for improving space-weather prediction relevant to technological systems. Reproducing this variability remains challenging for the SMRAI emulator (Surrogate Model for the REPPU Auroral Ionosphere; Kataoka et al., 2024, https://doi.org/10.1029/2023SW003720), where REPPU is the REProduce Plasma Universe global magnetohydrodynamic simulation. SMRAI is trained on ionospheric outputs from a REPPU MHD simulation and primarily produces smooth and gradual variations in auroral currents during substorms. Therefore, we evaluate the performance of SMRAI with SuperDARN line-of-sight velocity data assimilation (Nakano et al.,2025, https://doi.org/10.1029/2025SW004488), referred to as the SMRAI–SD framework. Two isolated substorm events on 30 and 31 October 2023 are analyzed to assess the performance of the SMRAI–SD. The SMRAI–SD reproduces auroral current variability in closer agreement with observations than SMRAI, as indicated by improved correspondence with the AL and AU indices. Although reproducing AE indices is not the primary objective, they are used to evaluate the performance of the SMRAI–SD approach and to identify its strengths and limitations through comparison with observations and examination of two-dimensional maps of ionospheric electric potential. SMRAI–SD reproduces abrupt changes in the ionospheric potential that are more pronounced than in the SMRAI. This study therefore evaluates whether such abrupt electrodynamic changes are physically consistent and under what conditions they are reliable. The results demonstrate that SuperDARN data assimilation enhances the ability of the SMRAI model to reproduce ionospheric auroral electrodynamics during substorm and supports its application to space-weather forecasting studies.</jats:p>
doi:10.1051/swsc/2026036.venue: Journal of Space Weather and Space Climate

doi:10.2118/234162-ms.title: Data-Driven Prediction of Electrical Submersible Pump Run Life Using Leakage-Resistant Machine-Learning Validation
doi:10.2118/234162-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrical submersible pumps (ESPs) are widely deployed to sustain production in mature and high-water-cut wells. Routine surveillance data capture equipment degradation and changing operating conditions and can therefore support remaining-useful-life (RUL) estimation and proactive maintenance planning. However, predictive performance may be substantially overstated when correlated daily observations from the same ESP run are distributed across training and test partitions. This study presents a comprehensive, leakage-resistant machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) framework that formulates ESP reliability prediction as two complementary tasks: continuous RUL regression and binary failure classification at 30-, 14-, 7-, and 1-day warning horizons. Sensor, production, equipment, and event-record data from Egypt's Western Desert were consolidated and temporally matched. Following data cleaning, preprocessing, and quality control, the final data set comprised 1,577 completed ESP runs—each defined by a matched installation and subsequent failure date—across 526 wells, together with 933,535 daily surveillance observations. Ten regression model families and six classification configurations were evaluated using a standardized pipeline incorporating engineering-based feature selection, training-only preprocessing, class-imbalance handling, hyperparameter optimization, cross-validation, early stopping, and learning-rate scheduling. On the held-out classification test set, the 30-day K-nearest-neighbor model achieved 98.98% accuracy, 0.889 failure-class precision, 0.909 recall, and an F1-score of 0.899. Random-row regression experiments yielded mean absolute errors of 3.61 days for K-nearest neighbors and 3.66 days for random forest; these results were treated as interpolation baselines rather than prospective deployment estimates. Blind field evaluation across five consecutive ESP runs from the fully withheld Well KX1 produced prediction errors of −27 to +1 days, corresponding to signed percentage errors from −9.75% to +0.24%, a mean absolute error of 12.4 days, a root mean square error of 15.0 days, and a mean absolute percentage error of 4.27%. Based on the operator-reported exposure of USD 250,000–300,000 per event, the five historical events represent USD 1.25–1.50 million in cumulative exposure. The pronounced class imbalance, predominance of nonfailure observations, and within-run correlation of daily records created substantial risks of information leakage and overly optimistic performance estimates. A multilayer validation framework was therefore implemented using failure-stratified, well-grouped, block-temporal, chronological, rolling-origin, and cluster-aware partitioning strategies, with all preprocessing fitted exclusively to the training partition. The deterioration observed under block-temporal and chronological evaluation confirmed that validation design materially influences apparent model performance. Overall, routine ESP surveillance data can support proactive diagnostic review, maintenance scheduling, ESP design optimization, and production planning, provided that performance claims are reported with the corresponding validation design, test population, and prediction uncertainty.</jats:p>
doi:10.2118/234162-ms.venue: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition

doi:10.1098/rspb.2026.0619.title: Socially guided individual learning mitigates the double-edged sword of pedagogy
doi:10.1098/rspb.2026.0619.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Social learning and innovation are fundamental processes in cultural evolution, yet their interaction remains poorly understood. Prior research suggests that inheriting social information reduces exploration. However, most studies have focused on the transmission of fully fledged solutions. Here, we investigate whether alternative types of information can facilitate cumulative cultural evolution without reducing exploration. Specifically, we conducted a pre-registered experiment with 400 adult participants comparing the inheritance of solutions with that of heuristics—simple rules that guide problem solving. We found that social learners who inherited a heuristic explored more frequently and broadly than those who received a solution. Their productions were also less similar to those of their demonstrators, suggesting that heuristics foster more independent exploration. Despite these differences, both heuristics and solutions enabled learners to surpass their demonstrator's performance. These findings highlight that the type of social information transmitted plays a crucial role in the evolvability of culture.</jats:p>
doi:10.1098/rspb.2026.0619.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences

doi:10.58445/rars.4055.title: Predictive Modeling of CFTR Modulator Efficiency: A Machine Learning Approach
doi:10.58445/rars.4055.abstract: Cystic Fibrosis (CF), a severe genetic disorder, causes thick mucus buildup that severely damages the lungs and pancreas, leading to chronic infections and progressive organ damage.This widespread damage makes it incredibly difficult for doctors to know which new CFTR modulator therapy will work best for each individual patient.This challenge inspired my project.I investigated whether machine learning models could predict how much a patient's lung function (FEV1%) would improve after starting a CFTR modulator therapy.To do this, I built a comprehensive dataset by combining real CFTR genetic information with carefully simulated patient clinical details like age, sex, and existing health issues, along with their responses to different modulator drugs.New genetic features were engineered, such as functional mutation classes and detailed genotype groups, to capture the biological complexity of CF.Then an extensive exploratory data analysis was performed to understand patterns in this integrated data.Next, supervised machine learning models, including Random Forest and Gradient Boosting Regressors, were developed and tested to forecast FEV1 percentage changes.These models were then fine tuned using advanced techniques like hyperparameter optimization and cross-validation to ensure their reliability.To understand why my models made certain predictions, SHAP analysis was used, which helped reveal the most influential patient characteristics.The findings show that these models can indeed predict patient responses.The Random Forest Regressor proved to be the most effective, achieving an R-squared (R²) score of 0.4801 on data the model had never seen before.This means my model explained nearly half of the variation in FEV1 percentage change, demonstrating a significant ability to predict individual patient outcomes.The analysis clearly showed that the specific treatment group, a patient's baseline lung function, and their genotype were the most critical factors determining how well they responded to therapy.For instance, simulated patients on Trikafta showed substantially greater FEV1 improvements compared to other treatments.This project successfully proves that machine learning can predict individual patient responses to CFTR modulator therapies using integrated genetic and simulated clinical data.This work provides a valuable proof-of-concept for personalized medicine in Cystic Fibrosis, offering a new way to think about optimizing drug selection and ultimately improving patient health.

doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.67s.73.title: Artificial Intelligence–Driven Intrusion Detection Systems: A Systematic Review of Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Adaptive Ensemble Approaches
doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.67s.73.abstract: This is a critical systematic review of 40 peer-reviewed articles published between 2021 and 2025 on artificial intelligence-enhanced Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS).To maintain rigour and transparency in the review, the PRISMA 2020 and Kitchenham guidelines are adhered to.The appropriate literature was also searched in six major databases, such as IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Scopus, and Web of Science, and concentrated on the IDS methods, which used machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), reinforcement learning (RL), and ensemble methods.The results show that there is a clear shift of traditional ML algorithms, including SVM and Random Forest, towards advanced deep learning and hybrid ensemble models that have a higher detection accuracy and flexibility in a variety of benchmark datasets, including CICIDS2017 and UNSW-NB15.The frameworks of reinforcement learning also increase the autonomy of IDS by learning on its own and adapting dynamically, but they have difficulties with the issues of computational efficiency, and the stability of the convergence.On the whole, the review demonstrates that there is ongoing methodological standardization deficit, diversity of datasets, and inter-study reproducibility absence.It finds that explainable, adaptive, and federated AI models should be the main focus of future IDS studies to attain scalable, transparent, and trustworthy cybersecurity frameworks that are able to conduct proactive and intelligent network protection.
doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.67s.73.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

doi:10.1021/acs.oprd.6c00199.title: Maximizing Pd/C Hydrogenation Performance with Continuous Flow CSTR Cascades at Ambient Pressure
doi:10.1021/acs.oprd.6c00199.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study demonstrates the efficient implementation of heterogeneous gas–liquid–solid hydrogenation at ambient pressure using a continuous-flow reactor composed of a vertical cascade of ten continuously stirred tank reactors (CSTRs). The system enables simple operation by continuously feeding a suspended catalyst slurry alongside hydrogen gas,without the need for complex catalyst immobilization. Active agitation throughout the cascade ensures homogeneous and vigorous mixing, which in turn facilitates rapid hydrogenation even under ambient pressure conditions. Under optimized conditions, the system achieved 80% conversion of ethyl cinnamate within 4.7 min of residence time and exhibited apparent gas–liquid mass transfer coefficients (kLa) in the range of 1000–5000 h–1,comparable to those reported for advanced microreactors. Moreover, the relatively large reactor volume enabled superior productivity compared to the microstructured reactors under ambient pressure. The results demonstrate the applicability of the reactor to continuous hydrogenation, with efficient mass transfer, simple operation, and compatibility with slurry-based catalytic processes.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fspor.2026.1914074.title: Teachers' perspectives on physically active learning and student wellbeing in the Nova Scotia Active Smarter Kids Project
doi:10.3389/fspor.2026.1914074.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Active Smarter Kids (ASK) is a Norwegian physically active learning (PAL) program that integrates physical activity into school lessons for students to learn while moving. In 2017, government departments in Nova Scotia (NS), Canada, partnered with ASK to adapt and implement it locally as the NS ASK Project. Since 2018, teachers in over 130 NS schools have been trained in ASK. International studies and a pilot report from NS have noted several benefits of ASK, such as increased physically active time, academic achievement, and executive function. However, a more comprehensive study of the NS ASK project has not been completed. This paper explored elementary and middle school teachers' perceptions of students' wellbeing and the implementation challenges from a PAL project from NS, Canada.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ten teachers (5 elementary, 5 middle school) participated in semi-structured interviews addressing their experience conducting ASK lessons, perceived contributions to students' wellbeing, and any implementation challenges they've encountered. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seven themes were developed: 1) Fostering belonging and relationship-building; 2) Opportunities for, and experiencing success in, physical activity; 3) The joy of learning with movement; 4) Sharpening engagement and focus; 5) Pedagogical approaches as catalysts for wellbeing; 6) ‘Running' out of resources; and 7) Navigating the status quo.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The project was perceived to support many facets of students' wellbeing through its flexible, adaptable approach, enabling the meeting of different needs and abilities, and positioning it as a promising health-promoting school initiative aligned with global wellbeing frameworks. Implementation challenges, such as a lack of space and curriculum and assessment pressures, can inform efforts to rethink educational systems of similar contexts to remove barriers for PAL.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
doi:10.3389/fspor.2026.1914074.venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living

doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15010440/v1.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Subsequent Drug Release Trajectories using Early Release Information in PLGA Microparticles
doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15010440/v1.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate prediction of drug-release behavior from PLGA microparticles may reduce the experimental effort required for formulation characterization, yet conventional prediction approaches rely primarily on static molecular and formulation descriptors and do not incorporate experimentally observed release behavior as it becomes available during an ongoing experiment. Here, we develop a machine-learning framework that integrates molecular and formulation descriptors with early-release measurements to predict subsequent drug-release trajectories from PLGA microparticles. A dataset comprising 4,913 release observations from 321 formulations was analyzed using random forest regression with formulation-grouped cross-validation. Using a common set of 89 formulations, we systematically evaluated the predictive value of increasing amounts of early-release information. Prediction accuracy improved with additional early measurements, but the incremental benefit progressively diminished, with two and three measurements capturing 64.7% and 91.9% of the total predictive gain achieved with four measurements, respectively. The value of early information also varied substantially across formulations, with greater benefits generally observed for formulations that were more difficult to predict from static descriptors alone. Trajectory-level analysis further revealed that early observations constrained subsequent release trajectories to different extents across formulations. These findings demonstrate that experimentally observed early-release behavior provides formulation-specific predictive information beyond static descriptors and establish a data-driven framework for quantifying information sufficiency in drug-release characterization.</jats:p>

doi:10.2118/234148-ms.title: Facies-Conditioned Physics-Guided Machine Learning for Interpretable Permeability Prediction in Heterogeneous Clastic Reservoirs
doi:10.2118/234148-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Permeability prediction in clastic reservoirs is challenged by the limited vertical coverage of core measurements, the indirect nature of wireline log responses, and variations in pore connectivity across sandy and shaly lithological intervals. This study presents a novel facies-conditioned physics-guided machine learning workflow applied to the Zubair Formation in a well (TU-Well), Tuba oil field, southern Iraq. The final dataset comprises 178 depth-matched observations integrating core analysis, Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) logs, and conventional well logs. The dataset was split into 133 observations for training and 45 for a fixed development test. Initially, Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost were evaluated as direct permeability models using well logs alone and then with NMR-derived permeability as an additional input. Subsequently, four independent operational clastic Electrofacies, Clean Sand, Shaly Sand, Transitional, and Shale, were identified from training-only gamma-ray and shale-volume data. The final architecture incorporates multi-resolution vertical context by sampling 10 continuous LAS curves within a ±5 m window around each core depth, generating 1,010 contextual values, which were then compressed into PCA20 and PCA60 representations for modeling. The final prediction is constructed as a hybrid model, combining an averaged CatBoost global context model with a strongly regularized soft-facies residual adapter, ensuring NMR permeability remains an explicit physical reference in the final reconstruction: K = KNMR+ ΔKglobal + ΔKfacies. While the best direct baseline model (CatBoost with logs and NMR) achieved an R2 of 0.6072 and RMSE of 197.46 mD, the final multi-resolution soft-facies approach yielded superior results: Random Forest achieved an R2 of 0.5978, XGBoost achieved 0.6561, and CatBoost achieved the highest performance with an R2 of 0.7265, RMSE of 164.76 mD, and MAE of 114.34 mD. The proposed hierarchy reduced RMSE by 16.56% relative to the best direct baseline and 50.90% relative to raw NMR estimates. The robustness of the approach was confirmed through three facies-stratified fourfold validations and one CORE_NO-grouped fourfold validation, where the hierarchy consistently improved RMSE across all 16 outer-fold comparisons.</jats:p>
doi:10.2118/234148-ms.venue: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1975841.title: How generative AI becomes embedded in design learning: a 14-instructional-day intensive longitudinal study of reciprocal dynamics between AI use and self-efficacy
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1975841.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Generative AI is increasingly embedded in design education, yet little is known about how students’ daily engagement with generative AI is dynamically associated with their learning-related capability beliefs across successive instructional days. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, this study examined the reciprocal next-instructional-day associations between daily generative AI use in design learning and daily design-learning self-efficacy, and further investigated whether baseline hassles were associated with individual differences in these dynamics. A 14-instructional-day diary study was conducted with 260 Chinese undergraduate design students, yielding 3,558 observed person-day assessments out of 3,640 possible assessments. Daily generative AI use and design-learning self-efficacy were assessed throughout the diary period, whereas hassles were measured at baseline. The data were analyzed using bivariate dynamic structural equation modeling within a Bayesian estimation framework. The results showed significant autoregressive effects for daily generative AI use (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                    = 0.198, 95% CrI [0.154, 0.237]) and daily design-learning self-efficacy (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                    = 0.138, 95% CrI [0.100, 0.175]). At the within-person level, higher-than-usual generative AI use on one instructional day positively predicted design-learning self-efficacy on the subsequent instructional day (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                    = 0.043, 95% CrI [0.006, 0.077]), while higher-than-usual design-learning self-efficacy also positively predicted generative AI use on the subsequent instructional day (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                    = 0.059, 95% CrI [0.023, 0.095]). At the between-person level, greater baseline hassles were associated with higher average generative AI use (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                    = 0.135), lower average design-learning self-efficacy (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                    = −0.254), and a stronger cross-lagged association from generative AI use to subsequent self-efficacy (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                    = 0.458). Gender did not significantly predict the main random effects. These findings indicate modest reciprocal next-instructional-day associations between generative AI use and design-learning self-efficacy, suggesting that the two may reinforce one another across instructional days. The stronger association from generative AI use to subsequent self-efficacy among students reporting greater baseline hassles further suggests that contextual demands may shape how generative AI becomes integrated into students’ day-to-day design learning.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fdgth.2026.1952669.title: Development of an explainable machine learning framework for early diabetes detection, multiclass classification, and risk stratification across age groups
doi:10.3389/fdgth.2026.1952669.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To develop and evaluate a novel machine learning (ML) framework tailored to a clinical diabetes dataset and to assess whether demographic stratification enhances model performance and interpretability for multiclass diabetes classification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A clinical dataset of 264 patients' records was used to classify individuals including non-diabetic (36.4%), prediabetic (15.2%), and diabetic (48.5%) individuals. Several supervised learning models were trained using 80:20 train-test split and optimized using RandomizedSearchCV and 10-fold cross validation. Model performance was evaluated using the metrics accuracy, precision, recall and the F1-score. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) was calculated for the best generalizing model. A structured ML framework was developed for this dataset, incorporating preprocessing, model optimization, age stratification analysis age (&lt;35 vs ≥35 years) and gender. SHAP was developed for model interpretability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ensemble methods demonstrated superior performance in comparison to linear or single-tree approaches, with Gradient Boosting showing the most stable generalization with a test accuracy of 0.981 and stable cross validation accuracy of 0.972. AUC-ROC analysis using Gradient Boosting yielded good discriminative ability across the three diabetes classes: 0.991 (non-diabetic), 0.986 (prediabetic) and 0.972 (diabetic). Stratified analysis showed improved reliability in individuals aged ≥35 years (accuracy = 0.94, F1-score = 0.92), while performance in younger individuals was unstable due to small sample size. SHAP analysis identified HbA1c, BMI, and age as dominant predictors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study presents a ML framework integrating age stratified modelling with explainable ML frameworks to improve interpretability. The findings offer clinically relevant results that can support clinical decision-making systems, individualized risk assessment, and potential applications for targeted intervention in diabetes progression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1201/9781003519348-15.title: Optimal Treatment Strategies for Prioritized Outcomes
doi:10.1201/9781003519348-15.abstract: Dynamic treatment regimes formalize precision medicine as a sequence of decision rules, one for each stage of clinical intervention, that map current patient information to a recommended intervention. Optimal regimes are typically defined as maximizing some functional of a scalar outcome's distribution, e.g., the distribution's mean or median. However, in many clinical applications, there are multiple outcomes of interest. We consider the problem of estimating an optimal regime when there are multiple outcomes that are ordered by priority but which cannot be readily combined by domain experts into a meaningful single scalar outcome. We propose a definition of optimality in this setting and show that an optimal regime with respect to this definition leads to maximal mean utility under a large class of utility functions. Furthermore, we use inverse reinforcement learning to identify a composite outcome that most closely aligns with our definition within a pre-specified class. Simulation experiments and an application to data from a sequential multiple assignment randomized trial (SMART) on HIV/STI prevention illustrate the usefulness of the proposed approach.

doi:10.2118/233879-ms.title: A Scientific Machine Learning Model for Real-Time Transient Prediction of Cuttings Bed Height in Long Horizontal Laterals
doi:10.2118/233879-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Poor hole cleaning remains the root cause of stuck pipe, elevated torque and drag, and non-productive time while drilling long laterals. Yet most cuttings transport prediction models are either too computationally expensive for real-time decisions or too limited in generalizability when based purely on field data. This study develops a scientific machine learning framework to predict the transient cuttings transport phenomena under varying operating conditions and enable real-time hole cleaning monitoring.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>A physics-informed neural network (PINN) model was developed using a modified multilayer perceptron with random Fourier feature embedding and tanh activation, which enables the PINN to resolve high-frequency input variations. The model takes input operational, fluid, and cuttings parameters. Its composite loss combines measurement-based data to fit with a physics residual derived from the Navier-Stokes equations that captures gravitational settling, buoyancy, and annular drag. The PINN is trained and validated on hydraulic numerical models published in the literature.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>On two wells held out of training, the PINN reproduces the bed blockage, suspended cuttings concentration, annular pressure and phase velocities of the reference simulator. Bed blockage is recovered with a coefficient of determination between 0.84 and 0.94 and a mean absolute percentage error below 5%, and the remaining channels lie between 0.95 and 0.97. The model returns a full clean-up transient in milliseconds, which neither empirical correlations nor numerical simulators can do at rig-floor speed, and its physics residual and solids mass balance can be checked without access to a simulator. It was observed that higher annular velocity and pipe rotation reduce bed blockage, with diminishing returns beyond roughly 120 rev/min, while a higher drilling rate and coarser cuttings raise the suspended loading and lengthen the clean-up cycle. This framework is aimed at drilling engineers who need to optimize hole cleaning efficiency both during well planning and during real-time operations. In the planning phase it can be used to select the pump rate, pipe rotation and mud rheology that keep the lateral clean within the fracture gradient at the shoe. On the rig, because a full clean-up transient is returned in milliseconds, the engineer can quantify the circulating bottoms-up before the string is pulled, rank the intervals where pack-off risk is building, and test a change in rate or rotation before deciding. In day-to-day use the engineer enters the current rate, rotation, drilling rate and mud properties and get the bed height along the wellbore, how long a bottoms-up will take, and how much bed is left when it finishes. It therefore equips drilling engineers with an interpretable, real-time prediction tool that has direct potential to reduce non-productive time caused by poor hole cleaning.</jats:p>
doi:10.2118/233879-ms.venue: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition

doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1894027.title: Machine learning, molecular docking, and experimental validation identify shared molecular signatures between idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension and malignant pleural mesothelioma: a retrospective study
doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1894027.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension (IPAH) exhibits cancer-like features, yet its pathogenesis remains unclear. Given molecular similarities between IPAH and malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM), this study aimed to uncover shared transcriptomic patterns.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GEO datasets for IPAH and MPM were analyzed. Overlapping DEGs and WGCNA modules were identified. PPI network analysis combined with LASSO, random forest, and SVM-RFE was used to identify candidate biomarker genes. A classification model was constructed and evaluated using leave-one-out cross-validation and bootstrap optimism correction. Immune infiltration was evaluated by ssGSEA. Molecular docking and MD simulations assessed drug binding to candidate target proteins. qRT-PCR validated candidate biomarker gene expression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Six concordantly upregulated and eleven concordantly downregulated DEGs were shared between IPAH and MPM. Upregulated genes were enriched in cell cycle regulation, while downregulated genes were enriched in neutrophil chemotaxis. WGCNA identified 58 overlapping genes. CXCR2, S100A9, and LCN2 were identified as candidate biomarker genes. A ROTS sensitivity analysis confirmed that all 1710 MPM DEGs were reproducible and directionally concordant at the matching FDR &lt;0.05 threshold despite the imbalanced case–control ratio. The classification model achieved AUCs of 0.909 and 0.875 in training and external validation sets, with a LOOCV AUC of 0.879 and an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.896. Immune infiltration revealed increased Th17 cells but decreased neutrophils in IPAH. CXCR2 and S100A9 expression correlated with neutrophil infiltration; LCN2 expression correlated with metabolic reprogramming. Navarixin showed the strongest binding affinity to CXCR2 (−10.1 kcal/mol). MD simulations confirmed stable binding of the CXCR2-Navarixin complex. qRT-PCR confirmed significant downregulation of all three genes in IPAH patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This hypothesis-generating study identifies shared transcriptomic signatures between IPAH and MPM, highlighting CXCR2, S100A9, and LCN2 as candidate biomarkers linked to immune dysregulation and metabolic reprogramming. The computational and correlative nature of these findings, together with the limited size of the external validation cohort, requires confirmation through functional experiments and validation in larger, independent, and multicentre cohorts before clinical translation can be considered.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.29303/jpm.v21i5.12561.title: Effect of the Guided Inquiry Learning Model on Students' Scientific Literacy Skills in Ecology Material
doi:10.29303/jpm.v21i5.12561.abstract: <jats:p>The low scientific literacy skills of students in Indonesia, as reflected in the results of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), indicate the need for the implementation of learning models that are able to develop students' scientific thinking skills. This study aims to determine the effect of the guided inquiry learning model on students' scientific literacy skills in ecology material. This study uses a quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental design using a Nonequivalent Control Group Design. The research sample consisted of two classes: the experimental class, which implemented the guided inquiry learning model, and the control class, which used the direct learning model. The research instrument was a scientific literacy test consisting of validated multiple-choice questions. Data analysis was carried out using normality and homogeneity tests, N-gain calculations to assess increases in scientific literacy skills, and independent-samples t-tests to test the research hypothesis. The results showed that the average pretest scores for the experimental and control classes were 37.92 and 38.02, respectively, indicating that the two classes' initial abilities were relatively similar. After treatment, the average posttest score for the experimental class increased to 77.60, while the control class's score reached 65.10. The independent sample t-test results showed a significance value of 0.000 (<0.05), thus accepting the alternative hypothesis. Based on the study's results, the guided inquiry learning model significantly improved students' scientific literacy in ecology. This finding suggests that the implementation of the guided inquiry learning model can be an effective alternative in improving students' scientific literacy skills through learning activities centered on investigation, problem-solving, and active student involvement in the scientific process.</jats:p>

doi:10.22219/raden.v6i2.45374.title: Development and preliminary evaluation of ROMI using Articulate Storyline for sixth-grade learning about Earth’s rotation
doi:10.22219/raden.v6i2.45374.abstract: <jats:p>Background- Critical thinking is an important skill for students, particularly in learning science concepts such as Earth’s rotation. Preliminary assessment showed that students’ critical thinking ability had a low category. Objectives- This study aimed to develop and conduct a preliminary evaluation of Rotation Media Interactive (ROMI) using Articulate Storyline for sixth-grade. Method- This study employed the ADDIE development model. The participants were sixth-grade students at a public elementary school in Palembang. The developed media was evaluated through expert validation, individual and small-group trials, and a field evaluation involving 18 students. Data were collected using expert validation sheets, student response questionnaires, and critical thinking tests. Results- ROMI obtained an average feasibility score of 94.71% from material, media, and practitioner validation, categorized as very feasible. Student responses indicated high practicality, with average scores of 93.06% in the individual trial and 93.15% in the small-group trial. In the field evaluation, the mean critical thinking test score increased from 62.89 to 93.89 after implementation, with a mean N-Gain of 0.835, categorized as high. Conclusions- ROMI received favorable expert evaluations and student responses and showed promising results in the preliminary field evaluation. However, the observed score increase cannot be attributed solely to ROMI. Further evaluation using larger samples and controlled or comparative designs is needed.</jats:p>

doi:10.52096/jsrbs.12.04.09.title: The Impact of Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) on Reducing Anxiety and Enhancing School Engagement: A Case Study at ‘Androkli Kostallari’ Elemantary School
doi:10.52096/jsrbs.12.04.09.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines the effectiveness of a Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) intervention in reducing anxiety and enhancing students' school engagement at Androkli Kostallari School in Shkozë. The target group consists of first, second, and fifth-grade students, selected due to a high prevalence of students from divorced families, a demographic known to face heightened emotional and behavioral challenges. The study employs a qualitative methodology, integrating descriptive data to assess the impact of the SEL intervention. Teachers, trained in SEL techniques, implemented activities in the classroom while receiving continuous mentorship. Data were collected through teachers' reports on student progress, with a focus on emotional, behavioral, cognitive, and physical aspects of student well-being. The results indicated significant improvements in students' emotional regulation, behavior, cognitive skills, and physical well-being, contributing to a more positive and engaging school environment. This study underscores the importance of SEL in fostering emotional resilience and academic success, particularly for students facing family-related stressors.</jats:p>
doi:10.52096/jsrbs.12.04.09.venue: Journal of Social Research and Behavioral Sciences

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1948734.title: Service-learning and patient safety in medical education: a pretest–posttest study with a complementary expert perspective
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1948734.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Home- and community-based services (HCBS) may support quality of life among older adults when expected services are perceived as available. This study examined whether the number of expected HCBS perceived as available was associated with self-rated quality of life (QOL) contemporaneously and at the next scheduled survey wave.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed longitudinal data from the Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey. Contemporaneous analyses included 24,180 person-wave observations from 8,699 individuals and used individual fixed-effects linear probability models with survey-year effects. Prospective analyses included 20,974 adjacent-wave pairs from 13,386 individuals and adjusted for baseline QOL, covariates, and origin-year effects. Sensitivity analyses examined alternative outcome scales, model specifications, interval length, service domains, and subgroup interactions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the contemporaneous model, one additional expected perceived as available was associated with a 0.00841 higher probability of good/very good QOL (95% CI: 0.00408–0.01275). In the baseline-adjusted prospective analysis, the coefficient was 0.00338 (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.089), decreasing to 0.00094 (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       =0.662) when restricted to three-year intervals. Prospective findings varied by model and outcome specification.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>More expected HCBS perceived as available was associated with better contemporaneous self-rated QOL. Prospective evidence was weaker and sensitive to analytical specification. Findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects and do not establish actual service use or objectively verified service provision.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fphy.2026.1992795.title: Deep learning assisted screening of light-responsive piezoelectric crystals for next-generation photoacoustic and photothermal spectroscopy
doi:10.3389/fphy.2026.1992795.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High piezoelectric materials are promising alternative resonator materials for quartz-enhanced photoacoustic spectroscopy (QEPAS) and laser-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy (LITES), as enhanced piezoelectric response directly improves acoustic detection sensitivity. However, the discovery of materials combining high piezoelectricity with visible-light responsiveness remains a significant challenge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We developed an improved crystal graph convolutional neural network (I-CGCNN) model for high-throughput screening of visible-light-responsive piezoelectric crystals. The model incorporates a specialized algorithm for learning bond feature vectors and synchronizes the updates of atomic and bond feature vectors during multilayer convolution. Using this model, we re-calculated the bandgap and piezoelectric moduli of all piezoelectric crystals in the Materials Project database.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The I-CGCNN model significantly outperforms existing graph neural networks in predictive accuracy for both bandgap and piezoelectric modulus. The high-throughput screening identified several promising candidate crystals that exhibit both strong piezoelectric response and visible-light responsiveness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The screened candidates show considerable potential for piezo-phototronic applications, and the superior predictive performance of I-CGCNN suggests that it provides a powerful tool for accelerating the discovery of novel piezoelectric semiconductors for next-generation photoacoustic and photothermal spectroscopy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1926616.title: Lecturer presence is linked to perceived learning, while pedagogical and technical factors are linked to satisfaction in synchronous hybrid teaching
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1926616.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hybrid teaching, in which students attend lectures either in the physical presence of a lecturer or synchronously via video link from another location, has become increasingly common at multi-campus institutions, yet research systematically comparing student satisfaction and perceived learning in this format remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined synchronous hybrid teaching in an undergraduate Social Work programme delivered across two Swedish campuses, in which the defining difference between student groups was not physical attendance as such, since students at both sites were present in university classrooms, but whether the lecturer taught in person or via videoconference from the other campus. A total of 282 students completed a study-specific questionnaire across three consecutive semesters, assessing overall satisfaction, perceived learning under both lecturer conditions, ability to focus, sense of community, and technical problems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Perceived learning was consistently higher when the lecturer was physically present than when teaching remotely (d = 1.24), a pattern that held within students at both campuses, indicating that it was not attributable to campus affiliation alone. Students at the satellite campus reported significantly higher overall satisfaction than students at the main campus, but this campus-level difference was no longer statistically significant once pedagogical and technical factors were accounted for in a multiple regression model; instead, perceived learning during remote-lecturer sessions, ability to focus, sense of community, and technical problems emerged as the strongest independent predictors of satisfaction, together explaining 57.4% of its variance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that satisfaction and perceived learning represent partly distinct dimensions of the hybrid teaching experience and suggest that local pedagogical support and reliable technical delivery during remote-lecturer sessions may matter more for student satisfaction than physical co-location with the lecturer itself.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fsufs.2026.1949662.title: Climate policy uncertainty and domestic–international grain-market risk spillovers: a TVP-VAR-BK analysis with machine learning early warning
doi:10.3389/fsufs.2026.1949662.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Climate-policy transition uncertainty may affect grain-market risk transmission.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We use 2010–2025 daily data for Chinese and US corn and wheat, US soybean landed cost, and GCPU in a TVP-VAR-BK connectedness model and machine-learning warning exercise.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>TCI averages 15.29% and peaks at 57.32%; short-horizon transmission dominates; XGBoost achieves PR-AUC of 0.986/0.949/0.781 at 1/5/20-period horizons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Climate-policy uncertainty is dynamically associated with grain-market risk and can support market-stability monitoring, but the evidence is associational rather than causal.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1201/9781003519348-11.title: Learning Individualized Treatment Rules with Optimal Treatment Grouping for Maximizing Mean Survival Time
doi:10.1201/9781003519348-11.abstract: With the advancement in medical research and real-world clinical practice, it is common to have a wide range of treatment options for specific diseases. This diversity poses challenges for developing optimal individualized treatment rules (ITRs), particularly when dealing with censored outcomes. To address this methodological gap, we develop an accelerated failure time (AFT)-type model that incorporates a Supervised Clustering approach based on Adaptive Fusion (AFTSCAF). This model simultaneously estimates the optimal ITR that maximizes mean survival times and identifies treatment grouping. Specifically, the optimization problem is formulated as an inverse probability of censoring weighted least squares (WLS) estimation, enhanced with a flexible fusion penalty that clusters treatments with similar treatment effects. The resulting penalized loss function is optimized using group-lasso and accelerated proximal gradient descent. We evaluate the proposed method under comprehensive simulation settings, including various survival distributions, sample sizes, and censoring rates, and the results demonstrate its superior performance. Finally, we apply the AFTSCAF method to head-and-neck cancer (HNC) datasets, developing ITRs for 1,625 HNC patients who underwent chemotherapy and identifying the optimal treatment groups.
doi:10.1201/9781003519348-11.venue: Empirical Processes and Statistical Reinforcement Learning

doi:10.1201/9781003519348-3.title: Minimax Optimality of the Moderated MMD and Empirical Moderated MMD-Based Two-Sample Test
doi:10.1201/9781003519348-3.abstract: In this chapter, we consider the moderated MMD-based two-sample test. An important quantity called maximal marginal degrees of freedom is introduced. Similar in spirit to the effective degrees of freedom, the maximal marginal degrees of freedom can also represent the complexity of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space. In this work, it plays an important role in the following two aspects. First, it controls the variance of the moderated MMD-based test statistic and therefore determines whether the minimax optimality can be attained. Second, it determines how many samples are required to make the empirical moderated kernel sufficiently close to the moderated kernel. We show that under proper assumption of the maximal marginal degrees of freedom, the moderated MMD-based two-sample test is minimax optimal, and present a condition on the size of the empirical moderated kernel so that the associated test is minimax optimal as well. Adaptive tests are proposed, which achieve an almost optimal rate without having to know the regularity condition of the underlying distributions. All tests are performed using the permutation approach with Monte Carlo approximation so that the type I error rate is controlled rigorously. The number of required Monte Carlo samples is also provided.
doi:10.1201/9781003519348-3.venue: Empirical Processes and Statistical Reinforcement Learning

doi:10.2118/234199-ms.title: Co-Optimization of Carbon Storage and Enhanced Oil Recovery Under Stochastic Geological and Market Uncertainty via Deep Reinforcement Learning
doi:10.2118/234199-ms.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Carbon dioxide-enhanced oil recovery (CO2-EOR) coupled with geological carbon storage (GCS) has the potential to simultaneously improve hydrocarbon recovery and permanently sequester anthropogenic CO2. Achieving these dual objectives requires operational decision-making under significant geological and economic uncertainty. Time-lapse geophysical monitoring provides field-observable information on subsurface fluid migration and has the potential to inform adaptive reservoir management. We investigate a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for the co-optimization of CO2 storage and enhanced oil recovery using time-lapse gravity monitoring. Our objective is to determine adaptive CO2-water-alternating-gas (WAG) injection policies that maximize economic performance while accounting for geological uncertainty, stochastic oil-price fluctuations, and monitoring costs.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Geological uncertainty is incorporated via stochastic porosity and permeability realizations generated at the start of each training episode, whereas market uncertainty is represented by a mean-reverting stochastic oil price model. We trained a Double Deep Q-Network (DDQN) agent using coupled reservoir simulation and forward gravity modelling, with time-lapse gravity observations serving as the system state. We compare policies learned from five monitoring configurations comprising borehole, surface, and hybrid surface-borehole gravity surveys, as well as a fully observable benchmark consisting of the complete pressure and saturation fields in the reservoir. Comparison of the learned policies demonstrates that (1) the proposed DDQN framework successfully learns robust CO2-WAG control policies under simultaneous geological and market uncertainty; (2) incorporating stochastic oil prices produces more variable reward trajectories and slower convergence but results in economically robust decision-making; (3) dense surface and hybrid gravity monitoring substantially improve learning performance relative to sparse monitoring configurations, with performance approaching that of the fully observable benchmark; and (4) with the exception of the borehole-based strategy, the learned adaptive policies consistently outperform conventional fixed WAG strategies involving regular switching between water and gas phases in cumulative net present value (NPV) while simultaneously increasing oil recovery and CO2 storage. These results demonstrate that integrating time-lapse gravity monitoring with DRL provides a practical framework for uncertainty-aware, observation-driven optimization of CO2-WAG operations by jointly accounting for monitoring geometry and cost, geological uncertainty, and stochastic oil-price conditions, thereby advancing intelligent reservoir management for carbon storage and utilization</jats:p>
doi:10.2118/234199-ms.venue: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition

doi:10.1201/9781003519348-2.title: A Semi-Parametric Model for Target Localization in Distributed Systems
doi:10.1201/9781003519348-2.abstract: Distributed systems serve as a key technological infrastructure for monitoring diverse systems across space and time. Examples of their widespread applications include: precision agriculture, surveillance, ecosystem and physical infrastructure monitoring, animal behavior and tracking, disaster response and recovery to name a few. Such systems comprise of a large number of sensor devices at fixed locations, wherein each individual sensor obtains measurements that are subsequently fused and processed at a central processing node. A key problem for such systems is to detect targets and identify their locations, for which a large body of literature has been developed focusing primarily on employing parametric models for signal attenuation from target to device. In this paper, we adopt a nonparametric approach that only assumes that the signal is nonincreasing as function of the distance between the sensor and the target. We propose a simple tuning parameter free estimator for the target location, namely, the simple score estimator (SSCE). We show that the SSCE is $\sqrt{n}$ consistent and has a Gaussian limit distribution which can be used to construct asymptotic confidence regions for the location of the target. We study the performance of the SSCE through extensive simulations, and finally demonstrate an application to target detection in a video surveillance data set.
doi:10.1201/9781003519348-2.venue: Empirical Processes and Statistical Reinforcement Learning

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1911550.title: Identification of SLC15A3 as a shared prognostic biomarker for AML and COVID-19 via integrative bioinformatics, machine learning and Mendelian randomization
doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1911550.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a lethal hematological malignancy with poor overall prognosis.COVID-19 co-infection further complicates clinical management and worsens survival outcomes of AML patients, highlighting the need to explore the molecular interplay between the two diseases. In this study, we initially screened 109 common differentially expressed genes shared by AML and COVID-19 from public transcriptomic datasets, which were closely involved in tumor progression and viral pathogenesis. We further characterized their biological functions, constructed protein interaction and TF-miRNA regulatory networks, and established an AML prognostic model to evaluate the tumor immune microenvironment. Combining survival analysis, clinical correlation, immune infiltration assessment and m
                    <jats:sup>6</jats:sup>
                    A modification analysis,
                    <jats:italic>SLC15A3</jats:italic>
                    was preliminarily screened as a candidate prognostic gene for AML. Subsequent weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), machine learning (ML) and Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses further identified
                    <jats:italic>SLC15A3</jats:italic>
                    as a promising prognostic biomarker for AML. Finally, RT-qPCR and Western blotting assays verified its aberrant expression in AML cells. Consistent with bioinformatic prediction,
                    <jats:italic>SLC15A3</jats:italic>
                    serves as a shared candidate biomarker for AML and COVID-19,although its mechanistic role linking AML and SARS-CoV-2-related inflammation requires further functional validation.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1832982.title: Learning-enabled collaborative intelligence in search and rescue robotics: a survey of paradigms, models, and challenges
doi:10.3389/frobt.2026.1832982.abstract: <jats:p>Search and Rescue (SAR) robotics increasingly depends on collaborative intelligence to operate effectively in dynamic, uncertain, and time-sensitive environments. Modern SAR missions require coordinated interaction among heterogeneous robotic agents as well as structured collaboration between humans and intelligent systems for perception, decision-making, and adaptive mission execution. This paper presents a structured narrative review supported by a systematic literature search of learning-enabled collaborative intelligence frameworks in SAR robotics, organized around three paradigms: human-to-machine (H2M), machine-to-machine (M2M), and machine-to-human (M2H) learning. The review examines recent developments in reinforcement learning, federated and decentralized learning, knowledge distillation, swarm intelligence, semantic communication, and the growing integration of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) for knowledge grounding, transfer, and explainability. Beyond algorithmic advances, the analysis emphasizes deployment-oriented challenges including partial observability, communication constraints, uncertainty management, model reliability, and real-time operational requirements. Rather than conducting a fully PRISMA-compliant systematic review, this work synthesizes representative and influential studies to identify emerging trends, architectural trade-offs, deployment limitations, and future research directions for scalable and trustworthy collaborative SAR systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fcimb.2026.1967577.title: Machine learning-based risk prediction for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in non-neutropenic intensive care unit patients, with an exploratory analysis of pathogen-related risk factors
doi:10.3389/fcimb.2026.1967577.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) is increasingly recognized in non-neutropenic patients, but validated bedside risk stratification tools remain scarce. We developed a machine learning model to predict IPA and tested whether corticosteroid effect depends on bacterial co-pathogen.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This multicenter retrospective cohort study enrolled 837 non-neutropenic adults hospitalized with pulmonary infections across three tertiary hospitals in China between December 2020 and December 2025. The discovery cohort was split into training and internal validation sets. Four classifiers were compared, with Random Forest selected for optimal performance. The final model was externally validated in an independent cohort. Feature importance was assessed using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis. Corticosteroid-bacteria interactions were examined using subgroup analyses and propensity score matching, with the synergy index S calculated to quantify biological interaction. A simplified bedside score was derived from the top-ranking predictors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The Random Forest model achieved external validation AUC of 0.865. Six predictors consistently dominated across all assessments:
                      <jats:italic>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</jats:italic>
                      isolation, hypoxemia (PaO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      /FiO
                      <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                      &lt;200 mmHg), diabetes mellitus, organ failure (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, SOFA &gt;5), lymphopenia (lymphocyte count &lt;0.8×10
                      <jats:sup>9</jats:sup>
                      /L), and ICU (intensive care unit) admission. Corticosteroid exposure did not rank among the top six predictors. However, its association with IPA diverged sharply by bacterial context: OR below 1 with
                      <jats:italic>P. aeruginosa</jats:italic>
                      (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.214–1.283) but OR above 1 with other Gram-negative bacilli (OR 2.17, 95% CI 0.722–6.535); P for interaction = 0.131; a directional pattern that persisted after propensity matching. The six-variable score derived from these predictors showed AUCs of 0.869 (training), 0.774 (internal validation), and 0.719 (external validation).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>IPA risk in non-neutropenic ICU patients is shaped more by bacterial co-pathogen context than by corticosteroid exposure alone. The divergent corticosteroid effects across bacterial species challenge the conventional assumption of a uniform steroid-associated risk. The externally validated six-variable score offers a practical, software-free tool to support pathogen-informed, individualized risk stratification and clinical decision-making in the ICU.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
doi:10.3389/fcimb.2026.1967577.venue: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1851960.title: From entrepreneurial learning engagement to entrepreneurial intention among Chinese university students: the roles of entrepreneurial self-efficacy and uncertainty avoidance
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1851960.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As universities play a growing role in fostering innovation and entrepreneurship to support economic growth, researchers have increasingly focused on understanding the mechanisms through which entrepreneurial education influences students' entrepreneurial intention. Accordingly, on the basis of learning engagement theory, social cognitive theory, and cultural dimension theory, this study investigated the relationships between entrepreneurial learning engagement, entrepreneurial self-efficacy, uncertainty avoidance, and entrepreneurial intention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to 1,578 university students in Jilin Province, China. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to examine the direct, mediating, and moderating effects among the study variables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Entrepreneurial learning engagement was positively associated with entrepreneurial intention both directly and indirectly through entrepreneurial self-efficacy. Multigroup analyses showed that its associations with self-efficacy and intention differed significantly between uncertainty-avoidance groups. In the high-avoidance group, only the indirect association was significant, whereas both direct and indirect associations were significant in the low-avoidance group. However, the between-group difference in the indirect association did not reach statistical significance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings highlight entrepreneurial self-efficacy as an important psychological correlate of both entrepreneurial learning engagement and entrepreneurial intention and indicate that these relationships differ across groups characterized by different levels of uncertainty avoidance. These patterns underscore the relevance of efficacy beliefs and uncertainty-related orientations for understanding students' entrepreneurial intention. Given the cross-sectional design, the findings should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than evidence of temporal ordering or causality. Future longitudinal or experimental research is needed to examine these relationships further.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/ijdrbe-06-2026-0116.title: Explainable machine learning for anticipating county-level disaster recovery burden in the built environment
doi:10.1108/ijdrbe-06-2026-0116.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to develop and evaluate an explainable machine-learning framework to anticipate county-level high recovery burden from natural disasters one year ahead using only public administrative and social-vulnerability data. Its substantive aim is to help built-environment decision makers shift from reactive post-event allocation to earlier, place-based prioritization of recovery and mitigation effort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A county-year panel was assembled for 3,042 US counties over 2014–2022 by combining FEMA Disaster Declarations Summaries with county-level CDC/ATSDR social vulnerability index data. The outcome was a high-burden county-year, defined as repeated county-level declarations involving public assistance and/or hazard mitigation programme activity. Class-weighted logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost were benchmarked using a temporally ordered train-validation-test split. SHAP values and model coefficients were used to interpret predictive drivers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The benchmark produced a moderate but decision-relevant predictive signal. Class-weighted logistic regression achieved the strongest out-of-sample performance on the hold-out period (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.626; area under the precision–recall curve 0.140; F1-score 0.262) and outperformed the more flexible tree-based models. Across models, stronger prior programme burden, recent major declarations, population size, mobile-home prevalence and social vulnerability were associated with higher next-year burden.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The dependent variable is an administrative proxy for recovery burden rather than a direct measure of physical loss, repair cost or household recovery outcomes. The empirical setting is the USA; transfer to other countries should therefore be treated as conceptual and methodological rather than statistical.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The framework offers a transparent annual screening tool for local governments, regional planning bodies and emergency-management agencies seeking to identify counties likely to face elevated recovery pressure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Because it relies on public tabular data rather than expensive proprietary inputs, it is potentially transferable to resource-constrained settings that need interpretable anticipatory analytics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The paper contributes a reproducible public-data pipeline that links explainable artificial intelligence to disaster-resilience planning in the built environment. It also responds to the journal’s growing interest in technology-enabled resilience by showing that interpretable models, rather than only complex algorithms, can support forward-looking preparedness and recovery prioritization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
doi:10.1108/ijdrbe-06-2026-0116.venue: International Journal of Disaster Resilience in the Built Environment

doi:10.58421/gehu.v5i5.2108.title: The Effectiveness of Digital Literacy and Uma Lengge Culture-Based Learning on Student Motivation
doi:10.58421/gehu.v5i5.2108.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to determine the effectiveness of digital literacy and Uma Lengge culture-based learning on student motivation. The study employed a quantitative method using a quasi-experimental design involving an experimental group and a control group. The research subjects consisted of 40 fifth-grade elementary school students. The research instrument utilized a 15-item Likert scale questionnaire covering the variables of digital literacy, Uma Lengge culture-based learning, and student motivation. Data collection was conducted through pre-tests and post-tests, then analyzed using IBM SPSS via descriptive statistical tests, regression tests, ANOVA tests, and t-tests. The results showed that the digital literacy variable had a mean score of 74.00, Uma Lengge culture-based learning scored 76.20, and student motivation scored 80.80. The correlation coefficient test results showed an R value of 0.350 with a significance level of 0.089, indicating that the relationship between the two variables and student motivation falls into the low to moderate category and is not yet statistically significant simultaneously. Uma Lengge culture-based learning has a more dominant influence than digital literacy in enhancing student motivation. This study demonstrates that the integration of digital literacy and local culture can create learning that is more contextual, engaging, and relevant for students.</jats:p>
doi:10.58421/gehu.v5i5.2108.venue: Journal of General Education and Humanities

doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1964400.title: Deep learning-based android malware detection under realistic evaluation constraints: an architecture-centric review and reliability-aware empirical validation
doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1964400.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deep learning (DL) has reshaped Android malware detection (AMD) by enabling models to learn from heterogeneous Android artifacts, including permissions, DEX and bytecode representations, API and system-call traces, network traffic, image encodings, and program graphs. However, high benchmark accuracy does not necessarily imply reliable, robust, explainable, reproducible, or deployable malware detection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines DL-based AMD under realistic evaluation constraints through an architecture-centric systematic review and reliability-aware empirical validation. A PRISMA-guided review of studies published between 2021 and 2026 was conducted to analyze architecture families, artifact representations, dataset transparency, validation realism, robustness and evasion evidence, explainability, reproducibility, and deployment readiness. Controlled empirical validation was also conducted on CICMalDroid 2020 using representative CNN, GRU, Transformer, and Hybrid CNN–LSTM models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
