doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1965013.title: Machine learning predictors of cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy in type 2 diabetes: insights from a prospectively collected single-center registry
doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1965013.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cardiac autonomic neuropathy (CAN) is a severe complication of type 2 diabetes (T2DM) associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Machine learning (ML) can integrate multidimensional clinical data and identify features associated with CAN. We aimed to characterize predictors of CAN categories using ML.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were obtained from a prospective single-center observational registry of patients with T2DM undergoing standardized cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests (CARTs) based on Ewing’s protocol. Demographic, anthropometric, clinical, laboratory, and medication data were analyzed. Patients were classified as CAN0 (no or borderline CAN), CAN1 (early CAN), or CAN2 (definite or severe CAN). Three extreme gradient boosting models were evaluated: a CART-inclusive model, a CART-excluded model restricted to patients with T2DM, and a CART-excluded model supplemented with non-diabetic controls without abnormal CART results. Model performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and feature contributions were interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations values.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 693 patients with T2DM, 19 (2.7%) had completely normal autonomic function, whereas 674 (97.3%) exhibited at least one borderline or abnormal CART result. Greater CAN severity was associated with older age, longer diabetes duration, higher systolic blood pressure, and poorer renal function. The CART-inclusive model achieved perfect discrimination in the best iteration (weighted AUC, 1.00; accuracy, 100%), with all five CARTs ranking among the leading predictors. After CART exclusion, performance declined markedly (weighted AUC, 0.64), with class-specific AUCs of 0.59 for CAN0, 0.59 for CAN1, and 0.68 for CAN2. Inclusion of non-diabetic controls improved the weighted AUC to 0.78, with the greatest improvement for CAN0 (AUC, 0.85), followed by CAN2 (0.78) and CAN1 (0.70). Age, diabetes duration, and renal function markers were recurrent non-CART predictors, while anthropometric, hematological, metabolic, and treatment-related features showed category- and model-specific contributions. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection demonstrated substantial overlap among CAN categories, particularly for CAN1.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CARTs remained essential for accurate CAN classification and staging. Routinely available clinical variables provided complementary phenotypic information but were insufficient to robustly distinguish CAN categories without CART data, particularly CAN0 and CAN1. ML may support multidimensional phenotyping and hypothesis generation but cannot replace standardized autonomic testing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.56557/ajocr/2026/v11i411233.title: Machine Learning-assisted Antenna Design and Optimization: A Comprehensive Review of Surrogate Modeling, Active Learning, and Intelligent Optimization
doi:10.56557/ajocr/2026/v11i411233.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid development of wireless communication systems has created an increasing demand for compact, broadband, high-performance, and application-specific antennas. Conventional antenna design approaches generally rely on analytical formulations, empirical relationships, parameter sweeps, and repeated full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations, which become computationally expensive as the number of design variables increases. To address these challenges, metaheuristic optimisation techniques such as Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) have been widely investigated for exploring complex antenna design spaces. More recently, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches have been introduced for antenna performance prediction, inverse design, and surrogate-assisted optimisation. These approaches can reduce the computational burden associated with repeated EM simulations; however, their effectiveness often depends on sufficiently large and representative simulation datasets. Hybrid ML–metaheuristic approaches further improve the optimisation process by combining predictive models with intelligent search algorithms, while Active Learning enables the selective acquisition of informative simulation samples. This review presents the evolution of computational antenna design from conventional and metaheuristic approaches to ML-based, hybrid, and Active Learning-driven methodologies. The reviewed studies are critically examined with respect to their design strategies, optimisation techniques, simulation requirements, data dependence, and computational efficiency. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of surrogate modelling and adaptive sample selection in reducing expensive full-wave simulations. The review identifies the limitations of existing approaches and highlights the need for autonomous, data-efficient, and simulation-efficient frameworks for high-dimensional microstrip antenna optimisation.</jats:p>

doi:10.1080/15295192.2026.2728637.title: Early Parenting Stress, Coparenting Quality, and Changes in the Home Learning Environment: Longitudinal Links to Children’s Language and Literacy
doi:10.1080/15295192.2026.2728637.abstract: SYNOPSISObjective. This study examined longitudinal associations among early parenting stress, parenting behaviors (i.e. parental warmth/responsivity and engagement in home learning activities [HLAs]), and coparenting quality at ages 1 and 3 years, and children’s language and literacy outcomes at age 5, in a socioeconomically disadvantaged sample. Design. Using data from the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing (N = 1,506), residualized change modeling tested whether parenting stress at age 1 predicted declines in parental warmth/responsivity and reduced engagement in HLAs from ages 3 to 5; whether those declines in parenting quality and HLAs mediated the associations between parenting stress and children’s language and literacy; and whether perceived coparenting quality, assessed at ages 3 and 5, moderated associations among parenting stress, parenting behaviors, and children’s language and literacy outcomes. Results. Parenting stress was associated with declines in parents’ warmth/responsivity as well as their HLAs engagement. Declines in parental warmth/responsivity, but not engagement in HLAs, mediated the association between parenting stress and children’s receptive vocabulary. No indirect effects were observed for letter-word identification and teacher-rated language and literacy. Perceived coparenting quality at age 5 moderated the association between parenting stress and teacher-rated language and literacy skills and the association between HLA engagement and children’s letter-word identification skills. Conclusions. The associations between parenting stress and children’s subsequent language and literacy development may operate through specific family processes, including changes in parental warmth/responsivity.

doi:10.58258/kaha6d73.title: STRATEGI GURU DALAM MENINGKATKAN MINAT BELAJAR SISWA KELAS V SEKOLAH DASAR
doi:10.58258/kaha6d73.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to describe the teacher's strategies in creating learning activities that attract the attention and engagement of fifth-grade students at SDN 1 Sigar Penjalin in the 2025/2026 academic year, as well as to identify the factors influencing the learning interest of fifth-grade students at SDN 1 Sigar Penjalin in participating in the learning process. This study employed a qualitative approach with a descriptive research design. The research subjects consisted of the fifth-grade teacher and fifth-grade students of SDN 1 Sigar Penjalin. Data were collected systematically through in-depth observation, semi-structured interviews, and relevant documentation. The results of the study showed that teachers’ efforts to create engaging learning were carried out through various adaptive strategies, namely classroom agreements and ice-breaking activities implemented by the homeroom teacher, storytelling strategies used by the Islamic Religious Education (PAI) teacher, and direct practice applied by the Physical Education teacher. These strategies were proven to be able to create a more conducive learning atmosphere, attract students’ attention from the beginning, increase their active participation, and enhance their learning interest sustainably. In addition, the factors influencing students’ learning interest included supporting factors such as innovative teachers’ instructional strategies, high students’ learning motivation, and a clean and conducive classroom atmosphere. Meanwhile, inhibiting factors included the loss of students' focus during long learning durations and the lack of media variety in some sessions.</jats:p>

doi:10.5256/f1000research.209452.r527774.title: Peer Review Report For: Designing an AI-Responsive Early Childhood Curriculum: A Conceptual Framework for Supporting Developmental Learning Trajectories in Preschool Education [version 2; peer review: 2 approved, 1 not approved]

doi:10.18094/josc.1936165.title: Learning Disaster Journalism in a Media Anthropology Classroom
doi:10.18094/josc.1936165.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Disaster journalism has not been institutionally or curricularly established within Slovenian higher education. This article examines how disaster journalism can be taught in a media anthropology classroom through a case study of an experimental pedagogical intervention carried out in 2024–2025 in a master’s-level Media Anthropology course at a Slovenian public university. Implemented in a non-journalism communication and media programme, the intervention introduced disaster journalism as a temporary analytical framework through two seminar-based assignments: the reading of peer-reviewed scholarship and qualitative case studies of media coverage of floods, bushfires, technological disasters, war, pandemic, and school shootings. The article is based on a qualitative interpretive synthesis of student seminar papers, class presentations, and reflective discussions rather than on a formal assessment of learning outcomes. The findings show that students engaged scholarly literature mainly through preferential readings, while the greatest conceptual challenges emerged in relation to Bourdieu’s journalistic field theory and the translation of disaster journalism terminology into Slovenian. In their empirical analyses, however, students applied the framework more critically and identified recurring patterns such as humanitarian normalisation, routinisation of crisis coverage, politicisation, and ethical tensions in victim representation. The article argues that disaster journalism can serve as a productive interdisciplinary framework for developing media literacy, ethical sensitivity, structural reflexivity, and critical engagement among students who are not journalism trainees. Overall, the intervention suggests that experimental pedagogy may provide a viable pathway for institutionalising disaster journalism in academic environments where it currently lacks curricular status.</jats:p>

doi:10.4274/jmsr.galenos.2026.2026-7-2.title: Can Machine Learning Detect and Predict Outcomes in Multiple Sclerosis? A Review of Diagnostic and Prognostic Approaches
doi:10.4274/jmsr.galenos.2026.2026-7-2.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and the McDonald criteria, whereas long-term management requires anticipating disability progression and symptom burden.This narrative review evaluates current evidence on machine learning (ML) approaches for (i) detecting and classifying MS and (ii) predicting disability progression and symptom severity in patients with established MS.Evidence was synthesized from 25 sources published between 2012 and 2026 (23 peer-reviewed journal publications, one arXiv preprint, and one article published in a journal outside the major biomedical indexes), encompassing MS diagnosis [MRI, optical coherence tomography (OCT), fluid biomarkers, and differential diagnosis] and prognostic outcome prediction (disability progression, symptom-specific severity, and contextspecific changes in disability).MRI remains the predominant data source for ML-based MS detection: deep learning models applied to structural MRI achieved accuracies of 70.2-98.8%in distinguishing MS from healthy controls, whereas conventional ML models achieved accuracies of 83.7-90.0%.A broader meta-review of more than 100 studies reported diagnostic accuracies ranging from 61% to 97%, while differentiation of MS from neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder achieved 74-88% accuracy, depending on data integration.For prognostic applications, tree-based ensemble models generally outperformed simpler regression models: a 231-patient cohort achieved an R 2 of 0.97 for two-year disability score prediction, although this estimate warrants cautious interpretation because of the strong autocorrelation of baseline Expanded Disability Status Scale scores.A 662-woman cohort achieved 85-88% classification accuracy for postpartum changes in disability, whereas a 23-patient cohort achieved 92.65% accuracy in predicting restless legs syndrome severity, with sleep quality identified as the leading predictor.Overall, ML can effectively detect MS-associated patterns in MRI and is increasingly being applied to OCT and fluid biomarkers.It can also generate clinically meaningful prognostic predictions after MS diagnosis, although categorical outcome prediction appears to generalize better than continuous regression.Dataset size, single-center study designs, and limited external validation remain the principal barriers to clinical deployment across both domains.Multimodal data integration and prospective multicenter validation therefore represent important priorities for future research.

doi:10.33619/2414-2948/131/68.title: Enhancing Students’ Autonomous Foreign Language Learning Through Information Technologies in Higher Education
doi:10.33619/2414-2948/131/68.abstract: <jats:p>Explores the role of information technologies in students’ independent foreign language learning in higher education institutions. The study focuses on the pedagogical potential of digital educational tools, including online learning platforms, mobile applications, multimedia resources, and communication technologies. Special attention is given to the development of students’ autonomy, motivation, and digital competence. The research analyzes the advantages of integrating information technologies into the learning process and their influence on improving language proficiency. The results indicate that the use of modern digital technologies significantly increases the effectiveness of independent learning and contributes to the formation of communicative competence in foreign languages.</jats:p>

doi:10.1142/s0218001426570296.title: Advanced AI-Based Multi-Stage Deep Learning Architecture for Robust Image Segmentation and Comprehensive Classification of Interstitial Lung Disorders in Next-Generation Medical Diagnostics
doi:10.1142/s0218001426570296.abstract: <jats:p>Current trends in interstitial lung disease research focus on early detection, precise diagnosis, and thorough characterization to optimize patient outcomes. Challenges persist because of heterogeneous patterns of disease, the scarcity of annotated datasets, and variability in image quality, resulting in inconsistent diagnosis and prognosis. To overcome this problem, this paper proposes image segmentation and comprehensive classification of interstitial lung disorders using Xception Spiking Fractional Neural Network (ISCC-ILD-XSFNN). The proposed model integrates Fuzzy Consensus Cubature Information Filtering (FCCIF), Structured Doubly Stochastic Graph-based Clustering (SDSGC), Self-Modulating Convolutional Neural Networks (SMCNet), and Xception Spiking Fractional Neural Networks (XSFNN) into a cohesive architecture. Initially, lung images from the MedGIFT database are preprocessed using FCCIF for normalization and noise reduction. The normalized images are segmented through SDSGC to identify affected lung regions. Subsequently, SMCNet extracts discriminative multi-scale features from segmented images. Finally, XSFNN classifies interstitial lung diseases into consolidation, ground glass, fibrosis, micronodules, emphysema, and normal classes. Experimental results demonstrate better and balanced classification performance, achieving 99.12% accuracy, 99.23% precision, 99.07% recall and 99.14% F1-score. Also, the per-class metrics remain consistently high across all six classes, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches. These results indicate that the proposed framework maintains balanced predictive performance across different ILD categories.</jats:p>
doi:10.1142/s0218001426570296.venue: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence

doi:10.4208/cicc.2026.146.02.title: Decoding Tunable Ring-Specific Adaptive Aromaticity in 1,3-Diaza-5,6-Diborabicyclo[3.1.0]hexatriene: Insights from a Combined DFT and Machine Learning Study
doi:10.4208/cicc.2026.146.02.abstract: <jats:p>Aromaticity, a cornerstone of chemical stability, is governed by Hückel’s and Baird’s rules for the ground $(S_0)$ and triplet excited $(T_1)$ states, respectively, yet these canonical rules are challenged by two-state aromaticity (adaptive aromaticity)—a burgeoning frontier in aromaticity research. Herein, density functional theory (DFT) investigations reveal that 1,3-diaza-5,6-diborabicyclo[3.1.0]hexatriene (1) and its all-carbon congener both exhibit $S_0$ entire-fused system aromaticity, but show striking $T_1$ divergence: the carbon analog loses aromaticity entirely, while compound 1 displays ring-specific adaptive aromaticity (5MR antiaromatic, 3MR aromatic). Nitroso/nitro substituents act as potent spin modulators, enabling switching between localized and whole-system $T_1$ aromaticity. A multiple linear regression model identifies spin localization and charge distribution as the principal contributors to $T_1$-state electron delocalization within the present dataset, while an Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) classifier reproduces the DFT-derived aromaticity categories with 93% accuracy on the held-out entry-level test set. This combined DFT–ML strategy provides a complementary data-driven framework for analyzing adaptive aromaticity in BN-doped heterocyclic systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.47637/justine.v1i2.1312.title: Perancangan dan Implementasi Sistem Informasi E-Learning Berbasis Web Mobile (Studi Kasus: SMP Negeri 02 Sungkai Utara)
doi:10.47637/justine.v1i2.1312.abstract: <jats:p>Pemanfaatan teknologi informasi dalam lembaga pendidikan telah memberikan dampak yang besar, seperti penggunaan e-learning yang menjadi alat bantu dalam memanajemen proses pembelajaran. Berdasarkan observasi yang telah dilakukan, SMP Negeri 02 Sungkai Utara belum memiliki media pembelajaran berbasis elektronik (e-learning) sebagai penunjang proses pembelajaran. Metode pembelajaran belum memiliki media untuk menghimpun materi tugas maupun absensi sehingga menghambat guru maupun siswa yang berhalangan hadir untuk memberikan/mendapatkan materi dan tugas. E-learning adalah media pembelajaran elektronik berbasis online, dengan e-learning memungkinkan proses pembelajaran dapat dilakukan secara berkesinambungan tanpa terbatas oleh ruang dan waktu selagi terhubung jaringan internet. Penggunaan metode waterfall dominan menggunakan pendekatan secara sistematis dan berurutan. Sistem informasi E-Learning berbasis web mobile menggunakan framework Codeigniter dan penyimpanan database MySQL telah diuji menggunakan black box dan berhasil diimplementasikan pada SMP Negeri 02 Sungkai Utara.</jats:p>

doi:10.17559/tv-20260304003434.title: Research on Interactive Control and Revenue Maximization of Distributed Battery Energy Storage Based on Machine Learning
doi:10.17559/tv-20260304003434.abstract: This paper discusses the application necessity and modeling feasibility of machine learning in the interactive control and dynamic game of distributed energy storage systems in distribution networks. By implementing multi-dimensional deep optimization of the network structure, training mechanism and experience replay strategy of the deep Q-learning algorithm, and introducing the sum-tree data structure to achieve efficient access and replay training of transformed data, the convergence speed, decision accuracy and control stability of the algorithm have been significantly improved, enabling it to meet the requirements of online real-time control. The research results show that compared with traditional methods and other learning algorithms, the proposed method demonstrates obvious application advantages. Meanwhile, this algorithm has a good adaptability to the discretization differences of the action space and can effectively suppress the convergence risk that may be caused by the significant expansion of the action space. In addition, combined with the capacity attenuation law of distributed energy storage, its operational characteristic model was constructed; Based on the life loss characteristics of distributed energy storage, the costs and economic benefits of its participation in grid operation were analyzed, the corresponding economic assessment model was established, and the controllable potential of distributed energy storage was quantitatively calculated.

doi:10.64643/ijirt.208470-459.title: AI And Machine Learning-Based Border Intrusion Detection System
doi:10.64643/ijirt.208470-459.abstract: Border areas require continuous monitoring to identify unauthorized movement and potential intrusion events.Conventional border monitoring systems generally depend on security personnel, cameras, or individual sensors, which can result in delayed detection and false alarms.This paper presents an Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning-Based Border Intrusion Detection System that combines multiple sensors, wireless communication, machine learning, and camera-based monitoring.The proposed system uses a Passive Infrared sensor to detect movement, an ultrasonic sensor to measure distance, and a vibration sensor to detect physical disturbance.An ESP32 microcontroller collects sensor readings and provides them to a Random Forest classification model for identifying normal and intrusion conditions.An ESP32-CAM is used for visual monitoring of the protected area.Long Range communication is used for wireless transmission of detected event information, while an OLED display, red and green light-emitting diodes, and a buzzer provide system status and alerts.The proposed system provides an automated and lowcost approach to border intrusion monitoring by combining information from multiple sensors with machine learning-based classification and visual verification.
doi:10.64643/ijirt.208470-459.venue: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology

doi:10.58578/masaliq.v6i6.12319.title: Praktik Assessment of Learning pada Evaluasi Matematika SMP: Studi Kasus Guru
doi:10.58578/masaliq.v6i6.12319.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to describe assessment of learning practices in the evaluation of mathematics learning at junior secondary schools (SMP), covering reflection on assessment, the determination of criteria, instrument selection, student involvement, the use of evaluation results, and implementation challenges. The study employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. Data were collected through interviews with mathematics teachers and analyzed descriptively according to themes in assessment practice. The interview findings showed that teachers reflected on assessment through collegial discussions and feedback, considered a range of mathematical competencies when determining criteria, and aligned instruments with learning objectives and student characteristics. The reported forms of assessment included written tests, oral tests, performance assessment, portfolios, self-assessment, and peer assessment. Evaluation results were used to inform the planning of subsequent instruction and remediation. The main challenges included difficulties in assessing problem-solving and critical thinking skills, as well as low motivation among some students. The reported practices reflect teachers’ efforts to integrate multiple sources of evidence into the assessment of learning outcomes, although operational indicators, rubrics, and transparency in assessment decision-making still need to be strengthened. These findings provide a contextual account of mathematics assessment practices in junior secondary schools and indicate aspects that need to be strengthened in their implementation. Because the study was based on interviews, further research using observation and document analysis is needed to examine the technical implementation of assessment in greater depth.</jats:p>

doi:10.5194/egusphere-2026-5409.title: Machine-learning bias correction of passive-microwave sea ice concentration against a SAR-derived product: impact on Arctic sea ice forecasts
doi:10.5194/egusphere-2026-5409.abstract: <jats:p>Abstract. Sea ice concentration (SIC) assimilation in operational systems relies predominantly on passive-microwave satellite retrievals, which present well-known limitations, such as smoothing of the ice edge and underestimation of SIC during the melt season. We develop a Random Forest model that bias-corrects AMSR2 SIC observations towards an existing deep learning, SAR-derived product (ML-SAR) in the Arctic. The bias-corrected AMSR2 observations, together with ML-SAR, are then assimilated into the 1/4° configuration of the Met Office Forecast Ocean Assimilation Model (FOAM) as the key experiment. Assimilating ML-SAR and bias-corrected AMSR2 produces a sharper ice edge during the ice growing season and reduces the 5-day forecast Integrated Ice Edge Error by 30 % in summer, relative to a control experiment assimilating only AMSR2 alongside the standard ocean observations. It also largely mitigates the SIC underestimation in the melt season, raising the Critical Success Index against the ice charts in all SIC categories and at all 5-day forecast lead times, by about 25 % on average, with respect to the control. Because the bias-corrected AMSR2 is assimilated wherever ML-SAR is absent, sea ice forecast improvements reach the whole Arctic, including regions of limited SAR coverage, and could not be obtained by assimilating ML-SAR alone. The additional ice volume produced by assimilating both ML-SAR and bias-corrected AMSR2, particularly in spring and summer, contributes to alleviating a known thin bias in the central Arctic in FOAM, but also leads to an overestimation of thickness in the Arctic marginal seas. Overall, the results demonstrate that, by combining the spatial completeness of passive-microwave observations with the fidelity of SAR-based data, this learned bias correction offers a computationally inexpensive, observation-based pathway towards improved Arctic sea ice prediction.</jats:p>

doi:10.4995/muse.2026.25477.title: Teacher support, student engagement, and learning in project-based learning: An exploratory two time point analysis
doi:10.4995/muse.2026.25477.abstract: <jats:p>Project-Based Learning (PBL) is a teaching methodology that enhances students’ engagement in learning. While there are some models that seek to comprehensively explain the factors associated with engagement, few studies focus on the process itself to understand the dynamics of PBL that lead to student engagement. This study aims to identify the factors that affect student engagement and performance during the PBL process. This exploratory study focused on a PBL experience conducted over two academic years, involving five secondary schools. Structural equation models were developed to analyze the relationships between the program structure and teacher behavior with student engagement and self-reported learning, both at the beginning and at the end of the project. Preliminary results from the study suggest that the initial phase of the project may be important for teachers to foster group autonomy, while in the final phase, it seems advisable to provide structure and emotional involvement in the learning process. This study offers initial evidence that could help promote student engagement in PBL.</jats:p>
doi:10.4995/muse.2026.25477.venue: Multidisciplinary Journal for Education, Social and Technological Sciences

doi:10.64643/ijirt.208559-459.title: Brightsteps AI Based Learning Platform or Children with Down Syndrome
doi:10.64643/ijirt.208559-459.abstract: BrightSteps is an all-around digital learning application that is designed for the children who are affected with Down syndrome for developing their daily life skills, interactive communication and essential academic background.Children with down syndrome have problems with reading, memory, communication and focusing on the topics that make their life challenging to perform their day-to-day tasks.Many existing systems are present but they provide specific personalization and are limited to particular modules.However, the application lacks AI based support, speech and overall progress.To address these problems our proposed system helps the children to provide a simple, interactive and user-friendly application that integrates activities like basic educational games, quizzes, visual learning, memory exercise, daily life communication practice and brain development games to enhance their skills.These platform helps the children to engage in different activities and helps to gain knowledge.It also allows the parents, teachers and even the mentors to monitor the children's daily activities, progress and encourage their skills.The main objective of the proposed system is to provide an opportunity to support the development of the children.These learning applications help to create an integrated platform for education and support the development of children with Down Syndrome.
doi:10.64643/ijirt.208559-459.venue: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology

doi:10.30560/sdr.v8n2p23.title: Remaining-Time Prediction for Hydrogen-Based Iron Ore Pellet Reduction: Cross-Study Evidence and Limits of Structured Learning
doi:10.30560/sdr.v8n2p23.abstract: <jats:p>Early prediction of a pellet-reduction endpoint must extrapolate beyond the observed trajectory and transfer to experiments outside model development. We examine both requirements using 32 published single-pellet curves from five studies and an expanded cohort of 51 curves from seven studies. Direct regressors and positive three-timescale models predict the first crossing of reported reduction degree 0.90 under nested leave-one-study-out evaluation. At the primary checkpoint of 0.4, study-equal mean absolute error in z = ln(1 + remaining time / 1 min) was 0.168 for Ridge, 0.257 for hierarchical maximum-a-posteriori updating and 0.306 for information-restricted updating. Removing either the single-curve study or the terminally normalised study and refitting the complete pipeline preserved the restricted model’s disadvantage in this metric. Its error nevertheless fell to 0.189 under an exploratory goal-centred prior, revealing substantial sensitivity to prior specification rather than consistent superiority over Ridge. Empirical calibration increased coverage by widening intervals; none of the four principal models accepted a plan at the declared relative-width tolerance of 0.30. Checks against original graphical markers also exposed unequal observation times behind nominally matched checkpoints. The results locate conditional benefits of structure while separating endpoint accuracy, parameter interpretation and planning usefulness. Because the trajectories are secondary graphical data and include terminal normalisation, these findings concern retrospective prediction rather than a validated online operating policy.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10934849/v1.title: Parameter compensation reveals weak physical effects in multi-parameter inverse learning
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10934849/v1.abstract: Inverse learning from sparse observations can reproduce measured responses while assigning them to an incorrect combination of physical parameters. This failure can remain hidden at low response error or optimized loss, especially when weak effects are absorbed by compensatory changes in another parameter. We formalize this as parameter compensation and establish local conditions for the existence, persistence and recoverability of compensatory representations. We demonstrate the principle in the minimal nontrivial two-parameter setting, providing a basis for hierarchical extensions. We then develop a bias-compensated neural network (BcNN) with two single-parameter anchors in adjacent physical representations that expose structured pseudo-solutions. Their ordered difference defines a physical gauge for complementary bias reparameterization. Across controlled theoretical benchmarks and sparse structural measurements, BcNN recovers weak physical effects more reliably than baseline PINN. These results show accurate response reconstruction is not sufficient evidence of physical recovery and that representation-dependent pseudo-solutions can provide information for inverse learning.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10934849/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.3389/fnhum.2026.1875156.title: Hierarchical affective predictive imbalance in adolescent borderline personality disorder: task-evoked fMRI evidence from multimodal machine learning
doi:10.3389/fnhum.2026.1875156.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Predictive-processing accounts of BPD, including the hierarchical-prior-imbalance account proposed by Herzog, offer a framework for interpreting affective instability and impulsivity. The present task-fMRI study evaluates whether discriminative task-evoked patterns are consistent with this framework; because it does not directly estimate prediction errors, precision weighting, or hierarchical belief updating, it is not a mechanistic test of predictive processing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate this question, this study developed a leakage-controlled multimodal machine learning framework for individualized classification of adolescents with BPD and healthy controls based on emotional Go/No-Go task-fMRI activity. Three feature domains were constructed: functional connectivity (FC), task-evoked general linear model (GLM)-derived temporal features, and clinical variables. Seven feature settings, including single-modality, dual-modality, and full multimodal combinations, were evaluated using multiple conventional machine learning classifiers, including logistic regression, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors, Gaussian naive Bayes, multilayer perceptron, random forest, and XGBoost or gradient boosting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results showed that task-evoked GLM-derived features provided the strongest single-modality discriminative information (AUC of 0.881 ± 0.055). SHAP analysis confirmed the predominance of GLM-derived features, accounting for 83.1% of total model attribution, compared to 9.5 and 7.5% for functional connectivity and clinical variables, respectively. At the neural level, discriminative features were distributed across visual/perceptual regions (calcarine, cuneus, occipital cortex), temporoparietal/default-mode hubs (angular and supramarginal gyri), frontal control regions (inferior frontal gyrus), and subcortical structures (putamen). This distributed pattern aligns with a hierarchical organization spanning perceptual input, contextual/self-referential processing, and top-down inhibitory control systems, consistent with the proposed model of hierarchical affective predictive imbalance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Task-evoked GLM-derived features were the primary source of discriminative information for adolescent BPD, with functional connectivity and clinical variables providing modest additional value. The resulting classification pattern is consistent with hierarchical predictive-processing accounts but does not establish a specific predictive-processing mechanism. The same regional pattern may also reflect visual attention, salience processing, and executive inhibitory control.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1930030.title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1930030.abstract: <jats:p>Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.</jats:p>

doi:10.64643/ijirt.209614-459.title: Assessing The Reality of Quantum Advantage in Machine Learning
doi:10.64643/ijirt.209614-459.abstract: Quantum computing has generated significant expectations for its potential to enhance machine learning (ML) tasks, with theoretical research proposing computational advantages ranging from polynomial to exponential speedups for specific subroutines.However, a critical disconnect remains: theoretical or asymptotic speedup claims do not automatically imply a practical, end-to-end advantage.Current evidence does not clearly establish whether these claimed advantages translate into measurable superiority over optimised classical approaches.This review critically assesses the relationship between theoretical claims of quantum advantage and the currently available practical and experimental evidence.We critically examine the evidence and assumptions underlying claimed speedups, including the overheads associated with data encoding and access, as well as the use of appropriate and competitive classical baselines for fair comparison.The scope of this assessment covers key limiting factors, such as scalability, trainability, hardware noise in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era, and overall resource requirements.By distinguishing between theoretical potential and demonstrated practical performance, this work identifies where current evidence is convincing and where it remains insufficient.The review identifies the specific conditions required for the credible validation of quantum advantage and argues that future progress must be positioned around rigorous, realistic, and end-to-end evaluation rather than theoretical complexity claims alone.
doi:10.64643/ijirt.209614-459.venue: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology

doi:10.22146/jcef.28456.title: Experimental Study and Physics-Informed Machine Learning on Sustainable Concrete Using Sugarcane Bagasse Ash and Distilled Sewage Water
doi:10.22146/jcef.28456.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing environmental burden associated with cement production and freshwater consumption has created a need for sustainable alternatives in concrete production. This study investigates the combined utilization of Sugarcane Bagasse Ash (SCBA) as a partial cement replacement and Distilled SewageWater (DSW) as an alternative mixing-water source in M25–grade concrete. Seven concrete mixtures (M0–M6) were prepared by incorporating 0–30% SCBA and 0–40% DSW while maintaining a constant binder content of 400 kg/m3 and water-to-binder ratio of 0.50. Compressive strength was experimentally evaluated after 7, 14, and 28 days of curing. The results demonstrated that moderate replacement levels improved strength, with the mixture containing 10% SCBA and 20% DSW achieving the highest compressive strengths of 20.8, 26.1, and 34.2 MPa at 7, 14, and 28 days, respectively. The improvement was attributed to the pozzolanic activity and micro-filler effect of SCBA, together with adequate water availability. Higher replacement levels resulted in strength reduction because of cement dilution and reduced calcium hydroxide availability. Furthermore, Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) models were developed to predict compressive strength using key mix–design parameters and curing age. Both models exhibited excellent predictive performance, with R2 values exceeding 0.999 during the evaluated stages. ANN provided slightly higher numerical accuracy, whereas PINN demonstrated more consistent validation and testing behaviour, indicating improved generalisation and physical consistency. The findings demonstrate that the integrated experimental, physics-informed modelling, and explainable–AI framework can support the development and optimization of sustainable SCBA–DSW concrete while reducing dependence on conventional cement and freshwater resources.</jats:p>
doi:10.22146/jcef.28456.venue: Journal of the Civil Engineering Forum

doi:10.59944/postaxial.v4i3.1961.title: The Utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Technology in Islamic Religious Education to Develop Students’ Spiritual Character at MTs Diniyyah Putri Lampung, Gedong Tataan District, Pesawaran Regency, Lampung Province
doi:10.59944/postaxial.v4i3.1961.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to examine the utilization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) and its contribution to strengthening students’ spiritual character at MTs Diniyyah Putri Lampung, Pesawaran Regency, Lampung Province. The study was motivated by the challenges of providing relevant and engaging Islamic Religious Education for a digitally oriented generation, whose familiarity with technology is not always accompanied by strong spiritual awareness. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. The informants included the Head of the Madrasah, IRE teachers, students, dormitory Ummi, and PMDL administrators. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participatory observations, and documentation of IRE learning activities. The findings indicate that AI was utilized through several applications, including AI-based chatbots to facilitate students’ religious inquiries and spiritual guidance, interactive digital applications to support dhikr and self-reflection (muhasabah), and visual-based AI learning platforms to present Islamic Religious Education materials in a more engaging manner. These applications supported interactive religious learning, encouraged students to reflect on their behavior and religious practices, increased learning motivation, and strengthened emotional engagement with Islamic learning. However, the findings also demonstrate that AI has a supportive rather than substitutive role in spiritual character formation. Teachers remain essential in modeling and cultivating values such as sincerity, patience, discipline, and closeness to Allah SWT through direct guidance and interpersonal interaction. The novelty of this study lies in identifying AI as a complementary pedagogical instrument that connects digital Islamic learning with students’ spiritual self-reflection, while emphasizing the irreplaceable role of teachers in authentic spiritual character formation. This study contributes to the development of technology-integrated Islamic Religious Education by proposing a balanced approach in which AI supports learning innovation without displacing teacher-mediated spiritual formation.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11084191/v1.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Stock Market Prediction: A Systematic Literature Review of Methods, Emerging Paradigms, Reproducibility, and Evaluation Gaps (2016-2026)
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11084191/v1.abstract: Stock prices are hard to predict: the underlying series are non-stationary, noisy, and non-linear, and over the past decade researchers have increasingly reached for artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) rather than classical linear econometrics. This paper reports a systematic literature review (SLR), conducted under PRISMA 2020, of 685 primary empirical studies drawn from three scientific databases (Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science) and published between 2016 and 2026. We ask four questions. First, which architectures does the field actually use, and how do shallow models, deep sequence networks, and hybrid ensembles compare across markets, horizons, and asset classes? Second, how has method evolved over the decade, from kernel machines through recurrent networks to Transformers, financial Large Language Models (LLMs), dynamic spatial-temporal Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), multimodal fusion, and friction-aware Deep Reinforcement Learning? Third, how reproducible is any of it? We audit code, data, and environment availability, sort the corpus into a three-tier reproducibility hierarchy, and give mathematical form to five recurring data leakage mechanisms. Fourth, how are models evaluated? Here we describe what we call the ``Lag-1 Shadowing Trap'', along with scale-dependent error metrics, ignored execution frictions, and a near-absence of statistical hypothesis testing. LSTM networks appear in 89.2% of the studies and hybrid frameworks in 61.9%, yet only 7.6% release working source code, more than 83% report no formal significance test, and 45.8% never assess trading utility at all. We close with a Four-Pillar Standardization Protocol intended to narrow the gap between the accuracies papers report and the returns those models can plausibly earn.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11084191/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.33619/2414-2948/131/61.title: The Use of Machine Translation as a Tool for Teaching Translation at University
doi:10.33619/2414-2948/131/61.abstract: <jats:p>The article examines the didactic potential of machine translation in university translator training. The study aims to identify learning tasks in which automated systems support the development of translation competence without replacing students’ independent analytical work. The research material includes publications on neural machine translation, digital competence, post-editing, methodological recommendations, and ISO 18587:2017. The methods comprise literature analysis, comparison of pedagogical approaches, classification of recurrent errors, and modeling of classroom assignments. The findings show that comparing a source text with machine-generated output helps students identify semantic, terminological, stylistic, and culture-specific errors. Post-editing develops fact-checking, terminology management, and the ability to assess whether a translation is suitable for a particular communicative purpose. Unsupervised reliance on online services, however, may weaken independent decision-making and encourage uncritical trust in automatically generated text. A staged classroom procedure is proposed: an initial translation without digital assistance, production of a machine-translated version, classification of discrepancies, reasoned editing, and final reflection. For language pairs involving Kyrgyz, special attention should be paid to culture-bound vocabulary and the limited availability of digital corpora. The study concludes that machine translation should be used as an auxiliary tool under teacher supervision. This approach combines traditional translation training with digital literacy, professional responsibility, and systematic post-editing skills.</jats:p>

doi:10.17559/tv-20260816003808.title: Comparative Study of SREM and RAM Methods for Machine Tool Selection
doi:10.17559/tv-20260816003808.abstract: This study performs a comparative evaluation of two multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) approaches, the Square-Root based Evaluation Method (SREM) and the Root Assessment Method (RAM) for machine tool selection, specifically wood planers and grinding machines. The performance effectiveness and ranking stability of both methods were evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (S) against ten widely used contemporary MCDM techniques: TOPSIS, SAW, MARCOS, ROV, FUCA, PIV, VIKOR, COCOSO, CRADIS, and EDAS. Experimental results and sensitivity analyses under different weight distributions indicate that SREM's capacity to maintain ranking stability relies on the adjustment coefficient k, which balances square-root and squared transformations. When k equals 0 (considering only the square-root transformation), SREM achieves very high ranking consensus, fully comparable to RAM and the other MCDM techniques (with mean S ranging from 0.9143 to 0.9580). However, increasing coefficient k (which raises the weight of the squared transformation) lowers SREM's ranking agreement, as the squared transformation exaggerates disparities among criteria containing extreme or outlier values, resulting in severe over-penalization or over-rewarding of specific alternatives. Although both SREM and RAM were verified as suitable for machine tool selection in the tested scenarios, a detailed assessment reveals that RAM proves superior to SREM in ensuring overall ranking consensus and stability for machine tool ranking.

doi:10.1093/9780198986201.003.0064.title: Can Failure Be Success? Interrogating Urban Climate Governance Fragmentation as ‘Adaptation by Learning’
doi:10.1093/9780198986201.003.0064.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Urban climate governance is often portrayed as fragmented, producing policy incoherence, uneven capacities, and inequitable outcomes. This article reframes fragmentation not only as a constraint, but also as a potential driver of ‘adaptation by learning’. Drawing on comparative case studies of Lincoln, San Francisco, and London, and three analytical drivers—(a) institutional and multi‑level governance; (b) political economy and resource constraints; and (c) knowledge, networks, and socio‑spatial inequality——the article shows how fragmentation generates both failures and conditions for urban climate governance experimentation, reflexivity, and mutual adjustment. Fragmentation can inhibit coherent climate action where silos, resource asymmetries, and competing mandates persist, yet it can also catalyse learning where diverse actors, intermediaries, and participatory processes convert governance failures into new practices, relationships, and organizational routines. The authors conceptualize adaptation by learning as a dynamic process through which actors reinterpret problems, renegotiate roles, and institutionalize new modes of coordination over time. By treating fragmentation as a condition to be intentionally governed rather than eliminated, this article advances a more adaptive, connected, and just model of urban climate governance enabled by bridging scales and cross-institutional intermediaries, community-driven participation, iterative learning from failure, and coordinated resources drawn from fragmented funding landscapes.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/ir-07-2026-0421.title: Geometrically constrained permutation invariant learning for hand-eye calibration with iteratively reweighted least squares and Levenberg–Marquardt refinement
doi:10.1108/ir-07-2026-0421.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to develop an accurate and robust hand-eye calibration framework for estimating the rigid transformation between a camera and a robot end-effector, particularly under non-ideal conditions involving noisy pose measurements, outliers and motion pairs of varying quality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed method models unordered relative pose pairs using a shared, attention based, permutation invariant encoder. Rotations are represented in the Lie algebra and mapped to SO(3) via the exponential map, while translations are estimated by least squares. The resulting initial estimate is then refined on SO(3) using iteratively reweighted least squares combined with Levenberg–Marquardt optimization, thereby improving robustness to measurement noise and outliers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate and robust hand-eye calibration. Geometry aware refinement enhances calibration stability in the presence of noise and outliers while preserving the physical consistency of the estimated rigid transformation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study develops a permutation invariant hand-eye calibration approach that integrates Lie group-based rotation modeling with robust refinement on SO(3), enabling reliable calibration under noisy and heterogeneous measurement conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
doi:10.1108/ir-07-2026-0421.venue: Industrial Robot: the international journal of robotics research and application

doi:10.4324/9781003743705-12.title: Integrating Flexible Grading and Formative Assessment to Promote Learning and Engagement
doi:10.4324/9781003743705-12.abstract: In this chapter, I will describe a series of interventions to promote student learning and engagement I have attempted in several of my recent Psychology undergraduate courses. Combining insights from small (∼25 person) seminar-style upper-division courses (PSYC169), larger (∼150 person) upper-division lecture classes (PSYC161) and a high-enrollment (∼600 person), online lower-division introductory course (PSYC2V), I review the strategies implemented in these varying contexts to co-construct a supportive and inclusive learning environment and meet students where they are when they join my classes. The discussion will focus on applications of innovative teaching techniques including “ungrading,” emphasis on peer feedback and formative assessments, and flexible grading policies to support all students. Strategies to support and mentor graduate teaching assistants in these courses will also be discussed. The chapter ends with a consideration of reasons why certain interventions were not fully successful, and recommendations for future efforts to promote student success.

doi:10.3389/fneur.2026.1954788.title: Deep learning–accelerated contrast-enhanced 3D MRI for acute optic neuritis: faster acquisition and improved lesion conspicuity
doi:10.3389/fneur.2026.1954788.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To compare a deep learning-accelerated contrast-enhanced 3D T1-weighted sequence (T1-CUBE-DLS) with standard parallel imaging-accelerated T1-CUBE for detecting acute optic neuritis (ON).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This prospective study enrolled 59 patients with suspected acute ON (38 females; mean age 41.2 ± 12.8 years). All underwent contrast-enhanced whole-brain 3.0 T MRI including both T1-CUBE-DLS and standard T1-CUBE sequences. Two blinded neuroradiologists independently scored motion artifacts, subjective noise, and optic nerve clarity. Consensus readings recorded enhancement laterality, involved segments, and visual conspicuity. Enhancement length was measured per optic nerve, with inter-observer reliability assessed via intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and Bland–Altman analysis. Clinical diagnosis by a senior neuro-ophthalmologist served as the reference standard.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Acute ON was confirmed in 43 of 59 patients (72.9%). T1-CUBE-DLS reduced acquisition time by 36.2%. Subjective noise was equivalent between sequences (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &gt; 0.05), but T1-CUBE-DLS showed significantly fewer motion artifacts and superior optic nerve clarity (both
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.05). No significant difference was detected in diagnostic performance between the two sequences: sensitivity (88.4% vs. 86.0%), specificity (93.8% vs. 93.8%), and accuracy (89.8% vs. 88.1%; all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &gt; 0.05). T1-CUBE-DLS demonstrated stronger visual conspicuity (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.011) and slightly longer measured enhancement length (mean difference, 0.836 mm;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.0001). ICC for length measurement was 0.91 for T1-CUBE-DLS vs. 0.83 for standard T1-CUBE, with narrower 95% limits of agreement (−1.37 to 1.51 mm vs. − 3.1 to 2.4 mm).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>T1-CUBE-DLS reduces acquisition time by 36.2%, with no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy detected, while improving enhancement conspicuity and measurement reproducibility, supporting its potential as a practical and efficient alternative for ON evaluation.</jats:p>

doi:10.68414/fxcq4238.title: Engaging HBCU Students in Active Learning for Blockchain, FinTech, and Generative AI: A Human-Centered Pedagogical Framework
doi:10.68414/fxcq4238.abstract: <jats:p>The convergence of blockchain, financial technology, digital assets, and generative artificial intelligence creates important opportunities and challenges for undergraduate education, especially at Historically Black Colleges and Universities. Students preparing for careers in business, computing, analytics, cybersecurity, and financial services need more than exposure to emerging technologies; they also need confidence, collaboration skills, ethical awareness, computational fluency, and experience applying tools to realistic problems. This paper proposes a human-centered pedagogical framework to engage HBCU students in active learning about blockchain, FinTech, and generative AI. The framework synthesizes classroom-tested strategies from computer information systems, business analytics, programming, mathematics, and interdisciplinary student research. It emphasizes structured collaboration, low-stakes practice, role rotation, peer evaluation, reflective learning, responsible use of generative AI, reproducible computational notebooks, and applied problem contexts such as credit risk, fraud detection, investment analysis, digital trust, and smart financial systems. The paper presents an evidence-informed model that instructors can adapt across introductory and advanced undergraduate courses. The framework suggests that active, collaborative, and AI-supported pedagogy can increase student participation, reduce anxiety around technical topics, support inclusive learning, and strengthen workforce readiness for emerging blockchain and FinTech ecosystems.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10833348/v1.title: Learning alignment topology improves structural variant discovery from long-read sequencing
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10833348/v1.abstract: Structural variant calling from long-read sequencing is increasingly limited not by read length itself, but by how heterogeneous alignment signals are combined into candidate events. Repetitive sequence, short variants and mobile element insertions can produce dispersed breakpoints and ambiguous local alignments that challenge fixed clustering strategies. We developed SGraSV, which uses self-supervised graph representation learning to capture relationships among read-level signals and local sequence context. Here, we show that SGraSV improves detection and breakpoint resolution across PacBio and Oxford Nanopore data and maintains high reproducibility across sequencing platforms. Evaluation in 65 individuals and independent analysis of 3,202 1000 Genomes Project genomes further support its ability to recover rare and difficult variants. In particular, SGraSV preserves characteristic insertion patterns for mobile elements that are often fragmented by existing callers. These findings support graph-based representation of alignment evidence as a practical strategy for improving structural variant discovery in heterogeneous genomic datasets.

doi:10.12688/f1000research.182491.2.title: Towards a New Learning Ecology: The Mediator Role of Teachers Facing Generative AI in the University Context of Peru, Chile, and Colombia
doi:10.12688/f1000research.182491.2.abstract: <ns3:p>Background The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has created an ontological disruption in higher education, challenging traditional pedagogical mediation and academic production. This study examines the transformation of the teaching role in university environments across Peru, Chile, and Colombia, addressing a knowledge gap in Latin American empirical research regarding faculty perceptions and daily practices with Large Language Models. Methods The research employed a descriptive-interpretative qualitative design with an open-ended survey approach interpreted through a hermeneutic lens. A non-probabilistic sample of 48 undergraduate and graduate professors from 20 Higher Education Institutions in the region participated. Data were collected through a validated 18-item structured online questionnaire and analyzed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis assisted by Atlas.ti software. Results The findings identify a transition from traditional instructional roles toward a “mediator-curator” model, where educators act as orchestrators of human-AI co-intelligence. Key applications include pedagogical re-engineering, such as dynamic curricular design, Socratic tutoring, and the shift from product-oriented to process-oriented assessment. Critical dimensions emerged regarding the need for pedagogical re-engineering, ethical challenges in academic integrity, and the development of critical AI literacy. National variations showed Chile focusing on pedagogical equity, Colombia on research productivity, and Peru on didactic agility. Conclusions The integration of GenAI in the Latin American university context requires a situated pedagogical response that transcends instrumental use. The study proposes a new learning ecology where the teacher facilitates critical interaction between students and generative systems. This shift necessitates a reconfiguration of teaching competencies toward epistemic curation and algorithmic responsibility to ensure meaningful and ethical learning.</ns3:p>

doi:10.64643/ijirt.208434-459.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Predict Human Vulnerability to Cyber Threats? A Machine Learning Approach to Cybersecurity Behaviour
doi:10.64643/ijirt.208434-459.abstract: Individual users, rather than the technical systems around them, are frequently a critical point of vulnerability in cybersecurity: a reused password, an unexamined link, a postponed software update, or a banking session conducted over an unsecured public network can expose individuals to significant cyber risks.Existing approaches to behavioural cybersecurity often reduce vulnerability to a single overall score, which may indicate that an individual is at risk without identifying the specific behaviours contributing to that risk.At the same time, the growing application of supervised machine learning in cybersecurity has focused predominantly on organisational networks, systems, and software rather than on individual behavioural profiles.This paper addresses this gap by developing a multidimensional framework for analysing human vulnerability to cyber threats.The framework incorporates eight behavioural domains-password management, authentication, phishing response, device security, privacy practices, network behaviour, digital payment security, and incident response-along with a transparent and leakage-aware procedure for behavioural risk scoring.It further proposes a supervised machine-learning pipeline using Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and K-Nearest Neighbours, with model assessment based on accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC rather than accuracy alone.A SHAP-based explainability layer is incorporated to connect model classifications with the behavioural factors underlying them, making the resulting assessment more transparent and actionable.By integrating behavioural cybersecurity measurement, machine learning, and explainable artificial intelligence, the study presents a structured and non-stigmatising approach to understanding individual cybersecurity vulnerability and provides a foundation for future empirical investigation and targeted cybersecurity awareness strategies.
doi:10.64643/ijirt.208434-459.venue: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1960438.title: Multistage CBAM-enhanced deep learning for three-class classification of radiographically derived bone mass status labels on knee radiographs
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1960438.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To develop and validate a deep learning model incorporating multistage convolutional block attention modules (CBAMs) for classifying the radiographically derived bone-mass labels (normal bone mass, osteopenia, and osteoporosis) of a public knee radiograph dataset, and to investigate the potential of knee radiography for opportunistic screening of abnormal bone mass.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study used the publicly available Multi-Class Knee Osteoporosis x-Ray Dataset, which was released on Kaggle and compiled from multiple publicly accessible knee radiograph sources. The class labels (normal bone mass, osteopenia, and osteoporosis) were assigned by the dataset provider on the basis of radiographic features and were not verified against dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) T-scores; the model therefore classifies the dataset's radiographic labels rather than DXA-defined bone mass status. After assessing image integrity, label consistency, and data usability, a total of 1,947 knee radiographs were included, comprising 780 images labeled as normal bone mass, 374 as osteopenia, and 793 as osteoporosis. The dataset was stratified into training, validation, and test sets at a ratio of 70:20:10. All images were resized to 224 × 224 pixels and normalized using the ImageNet mean and standard deviation. A multi-stage convolutional block attention module (CBAM)-enhanced classification model was developed based on a VGG19-style convolutional neural network and compared with the ResNet50, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet121, and VGG19 baseline models, as well as several attention-based ablation models. Model performance was evaluated using overall accuracy, class-wise precision, recall, and F1-score, together with confusion matrices and one-vs.-rest receiver operating characteristic curves. Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) was further used to visualize and assess the image regions contributing to model predictions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On the independent test set, the multistage CBAM model achieved the highest overall accuracy of 90.77% (177/195), outperforming VGG19, ResNet50, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet121, and a reproduced model from the literature. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) was 0.982 for normal bone mass, 0.991 for osteopenia, and 0.981 for osteoporosis. The confusion matrix showed 68/78, 34/38, and 75/79 correctly classified images in the three categories, respectively, with most errors occurring between adjacent bone-mass states. Ablation experiments showed that multistage CBAM outperformed attention-free VGG19, SE-VGG19, ECA-VGG19, and stacked CBAM. Grad-CAM highlighted primarily the distal femur, proximal tibia, and periarticular osseous structures. All results were obtained from a single stratified split and a single random seed (42); because of limited computational resources, repeated runs over multiple seeds and k-fold cross-validation could not be performed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The multistage CBAM-enhanced model effectively distinguished the radiographically derived bone-mass labels (normal bone mass, osteopenia, and osteoporosis) of this public knee radiograph dataset. Because the labels were not verified against DXA, the model should be regarded as a classifier of the dataset's radiographic labels rather than of DXA-defined bone mass status. It may serve as an adjunctive tool for opportunistic screening of abnormal bone mass and provide imaging-based prompts for subsequent DXA assessment and fracture-risk evaluation, subject to further validation against DXA-derived ground truth, de-duplication and patient-level partitioning, and external data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.64643/ijirt.208760-459.title: A Review of Explainable AI Techniques in Machine Learning
doi:10.64643/ijirt.208760-459.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used in healthcare, finance, education, cybersecurity and other decision support applications.As predictive systems become more complex, it is often difficult for users to understand why a model produces a particular output.This issue is commonly described as the black box problem.Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) addresses this concern by providing information that helps humans understand model predictions and behaviour.This paper reviews major XAI approaches and organizes them according to explanation scope, model dependence and the stage at which interpretability is introduced.Prominent techniques including SHAP, LIME, saliency maps, attention-based approaches, counterfactual explanations and surrogate models are discussed.Their working principles, strengths, limitations and typical application areas are compared.The paper also examines important criteria for judging explanation quality, including fidelity, stability, robustness, completeness and human interpretability.A key observation from the reviewed literature is that an explanation that appears convincing to a human is not necessarily a faithful representation of the underlying model.The review therefore distinguishes plausibility from faithfulness and highlights the need for systematic evaluation.Finally, research gaps involving standardized benchmarks, causal reasoning, fairness, privacy, robustness and domain-specific explanations are discussed.The review concludes that there is no single XAI method that is optimal for every model or application; the choice should depend on the model, data, decision context and needs of the intended user.
doi:10.64643/ijirt.208760-459.venue: International Journal of Innovative Research in Technology

doi:10.1108/lodj-01-2024-0057.title: The impact of authentic leadership on organizational learning: mediating roles of organizational culture and knowledge sharing
doi:10.1108/lodj-01-2024-0057.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing upon social information processing theory, this research examines the impact of authentic leadership on organizational learning through the mediating roles of organizational culture and knowledge sharing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using purposive sampling, we targeted all senior managers of nonprofit sport organizations in Gilan Province, Iran. Of the 189 questionnaires distributed, 182 usable responses were retained for analysis. The collected data were subsequently analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling with SmartPLS 4.0.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings provide evidence that authentic leadership has a significant positive effect on organizational learning, organizational culture and knowledge sharing. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that organizational culture and knowledge sharing serve as important mechanisms through which authentic leadership contributes to the development of organizational learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nonprofit sport organizations should invest in targeted leadership development programs to strengthen authentic leadership capabilities among current and emerging leaders. Simultaneously, managers should cultivate transparent and collaborative organizational cultures that promote knowledge sharing through open communication and trust-based relationships. Together, these initiatives can enhance organizational learning and contribute to the long-term effectiveness of nonprofit sport organizations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This article presents an integrated model explaining how authentic leadership influences organizational learning in the underexplored context of Iranian sports organizations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
