doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1964709.title: Association between the triacylglycerol–glucose index, TyG-BMI and hypertension in children and adolescents: a cross-sectional study with machine-learning-based risk stratification
doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1964709.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hypertension in children and adolescents is closely linked to obesity and metabolic disturbance. The triacylglycerol–glucose (TyG) index and TyG-BMI are surrogate markers of insulin resistance, but their associations with pediatric hypertension remain incompletely characterized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 25,886 children and adolescents aged 7–17 years from 18 prefecture-level cities in Henan Province, China. The TyG index was calculated as ln[triglycerides (mg/dL) × fasting plasma glucose (mg/dL)/2] and TyG-BMI as TyG × BMI. Hypertension was defined as a blood pressure at or above the 95th percentile for age, sex and height (mean of the last two of three measurements). Logistic regression (Models I–IV) estimated odds ratios (ORs) per 1 SD and across quartiles, with non-linearity and effect modification assessed on both scales. Eleven machine-learning models were developed on a stratified 70:30 split, with imputation and feature selection performed strictly within the training set and discrimination (area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve, AUC) evaluated in the held-out validation set.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 25,886 participants, 1,798 (6.95%) had hypertension. Median TyG was 8.05 (IQR 7.77–8.35) and median TyG-BMI 154 (IQR 133–180). Each 1-SD increment in TyG was associated with hypertension in all models (Model IV 1.306 (95% CI 1.145–1.489)), and the association was graded across quartiles; TyG-BMI showed stronger associations (Model IV 2.109 (95% CI 1.985–2.241)). No multiplicative product term was significant after correction, whereas on the additive scale all six relative excess risk estimates were positive with confidence intervals excluding zero. In the held-out validation set, discrimination was moderate (best AUC 0.7544, 95% CI 0.7302–0.7777, for TyG and 0.7534, 0.7298–0.7759, for TyG-BMI), and adding either index to the same baseline model already containing BMI increased discrimination only marginally (about 0.003 in AUC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher TyG and TyG-BMI were associated with hypertension in Chinese children and adolescents, more strongly for TyG-BMI. No multiplicative interaction survived correction, but all additive-scale estimates were positive, so effect modification cannot be excluded. Machine-learning models built from routinely available variables showed only moderate discrimination and remain hypothesis-generating tools for risk stratification rather than validated prediction models. Longitudinal studies are needed to assess causality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.14445/23488387/ijcse-v13i9p101.title: Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning Models with SHAP Explanations towards Transparent Fake News Detection
doi:10.14445/23488387/ijcse-v13i9p101.abstract: <jats:p>The generation of fake news on online platforms has grown into a serious problem, compromising public trust, public opinion and the possibility of information-based decision making. In this study, an intelligent Fake News Detection (FND) system to automatically classify news articles as fake or real was developed using techniques of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Machine Learning (ML) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). A publicly available dataset consisting of 44,856 news articles from the LIAR data set and the Kaggle repository was used, of which 80% was used for training and 20% for testing. The data preprocessing included the following steps: Removing punctuation, Lowercase, Stop-word removal, Tokenization, Stemming, Lemmatization, and TF-IDF (Term Frequency – Inverse Document Frequency) Feature Extraction. The classification algorithms used were Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), which were trained and evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. Experimental results indicated that SVM outperforms the other models with respect to accuracy (99.21%), precision (99.25%), recall (99.23%), F1-Score (99.24%) and AUC-ROC (99.96%). To make the classifications auditable, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied uniformly to all five trained models rather than to the best model alone, permitting a direct comparison of the lexical evidence on which each classifier relies. The attributions converge: four of the five models rank the token “said” as the single most influential feature, and in every case, it shifts the prediction towards REAL, indicating that the models are detecting the attribution conventions of professional reporting rather than topic alone. The results show that the proposed NLP-ML-XAI framework is accurate, interpretable, and reliable for automatic fake news detection, which could be deployed by media organizations, fact checkers, and digital platforms to prevent spreading fake news online.</jats:p>
doi:10.14445/23488387/ijcse-v13i9p101.venue: International Journal of Computer Science and Engineering

doi:10.1108/tlo-11-2025-0282.title: Emotional intelligence and leadership development: past patterns, present realities and future directions in learning-oriented research
doi:10.1108/tlo-11-2025-0282.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study systematically examines the intersection of emotional intelligence (EI), leadership and learning-oriented development to understand how the field has evolved and its implications for human resource development (HRD) theory and practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A bibliometric analysis of 72 Scopus-indexed, ABDC-ranked journal articles published between 2015 and 2025 was conducted using Bibliometrix and VOSviewer. The analysis examined publication trends, collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence patterns and thematic evolution within the field.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seven thematic clusters emerged, with EI functioning as a central construct linking leadership, workplace learning and organizational outcomes. The findings indicate a shift from viewing EI as a fixed trait to conceptualizing it as a developable capability shaped through learning, reflection and relational experiences. The field has evolved from early conceptual exploration (2015–2018) to more empirical and context-driven research, particularly in the postpandemic period (2022–2025). While transformational leadership and EI remain dominant themes, adaptive, digital and crisis leadership have emerged as important areas of inquiry. The analysis also reveals a geographically diverse research landscape, although international collaboration remains uneven across regions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric overview of the intersection between EI, leadership and learning and advances a learning-oriented perspective by positioning EI as a key capability within leadership development frameworks. By integrating leadership, workplace learning and organizational context, the study contributes to HRD and leadership scholarship and offers a structured foundation for future research and practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.2002414.title: A conceptual framework: what is impactful learning? A case study of teaching organic chemistry for pre-medical students
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.2002414.abstract: <jats:p>Organic chemistry occupies a contested place in pre-health education: required of nearly all premedical students, experienced as difficult, and justified on grounds that it “teaches you to think”, a claim too vague to evaluate or teach toward deliberately. Existing frameworks do not resolve this tension. This paper adopts a conceptual analysis approach, drawing on Ausubel's rote/meaningful learning distinction and the traditional transfer-of-learning literature, to propose impactful learning as a third pedagogical stage following rote and meaningful learning. Impactful learning is defined as the stage where procedural and reasoning skills exercised in mastering a discipline's content become generalizable cognitive tools deployable outside that discipline. Three key concepts are examined: the unit of transfer (the cognitive procedure, not the content), the extraction dimension (detachment of a practiced operation from the content that trained it), and the conditions under which such transfer becomes pedagogically achievable. These concepts are developed through three organic chemistry tasks as worked examples—resonance structures as constraint-satisfaction reasoning, reaction mechanisms as iterative-hypothesis testing, and stereochemistry as symbolic-to-spatial translation—each mapped onto a corresponding form of clinical reasoning. We further propose a four-step explicit transfer scaffolding model (Name, Perform, Bridge, Generate) as a testable methodological companion, grounded in Gick and Holyoak's analogical transfer research and Detterman's critique of spontaneous far transfer. The paper argues that naming impactful learning as a distinct pedagogical target, rather than assuming it as an automatic byproduct of meaningful understanding, has direct implications for instructional design and assessment in service courses across STEM disciplines.</jats:p>

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aec2068.title: Learning to infer transitively on a mental line in premotor cortex
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aec2068.abstract: <jats:p>Transitive inference (TI) is a form of deductive reasoning that enables the derivation of unknown relationships among premises. It is hypothesized that this cognitive process relies on mapping stimuli onto a “mental line,” a linear workspace organized by arbitrarily assigned ranks. However, its neural basis remains unclear: Does this mental line have a neural correlate and how is it learned? This study investigates the role of dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) in encoding the hypothesized mental line as monkeys acquire item relationships for motor decisions. Findings reveal that PMd multiunit activity organizes along a theoretically predicted direction, supporting a geometrical model that explains behavior. Moreover, a learning process is observed, where the mental line rotates to align with motor planning.</jats:p>

Five machine learning methods are deployed and benchmarked: (i) Sparse Identification of Non-linear Dynamics (SINDy) with a generic polynomial library, which recovers the predator equations exactly (

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1942203.title: Development and external validation of interpretable machine learning models for 7-, 14-, and 28-day mortality in sepsis-associated liver injury
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1942203.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mortality in sepsis-associated liver injury (SALI) remains high, and early risk stratification is difficult. Existing prognostic models commonly focus on a single endpoint, usually 28-day mortality, and rarely undergo independent external validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We developed machine-learning models using clinical features recorded during the first 24 h to predict all-cause in-hospital mortality within 7, 14, and 28 days. In MIMIC-IV (v3.1), 1,550 adults meeting the prespecified SALI criteria were allocated to a training cohort (n = 1,119) and a held-out internal validation cohort (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 431). An independent Chinese cohort from Xiaogan Central Hospital (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 229; 28-day in-hospital mortality, 45.9%) was used for external validation. One hundred candidate pipelines were evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. SHAP was used to describe feature attribution across prediction horizons.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      AUROCs in the held-out internal validation cohort were 0.840, 0.841, and 0.850 for 7-, 14-, and 28-day mortality, respectively; corresponding external AUROCs were 0.720, 0.717, and 0.763. The external 28-day model outperformed modified SOFA (0.763 vs. 0.673;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.011) and MELD-Na (0.763 vs. 0.636;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.002). A parsimonious logistic-regression sensitivity model achieved an external 28-day AUROC of 0.762, not significantly different from the full model (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.970). The 14-day model was miscalibrated externally; recalibration improved the calibration slope from 0.563 to 0.970 but did not materially improve the Brier score. SHAP rankings varied across horizons and were interpreted descriptively rather than causally.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The models showed moderate transportability to one independent retrospective cohort. Multicentre prospective validation is needed before clinical implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1021/acs.jcim.6c03208.title: Interpretive Limits of Cross-Split AUPRC Differences in Deep Learning-Based Antibiotic Screening
doi:10.1021/acs.jcim.6c03208.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Deep learning expands the chemical space accessible to antibiotic discovery, making interpretation of evaluation results increasingly important when only a few compounds can be prioritized from vast candidate libraries. AUPRC depends on test-set prevalence, while molecular splitting can alter training-to-test structural relatedness and test-set class composition, so when prevalence differs across splits, a cross-split AUPRC difference alone cannot quantify how much of the performance change is attributable to structural differences. Cross-split comparisons should therefore report test-set size, positive count, prevalence, splitting method, and the precision-recall summary metric, while direct model comparisons should use the same fixed independent test set whenever possible. Claims about practical screening utility should also consider top-k performance, early enrichment metrics, or prospective experimental hit rates under a prespecified budget, so that evidence remains aligned with the scientific claims it is intended to support.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4508-4.ch001.title: Designing Low-Cost, AI-Supported Instructional Tools for Individualised Learning in Inclusive Primary and Secondary Education
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4508-4.ch001.abstract: <jats:p>Inclusive classrooms require teachers to address diverse learner needs while maintaining meaningful participation and access to the curriculum for all pupils. This chapter explores how low-cost and freely available artificial intelligence (AI) tools can support individualised learning and inclusive instructional design in primary and secondary education. Drawing on the principles of Inclusive Education, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and Differentiated Instruction, it presents practical applications of AI for text adaptation, visual supports, accessibility, communication, multilingual learning, and personalised learning. A Five-Step Framework for AI-Supported Inclusive Instructional Design is proposed to guide teachers in identifying learner needs, selecting appropriate tools, developing accessible materials, implementing instructional supports, and evaluating their effectiveness. The chapter argues that AI is most valuable when used as a teacher-controlled tool that enhances accessibility, participation, and equitable learning opportunities for all pupils.</jats:p>

doi:10.58421/misro.v5i3.2138.title: Improvement in Junior High School Students’ Mathematical Critical Thinking Ability through the Teams Games Tournament (TGT) Learning Model Assisted by Wordwall on the Topic of Two-Variable Linear Equation Systems (SPLDV)
doi:10.58421/misro.v5i3.2138.abstract: <jats:p>This research was motivated by junior high school students' low mathematical critical thinking ability in Two-Variable Linear Equation Systems (SPLDV), shown by their difficulties interpreting word problems, constructing mathematical models, and drawing logical conclusions. This study aims to describe the change in students' mathematical critical thinking ability on SPLDV after learning with the Teams Games Tournament (TGT) model assisted by Wordwall. Using a quantitative pre-experimental approach with a One Group Pretest-Posttest Design, the sample comprised 28 eighth-grade students (class VIII-B) of SMP Negeri 1 Sipispis, selected through purposive sampling. The instrument consisted of five essay items, one for each of five critical thinking indicators, scored with a 0–4 rubric. A pilot test with 25 students showed item-total correlations of 0.59–0.85 (rtable = 0.396) and a Cronbach's Alpha of 0.76. Data were analyzed using normality tests on the difference scores, a paired-samples t-test (α = 0.05), effect size, and normalized gain. The mean score increased from 36.61 (pre-test) to 75.71 (post-test); the mean difference of 39.11 points was statistically significant (95% CI [33.33, 44.89]; t(27) = 13.88, p < 0.001; Cohen's dz = 2.62), with a normalized gain of 0.62 (moderate), and all 28 students improved. Scores rose on all five indicators. Because the design had no control group, the improvement cannot be attributed solely to the treatment and should be confirmed with a quasi-experimental design.</jats:p>
doi:10.58421/misro.v5i3.2138.venue: Journal of Mathematics Instruction, Social Research and Opinion

doi:10.15408/elementar.v5i2.49692.title: DIFFERENTIATED LEARNING STRATEGIES TO IMPROVE THE INTERPERSONAL SKILLS OF STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES IN SCIENCE LEARNING
doi:10.15408/elementar.v5i2.49692.abstract:
<jats:p>This study aims to analyze the role of differentiated learning in developing the interpersonal skills of students with disabilities through Natural Science (IPA) learning in an inclusive educational environment. Interpersonal skills, such as social participation, communication, collaboration, and self-confidence, are important competencies that support the academic and social success of students with disabilities, but are often not optimally developed in inclusive practices. This study used a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) design with a descriptive qualitative approach. Data were obtained from reputable national and international journal articles published between 2021 and 2025 and analyzed using thematic analysis techniques. The synthesis results indicate that differentiated learning—especially in the aspect of process differentiation—plays a significant role in improving the quality of social interactions of students with disabilities through flexible grouping, collaborative role assignments, and adjustments to learning activities according to students' readiness and learning profiles. Inquiry-based and collaborative IPA learning has proven to be an effective social space for inclusively training students' communication, cooperation, and self-confidence. These findings confirm that differentiated learning functions not only as an academic strategy but also as a social learning mechanism that supports the development of interpersonal skills in students with disabilities. The implications of this research emphasize the importance of deliberate instructional design, teacher competency in differentiation, and the integration of social goals in inclusive science learning.
Keywords: differentiated learning, interpersonal skills, students with disabilities, inclusive education, science learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.22373/1gqr4h33.title: PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS OF MACHINE LEARNING AND INDOBERT IN CLASSIFYING SENTIMENTS ON INDONESIA'S FREE NUTRITIOUS MEAL
doi:10.22373/1gqr4h33.abstract: <jats:p>Natural Language Processing (NLP) is a branch of artificial intelligence that is widely used to analyze whether a sentence contains positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, particularly in the context of expressing opinions in the online environment. This study compares several models to identify the most optimal one, namely Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machine (SVM), XGBoost, and IndoBERT. The dataset used in this research was obtained from Kaggle and consists of 5,644 data points in the neutral class, 2,934 data points in the positive class, and 2,606 data points in the negative class. Prior to model implementation, the dataset underwent a preprocessing stage that included case folding, cleansing, tokenization, stemming, and stopword removal. Subsequently, the data were trained using the four aforementioned methods. The results indicate that Naïve Bayes achieved an accuracy of 75%, SVM reached 79%, XGBoost obtained 76%, while IndoBERT achieved the highest accuracy at 85%. Therefore, it can be concluded that, using this dataset, IndoBERT performed sentiment classification very effectively.</jats:p>

doi:10.70148/rise.v3i6.3.title: Developing Islamic Innovative Pedagogy in Early Childhood Education: A Faith-Informed Framework for Holistic and Sustainable Learning
doi:10.70148/rise.v3i6.3.abstract: <jats:p>Islamic early childhood education (ECE) lacks a sufficiently articulated pedagogical framework that connects Islamic epistemology with contemporary child-centred practice and Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) priorities. This conceptual paper develops Islamic Innovative Pedagogy (IIP) to address that integration problem. Using an integrative conceptual review and framework-development synthesis, the paper brings together foundational Islamic education scholarship, recent ECE literature, and policy sources on quality, inclusion and sustainability. The synthesis is organised around tawhid, tarbiyah, ta’dib and ta‘lim and is informed by comparison with integrated Islamic education and contemporary child-centred pedagogy. IIP comprises four interrelated dimensions: Tawhidic worldview integration, holistic child development, innovative child-centred methodologies, and inclusive and sustainable learning ecosystems. Its distinctive contribution lies not in introducing these elements individually, but in configuring them as an ECE-specific architecture linking worldview, developmental aims, pedagogical practice, ecosystem conditions and SDG 4. The framework offers a theoretically informed basis for curriculum design, teacher professional learning, quality discussion and future research in Islamic ECE. As a conceptual model, however, its feasibility, effects and transferability require empirical validation across diverse ECE contexts.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1956632.title: Development and validation of a prognostic prediction model for elderly patients with sepsis-associated acute kidney injury based on interpretable machine learning
doi:10.3389/fmed.2026.1956632.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Elderly patients with sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (SA-AKI) have high short-term mortality; early identification of high-risk individuals is critical for personalized intervention. Traditional clinical scoring systems relying on linear assumptions and conventional machine learning models often lack interpretability, hindering translation to clinical practice. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable prognostic model for 28-day in-hospital mortality in elderly SA-AKI using routinely available clinical variables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Clinical data of 11,468 elderly SA-AKI patients were retrospectively extracted from the MIMIC-IV database and divided into training and internal test sets at a 7:3 ratio using stratified random sampling. A dual feature selection strategy combining LASSO regression and random forest was applied. Five machine learning models—decision tree, logistic regression, random forest, LightGBM, and XGBoost—were constructed in parallel. Model discrimination and calibration were evaluated by AUC, Brier score, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      1 score. External independent validation was performed using a clinical cohort of 257 patients from the General Hospital of Ningxia Medical University. The SHAP method was used for global and individual-level interpretability of the optimal model.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dual feature selection identified 10 independent predictors: age, weight, red blood cell distribution width, arterial partial pressure of oxygen, blood lactate, prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, and respiratory rate. Among the five models, XGBoost demonstrated the best performance, with training AUC 0.9898 (accuracy 0.9472) and external validation AUC 0.9156 (accuracy 0.8560), indicating strong generalizability. SHAP global importance ranking showed age as the primary driver, followed by serum creatinine and arterial partial pressure of oxygen. Each core feature exhibited a nonlinear association with 28-day mortality risk, with clear model-derived risk inflection points rather than clinical intervention thresholds.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The XGBoost-based interpretable model exhibits excellent discriminative performance and robust external generalizability for predicting 28-day mortality in elderly SA-AKI. The SHAP attribution framework renders model decisions transparent, providing quantitative evidence-based support for early risk stratification and hypothesis generation for individualized organ-protective strategies in the ICU.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1021/acsami.6c13144.title: Deep Learning-Assisted Noise-Robust Optical Encryption Enabled by Pentachromatic Phototransistors
doi:10.1021/acsami.6c13144.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Optical communication requires effective encryption strategies for secure information transmission. The use of different wavelengths allows optical information to be configured in different ways, while broadband photoresponse enables these wavelength signals to be detected within a single device. Based on this approach, this study fabricated a broadband transparent phototransistor that operates across ultraviolet to infrared wavelengths. The IGZO/Ag2O/IGZO stacked structure exhibited a lower oxygen-related defect component and improved device stability. The responsivity increased by a factor of 2.38 and the noise equivalent power decreased by a factor of 1.95 compared to the IGZO/Ag2O device. The broadband photoresponse properties of the device enabled the separation of key and data channels, while a dynamic key enhanced security. This approach restricts pattern recognition compared to using fixed keys, resulting in a higher security rate. The learning-based approach was evaluated under noise and sensitivity-drift conditions, together with the effect of photoresponse stability under repetitive operation. These results contribute to the fabrication of broadband transparent phototransistors, facilitating high-performance optical encryption systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11371914/v1.title: Research Competence and Academic Performance in Senior High School Learners Through an AI Supported Seamless Learning Approach Using Project ARDI
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11371914/v1.abstract: This study explored the adoption of a seamless learning approach through Project ARDI (Automated Research Data Interpreter) in research-based teaching in senior high schools. Based on technology-enhanced, project-based, and seamless learning theories, the study focuses on assessing learners’ research skills, performance, and experience in a research-based educational context. A mixed-methods design with a convergent parallel approach was used with 30 senior high school students who took Practical Research 2. Survey, pretest and posttest scores, and academic records were used for quantitative data collection, whereas learner reflection and feedback provided the qualitative data. Techniques for data analysis include descriptive statistics, paired-sample t-test, correlation, and thematic analysis. Before the adoption of Project ARDI, learners had moderate research skills and were progressing toward mastery based on the assessment test and very satisfactory academic performance. After its adoption, higher levels of engagement, benefits, productivity, and attitudes toward research were noted. Differences were evident between the scores obtained on the pretest and posttest, as well as between the performances in the first and second quarter. Nonetheless, due to the action research design used, it would be safe to conclude from these findings the existence of associations rather than causes of the same. In terms of qualitative analysis, an improvement in research confidence, structured support, research involvement, collaboration, and a combination of formal and informal learning was reported. From the findings gathered, it can be concluded that participation in Project ARDI was associated with higher levels of perceived research engagement, research competence, and academic performance. Differences with large effect sizes were found between the pretest and posttest scores and between the performances in the first and second quarter.

doi:10.1117/1.nph.13.4.045001.title: Multiscale neural signatures of long-lag repetition learning: a simultaneous fNIRS–EEG study
doi:10.1117/1.nph.13.4.045001.abstract: <jats:p>SignificanceRepetition-based learning supports word recognition and reading fluency, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly where deficits in consolidating repeated linguistic input may underlie reading and language difficulties. Establishing reliable neural markers of repetition-based learning is a critical first step toward characterizing the phenotypes of these difficulties in children.AimWe developed a whole-brain simultaneous functional near-infrared spectroscopy–electroencephalography (fNIRS–EEG) approach to capture fast temporal electrophysiological and spatially accurate hemodynamic signals during long-lag repetition learning.ApproachThirty participants performed a semantic judgment task with words repeated across four runs with intervening items, modeling repetition demands central to reading instruction. A multimodal decoding framework integrating electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cross-modal fNIRS–EEG correlation features was used to classify repetition-based learning.ResultsRepeated words showed response time reductions. EEG captured a frontal N400-range repetition-related negativity and attenuation of alpha–beta suppression, reflecting changes in recognition-related and post-recognition processing. fNIRS revealed left inferior frontal and superior temporal efficiency increases alongside right supramarginal activation, suggesting integrative processing. Multimodal classifiers outperformed unimodal classifiers, indicating that each modality captured complementary aspects of learning.ConclusionsCombining fNIRS and EEG with multimodal machine learning provides a richer characterization of repetition-based learning than either modality alone, establishing a framework for phenotyping language learning capacity and identifying neural markers of reading difficulties in pediatric populations.</jats:p>

doi:10.51878/learning.v6i4.14083.title: ANALISIS RESPON SISWA TERHADAP IMPLEMENTASI MODEL KOOPERATIF TIPE THINK-TALK-WRITE DALAM PEMBELAJARAN ANTROPOLOGI DI KELAS XI SMAN 1 MALUNDA
doi:10.51878/learning.v6i4.14083.abstract:
<jats:p>ABSTRACT
Anthropology learning in schools needs to provide opportunities for students to actively engage in understanding social and cultural phenomena. However, teacher-centered learning that relies heavily on explanations may limit students’ opportunities to discuss, conduct field-based inquiry, and communicate their ideas. This study aimed to analyze students’ responses to the implementation of the cooperative Think-Talk-Write (TTW) learning model in Anthropology learning among Grade XI students at SMAN 1 Malunda. The study employed a qualitative approach with a descriptive research design. The participants consisted of an Anthropology teacher and Grade XI students. Data were collected through observation, interviews, and documentation and analyzed through data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings showed that TTW was implemented through the think, talk, and write stages, adapted to the characteristics of social and cultural inquiry. Students’ responses were generally positive, as they found the learning more engaging, participated actively in discussions, became more confident in expressing their opinions, understood the material more easily, and were motivated through group work and field activities. Challenges involving differences in students’ abilities, limited confidence among some students, and time constraints were addressed through motivation, guidance, and group-based learning. These findings indicate that TTW has potential as an active, collaborative, and contextual alternative for Anthropology learning.
ABSTRAK
Pembelajaran Antropologi di sekolah perlu memberikan kesempatan kepada siswa untuk terlibat secara aktif dalam memahami fenomena sosial dan budaya, tetapi pembelajaran yang masih berpusat pada penjelasan guru dapat membatasi ruang siswa untuk berdiskusi, melakukan kajian lapangan, dan menyampaikan hasil pemikirannya. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis respons siswa terhadap implementasi model pembelajaran kooperatif tipe Think-Talk-Write (TTW) dalam pembelajaran Antropologi di kelas XI SMAN 1 Malunda. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan jenis penelitian deskriptif. Subjek penelitian terdiri atas G-A dan siswa kelas XI. Data dikumpulkan melalui observasi, wawancara, dan dokumentasi, kemudian dianalisis melalui reduksi data, penyajian data, serta penarikan dan verifikasi kesimpulan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa TTW diimplementasikan melalui tahap think, talk, dan write yang disesuaikan dengan karakteristik kajian sosial dan budaya. Respons siswa cenderung positif karena siswa merasa lebih tertarik, aktif berdiskusi, lebih berani menyampaikan pendapat, lebih mudah memahami materi, serta termotivasi melalui kerja kelompok dan kegiatan lapangan. Kendala berupa perbedaan kemampuan, rendahnya kepercayaan diri sebagian siswa, dan keterbatasan waktu diatasi melalui motivasi, pendampingan, dan pembelajaran kelompok. Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa TTW berpotensi menjadi alternatif pembelajaran Antropologi yang lebih aktif, kolaboratif, dan kontekstual.</jats:p>
doi:10.51878/learning.v6i4.14083.venue: LEARNING : Jurnal Inovasi Penelitian Pendidikan dan Pembelajaran

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-75649-z.title: Early childhood teachers’ practices and perspectives on the integration of smart devices in children’s learning environments
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-75649-z.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Digital technology is increasingly used in early childhood education to support children’s engagement, interaction, and learning. However, limited research has examined how teachers interpret and integrate smart devices into classroom practice, particularly in underrepresented contexts such as Saudi Arabia. This study explores early childhood teachers’ perceptions and practices regarding the integration of smart devices in children’s learning. A qualitative research design was employed with 63 early childhood teachers in Al-Ahsa, Saudi Arabia. Data were collected through classroom observations and semi-structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed four interconnected domains of practice concerning teachers’ integration of smart devices in early childhood settings: children’s digital self-regulation, guidance for technology use, digital collaboration and social interaction, and digital creativity and innovation. The findings suggest that smart-device integration is shaped by teachers’ intentional decisions, pedagogical guidance, and attention to children’s learning needs. The study contributes context-sensitive evidence to the literature on digital technology in early childhood education by providing an empirically grounded account of interconnected pedagogical practices within the Saudi Arabian context. It also highlights the role of teachers in creating meaningful digital learning experiences in which smart devices complement, rather than replace, meaningful interaction and other age-appropriate learning opportunities.</jats:p>

doi:10.53761/npzx9z18.title: Ubuntu Pedagogy: An Enabling and Empowering Approach for Peer Assisted Learning
doi:10.53761/npzx9z18.abstract: <jats:p>Peer assisted learning (PAL) is integral to student learning in higher education and provides opportunities for learning that extend beyond academic support. This study explores how students perceive the peer support received from tutors, mentors, retention officers and teaching assistants.  Principles of Ubuntu pedagogy, namely support from a position of love and care, building positive relationships, working collectively and nurturing students’ minds underpin this study. Qualitative surveys with closed and open-ended questions were administered for data generation to garner perceptions of academic and social interventions. It allowed participants to articulate their experiences and viewpoints in their own words, providing rich insights and perspectives. Findings revealed that those who provided peer support are epistemic agents facilitating pedagogical encounters, and in this dialogical process both epistemic agents and students develop reciprocally. This study foregrounds a novel approach to peer support where the principles of Ubuntu are central to opening vistas for student learning, empowerment and success. The study contributes to strategies on the role of indigenous knowledge systems in transforming peer-to-peer engagement and recommends that tacit Ubuntu values be made overt in PAL training programmes.</jats:p>
doi:10.53761/npzx9z18.venue: Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4488-9.ch004.title: Transformative Pedagogies for Student Retention in Health Sciences Education
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4488-9.ch004.abstract: <jats:p>Student retention remains a challenge in nursing and health sciences education, where students must achieve academic, clinical and professional competence. Traditional content-driven pedagogies often fail to address diversity and engagement, contributing to disengagement and attrition among students. This chapter explores how student-centred, digitally enabled and collaborative pedagogies can improve retention in health sciences education. Drawing on global and African scholarship, it examines strategies such as collaborative learning, interprofessional education, simulation-based learning, reflective practice, and technology-enhanced environments to strengthen engagement and self-directed learning. It also considers the role of learning environments, learning analytics and artificial intelligence in supporting personalised learning and identifying at risk students. Using examples from the Global South, the chapter highlights how equity-oriented pedagogies, curriculum reform, faculty development, and institutional leadership can foster inclusive and sustainable learning environments.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4488-9.ch004.venue: Transforming Student Persistence in Higher Education

doi:10.59992/ijci.2026.v5n10p2.title: A Hybrid Deep-Learning and Impedance-Based Scheme for Fault Classification and Location in Transmission Lines: A Physics-Validated, Leakage-Free Evaluation
doi:10.59992/ijci.2026.v5n10p2.abstract: <jats:p>Deep-learning fault classifiers and locators for transmission lines are often evaluated on unvalidated simulations, with possible data leakage and without comparison against the impedance-based methods used in practice. This study builds an exact time-domain simulator of a 400 kV, 200 km two-source line, whose fault currents agree with symmetrical-component calculations within 2%, and generates 22,600 independent scenarios covering ten fault types, fault resistance, location, inception angle, loading and source strength. Single-ended 25 ms windows sampled at 4 kHz were used to train one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (CNNs), which were compared with feature-based classifiers and with the reactance and Takagi locators. The CNN classified faults with 99.91% accuracy in 0.4 ms per window, but feature-based classifiers were equally accurate, and all learned classifiers failed for fault resistances beyond the training range until that range was included in training, which in turn increased false alarms under strong noise. CNN regression located faults with a mean absolute error of 5.81 km, better than other learned models but far worse than the Takagi method on the third post-fault cycle. A hybrid scheme, in which the CNN supplies the fault type and the Takagi method the distance, reduced the error to 1.40 km, located 93.8% of faults within 2% of the line length, and remained accurate for weak sources, noise and high fault resistance. Deep learning is thus best used for fast classification, and physics-based methods for precise location.</jats:p>
doi:10.59992/ijci.2026.v5n10p2.venue: International Journal of Computers and Informatics

doi:10.55041/ijcope.v2i10.064.title: Adaptive Privacy-Preserving Big Data Analytics: A Hybrid Machine Learning and Deterministic Guardrail Framework
doi:10.55041/ijcope.v2i10.064.abstract:
<jats:p>The exponential expansion of consumer financial services has led to massive volumes of structured transaction and account data being migrated to public cloud data lakes for high-throughput distributed analytics. However, financial datasets intrinsically contain sensitive Personally Identifiable Information (PII) subject to stringent regulatory frameworks including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Indian Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act of 2023. Conventional privacy solutions exhibit a debilitating trilemma: cryptographic methods such as Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) impose prohibitive computational latency; static dictionary-based anonymization collapses under schema drift and lexical variations; and unconstrained machine learning classifiers suffer from train/serve distribution shifts where subtle format discrepancies precipitate catastrophic privacy leaks.

In this paper, we propose a scalable, cloud-native privacy preserving big data analytics framework anchored by an Adaptive Dual-Tier Privacy Engine. Our architecture couples an adaptive multi-stage gradient boosted decision tree (XGBoost) classifier— trained on a 25-dimensional structural, keyword, sample-level, and regular expression feature space—with deterministic safety-net guardrails (Force-Protect and Force-Keep). This hybrid design guarantees zero exposure of mission-critical identifiers while completely insulating downstream business analytical features against corruption. Masked datasets are securely persisted to AWS S3 and processed through distributed Apache Spark (PySpark) clusters via the S3A connector across four analytical dimensions: descriptive statistics, bivariate fraud detection with two-factor authentication (2FA) correlation, credit risk profiling, and multi tier customer segmentation. Validated against a high-cardinality 100,000-record banking benchmark across 57 attributes, our system demonstrates 100% mitigation of critical PII leakage, overcomes real-world distribution skew on complex identifier formats, preserves analytical utility with zero loss of statistical fidelity, and maintains sub-minute distributed pipeline throughput.

Index Terms—Privacy-Preserving Big Data Analytics, Cloud Computing, Apache Spark, XGBoost, Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Hybrid Guardrails, Train/Serve Skew, Financial Data Governance.</jats:p>
doi:10.55041/ijcope.v2i10.064.venue: International Journal of Creative and Open Research in Engineering and Management

doi:10.3928/01484834-20260914-01.title: The Story of Learning: Integrating ePortfolios in Nursing Education
doi:10.3928/01484834-20260914-01.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The transition to competency-based nursing education under the 2021 AACN
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Essentials</jats:italic>
                      has increased the need for evidence of competency development beyond course grades. This nursing program implemented a program-wide ePortfolio using Google Sites to document learning, support reflection, and demonstrate attainment of competencies.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Faculty revised program outcomes to align with the AACN
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Essentials</jats:italic>
                      and other standards, then mapped where competencies were introduced, reinforced, and demonstrated. These maps informed a common ePortfolio template, selection of key course-embedded assignments, and structured reflection, rubrics, and feedback. Implementation included faculty development, student orientation, and a year-long soft launch.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The ePortfolio enhanced curricular alignment, made competency progression more visible, and supported student reflection, self-assessment, and professional identity development. It also facilitated advising, program assessment, and accreditation documentation, though workload, digital literacy, and gaps for transfer and accelerated students posed challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intentionally integrated ePortfolios can strengthen reflection and assessment in nursing education.</jats:p>

doi:10.70148/rise.v3i6.2.title: Implementing Research-Based Science Activities in a Rural ESL Classroom: Usability, Pupil Learning and Instructional Value
doi:10.70148/rise.v3i6.2.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the implementation of a researcher-designed Science Research-Based Activity (SRA) sequence in a rural Year 5 ESL classroom in Sarawak with limited infrastructure and teaching materials. The sequence organised Survey, Case Study, and Experimental Science Activities as a connected progression. Using Action Research supported by the Successive Approximation Model, 23 pupils completed nine cycles from 24 November to 11 December 2025, with 595 minutes (9 hours 55 minutes) of planned instructional time. Data included written pupil responses, classroom observations, semi-structured interviews with the teacher-researcher, reflection records, field notes, pupil artefacts, activity outputs, and cycle-level classroom-performance ratings. Engagement and activity-specific Learning Outcomes were summarised descriptively, while qualitative data were analysed thematically. Engagement increased broadly from M = 5.17 (SD = 1.37) out of 8 in Cycle 1 to M = 7.43 (SD = 0.79) in Cycle 9. Learning Outcomes varied with task demands, ranging from M = 5.35 (SD = 1.58) to M = 7.57 (SD = 1.70) out of 12, and generally improved within phases. High engagement did not always coincide with strong scientific explanation, particularly during hands-on work. The SRA sequence was workable when clear stages, adaptive scaffolding, accessible materials, language support, and teacher adjustment were used. Findings are specific to this classroom and do not establish causal effectiveness.</jats:p>

doi:10.14719/pst.16505.title: Leveraging satellite products and machine learning/deep learning models for the upgrading of agro-advisory systems in India: A bibliometric and systematic narrative review
doi:10.14719/pst.16505.abstract: <jats:p>A comprehensive bibliometric review was conducted to evaluate the most relevant literature retrieved from the Scopus database, resulting in the identification of 125 relevant publications from an initial pool of 1948 records through a screening process based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). The bibliometric analysis revealed a significant increasing trend in year-wise publications and citations, wherein India and the US emerged as the leading contributors with total publications of 34 and 25 respectively. Notably, the systematic narrative review highlights that agro-advisory systems (AAS) have increased farmer income by 83 %, improved crop yields by 6–25 % and enhanced farm profitability by 15–26 % in India. Despite these achievements, conventional AAS frameworks that rely predominantly on automatic weather stations (AWS) continue to face critical limitations, including sparse spatial coverage, restricted agro-meteorological observations, data discontinuities and inadequate representation of local microclimatic variability. To address these limitations, the study highlights the importance of integrating AWS observations with high-resolution satellite products through downscaling and subsequent assimilation within the Weather Research and Forecasting Data Assimilation (WRFDA) framework to improve the spatial accuracy of weather forecasts and facilitate the delivery of reliable block-level and village-level agro-advisories. However, the operational implementation of satellite-assisted weather forecasting using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model is often constrained by latency in data availability, as many high-resolution satellite products require several hours to multiple days for processing and dissemination. In order to overcome this limitation, the review further demonstrates the considerable potential of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models trained using historical satellite observations along with meteorological predictors derived from numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems for enhancing downscaling capabilities and improving forecast accuracy. The results inferred that the satellite-based weather forecasting using ML and DL architectures achieved strong predictive performance, with reported R² values of up to 0.982, 0.976 and 0.95 for rainfall, temperature and aerosol concentration respectively. These findings demonstrate the increasing potential of satellite-driven ML and DL approaches for high-resolution weather forecasting and their applicability to next-generation, location-specific agro-advisory services. However, their operational utilisation depends on the availability of adequate computational infrastructure, skilled human resources, economic feasibility, institutional coordination and farmer acceptance. Therefore, the future of satellite-based AAS lies in developing computationally efficient, economically viable and farmer centric decision support platforms capable of translating complex forecast information into timely, understandable and actionable recommendations for climate-resilient agriculture.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1842508.title: Global thyroid cancer incidence in relation to dietary and socioeconomic factors: an ecological machine learning study
doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1842508.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thyroid cancer incidence has risen dramatically worldwide, with marked geographic heterogeneity suggesting dietary and environmental contributions beyond screening effects. The roles of specific dietary patterns in thyroid cancer remain poorly characterized at the global level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Age-standardized thyroid cancer incidence was the prespecified primary outcome. We aimed to (1) build machine learning models predicting country-level thyroid cancer incidence from dietary and socioeconomic features, (2) quantify confounder-adjusted dietary associations with incidence, including prespecified sensitivity analyses of the iodine-rich food availability index, and (3) identify key dietary predictors through explainability analyses and a descriptive decomposition of the development pathway. Mortality was analyzed only as a secondary outcome in order to evaluate whether the incidence patterns could be attributed to differential cancer detection rather than to differences in disease occurrence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We integrated GLOBOCAN 2022 (cancer outcomes), FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets (113 food items, 2010–2022; primary exposure 2015–2019 mean), the UNDP Human Development Report 2025 statistical annex (HDI 2023 and its life expectancy, education, and income sub-indices), and WHO obesity prevalence (2022) across 163 countries, yielding 155 harmonized variables and 150 numeric predictors. All modeling was performed inside a nested cross-validation framework: multiple imputation by chained equations, standardization, four-method consensus feature selection, and hyperparameter search were fitted exclusively on the training partition of each outer fold (10 folds × five repetitions), and performance was summarized from pooled out-of-fold predictions with 95% confidence intervals obtained by resampling countries (2,000 bootstrap replicates). Three analyses separated dietary signal from confounding: block-wise models comparing socioeconomic-only, diet-only and combined feature sets; leave-one-region-out validation across six world regions; and confounder-adjusted partial correlations under a basic (HDI, obesity) and an extended adjustment set (HDI, obesity, the three HDI sub-indices, and region fixed effects), with Benjamini–Hochberg and Bonferroni correction applied across all comparisons. Iodine-related exposure was represented by an iodine-rich food availability index constructed from seafood, dairy, and egg supply; its construction was interrogated in four sensitivity analyses in which the components were entered separately and jointly, four weighting schemes were compared, total animal protein supply was added to the adjustment set, and an iodine-poor animal-origin food index was used as a specificity control. Binary classification and all mortality analyses were secondary.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s12889-026-29774-z.title: Multimodal analysis of sleep disturbances and heart disease in older adults: a machine learning and exploratory path analysis approach
doi:10.1186/s12889-026-29774-z.abstract: Sleep disturbances and heart disease are common among older adults, yet the psychological and functional pathways linking sleep symptoms to heart disease remain insufficiently characterized. This study examined the association between sleep disturbance indicators and heart disease among older adults using multivariable regression, exploratory path analysis, and machine-learning approaches in a cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 wave of the Mexican Health and Aging Study. This cross-sectional analysis used data from the 2018 wave (wave 5) of the Mexican Health and Aging Study and was restricted to respondents aged 50 years or older. Participants were categorized according to self-reported heart disease status. Sleep disturbance indicators included difficulty falling asleep, waking up at night, waking up too early, and feeling refreshed upon waking. Depressive symptoms were assessed using the CESD-9 score. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to estimate odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. An exploratory path analysis was applied to examine pathways involving depressive symptoms and fatigue. As an exploratory, complementary analysis, random forest was used to assess variable importance and internal classification performance rather than clinical prediction. Among 12,709 participants aged 50 years or older, 1,585 had heart disease and 11,124 were controls. In the primary model, which estimated the total association without adjusting for depressive symptoms and fatigue, waking up at night most of the time was associated with higher odds of heart disease compared with never having this symptom (adjusted OR 1.70, 95% CI 1.41–2.03, p < 0.001), as were waking up at night sometimes (adjusted OR 1.28, 95% CI 1.10–1.48, p < 0.001) and difficulty falling asleep most of the time (adjusted OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.07–1.52, p = 0.007). Feeling refreshed upon waking most of the time was inversely associated with heart disease (adjusted OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.69–0.94, p = 0.007). Waking up too early was not associated with heart disease (adjusted OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.94–1.30, p = 0.223). These associations were less precise and were no longer statistically significant in the respondent-weighted sensitivity analysis, whereas the nighttime-awakening associations remained robust when the three CESD-9 items overlapping with sleep and fatigue were removed. The exploratory random forest analysis showed limited internal classification performance, with an AUC of 0.72 (95% CI 0.71–0.73) and a precision-recall AUC of 0.24 based on 10-fold cross-validation; at the Youden-optimal threshold sensitivity and specificity were both 0.67. Hypertension, age, fatigue, ADL score, CESD-9 score and stroke history were the most informative classification variables. Exploratory path analysis indicated that depressive symptoms and fatigue were associated with both the sleep disturbance indicators and heart disease status; these indirect associations are interpreted descriptively rather than as evidence of temporal mediation. Sleep disturbance indicators were independently associated with heart disease among older adults. Exploratory path analysis and machine learning further suggested that fatigue and depressive symptoms were associated with sleep disturbance and with heart disease status. Because this was a cross-sectional analysis, the findings should be interpreted as associative rather than causal. The random forest findings represent exploratory classification and should not be interpreted as a clinically validated prediction model.

doi:10.1080/00220272.2026.2746353.title: From listening to doing: how project-based learning shapes academic emotions in lower-secondary mathematics
doi:10.1080/00220272.2026.2746353.abstract: Project-based learning (PjBL) is widely promoted as a student-centred approach, yet limited evidence explains how it shapes discrete academic emotions in lower-secondary mathematics. This study examined Grade 7 students’ mathematics-related academic emotions and unit-level mathematics achievement during the unit ‘Data Collection, Organization, and Description’. Two intact Grade 7 classes in a lower-secondary school in central China participated in a quasi-experimental study: one class (n = 40) completed a seven-lesson PjBL project, while the control class (n = 40) received lecture-based instruction. Students completed a 26-item academic emotion questionnaire at three phases, measuring enjoyment, pride, anger, anxiety, shame, hopelessness, and boredom. Unit-level mathematics achievement, interviews, and classroom observations were also used. Both groups improved emotionally, but the PjBL group showed larger changes, particularly in pride, anger, anxiety, and boredom. Enjoyment and hopelessness improved more descriptively, while shame declined temporarily before recovering. The raw post-test achievement difference was not significant, but ANCOVA controlling for pre-test achievement showed a significant adjusted advantage for the PjBL group. Interviews and observations suggested that authentic tasks, visible outcomes, peer interaction, and teacher scaffolding made mathematics more meaningful and manageable. Findings should be interpreted as short-term, unit-specific evidence rather than as a general effect of PjBL.

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4488-9.ch009.title: Cultural & Inclusive Experiential Learning as a Model of Persistence
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4488-9.ch009.abstract: <jats:p>Study abroad has long been recognized as a high-impact practice within higher education, yet often feels exclusively designed for students from dominant identities. This chapter offers a model of possibility for study abroad programs when such experiential learning opportunities are built with minoritized students, faculty, and staff in mind. When these opportunities are built from a culturally responsive lens, they cultivate accessible global experiences for minoritized participants and they shape the ways in which students persist through their higher education journeys. Drawing on three distinct sets of data, the purpose of this chapter is to describe a transformative global experiential learning program, CIELO (Cultural and Inclusive Experiential Learning Opportunities) and illustrate the ways in which participants contribute to student growth and persistence. The chapter addresses the following central question: In what ways do global cultural and experiential learning opportunities shape the postsecondary experiences of minoritized students, faculty, and staff?</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-75865-7.title: Botune: an AI-supported scaffolding system for children’s drawing-based narrative expression in nature learning
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-75865-7.abstract: Nature exploration fosters children’s cognitive development and environmental awareness; however, kindergarten curricula are often constrained by limited resources and repetitive interaction, leaving children’s observations only weakly integrated into structured understanding and expression. We present Botune, an AI-supported creative-expression tool for kindergarten planting activities that integrates plant observation, drawing, spoken narration, and animation-based sharing. We conducted an exploratory, fixed-order within-participant study in kindergarten planting classes with 27 children and three educators; 24 complete cases were analysed after excluding data from three children who did not complete the drawing task. The traditional activity preceded the Botune-supported activity by seven days. The proportion of activity time spent observing and teacher-rated involvement scores during sharing were higher in the later session. The later narrations contained significantly more actions and character interactions; character counts were descriptively higher but did not remain statistically significant after Holm correction, and state- or emotion-related expressions did not differ significantly. These semantic counts index narrative elaboration rather than overall narrative quality or general narrative ability. These differences cannot be attributed to Botune alone. Scientific knowledge and conceptual understanding were not directly assessed by these measures. The study offers exploratory observations and design considerations for AI-supported narrative expression in kindergarten nature learning.

doi:10.1002/9781394392834.ch1.title: Tiny Machine Learning Basic Concepts
doi:10.1002/9781394392834.ch1.abstract: The artificial intelligence field is booming in unexpected ways and has entered into diverse research areas, unlike conventional machine learning methods, which often require substantial computational power, high-performance servers, or network nodes. Tiny machine learning (TinyML) techniques execute efficiently on small embedded devices such as sensors and microcontrollers. Machine learning capabilities are pushed to the extreme edge, enabling fast real-time responsiveness. TinyML is a composition of mainly software, hardware, and algorithms. The hardware comprises Internet of Things (IoT) devices with or without hardware accelerators. The current scenario advocates the use of TinyML as a possible solution to reduce carbon footprints and considers it extremely useful in low-profile devices with limited computing power. TinyML represents a significant paradigm shift by making it possible to execute ML tasks directly on IoT devices with strict limitations. In this chapter, basic concepts of TinyML, components, applications, and benefits are discussed. This chapter also discusses the challenges and issues in implementing systems using TinyML.

doi:10.1002/9781394392834.ch4.title: Hardware Platforms for Tiny Machine Learning
doi:10.1002/9781394392834.ch4.abstract: Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) integrates machine learning functionality with low-power, resource-limited devices, such as microcontrollers and edge devices, to enable smart Internet of Things and edge use cases. As the Internet of Things and edge computing surge, TinyML unlocks opportunities in smart wearables, industrial predictive maintenance, precision agriculture, and autonomous devices. This chapter presents a comprehensive analysis of the hardware platforms powering TinyML, emphasizing their computation speed, power consumption, memory requirements, and ease of integration with machine learning models. The ARM Cortex-series, ESP32, Raspberry Pi, and AI accelerators like Google Edge TPU and NVIDIA Jetson Nano are regarded highly as the market leaders in this domain. Each platform has specific advantages according to its respective application requirements, like latency, power consumption, and inference rate. The trade-offs are highlighted in the analysis presented. By integrating real-world case studies and benchmarking metrics, this chapter equips developers with actionable insights to navigate design trade-offs, optimize resource allocation, and select platforms aligned with deployment goals. Ultimately, this resource empowers engineers and researchers to harness TinyML's potential, fostering innovation in scalable, sustainable, intelligent edge solutions.

doi:10.4119/unibi/3020849.title: Efficient Implementation of Machine Learning Algorithms on Reconfigurable Architectures Using High-Level Synthesis
doi:10.4119/unibi/3020849.abstract: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) can offer high performance and energy efficiency when used to accelerate compute-intensive workloads. However, the often fairly long development time associated with the commonly used RTL design flows hinders their adaptation in fast-paced domains such as machine learning. Therefore, this thesis analyzes the extent to which High-Level Synthesis (HLS) can be used to efficiently implement machine learning algorithms on FPGAs. In addition to design-time improvements through HLS, the implementation's efficiency in terms of performance, resource utilization, and energy consumption is evaluated. To address bottlenecks in the interaction between software and FPGA hardware, the runtime framework CLAP was developed. It provides a unified C++ API for interacting with AMD/Xilinx FPGAs, independent of the execution target, i.e., PCIe-based accelerators, embedded Linux running on a reconfigurable MPSoC, or bare-metal on an embedded processor. In combination with CLAPPy, a Python binding, and the automatic project-generation tool CLAPify, the framework can significantly reduce the manual work required to create host applications and enables easy integration of FPGA accelerators into existing C++ and Python projects. Additionally, FPGA4ML, a wrapping framework for the Python package hls4ml, was developed to automatically transform trained neural networks into fully functional FPGA implementations. Binary Neuronal Associative Memories (BINAM), Self-Organizing Maps (SOM), and different autoencoder models were implemented and evaluated to analyze the usability and efficiency of HLS-based hardware designs for machine learning. While the BINAM and SOM designs were implemented from scratch, the autoencoders were realized using FPGA4ML. For each algorithm, an extensive design space exploration was performed to evaluate resource utilization, performance, and energy efficiency. The results of these evaluations demonstrate that HLS-based designs can achieve performance comparable to GPU and RTL-based FPGA implementations. Depending on the target application, software-based solutions on CPUs were even outperformed by up to two orders of magnitude at a significantly higher energy efficiency. Overall, this work demonstrates that HLS-based FPGA development is a viable approach for implementing machine learning algorithms. In combination with easy-to-use frameworks for runtime development and design space exploration, HLS can significantly reduce development time while maintaining high performance and energy efficiency.
