doi:10.1002/9781394392834.ch18.title: Hands‐On Project and Case Studies
doi:10.1002/9781394392834.ch18.abstract: TinyML is a technology that incorporates artificial intelligence into edge machines, which allows machine learning models to be executed on very low-power microcontrollers with small memory and processing units. In contrast to cloud-based AI-based solutions, TinyML does not require the cloud to run inference on an embedded system, but instead it allows real-time decision-making and is less energy-intensive, less bandwidth-intensive, and less latency-intensive. It can be a good fit in Internet of Things (IoT) systems where power and computational requirements are of significant concern. The chapter is a well-organized, practical introduction to the implementation of TinyML, which includes the choice of the model, its optimization, deployment, and evaluation of the system. It solves the real world issues in implementing deep learning models to predictive maintenance, anomaly detection and environmental monitoring. Inference speed, memory footprint and energy utilization are used to measure performance. Real-world efficiency is measured with profiling instruments like EEMBC(r) MLMarktm and the Power Profiler Kit and trade-offs between accuracy and resource usage are analyzed with them. The discussion proposes both software and hardware ecosystems of TinyML. Arduino supported platforms consist of Nano 33 BLE Sense, STM32 boards and TensorFlow Lite on Microcontrollers-enabled platforms. Model conversion and deployment The TensorFlow Lite, Edge Impulse and TinyMLgen software are used to convert and deploy models. The chapter describes how small convolutional and recurrent neural networks can be applied to either classification or regression to fit into limited hardware. The main case study is concerned with predictive maintenance of industrial motors using the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense, which has onboard vibration and temperature sensing. Once accelerator, acoustic, and thermal data has been gathered, post-training quantization and knowledge distillation is used to deploy optimized neural networks. Such methods massively decrease the size of models and their fault detection accuracy remains at more than 90 percent. Transfer learning, pruning, compression using sparsity and integer-only inference are also discussed in order to enhance runtime efficiency. The use of TensorFlow Lite Converter, STM32Cube.AI and GLOW compilers to show deployment workflows is illustrated. The chapter also focuses on hardware-software co-design, whereby microcontroller choice is based on user requirements (in terms of operation), memory, and power requirements. TinyML frameworks with the help of clouds and federated learning methods are explained as they allow updating models safely without violating privacy. Security issues involve encryption and privacy inference protection of the sensitive IoT setting. Multi-edge IoT network scalability is investigated by collaborative and hierarchical learning techniques. The future possibilities are presented as emerging technologies consisting of neuromorphic computing, spiking neural networks and hardware accelerators, as a way of enhancing efficiency. On the whole, this paper will cover the gap between machine learning studies and embedded sensors by offering a practical roadmap towards creating intelligent edge systems requiring energy efficiency, security, and scalability.

doi:10.1002/9781394392834.ch20.title: Future Directions in Tiny Machine Learning
doi:10.1002/9781394392834.ch20.abstract: Tiny machine learning (TinyML) represents a transformative frontier in the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI), merging machine learning capabilities with ultra-low-power embedded systems to enable real-time inference at the edge. As data generation accelerates across billions of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, the need for intelligent edge computing that operates efficiently without relying on cloud infrastructure has become critical. TinyML addresses this demand by enabling localized AI processing on constrained devices with limited memory, computation, and energy resources. This chapter provides a comprehensive exploration of the cutting-edge advancements and research trends shaping the present and future landscape of TinyML. We begin by analyzing the core technological enablers of TinyML, including the rise of energy-efficient microcontrollers, specialized AI hardware accelerators, and neuromorphic computing platforms that emulate human brain-like functionality. Innovations in model compression techniques—such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation—play a central role in shrinking complex deep learning models into formats suitable for resource-constrained environments. Additionally, adopting federated learning architectures allows distributed training and data privacy preservation directly on edge nodes, enabling collaborative intelligence without centralized data aggregation. The chapter also highlights the emergence of event-driven AI, which processes sensory inputs based on relevance or change detection rather than continuous sampling, thus reducing power consumption and latency. These techniques are further enhanced by software frameworks tailored for TinyML deployment, including TensorFlow Lite Micro, Edge Impulse, and TVM. Their integration enables scalable development across various application domains. Real-world implementations of TinyML are explored in depth, with practical use cases spanning healthcare, industrial IoT, agriculture, and smart cities. In healthcare, wearable biosensors powered by TinyML enable continuous physiological monitoring, early disease detection, and personalized health feedback. In industrial environments, TinyML enables predictive maintenance systems that detect anomalies in machinery before catastrophic failures occur. Additionally, autonomous drones and surveillance systems powered by on-device AI offer scalable solutions for crowd analytics, traffic monitoring, and environmental sensing in urban settings. Despite its growing potential, TinyML faces significant challenges, particularly concerning energy constraints, data privacy, and security. To address these issues, emerging solutions such as homomorphic encryption for secure inference, blockchain-based identity management for trusted edge collaboration, and hardware-rooted trust anchors for secure boot processes are examined. Furthermore, the ethical dimensions of deploying AI at the edge—such as algorithmic bias, data ownership, and transparency—are critically assessed. Looking forward, the chapter investigates future research directions and anticipated breakthroughs. The integration of TinyML with 6G-enabled IoT ecosystems is poised to enable intelligent, real-time, and ultra-reliable machine-type communication. Biomedical AI applications powered by TinyML are expected to revolutionize early diagnostics and personalized treatment using implantable or ingestible AI chips. Additionally, advances in cognitive computing and neuromorphic architectures hold promise for self-learning edge devices that adapt dynamically to contextual changes in their environments.

doi:10.5281/zenodo.23403869.title: Discovery Is a Human-AI Loop
doi:10.5281/zenodo.23403869.abstract: This compendium examines a single methodological question: how far can one researcher expand scientific search by combining human creativity with ChatGPT, executable computation, external evidence, and deliberate falsification? ChatGPT is treated as a research instrument for formalization, coding, search, control design, and criticism, not as an autonomous discoverer or a source of experimental evidence. The archive contains 74 experimental lines spanning artificial cognition, Consequential Necessity, machine learning, genomics, complex systems, synthetic artificial life, computational physics, accelerator models, neutrino cosmology, the Voynich Manuscript, seismology, music, and human-AI interfaces. The studies vary in maturity from exploratory prototypes to controlled computational campaigns and frozen prediction ledgers. Positive, negative, and inconclusive results are retained, and each line is interpreted according to explicit evidence and provenance rules. Across domains, the most persistent methodological pattern was a reduction in the cost between reframing a problem and attacking the resulting hypothesis. Human judgment supplied unusual representations and decided what questions mattered; ChatGPT accelerated translation into equa- tions, code, baselines, and alternative explanations; numerical or external evidence determined what survived. Repeated failures showed that complexity, model agreement, visual plausibility, and novelty are not substitutes for controls. The central conclusion is therefore methodological rather than a catalogue of established discoveries: a human-AI loop can widen the number and diversity of scientific hypotheses that one person can make executable and falsifiable. A final conceptual Part derives Hypothesis Language Generation (HLG), a proposed architecture in which persistent internal hypotheses are generated, tested, consequentially reduced, and only then rendered into language. HLG is presented as a falsifiable next-stage architecture, not as a demonstrated replacement for language models. Any domain-specific claim remains subject to independent replication, stronger controls, and evidence beyond this compendium. Keywords: ChatGPT; human-AI collaboration; Hypothesis Language Generation; scientific search; computational experiments; falsification; representation; reproducibility.

doi:10.24042/desimal.v9i3.33155.title: Design Thinking for Mathematical Critical Thinking in Digital Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
doi:10.24042/desimal.v9i3.33155.abstract: <jats:p>Mathematical critical thinking in digital learning requires purposeful interaction among pedagogical tasks, digital tools, and students' interpretation and justification of mathematical ideas. This systematic literature review examines the complementary functions of GeoGebra, Problem-Based Learning (PBL), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Meaningful Learning, and Design Thinking. The manuscript reports a qualitative thematic synthesis of 15 primary empirical studies published within the 2020–2026 search period and identified through Scopus, ERIC, Google Scholar, DOAJ, and Garuda. The available reporting record does not preserve complete database-specific retrieval and screening counts or item-level methodological appraisal results; the review therefore does not claim a fully reproducible PRISMA 2020 selection record. Across the cited evidence, GeoGebra provides dynamic mathematical representations; PBL structures problem-centred inquiry; AI offers feedback and alternative approaches that require mathematical verification; and Meaningful Learning emphasizes connections with prior knowledge. Design Thinking is proposed as a learner-centred organizing process through Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test. These differentiated functions support a conceptually coherent, potentially testable instructional pathway rather than a demonstrated effect of the combined intervention. Future research should verify the primary-study corpus, document review procedures in full, and test the proposed relationships in classroom settings.</jats:p>

doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.72s.150.title: A Machine Learning Approach to Predict Hypertension Using Cross-Sectional & Two Years Follow Up Data from A Health & Demographic Cohort
doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.72s.150.abstract: Background: Hypertension is a major public health problem and an important modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, chronic kidney disease, and premature mortality.Machine learning techniques have shown considerable potential for improving hypertension prediction by analyzing complex interactions among multiple demographic, clinical, and lifestyle variables.Aim: To evaluate the performance of different machine learning algorithms for predicting hypertension using crosssectional and two-year follow-up data from a health and demographic cohort.Methods: A prospective observational cohort study was conducted among 2,000 adults aged ≥18 years using baseline cross-sectional and two-year follow-up data.Demographic, anthropometric, clinical, and lifestyle variables were collected using standardized methods.Data preprocessing included missing value handling, normalization, categorical encoding, and feature selection.The dataset was divided into training and testing sets for model development.Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Artificial Neural Network models were developed and evaluated.Model performance was assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, and area under the curve (AUC).Results: Among the 2,000 participants, 720 (36.0%) had hypertension and 1,280 (64.0%) were non-hypertensive.Hypertension was significantly associated with age ≥50 years, body mass index ≥25 kg/m², diabetes mellitus, family history of hypertension, smoking, and physical inactivity (p<0.05).XGBoost demonstrated the best predictive performance with an accuracy of 92.7%, sensitivity of 91.8%, specificity of 93.4%, precision of 91.1%, F1-score of 0.914, and AUC of 0.971.Random Forest showed the second-highest performance with an accuracy of 91.8% and AUC of 0.963.Feature importance analysis identified age, body mass index, systolic blood pressure, family history of hypertension, and diabetes mellitus as the strongest predictors of hypertension.Conclusion: Machine learning algorithms, particularly XGBoost, demonstrated excellent performance in predicting hypertension using combined cross-sectional and longitudinal cohort data.These models may facilitate early identification of high-risk individuals, support personalized preventive strategies, and improve clinical decisionmaking.Further external validation using doi:10.1007/s13202-026-02214-9.title: Machine learning-based interfacial tension prediction for nanoparticles-assisted enhanced oil recovery
doi:10.1007/s13202-026-02214-9.abstract: Accurate interfacial tension (IFT) prediction is crucial for optimizing enhanced oil recovery (EOR), as traditional measurement methods are time-consuming, costly, and often impractical under reservoir conditions. This study presents a novel machine learning (ML) framework for robust IFT prediction. A comprehensive dataset of 474 data points was curated from published literature, uniquely encompassing a wide variability in reservoir conditions and complex chemical formulations, including 10 distinct nanoparticle (NP) types, 4 surfactant classes, and various polymers. Multiple ML models were developed, including Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest (RF), and novel hybrid ensembles (ANN-RF and ANN-XGBoost). The results demonstrated that hybrid and deep learning approaches significantly outperformed simpler models. The hybrid ANN-RF model achieved superior validation accuracy (R 2 = 0.973, RMSE = 1.730), while the standalone ANN (Test R 2 = 0.942) and XGBoost (Test R 2 = 0.940) also showed strong generalization. A comprehensive sensitivity analysis identified chemical additive concentration as the dominant predictive factor, followed by NP concentration. Crucially, it revealed that salinity’s significant impact is driven primarily by high-order interaction effects. This work establishes a powerful, validated data-driven tool, highlighting the potential of ML to reduce experimentation and accelerate the design of optimized chemical EOR formulations. The novelty lies in combining hybrid models with comprehensive sensitivity analysis to deconstruct the complex, interaction-driven physics of NP-assisted EOR systems.

doi:10.1007/s44196-026-01648-7.title: GenOpt-FedGNN: GAN-Augmented Federated Graph Learning with GWO and ASIO-Inspired Adaptive Aggregation for Imbalanced Fraud Detection
doi:10.1007/s44196-026-01648-7.abstract: Detecting fraud in distributed financial transaction systems is challenging. It is extremely rare to find a fraudulent record. The interactions among transactional records have a relational structure and the data can’t be stored centrally by every participating institution. The paper introduces the federated graph learning framework i.e. GenOpt-FedGNN. The framework combines Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) with client local learning, graph neural classification, and the aggregation of the trained models through adaptive process of Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO) and Asteroid Satellite Inspired Optimization (ASIO). Each client preprocesses their own transactions independently, produces more minority fraud samples to train a class weighted Graph Neural Network (GNN), and builds a transaction graph. Each client sends updates regarding model and validator to the server. The framework is tested with a set of 200,000 PaySim transactions. Transactions were randomly sampled and distributed among the five distributed clients with 30 communication rounds. Six configurations (FedAvg, GWO and ASIO with and without GAN augmentation), have been compared by Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Specificity, False Positive Rate, False Negative Rate and Confusion-matrix measures. The ablation analysis demonstrated that GAN augmentation doubled local fraud training samples and reduced class-imbalance ratio. But, the local fraud data has been extremely imbalanced. Overall, at the final round, the accuracy was highest with ASIO-GAN (96.40%), the specificity (96.41%), precision (1.58%), F1-score (3.11%), and the lowest False Positive Rate (3.59%). The best Balanced Accuracy (94.16%) was found for FedAvg-GAN, and the best PR-AUC (60.02%) was found for ASIO-NoGAN. The GWO GAN-based configurations got best PR-AUC of 59.20%. The ablation results on the other hand further showed that using GAN for augmentation resulted in a consistent increase in the Accuracy, Precision, F1-Score, Specificity and false alarm control compared to using it without GAN. So augmentation with GAN and aggregation with Adaptive Aggregation can affect the sensitivity–specificity trade-off but not necessarily all the other aggregation metrics. The proposed framework is reproducible and data local to the raw data for the graph-based fraud detection application which features extreme class imbalance.

doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.6c03879.title: Resolving the Data Dilemma in Catalyst Design: A Generative-Enhanced Manifold-Preserving Machine Learning Method for CO2-to-Aromatics
doi:10.1021/acs.iecr.6c03879.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Direct CO2 hydrogenation to aromatics (CTA) offers a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based aromatic production, yet its catalyst design is severely hindered by data scarcity, feature heterogeneity, and conflicting multiobjective requirements. Therefore, this study proposes a generative enhancement and manifold preservation-driven interpretable machine learning (GEMP-ML) framework. It integrates heuristic hybrid encoding, hierarchical missing value management, generative data augmentation, and active-learning-based sample screening to construct an information-enriched catalyst training set. To enable semantically faithful numerical representation of high-cardinality categorical features, a best-first sampling strategy is designed to identify the optimal hybrid encoding scheme from 89 candidate combinations specifically for these categorical variables. Combined with hierarchical semantic missing-value management and high-fidelity imputation algorithms, the data integrity of the CTA dataset is restored while preserving the semantic integrity of categorical features. GMM-based generative augmentation combined with diversity-aware active learning improved the utilization of synthetic data, and the CatBoost surrogate model achieved an average test set R2 of 0.973 across the three targets. Complementary interpretability analysis further identifies key descriptors governing catalyst performance, guiding the Pareto optimization of catalyst formulations and operating parameters. The recommended Zn–Al/HZSM-5 catalyst is predicted to achieve approximately 36.5% CO2 conversion, 78.6% C5+ selectivity, and 0.35% CO selectivity. The model is further validated against two independent experimental datasets covering 100 h time-on-stream, with prediction errors of &lt;8%, supporting its ability to reproduce the observed performance trends under the evaluated conditions. This generalizable framework provides a systematic, data-driven paradigm for accelerating the design of high-performance catalysts in data-sparse catalytic systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s00406-026-02408-6.title: Reinforcement learning deficits in at-risk mental state for psychosis: the role of primary negative symptoms
doi:10.1007/s00406-026-02408-6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Negative symptoms such as amotivation begin to emerge in the at-risk mental state for psychosis (ARMS), and in some cases, these symptoms are idiopathic (i.e., primary negative symptoms, PNS). While deficits in reinforcement learning (RL) are evident in patients with first-episode and chronic schizophrenia and are associated with the severity of negative symptoms, whether these deficits are present during ARMS warrants further investigation. Additionally, it is unclear whether these deficits, especially those driven by rewards, are particularly characteristic of ARMS individuals with PNS. This study compared 97 ARMS individuals and 37 healthy controls (HC) on probabilistic RL. We then compared ARMS individuals with PNS (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 15), those without PNS (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 82), and HC on probabilistic RL. Reward- and punishment-driven RL (both trial-by-trial and procedural) and value-guided choice were assessed using two probabilistic RL tasks: Go/NoGo (GNG) and Gain vs. Loss-Avoidance (GLA) tasks. Compared with HC, ARMS individuals showed impairments in overall procedural RL on both RL tasks, as well as subtle, task-specific alterations in value-guided choice. Furthermore, ARMS-PNS individuals, relative to HC, showed particular deficits in reward-driven RL (trial-to-trial RL on GLA task and procedural RL on both tasks), as well as impaired positive expected value representations to guide decision-making on GLA task. Extending the results in patients with established psychosis, our findings indicate that deficits in RL exist before the onset of a psychotic disorder. With a modest sample of ARMS-PNS individuals, preliminary evidence suggests that deficits in reward-driven RL may be more specific to PNS.

doi:10.32628/cseit2612553.abstract: <jats:p>Effectiveness of anticancer drug varies among various types of cancers so understanding their response towards these medications is essential. The paper describes an algorithm to classify drug response patterns from the lung cancer subset of GDSC2 data set through machine learning techniques. Continuous LN_IC50 response values are classified as sensitive and resistant based on predetermined cut-off points for creating a balanced dataset for modeling purposes. Eight out of nine numbers are obtained by drugs, cells lines targets pathways related responses while selecting them via selectkbest method through ANOVA Ftest. Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest and XGBoost models were trained and evaluated on a held-out test set of 6,404 samples from an unbalanced dataset containing 32,018 records. Test accuracy of these models was between 92.61% and 92.96%, whereas their ROC-AUC value ranged from 0.978 to 0.981. Integrated with a Django based research tool by means of an algorithm that combines predictions via vote for producing outputs from this system. This device is meant solely to serve as an educational tool; it cannot be used by patients for self-diagnosis, healthcare decisions, or prescription of medications.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/978-3-032-40124-3_10.title: Statistical Model Checking in 2026: Simulation, Learning, and Exhaustive Verification
doi:10.1007/978-3-032-40124-3_10.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Statistical model checking (SMC) analyses stochastic models by simulation: it samples many runs, evaluates the property of interest on each of them, and returns an estimate together with a statistical guarantee. It only needs the ability to draw runs from a model or system, which makes it widely applicable—at the cost of statistical instead of hard guarantees. Yet rare events, unbounded properties, and nondeterminism remain hard for simulation alone. In 2026, SMC is therefore practised as simulation, learning, and exhaustive verification working together. We recall the essence of SMC, and survey the work of the past few years on these three problems and SMC’s statistical methods themselves. We then examine how SMC combines with reinforcement learning and with probabilistic model checking, and introduce the contributions to the SMC track at ISoLA 2026.</jats:p>

doi:10.55640/ijidml-v03i10-03.title: An Analytical Study of a Governed Lakehouse Framework in Multi-State Medicare Claims and Provider Data for Fraud, Waste, and Abuse Detection
doi:10.55640/ijidml-v03i10-03.abstract: <jats:p>Medicare fraud detection, waste, and abuse is hampered by the high volume of claims, highly fragmented data-analysis systems, limited visibility into data quality, and significant class imbalance. This study assessed the potential of an Original Medicare Part B (OMB) Bronze-Silver-Gold lakehouse to improve data quality, traceability, analytical efficiency, and provider-level risk identification across OMB-covered populations in California, New York, Florida, Texas, and Pennsylvania in 2024. Using Apache Spark/PySpark with Delta-format tables, the study sampled 1,500,000 provider-service records in proportion to state Traditional Medicare enrollment, representing 214,873 unique NPIs, consolidated them with CMS provider files and HHS-OIG provider-exclusion data, interpreted 30 features, and used four models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Isolation Forest. During Silver-layer screening, 27,362 records (1.82%) triggered one or more quality rules and were quarantined; NPI enrichment had 99.7% compliance, and Gold-layer data quality had 99.2% compliance. This reduced query time from a median of 18.4 seconds to 5.7 seconds (approximately 69%). XGBoost performed best among the supervised models, with ROC-AUC = 0.91, PR-AUC = 0.34, and F1 = 0.66. State elevated/high-risk flags were not confirmed as fraud; they were a priority for investigation and ranged from 2.2%–3.4% of unique providers within each state. Manually managed, repeatable pipelines provide defensible Medicare FWA prioritization, and repeatable, source-to-feature, auditable pipelines can support multi-state, analytic workflows where needed. Areas to explore include longitudinal claims, Part D, DMEPOS, enforcement outcomes, graph analytics, and prospective investigator validation.</jats:p>

doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.88s.94.title: An Explainable Federated Vision–Language Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserving Automated Medical Report Generation Across Distributed Healthcare Institutions
doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.88s.94.abstract: <jats:p>Automated generation of medical reports using AI can help speed up diagnosis and reduce doctor workload, but currently, the most efficient forms of automation use centralized training, which requires hospitals to share sensitive patient data. This raises concerns about the privacy and regulatory issues of sharing patient information to generate reports. In addition, clinicians have difficulty trusting AI-assisted diagnosis because the visionlanguage models used for automated report generation are not easily interpretable. To tackle these issues, an Explainable Federated Vision-Language Learning Framework (EFVLL) has been created to generate automated medical reports that preserve patient privacy through distributed healthcare institutions. Hospitals can use federated learning to build a collaborative global vision-language model without having to share raw patient information. The EFVLL framework also includes an explainable attention mechanism that will help clinicians understand how specific areas of the image and text are related to the report being generated, increasing the transparency and interpretability of automated reports. Further, the EFVLL will improve generalization across non-homogenous datasets and comply with data privacy and regulatory requirements. The EFVLL framework has been validated with multiple large standard datasets (e.g., RSNA), and therefore it is suitable for implementation and use in a distributed healthcare environment.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s44411-026-00911-9.title: A Multi-Parametric Risk Stratification Model for Early-Pregnancy Prediction of Preeclampsia: Integrating First- and Second-Trimester Biomarkers with Machine Learning
doi:10.1007/s44411-026-00911-9.abstract: Preeclampsia remains a major contributor to maternal and perinatal morbidity. This study aimed to develop and internally evaluate an interpretable machine-learning framework integrating routinely available first- and second-trimester parameters for preclinical risk stratification. This retrospective case-control study included 524 singleton pregnancies (262 with preeclampsia and 262 normotensive controls). Seven prespecified predictors—12-week mean arterial pressure (MAP), pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A), alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), unconjugated estriol, eosinophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (ELR), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and lymphocyte count—were evaluated using logistic regression, random forest, Gaussian naive Bayes, support vector machine, and k-nearest neighbors. Internal validation used stratified 10-fold cross-validation with identical fold assignments across classifiers. A five-variable weighted clinical risk score was also constructed. MAP showed the highest univariable discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] = 0.891). In cross-validation, Gaussian naive Bayes achieved the numerically highest mean AUC (0.948 ± 0.024), accuracy (0.885 ± 0.031), recall (0.893 ± 0.044), and F1 score (0.886 ± 0.032), while random forest had the highest mean precision (0.891 ± 0.042). The weighted clinical risk score achieved an AUC of 0.885 and 81.9% accuracy. The framework showed strong internal discrimination but remains exploratory. Because the score incorporates approximately 16-week AFP and estriol measurements, it should not be interpreted as a purely first-trimester aspirin-selection model. Prospective external validation, calibration, and subtype-specific assessment are required before clinical use.

doi:10.14202/vetworld.2026.4641-4656.title: Machine learning-based segmentation and quantitative histological assessment of bovine liver fibrosis: Comparative performance of three open-source models
doi:10.14202/vetworld.2026.4641-4656.abstract:
<jats:p>Background and Aim: Conventional semiquantitative histopathological scoring of hepatic fibrosis is affected by interobserver variability and provides limited quantitative information on the spatial distribution and progression of collagen deposition. Machine learning (ML)-based image analysis may provide a reproducible approach for objective fibrosis assessment in veterinary pathology. This study compared three open-source ML models, Trainable Weka Segmentation (TWS), Ilastik, and Fiber-ML, for segmentation and quantitative assessment of bovine liver fibrosis and evaluated their diagnostic performance, agreement with METAVIR staging, and computational efficiency.

Materials and Methods: This cross-sectional observational study included liver samples from 35 cattle diagnosed with hepatic fibrosis according to the clinical sign records. Masson’s trichrome-stained sections were classified according to METAVIR stages F0–F4 (F0 represents normal liver samples, n=7). A total of 525 images were obtained from perisinusoidal, pericentral, and periportal regions. Images from 25 animals (375 images) constituted the training/validation dataset with five-fold cross-validation, whereas images from 10 animals (150 images) formed an independent testing dataset. A similar dataset was annotated by experts to generate manual ground-truth segmentation, and images from the same animal appeared in both training and testing datasets. Model performance was assessed using collagen proportionate area (CPA), Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, correlation with METAVIR scores, and computational-resource requirements.

Results: Ilastik and Fiber-ML generally achieved greater segmentation agreement than TWS (p ≤ 0.05), with DSC values reaching 0.91 and 0.92, compared to 0.87 in TWS, depending on the hepatic region. Overall model pixel-level segmentation accuracy ranged from 84.7% to 91.8%, with the highest performance observed in the periportal region. CPA measurements generated by the models showed strong positive correlations with METAVIR stages (ρ = 0.97–0.99). Fiber-ML required substantially less computational resources, while Ilastik recorded fewer software errors than TWS, including shorter training time and lower CPU and RAM utilization. All computational benchmarking was conducted under identical hardware and software conditions.

Conclusion: Open-source ML models enabled objective segmentation and quantitative assessment of bovine hepatic fibrosis. Ilastik and Fiber-ML demonstrated strong agreement with expert-derived reference segmentation and fibrosis staging, while Fiber-ML offered additional computational efficiency. These findings support ML-assisted digital histopathology as a future complementary tool for quantifying and spatially characterizing hepatic fibrosis in cattle. Further validation is required before their reproducibility and diagnostic applicability can be established.

Keywords: bovine liver fibrosis, collagen proportionate area, digital histopathology, hepatic fibrosis, machine learning, METAVIR staging, segmentation, veterinary pathology.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-75703-w.title: Adaptive storage optimization for deep learning workloads in converged HPC-cloud environments: a reinforcement learning approach
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-75703-w.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Storage systems remain a significant bottleneck in large-scale deep learning training. Most evaluation studies rely on synthetic benchmarks that do not capture the I/O heterogeneity present in real training pipelines. Automated configuration methods often treat parameter selection as stateless, overlooking the temporal structure of recurring training phases. These challenges are addressed using a converged HPC-cloud platform that integrates Lustre with S3-compatible object storage. Three workloads with distinct I/O characteristics were evaluated: ResNet-50 on ImageNet-1K, 3D U-Net on the Medical Segmentation Decathlon, and Whisper Large on LibriSpeech. Time-to-convergence was used as the primary metric. We introduced a deep reinforcement learning framework that combines Proximal Policy Optimization and Soft Actor-Critic with a Transformer-based state encoder to predict workload phase transitions rather than merely respond to them. The learned policies reduced checkpoint write latency by up to 74.6% and improved GPU utilization across all three workloads. The approach generalizes across heterogeneous I/O profiles without per-workload reconfiguration. The results indicate that temporally aware storage control can improve the efficiency of distributed training pipelines in heterogeneous HPC-cloud environments.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s12893-026-04287-z.title: Machine learning-based prediction of 30-day outcomes after surgery for left-sided infective endocarditis
doi:10.1186/s12893-026-04287-z.abstract: Surgery is often essential for patients with left-sided infective endocarditis (IE). Accurate preoperative risk assessment remains challenging. This study aimed to develop and internally validate machine learning (ML) models to predict 30-day postoperative mortality or major complications in patients undergoing surgery for left-sided IE. A retrospective analysis of adult patients between May 2009 and May 2025 was performed. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death or major complications within 30 days, including postoperative stroke, malignant arrhythmia, prolonged ventilation, acute kidney injury requiring dialysis, shock, and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. An ML-based pipeline was used to select variables. Eight ML algorithms were evaluated with 6 strategies to address class imbalance. Model performance was assessed in terms of discrimination, calibration, and overall prediction error using out-of-fold (OOF) predictions in the training set, and the selected final model was subsequently evaluated in the test set. Model interpretation was performed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis, and an online tool was developed for clinical implementation. Among the 992 included patients, 100 (10.1%) experienced the primary outcome. Ten predictors were selected for model development. Of the 56 candidate models evaluated, 13 met the screening criteria based on OOF predictions. The categorical boosting (CatBoost) model trained with random over-sampling (RO) showed the lowest OOF Brier score and was selected as the final model. In the test set, CatBoost-RO achieved an AUC of 0.814 (95% CI: 0.724–0.904), a calibration intercept of -0.036 (95% CI: -0.474–0.401), a calibration slope of 0.995 (95% CI: 0.658–1.331), and a Brier score of 0.065 (95% CI: 0.053–0.078). SHAP analysis identified total bilirubin and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide as the most influential predictors. The CatBoost model trained with RO showed favorable discrimination, calibration, and low prediction error for estimating the risk of 30-day death or major complications after surgery for left-sided IE, which may support preoperative risk stratification in this population, although external validation is warranted.

doi:10.1186/s40101-026-00451-9.abstract:

                  <jats:p>
                    Classroom overcrowding affects hundreds of millions of students globally, yet its physiological impact on cardiac autonomic function remains uncharacterized. This controlled within-subjects experiment enrolled 30 healthy university students who attended standardized 30-min lectures under three calibrated density conditions: low (30 students/150 m

Subjective workload was assessed via the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), and RoBoSS-SVM (a Support Vector Machine using the Robust, Bounded, Sparse, and Smooth loss function) with Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) classified density conditions from HRV features. Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed significant density effects on all 25 HRV parameters (all

                     < 0.001), with 64% demonstrating exceptionally large effect sizes (
                    <jats:italic>η</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    p ≥ 0.50). Parasympathetic markers showed the largest responses: pNN50 declined 52% (
                    <jats:italic>η</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    p = 0.702), HF power declined 51% (
                    <jats:italic>η</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    p = 0.654), and RMSSD declined 32% (
                    <jats:italic>η</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    p = 0.420) from low to high density—while sympathetically influenced indices showed substantially smaller effects, confirming parasympathetic withdrawal as the predominant autonomic mechanism. These suppression magnitudes approach levels associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. NASA-TLX scores increased 74% across conditions (

The excellent classification performance supports feasibility of real-time wearable monitoring for evidence-based classroom capacity management.

doi:10.1038/s41524-026-02302-8.title: Tracking the lithiation state of LixSi from machine-learned XPS binding energies
doi:10.1038/s41524-026-02302-8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) is a powerful technique to probe chemical states and interfacial processes in battery materials, but a quantitative interpretation is often hindered by the complex, heterogeneous microstructures that form during operation and dominate electrochemical cycling. Silicon-based anodes represent a paradigmatic example in Li batteries, as (de)lithiation proceeds through the formation of strongly disordered Li
                    <jats:sub>x</jats:sub>
                    Si phases and crystal-amorphous transformations that are hard to characterize. Here, we introduce a computational framework that combines machine-learning (ML) prediction of core-level binding energies to large-scale atomistic simulations—grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) complemented with molecular dynamics (MD), driven by an ML potential—for a systematic sampling of lithiation states and local atomic environments. This approach yields stoichiometry maps that capture the main spectroscopic trends observed in
                    <jats:italic>operando</jats:italic>
                    and ex situ XPS measurements, including the distinctive Si 2
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    signatures associated with the crystal-to-amorphous disordering during early delithiation.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.67785/pjpp.7.372.title: Sequential Impact Analysis of Instructional Leadership Quality on Student Learning Outcomes at the Elementary Level
doi:10.67785/pjpp.7.372.abstract: <jats:p>This study was analysing the sequential impact analysis of instructional leadership quality on student learning out comes at elementary level. The main objective of the study was to identify the association between instructional leadership quality and students' learning outcomes. The main research question which was to be answered to what extent there will be the association exist between leadership quality and students' learning outcomes? The population of the study were all the elementary schools of district Khushab. From 120 primary schools of district Khushab, 60 elementary schools were selected by multistage sampling technique. This study was quantitative in nature so, self-developed questionnaire was used to gather the data from the respondents. Descriptive statistics i.e. frequency, percentage, mean and standard deviation were used in analyzing the data. The conclusion of the study was that there was a clear and significant association between instructional leadership quality and students' learning outcomes at elementary level. On the basis of conclusion, it was recommended that instructional leadership practices should be monitored and evaluated regularly to identify the areas for improvement and ensure effective implementation of practices.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/978-3-032-40124-3_7.title: Automated ADAS Testing Using Automata Learning: A Case Study in Learning-Based Testing
doi:10.1007/978-3-032-40124-3_7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>As part of the ongoing effort in the automotive domain to achieve automated driving, advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) are designed for increasingly complex driving tasks. This includes safety-critical features such as automated lane-keeping and emergency braking. Consequently, validation and verification of ADAS are highly important. However, with the growing complexity of the automated driving tasks, the corresponding ADAS also increase in complexity, which makes validation and verification more costly. Hence, automation is needed. In this work, the domain of ADAS serves as a case study for learning-based testing (LBT). In particular, we apply active automata learning to infer formal behavioral models of ADAS during testing. This entails several challenges since such systems feature a mixture of continuous and discrete behavior as well as domain constraints. The setting exhibits a large search space with only a small portion of valid test cases. We exemplify how the right abstractions implemented through mappers can be used to deal with these challenges. Finally, we demonstrate the use of two different automata learning approaches in learning-based testing of an adaptive cruise controller and show that they are able to generate critical test cases.</jats:p>

doi:10.55205/joctensa.5220262015827.title: Predicting Cross-Country Waste Recycling Performance Using Regression and Explainable Machine Learning
doi:10.55205/joctensa.5220262015827.abstract: Recycling is central to sustainable waste management and the circular economy, yet performance varies substantially across countries. This study examines economic and waste-related factors associated with municipal recycling performance and evaluates whether machine learning (ML) models improve prediction relative to conventional statistical modelling. The analysis included 84 countries with populations of at least one million using World Bank What a Waste 3.0 data. Municipal recycling rate was modelled using GDP per capita, municipal solid waste (MSW) generation per capita, and food, plastic, and paper and cardboard waste shares. Multiple linear regression (MLR) was compared with Random Forest (RF), XGBoost, and Support Vector Regression (SVR) using nested repeated five-fold cross-validation, while SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were used to interpret the best-performing ML model. ln(GDP per capita) was the only statistically significant independent predictor in MLR and the dominant RF predictor, accounting for 47.67% of global SHAP importance. Food waste (18.95%), paper and cardboard (14.71%), and MSW generation (14.69%) also contributed meaningfully, whereas plastic waste showed limited importance (3.98%). RF achieved the strongest predictive performance (R2=0.312), outperforming MLR (R2=0.229), while XGBoost showed a modest improvement (R2=0.263) and SVR did not (R2=0.215). Income-stratified SHAP analysis showed that GDP remained dominant across income groups, while waste-related importance varied. These findings demonstrate the value of explainable ML as a complement to conventional statistical modelling.

doi:10.3390/diagnostics16203369.title: Stage Migration, Treatment Patterns, and Machine Learning-Based Prediction of 12-Month Mortality in Lung Adenocarcinoma Across the COVID-19 Era: A SEER Population-Based Study
doi:10.3390/diagnostics16203369.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: The COVID-19 pandemic coincided with widespread disruption of cancer care. We examined changes in lung adenocarcinoma presentation and outcomes across the COVID-19 era and whether diagnosis-time information identifies patients at risk of early death. Methods: Adults with microscopically confirmed lung adenocarcinoma diagnosed during 2018–2023 were identified from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results 17 Registries database and grouped into three diagnostic periods. Logistic regression, time-varying Cox, and Fine-Gray models evaluated stage, metastasis, surgery, delay, and mortality. Four machine-learning algorithms using only diagnosis-time variables were developed (2018–2021; n = 87,281) and temporally validated (2022; n = 22,012). Results: Among 133,306 patients, COVID-19 versus pre-COVID-19 differences were significant but small in absolute terms: stage IV disease 47.9% versus 47.4% (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 1.03; 95% CI, 1.00–1.06), organ-specific metastasis 45.8% versus 44.4% (OR, 1.06; 1.04–1.09), and treatment delay exceeding 90 days 11.1% versus 10.2% (OR, 1.11; 1.06–1.17). Post-COVID-19 (2022–2023) diagnosis showed less advanced disease but substantially longer delay (14.5% versus 10.2%; OR, 1.45; 1.39–1.52). Gradient boosting achieved a 2022 ROC AUC of 0.840 (0.834–0.845); it flagged 46.8% of patients and correctly flagged 81.6% of those who died, against 44.0% and 75.4% for stage IV classification. Conclusions: COVID-era changes in stage and metastatic presentation were small in absolute terms, whereas the increase in treatment delay was larger and persisted. A diagnosis-time model modestly improved identification of early death beyond stage alone, flagging 28 more patients per 1000, of whom 21 died within the year. These findings support further evaluation; external validation is required before clinical use.</jats:p>

doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.72s.90.title: Effectiveness of Implementing Blended Learning Model with SMART BADMINTON ZR Application in Badminton Learning in Physical Education
doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.72s.90.abstract: This study aims to investigate the effectiveness of implementing a blended learning model using the SMART BADMINTON ZR application on improving student performance in basic serving and smashing techniques in badminton courses.Method: This study used a quasi-experimental design with a pretest-posttest control group.A total of 64 Physical Education students from Dharmas Indonesia University participated and were divided into an experimental group (n=32) that used the blended learning model based on the SMART BADMINTON ZR application, and a control group (n=32) that used conventional face-to-face learning methods.The intervention was carried out over 16 meetings.Student performance was measured using a serve and smash technique test with a 1-4 scale process-work rubric.Data were analyzed using paired-samples t-test and independent-samples t-test with a significance level of α = 0.05.Results: The results showed a significant improvement in both skills (serve and smash) in the experimental group compared to the control group (p < 0.05).The experimental group showed an average posttest score of 45.88, higher than the control group with an average of 40.78.Conclusion: The integration of technology through a blended learning model with the SMART BADMINTON ZR application has been proven effective in improving students' understanding, motor performance, and engagement in sports learning.Flexibility in independent learning, better visualization of techniques, quick feedback, and increased motivation are key factors in the success of this approach.

doi:10.3390/jof12100778.title: Accurate Extraction of Phenotypic Parameters for DUS Testing of Oudemansiella raphanipes Based on Deep Learning
doi:10.3390/jof12100778.abstract: <jats:p>To enable the rapid and accurate acquisition of phenotypic parameters during distinctness, uniformity, and stability (DUS) testing of edible mushroom varieties, and to address the low efficiency, strong subjectivity, and insufficient standardization of conventional manual measurement methods, this study used the fruiting bodies of Oudemansiella raphanipes as the research object and proposed an automatic phenotypic parameter extraction method based on deep learning instance segmentation. An instance-segmentation dataset containing 473 O. raphanipes images and 1419 annotated objects was constructed, and the YOLOv11s-seg model was improved by introducing the lightweight feature-extraction network StarNet_s050 to construct the YOLOv11s-star-seg model, thereby improving model inference efficiency and meeting practical application requirements. Under standardized imaging conditions, pileus and stipe regions were obtained from the instance-segmentation results, and image-scale calibration was combined to automatically extract DUS phenotypic parameters, including pileus diameter, pileus context thickness, stipe length, and stipe diameter, while quantitatively describing stipe shape. The experimental results showed that the YOLOv11s-star-seg model performed well in the instance segmentation of O. raphanipes, achieving an mAP50 of 99.1%, an F1 value of 98.9%, and an mIoU of 97.86%; compared with the YOLOv11s-seg model, the number of parameters was reduced by 39% and the inference time was reduced by 27%, thereby achieving model lightweighting while maintaining high segmentation accuracy. The automatically extracted results showed high consistency with the manual measurements; the coefficients of determination (R2) from linear regression fitting for stipe length, stipe diameter, and pileus diameter all exceeded 0.96, indicating that the method can effectively replace part of the manual measurement process. The results can provide technical support for the digitalization of DUS testing of O. raphanipes, intelligent breeding of edible mushrooms, and accurate phenotypic identification.</jats:p>

doi:10.1002/fer3.70055.title: AI‐Supported Research‐Led Teaching in Syntegrative Project‐Based Learning: Educator Questioning, Feedback, and Student Learning Outcomes in Authentic Industry Projects
doi:10.1002/fer3.70055.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new possibilities for connecting research‐led teaching with authentic industry projects, yet its educational value depends on how educators organize inquiry rather than on technological use alone. This study examined the relationships among AI‐supported research‐led teaching (AIRLT), educator questioning (EQ), educator feedback (EF), student inquiry engagement (SIE), and authentic project learning outcomes (APLO) within Syntegrative Project‐Based Learning. A quantitative cross‐sectional survey was conducted with 898 undergraduate students from 12 universities in Vietnam who had participated in authentic industry or organizational projects involving AI‐supported inquiry and educator guidance. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) showed that AIRLT was positively associated with EQ (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                     = 0.642) and EF (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                     = 0.611). Both EQ (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                     = 0.463) and EF (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                     = 0.349) were positively associated with SIE, which, in turn, showed a strong positive association with APLO (
                    <jats:italic>β</jats:italic>
                     = 0.689). All six specific indirect effects were significant, indicating statistically significant indirect associations among AI‐supported teaching, educator guidance, student inquiry, and perceived authentic learning outcomes. The findings contribute an educator‐mediated perspective to Syntegrative Education by showing that AI is most educationally meaningful when embedded in purposeful questioning, feedback, and sustained student inquiry. The study highlights the importance of designing AI‐supported industry projects around evidence evaluation, iterative feedback, reflection, and active investigation of authentic problems rather than treating AI use as an educational objective in itself.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3390/jcm15208043.title: The Learning Curve in Robotic HPB Surgery: Myth, Metrics, and Misinterpretations
doi:10.3390/jcm15208043.abstract: <jats:p>Background: The evolution of robotic surgery has widened the indications for minimally invasive hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) surgery, making possible the execution of more complicated cases. Within this context, the learning curve concept is now an essential factor when assessing surgical training and expertise, as well as patient safety within a robotic HPB program. Nevertheless, existing methodologies often make use of procedure volume and surrogate intraoperative measures, which may be an insufficient way to define surgical competence. Methods: This narrative review examines the learning curve concept in robotic HPB surgery, focusing on existing performance metrics, methodological limitations, procedural complexity, risk adjustment, and the influence of team-related and institutional factors. Results: The time of operation, the estimated blood loss, the rate of conversion, and postoperative morbidity are frequently applied to assess learning curves. Nevertheless, these metrics are affected by the criteria of patient selection, the level of complexity of the procedure, and some other factors like institutional characteristics and experience of the team performing the procedure. As a result, one single value or an inflection point might fail to adequately capture the concept of surgical competence. The concepts of competency, proficiency, and mastery are distinct stages of learning, whereas the speed of learning for such skills as technical proficiency, clinical outcomes, oncological sufficiency, and intraoperative decision-making might be different. Conclusions: The learning curve in robotic HPB surgery should be viewed as a multi-dimensional and complex process and not a straightforward correlation between the number of cases and the results. The future assessment of the learning curve needs to consider different domains, including technical, clinical, oncological, cognitive, and team-related aspects, taking into account the level of complexity and institutional context of each case.</jats:p>

doi:10.21528/lnlm-vol24-no1-art2.title: Data Labeling with Local and Global Consistency Using Phylograms
doi:10.21528/lnlm-vol24-no1-art2.abstract: <jats:p>One of the main challenges in machine learning tasks is unlabeled data. Consequently, semi-supervised learning is an approach commonly used in labeling data tasks. The use of diffusion kernels is one of the powerful methods in this set of learning. This paper introduces Phylogram based Data Labeling (PhyDL), an innovative method that combines the benefits of phylogram analysis with Learning with Local and Global Consistency (LLGC). PhyDL leverages phylogram analysis to act as an aggregator of information from labeled samples, capable of correcting possible labeling errors. PhyDL constructs a phylogram using community detection algorithms, FastGreedy and Edge Betweenness, to identify and leverage the structure of the data, with FastGreedy emerging as the best-performing algorithm among those evaluated. We implemented PhyDL and evaluated its performance on the TwoMoons, MNIST, MUSK, HEART, and SONAR datasets. PhyDL outperformed LLGC on 4 out of 5 evaluated datasets, highlighting its effectiveness in semi-supervised learning scenarios. On the TwoMoons, MNIST, MUSK, and SONAR benchmarks, the method showed steady accuracy gains, with consistent improvements as the number of labeled samples increased. However, on the HEART dataset, standard LLGC achieved better results, indicating that PhyDL’s community-based diffusion can be limited by certain underlying spatial structures. Furthermore, the experiments revealed that the Edge Betweenness algorithm is unsuitable for these specific high-dimensional tasks. Ultimately, this study showcases PhyDL’s potential, when equipped with the FastGreedy algorithm, to significantly improve data labeling performance in semi-supervised scenarios, effectively leveraging the structural topology of complex datasets.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78417-9.title: A genetically encoded local learning rule enables physical learning in engineered bacteria
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78417-9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Training physical neural networks directly in matter remains difficult because most platforms do not store and update weights within the same physical substrate. Here we show that engineered
                    <jats:italic>Escherichia coli</jats:italic>
                    can implement a genetically encoded local learning rule acting on persistent biological memory. We introduce memregulons: bacterial memory elements in which coupled plasmids store an analogue weight as the relative abundance of P1 within the P1 + P2 plasmid pool. Environmental inputs activate local promoters, and a shared sublethal kanamycin signal converts promoter activity into differential growth that lowers the stored P1 fraction. Across single-strain trajectories, combined plate-reader and flow-cytometry measurements are consistent with activity- and variance-dependent weight change. At the single-cell level, repeated negative learning reshapes the stored weight distribution as it approaches the lower boundary. In mixed populations and co-cultures, one shared negative learning signal selectively rewrites active memregulons, enabling externally routed supervised tic-tac-toe lessons. We then generalise the architecture across orthogonal chemical inputs and combinatorial promoters, and combine measured co-culture updates with external game analysis and simulate negative pruning in nonlinear-classifier architectures. These results establish physical learning in living matter through local negative updates of genetically encoded analogue weights.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3390/e28101137.title: Clone-Node Detection in Wireless Sensor Networks Using Behavioral Analysis and Machine Learning
doi:10.3390/e28101137.abstract: <jats:p>Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) remain vulnerable to clone-node attacks, in which malicious replicas use the identity or credentials of legitimate sensor nodes. This study presents an intelligent learning-based approach for clone-node detection using behavioral characteristics related to communication, topology, traffic, distance, and energy consumption. Since the WSN-DS dataset does not contain a native clone-node class, a controlled synthetic clone-node scenario was developed from legitimate sensor observations by preserving node identities while introducing behavioral changes associated with replication. A group-aware evaluation strategy was used to evaluate Logistic Regression, Random Forest, 1D-CNN, and a correlation-enhanced DCNN under the same experimental conditions. The results showed different detection characteristics among the evaluated models. Random Forest achieved the strongest overall classification performance, while Logistic Regression also provided strong discrimination with a low false-positive rate. The deep-learning models achieved high clone-detection recall, with the correlation-enhanced DCNN reaching 99.46% recall. These results demonstrate that different learning approaches provide different advantages for clone-node detection and highlight the importance of considering accuracy, detection sensitivity, and false-positive behavior together. The findings provide a useful basis for developing more reliable and adaptive intelligent clone-node detection methods for resource-constrained WSN environments.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/su182010532.title: Tracing Sustainability Knowledge from Course Aims and Content to Learning Outcomes: An Element-Level Analysis of an Interior Architecture Curriculum
doi:10.3390/su182010532.abstract: <jats:p>Curriculum studies in sustainable design commonly map themes or Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), but such mapping does not show whether specifically named disciplinary knowledge remains identifiable in formal learning outcomes. This study therefore examines how sustainability-related knowledge is represented across course aims/content and learning outcomes in a publicly documented 2025–2026 undergraduate Interior Architecture curriculum. Across all 70 course records, aims and content from 67 records yielded 1168 named knowledge elements; 169 sustainability-related elements in 17 courses met conservative inclusion criteria across seven domains. Each element was coded as preserved, generalized, displaced, or not represented. Independent re-unitization of a predefined 14-course validation sample yielded Krippendorff’s unitizing alpha of αU = 0.84, while independent recoding of all 169 included elements yielded 81.7% pre-adjudication agreement (Cohen’s κ = 0.725); final adjudicated transformation classifications were used for analysis. Overall, 45.0% were preserved at equivalent specificity, 30.2% generalized, 4.1% displaced, and 20.7% not represented. Preservation was highest for materials, water, resources, and circularity (77.8%) and indoor environmental quality, health, and safety (69.6%) but lower for climate/energy performance (22.2%) and heritage/adaptive reuse (20.7%). Leave-one-course-out estimates ranged from 41.1% to 48.3%. The study distinguishes curricular presence from outcome-level specificity and provides a transparent element-level diagnostic for examining how sustainability knowledge is formally recontextualized across curricular fields without treating documentary visibility as evidence of teaching or learning.</jats:p>

doi:10.31127/tuje.1968300.title: Predictive Modeling of Urban Heat Stress Using Machine Learning: A 2050 UTCI-Based Assessment
doi:10.31127/tuje.1968300.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Urban heat islands and increasingly severe thermal stress pose critical challenges to sustainable urban development, yet physics-based simulation tools remain computationally expensive and ill-suited to early-stage climate-responsive design. This study applies machine learning to predict outdoor air and surface temperature using 20 years (2005-2025) of daily maximum temperature data ranging from 15°C to 40°C. Four algorithms were evaluated: Linear Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XG Boost). Gradient Boosting achieved the best performance with RMSE = 1.869, MAE = 1.405, and R² = 0.708, indicating robust predictive ability across diurnal temperature and seasonal patterns. 2050 projections, based on direct extrapolation of the trained model's seasonal temperature pattern, show a shift toward moderate-to-strong Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) heat stress conditions across the majority of the year, underscoring the need for climate-responsive urban design even under conservative, non-scenario-scaled projections. The results strengthen the acceptance of data-driven ML frameworks for the application in urban planning and climate-responsive architectural design practice.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/s26206572.title: Non-Invasive Blood Glucose Monitoring Using Machine Learning and Optical Approaches: A Systematic Literature Review and a Proposed Framework for Reproducible and Clinically Reliable Research
doi:10.3390/s26206572.abstract: <jats:p>Diabetes Mellitus is the leading healthcare challenge. For effective management of this disease, patients need to check their blood glucose levels regularly; however, the standard method of taking a drop of blood and placing it on a test strip does not allow for continuous monitoring and is dreaded by most people, who find it painful and uncomfortable. Researchers worldwide are trying to develop non-invasive blood glucose monitoring (NIBGM) devices; most of them have reported promising accuracy using a combination of optical techniques and machine learning, but the CE/FDA marked solution still cannot reach the market. The main objective of this systematic review is to critically analyse recent quantitative research works in optical NIBGM, highlight their strengths, and identify the main factors that hinder regulatory approvals and the commercialisation of these devices. Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, ScienceDirect, SPIE Digital Library, and Optica Publishing Group databases were searched between 1st September 2015 and 1st August 2026 using specific keywords. From the initial 1143 records, 245 studies were considered for full-text quality assessment, and 208 were excluded based on a post hoc quality score threshold. The sensing modality, wavelength, sample size, reference device, glucose range, validation strategy, accuracy metrics, and use of demographic variables as model inputs for the 37 included studies are reported. By applying an author-defined three-tier rubric, the risk of shortcut learning in each study was highlighted. Based on these findings, a common framework of fifteen concrete, evidence-grounded recommendations for future NIBGM studies was proposed.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-70508-3.title: Externally validated machine learning models for prediction of treatment selection and clinical outcomes in posterior communicating artery aneurysms
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-70508-3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Posterior communicating artery (PCOM) aneurysms account for approximately 25% of intracranial aneurysms and present clinical challenges regarding optimal treatment selection. This study developed and validated machine learning models to predict treatment modality, complications, and functional outcomes in PCOM aneurysm management using a comprehensive institutional database of 75 patients treated between 2002 and 2023. Five machine learning algorithms—Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and XGBoost—were systematically compared across 7 outcome variables: treatment type (open vs. endovascular), specific open surgical treatment, specific endovascular treatment, intraoperative rupture, complications, angiographic obliteration, and discharge modified Rankin Scale score. Models were developed using preoperative patient-specific (age, sex, family history) and aneurysm-specific (size, presentation, morphology, location) parameters, with rigorous preprocessing that included class-balancing strategies, feature engineering, and regularization to minimize overfitting. Cross-validation performance demonstrated high accuracy for treatment prediction (78.7% Random Forest), complications (94.7% Random Forest; however, sensitivity of 0% indicates that this accuracy should not be interpreted as clinically useful event detection), intraoperative rupture (92.0% Random Forest), and angiographic obliteration (87.3% Random Forest). External validation on an independent cohort from the University of Louisville (n=20–28; n=20 most complete cases for the primary external cohort, with up to n=28 for selected endpoints with available labels) revealed variable generalizability: treatment prediction maintained 78.1% accuracy, and complication prediction showed reduced external performance (70.3%), highlighting institution-specific factors. Comprehensive sensitivity analyses demonstrated that class balancing significantly improved minority class recall (0.0% → 52.2%–86.3%) for rare outcomes. Feature importance analyses identified age, aneurysm size, admission modified Rankin Scale score, and Hunt-Hess grade as the most influential predictors across multiple outcomes. This study represents the first externally validated, multioutcome machine learning framework for PCOM aneurysm management, providing quantitative risk estimates and evidence-based decision support for treatment selection and outcome prediction.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/eng7100566.title: A Two-Stage Unsupervised–Supervised Machine Learning Framework for Maximum Power Point Tracking of Photovoltaic Systems
doi:10.3390/eng7100566.abstract: <jats:p>Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) is essential for maximizing photovoltaic (PV) energy extraction under changing operating conditions. This paper investigates a two-stage machine-learning framework combining K-means or fuzzy C-means (FCM) clustering of irradiance–temperature conditions with region-specific support vector regression (SVR), Gaussian process regression (GPR), and bagged ensemble trees (BET) to estimate the maximum-power-point reference voltage. The predicted voltage is supplied to a proportional–integral–derivative (PID)-controlled boost converter, and closed-loop performance is evaluated in MATLAB R2024/Simulink under changing irradiance, temperature, and load. Under the original evaluation protocol, two-cluster K-means—BET achieved the lowest MAE among the K-means prediction configurations, whereas integrated-energy rankings did not consistently follow voltage-prediction rankings. An additional leakage-controlled assessment used 70% of data for training and 30% for independent test observations, with clustering, standardization, and five-fold cross-validated Bayesian hyperparameter optimization performed using training observations only. In this stricter comparison, unclustered SVR achieved the lowest overall MAE, while FCM with three clusters improved BET MAE by approximately 9.7%. These results show that clustering benefits depend on the regression model and evaluation protocol. The closed-loop energy findings apply to the original simulated configurations; the new strict hold-out models were not separately tested in closed-loop simulation. Hardware implementation and broader-dataset validation remain future work.</jats:p>

doi:10.1057/s41267-026-00914-2.title: Simulating competitive collocation strategies with deep reinforcement learning
doi:10.1057/s41267-026-00914-2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper introduces a simulation model based on deep reinforcement learning to study competitive collocation strategies of two internationalizing firms. Drawing on the strategic interaction and competitive collocation literature in IB, we explore the factors determining the performance-optimizing degree of collocation in market-seeking internationalization for a duopoly in product markets. Our simulation suggests that a high degree of collocation between the two firms is optimal in many circumstances. Whereas mid-to-high levels of collocation are driven by low competitive intensity, low entry barriers, low home-market size, and high market-size variation, complete collocation emerges under high competitive intensity, low first-mover advantage, and smaller home-market size. High entry barriers, combined with low variation in market size and strong liabilities of foreignness, drive the opposite case of complete mutual avoidance. A key takeaway from the simulation is a focus on the competing firm in global expansion: in many cases, it becomes key to limit the rival’s growth options and to enter key markets before access becomes more restricted. We discuss the possibilities of using computer-simulation-based approaches to theorizing on internationalization.</jats:p>

doi:10.1111/exsy.70457.title: Heterophily‐Aware Motif‐Guided Contrastive Learning for Robust Social Recommendation
doi:10.1111/exsy.70457.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The homophily principle serves as the core foundation of graph neural network (GNN) based social recommendation, which assumes socially connected users share similar preferences and enables neighbourhood aggregation for user representation learning. Most existing methods directly aggregate information from original social graphs, but this strategy is severely suboptimal due to the prevalent low preference‐aware homophily in real‐world social networks. We further reveal that nonpreference‐driven social connections introduce massive noise into GNN aggregation, leading to representation degradation, over‐smoothing and even performance decline. Existing efforts mostly focus on individual subproblems of social denoising, high‐order modelling or representation enhancement and fail to provide a systematic solution for these cascading challenges. In this paper, we propose H2Rec, a heterophily‐aware motif‐guided contrastive learning framework for low‐homophily social recommendation. It integrates a dual‐branch social aggregation module, a homophily‐enhanced contrastive alignment objective and a user‐adaptive fusion mechanism to suppress noise and learn robust user representations end‐to‐end. Extensive experiments on real‐world benchmarks show that H2Rec significantly outperforms state‐of‐the‐art methods on mainstream evaluation metrics.</jats:p>

doi:10.1177/14613484261498624.title: A novel intelligent fault diagnosis model for planetary gearboxes using wavelet-based synchroextracting transform-based deep learning networks
doi:10.1177/14613484261498624.abstract: <jats:p>Abstract Planetary gearboxes are critical components in rotating machinery where timely fault diagnosis is essential for operational safety and reliability. However, diagnosing faults from vibration signals generated by these complex systems remains challenging due to their non-stationary nature and inherent complexity. To address the challenges, this paper proposes a novel intelligent fault diagnosis model integrating wavelet-based synchroextracting transform (WSET) with a convolutional neural network-bidirectional long short-term memory-black winged kite optimization algorithm-least squares support vector machine (CNN-BiLSTM-BKA-LSSVM) framework. First, the WSET is employed to preprocess raw vibration signals, leveraging the multi-resolution analysis capability of wavelets to suppress noise and extract time-frequency synchronized features, thereby enhancing the separability of fault patterns. Subsequently, a CNN architecture is designed to automatically learn high-level features from the preprocessed signals, capturing local spatial correlations and hierarchical fault signatures. To further improve classification performance, the LSSVM classifier is integrated with the CNN’s feature extraction layer, and its hyperparameters (e.g., kernel parameter and penalty factor) are optimized via the BKA optimization algorithm to enhance the diagnostic performance. Experimental validation is conducted using a planetary gearbox fault dataset under healthy and multiple fault conditions. Comparative results with some existing deep learning methods demonstrate that the proposed intelligent fault model achieves high diagnostic accuracy across all fault types.</jats:p>
