arxiv:2610.23826.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting the role of human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

arxiv:2610.23779.title: Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks
arxiv:2610.23779.abstract: Understanding how stochastic gradient descent learns internal representations in wide neural networks trained on rich target functions is a central problem in machine learning. We study this question in two-layer neural networks learning target functions represented by networks of the same architecture, with arbitrary nonlinearity, and with network width and input dimension growing proportionally. In this regime, standard approaches for describing the learning dynamics require tracking a diverging number of overlaps, which measure correlations between learned and target features, leaving no obvious description in terms of a few order parameters. Here, we develop a mesoscopic description of learning by characterizing the distribution of overlaps. In the early stages of learning, we find that a Gaussian description of overlap statistics reduces the learning dynamics to a few collective variables that track learning of the target function's linear and quadratic components. We then estimate the timescale of specialization, when Gaussian closure breaks down and individual learned features begin to strongly correlate with specific target features. We find that specialization in extensive-rank networks is accelerated via a quadratic shielding mechanism, whereby learning the linear and quadratic components of the target function filters gradient fluctuations. We finally describe how the activation function determines the pattern of specialization and characterize the subsequent refinement of learned features. Together, these results show how collective learning gives way to individual feature discovery and clarify when learning in large neural networks admits a simple statistical description.

arxiv:2610.23703.title: Blitz: Accelerating the Diffusion Modules of AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2
arxiv:2610.23703.abstract: Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.

arxiv:2610.23650.title: JAXtari: High-Throughput and Easy-to-Modify Arcade Learning Environment
arxiv:2610.23650.abstract: The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) has been a cornerstone of Deep Reinforcement Learning research, providing a standardized benchmark for evaluating general agents. However, its lack of native support for object-extraction and environment modification restricts research into evaluating whether agents learn robust causal models or rely on brittle visual heuristics. Furthermore, the ALE's dependence on CPU-based emulation creates a significant bottleneck in modern GPU-accelerated training pipelines, limiting both experimental scale and iteration frequency. In this work, we introduce JAXtari, an open-source, high-performance reimplementation of Atari 2600 environments. By leveraging massive GPU parallelization, JAXtari allows PPO agents to finish training on 100M environment steps on a single A100-GPU in under an hour. Beyond speed, it provides object-centric observations and a flexible modification system, allowing researchers to, e.g. develop neuro-symbolic methods or discover novel shortcuts and subsequently train and adapt their agents rapidly, sometimes in only minutes.

arxiv:2610.23222.title: qGAMMA: A Framework for Optimal DNN Mapping on Multi-Precision Accelerators
arxiv:2610.23222.abstract: This work describes qGAMMA, a flexible framework for exploring and optimizing the mapping of mixed-precision Deep Neural Network (DNN) models onto general-purpose spatial accelerators that support a range of fixed- and floating-point precisions. qGAMMA navigates the design space using a domain-specific genetic algorithm and an analytical performance model based on hardware synthesis results. The framework identifies the optimal mapping and accelerator configuration that minimizes target metrics. Extensive evaluations across DNN workloads show that qGAMMA offers valuable insights for designing mixed-precision applications, enabling better trade-offs between performance, energy efficiency, and resource utilization.

arxiv:2610.23047.title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
arxiv:2610.23047.abstract: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.

arxiv:2610.22811.title: Replay Pruning and Few-Bit Integer Inference for Hardware-Efficient Speed-Sign Recognition
arxiv:2610.22811.abstract: Speed-limit sign recognition on an automotive camera system-on-chip (SoC) must fit a detector and a classifier (the reader) into the memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets of the device. In our two-stage recognizer, the detector, a YOLO-family network with ReLU and hard-sigmoid operators, is compressed by channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade identifies the channels to remove, the recorded deletions are replayed on the original task-trained network, the parent, and one continuous knowledge-distillation recovery follows. On a YOLOv5n, replay removes 60.3% of the parameters at the accuracy of the parent and, in validation mAP50-95 over five matched seeds, outperforms iterative pruning and training from scratch, and its per-step variant (per-step replay) is the most accurate pruning method. On a YOLOv8n, replay and per-step replay outperform every other method and the unpruned parent. The reader, a five-layer CNN with 18k parameters, and the post-processing of the YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n heads use integer arithmetic only. With 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W4A8), the reader matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory, and an executable streaming model reproduces the INT8 class predictions of its runtime on all 9,850 test crops. On a Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only in the implicit formulation of TensorRT, and the replay detector runs fastest on the deep-learning accelerator (DLA). Trained on public data only, the combined system of 0.72 M parameters recognizes 95.2% of the signs of a held-out automotive camera at 90% precision and 94 frames per second.

arxiv:2610.22603.title: At the Limits of Computability: Steps Towards Autonomous AI Discovery on the Busy Beaver Frontier
arxiv:2610.22603.abstract: Recent breakthroughs in AI for mathematics---ranging from Olympiad medal performances to resolving long-standing open conjectures---have rapidly expanded what automated systems can achieve. Yet these successes primarily concern predefined, human-formulated problems, leaving open how AI systems can autonomously uncover mathematical structure and formulate new questions. To push beyond static challenges, we explore the Busy Beaver (BB) domain, an uncomputable frontier that is fundamentally open-ended. Because no algorithm can compute the Busy Beaver number $\mathrm{BB}(n)$ for every $n$, this domain provides a natural setting for sustained exploration through mathematical conjecture and proof. In this paper, we introduce a Gemini-based agentic pipeline that automatically discovers accelerations of Turing machines, expressed as compact mathematical rules summarizing many execution steps. Our system integrates pattern recognition, automated conjecturing, informal mathematical reasoning, and formal theorem proving in Lean. With this framework, our system autonomously discovered and formally verified novel Collatz-like accelerations for eleven machines in $\mathrm{BB}(6)$. Subject to community acceptance, we provisionally classify these machines as Cryptids, namely machines whose blank-tape executions admit exact, compact mathematical descriptions but whose halting behavior remains unresolved. These results advance the analysis of $\mathrm{BB}(6)$ holdouts on the Busy Beaver frontier and demonstrate the potential of autonomous AI systems for open-ended mathematical discovery in fundamental computer science.

arxiv:2610.22543.title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction
arxiv:2610.22543.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at 92-100% of positions, but not which position comes next. Based on this observation, we introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), which learns to predict this order. A 0.62M-parameter model reads only the target's output distributions and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, and the target verifies all of them in a single pass by checking whether each equals its own next state. On the verification side, our analysis shows that prior block-diffusion verification approaches either assume $T=0$ or a sequential proposal interface. To support tree-based speculation at any temperature, we propose using coupled-noise match verification for diffusion blocks, following shared-Gumbel-noise coupling approaches. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to 6.8x and reaches up to 3.2x the throughput of standard decoding, beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that the learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT-dLLM/

arxiv:2610.22436.title: Generative adversarial networks with Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification for structural health monitoring: Fibre Bragg grating data augmentation comparison in Hawk T1A aircraft
arxiv:2610.22436.abstract: The signal generation capabilities of a novel data augmentation framework are examined in aerospace structures. First, the framework learns class-conditional temporal and spectral characteristics of the measured structural responses. It uses conditional generative adversarial network training and Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification as a Bayesian approximation. This step enables stochastic signal synthesis and uncertainty quantification. Second, the generated responses are rigorously compared against experimental measurements across time, frequency, uncertainty, variability, and feature domains to assess physical realism, statistical consistency, and distributional fidelity. Finally, the synthetic data are evaluated to determine whether they should be incorporated into a supervised damage classification workflow. The framework is validated on the full-scale benchmark dataset from a BAE Systems Hawk T1A aircraft tested at the University of Sheffield's Structural Dynamics Laboratory for Verification and Validation. The test involves acceleration, fibre Bragg grating strain, and nonlinear dynamic response measurements. The results demonstrate that the model accurately captures dominant structural dynamics, it guides on signal use for classification improvement based on uncertainty characteristics, and it provides meaningful uncertainty estimates linked to signal complexity and excitation characteristics. Importantly, the framework offers a realistic generative modelling plan as a robust digital twin component for data-driven structural health monitoring, supporting resilient decision-making for condition assessment in safety-critical aerospace systems.

arxiv:2610.22432.title: An Adaptive-Horizon Graph Neural Operator for coupled surrogate morphodynamic modelling
arxiv:2610.22432.abstract: Morphodynamic simulations require repeated coupling between hydrodynamic solvers, sediment transport modules, and bed updating. For long duration, multi-scenario simulations on large unstructured meshes, such coupling is computationally demanding. This study proposes an Adaptive-Horizon Graph Neural Operator (AH-GNO) that formulates bed evolution as a graph operator learning problem from recent hydrodynamic and topographic states to predict future bed elevation increments. The model operates directly on the native unstructured meshes. The approach integrates area-weighted graph learning, historical state selection, and forecast horizon estimation, allowing the effective history length (K) and update interval (B) to vary with the evolving flow and bed state. Using Telemac2D/GAIA solutions as supervised numerical references, the framework is evaluated on the official Bump and Yen bend benchmarks and on a field-scale application (Waiho River, New Zealand). Results show that the AH-GNO reproduces the main patterns of bedform migration, bend-scale erosion and deposition, and localized bed adjustment. Across the three cases, the tested CPU-GPU deployment reduced post-training bed-update workflow time from 12~1204 s with GAIA to 0.08~3.34 s with AH-GNO. This improvement corresponds to deployment-specific accelerations of approximately 150~360 times relative to 4-core GAIA CPU configurations, and with 105~186 times gains for 20-core CPU configurations. These results suggest that, while retaining hydrodynamic feedback from TELEMAC-2D, a learned operator for bed updating can provide an efficient acceleration component for morphodynamic scenario analysis and rapid coupled simulation.

arxiv:2610.22431.title: GPU-Accelerated Robust MA--RIS Pre-Optimization for Communication and Target Illumination
arxiv:2610.22431.abstract: Movable antennas (MAs) and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) offer strong spatial control for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), but repeatedly adapting MA positions and RIS phases to each channel realization can be impractical. This letter develops a GPU-accelerated robust pre-optimization framework that jointly selects slow-timescale MA geometry and RIS phases and returns a reusable Pareto set balancing expected worst-user rate and transmit-side worst-target illumination. The illumination objective measures directional transmitted power rather than complete echo-detection or parameter-estimation performance. The proposed Regime-Aware Multiobjective Pre-optimization (RAMP) preserves regime-specific Pareto populations, regulates cross-regime mating using Pareto-survival feedback, and constructs a worst-regime robust archive. Numerical results demonstrate competitive robust Pareto quality against the considered evolutionary baselines while avoiding online physical re-optimization.

arxiv:2610.22377.title: Memory Bandwidth, Not FLOPs: Profiling and Accelerating Query-Based Segmentation Decoders on Edge GPUs
arxiv:2610.22377.abstract: Query-based segmentation models achieve strong performance even under real-time inference on workstation GPUs. On edge devices, however, we show their transformer decoders are deeply memory-bandwidth-bound, a bottleneck invisible to standard FLOP analysis that worsens with input resolution and limited DRAM bandwidth. An FP16 roofline analysis with tensor-core GEMMs active and hardware DRAM counters shows that the non-tensor-core aggregates of FastInst and Mask2Former reach only $2.5\%$ to $6\%$ of the CUDA-core ridge yet account for $53\%$ to $70\%$ of decoder time and $61\%$ to $71\%$ of decoder bytes. The largest individual kernels sustain up to $90\%$ of nominal peak DRAM bandwidth, effectively saturating the memory bus. The bottleneck is therefore not primarily low GEMM intensity, but cross-kernel activation traffic. CompactInst addresses this bottleneck using parameter-free spatial pooling at $4{\times}$, which reduces the bytes moved within the transformer decoder, while a two-convolution refinement head recovers spatial detail. Under TensorRT FP16 on Jetson Orin Nano, CompactInst delivers decoder speedups from $2.35{\times}$ to $4.74{\times}$ and model speedups from $1.57{\times}$ to $2.62{\times}$ as input resolution grows, while closely matching accuracy ($-0.4$ AP on COCO val2017, $+0.2$ AP on Cityscapes test). A heavier variant with $2.57{\times}$ more decoder FLOPs still runs its decoder $1.74{\times}$ faster on the most bandwidth-constrained device, confirming at the deployment level that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, govern latency.

arxiv:2610.23783.title: Sampling the XY model with an attention-based neural network
arxiv:2610.23783.abstract: We present a transformer-based variational autoregressive network for sampling lattice systems with continuous degrees of freedom and apply it to the two-dimensional XY model near the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition. The architecture is combined with physics-informed ingredients: locality-informed attention and approximate probabilities. The resulting sampler significantly outperforms existing neural samplers. We train the model on lattices up to $96\times96$, verify with a mode-dropping estimator that no parts of the configuration space are missed, and reproduce the energy, magnetization and helicity modulus obtained with the traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm.

arxiv:2610.22382.title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
arxiv:2610.22382.abstract: LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.

doi:10.5281/zenodo.22759465.title: From Notebook to Control Room: Reproducible MLOps for Accelerator Digital Twins
doi:10.5281/zenodo.22759465.abstract: Scientific user facilities like the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS), the world’s brightest X-ray free-electron laser at the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, require rapid, continuous control adjustments to maximize beam time and experimental throughput. Machine Learning (ML) surrogate models can help operators navigate complex parameter spaces, but only if those models can be deployed reliably and updated without disrupting operations. How do you reliably and sustainably move ML models from various researchers’ training environments into a facility production system? In this talk, we present a reproducible MLOps framework that addresses this challenge in the context of digital twin deployments for online accelerator control. We discuss how we standardized the Kubernetes-based deployment of digital twins and ML inference services by prioritizing reproducibility across environments through container-based packaging, rigorous model versioning and experiment tracking integrated into the deployment pipeline, minimal boilerplate templates so domain scientists can onboard models without DevOps expertise, and flexible configuration to adapt across diverse control scenarios. The framework is built around a software ecosystem that provides abstraction layers to wrap simulator-specific backends (PyTorch-based neural network surrogates and physics simulations) behind a common Python API. This design means the deployment infrastructure generalizes across model types rather than being tied to any single simulation code or modeling approach. The same model instance can be used directly in Python-native workflows for development and testing, or deployed as a process variable server integrated with existing control system infrastructure, without changes to the underlying model code. This approach demonstrates how such software infrastructure can lower the barrier to AI integration in research facilities, allowing scientists to focus on model development while RSEs maintain the reliability, observability, and sustainability of the deployment stack. We discuss lessons learned, remaining challenges around hybrid ML-simulation system models, and paths toward tooling that is shareable across facilities.
doi:10.5281/zenodo.22759465.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32084.title: Traditional Machine Learning versus Large Language Models for Predicting Ship Turnaround Times at Brazilian Ports
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32084.abstract: <jats:p>Predicting ship turnaround time at ports is an operationally valuable regression problem on heterogeneous, text-rich tabular data. We ask whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can match purpose-built Machine Learning (ML) on this task, using a leakage-controlled pipeline over seven years of Brazilian (ANTAQ) data. On a fixed 200-berthing test set, with 20 seeds and seed-paired statistics (Wilcoxon, Cohen’s d), we compare five families that read the same cases: classical ML on engineered tabular features plus multilingual sentence embeddings; frontier LLMs (Qwen3-32B, DeepSeek-V3) prompted zero-, 5and 20-shot; a small generative LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B) fine-tuned on 100–6000 serialized records; an encoder with a regression head fine-tuned on 100–12000 records; and a tabular foundation model (TabFM) reading the raw table in-context. Tuned XGBoost attains R2 ≈ 0.73. Every prompted configuration stays at R2 ≤ 0 and in-context examples do not help; generative fine-tuning barely clears zero, reaching only R2 ≈ 0.10 at 6000 examples. The encoder is the only text regime to rise substantially above R2 = 0, reaching ≈ 0.43 at 12000 examples yet still trailing all ML. In contrast, TabFM, with no task training, matches or beats a data-matched XGBoost at every budget (100–6000; R2 up to ≈ 0.60), leading the low-data regime, though full-data XGBoost still wins and TabFM is far costlier at inference. The predictive signal is tabular, not textual: text-only LLMs miss it, whereas a tabular foundation model recovers it in-context and engineered boosting wins at scale.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32084.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32067.title: PLC-Embedded Virtual Pressure Sensor with Continual Learning for Mining Tailings Pumping
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32067.abstract: <jats:p>Reliable pressure measurement in mining tailings pipelines is essential for safe and efficient operation, but physical sensors are prone to failures. This work proposes a virtual pressure sensor based on a compact LSTM network embedded in a PLC. Non-stationary data and hardware constraints introduce covariate shift and catastrophic forgetting in continuous learning. Three training strategies are compared: static dataset (A1), sequential learning without mitigation (A2), and learning with experience replay and targeted oversampling (A3). Results show that A2 suffers severe degradation (R2 = 0.48), while A3 achieves the best performance (RMSE = 0.36 bar, R2 = 0.94) without increasing inference cost. The model is validated in a SIMATIC PCS 7 environment, confirming real-time feasibility with 517 parameters.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32067.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32014.title: Exploring Problem Statements and Source Code Submissions in Online Judges via 2D Embedding Projections
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32014.abstract: <jats:p>Online Judges (OJs) are widely used as supporting tools in computer programming courses. These platforms store large collections of problem statements and student code submissions, offering rich opportunities for analyzing behaviors and performance patterns. However, their built-in analytics capabilities are limited, making systematic data exploration difficult. In this paper, we investigate how embeddings of problem statements and student source code, combined with multidimensional projection techniques, can support exploratory analysis of student activity. We evaluate multiple embedding models for Portuguese problem statements, as well as for source code, using metrics such as Neighborhood Preservation, Trustworthiness, Spearman correlation, and Stress. Our results indicate that ModernBERT-PT and GraphCodeBERT are the most suitable embeddings for Portuguese statements and source code, respectively. Regarding projection methods, t-SNE outperformed UMAP and TriMap in preserving local structure. Two case studies illustrate the practical value of the approach, showing how projections reveal groups of students with similar topic preferences and highlight potentially suspicious submissions.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32014.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.1108/jcms-06-2026-0114.title: Tail-risk-constrained portfolio optimization with cluster pre-selection and machine learning: risk-adjusted evidence from the S&P 500
doi:10.1108/jcms-06-2026-0114.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Standard Gaussian risk frameworks underestimate extreme joint losses in large equity universes, exposing investors to unbudgeted drawdowns. This article develops and tests a portfolio-construction pipeline that disciplines tail risk while exploiting forward-looking return signals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The four-stage pipeline integrates a rolling tail-index (Hill) filter, cluster pre-selection, a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) risk-parity optimizer with Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) and extreme value theory (EVT) marginals and a Student-t copula, and an eight-classifier machine-learning ensemble that reallocates weights within the risk budget. It is tested on S&P 500 constituents across 75 monthly walk-forward windows (January 2020–January 2026), net of transaction costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among twelve strategies, the pipeline delivers the highest Sharpe ratio (1.106) and monthly win rate (76.0%), surpassing risk parity, Hierarchical Risk Parity and the Gaussian CVaR specification it generalizes; block-bootstrap inference confirms its advantage over passive exposure (resampled mean Sharpe 1.316). Risk parity accumulates greater terminal wealth, a trade-off, since tail constraints curb high-momentum exposure in bull markets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis is limited to S&P 500 constituents and a January 2020–January 2026 evaluation period. Results may differ in other asset classes, international markets or under alternative transaction-cost assumptions. Future research could examine adaptive clustering schemes, alternative dependence structures and real-time implementation constraints.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For investors prioritizing risk-adjusted efficiency over cumulative wealth, the framework is a transparent capital-allocation tool whose tail discipline holds at roughly 97 basis points annually.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To the authors' knowledge, this is the first to combine tail-index screening, clustering, GARCH-EVT-copula CVaR optimization and a machine-learning overlay within one framework, jointly addressing the dimensionality, distributional misspecification and information-neglect problems that defeat these tools in isolation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.61669/001c.172640.title: From Chaos to Consistency: A Human-Centered Framework for AI-supported Assessment at a Mission-Driven Liberal Arts College
doi:10.61669/001c.172640.abstract: <jats:p>This practitioner inquiry reports on a pilot at a small Catholic liberal arts college that used generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-supported tools to help faculty complete program-assessment documentation during a structured Education Day. Grounded in Catholic social teaching and human-centered AI principles, the pilot tested a framework organized around human judgment, ethical stewardship, and formative human-AI partnership. Survey results from the pilot cohort (N = 10; item-level valid responses varied) showed strong faculty endorsement, including unanimous agreement that the process deepened thinking about evidence of student learning and unanimous intent to use AI-supported tools in future cycles. Qualitative findings identified five themes: efficiency and cognitive scaffolding, human-in-the-loop validation, platform reliability and trust, data governance, and institutional support infrastructure. Findings suggest that mission-driven institutions can integrate AI into assessment responsibly when faculty formation, verification checkpoints, and governance structures precede broad implementation.</jats:p>
doi:10.61669/001c.172640.venue: Intersection: A Journal at the Intersection of Assessment and Learning

doi:10.68079/moglkx.2026.3.08.title: 智能时代人机协作中的角色重塑：边界演化、行为适应与非标准化判断力
doi:10.68079/moglkx.2026.3.08.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has profoundly reshaped human-machine collaboration within organizations.The traditional "substitution-augmentation" dual framework fails to explain a practical paradox: sophisticated creative work can be imitated by algorithms, while low-threshold emotional labor cannot be replaced by machines.This raises two research questions concerning the essence and dynamic evolution of human-machine collaboration boundaries.From the perspective of organizational behavior and integrating multidisciplinary theories, this paper constructs the theoretical framework of the algorithmizability boundary.The research indicates that the boundary is jointly determined by three dimensions, namely rule clarity, data completeness and value embeddedness, and evolves continuously within the closed loop of technology, task, subject and institution.Based on case analyses of four major industries, this paper verifies the effectiveness of the four-dimensional [作者简介] 杨丽茵，女，澳门科技大学商学院工商管理专业博士生，2766649066@qq.com。《澳门管理科学》•企业管理 2026 年第 3 期 -93 -co-evolution model.The study finds that the core value of human beings in the intelligent era lies in non-standardized judgment integrating technical understanding, experience accumulation and empathy, whose essence is the creativity to produce original solutions in complex scenarios.This research provides comprehensive theoretical and practical guidance for organizational strategy, human resource management and leadership transformation, facilitating the shift of management paradigms from efficiency optimization to creativity stimulation.

doi:10.3389/fenvs.2026.1939822.title: Advanced meteorological modeling framework integrating quantum computing and machine learning for hurricane track prediction beyond traditional forecasting limitations
doi:10.3389/fenvs.2026.1939822.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Accurate prediction of hurricane tracks, intensity, and rapid intensification remains a major challenge in meteorological forecasting. This study investigates whether a hybrid quantum-classical approach, called the Quantum-Enhanced Neural Network (QENN), can improve tropical cyclone prediction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>QENN combines atmospheric features from multiple sources with a four-layer, 50-qubit variational circuit, grouped Pauli measurements, and a classical temporal prediction model. The evaluation included 847 Atlantic tropical cyclones recorded between 1980 and 2024. Separate hurricane-disjoint partitions were used for model development, validation, testing, and the 2024 holdout evaluation. Model reliability was further examined through ten random-seed runs, storm-level bootstrap confidence intervals, calibration analysis, comparisons with recent forecasting models, and a width-matched classical ablation study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On the locked 2016–2023 test set, QENN achieved a 120-h track mean absolute error of 83.7 km (95% confidence interval [CI]: 78.9–88.6 km), compared with 312.0 km (95% CI: 299.6–325.1 km) for the operational classical ensemble, representing a 73.2% reduction in relative error. For rapid-intensification prediction, QENN achieved a balanced accuracy of 94.7% (95% CI: 91.2%–97.1%), while the classical baseline achieved 67.3%. The median wall-clock time was 50.0 min for QENN and 210.0 min for the classical ensemble, equivalent to a 4.20-fold speed-up and a 76.2% reduction in runtime. In the 2024 holdout evaluation, which included six storms, the mean landfall-position error was 45 km (95% CI: 39–51 km).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results indicate that quantum-enhanced correlation features may improve forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency within the proposed experimental framework. However, the runtime comparison does not establish a formal quantum computational advantage. Further testing under operational forecasting conditions and validation on quantum hardware are needed to assess the reliability, generalizability, and practical value of the approach.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10941201/v1.title: Contour-free multi-instance learning versus conventional CT features for preoperative Ki-67 stratification in gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumors: a retrospective comparison
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10941201/v1.abstract: Background : Manual tumor contouring adds a separate preprocessing step to CT-based prediction. We therefore evaluated whether complete-series multiinstance learning (MIL) could perform preoperative Ki-67 stratification from dual-phase CT without tumor contours and provide greater discrimination than conventional CT features. Methods : This retrospective study included 61 patients. Ki-67 cutoffs of 5%, 8%, and 10% defined three cutoff-specific tasks. Patients whose reported Ki-67 interval spanned a cutoff were excluded only from the corresponding task. Twenty-one conventional variables were analyzed with two conventional models, and frozen ResNet-18 features from the complete arterial and venous phase series were analyzed separately with five MIL methods. Four prespecified equal-logit fusion combinations were evaluated. Patient-level stratified fivefold cross-validation was repeated 10 times. Assessment comprised AUROC, AUPRC, calibration assessment, decision-curve analysis, paired bootstrap comparisons with Holm correction, and a post-training attention audit. Results : The three tasks included 59, 54, and 56 patients, with 41, 26, and 15 positive cases. The highest AUROCs were 0.645 (95% CI, 0.485–0.781) at 5%, 0.646 (95% CI, 0.496–0.788) at 8%, and 0.605 (95% CI, 0.442–0.753) at 10%. The maximum AUPRCs at 5%, 8%, and 10% were 0.822, 0.637, and 0.346. Every AUROC confidence interval included 0.5, and no comparison among the prespecified individual models or between fusion and its components remained significant after Holm correction. In the attention audit, 34 of 60 tests remained significant after global Holm correction, with 21 estimates above and 13 below their prespecified references. Conclusions : Complete-series MIL was applied separately to arterial and venous CT series for cutoff-specific Ki-67 stratification and did not require tumor contour inputs. It showed no clear discrimination advantage over conventional CT features in this cohort. External validation and direct assessment of annotation burden are required before clinical use.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10941201/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1885067.title: Evaluating the associations of learning environment with student engagement and learning gains among undergraduate students at a medical university in western China
doi:10.3389/fpubh.2026.1885067.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As quality improvement in medical education increasingly focuses on the learning processes that students actually experience, it is important to clarify which learning-environment domains are most closely associated with student engagement and how engagement relates to learning gains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this pooled repeated cross-sectional study, we analyzed 11,717 student responses from four administrations (2021–2024) of the National College Student Survey among undergraduate students at a medical university in western China. The learning environment was assessed across five domains: classroom teaching quality, facilities and resources, developmental support, interpersonal support, and teaching administration. Student engagement was measured across behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions. Learning gains were assessed across six domains. Hierarchical multiple linear regression, cross-sectional indirect association analysis, year-stratified analyses, and k-means clustering were used to examine associations among perceived learning environment, engagement, and learning gains and to explore heterogeneity among students.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Survey year and background characteristics explained only 1.5–4.0% of the variance in engagement, whereas the five learning-environment domains explained an additional 22.5–27.6%. Classroom teaching quality showed the largest positive associations with behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, which were statistically significant in every survey wave, and developmental support was also positively associated with all three dimensions. Engagement statistically accounted for 31.93% of the cross-sectional association between perceived learning environment and learning gains (total indirect association = 0.234; total association = 0.734). Person-centered analysis identified a convergent-low profile comprising 37.2% of students, whose scores on perceived learning environment, engagement, and learning gains were all below the sample average; background characteristics were only weakly associated with membership in the three profiles (Cramér’s
                      <jats:italic>V</jats:italic>
                      ≤ 0.063).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that, in improving educational quality, medical universities should give greater attention to the classroom teaching and developmental support processes that students experience directly in their everyday learning, and should incorporate student engagement and learning experiences into routine, ongoing quality monitoring alongside conventional outcome assessment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11394067/v1.title: Sentiment Classification of Saudi Stock Market Tweets: Lexicon-Based Weak Supervision, Classical Machine Learning, and Zero-Shot Open-Source Large Language Models
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11394067/v1.abstract: Social media platforms have become a rich, real-time source of investor opinion, yet Arabic-language financial text remains under-studied, and much applied work validates classifiers against labels produced by the very rules they later learn to imitate. This study examines sentiment classification of 1,000 Arabic tweets about companies listed on the Saudi Exchange (Tadawul), issued by 41 accounts. Using a domain lexicon of 180 financial terms, tweets were assigned positive, negative or neutral labels, and four classical models (Multinomial Naïve Bayes, Logistic Regression, Random Forest and a linear Support Vector Machine) were trained on TF-IDF features. Under stratified five-fold cross-validation the linear SVM reproduced the lexicon labels with an accuracy of 0.861 and a macro-F1 of 0.819, whereas Naïve Bayes reached only 0.446 macro-F1. We then added a zero-shot open-source large language model (LLM), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run locally with 4-bit quantisation and no task-specific training. Its agreement with the lexicon labels was low (accuracy 0.376, macro-F1 0.401, Cohen’s κ = 0.19), driven by a strong tendency to label lexicon-neutral tweets, such as dividend declarations and earnings announcements, as positive. A diagnostic analysis showed that this disagreement reflects, to a large extent, weaknesses in the lexicon labels: the lexicon terms were not subjected to the same orthographic normalisation as the tweets, so only 42.4% of tweets matched any term; after correcting this, the match rate rose to 67.8%, 30% of labels changed, and LLM–lexicon agreement rose to 57.5% (κ = 0.31). We conclude that high accuracy against rule-derived labels demonstrates label reproduction rather than sentiment understanding, that zero-shot LLMs offer a label-free, domain-aware alternative whose outputs differ systematically from lexicon rules, and that a human-annotated reference set is indispensable for establishing which is correct. We release the pipeline, prompt and an annotation protocol to support such validation.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11394067/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.74s.34.title: Learning Task-Preserving Encoded Representations for Privacy-Sensitive Data Outsourcing
doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.74s.34.abstract: This paper addresses a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning: how to train accurate cloud-hosted models on sensitive data without ever exposing that data to the cloud.It introduces LTPER (Learning Task-Preserving Encoded Representations), a two-zone framework in which a Supervised Residual Autoencoder (SRAE) is trained entirely on the data owner's local hardware and only the resulting encoded artifact Ψ is forwarded to the cloud for downstream model training.The encoder is optimized simultaneously under four objectives designed to work in concert: a reconstruction term that anchors the encoding to input geometry, a multi-layer classification term that enforces task relevance at every encoder depth, a center loss that tightens intra-class clusters, and a PCA cosine alignment term that aligns the encoding topology with the principal variance directions of the original data.This paper further introduces a layer-stacking strategy that concatenates encoder outputs from all depth levels into a single 480-dimensional vector, recovering multi-scale structure that single-bottleneck approaches discard.LTPER is validated on five benchmark datasets spanning images, medical scans, gene-expression arrays, and multi-omics records.The encodings match or exceed unprotected baselines across four classifier families while resisting reconstruction attacks.This paper also provides a four-scenario adversary analysis that formally establishes the security boundaries of the proposed system.
doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.74s.34.venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology

doi:10.4271/2026-99-2936.title: Trust-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for Access Control in Satellite Communication Systems
doi:10.4271/2026-99-2936.abstract:
<jats:p><div class="section abstract">
                <div class="htmlview paragraph">The rapid evolution of satellite communication systems enables direct network
                    access for terrestrial users via portable devices, but also introduces critical
                    security challenges in access control. In particular, identity hijacking attacks
                    allow malicious users to exploit legitimate access channels, leading to
                    inefficient occupation of scarce satellite resources. Existing approaches mainly
                    depend on trust evaluation or heuristic-based decision strategies, which are
                    inadequate for adapting to dynamic environments. To address this issue, this
                    paper proposes a trust-aware deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework for
                    satellite access control, which jointly considers user behavior evaluation and
                    decision optimization. Specifically, a Bayesian trust evaluation model is first
                    developed to quantify the credibility of user behavior by incorporating
                    historical interaction records as prior information. Unlike conventional static
                    trust schemes, an adaptive mechanism is introduced to enhance sensitivity to
                    behavioral dynamics. Building upon the trust assessment, the satellite access
                    process is formulated as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where system states
                    integrate channel conditions, user trust levels, and service demands. A Deep
                    Q-Network (DQN) is then employed to learn optimal admission and scheduling
                    policies that maximize long-term system utility under resource constraints.
                    Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly
                    outperforms conventional greedy and threshold-based strategies. In particular,
                    it effectively mitigates the impact of malicious behaviors and improves system
                    utility by over 80%, while achieving more efficient resource utilization in
                    dynamic environments.</div>
            </div></jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10122799/v1.title: Machine translation of modern Chinese poetry into Japanese: A comparative evaluation of LLMs, neural machine translation systems, and prompt strategies
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10122799/v1.abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has renewed interest in the role of machine translation (MT) in literary contexts, yet its applicability to poetry translation remains insufficiently understood. This study examines the Chinese-to-Japanese MT of modern Chinese poetry by comparing two LLM-based systems, ChatGPT and DeepSeek, with two widely used online NMT-based systems, Google Translate and DeepL. It further investigates how prompt strategy affects LLM-based poetry translation. Twelve poems were selected from Yu Xiuhua’s 2024 poetry collection Houshan Huakai ( Flowers Blooming on the Back Hill ) through stratified random sampling. The resulting translations were evaluated by eight expert raters using a multidimensional human evaluation framework covering fidelity, fluency, language style, machine-translation style, and overall quality. Linear mixed-effects models were used to account for variation across raters and source poems. The results show that, under the minimal prompt condition, the LLM-based systems received higher ratings than the online NMT-based systems in fidelity, fluency, language style, and overall quality, and showed fewer machine-translation traces. The effect of prompt strategy was model-dependent: the explanatory prompt improved DeepSeek’s performance in several dimensions, but did not improve ChatGPT’s performance. Under the explanatory prompt condition, no statistically significant differences were found between ChatGPT and DeepSeek, suggesting a degree of prompt-induced convergence in evaluated translation quality. These findings indicate that LLM-based poetry translation should be understood as an interaction between model characteristics and prompt design, and that machine-translated poetry should be evaluated beyond fluency and semantic accuracy, with closer attention to poetic style and machine-translation traces.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10122799/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.35378/gujs.1767589.title: Predictive Modeling of Heart Disease with Machine Learning Algorithms
doi:10.35378/gujs.1767589.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Machine learning is recognized as one of the fastest-growing technologies and is widely applied across various fields. The healthcare sector benefits significantly from advances in this technology. In recent years, the prevalence of heart attacks and heart failure has increased across different age groups. Heart failure is a condition in which the heart is unable to deliver sufficient blood to meet the body's metabolic demands and may arise from various underlying causes. A dataset comprising 918 records was analyzed, with missing values addressed, outliers handled, and appropriate preprocessing procedures applied. The dataset was then classified using eleven machine learning algorithms, with feature standardization applied selectively to scale-sensitive models. GridSearchCV was used for hyperparameter optimization, and the models were evaluated using standard classification performance metrics.</jats:p>

doi:10.1515/cclm-2026-1514.title: Enhanced detection of bladder cancer using machine learning analysis of routine urinary sediment data
doi:10.1515/cclm-2026-1514.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec id="j_cclm-2026-1514_abs_001">
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Bladder cancer (BC) has a high recurrence rate, requiring invasive procedures such as cystoscopy and histopathological examination. Existing non-invasive methods, including urine cytology, fluorescence
                      <jats:italic>in situ</jats:italic>
                      hybridization (FISH), and tumor markers like nuclear matrix protein 22 (NMP22), have limited sensitivity and specificity. This study assessed the potential of low-cost, non-invasive urine sediment data for BC detection using a machine learning model.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_cclm-2026-1514_abs_002">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Urine sediment data from 1,341 patients (577 with BC and 764 with benign conditions) were obtained using a fully automated urinary particle analyzer (UF-5000). One preoperative sample per patient was included. A soft-voting ensemble model combining random forest and logistic regression was developed. Class imbalance was addressed using the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique, and feature selection was guided by the variance inflation factor. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), balanced accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, with 95 % confidence intervals estimated via bootstrapping. Model stability was evaluated using fivefold cross-validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_cclm-2026-1514_abs_003">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The ensemble model achieved an AUC of 0.89, with a sensitivity of 0.80 and specificity of 0.88. Balanced accuracy was 0.84, and cross-validation demonstrated stable performance (accuracy 0.80). Feature importance analysis identified atypical cells and red blood cells as the most influential predictors, particularly of non-muscle-invasive BC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_cclm-2026-1514_abs_004">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This urine sediment–based, non-invasive approach shows promise for the early detection and monitoring of BC. Its integration into routine clinical workflows may enhance screening efficiency without additional costs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31693.title: Classical Tricks for Better Topics: Can Traditional Text Mining Techniques Improve Generative Topic Modeling?
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31693.abstract: <jats:p>Topic modeling is widely used to discover and organize latent themes in large text collections. While recent embedding-based methods have improved topic discovery by leveraging dense semantic representations, they typically represent topics as lists of keywords, often providing limited insights into the underlying theme. More recently, Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches, such as TopicGPT, have introduced generative topic modeling methods capable of producing human-readable topic labels and descriptions. However, the effectiveness of these methods depends heavily on the quality and representativeness of the documents selected to guide topic generation. In this paper, we propose Core-Periphery Sampling (CPS), a hybrid strategy that combines classical text representation and clustering methods with a TopicGPT-inspired pipeline. CPS selects both central documents and boundary instances that capture transitional and potentially informative cases, providing the generative model with an informed and diverse subset for topic induction. Experimental results show that CPS outperforms random sampling, particularly when the underlying document representation yields well-separable clusters. Although BERTopic remains stronger on clustering-oriented metrics, CPS offers an effective, computationally simple mechanism for guiding LLM-based topic generation via informed document selection, resulting in coherent and contextually grounded topic descriptions.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31693.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.51878/vocational.v6i4.16152.title: PENGARUH MOTIVASI BELAJAR DAN SELF-REGULATED LEARNING TERHADAP HASIL BELAJAR SISWA SMK PADA ELEMEN GAMBAR TEKNIK
doi:10.51878/vocational.v6i4.16152.abstract: <jats:p>Student learning outcomes on the elements of engineering drawing, especially the skill of drawing manual for simple residential plans, are still not optimal. This condition can be seen from the lack of activeness, enthusiasm, perseverance, ability to manage time, and students' independence in completing learning tasks. This condition shows the need to examine internal factors related to learning outcomes, especially learning motivation and self-regulated learning. This study aims to determine the influence of learning motivation on learning outcomes, the influence of self-regulated learning on learning outcomes, and the simultaneous influence of both on student learning outcomes on engineering drawing elements. The research uses a quantitative approach with an ex post facto type of research. The research was carried out at SMK Negeri 3 Jombang with a sample of 70 students of class X DPIB. Data were collected using a learning motivation questionnaire, a self-regulated learning questionnaire, and a learning outcome practice test in the form of drawing a simple residential plan manual. Data analysis was carried out through descriptive statistics, analytical prerequisite tests, and multiple linear regression to test hypotheses partially and simultaneously. The results showed that learning motivation had a positive and significant effect on learning outcomes with a significance value of 0.042 < 0.05. Self-regulated learning also had a positive and significant effect on learning outcomes with a significance value of 0.004 < 0.05. Simultaneously, learning motivation and self-regulated learning had a positive and significant effect on learning outcomes with a significance value of 0.002 < 0.05. The determination coefficient value of 0.473 showed a contribution of 47.3% to learning outcomes. The conclusions of the study showed that learning motivation and self-regulated learning had a significant effect on student learning outcomes in engineering drawing elements.</jats:p>

doi:10.4271/2026-99-2990.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Downlink User Scheduling in LEO Satellite Massive MIMO Systems
doi:10.4271/2026-99-2990.abstract:
<jats:p><div class="section abstract">
                <div class="htmlview paragraph">Low earth orbit (LEO) satellite communication system is expected to play a key
                    role in the 6G wireless networks. Due to the limited communication resource and
                    inter-user interference (IUI), the user equipments (UEs) must be well scheduled
                    to maximize spectral efficiency. However, rapid channel variations and high
                    mobility in LEO system make the conventional user scheduling strategies relying
                    on instantaneous channel state information impractical. To address this
                    challenge, this paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework
                    based on batch normalization in CrossQ algorithm to optimize the downlink user
                    scheduling in a LEO satellite massive multi-input multi-output (MIMO) system.
                    The scheduling task is modeled as a Markov decision process (MDP), where the
                    observation space integrates high-dimensional features including large-scale
                    fading (LSF) coefficients, channel matrix, and temporal features capturing the
                    orbital progress of the satellite. Unlike traditional DRL methods, the
                    CrossQ-based algorithm applies batch normalization (BN) within the critic
                    networks to eliminate the need for slowly-moving target networks, fostering
                    training stability and sample efficiency. A continuous priority score vector is
                    mapped to discrete scheduling decisions through a top-z selection logic,
                    allowing the agent to effectively identify spatially orthogonal user subsets to
                    suppress the IUI. To guide the agent toward the true optimization direction, a
                    differential reward mechanism is designed. Simulation results demonstrate that
                    the proposed CrossQ-based scheduler consistently achieves nearly optimal
                    performance at different signal-to-noise ratios (SNR), reaching at least 91% and
                    94% of the Monte Carlo search ceiling under different user densities. Moreover,
                    the trained model provides scheduling strategy in millisecond inference time,
                    making it a practical and robust solution for future 6G non-terrestrial
                    networks.</div>
            </div></jats:p>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.30418.title: Local Anonymization of Free-Text Robbery Police Reports in Brazilian Portuguese: a Safety-Recall-Oriented Multi-Model Benchmark
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.30418.abstract: <jats:p>Brazilian public-safety agencies release structured crime statistics but withhold the free-text narrative field of police reports, which is rich in modus operandi and contextual information, because it contains personal data protected by the Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD). We address this deadlock for robbery reports with a fully local (on-premise) two-stage anonymization pipeline: a deterministic regular-expression stage for structured personally identifiable information (PII) and a pluggable semantic layer (dedicated NER, local LLMs served by Ollama, union and chained hybrids, and Microsoft Presidio as a system baseline). We contribute (i) an expert-annotated gold standard of 996 robbery narratives, released with the source code; (ii) an entity-level evaluation protocol whose headline metric is safety recall (how much PII actually did not leak), complemented by a re-identification-criticality analysis and bootstrap confidence intervals; and (iii) an empirical benchmark of nine engine configurations quantifying the safety–utility trade-off. The union of spaCy and qwen3:8b over the regex stage reaches the highest macro safety recall (0.986, 95% CI [0.972; 0.994]; micro 0.973) and is the most conservative (highest-recall) option, while qwen3:8b alone gives the best overall balance (safety recall 0.966, precision 0.80, micro-F1 0.826, text retention 96%) and is our recommendation for general use. In this configuration, direct identifiers (names, documents, phones, e-mails) are removed at 99–100%, with residual leakage concentrated in location quasi-identifiers. Safety recall measures PII removal, not residual reidentification risk: these figures bound leakage rather than certify anonymity. We recommend qwen3:8b for general supervised anonymization, and the union when leakage must be minimized, and discuss conditions for replication across Brazilian police forces.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.30418.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.63498/injelps116.title: Total Quality Management (TQM) for reading improvement
doi:10.63498/injelps116.abstract: Aim: This study examined the application of Total Quality Management (TQM) principles in a citizen-centered reading intervention for Grade 3 learners.Specifically, it determined learners' reading levels before and after the intervention, assessed changes in reading performance, explored internal and external stakeholders' perceptions of the implementation, and identified areas for improvement.Methodology: The study employed an action research design using a mixed-methods approach.Participants included 30 Grade 3 learners initially classified at the frustration reading level, four Master Teachers, four Grade 3 teachers, two school principals, 30 parents, and eight Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials.Data were collected through pre-and post-reading assessments and semi-structured interviews.Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, while qualitative data were examined through coding, thematic analysis, and content analysis to identify stakeholder perceptions, implementation challenges, and effective practices.Results: Before the intervention, all 30 learners were classified at the frustration reading level.Following the intervention, all learners progressed to either the instructional or independent reading level.Stakeholder feedback indicated positive perceptions of the intervention, particularly regarding structured implementation, shared responsibility, parental involvement, and community participation.Qualitative findings also indicated improvements in learner motivation, vocabulary development, reading fluency, and comprehension.However, areas for improvement included stakeholder engagement, scheduling and time management, teaching strategies and materials, and learner motivation and incentive strategies.Conclusion: The findings suggest that integrating TQM principles into reading interventions can support improvements in learners' reading levels and promote collaborative educational practices.Systematic planning, continuous monitoring, stakeholder participation, and feedback may help strengthen foundational reading instruction.Addressing implementation challenges and sustaining stakeholder engagement are important considerations for improving and maintaining the intervention.
doi:10.63498/injelps116.venue: International Journal of Education, Learning, and Pedagogical Sciences (INJELPS)

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1927981.title: Machine learning-assisted chemometric analysis of salivary ATR-FTIR spectra for the diagnosis of oral submucous fibrosis
doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1927981.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Oral submucous fibrosis (OSMF) is a chronic, potentially malignant disorder strongly linked to areca nut chewing. Clinical diagnosis is challenging, and histopathology, though the gold standard, is invasive and subject to inter-observer variability. Saliva analysis using Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy offers a promising non-invasive alternative. This study evaluated salivary ATR-FTIR spectral analysis integrated with machine learning for classification of OSMF, individuals with adverse oral habits, and healthy controls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methodology</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Unstimulated saliva samples were collected from 450 participants comprising 150 patients with clinically diagnosed OSMF, 150 individuals with adverse oral habits without clinical evidence of OSMF, and 150 healthy controls. After centrifugation, the saliva supernatant was analyzed by ATR-FTIR spectroscopy over 400–4000 cm
                      <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                      ¹. Spectra underwent baseline correction and normalization followed by Savitzky–Golay smoothing. For machine-learning analysis, Standard Scaler and PCA were incorporated within the classification pipeline. Decision Tree, Random Forest, support vector machine (SVM), and XGBoost classifiers were evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. Hyperparameter optimization and performance estimation used the same cross-validation framework. An independent cohort of 90 participants was used for validation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      XGBoost showed the highest cross-validation performance, with accuracies of 90.62% for Normal versus Habit, 97.67% for Normal versus OSMF, and 91.30% for three-class classification. Statistical analysis identified 157 nominally significant wavenumbers (p&lt;0.05) within a continuous region from 1581 to 2142 cm
                      <jats:sup>−</jats:sup>
                      ¹ corresponding to protein and collagen bands. Principal component analysis showed that PC1 and PC2 explained 89.26% and 6.95% of the total variance, respectively (96.21% cumulatively). In the independent validation cohort, accuracy was 80.0% for OSMF versus Normal and 71.7% for Habit versus Normal.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Salivary ATR-FTIR combined with machine learning demonstrated promising classification performance and preliminary performance in an independent cohort. The identified spectral region is biologically plausible in the context of altered salivary biochemical composition associated with inflammation and fibrosis, but it should not be regarded as a validated disease-specific biomarker. Salivary ATR-FTIR is best considered a complementary, non-invasive screening and risk-stratification approach rather than a replacement for clinical/oral examination or histopathological assessment when biopsy is indicated. Larger, diverse, multicenter studies with rigorous validation are needed before clinical implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.27465.title: A Brazilian Dataset for Financial Sentiment Analysis: An Active Learning-Based Annotation Framework
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.27465.abstract: <jats:p>This paper introduces a new expert-annotated dataset for financial sentiment analysis in Brazilian Portuguese, constructed from earnings call transcripts of the banking sector. The dataset was developed using a two-stage active learning pipeline designed to reduce annotation cost while preserving data quality. In the first stage, clustering and active learning were combined to filter relevant sentences from noisy transcripts. In the second stage, a Query by Committee strategy combining the transformer models BERTimbau and DeB3RTa was employed to select informative samples for expert annotation. The resulting dataset contains 719 annotated sentences with agreement analysis across multiple annotators. We further evaluated BERTimbau, DeB3RTa, and the external transformer model BERTuguês under three experimental settings, including fine-grained eight-class classification and complementary three-class scenarios. In the eight-class setting, BERTuguês and BERTimbau achieved comparable F1-macro scores (0.43±0.03 and 0.43 ± 0.01, respectively). In the sentiment-only three-class setup, BERTimbau achieved the best performance (0.68± 0.06). These results suggest that the dataset supports both fine-grained and coarse-grained sentiment analysis while remaining useful for models not involved in the active learning process.</jats:p>

doi:10.61669/001c.172639.title: Leading Continuous Improvement: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Assessment in Higher Education
doi:10.61669/001c.172639.abstract: <jats:p>Assessment is most powerful when understood as a leadership-driven process of continuous improvement—iterative, evidence-informed, and oriented toward genuine learning rather than compliance. However, the coordination costs of meaningful assessment have historically exceeded most programs’ capacity to sustain it. This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, and in particular retrieval-augmented reasoning environments, can function as leadership-support tools that change the conditions under which assessment becomes practically feasible without displacing the human judgment it requires. Drawing on leadership education and assessment scholarship, we develop a three-level framework—individual and course, program, and institutional—and present six practice-based use cases illustrating AI-supported assessment at each level, including an AI-populated curriculum alignment matrix and an AI-assisted synthesis of external program reviews. We also directly address the tensions practitioners must navigate: data contamination from AI-generated student work, reliability-validity trade-offs, the limitations of AI detection tools, and the faculty professional development gap. Implications for assessment leaders are discussed.</jats:p>

doi:10.63498/injelps117.title: Doray the Catbaloganon Explorer on Probability: Validation of a Mathematics Strategic Intervention Material (SIM)
doi:10.63498/injelps117.abstract: Aim: This study aimed to develop and validate Doray the Catbaloganon Explorer on Probability, a culturally contextualized and gamified Strategic Intervention Material (SIM) for teaching probability to Grade 8 learners. Methodology:The study employed a descriptive-evaluative research design.Five experts and Grade 8 students evaluated the developed SIM in terms of content validity, clarity and readability, engagement and motivation, practicality and usefulness, design and visual appeal, and usability.Results: All 14 indicators obtained an Item-Level Content Validity Index (I-CVI) of 1.00, resulting in a Scale-Level Content Validity Index (S-CVI) of 1.00, indicating excellent content validity.The SIM received Very High/Excellent ratings across all evaluation dimensions, with mean scores ranging from 4.89 to 4.98 and standard deviations ranging from 0.02 to 0.08.Reliability received the highest rating among both experts (M = 4.97, SD = 0.03) and students (M = 4.98, SD = 0.02). Conclusion:The developed SIM demonstrated excellent content validity and very high ratings for instructional quality, usability, and acceptability.It may therefore be used as a supplementary instructional resource for teaching probability to Grade 8 learners.
doi:10.63498/injelps117.venue: International Journal of Education, Learning, and Pedagogical Sciences (INJELPS)

doi:10.61669/001c.172677.title: Capacity and Disposition: A Framework for Understanding GenAI Engagement in Assessment Practice
doi:10.61669/001c.172677.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has made assessment work faster, messier, and more consequential. This conceptual article argues that assessment professionals’ engagement with GenAI is shaped less by simple enthusiasm or resistance than by the relationship between two conditions: the time professionals have to learn, test, and implement AI responsibly, and the disposition they bring to AI-mediated assessment practice. Institutional support functions as the environment that expands or constrains both. The article proposes the Capacity-Disposition Framework, a model that identifies four engagement conditions: The Calendar Trap, The Margin Lab, The Evidence Gate, and The Practice Commons. The framework helps assessment leaders diagnose uneven AI adoption, protect time for meaningful experimentation, honor appropriate skepticism, and connect AI use to validity, equity, transparency, and continuous improvement rather than speed alone.</jats:p>
