doi:10.1007/978-981-95-5156-9_62.title: Quantitative Research of the User Perception of Informal Learning Space on Campus in Cold Region
doi:10.1007/978-981-95-5156-9_62.abstract: In the era of educational reform, people’s learning mode has gradually changed from traditional school organized learning to unorganized and independent informal learning. To support this learning mode, higher design requirements have been put forward for the informal learning space. From the perspective of users’ spatial perception, this paper takes Harbin Institute of Technology as an example to study the informal learning space of campus in cold region, which solves the lacking attention to informal learning space of cold region campus in existing studies. In the study, questionnaire survey and field investigation were used to grasp the status quo of informal learning space on campus in cold region. Semantic differential method and factor analysis were used to make a quantitative analysis of users’ spatial perception. It is found that informal learning space of cold region campus can be divided into three types: point space, line space and plane space. The internal interpretation of the spatial perception in the three types is basically the same, which can be summarized into four types of factors. Based on these findings, this paper puts forward some suggestions on the optimal design of informal learning space on campus in cold regions from three aspects: outdoor design of interior space, steady state space design and collaborative space design.

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31915.title: Beyond Efficiency: The Impact of Instance Selection on Semantic Locality in Transformer-based Text Classification
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31915.abstract: <jats:p>Transformer-based models achieve high performance in text classification tasks. In parallel, Instance Selection (IS) techniques have been widely adopted to reduce training sets by removing redundant or noisy examples, lowering computational cost while preserving predictive effectiveness. However, little is known about how these techniques affect the semantic organization of the representation space learned by Transformer models. This work investigates the impact of two recent IS methods, E2SC and biO-IS, on the semantic locality structure of BERT representations and on locality properties previously associated with the quality of model explanations. Models were trained on the original AGNews dataset and on reduced training sets produced by each IS method. Semantic locality was characterized using CLS embeddings from the last BERT layer, average neighborhood similarity and class entropy computed over k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN), complemented by a qualitative analysis based on neighborhood word clouds. The results reveal a dissociated effect of Instance Selection on locality: while both methods increase neighborhood similarity, only biO-IS consistently increases the concentration of instances in highly homogeneous regions. These findings indicate that different Instance Selection strategies modify the geometry of the learned representation space in distinct ways, suggesting that their effects extend beyond computational efficiency and may influence locality properties relevant to explanation methods.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31915.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.37850.title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Stock Volatility Prediction: Methods, Challenges and Future Directions
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.37850.abstract: <jats:p>Predicting stock fluctuations is extremely important for risk management and asset allocation. Traditional models like Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) cannot handle the complex and ever-changing stock market data, so machine learning prediction methods have been widely adopted. This paper conducts a review study by collecting relevant literature. The research steps are as follows: first, screen the relevant literature on stock volatility prediction; then, divide the models in the literature into two categories: traditional machine learning and deep learning; next, compare the application scenarios, actual effects, and shortcomings of each type of model, and summarize the common methods used in existing research for data processing and feature creation. After organizing the data, it was found that this industry has three main practical problems: the predicted results given by the model are unclear in terms of their causes, the predictions are inaccurate in different market environments, and it is difficult to develop high-quality analytical indicators. To address these issues, several research directions can be proposed: developing a logically understandable combined model that can adapt to different markets and combine data from various sources for use. This review can provide a reference for those who will conduct related research in the future.</jats:p>
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.37850.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

doi:10.4271/2026-99-2995.title: Adaptive Optimization of Fault Diagnosis Models Based on Reinforcement Learning and Robustness Quantification Feedback
doi:10.4271/2026-99-2995.abstract:
<jats:p><div class="section abstract">
                <div class="htmlview paragraph">Spacecraft operate in a highly complex in-orbit environment. Telemetry data from
                    power systems is often plagued by multi-source disturbances such as plasma
                    noise, electromagnetic interference, and communication packet loss, which places
                    very strict demands on fault diagnosis model reliability. Using dynamic
                    disturbance test manifolds and the comprehensive robustness quantification index
                    (RQI) for evaluation, we found a critical vulnerability: baseline models such as
                    the joint loss enhanced global sparse attention transformer
                    (JLE-GSA-Transformer) perform well in resisting continuous signal disturbances,
                    but their performance drops sharply when temporal structures are disrupted due
                    to data missingness. This finding highlights that static diagnostic models have
                    fragile robustness boundaries when operating under extreme non-stationary
                    conditions. To solve this problem, this paper puts forward an adaptive
                    optimization method that combines deep reinforcement learning (RL) with
                    quantitative robustness feedback. By making use of the dynamic disturbance
                    manifold, this method embeds the RQI into the reward function of the RL
                    algorithm. Through continuous updates to the agent’s policy, it drives the
                    adaptive adjustment of key parameters in the JLE-GSA-Transformer, mainly
                    including the coding structure of global sparse attention (GSA) and the
                    discriminative boundaries of temporal cosine-center joint loss. This closed-loop
                    mechanism can significantly improve the stability, adaptability, and long-term
                    reliability of the model when it works in complex environments with multi-source
                    disturbances.</div>
            </div></jats:p>

doi:10.3998/tia.8087.title: Unveiling the roles, tasks, and competencies of Center for Teaching and Learning (CTL) directors: Insights from a Delphi study
doi:10.3998/tia.8087.abstract: <jats:p>This study identifies and defines the essential roles, tasks, and competencies of Center for Teaching and Learning (CTL) directors in U.S. higher education, synthesizing them into a unified framework that reflects the multifaceted nature of CTL leadership. Using a three-round Delphi method with 54 CTL directors, the study reached consensus on core leadership functions while highlighting contextual variations across institutions. Findings reveal the breadth of directors’ responsibilities, the competencies required for success, and their perspectives on future directions for CTLs. Implications for institutional development and leadership growth are discussed.</jats:p>
doi:10.3998/tia.8087.venue: To Improve the Academy: A Journal of Educational Development

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11173311/v1.title: Attack-aware Federated Learning via Prototype-guided Cross-cluster Knowledge Transfer for Label-space Heterogeneous Intrusion Detection
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11173311/v1.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative intrusion detection without requiring the direct sharing of distributed network data. However, label-space heterogeneity, where clients observe different attack families, challenges conventional aggregation and existing clustered collaboration strategies, which may either mix incompatible knowledge or isolate complementary attack expertise. To address this challenge, we propose Attack-Fed, a two-level attack-aware federated learning method that jointly considers attack-space compatibility and complementary knowledge across clients. Unlike collaboration strategies restricted to independent client clusters, Attack-Fed combines attack-aware clustering with selective cross-cluster knowledge transfer. At the first level, an Attack Category Profile (ACP) characterizes clients' attack expertise and guides Affinity Propagation to identify compatible attack spaces. At the second level, prototype-guided knowledge transfer exploits complementary attack relationships between clusters to reduce knowledge isolation while limiting the exchange of potentially irrelevant knowledge. This two-level design enables specialized intra-cluster learning and targeted inter-cluster knowledge sharing under heterogeneous label spaces. Extensive experiments on intrusion detection datasets evaluate Attack-Fed against conventional and clustered federated learning baselines, demonstrating its performance under varying degrees of label-space heterogeneity. \end{abstract}
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11173311/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.1021/acs.inorgchem.6c04676.title: Quantifying Base-Dependent Lewis Acidity in Substituted Boranes through DFT and Machine Learning
doi:10.1021/acs.inorgchem.6c04676.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The dependence of Lewis acidity on the interacting base is established. Here, density functional theory calculations and machine-learning analysis quantify substituent effects and base dependence within a combinatorial library of 816 trisubstituted boranes constructed from 16 substituents. Interactions with five probe bases (H2O, NH3, C5H5N, PMe3, and Cl–) yield 3927 calculated adduct formation free energies in dichloromethane. Electron-withdrawing substituents generally enhance borane Lewis acidity, whereas electron-donating substituents attenuate it. The magnitude of these effects varies with the base, producing changes and occasional reversals in relative acidity rankings. PMe3 shows the strongest dependence on substituent identity among the investigated bases. Weak linear correlations between isolated-borane global hardness and adduct formation free energy indicate limited predictive power for this single descriptor. Random forest models describe the computed trends, while SHAP analysis identifies the summed Hammett σp parameter, the borane–base frontier orbital energy gap, and borane electrophilicity as the most influential descriptors in the model. These results provide a quantitative map of substituent effects and the transferability of relative borane acidity rankings across the investigated bases.</jats:p>

doi:10.63468/pss.115.title: AI-supported education, cognitive curiosity, and psychological well-being among Pakistani university students: The mediating role of learning engagement in a cross-sectional study
doi:10.63468/pss.115.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the relationships among AI-supported education, cognitive curiosity, learning engagement, and psychological well-being among Pakistani university students, with learning engagement investigated as a mediator. A quantitative cross-sectional design was employed, and data were collected from 395 university students in Punjab and Sindh, Pakistan, using an online structured questionnaire. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, multiple linear regression, and mediation analysis. The findings revealed significant positive correlations between AI-supported education and psychological well-being (r = .391, p < .01), cognitive curiosity and psychological well-being (r = .447, p < .01), and learning engagement and psychological well-being (r = .563, p < .01). The multiple regression model was statistically significant, F(3, 391) = 74.47, p < .001, explaining approximately 36.4% of the variance in psychological well-being (R² = .364). Learning engagement emerged as the strongest significant predictor (β = .418, p < .001), followed by cognitive curiosity (β = .211, p < .001), whereas AI-supported education demonstrated a positive but statistically non-significant adjusted association (β = .087, p = .075). The mediation analysis revealed positive indirect effects of AI-supported education (ab = .200) and cognitive curiosity (ab = .170) on psychological well-being through learning engagement. These findings highlight the mediating role of learning engagement in the associations between the study variables. Overall, AI-supported education, cognitive curiosity, and learning engagement were positively correlated with psychological well-being. Given the cross-sectional research design, causal relationships cannot be established.</jats:p>

doi:10.54536/ajsts.v5i2.8655.title: Sustainable Market Forecasting of Electric Vehicle Adoption Using Machine Learning Techniques in Emerging Economies
doi:10.54536/ajsts.v5i2.8655.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid transition toward sustainable transportation has increased the importance of electric vehicle (EV) adoption forecasting, particularly in emerging economies where market growth is influenced by economic conditions, charging infrastructure availability, vehicle costs, and policy environments. The scale of EV market penetration, however, is not a straightforward prediction owing to the fact that it can differ based on adoption rates, infrastructure deployment, and socioeconomic conditions in individual countries. This study proposes a machine learning tool to develop a sustainable market forecasting model to forecast adoption of EVs in emerging economies based on past market, economic, infrastructure and policy indicators. An EV adoption dataset was used, which consists of EV sales share, charging infrastructure, economic indicators, vehicle price data, and policy features across 26 emerging economies spanning 2010 to 2025. A set of forecasting models, such as Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, XGBoost, Gradient Boosting and an ensemble approach, was tested with an unseen test period from 2025, employing a leakage aware time-series validation strategy. The ensemble forecasting model presented here proved to have a high level of predictive skill with R², RMSE and MAE values of 0.9010, 5.0773 and 3.7198, respectively. The historical trends of EV adoption, development of charging infrastructure, economic factors, and policy considerations were identified as primary drivers of future EV market growth through feature analysis. The results illustrate how machine learning-based forecasting can help offer decision-support information to policymakers, industry, and sustainable transportation planners. The suggested model is a step towards more data-informed EV transition planning, as it facilitates accurate market prediction and assists in sustainable mobility planning in new economies.</jats:p>
doi:10.54536/ajsts.v5i2.8655.venue: American Journal of Smart Technology and Solutions

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32102.title: The Role of Retained-Layer Representations in Data Selection for Compressed Transformer Fine-Tuning
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32102.abstract: <jats:p>Fine-tuning of Transformer-based models can be made more efficient by reducing the model, the training set, or both. However, layer pruning and training-instance selection are often treated as independent decisions, even though pruning layers changes the representation space in which examples are evaluated. This paper investigates whether data selection for fine-tuning compressed Transformer-based models should account for the representation space defined by the retained layers. We evaluate this hypothesis using BERT-base, selecting layers through kernel–target alignment (KTA) to favor task-relevant representations and centered kernel alignment (CKA) to penalize redundancy. The selected layers then define the representation kernel used for Nyström-based training-instance selection, followed by candidate-pool construction and balanced downselection. In experiments with BERT-base on SST-2 and QNLI across 12 seeds, the evaluated configuration achieves the highest average accuracy among the compressed variants considered in our experimental setting. On QNLI, it reaches (61.36±6.44)% accuracy and improves over BI+Nyström-Uniform by (6.25) paired percentage points, with 9/11 wins and BH-FDR (¯0.0205). On SST-2, it reaches (79.88 ± 6.08)% accuracy and remains competitive among the compressed configurations. Across both tasks, it reduces the aggregate FLOPs proxy by about 69% and peak CUDA memory by 13–19% relative to full BERT, although selection overhead still limits wall-clock gains. These results provide initial evidence that the representation space defined by the retained layers is a relevant consideration for data selection in compressed BERT fine-tuning.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32102.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.26483.title: Monitoring Explanation Drift in Longitudinal NLP Pipelines: A Cross-Domain Study under Temporal Distribution Shift
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.26483.abstract: <jats:p>This paper studies explanation drift : the temporal instability of ranked human-readable terms produced by fixed explanation mechanisms in longitudinal NLP pipelines. We compare corpus-level TF–IDF explanations with model-level explanations derived from logistic-regression coefficients in arXiv and PubMed abstracts from 2014 to 2024. The vocabulary is learned only from the 2014–2016 reference window and then frozen, approximating a deployed monitoring scenario. arXiv is used as the primary supervised setting, while PubMed provides a cross-domain robustness check with query-defined weak labels. Results show that model-level explanations drift more than corpus-level TF–IDF summaries. On arXiv, mean DriftScore is 0.50 for model-level explanations and 0.15 for TF–IDF, a 3.33-fold increase with strong statistical support (padj = 0.0040). On PubMed, the same direction appears with smaller magnitude, 0.20 versus 0.13, but is not significant after Bonferroni correction (padj = 0.0938). The proposed audit rule produces no automatic alerts under the strict configuration because observed drift does not strictly exceed the null 95th percentile, illustrating the distinction between measurable explanation turnover and drift that is sufficiently unusual to trigger operational review.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.26483.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.23960/jpmipa.v27i4.pp1853-1856.title: The Influence of the Guided Inquiry Learning Model in Supporting Chemistry Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
doi:10.23960/jpmipa.v27i4.pp1853-1856.abstract: <jats:p>This study systematically examines the implementation of guided inquiry-based learning in chemistry learning. The study covers guided inquiry implementation, applicable chemical materials, measured variables, research media, and gaps. The research was conducted through a systematic literature review by following the PRISMA framework based on identification, screening, feasibility, and inclusion to ensure rigorous and transparent article selection. The selected articles published between 2016 and 2025 were retrieved using the ScienceDirect, Scopus, ERIC, and Google Scholar databases, resulting in 24 articles. The articles were then analyzed using a thematic synthesis approach, following Braun & Clarke's steps, to answer the research questions. This review aims to provide teachers and researchers in chemistry education with information on the influence and application of the guided inquiry learning model. The review shows that the guided inquiry learning model has been integrated with various learning approaches and models, such as green chemistry, STEM, SETS, scientific, experimental, contextual, simulation, and other learning models. Chemical equilibrium is the most researched material, while reaction rate is still relatively understudied. The most commonly measured aspect was learning outcomes, followed by critical thinking, high-level thinking skills (HOTS), and science process skills. In terms of learning tools, students’ worksheets (LKPD) are the most widely used because they can systematically facilitate guided inquiry. The analysis also shows that research is still dominated by a quantitative approach focused on learning outcomes. At the same time, research that measures cognitive and affective aspects, such as comprehension and self-efficacy, remains limited. The use of other media is still limited. Guided inquiry learning using electronic modules is a promising research opportunity because it can support all stages of inquiry in a structured way and integrate digital features that increase student engagement and help visualize abstract chemistry concepts. Keywords: guided inquiry learning, chemistry, high school.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/feart.2026.1883390.title: Core driving determinants of India’s steel demand: evidence from ARDL-ECM and machine learning cross-validation
doi:10.3389/feart.2026.1883390.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Steel consumption dynamics, as the foundation of modern industry, serve as a critical indicator of a nation’s macroeconomic health and the fluctuations of industrial activity. In the context of the global low-carbon transition and the structural adjustments in China’s demand, India’s potential to become a new growth engine for the global steel supply-demand system depends on the accurate identification of its key explanatory factors. However, existing studies mostly rely on traditional linear regression frameworks, overlooking the distinct long-run and short-run relationship and lacking cross-model empirical validation. To address this gap, this paper constructs an integrated analytical framework combining econometric regression with machine learning, using time-series data from 1970 to 2025. The Autoregressive Distributed Lag-Error Correction Model (ARDL-ECM) model is employed to examine long-run relationships and short-run dynamics, with robustness checks via variable substitution. Quadratic polynomial ridge regression and dynamic Support Vector Regression (SVR) are further applied to validate the relative importance of each factor. Empirical results show that: (1) a long-run equilibrium exists between India’s
                    <jats:italic>per capita</jats:italic>
                    steel demand and its explanatory variables; (2) GDP
                    <jats:italic>per capita</jats:italic>
                    is the most stable explanatory variable, with significantly positive effects in both the long and short run; (3) gross fixed capital formation rate and industrial value added (including construction) as a share of GDP generally exhibit a positive relationship, but the significance of this relationship varies depending on the model specifications and the definition of the indicators; (4) Urban population growth rate exhibits a negative conditional relationship with
                    <jats:italic>per capita</jats:italic>
                    steel demand, while the iron ore price coefficient is negative but statistically insignificant; (5) the error correction term is significantly negative, indicating that short-run deviations are corrected toward long-run equilibrium. Machine learning validation further confirms that economic development, investment, and lagged steel demand are key variables for explaining and predicting India’s steel demand changes.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1969295.title: Deep learning-based genetic disease prediction with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout uncertainty estimation: a comparative study with classical machine learning baselines
doi:10.3389/fgene.2026.1969295.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Deep neural networks have been successfully applied to structured clinical data with a good predictive performance, but their point predictions do not reflect an indication of confidence, which limits their trustworthiness in screening for genetic conditions where an overconfident misclassification may delay the appropriate confirmatory testing or intervention. Methods: A feed-forward neural network (128-64-32 hidden units, batch normalization, and dropout p = 0.3) was trained to classify patients into five genetic-disease-associated groups based on twelve regularly accessible clinical and molecular biomarkers, using a publicly available, pre-labelled structured biomedical dataset (n = 1,000) whose real-world clinical vs. synthetic provenance could not be independently confirmed (see Section 2.1 and Limitations). Performance was assessed using stratified 5-fold cross-validation versus four traditional baselines (logistic regression, random forest, SVM, gradient boosting; McNemar’s test for pairwise significance). We quantified predictive uncertainty using Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout (T up to 200 stochastic passes), decomposed it into epistemic and aleatoric components, and evaluated it thru calibration analysis (ECE, MCE, Brier score, negative log-likelihood), an uncertainty-quality analysis (low/medium/high uncertainty strata), a selective-prediction (risk-coverage) analysis, a seven-configuration ablation study, and robustness testing across random seeds, reduced training data, and Gaussian feature noise. Results The developed network achieved 94.30% +- 1.36% cross-validated accuracy which was statistically comparable to logistic regression (p = 0.092) and gradient boosting (p = 0.238) but considerably inferior to random forest (95.50% +- 1.26%, p = 0.0018) and SVM (95.30% +- 1.36%, p = 0.0063). MC-Dropout obtained 93.33% accuracy (macro F1 = 0.933, macro ROC-AUC = 0.971, MCC = 0.917) with ECE = 0.076 on a held-out test partition—numerically the highest (worst) ECE among the six model/inference configurations evaluated, exceeding all four classical baselines (ECE 0.024–0.066), although MC-Dropout inference reduced negative log-likelihood substantially relative to deterministic inference (0.370 vs. 0.445), indicating its calibration benefit is concentrated in reducing the penalty for confident errors rather than in bin-wise confidence-accuracy alignment. Errors were about twice as likely in the highest (most uncertain) tercile of predictions than in the lowest (12.0% vs. 6.0% mistake rate), and 60% of all misclassifications were within the high-uncertainty group. Removing the most doubtful 20%–30% of predictions yielded a retained-sample accuracy of above 95%. Accuracy and calibration were consistent across five random seeds (93.07%) and deteriorated gracefully with increasing predictive entropy under synthetic feature-noise perturbation. Conclusion: On this structured, moderate-sized genetic-disease benchmark dataset—evaluated entirely through internal computational validation, without external or prospective clinical testing—classical machine learning algorithms achieved statistically comparable or slightly higher raw classification accuracy than this deep learning approach under standard, non-tuned hyperparameters for all models.</jats:p>

doi:10.1017/s2058631026101329.title: Humanist learning and artificial intelligences: critical literacies for digital worlds
doi:10.1017/s2058631026101329.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Shifting technological landscapes have been shaping the epistemologies, methods, and workflows of classicists, historians, and archaeologists for more than a century. Yet these technologies and their impacts have not always been subject to reflexive interrogation within our disciplines. As artificial intelligence (AI) technologies – especially generative AI – have become widely accessible, there has been a wave of concern among educators around student learning outcomes and academic honesty. In addressing these challenges, we must also engage in critical reflection around the use of AI technologies in our research and teaching from humanist and social scientist perspectives in order to serve critical learning outcomes and counter rising digital colonialism. This paper first situates the conversation within the context of corporate AI economies and the intersections between AI technologies and antiquity-focused fields. It then proposes three AI-focused literacies for cultivating core ancient Mediterranean studies competencies and fostering critical thinking: the ability to identify and analyse the impact of taxonomic frameworks and data training inputs on algorithmic outputs; the ability to understand the development of computational models and algorithmic reasoning and their applications; and the ability to critically evaluate the ethical and environmental impacts of algorithmic reasoning and AI technologies. Critical assessment of the foundational structures and logics of AI systems and economies situates both educators and learners to critically assess the political, social, and environmental impacts of such systems on the study of the past and the world in the present.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/atsip-08-2025-0072.title: Mutual learning of self-supervised ViTs for image classification with limited labeled data
doi:10.1108/atsip-08-2025-0072.abstract: <jats:p>With the rapid advancement of self-supervised learning in computer vision, pretrained models have shown remarkable transferability across a wide range of downstream tasks by effectively leveraging large-scale unlabeled data. However, prevailing approaches predominantly adopt supervised fine-tuning strategies on individual models, often overlooking the potential complementarity between different pretrained models during adaptation. This limitation constrains the further improvement of model performance. To address this, the authors propose a bidirectional mutual learning framework that enables two distinct self-supervised models to be jointly fine-tuned on a target task. By exchanging predictions during training, the models share knowledge and collaboratively enhance their representations. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that their method consistently outperforms conventional full-parameter fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) in classification performance. Notably, the superior results achieved on the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) data set highlight the potential of their method in medical imaging analysis.</jats:p>
doi:10.1108/atsip-08-2025-0072.venue: APSIPA Transactions on Signal and Information Processing

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31150.title: Ontology-Enriched GraphRAG: A Case Study in Portuguese Geoscience Question Answering
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31150.abstract: <jats:p>Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) significantly enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) in Question-Answering (QA) tasks. However, traditional text-based retrieval may prove insufficient in specialized domains, such as geoscience, where critical information is highly interconnected and distributed across complex concepts, relations, and interpretative descriptions. While Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) addresses part of this limitation by structuring evidence into entity-relation graphs, it remains susceptible to terminological inconsistencies, synonyms, and domain-specific variants. To bridge this gap, this paper presents a controlled empirical study evaluating ontology-enriched GraphRAG for Portuguese geoscience QA. We systematically compared four generation strategies: LLM-only, textual RAG, standard GraphRAG, and ontology-enriched GraphRAG. The ontology-driven approach grounds text-extracted entities in formal reference ontologies using a cascading matching strategy that starts with embedding-based semantic similarity, followed by URI-based, label-based, and alternative-label-based matching. Evaluated across semantic, lexical, contextual, and graph-level metrics, our results confirm that external retrieval is indispensable, as retrieval-based strategies outperform the LLM-only baseline. Textual RAG achieved the strongest lexical overlap, while ontology-enriched GraphRAG achieved the highest Correctness, Completeness, and Contextual Recall. GraphRAG provided stronger grounding and question alignment, as reflected by higher Faithfulness and Answer Relevancy. Beyond these answerand context-level gains, the most substantial effect of ontology enrichment was structural, driving a substantial expansion in graph semantic coverage, graph size, and matching rate. These findings suggest that ontology grounding acts primarily as a powerful enabling mechanism for semantic representation; however, its impact on answer quality depends on retrieval, subgraph selection, and prompt construction.</jats:p>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31994.title: Knowledge Discovery of Emerging Developer Skill Profiles in Telegram Community Using Semantic Embeddings
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31994.abstract: <jats:p>This article proposes a pipeline to discover professional profiles of software developers from job posts published on Telegram. The corpus consists of 22,243 messages collected between May 2021 and January 2026 from a public Brazilian group dedicated to IT vacancies; a two-stage filter combining deterministic rules and semantic validation reduced the set to 7,264 valid posts. A taxonomy of 108 technical and contractual competences was applied to the corpus, three embedding models were compared, and the reduced space was partitioned with K-Means. The number of clusters followed internal indices restricted by admissibility criteria defined beforehand and decided by an independent evaluator, resulting in 23 profiles with mean topic coherence of 0.522. Labelling and auditing relied on models from different families, so that no model judged its own output. This choice mattered: the cross-architecture protocol spread the scores instead of concentrating them, and showed that about a fifth of the corpus forms clusters built around posting format rather than occupational content. With each competence expressed as a share of monthly posts and multiple-testing correction applied, only three of 50 series decline significantly and none rises.</jats:p>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32086.title: Beyond Retrieval: Bidirectional Neuro-Symbolic Validation for Reliable Graph-RAG
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32086.abstract: <jats:p>Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and its graph-based extensions improve factual grounding in LLMs but do not guarantee logical consistency when responses must satisfy explicit domain constraints. We propose a bidirectional neuro-symbolic validation framework for Graph-RAG that combines First-Order Logic reasoning over a domain knowledge graph with an Annotated Datalog engine built on PyReason, propagating confidence bounds across inferred facts. A bidirectional mechanism supports symbolic enrichment, post-hoc validation with corrective rewriting, and direct symbolic execution. In a Brazilian public university advisory benchmark, the framework achieves strict accuracy of 84.2% and weighted accuracy of 87.7% (with partial-credit weighting), an 87% reduction in factual errors relative to LLM-only; a backend-sensitivity study with gemma4:12b preserves the baseline ordering with no answer labeled incorrect (0/57).</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11396505/v1.title: Aesthetics Prediction of Websites using Federated Learning
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11396505/v1.abstract: Interface aesthetics is considered subjective in nature. Most existing approaches to aesthetic prediction generally rely on centralized data collection and use average ratings, often ignoring individual user choices. To address this, we propose a Federated Learning-based model. To construct the base model, we considered EfficientNet-B0, ResNet- 50, and Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16). To test these three models, we developed a dataset of 100 website interfaces (50 mobile and 50 desktop/laptop) and had 100 users rate them using the Latin Square Method. It was observed that EfficientNet-B0 outperformed the others. Consequently, we considered EfficientNet-B0 as the base model. In the empirical study, we found that users can be grouped into five types based on their gender and occupation. Accordingly, five clients were considered for our Federated Learning algorithm. The Federated Average (FedAvg) algorithm achieved a promising MSE of only 0.0534.

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31988.title: Where Does Hardness Come From? An Instance Hardness Analysis of Substance-Use Prediction in Brazilian Adolescents
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31988.abstract: <jats:p>The intrinsic difficulty of a classification dataset is routinely measured, yet its origin is rarely examined: is an instance hard because of the features that describe it, or because of the target to be predicted? We study this through Instance Hardness (IH) in a real, highly imbalanced problem — predicting frequent substance use among 165,838 Brazilian adolescents from the 2019 PeNSE survey, a setting that is hard by construction: the data are self-reported and the positive class has a prevalence of only about 4%. Hardness is quantified per instance in two independent ways — empirically, as the misclassification propensity across a committee of four learning architectures, and geometrically, from local class overlap (kDN), which uses no model. Three findings emerge across ten data partitions. First, IH is largely but not uniformly model-invariant (Spearman ρ > 0.94 among the four committee members; ≈ 0.79–0.97 against a fifth, neural architecture), which justifies treating hardness as a property of the data rather than of any single learner. Second, local overlap explains only part of the difficulty: kDN predicts true errors with an AUC of ≈ 0.73, against ≈ 0.95 for empirical IH, leaving a substantial residual attributable to non-local structure such as label noise or feature interactions. Third, through a controlled ablation, hardness responds to the target, not the features — removing an entire block of strong features leaves the hardness distribution essentially unchanged, whereas enlarging the target raises mean hardness roughly 2.5×. In this domain, difficulty is governed by what is predicted, not by which variables are used to predict it; past a reasonable feature set, the performance ceiling is more productively addressed by reconsidering the target than by further feature engineering.</jats:p>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32143.title: A Comparative Evaluation of Embedding Models for Retrieval and Clustering of Brazilian Legislative Amendments
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32143.abstract: <jats:p>The large volume of amendments submitted in the Brazilian legislative process makes semantic analysis and consolidation labor-intensive. We present a comparative evaluation of 14 distinct base representation models, including BM25L and embedding models spanning open-source multilingual, proprietary, Portuguese-adapted, and legislative-specialized architectures, for retrieving and clustering legislative amendments. Across three corpora totaling 2,462 documents, we assess retrieval, clustering, text segmentation, and thematic granularity. Results show that large-scale open-source multilingual models constitute the best-performing group overall, with Octen-Embedding-8B exhibiting the most consistent performance. gemini-embedding-2 is highly competitive in sentence-similarity mode, while preprocessed BM25L remains a strong baseline, outperforming specialized encoders. Finally, removing structural metadata improves performance, whereas removing justifications degrades global structure; thematic aggregation improves local accuracy at the expense of global consistency.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s00784-026-07181-3.title: Accuracy of transfer learning in predicting peri-implantitis onset from intraoral radiograph: A multi-center longitudinal retrospective study
doi:10.1007/s00784-026-07181-3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The growing application of artificial intelligence in dentistry has opened new opportunities for predicting peri-implantitis (PI) using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Transfer learning, where knowledge from a model pre-trained on a large dataset is adapted to a new, domain-specific task, may enhance performance, particularly when medical datasets are limited. This study evaluated the ability of several pre-trained CNN architectures applied to baseline 2D intraoral radiographs to predict peri-implantitis onset.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A retrospective multi-center study was conducted at the University of Michigan and King’s College London. A total of 195 implants (146 from Michigan and 49 from London) placed in 108 maintained patients were included. For each implant, a baseline periapical radiograph taken up to one year after prosthetic restoration was analyzed. Five pre-trained CNN architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, EfficientNet) were combined with four transfer learning strategies: feature extraction (hybrid and non-hybrid), partial fine-tuning (50% of layers), and full fine-tuning. Models were trained using patient-wise splits to avoid leakage, and performance was evaluated on an independent test set using accuracy, area under the ROC curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All CNN architectures showed variable performance across transfer learning strategies. The non-hybrid feature extraction approach provided the most consistent discrimination, with the best models achieving AUC values between 0.74 and 0.83. InceptionV3 reached the highest AUC (0.83). Fine-tuning strategies yielded modest or low performance, with AUCs generally ranging from 0.42 to 0.69 across architectures.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Non-hybrid feature extraction applied to pre-trained CNNs showed the most promising, though moderate, performance for predicting PI onset from baseline intraoral radiographs. These findings indicate that transfer learning may assist early risk stratification in implant dentistry, but larger prospective studies are needed before clinical adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical relevance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deep learning models may serve as adjunctive tools to identify implants at higher risk for future PI based on routine baseline radiographs, supporting more individualized maintenance protocols and earlier preventive interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.30058.title: Text to SPARQL via LLMs fine-tuned with rewards and reasoning
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.30058.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models have made notable progress in translating natural-language questions into SPARQL queries for knowledge graphs. Recent studies from the first Text2SPARQL challenge have explored zero-shot and few-shot scenarios, as well as in-context learning techniques. With state-of-the-art (SoTA) results, the challenge exposes significant gaps, including limited use of open-source models and a scarcity of open-source fine-tuning, especially for reasoning. In this sense, we propose a new method for the Text2SPARQL task that combines pre-fine-tuning with explicit reasoning and a subsequent reward-based fine-tuning stage. First, we perform a fine-tuning to generate both a reasoning chain and the corresponding SPARQL query. Next, we apply reinforcement learning guided by reward functions. Our experiments show that the proposed model outperforms all baselines and six SoTA methods.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.30058.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.4271/2026-99-2988.title: Performance Prediction of Hall Thrusters with Deep Learning Algorithms
doi:10.4271/2026-99-2988.abstract:
<jats:p><div class="section abstract">
                <div class="htmlview paragraph">Accurate performance prediction is essential for improving the reliability and
                    service life of Hall thrusters in space applications. Because conventional
                    scaling-based prediction methods are often limited when the operating state and
                    magnetic-field structure become complex, this study develops a deep-learning
                    framework for rapid prediction of key Hall-thruster performance indicators.
                    Three representative neural-network architectures, namely Multi-Layer Perceptron
                    (MLP), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Bidirectional Long Short-Term
                    Memory (BiLSTM), are constructed and comparatively evaluated. Among them, BiLSTM
                    achieves the best overall performance, with a Mean Absolute Percentage Error
                    (MAPE) of 6.44% on the test set. Additional validation based on real
                    Hall-thruster experimental data gives a MAPE of 3.884%, indicating that the
                    proposed model has good generalization ability and can provide an effective
                    data-driven tool for Hall-thruster performance prediction.</div>
            </div></jats:p>

doi:10.51574/kognitif.v6i4.5538.title: Analysis of the Challenges and Strategyes Faced by Teachers in Enhancing Primary School Pupils’ Interest in Learning Mathematics
doi:10.51574/kognitif.v6i4.5538.abstract: <jats:p>Interest in learning is the primary driver of success in learning mathematics; however, many primary school pupils still view mathematics as a difficult, daunting and boring subject, resulting in low levels of interest that directly impact their learning outcomes. This situation requires teachers to face various challenges in the classroom whilst devising appropriate Strategyes to enhance pupils’ interest in learning, yet research examining both aspects simultaneously from the teachers’ perspective remains limited. This study aims to describe the challenges faced by teachers in enhancing pupils’ interest in learning mathematics, to analyse the Strategyes used by teachers to overcome these challenges, and to describe teachers’ perceptions of changes in primary school pupils’ interest in learning mathematics following the implementation of these Strategyes. The method used was a descriptive qualitative approach, with data collection involving semi-structured in-depth interviews with three primary school teachers: Ms EN, a Year 5 teacher with 12 years’ teaching experience; Ms ONR, a Year 2 teacher who began teaching in 2022; and Ms FD, a Year 2 form tutor with 9 years’ teaching experience. Data analysis was carried out through data reduction, data presentation and drawing conclusions following the Miles and Huberman model, with data credibility maintained through member checking and peer debriefing. The research findings indicate that the main challenges faced by teachers in fostering pupils’ interest in learning include pupils’ poor mastery of basic mathematics, negative perceptions of mathematics lessons, diversity in pupils’ personalities and abilities, a lack of parental involvement, and limited teaching time. To enhance pupils’ interest in learning, teachers implemented various innovative Strategyes such as Problem-Based Learning (PBL), the use of concrete materials, game-based learning, personalised approaches, and the provision of motivation and rewards. According to the teachers’ perceptions, the implementation of these Strategyes increased pupils’ enthusiasm, conceptual understanding, and interest in learning mathematics. These findings indicate that the success of teachers’ Strategyes in enhancing pupils’ interest in learning needs to be supported by active parental involvement and the provision of adequate school facilities; thus, the results of this study can serve as a practical reference for teachers and a basis for consideration by schools in designing more meaningful mathematics learning at primary school level.</jats:p>
doi:10.51574/kognitif.v6i4.5538.venue: Kognitif: Jurnal Riset HOTS Pendidikan Matematika

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1928492.title: Working memory, mathematics motivation, and problem solving in English learners with and without risk for mathematics learning difficulties: evidence from a high-poverty urban district
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1928492.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined whether working memory (WM) and general mathematics motivation were associated with word-problem-solving accuracy among 76 third-grade Latino English Learners (ELs), 43 of whom were identified as at risk for mathematics learning difficulties (MLD), in a high-poverty urban school district. Students completed WM tasks, a mathematics motivation scale, and standardized word-problem-solving measures. In the primary multilevel model, WM and motivation were each positively and uniquely associated with posttest word-problem-solving accuracy, and both associations remained significant after correction for multiple tests. Both associations also held after controlling for English proficiency and appeared for problems read aloud as well as problems students read independently. However, each association weakened under some alternative analyses. The WM association was no longer significant when prior word-problem performance was controlled, and the motivation association was not significant when motivation was measured at a single time point or when cluster-robust standard errors were used. Exploratory analyses did not detect mediation or moderation, but these tests had low statistical power. The findings offer cautious, correlational evidence that WM and motivation are distinct correlates of word-problem solving among ELs, including those at risk for MLD. Longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to test whether supporting both cognitive and motivational factors improves these students’ outcomes.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10605-z.title: Design, implementation, and evaluation of an educational escape room for critical care learning among emergency medicine residents
doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10605-z.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Traditional teaching methods often fail to adequately prepare emergency medicine (EM) residents for high-stakes critical care scenarios. Although gamified escape rooms show promise as active learning strategies, research has primarily focused on undergraduate learners. This study aimed to design, implement, and evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and perceived learning associated with a theory-informed educational escape room focused on critical care concepts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study was conducted at a medical Skills Laboratory (Tehran University of Medical Sciences) among EM residents with > 6 months of clinical experience. A theory-informed educational escape room was designed by a multidisciplinary team, integrating clinical scenarios, puzzles, and ACGME competencies. The intervention included the escape room simulation followed by a structured three-phase debriefing (reactions, scenario analysis, and summary). Data were collected to evaluate participants’ satisfaction with the educational escape room experience and their perceptions of learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A structured, multistep process led to the development of an educational escape room for EM residents, comprising five scenario-based challenges aligned with core competencies in resuscitation, airway management, trauma management, anaphylaxis, and poisoning. Of 24 eligible residents, 9 (37.5%) volunteered to participate; 3 participated in the pilot session and 6 completed the final intervention. The intervention was successfully implemented in this small volunteer sample following pilot testing and subsequent refinements. In the final intervention group, high participant satisfaction was observed, with an overall mean ± SD score of 4.35 ± 0.41, including 4.42 ± 0.51 for the debriefing session, 4.23 ± 0.44 for the quality of the educational escape room and 4.5 ± 0.45 for alignment with learners’ needs. Perceived learning was also rated favorably, with a mean ± SD score of 4.30 ± 0.53 in the final intervention group.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot evaluation suggests that a structured, scenario-based educational escape room can be implemented in a small volunteer sample of EM residents and was well received by participants. Participants reported high satisfaction with the escape room experience and favorable perceptions of learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.title: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.abstract: This paper introduces a new expert-annotated dataset for financial sentiment analysis in Brazilian Portuguese, constructed from earnings call transcripts of the banking sector.The dataset was developed using a two-stage active learning pipeline designed to reduce annotation cost while preserving data quality.In the first stage, clustering and active learning were combined to filter relevant sentences from noisy transcripts.In the second stage, a Query by Committee strategy combining the transformer models BERTimbau and DeB3RTa was employed to select informative samples for expert annotation.The resulting dataset contains 719 annotated sentences with agreement analysis across multiple annotators.We further evaluated BERTimbau, DeB3RTa, and the external transformer model BERTuguês under three experimental settings, including fine-grained eight-class classification and complementary threeclass scenarios.In the eight-class setting, BERTuguês and BERTimbau achieved comparable F1-macro scores (0.43±0.03 and 0.43 ± 0.01, respectively).In the sentiment-only three-class setup, BERTimbau achieved the best performance (0.68 ± 0.06).These results suggest that the dataset supports both fine-grained and coarse-grained sentiment analysis while remaining useful for models not involved in the active learning process.

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.29261.title: STAB: A Complexity-Ladder Framework for Evaluating Local LLMs as Autonomous Agents
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.29261.abstract: <jats:p>O uso de Large Language Models (LLMs) em sistemas agênticos locais enfrenta desafios críticos de consistência e confiabilidade, especialmente em hardware de consumo. Este trabalho apresenta o protocolo STAB, uma metodologia de avaliação em escada de complexidade (S1→S4) combinada a um protocolo de estabilidade temporal para diagnosticar falhas em agentes on-premise. Avaliamos oito modelos de quatro famílias (Qwen, Gemma, Llama e Mistral) em servidor com GPU NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12 GB VRAM). Os resultados revelam que as falhas agênticas originam-se predominantemente na camada de instrução e decisão contextual, e não na capacidade bruta dos modelos. Identificamos o fenômeno de tool-skipping por nomeação semântica (H12) e demonstramos que conformidade de formato e acurácia semântica são dimensões ortogonais (H10). O modelo gemma4:e4b destacou-se como referência de maior confiabilidade, mantendo desempenho perfeito em todos os níveis de complexidade.</jats:p>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32136.title: A Hybrid Clustering-Based Approach for Renewal Opportunity Prioritization in Payroll-Deducted Loan Portfolios
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32136.abstract: <jats:p>The identification of renewal opportunities in payroll-deducted loan portfolios is an important task for financial institutions, as it helps sales teams prioritize contracts with greater operational potential for refinancing. In practice, however, historical labels indicating effective renewal conversions are often unavailable, inconsistent, or unreliable, limiting the direct use of traditional supervised learning approaches. This paper proposes a hybrid data mining approach for renewal opportunity prioritization in payroll-deducted loan portfolios. The method integrates information from loan contracts, payroll margin records, and liquidation history to build an analytical dataset. K-Means clustering is applied to identify contractual profiles, and the cluster with the highest operational adherence to renewal opportunities is used to generate pseudo-labels. Based on these pseudo-labels, a Random Forest model is used as an auxiliary supervised model to produce an operational prioritization score. Experiments were conducted as a pilot study using a real-world dataset with 739 contractual instances from a small municipal agreement. The results indicate that the selected target cluster is characterized by intermediate remaining term, relevant paid percentage, and low available margin. The proposed approach does not estimate actual renewal conversion probabilities, but provides an interpretable decision-support artifact for prioritizing renewal opportunities in scenarios where explicit conversion labels are not available.</jats:p>

doi:10.48079/jika.v9i2.217.title: PSYCHOSOCIAL ANALYSIS AND SATISFACTION OF GENERATION Z IN CLINICAL LEARNING AND RETENTION OF NEW HEALTHCARE PRACTITIONERS AT HERMINA HOSPITAL GROUP
doi:10.48079/jika.v9i2.217.abstract:
<jats:p>Clinical learning is a crucial phase in healthcare education, as it bridges academic knowledge with real-world hospital practice. However, for Generation Z students, psychosocial stressors may negatively affect their learning satisfaction and their likelihood of remaining in the healthcare profession. The purpose of this study is to evaluate the relationship between the clinical learning environment and academic stress, and how these factors influence the satisfaction and retention of Generation Z healthcare students.
This research adopted a quantitative, cross-sectional design. A total of 211 students from healthcare programs having completed clinical placements in various hospitals were selected through simple random sampling. Data collection was carried out using the Academic Stress Scale and the Clinical Learning Environment Inventory.
The study results indicated that the majority of respondents—62.1%—experienced low satisfaction and retention, and 99.1% rated the CLEI as unsupportive. Bivariate analysis revealed no significant relationship between CLEI and satisfaction or retention (p = 1.000; odds ratio = 1.646). In contrast, higher levels of maladaptive academic stress, as measured by the ASS, were significantly associated with lower satisfaction and retention (p = 0.005). The odds ratio (OR) of 19.050 (95% CI: 6.383–56.852) suggests that students with maladaptive academic stress were 19 times more likely to report low satisfaction and retention compared to those with adaptive stress.
The study concludes that psychosocial factors significantly influence the satisfaction and retention of Generation Z health students. As a result, improving clinical mentorship and providing robust psychosocial support are crucial for preparing future healthcare professionals.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11104077/v1.title: Integrated debris-flow susceptibility assessment along the Karakoram highway using statistical, multi- criteria, and explainable machine-learning models
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11104077/v1.abstract: Globally, Debris Flows are the most abundant geomorphological hazard, causing significant loss of life and severe damage to infrastructure, especially in mountainous areas. The Karakoram Highway (KKH), which passes through rugged terrain, plays a vital role in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor and is particularly vulnerable due to extreme topographic relief, active neotectonics, and complex hydrometeorological conditions. Besides its strategic significance, the regional-scale susceptibility mapping that systematically compares with a subjective, expert-driven approach with a data-driven machine learning model remains limited in the area. In this study, a comparative debris-flow susceptibility framework was developed using an independently compiled inventory of 104 occurrences, including 62 field-verified sites and 42 remotely identified sites. An integrated analytical framework was used to compare multi-criteria decision-making methods (AHP and ANP), the Statistical Frequency Ratio (FR) approach, and machine-learning algorithms (XGBoost and Random Forest) across thirteen geo-environmental conditioning factors and to evaluate regional debris-flow susceptibility. The results indicate that Random Forest achieved the highest AUC (0.852), followed by XGBoost (AUC = 0.839), FR (AUC = 0.784), ANP (AUC = 0.775), and AHP (AUC = 0.766). The Debris flow hazard in this area is frequently controlled by topographical factors, including elevation and slope, combined with intense seasonal precipitation. The resulting high-resolution susceptibility maps support disaster risk reduction, resilient infrastructure development, and targeted emergency response strategies for the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).

doi:10.3389/fbuil.2026.1976552.title: Unsupervised geomechanical state reconstruction in deviated wellbore using a hybrid Transformer graph attention deep learning architecture

<jats:p>
                    Discrete interval state reconstruction of wellbore trajectory dynamics and downhole geomechanical conditions is essential for mitigating non-productive time (NPT) and optimising the rate of penetration (ROP). Conventional automated monitoring relies on empirical geomechanical formulas that fail to capture non-linear dynamics, or on supervised learning paradigms requiring manually labelled drilling dysfunction datasets, which are scarce and prone to human bias. This study introduces a Domain-informed, unsupervised hybrid deep learning architecture that couples multi-head self-attention mechanisms with spatial-cosine Graph Attention Networks (GATs) to model unlabelled logging-while-drilling (LWD) and mechanical data. Evaluated on a 205-sample directional dataset spanning 1,500 m to 6,600 m measured depth, achieving a true 24.88 m spatial resolution across 16 primary and Domain-informed variables, the proposed Hybrid Transformer GAT Autoencoder, comprising an ultra-lightweight total of 4,316 trainable parameters, was validated using a 5-fold spatially stratified Group-K-Fold protocol. doi:10.1142/s0129183126430102.title: Physics-informed quantum machine learning for parameter recovery in the underdamped harmonic oscillator
doi:10.1142/s0129183126430102.abstract: <jats:p>Physics-informed neural networks are widely used for inverse problems governed by differential equations, whereas evidence for physics-informed quantum models remains limited. We study a hybrid quantum model for recovering the damping coefficient of an underdamped harmonic oscillator from sparse noisy observations. The model contains 109 architecture parameters in classical input and output layers and a six-qubit parameterized quantum circuit; the damping coefficient is optimized as one additional scalar. The main comparison uses 15 independent paired replicates in each of four oscillator regimes. Against a 2209-parameter classical multilayer perceptron, the quantum model has lower mean absolute damping error in all four regimes. Exact paired Wilcoxon tests with Holm correction support a difference only in the fourth regime ([Formula: see text]); the other corrected tests are not significant. A tuned DeepXDE baseline has a descriptively lower mean error in the first regime, while the quantum model has lower means in the remaining three, but this cross-framework comparison was not included in the frozen confirmatory test. Ablations show that both data and physics terms are needed, that circuit-depth effects are regime dependent and that the observed ranking is robust to the tested observation-noise and training-size changes. All quantum experiments use an analytic classical simulator.</jats:p>
doi:10.1142/s0129183126430102.venue: International Journal of Modern Physics C

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31615.title: Integrando Dados Textuais e Estruturados para Compreender Fatores Associados à Infrequência Escolar
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31615.abstract: <jats:p>School dropout is influenced by both academic and socio-demographic factors, yet Educational Data Mining (EDM) studies predominantly rely on structured quantitative data. As a result, contextual information contained in textual records remains underexplored. This paper proposes a Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) process that integrates unstructured and structured data from FICAI, a school absenteeism monitoring system used in southern Brazil. The approach applies topic modeling to reports produced by child protection counselors to identify latent topics associated with school absenteeism. These topics are then combined with demographic and institutional attributes and analyzed through Association rules. The study analyzes records from approximately 89,800 students. The results show that text mining uncovers factors overlooked by traditional institutional diagnoses. The discovered associations indicate that the pedagogical triad reflects symptoms rather than causes of disengagement, reveal distinct risk profiles across educational stages, and provide evidence to support targeted dropout prevention policies.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41746-026-03392-w.title: A generalizable deep learning model for predicting opioid use disorder using language modeling for cross-EHR data harmonization
doi:10.1038/s41746-026-03392-w.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The opioid use disorder (OUD) epidemic in the United States has been a major public health crisis. We developed OUD-REY (
                    <jats:underline>OUD R</jats:underline>
                    isk
                    <jats:underline>E</jats:underline>
                    valuator at 1
                    <jats:underline>Y</jats:underline>
                    ear) - a deep learning model that uses longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data from the All of Us research program to predict risk of OUD at one year for patients with an opioid prescription. On internal validation, OUD-REY achieved an AUROC of 91.2% and AUPRC of 77.0%. We leveraged a pretrained language model to accommodate thousands of unseen, out-of-vocabulary clinical features in a patient’s longitudinal EHR history. We externally validated our model on a new dataset released by All of Us that was temporally separated from our development set and on a dataset containing ~6 million patients from medical centers of the Veterans Affairs (VA) nationwide over a span of 20 years. On external validation, our model had an AUROC and AUPRC of 86.4% and 23.1% (OUD prevalence of 2.9%), respectively, on our temporally separated All of Us validation set. It had an AUROC and AUPRC of 85.5% and 19.5% (OUD prevalence of 3.5%), respectively, on the VA dataset. Our fairness auditing showed that the model was generally fair for patients with different genders, race, and ethnic backgrounds. This model may potentially improve prevention and care of OUD.

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31012.title: When Degree Anonymity Is Not Enough: Assessing Structural Re-identification Risk in Social Graphs
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31012.abstract: <jats:p>Removing identifiers and equalizing node degrees do not guarantee graph privacy, as network topology acts as a structural quasi-identifier. Evaluating rather than assuming privacy, this article frames structural re-identification risk assessment as a reproducible evaluation problem and presents a configuration-driven pipeline that anonymizes graphs, validates anonymity, and reports privacy-utility metrics. We adopt the structural k-anonymity paradigm as our core design choice, evaluating it on Facebook Ego-Nets and Email-Enron across k ∈ {2, 5, 10, 20}. Under a 1-hop subgraph adversary (d = 1), effective protection reduces to degree-based anonymity: the 1-hop re-identification rate exceeds the degree-based rate by approximately 6× on Facebook and 38× on Enron at k = 2, indicating that neighborhoods can remain structurally distinguishable. We position this assessment relative to differential privacy (a difference of premises: publishing the whole graph versus releasing queries) and to stronger learned de-anonymization adversaries. Furthermore, increasing k does not improve privacy monotonically, as aggressive anonymization distorts degree distributions and shifts vulnerability patterns. Since our scenarios model basic adversaries, these risk rates represent lower bounds, indicating that graphs anonymized by degree-based protection should undergo structural risk assessment before publication.</jats:p>

doi:10.61669/001c.172641.title: Assessment Professionals’ Journey to Owning GenAI Adoption
doi:10.61669/001c.172641.abstract: <jats:p>This Special Issue started with a question - what can assessment practitioners do to optimize GenAI adoption across contexts? While GenAI is no longer considered passing or irrelevant in assessment work, scholarly sharing of its applications have been primarily bound to the classroom assessment context. Professionals have, and must continue to, build knowledge and skill in navigating the GenAI to maintain momentum in relentlessly pursuing continuous improvement within their institutions, whether they are encouraging and seeking rapid integration or more cautiously approaching these technological breakthroughs. The articles in this Special Issue take GenAI implementation from integration on the margins and in the classroom only to being embraced with intentionality across the institution. Through stories of practice, basic research, and frameworks, they focus on way that the assessment practitioner can own GenAI adoption, expanding the conversation. Practitioners can walk away with a perspective shift on GenAI- from a potential threat to a willing partner.</jats:p>
doi:10.61669/001c.172641.venue: Intersection: A Journal at the Intersection of Assessment and Learning

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11390685/v1.title: Measuring brands in machine answers: A scoping review and validity framework for large language model brand-visibility audits
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11390685/v1.abstract: Firms increasingly track how often large language models (LLMs) and AI answer engines mention, rank and recommend their brands, yet the audits behind these “AI visibility” metrics reach conflicting conclusions. This scoping review, reported under PRISMA-ScR, maps 38 empirical studies (2024–2026) that query LLMs and measure outcomes at the brand or business level, and appraises them against nine measurement-validity criteria drawn from marketing measurement theory. The evidence base is young and fragile: 35 studies are not peer reviewed, half come from authors with commercial stakes in visibility services, and two vendor groups account for 12 papers. Few studies validate scores against external brand or market benchmarks (2) or repeat measurement over time (7), and results are sensitive to paraphrasing, query language and the number of draws. Drawing on consideration-set theory, I propose a two-stage account that can reconcile many apparent contradictions: inclusion in an answer (membership) appears to track how extensively a brand is documented online, while selection among included brands may be more responsive to attribute evidence, a conjecture the evidence supports only partly. Designs that supply a candidate list observe only selection. Six propositions and a minimum design and reporting standard for brand-visibility audits follow.

doi:10.46328/ijte.8031.title: <b>STEAM and Computational Thinking in Technology-Enhanced Education: A Systematic Review of Learning Design </b>
doi:10.46328/ijte.8031.abstract: <jats:p>This systematic literature review examines how STEAM (science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics) and computational thinking (CT) activities are conceptualized and implemented in technology-enhanced learning environments in primary and lower secondary education. Guided by PRISMA 2020 procedures, 34 empirical studies were analyzed using inductive content analysis to identify recurring pedagogical structures. Seven categories emerged: problem-based, inquiry-based, and project-based pedagogical forms; a social dimension of collaborative learning; and modal formats including role-playing, game-based, and experiential learning. These categories reflect patterns of pedagogical organization rather than disciplinary content alone. Interpreted through the lens of active learning, the findings indicate that STEAM and CT activities are predominantly structured as activity-centered, interdisciplinary, and iterative learning processes. CT appears not as an isolated technological skill but as a structuring principle for organizing reasoning, problem decomposition, and solution refinement across subject domains. Overall, the reviewed studies suggest that STEAM–CT integration increasingly functions as a model of learning design and orchestration: CT organizes sequences of cognitive actions, while active learning formats cultivate epistemic practices (investigating, designing, testing, and refining) realized through the interaction of tools, artifacts, and collaborative structures. This positioning highlights STEAM and CT as integral to contemporary science, mathematics, and technology education.</jats:p>
doi:10.46328/ijte.8031.venue: International Journal of Technology in Education

doi:10.25258/ijddt.16.74s.32.abstract: Cloud computing is commonly used by contemporary organizations due to the flexibility and reduced costs of cloud computing.Despite the advantages of cloud computing, cloud computing has several security challenges.Cloud computing is a distributed system with high dynamics, which makes cloud computing more vulnerable to cyber attacks, unauthorized access, and various attacks from the networks.The intrusion detection system is based on signature and rulebased systems.Because of this, the intrusion detection system is not effective in detecting new attacks.It learns from the data that has already been available and tries to learn how different types of attacks look.After this, it is capable of recognizing abnormal patterns in the network, which might mean that there is a potential threat in the system.The main purpose of this project is to ensure that there is a reduction in false alarms in the system.It is not easy to spot real alarms in the system if there is a high rate of false alarms.This is because it is not easy to monitor the system.This is where the reduction of false alarms is going to take place, making it easy to monitor the system.This system is also designed in a way that it can function well in cloud environments.This is because in cloud environments, there is a constant change in workload.It is not easy to deal with constant changes in workload.This is where machine learning comes in handy.Machine learning in cloud security makes it easy to detect attacks.This is because it is monitored in real time.This makes it easy to ensure that cloud computing is safe from different types of attacks.

doi:10.1007/s00138-026-01939-1.title: Edge-deployed streaming real-time trajectory prediction
doi:10.1007/s00138-026-01939-1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Future trajectories of neighboring traffic agents heavily influence the path planning and decision-making of autonomous vehicles. While traditional trajectory forecasting focuses on snapshot-based predictions that treat scenarios independently, real-world deployment demands continuous, real-time data stream processing with low latency and temporal consistency. To address these requirements, we introduce a lightweight, streaming-based trajectory forecasting framework that propagates temporal context across successive timesteps. By utilizing the predicted endpoints of previous forecasts as structural anchors, our approach efficiently guides a scene encoder to extract highly targeted context encodings without requiring multi-stage refinement or segment-wise decoding. To ensure deterministic execution bounds on real-world robotics hardware, we enforce static token boundaries via proximity-based sampling to satisfy edge-compilation constraints. Evaluated on the Argoverse 2 multi-agent and single-agent benchmarks, our method achieves state-of-the-art streaming accuracy while requiring fewer computational resources than snapshot baselines. Furthermore, hardware deployment tests on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano platform demonstrate that our model maintains an inference frequency exceeding 10 Hz while preserving a highly favorable latency-accuracy trade-off, proving its viability for deterministic, low-power, real-time execution in dense, continuous traffic environments.</jats:p>

doi:10.22158/asir.v10n4p1.title: Predicting Passing-Play Outcomes in American Football: A Comparative Study of Traditional Machine Learning Algorithms and Fine-Tuned Large Language Models
doi:10.22158/asir.v10n4p1.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines American football passing play strategies based on an analysis of 100 NFL games, addressing the notable lack of research on offensive passing strategies. The yardage prediction task is formulated as a regression task, and the touchdown prediction task is formulated as a classification task. A regression analysis was conducted using four traditional machine learning models, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs), K-Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, and LightGBM, and a LoRA-fine-tuned Llama 3 (8B) model. The SVM model showed optimal performance with a Mean Absolute Error of 6.996 yards, marginally outperforming the Llama 3 model (7.059 yards).
