In contrast, the fine-tuned Llama 3 significantly outperformed all traditional algorithms for the classification task, with a Macro F1 of 0.712 compared to the highest Macro F1 of 0.614 for traditional algorithms. Therefore, I advocate large language models (LLMs) for classification tasks and traditional machine learning algorithms for regression tasks. Sports analytics models can be selected based on the findings of these studies.</jats:p>

doi:10.3847/1538-4357/aeab97.title: J-PLUS: Identifying Outlier Spectral Energy Distributions in the Fourth Data Release Using Unsupervised Machine Learning
doi:10.3847/1538-4357/aeab97.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The selection of candidates belonging to rare or underrepresented stellar populations, as well as novel objects, is essential for spectroscopic follow-up. In this work, we demonstrate how combining broadband and narrowband photometric information with machine learning techniques enables this selection. Using photometric data in 12 filters from the Javalambre Photometric Local Universe Survey (J-PLUS) as input, we applied an anomaly detection technique based on autoencoders to identify spectral energy distributions (SEDs) that deviate from the dominant pattern in the sample of J-PLUS objects. Subsequently, we applied the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) algorithm to the J-PLUS colors of the population of outlier SEDs. Combining information from the SIMBAD database and other astronomical surveys to classify the outliers identified by the autoencoder, we are able to characterize overdensities in the t-SNE map. Our study specifically focuses on well-defined islands in the t-SNE space, corresponding to specific populations. We identified a large sample of white dwarfs and low-mass stars, including a small subset of polluted white dwarfs, and report potential candidates for spectroscopic follow-up, including 19 carbon-rich stars, 11 cataclysmic variables, and 170 white dwarf–main-sequence binaries, all previously unreported in the literature.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s43246-026-01354-z.title: Trustworthy machine learning of diffractograms to prevent silent failure of apparently accurate models
doi:10.1038/s43246-026-01354-z.abstract: For automated analysis of diffractograms, it seems straight forward to use machine-learning models developed for images, which can indeed generate highly accurate predictions. However, the fundamental difference between images and diffractograms can introduce hidden vulnerabilities. As a case study, we analyze $$\upalpha$$- and $$\upbeta$$-phase fractions in Ti–6Al–4V using two independent synchrotron 2D X-ray diffractogram datasets. We analyze the performance of two neural networks: “IE,” pre-trained only on ImageNet (a database of natural images), and “ISE,” additionally trained on a large corpus of simulated X-ray diffractograms. Subsequently fine-tuned with just 250 experimental diffractograms, both models achieve similarly high predictive accuracy. However, robustness tests and attention mapping reveal fundamentally different internal logic. IE suffers from “surface-texture bias,” predicting phase fractions from irrelevant background and pixel noise. ISE, in contrast, evaluates physically relevant features – Bragg reflections – in the diffractograms. Accordingly, prediction accuracy alone does not validate machine-learning models. Trustworthy models for diffractogram analysis require physics-driven pre-training. Machine-learning models can accurately predict outcomes from diffractograms, but differences between images and diffractograms may introduce vulnerabilities. Here, the authors compare neural networks trained on natural images and simulated diffractograms, revealing that physics-driven pre-training enhances model robustness by focusing on relevant features, underscoring the need for domain-specific training in scientific applications.

doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.37789.title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Telecom Customer Churn Prediction: Methods, Challenges and Future Directions
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.37789.abstract: <jats:p>Customer churn happens when users stop using a service, and a high churn rate erodes revenue and market position. Simple statistical methods often miss high-risk users in large telecom datasets, while earlier studies rely on static public data, mix different customer types, and rarely test models in a live business setting. This study reviews machine learning and deep learning methods used to predict telecom churn and compares what each can and cannot do. The traditional group covers Random Forest, Decision Tree, Support Vector Machine and K-Nearest Neighbors, and traces how each one builds a prediction from features such as call time, monthly charges and contract type. The deep learning group covers artificial neural networks, convolutional neural networks and the Transformer, with a close look at data needs, computing cost, model structure and the ability to capture non-linear behaviour. The review finds that no single model fits every situation. Random Forest captures non-linear patterns well and reaches about 87 to 95 percent AUC on telecom data, while Logistic Regression remains a fast, readable baseline. Decision Tree and KNN are simple but weaker on complex data, and SVM suits small, high-dimensional cases; deep models scale to large messy data but cost more to train. Three open problems are also identified, limited expert input, privacy rules and data silos, and weak cross-domain transfer, each matched with a way forward: knowledge-informed expert systems, federated learning, and transfer learning with domain adaptation.</jats:p>
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.37789.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32096.title: Residual Hybrid Learning for Data-Limited Formula 1 Lap Time Prediction Across Multiple Circuits
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32096.abstract: <jats:p>Lap time prediction in Formula 1 is a key element of race strategy analysis, as small changes in race pace can affect pit stop timing, tire compound selection, and the viability of tactics such as the undercut or overcut. This work uses publicly available telemetry data extracted with the FastF1 library and examines five Formula 1 circuits from the 2022 to 2025 seasons that fall under a single technical regulation. The methodology uses residual learning in a two-stage deep learning forecasting approach to address data limitations and improve the accuracy of drivers’ lap time predictions across multiple seasons. First, a Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) model predicts the aggregated lap time series for all drivers on each circuit. Then, a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network predicts the residuals, filtered by driver and year. In addition, we propose a score that balances performance and model variation, helping identify the most suitable model. We call our approach Hybrid MLR-LSTM. It achieves the best training performance across all circuits. In testing, the hybrid model performs best on Italy and achieves performance comparable to competing models on the other circuits. To support reproducibility, the code repository is publicly available at https://github.com/emipe09/HybridLSTM-F1.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32096.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31129.title: Classification of Descriptive Sufficiency in Public Expenditure Liquidation Records
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31129.abstract: <jats:p>This study proposes a supervised Natural Language Processing approach based on BERTimbau to classify public expenditure liquidation records according to the descriptive sufficiency of their content. The research is grounded on the premise that generic, vague, or overly document-dependent descriptions reduce transparency and hinder institutional and social oversight of public spending. A labeled dataset of 600 records was constructed by random sampling with artificial class balancing from a corpus of 4,083 permanent equipment liquidation records from the State Executive Branch of Mato Grosso, Brazil, for fiscal year 2025, with labeling validated by two independent auditors via Cohen’s Kappa (κ = 0.900). Three supervised strategies were evaluated under stratified 10-fold cross-validation: TF-IDF + SVM (baseline), BERTimbau Feature-Based, and BERTimbau Fine-Tuning. The results demonstrate that both BERTimbau configurations outperformed the baseline with medium-to-large effect sizes, significant for Feature-Based, with Fine-Tuning achieving macro-F1 of 92.66% and accuracy of 92.67%, confirming the feasibility of contextualized Portuguese-language models for supporting preventive, risk-focused governmental auditing.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31129.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32039.title: A Multi-Parser Benchmark over Android Bug-Report Logs
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32039.abstract: <jats:p>Log parsing turns free-text log lines into event templates and is the first step of most log-mining pipelines, yet parser behavior on mobile-platform logs remains poorly characterized. We present ABRLogParser, a multi-parser benchmark that expands the ABRLog Android bug-report dataset by applying thirteen classical parsers to its eight regular-expression block types: 342 files, 14 devices, 32.0 million log lines. Every (file, parser) pair yields a released structured output and template summary, and each parser is characterized by content (how aggressively it abstracts lines into templates) and by execution (coverage, failure modes, runtime). Abstraction spans a factor of 906 across parsers and throughput about fiftyfold; parsers carrying the LogPAI server-log defaults degenerate into near-identity transforms on Android; and we map where each one breaks down on large inputs. The corpus has no ground-truth templates, so the artifact is a substrate for parser comparison, not an accuracy benchmark.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32039.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.4271/2026-99-2908.title: Active Control of Attitude-Maneuvering-Induced Vibration of Membrane Antenna Based on Reinforcement Learning
doi:10.4271/2026-99-2908.abstract:
<jats:p><div class="section abstract">
                <div class="htmlview paragraph">Space membrane structures, prized for their lightness, affordability, and ability
                    to fold and unfold, hold immense promise for missions like deep space
                    exploration, high-definition Earth observation, and advanced satellite
                    communications. However, these structures are typically large-size,
                    ultra-lightweight, highly flexible, and have very low damping. This leads to
                    complex dynamic behavior featuring significant geometric nonlinearity, strong
                    coupling between rigid and flexible motions, and uncertain parameters.
                    Consequently, creating accurate yet simple mathematical models for designing
                    controllers is exceptionally difficult, and traditional control methods that
                    rely on such models often fall short. To tackle this problem, this study focuses
                    on a membrane antenna spacecraft equipped with cable actuators, aiming to
                    suppress its vibrations during attitude maneuvers. Using the Deep Deterministic
                    Policy Gradient (DDPG) algorithm, an intelligent vibration controller based on
                    the Actor-Critic architecture is designed. This approach is data-driven, meaning
                    it learns effective control strategies directly through interaction with the
                    system’s environment, bypassing the need for a precise pre-defined mathematical
                    model. Simulation results show that the controller demonstrated superior
                    vibration suppression and strong adaptability across several key scenarios.</div>
            </div></jats:p>

doi:10.4271/2026-99-2981.title: A Deep Learning Approach for Space Target Pose Estimation Based on Multi-Task Joint Training
doi:10.4271/2026-99-2981.abstract:
<jats:p><div class="section abstract">
                <div class="htmlview paragraph">The growing number of space objects raises collision risks and demand for
                    on-orbit maintenance. Since most servicing tasks require observing the target,
                    relative pose estimation is key for debris removal and satellite servicing. The
                    complex orbital environment poses significant challenges for conventional
                    feature extraction networks.. To address these challenges, this paper presents a
                    multi-task convolutional neural network for space target pose estimation. The
                    network uses a MobileNetV3-based encoder to extract image features and an
                    Adaptively Spatial Feature Fusion (ASFF) module for adaptive multi-scale feature
                    fusion. Although MobileNetV3 and ASFF have rarely been combined in the aerospace
                    field, their combination offers significant advantages in low parameter count
                    and reduced computational load, showing strong potential for spacecraft pose
                    estimation. Two parallel prediction heads are employed: an EfficientPose head
                    consisting of classification, bounding box regression, rotation matrix
                    regression, and translation vector regression, together with a Heatmap head.
                    This design leads to more robust and accurate pose estimation. The loss function
                    follows a multi-prediction-head joint approach, where each component is weighted
                    to form the final loss for multi-task optimization. The network is trained,
                    validated, and tested on a simulation dataset of the DAWN satellite built with
                    Unity. The dataset includes illumination variations, large distance changes, and
                    multi-view target appearances, thus capturing the complex scenes typical of
                    vision-based recognition tasks. Experimental results show that after 40 training
                    epochs, the model achieves an average position error of about 0.05 m and a
                    rotation error of about 0.8° on the test set. These results demonstrate the
                    effectiveness and accuracy of the proposed network for space target pose
                    estimation.</div>
            </div></jats:p>

doi:10.58304/tc.261016.title: Cartoon Word Lists for Second Language Learning Based on Extensive Viewing of Cartoons
doi:10.58304/tc.261016.abstract: This study created Cartoon Word Lists (CWLs) for second language learning through extensive viewing of cartoons.We built the English Cartoon Corpus (ECC), consisting of 8,016,916 words from a total of 3,756 episodes streamed on Netflix.The ECC comprised four subcorpora grouped by recommended viewing age (i.e., toddlers, young children, older children, and adults).Then, the words that met the following three conditions were selected: (1) used 30 times or more per million words; (2) having a dispersion (Juilland's D) value of 0.6 or higher; and (3) not listed in the 2,809 flemmas from the New General Service List version 1.2 (NGSL 1.2, Browne et al., 2024).This resulted in the extraction of 271, 266, 137, and 235 flemmas in the CWLs for Toddlers, Young Children, Older Children, and Adults, respectively.We calculated the lexical coverage in the scripts of other cartoons that were not included in the ECC.The results showed that the NGSL 1.2 alone covered over 90% of the corpus, while the addition of the CWLs increased coverage to over 95%, indicating a substantial gain in lexical coverage for cartoon viewing.

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.27518.title: A Composite Metric for Abstractive Summarization Evaluation: Integrating Lexical, Semantic, and Factual Dimensions
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.27518.abstract: <jats:p>Automatic evaluation of abstractive summarization remains challenging because traditional lexical-overlap metrics often fail to capture semantic adequacy and factual consistency. This work proposes a composite evaluation metric integrating lexical, semantic, and factual dimensions. Metrics from each family are combined using a hierarchical weighted formulation, with both intra-family and inter-family weights optimized via Bayesian Optimization using the SummEval benchmark [Fabbri et al., 2021]. The resulting metric assigns 19% weight to lexical overlap, 58% to semantic similarity, and 23% to factuality, and achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.488 on the test set, outperforming the best individual metric, BERTScore-Precision (0.467). These results indicate that combining complementary evaluation dimensions yields a more robust and human-aligned signal for abstractive summarization.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.27518.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.1007/978-981-95-5156-9_71.title: Fostering Supportive Environments for Knowledge Creation: Comparative Study of Campus Learning Space Layouts Based on Knowledge Creation Behaviours
doi:10.1007/978-981-95-5156-9_71.abstract: In the era of knowledge innovation, global production and economic development are highly dependent on knowledge. Universities, as national centres of knowledge creation, need to use campus space as a carrier to enhance the quality and efficiency of knowledge creation. However, the relationship between campus space and knowledge creation has not been fully understood. Accordingly, this study aims to demonstrate the differences between different spatial layouts in supporting knowledge creation, in order to explore the mechanisms by which campus learning space layouts improve knowledge creation. The study establishes a knowledge production process-behaviour-space ternary model based on the SECI knowledge creation theory. Observational experiments and semi-structured interviews are conducted in two representative spatial layouts of university learning spaces, and the intensity and distribution characteristics of knowledge creation behaviours in the corresponding spaces are analysed based on knowledge behaviour codings. The SYNTACTIC toolset is introduced to couple it to the topology of the university learning space layout, thus proposing a mechanism for campus space to promote knowledge creation. The results of the study show that the knowledge creation behaviours occurring in a space are mainly influenced by the scale and openness of the spatial layout. Specific combinations of knowledge creation spaces can achieve better results in promoting knowledge creation. Spatial layouts that connect different stages of the knowledge creation process in a traffic sequence perform better in supporting knowledge creation. This study provides a theoretical basis for updating the stock of university campus space towards new quality productivity enhancement.

doi:10.3389/fcell.2026.1978214.title: DeepFusion-HSK: a multimodal deep learning for subtype classification of herpes simplex keratitis with multicenter validation
doi:10.3389/fcell.2026.1978214.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To develop and evaluate a multimodal deep learning (DL) model for subtype classification of viral keratitis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective multicenter study included 3,501 slit-lamp images (807 eyes) as the internal development set and two external validation cohorts (2,957 images total). DeepFusion-HSK integrates three complementary illumination modalities—diffuse light imaging (DLI), slit-beam imaging (SBI), and fluorescein staining imaging (FSI)—through a novel fusion architecture. The framework uses a tri-way higher-order interaction layer to capture cross-modal pathological signatures, dual-task learning with auxiliary heads to prevent modality-specific feature degradation, and a dynamic gating mechanism that uses high-confidence coarse priors to calibrate fine-grained predictions and mitigate softmax probability spillover. To simulate real-world data deficiency, we evaluated model resilience under complete FSI dropout.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On the internal test set, DeepFusion-HSK achieved an accuracy of 85.1% (95% CI: 78.5%–90.0%) and AUCs of 0.947–0.949 for discriminating epithelial herpes simplex keratitis (E-HSK) and non-epithelial herpes simplex keratitis (NE-HSK), significantly outperforming Swin-Transformer, EfficientNetV2, and ResNet50. External validation confirmed robust generalization, with accuracies of 81.7% on Dataset I and 78.2% on Dataset II, demonstrating clinical resilience. Ablation studies confirmed the hierarchical synergy of multimodal inputs: the best single modality (FSI) yielded 78.5% accuracy, the optimal dual-modality combination (DLI + FSI) reached 81.7%, and full tri-modal fusion improved performance to 85.1%, validating that integrated global morphology, depth contour, and superficial ulcer signatures are essential for robust HSK subtyping.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DeepFusion-HSK offers a robust, generalizable, and clinically deployable solution for therapeutic HSK subtyping. Its resilience to missing imaging modalities makes it well suited for heterogeneous real-world ophthalmic practice, providing a decision-support tool to reduce vision-threatening misdiagnoses and guide therapy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
doi:10.3389/fcell.2026.1978214.venue: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31964.title: A generative model-driven pipeline for post-hoc prioritization of candidates in nonlinear optical materials discovery
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31964.abstract: <jats:p>Discovering nonlinear optical (NLO) materials for quantum photonic applications remains challenging because of the vastness of chemical space and the high cost of first-principles calculations. Generative machine learning models, such as the Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE-χ2), enable targeted generation of novel candidates, but their outputs do not guarantee physical feasibility. In this work, we propose a generative model-driven pipeline to post-hoc prioritize 1,000 synthetic candidates previously generated by a CVAE-χ2 conditioned to a band gap range of 2–4 eV. The pipeline sequentially applies band gap filtering, thermodynamic stability estimation via the energy above the convex hull (ΔEhull) obtained from the nearest neighbor in the Materials Project database, non-centrosymmetric symmetry selection, and a heuristic SPDC figure of merit. This multi-criteria data-mining strategy reduced the original candidate set to a single physically consistent material (Cristal_CVAE_382), which showed competitive performance compared with commercial NLO crystals such as PPLN, PPKTP, and BBO. The proposed approach provides an effective and reproducible screening strategy that bridges generative artificial intelligence and materials science, significantly narrowing the search space for subsequent DFT calculations and experimental synthesis in the pursuit of future quantum technologies.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31964.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31792.title: KG-RAG: A Hybrid Retrieval Architecture for Institutional Normative Documents
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31792.abstract: <jats:p>Higher education institutions deal with complex hierarchical normative documents, a scenario where traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems suffer from context fragmentation and hallucinations. Furthermore, public data management requires strictly local processing to ensure technological sovereignty. To address these limitations, this paper proposes and evaluates the Knowledge Graph RAG (KG-RAG) architecture, a hybrid pipeline applied to the documentary ecosystem of the Federal University of Western Pará (UFOPA). The model integrates an institutional ontology, Contextual Chunking, and query decomposition to isolate administrative boundaries before response generation, processing a corpus of 11,047 chunks. An empirical evaluation using the RAGAS framework demonstrated that the approach outperformed a standard hybrid baseline, achieving gains of 30.1% in Faithfulness and 35.2% in Context Recall. The results provide evidence that retrieval guided by logical relationships mitigates context loss in deep normatives, ensuring informational accuracy and privacy in closed government environments.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31792.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.61669/001c.172638.title: AI-Assisted Sentiment Analysis of Student Voice: A Human-Validated Comparison of Lexicon and Transformer-Based Tools
doi:10.61669/001c.172638.abstract: <jats:p>Open-ended survey responses offer rich insights into the student experience, yet analyzing this qualitative data at scale is often time-consuming and labor-intensive. This study evaluates whether off-the-shelf sentiment analysis tools can validly classify such data for institutional assessment. Analyzing 1,220 free-text responses from undergraduate students at a private liberal arts university, we compared the performance of four tools: two lexicon-based (TextBlob and VADER) and two transformer-based (BERT-nlptown and RoBERTa-cardiffnlp) against manual coding. Evaluation metrics included accuracy, macro F1 score, and Cohen’s kappa (κ). While BERT-nlptown performed best, it achieved only moderate agreement with human coding (κ = .42). Furthermore, lexicon-based approaches misclassified roughly 20% of responses due to limited vocabulary coverage. Notably, all tools struggled to accurately classify negative, neutral and mixed sentiments. We recommend conducting lexicon-coverage diagnostics, few-shot prompting, domain-specific finetuning, and human-in-the-loop oversight to ensure valid, reliable, and trustworthy institutional assessment.</jats:p>
doi:10.61669/001c.172638.venue: Intersection: A Journal at the Intersection of Assessment and Learning

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11027924/v1.title: Active learning-driven experimental design for torrefaction process optimization using multi-objective Gaussian process surrogates
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11027924/v1.abstract: Data-driven optimization of biomass torrefaction is constrained by the high cost and time required for experimental exploration. We present an active learning framework that couples Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) surrogates with a multi-objective acquisition function to recommend the most informative next experiments for improving mass yield, higher heating value (HHV), and energy yield (EY). Using 486 torrefaction observations, GPR models with automatic relevance determination (ARD) kernels achieved cross-validated R² values of 0.854 (mass yield), 0.971 (HHV), and 0.869 (EY), outperforming random forest, support vector regression, and neural networks. A hybrid acquisition function balanced uncertainty reduction (40%) with expected improvement for mass yield (30%) and HHV (30%), while diversity-aware batch selection (K = 10) ensured spatial coverage. Cross-validated calibration confirmed 93.2% coverage for mass yield. ARD length scales identified temperature and residence time as dominant features. The recommended batch spans 200–315°C and 30–1089 s within the conventional torrefaction regime. Ablation and sensitivity analyses demonstrated component contributions and robustness. The Pareto front shows recommended points near the trade-off curve. This interpretable, uncertainty-aware framework provides a systematic methodology for accelerating torrefaction process development.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11027924/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.3389/fmicb.2026.1967486.title: CIT8, a machine learning-optimized antimicrobial peptide, exhibits potent activity against carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
doi:10.3389/fmicb.2026.1967486.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    As the burden of antimicrobial resistance continues to rise worldwide, the need for novel antimicrobial therapeutics has become increasingly urgent. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising strategy for accelerating antimicrobial peptide discovery; however, experimental characterization remains essential to define the biological properties and broader applicability of ML-optimized peptides. CIT8 is a 13-residue, citropin-based peptide previously developed through ML-optimization with potent antimicrobial activity against methicillin-resistant
                    <jats:italic>Staphylococcus aureus</jats:italic>
                    (MRSA). Here, we demonstrate that its activity extends to multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Among these, CIT8 displayed the most potent activity against
                    <jats:italic>Acinetobacter baumannii</jats:italic>
                    , maintaining an MIC of 4 μg/mL against 15 of 16
                    <jats:italic>A. baumannii</jats:italic>
                    strains tested, including multiple carbapenem-resistant (CRAB) clinical isolates. At 20 μg/mL (5 × MIC), CIT8 reduced an initial population of approximately 5 × 10
                    <jats:sup>7</jats:sup>
                    CFU/mL of exponential-phase
                    <jats:italic>A. baumannii</jats:italic>
                    to below the limit of detection within 15 min. Consistent with its rapid bactericidal activity, CIT8 induced rapid, dose-dependent membrane depolarization and permeabilization, accompanied by leakage of intracellular ATP. In addition, CIT8 and, even more notably, its D-enantiomer CIT8-D exhibited strong antibiofilm activity while maintaining relatively low mammalian cytotoxicity, with therapeutic indices of &gt;32 for CIT8 in both cell lines and 16.2 and 18.5 for CIT8-D in HaCaT and HKC-8 cells, respectively. Moreover, CIT8 potentiated the bactericidal activity of meropenem against CRAB, with the combination exhibiting bactericidal synergy by time-kill assay. These findings highlight CIT8 as a promising scaffold for further optimization and preclinical evaluation against multidrug-resistant
                    <jats:italic>A. baumannii</jats:italic>
                    .
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fmech.2026.1900959.title: Multi-objective optimization of lane-changing trajectories for autonomous vehicles based on deep reinforcement learning
doi:10.3389/fmech.2026.1900959.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The viability of autonomous driving technology largely depends on driving efficiency and driving safety, in which the accuracy of lane-changing trajectory planning is particularly important. Existing methods still suffer from low prediction accuracy and insufficient multi-objective collaborative optimization.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A multi-objective optimized lane-changing trajectory planning method for autonomous vehicles based on the improved deep deterministic policy gradient is proposed. A trajectory prediction module is constructed by combining the temporal convolution network, the spatial multi-head attention mechanism, and a Transformer encoder–decoder, and the driving risk field is integrated into the multi-objective reward function.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A performance comparison analysis was conducted between the trajectory prediction module and other methods, and the prediction root mean square errors for going straight, turning left, and turning right were 1.59, 1.19, and 1.27 m, respectively. The proposed method achieved obstacle avoidance and target advancement success rates of 98.92% and 98.26%, respectively, both of which outperformed the comparison method. In the lane-changing overtaking and lane-changing obstacle avoidance scenarios, the vehicle lane-changing correction was more timely, the vehicle speed fluctuation was smaller, and the front wheel angle control was smoother, all of which were better than those of the comparison method.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed lane-changing trajectory planning method effectively improves the trajectory prediction accuracy and planning performance, and can provide a theoretical basis for related research fields.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10633-9.title: The effectiveness of e-learning in maternal and neonatal health education: a systematic review and meta-analysis
doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10633-9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>E-learning is increasingly used in health professions education, including maternal and neonatal care. This systematic review evaluated the effects of e-learning interventions on knowledge and clinical skills among learners receiving maternal and neonatal health education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We searched PubMed, Scopus, ProQuest, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ERIC, MEDLINE, SID, and Magiran from inception to June 2025. Additional searches were conducted in relevant systematic-review databases, Google Scholar, and grey-literature sources. Two reviewers independently screened studies and assessed risk of bias using RoB 2.0 for randomized controlled trials and the JBI quasi-experimental checklist. Certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Where sufficient quantitative data were available, meta-analyses were conducted using RevMan 5.4 and Comprehensive Meta-Analysis version 4.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Sixteen interventional studies were included, comprising randomized controlled, quasi-experimental, and before-and-after interventions. Interventions included web-based modules, videos, simulations, serious games, mobile applications, and blended learning. In controlled studies, e-learning showed a favorable but non-significant effect on knowledge (SMD = 0.89, 95% CI − 0.22 to 1.99;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.12; I² = 93%; very low-certainty evidence). For clinical skills, the pooled effect favored e-learning (SMD = 0.43, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.82;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.03; I² = 38%; low-certainty evidence). In two uncontrolled before-and-after studies, knowledge improved after e-learning (SMD = 1.108, 95% CI 0.273 to 1.943; I² = 88%); very low-certainty evidence, but the absence of a control group and substantial heterogeneity limit causal interpretation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>E-learning may improve clinical skills in maternal and neonatal health education (low-certainty evidence), whereas evidence for an advantage in knowledge acquisition is less certain. Interpretation is constrained by substantial heterogeneity, incomplete outcome reporting, risk of bias, and the limited number of studies contributing to each meta-analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31025.title: Which Feature-Classifier Combinations for Video Sign Language Recognition?
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31025.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a comparative investigation of five feature extractors frequently used for video-based sign language recognition: I3D-RGB, I3D-OF, MediaPipe, Pose, TSM, and SlowFast. Many studies utilize these features, yet there is a lack of comparative analysis regarding their complexity and discriminative power when combined with linear, non-linear, and deep neural classifiers. Test results based on the public UFOP-LIBRAS-ISO dataset indicate that the top two performances were achieved by the TMS+LR combination (F1-score of 99.30%) and the SlowFast+LR combination (F1-score of 98.40%). Conversely, the complexity ranking begins with Pose as the least computationally demanding, followed by TSM, I3D-RGB, I3D-OF, MediaPipe, and SlowFast, with the latter being the most complex.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31025.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31993.title: Risk assessment of revictimization in cases of domestic violence against women
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31993.abstract: <jats:p>Risk assessment tools for domestic violence against women show limited predictive accuracy when grounded only in structured professional judgment. In Brazil, the National Risk Assessment Form (FONAR) lacks statistically grounded weighting, constraining its effectiveness. This study evaluates FONAR’s predictive capacity and tests whether judicial-data enrichment improves revictimization risk estimation. Administrative and judicial records were integrated through probabilistic linkage, yielding 8,694 cases (1,429 revictimizations) from 10,069 FONAR forms collected between March 2022 and September 2024. Propensity score matching (1:1, nearest-neighbour with caliper on the logit) estimates an effect of protective measures on revictimization of 0.1246 (ATC; 95% CI [0.1089, 0.1412]) and 0.1226 (ATT; 95% CI [0.1064, 0.1399]), consistent with selection of higher-risk cases for treatment. Supervised models were tested under two configurations: FONAR-only and enriched. XGBoost performed best (AUC = 0.6139, recall = 0.8027), outperforming FONAR-only (AUC = 0.5709). Protective-measure indicators and prior judicial proceedings dominate predictions, acting as proxies for case severity rather than causal drivers. The study contributes an empirical assessment of FONAR, evidence that data integration improves risk modelling, and a pipeline to support judicial decision-making.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.31993.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32002.title: Lightweight SPIT Detection Under Adversarial Mimicry
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32002.abstract: <jats:p>Spam over Internet Telephony (SPIT) detection faces escalating adversarial evasion via behavioral mimicry, while deep learning defenses often struggle to meet real-time scalability and transparency requirements. We formalize the “Fraudster’s Trilemma” and evaluate lightweight classifiers over an eight-dimensional feature space spanning physical, volumetric, and behavioral planes, using a simulation of 500,000 subscriber profiles across three stages of adversarial complexity (E1–E3). Ablation evidence indicates that the behavioral vector collapses under calibrated mimicry (F0.5 = 0.03 under Random Forest at E3), while the infrastructure-bound physical vector sustains an independent boundary of F0.5 = 0.98; the volumetric vector collapses under a linear boundary but persists under tree ensembles, which recover the class boundary from dispersion statistics that this benchmark does not equalize. Lightweight ensembles sustain high precision on this benchmark while scoring each subscriber independently, and per-decision SHAP attributions give operators an auditable justification for each blocking decision.</jats:p>
doi:10.5753/kdmile.2026.32002.venue: Anais do XIV Symposium on Knowledge Discovery, Mining and Learning (KDMiLe 2026)

arxiv:2610.26802.title: Scaling Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Brain Encoding
arxiv:2610.26802.abstract: Brain encoding models aim to predict neural responses to stimuli. The most widely used approach fits readouts from frozen pretrained backbones. Using neural data to train large models from scratch or fully fine-tune them after task-pretraining has proven difficult because neural data is costly and limited. We show that parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables us to effectively adapt very large pretrained backbones for brain encoding with a small number of trainable parameters. To make it computationally practical, we exploit the backbone's causal structure to predict multiple timepoints in a single pass instead of using sliding windows, significantly reducing feature-extraction cost. This enables efficient fine-tuning of multimodal backbones with up to 104B parameters, the largest model adapted for brain encoding to our knowledge. Trained with a low-rank adapter (LoRA) and a lightweight readout, our approach consistently improves brain encoding performance across nine diverse multimodal backbones. On the same Qwen3-Omni backbone as the prior state-of-the-art (SoTA), our method BrainLoRA achieves the best published performance on the Algonauts 2025 Challenge. We also show the adapted multimodal backbones remain interpretable: modality attribution recovers the canonical sensory topography that prior work often obtains by construction from separate unimodal encoders, and neural adaptation increases the contribution of audio inputs and cross-modal mixing within the backbone. To scale out the number of adapted models, we develop a multi-LoRA kernel that accelerates joint training of multiple LoRAs on a shared backbone. This enables an ensemble of 200+ adapted models that ranks first on the public Algonauts post-challenge leaderboard at the time of writing. Together, our results highlight PEFT as an efficient and powerful paradigm for brain encoding.

arxiv:2610.26748.title: Gradient descent reaches arbitrary accuracy in a fixed number of large steps on multiclass logistic regression
arxiv:2610.26748.abstract:
We show that gradient descent (GD) with step size $η$ can achieve $\varepsilon$ optimality gap on the multiclass logistic regression loss in a number of iterations $T$ that is independent of $\varepsilon$. To do so, the step size $η$ must be chosen large enough as a function of $\varepsilon$ (and properties of the linearly separable dataset), while $T$ is a constant that only depends on the data. The relevant properties of the data include the number of points and their margin (for $T$), and one additional quantity (for $η$) that turns out to be necessary in dimension $d \geq 3$. The proofs build on the known fact that, as $η\to \infty$, suitably rescaled GD becomes the perceptron algorithm, and the latter finds a perfect classifier in $T$ iterations. A similar claim was shown for two classes in dimension $d = 2$ using other proof techniques.
  This result adds to previous works that showed GD on the logistic regression loss can be accelerated by taking large step sizes. Those provoke a wild, oscillatory initial phase, followed by a stable phase. We provide results of this (qualitatively different) nature, too.

arxiv:2610.26351.title: PhyPro-FM: A Physics and Prompt-Guided Graph Foundation Model for Contingency Analysis
arxiv:2610.26351.abstract: The continuous evolution of next-generation power systems, characterized by the high penetration of renewable energy resources and dynamic topology variations, poses formidable challenges to traditional N-1/N-2 contingency analysis in terms of computational efficiency and scalability. While deep learning-based methods offer accelerated inference, existing studies predominantly treat contingency analysis as a pure regression problem, often overlooking the physical essence of grid operation and engineering requirements of real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes a physics and prompt-guided graph foundation model (PhyPro-FM) for generalizable and engineering-viable contingency analysis. The proposed architecture integrates graph neural networks with a learnable global query mechanism and, notably, introduces a prompt-guided learning paradigm. By leveraging historical snapshots as few-shot prompts, the model dynamically captures correlations between target and historical operating conditions, significantly enhancing generalization capabilities under unseen topologies. Furthermore, we design a physics-informed training mechanism that prioritizes branch power flow errors over nodal voltage errors, aligning the optimization objective with critical grid security constraints. To ensure engineering applicability, a physics-informed inference mechanism is also developed, incorporating a residual-based correction module and a specialized post-processing strategy for singular branches to circumvent numerical instability. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that PhyPro-FM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and generalization, validating its superior physical consistency and robustness for practical engineering applications.

arxiv:2610.26123.title: Optimal Multi-Kernel Combination for Online Multi-Label Classification
arxiv:2610.26123.abstract: Multi-label classification is particularly challenging in streaming scenarios, where data arrives sequentially. Online kernel methods offer a promising solution. However, prevailing methods rely on a single preselected kernel, making them prone to suboptimal choices since the global data distribution is unknown in advance in online settings. Although the recent method, Online Kernel Selection for Online Multi-label Classification (OKS-OMC), enables data-driven kernel selection, it fails to fully harness the complementary information from multiple kernels and encounters the curse of kernelization. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel online multi-kernel combination method for large-scale multi-label classification. First, an efficient and robust online single-kernel multi-label method is designed. Second, learning an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers is formalized as a structural risk minimization problem. An improved alternating optimization procedure is developed, in which the combination coefficients are updated by directly minimizing the objective function, while each kernel classifier is updated by minimizing a surrogate upper bound. This procedure decouples the learning of kernel classifiers from combination coefficients, allowing independent classifier updates via our single-kernel method and accelerating convergence to high-quality solutions. Our multi-kernel method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best fixed single-kernel models chosen in hindsight. Ablation studies confirm that our method's components outperform their counterparts in OKS-OMC. Comprehensive evaluations across 11 datasets and seven metrics demonstrate our method's overall superiority over existing online multi-label methods.

arxiv:2610.26025.title: TamedFlow: Trajectory-Aware Distillation\\for Teacher-Assisted Diffusion Sampling
arxiv:2610.26025.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) deliver high-fidelity image and video generation, but inference requires many sequential model evaluations. Two acceleration strategies are increasingly important: model compression makes each evaluation cheaper, while adaptive inference avoids selected teacher computation through reuse, forecasting, or speculative execution. Their combination, however, is brittle: directly applying the evaluated adaptive methods to a compressed student can degrade quality, an observed failure mode we call the \textbf{Combination Gap}. We link this gap to a mismatch between pointwise distillation and short-horizon execution: a student trained at teacher states need not remain reliable when its own predictions are chained. We propose \textbf{TamedFlow}, which trains a compressed DiT for this deployed role through cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision. At inference, a lightweight Learnable Trajectory Estimator routes completed drafts: accepted drafts bypass the teacher, while rejected drafts roll back and receive one teacher rescue step. Distilling DiT-XL/2 into DiT-B/2, TamedFlow reaches FID $2.58$ at $2.25\times$ measured speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet $256\times256$. Ablations support trajectory supervision, and routing controls favor LTE over random decisions at nearly matched latency. Evaluations on ImageNet $512\times512$, MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics extend the empirical scope.

arxiv:2610.26008.title: Accelerated Drift of Scientific Prose in the LLM Era: Evidence from an Interrupted Time-Series Analysis
arxiv:2610.26008.abstract: Every scientific text is embedded in the writing norms of its time: it reflects earlier publications while also shaping the texts that follow. The growing use of LLM-based writing tools introduces a new factor in this evolving system, but the linguistic changes coinciding with their emergence remain insufficiently understood. We investigate whether the trajectories of scientific-preprint writing changed in rate or direction after conversational LLMs became publicly accessible, using the release of ChatGPT in November 2022 as the observational breakpoint. We compare pre- and post-2022 trajectories across vocabulary, punctuation, readability, and syntax in abstracts from arXiv's artificial intelligence, statistics, and quantitative biology categories and from medRxiv. Using interrupted time-series regression, we find substantial post-2022 changes across multiple feature families and research domains, including increases in average word length, reduced formula-based readability, and declines in maximum dependency-tree depth and sentence-level depth variation. Individual features follow different dynamics: some lexical markers accelerate persistently, while others rise and then recede. Our findings show that isolated marker frequencies capture only part of the shift: changes in the rate, direction, and structure of linguistic trajectories provide complementary evidence of broader post-2022 change in scientific-preprint writing. More broadly, these findings motivate monitoring scientific writing as a multidimensional, evolving system rather than through a fixed set of LLM-associated markers.

arxiv:2610.25966.title: Behavioral Probes for Information Flow in LLM Swarms
arxiv:2610.25966.abstract: Most existing approaches to LLM swarm optimization are utility-driven, focusing on final task utility while leaving the processing, integration, and reliance of information within individual interactions largely implicit. To address this, we study LLM swarm interactions from an information-flow-based view and introduce behavioral probes to quantify information flow patterns. Specifically, we repurpose External Context Score (ECS) and Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)---originally designed for hallucination analysis---to measure a node's external-context dependence and parametric-knowledge dependence, respectively. Across controlled and realistic swarm settings, we observe consistent patterns: ECS increases with input relevance and distinguishes useful multi-source contributions, while PKS decreases as informative context accumulates. Building on this heuristic interpretation, we demonstrate how these probes can complement utility-driven structure optimization in two controlled applications. Probe-guided node pruning reduces redundant communication and token consumption, and probe-guided reasoning-path search accelerates convergence compared to utility-only baselines. Our empirical results suggest that behavioral probes can make the internal information flow of LLM swarms observable and serve as effective auxiliary signals for structure optimization.

arxiv:2610.25961.title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
arxiv:2610.25961.abstract: Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.

arxiv:2610.25834.title: FrontierRefactor: Benchmarking Multi-Scale Performance-Oriented Codebase Refactoring
arxiv:2610.25834.abstract: Autonomous codebase refactoring requires coding agents to restructure working software while strictly preserving externally observable behavior and prioritizing execution performance and compute efficiency over stylistic preference. Existing benchmarks: refactoring benchmarks assess functional correctness while overlooking runtime regressions, whereas code performance benchmarks target isolated micro-kernels that ignore codebase-scale complexity. We observe that refactoring scale is governed by the scope of the observable contract, the caller-visible interface fixing behavioral invariants while freeing private implementations for optimization. Building on this insight, we introduce FrontierRefactor, a benchmark of 60 qualified engineering tasks spanning four scales, from computational kernels to full repositories, across in-place optimization and cross-language rewriting. Evaluating frontier coding agents through a reference-free cascaded protocol across 1,080 execution runs reveals that correctness and speedup are largely decoupled: 41.2% of submissions satisfy functional equivalence yet fail to deliver verified performance improvements, with 19.3% suffering performance regressions and 21.9% trapped in measurement noise. Refactoring paradigms reveal orthogonal engineering bottlenecks: while cross-language rewrites gain speedups from native compilation after passing functional checks, agents struggle with contract fidelity, with pass rates dropping from 65.0% on modules to 32.6% at package scale; conversely, in-place optimization reliably preserves behavioral contracts at 86.5% but rarely achieves acceleration without physical performance profiling. Trajectory analysis shows that agents fall victim to uncalibrated micro-benchmarking illusions, an operational blind spot that multi-turn execution-timing feedback directly resolves, raising strict success from 16.0% to 40.0%.

arxiv:2610.25723.title: Learning to Couple: Context-Adaptive Joint Denoising for Diffusion Language Models
arxiv:2610.25723.abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by predicting multiple tokens in parallel, but factorized denoisers treat simultaneous predictions as conditionally independent. Decoding heuristics reduce the resulting errors by controlling which tokens are committed, but leave the underlying distribution factorized. Joint modeling addresses the source of the problem, yet existing methods attach separately learned layers to frozen denoisers, leaving the backbone unadapted to the joint objective and the coupling parameters fixed across contexts. We propose Codpula, a context-parameterized denoiser combining a Transformer with a tractable probabilistic inference layer. Given a partially masked input, the Transformer produces token potentials that shape per-position predictions and compact gates that modulate the layer's coupling parameters, yielding a context-dependent joint distribution while retaining exact conditional inference. We jointly optimize both components under a conditional denoising objective using a dual-flow multiplicative update that preserves valid probabilistic parameters. At inference, Codpula supports standard heuristics and uses conditional queries to adapt commitments to dependencies among proposed tokens without extra Transformer evaluations within a step. Codpula sets new state-of-the-art results across a broad suite of reasoning benchmarks while advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier in mathematical reasoning and code generation.

arxiv:2610.25544.title: Reinforcement learning on the EPRI AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment benchmark: diagnosing over-commitment and guiding MILP with learned policies
arxiv:2610.25544.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly proposed as a fast solver for unit commitment (UC), but standalone agents remain far more expensive than mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). In the first study of RL on the 51-generator, 72-hour benchmark of the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment competition, we trace this gap to the agents' own exploration, close most of it, and show that the resulting policy can accelerate an exact solver. In every configuration tested, Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) and an action-branching Deep Q-Network (DQN) trained from scratch committed about twice the units of a thermal-only MILP optimum, at 39-64% higher cost, whereas a merit-order rule came within 1.6-7% (10-24% when unserved energy is priced). When each unit's decision is sampled independently, spare units insure against random de-commitments. Consistent with this, injecting exploration noise during fine-tuning enlarged a lean policy's fleet, a reward without shaping terms did not remove the over-commitment, and under their training noise the agents outperformed the rule subjected to comparable noise. Imitating the MILP solutions and fine-tuning conservatively brought PPO within 2.6% of the optimum, and these policies had the lowest penalised cost of any evaluated (about 5%). Fixing the fine-tuned policy's confident decisions made the MILP 3.8-8.5 times faster within 0.10-0.25% of the best solution, with a smaller worst case than an imitation-only policy fixing as many variables (1.1% against 8.9%). Because dispatch method and benchmark scope alone shift the reported optimality ratio by up to 3.6% and 9%, we propose a reporting protocol.

arxiv:2610.25376.title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
arxiv:2610.25376.abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

arxiv:2610.25104.title: Non-Acceleration of the Heavy-Ball Method in 1D
arxiv:2610.25104.abstract: Despite having an asymptotically optimal rate of convergence on convex quadratics, the acceleration of Polyak's heavy-ball method and a characterization of its dynamics within more general settings have remained long standing open problems. Recently, the work of Goujaud et al. [Math. Program. (2025)] made progress regarding acceleration in the context of smooth, strongly convex minimization: for a small enough inverse condition number, either the method does not accelerate on quadratics, or there exists a smooth strongly convex function such that heavy-ball cycles over the roots of unity. The constructed functions have two variables, thus leaving the question of acceleration over univariate functions open. In this work, we use a Fourier-based analysis to i) provide a proof for the non-acceleration of the heavy-ball method over the class of univariate smooth strongly convex functions. We also ii) provide a strict enlargement of the previous root-of-unity cycling region, with insights regarding the "fractional" sets of Goujaud et al. [arXiv:2502.19916], and iii) give a higher dimensional cycling instance which is not covered by root-of-unity cycling.

arxiv:2610.25048.title: PACT: NVFP4 Data-Flow LoRA Fine-Tuning on Consumer GPUs
arxiv:2610.25048.abstract: Fine-tuning language models on consumer GPUs is constrained by computation and memory. Although LoRA reduces trainable parameters and optimizer state, frozen projections remain expensive, and activations retained for backward can dominate memory usage. We present PACT, a LoRA fine-tuning system that accelerates frozen projections with native NVFP4 GEMMs while reducing quantization and dequantization overhead and limiting quantization error. To reduce activation memory, PACT reuses quantized RMSNorm outputs and saves gate/up activations in NVFP4 for backward. To limit numerical error, it preserves BF16 inputs for forward nonlinear operations and calibrates frozen weights offline using GPTQ adapted to NVFP4 scales and quantized activations. Fused nonlinear kernels and cached forward and backward weight layouts reduce quantization and dequantization overhead. Evaluations across multiple models and tasks on a 16\,GB RTX~5080 show lower memory usage and faster LoRA fine-tuning with competitive accuracy, enabling model adaptation on resource-constrained consumer hardware.

arxiv:2610.25017.title: Decentralized Online Exp-Concave Optimization
arxiv:2610.25017.abstract: Decentralized Online Convex Optimization (D-OCO) is a fundamental framework in which a set of local agents aims to minimize a sequence of global loss functions using only local computations and communications. While recent work has established near-optimal regret guarantees for convex and strongly convex losses, the case of exp-concave losses remains an open challenge: specifically, whether logarithmic regret is achievable. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively by proposing Decentralized Online Newton Step (D-ONS), which adapts the idea of blocking and accelerated gossip to the Online Newton Step algorithm in a non-trivial manner. Concretely, our algorithm achieves a regret bound of $O\left(Nd(1-σ_2)^{-1/2}\,\log^2(T) \right)$ where $N$ is the number of agents, $d$ is the dimension, $T$ is the horizon, and $1-σ_2$ represents the spectral gap of the network. To our knowledge, this is the first logarithmic regret bound for decentralized online exp-concave optimization. We further establish a nearly matching lower bound of $Ω\left(Nd (1-σ_2)^{-1/2}\,\log(T/N) \right)$ showing the near optimality of our upper bound. Finally, we extend our algorithm to decentralized online linear regression in which the feasible domain is unbounded and features and labels are locally observed. By gossiping covariance and label-feature statistics, we also achieve logarithmic regret.

arxiv:2610.24970.title: PRECOCIAL: Pretraining with Code Curriculums via Iterative Search for Accelerated Learning
arxiv:2610.24970.abstract: Fully synthetic pretraining data generated by symbolic programs can bootstrap downstream training on naturalistic tasks, such as language modeling, but the generating programs have so far been designed by hand. We introduce PRECOCIAL, a method for automatically optimizing programs that generate synthetic pretraining data. Starting from an initial generator program, an LLM iteratively rewrites the program, and each rewrite is scored by pretraining a randomly-initialized transformer on its data and fine-tuning it on the downstream task. Because every score requires training, PRECOCIAL keeps a single network for the entire search, continuing its pretraining for each accepted program instead of training a new network per candidate, making it significantly more efficient. On four language and code datasets, at a fixed fine-tuning budget, optimized programs reach lower perplexity than hand-designed curricula, published procedural generators, random program mutation and the program the LLM writes in the first iteration of the search, and reach the same perplexity as the hand-designed curricula with 9-33% fewer fine-tuning steps. PRECOCIAL also ends with lower perplexity than FunSearch and AlphaEvolve, which train a new network for every candidate, at the same number of evaluations and a lower cost. We also observe that an optimized program generator from one domain transfers to datasets in other domains. Additionally, optimized programs allow for better downstream performance on four different reasoning and problem-solving tasks.

arxiv:2610.24739.title: Toward Collective Model Intelligence: Characterizing and Coordinating Models
arxiv:2610.24739.abstract: Independently developed AI models accumulate diverse and complementary capabilities, but a growing model collection does not automatically realize Collective AI. Addressing this gap requires understanding model capabilities with limited evaluation, organizing complementary models to collaborate on diverse tasks, and executing model calls efficiently under resource constraints. We present a systematic approach to pursuing Collective Model Intelligence through three connected components. First, Model Eval constructs evidence-based capability profiles by combining query-level performance estimation with cross-domain prediction, reducing the need for exhaustive evaluation. Second, Mio (Models in One) organizes complementary model candidates and supports task-conditioned, cost-aware selection and collaboration as task requirements evolve. Third, Mos (Model Serving OS) separates model selection from execution and provides endpoint scheduling and shared model deployment and distribution. Experiments show lower capability-estimation errors under limited evaluation. Across nine public benchmarks, Mio 1.0 Lite achieves the highest average score and lowest average cost among compared methods, with per-request costs 73.7-97.5% lower than those of the best-scoring alternatives. A prewarmed shared cache accelerates model-file retrieval by up to 23.3 times. This work lays a foundation for Collective Model Intelligence by characterizing and coordinating the diverse capabilities of an expanding model universe.

arxiv:2610.24538.title: Accelerating Finite-Sum Bilevel Optimization with Fully First-Order Oracles
arxiv:2610.24538.abstract: We study nonconvex--strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives and fully first-order oracles. We propose Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (SICBO), which combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. Under componentwise lower strong convexity, SICBO finds a point $x$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nablaΦ(x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ within $\tilde{O}(N+\sqrt{N}κ^{7/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient calls, where $N$ is the total number of components and $κ$ is the normalized lower-level condition number. The bound achieves square-root finite-sum dependence using only gradients and preserves the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number exponent for smooth problems. Our improvement follows from a curvature-dependent bound for nonlinear correction errors, which permits epochs of length $\tildeΘ(\sqrt{N/κ})$ with batches of size $\tildeΘ(\sqrt{Nκ})$. A single-level reduction shows that the dependence on $N$ and $\varepsilon$ is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed $κ$.

arxiv:2610.24536.title: A Multi-Step Inertial ADMM Algorithm for Federated Learning
arxiv:2610.24536.abstract: Federated learning has recently emerged as an important paradigm for large-scale distributed model training, which can be naturally formulated as a class of distributed learning problems. The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a widely used approach for solving such problems. However, its practical performance is often hindered by significant communication overhead and system heterogeneity. In this paper, we propose a multi-step inertial ADMM algorithm, called MiFedADMM, for federated learning. The proposed method leverages multiple historical iterates on the server side to construct a higher-order extrapolation after each aggregation to accelerate the convergence behavior. Under mild assumptions, we establish convergence results for the single-step variant of the proposed method and derive an O(1/K) convergence rate. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and improved performance of the proposed method compared with existing approaches.

arxiv:2610.24535.title: From Score to Diagnosis: Search-Independent Post-Diagnosis for Symbolic Regression
arxiv:2610.24535.abstract: Symbolic regression (SR) solvers employ diverse search mechanisms, yet most rely on the same low-information scalar fitness. Such scores provide little guidance on why a skeleton fails or how it should be revised. Recent methods develop new methods to address this bottleneck. Their enhanced feedback mechanisms are tightly coupled to their search processes and are difficult to reuse across diverse SR solvers. Instead, we ask whether a shared feedback mechanism can further improve diverse solvers facing the same bottleneck. To this end, we propose PostDiag, a search-independent feedback mechanism, which can be shared to different SR solvers. PostDiag introduces Patch-wise Feature Profiling (PFP) to capture local behavior through patch-wise features of level, trend, and roughness. Based on PFP, PostDiag quantifies Skeleton Expressiveness Risk by comparing the fitted candidate with the observations, and Skeleton Stability Risk by measuring variability of behavior after bootstrap refitting. The Diagnostic Risk Plane (DRP) combines two risks to determine whether a skeleton should be preserved, repaired, simplified, or rewritten, while the patch-wise discrepancies provide evidence for the intervention. An LLM editor then performs the diagnosis-guided intervention, and the validated revision is returned to the original solver through a lightweight adapter. Experiments across multiple LLM-based and GP-based SR solvers show that PostDiag consistently improves accuracy and accelerates convergence.

arxiv:2610.24534.title: Structured Latent Dynamics for Long-Horizon Embodied World Models
arxiv:2610.24534.abstract: Reliable long-horizon prediction remains a central challenge for embodied world models. Although recent generative models can synthesize visually plausible action-conditioned futures, their latent dynamics are typically learned through unconstrained transition modules, which may gradually deviate from coherent physical evolution as predictions are recursively rolled forward. We investigate whether explicitly structuring latent state evolution can improve the stability and utility of such imagined trajectories. To this end, we introduce HWM, a structured dynamics framework that represents backbone latents in a learned phase space consisting of generalized coordinates and momenta. Future states are propagated through dissipative Hamiltonian dynamics and mapped back to the original latent representation through a learnable inverse interface. The resulting formulation can be integrated into existing world-model architectures without redesigning their perception or decoding components, while multi-step transition supervision encourages the structured rollout to remain aligned with the latent trajectories induced by real observations. Controlled simulation experiments show that HWM produces more accurate estimates of velocity, acceleration, and jerk and substantially reduces long-horizon energy drift relative to unstructured latent dynamics. We further evaluate the approach across three distinct embodied world-model settings, covering single-arm multi-view prediction with Ctrl-World, dual-arm single-view prediction with EVAC, and task-oriented single-arm prediction with Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B. On RoboCasa, incorporating HWM into Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B yields a 2.7% relative improvement in task success. On real-world AgiBot World trajectories, it improves nDTW by 9.7% with Ctrl-World and Logic by 8.4% with EVAC.

arxiv:2610.24355.title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
arxiv:2610.24355.abstract: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. We present Koi, a self-calibrating cluster planner for heterogeneous, multi-cloud fleets. Koi uses a Recursive Language Model (RLM) hierarchy to propose hypotheses and reason over deployment while deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement. It represents inference behavior as a fixed causal graph linking decisions (e.g., accelerator, parallelism), runtime mediators (e.g., KV-cache pressure, communication overhead), and outcomes (e.g., latency, throughput). Each deployment strengthens or weakens scoped causal relationships, building a comprehensive playbook for inference that the planner employs to guide future decisions. Job-wise configurations are composed into cluster-wide plans and evaluated against serving objectives, resource constraints, SLO risks, and cost. Across benchmarks, Koi achieves 1.18x greater goodput than the strongest baseline while reducing $/token by 20% in a real heterogeneous cluster. Ablations isolate the contribution of Koi's architecture: a pure language model attains a composite score of 35.3, the same model equipped with Koi's deterministic tools reaches 51.6, and the full Koi planner reaches 70.8.

arxiv:2610.24349.title: FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines for Physical AI Inference
arxiv:2610.24349.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3-3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38-12.66x speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.

arxiv:2610.24185.title: Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree for Inference-time Search Under Sparse Reward
arxiv:2610.24185.abstract: Tree-based samplers offer a compelling alternative for scalable inference-time search, bypassing the per-step reward and gradient dependencies that introduce systematic bias into SMC-style frameworks. Despite this advantage, contemporary tree samplers fail to achieve broad exploration. Their reliance on learned, DDPM-like transitions inherently couples neighbor states in a trajectory, thereby restricting child-parent feature divergence in the tree sampler. Consequently, these samplers suffer from restricted coverage of the target marginal distribution, severely hindering the exploration critical for efficient search under sparse reward. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a simple yet effective Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree (BSIT) sampler that decouples child node generation from explicit parent dependencies. By expanding the degrees of freedom during child node sampling, BSIT encourages diverse trajectory rollouts and unlocks broader path-space diversity-the exact catalyst needed for efficient exploration. Crucially, we show that BSIT's improved exploration accelerates convergence to the target distribution while achieving broader distributional coverage than samplers that rely on DDPM-like transitions for child-node generation, all without incurring additional function evaluations or reward feedback, thereby providing a highly efficient basis for rare target search.
