The findings reflect context-bound perceptions rather than measures of learning outcomes; they nevertheless suggest that sequencing games after conceptual input and combining competitive and skill-oriented platforms may support positive affective states in online language classes. Thus, the study contributes qualitative evidence to a field predominantly served by quantitative designs. Implications and directions for triangulated future research are discussed.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fnut.2026.1958865.title: Nutritional status, inflammatory burden, and CT-derived muscle phenotypes for predicting chronic postsurgical pain after total hip arthroplasty: an explainable machine learning study
doi:10.3389/fnut.2026.1958865.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hip fracture (HF) is a common fragility fracture in older adults and may lead to persistent pain and impaired recovery. Chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) after total hip arthroplasty (THA) negatively affects rehabilitation and quality of life. This study aimed to develop and validate a machine learning model integrating clinical variables, peri-hip muscle characteristics, and nutrition-related inflammatory indicators for CPSP prediction after THA in patients with HF.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This single-center cohort study included patients with HF undergoing primary unilateral THA between October 2022 and March 2026. Patients from October 2022 to September 2024 were randomly divided into training and internal validation sets, while those from October 2024 to March 2026 served as an independent temporal test set. CPSP was defined as surgery-related pain persisting for ≥3 months with NRS ≥4. Candidate predictors included clinical, psychological, nutritional, inflammatory, and CT-derived muscle parameters. LASSO and Boruta were used for feature selection, and six machine learning algorithms were compared. SHAP analysis was applied to interpret the optimal model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 881 patients, 137/529 (25.9%) developed CPSP in the development cohort. Seven predictors were selected: GNRI, gluteus medius/minimus muscle density, gluteus medius/minimus cross-sectional area, NLR, age, preoperative anxiety, and PNI. The SVM model showed the best performance, achieving an AUC of 0.854 in the temporal test set, with accuracy of 0.770, sensitivity of 0.789, specificity of 0.763, NPV of 0.913, F1-score of 0.637, and Brier score of 0.125. SHAP analysis identified GNRI as the most influential predictor (35.4%), followed by muscle density (13.6%) and NLR (12.5%).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A machine learning model integrating clinical, CT-derived muscle, and nutrition-related inflammatory features showed good predictive performance for CPSP after THA in patients with HF and may support early risk stratification and individualized perioperative management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.30872/jlpf.v7i2.6790.title: Scientific Argumentation in Physics Learning and Its Influence on Scientific Literacy: A Systematic Literature Review
doi:10.30872/jlpf.v7i2.6790.abstract: <jats:p>This study uses a systematic literature review approach. There are 22 articles that are analyzed in depth and comprehensively using the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis) method. The stages of the PRISMA method consist of identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion. The databases used are Scopus and Google Scholar. This study consists of 3 research questions, namely (1) research trends on scientific argumentation in physics learning; (2) implementation of scientific argumentation in physics learning; and (3) the influence of scientific argumentation on students' scientific literacy. The findings of this study are: (1) research trends on scientific argumentation in physics learning are mostly conducted in Indonesia; the year of most publications is 2025, the most frequently used research method is the quantitative approach, and the research subjects are junior high and senior high school students; (2) this study explains that scientific argumentation in physics learning integrates one or more STEM components and the most widely used Toulmin argumentation pattern; (3) scientific argumentation in physics learning has a positive influence on students' scientific literacy skills.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-9953-9.ch010.title: Mathematical Meaning in Maker-STEAM (M3S)
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-9953-9.ch010.abstract: <jats:p>Despite the rapid proliferation of STEAM and maker-inspired education, a fundamental conceptual tension persists: mathematics is repeatedly positioned as a peripheral tool for measurement and computation rather than as the integrative core of interdisciplinary design. This theoretical chapter responds to this gap by developing the Mathematical Meaning in Maker-STEAM (M3S) Framework—a four-dimensional conceptual model grounded in an integrative conceptual synthesis of mathematics education, maker pedagogy, design-based learning, representational theory, and equity-oriented teaching. The four dimensions—Mathematical Modeling and Quantification, Design and Iterative Reasoning, Representational Mobility, and Equity-Oriented Teacher Mediation—are theorized as mutually constitutive aspects of a coherent pedagogical ecology. Crucially, the framework also integrates aesthetic design reasoning as a mathematically generative strand of arts integration in STEAM. The chapter is supplemented by two illustrative vignettes and an analytic rubric for classroom-based assessment.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-9953-9.ch010.venue: Transforming STEAM Education With Maker-Inspired Learning Environments

doi:10.3744/snak.2026.63.5.388.title: Deep Learning-based Fuel Oil Consumption Prediction for Twin-screw Ship
doi:10.3744/snak.2026.63.5.388.abstract: With growing pressure from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to reach net-zero emissions by 2050, accurate prediction of ship Fuel Oil Consumption (FOC) has become increasingly important. Although numerous deep learning-based FOC prediction models have been proposed, studies targeting twin-screw ships remain scarce. In this paper, we propose a dual-branch deep learning architecture for multi-step FOC prediction of twin-screw ships, designed to capture the distinct operational characteristics of the port and starboard propulsion shafts. Each branch independently encodes feature-axis relationships using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) encoder and temporal patterns using a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) encoder. A Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) block is employed to adaptively fuse the encoded representations, and an autoregressive GRU decoder then generates multi-step FOC predictions. The model is trained on five months of operational data from a RO-RO passenger ship navigating the Gunsan–Shidao route, supplemented with wave data from the Copernicus Marine Environment Monitoring Service (CMEMS). Experiments under various prediction conditions demonstrate that the proposed model consistently outperforms nine baseline models, including LSTM, GRU, transformer variants, and recent hybrid architectures, across the RMSE, MAE, and MAPE metrics.
doi:10.3744/snak.2026.63.5.388.venue: Journal of the Society of Naval Architects of Korea

doi:10.37329/ijms.v4i3.5753.title: Ethnopedagogy of the Ngerebeg Tradition in Tegal Darmasaba Traditional Village as A Social Studies Learning Resource
doi:10.37329/ijms.v4i3.5753.abstract: <jats:p>Ethnopedagogy is essential for supporting contextual social studies instruction grounded in culture and local wisdom. This study analyzes the Ngerebeg tradition in the Tegal Darmasaba Traditional Village. The primary focus is on identifying values ​​that can serve as resources for social studies learning via an ethnopedagogical approach and determining how to integrate them into the curriculum. Conducted over a three-year period (2023-2025), the research aims to: 1) analyze the potential ethnopedagogical values ​​represented in the Ngerebeg tradition; 2) analyze the social studies content and concepts reflected in the tradition; and 3) analyze methods for implementing these elements in social studies instruction. A qualitative ethnographic research method was employed, with the Ngerebeg tradition serving as the object of study. Research subjects were selected using purposive and snowball sampling techniques, the total sample consisted of 28 individuals, five of whom were selected purposively. Data analysis utilized an ethnographic thematic approach. Empirical ethnographic findings reveal that the Ngerebeg tradition embodies religious, educational, economic, artistic, social, political, theoretical, and symbolic values. Furthermore, analysis and pedagogical recommendations indicate that the philosophical and practical aspects of the Ngerebeg tradition reflect social studies subject matter. Ethnopedagogical application of the Ngerebeg tradition can be achieved through field studies, the development of learning resources, and the creation of instructional media. The study concludes that the Ngerebeg tradition holds educational and contextual value and aligns with the social studies curriculum for middle school.</jats:p>

doi:10.1075/aila.00073.haf.title: Digital spaces and language learning
doi:10.1075/aila.00073.haf.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this commentary, I consider contributions to the special issue on Challenges and Affordances in Digital Spaces. The contributions both build on well-established areas of interest in language learning and technology (like digital multimodal composing, for example) and attend to relatively new frontiers in the digital domain (like AI and platformization). I comment on three inter-related themes that are raised in the special issue: (1) process and distributed agency, (2) criticality and creativity, (3) power, platforms and legitimacy. I close with a call for more research to better understand how language and literacy educators can rise to meet increasing challenges in ways that promote active and critical learning, meaningful activity, and individual agency.</jats:p>

doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld37944.title: Spatial Modeling of Urban Land Surface Temperature with Interpretable Machine Learning: Cross-City Generalization Across Three Chinese Cities
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld37944.abstract: <jats:p>This study developed spatial predictive models of urban land surface temperature in Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou using four methods—multiple linear regression, random forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM—to assess cross-city generalization. Ensemble tree models performed far better than the linear model in all three cities, with XGBoost achieving the best accuracy in Beijing and Shanghai and LightGBM performing slightly better in Guangzhou. Predictive performance degraded dramatically after cross-city transfer, and increasing the number of training cities did not consistently restore predictive skill, indicating that surface temperature is strongly shaped by local geographical factors. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis revealed significant differences in dominant factors across cities: Digital Elevation Model (DEM) contributed most in both Beijing and Guangzhou, while the built-up index and distance from the city center were the key drivers in Shanghai. Spatial residual analysis showed more pronounced spatial variation in prediction errors in Beijing, whereas residuals in Shanghai and Guangzhou were mainly distributed near zero. These results indicate that machine learning has substantial limitations for cross-regional prediction of urban land surface temperature, and that local calibration or domain adaptation strategies are needed for cross-city applications.</jats:p>
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld37944.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld37894.title: Forecasting Stock Market Synchronicity: An Out-of-Sample Comparison of Statistical and Machine Learning Models
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld37894.abstract: <jats:p>Stock–market synchronicity measures the extent to which individual stock returns move with the overall market and is relevant to risk assessment and portfolio allocation. This study examines whether next-quarter synchronicity can be predicted and whether machine-learning models improve on simpler benchmarks. Daily price and volume data for 25 U.S. large-cap stocks from 2010 to 2025 were used to estimate quarterly R² values from regressions of individual stock returns on SPY returns. A persistence benchmark, ordinary least squares (OLS), decision tree, and random forest were evaluated on an untouched 2022–2025 test set using MAE, RMSE, predictive R², and out-of-sample R². OLS achieved the lowest RMSE (0.1873), the highest predictive R² (0.3255), and a 10.5% reduction in squared forecast error relative to persistence, although persistence produced the lowest MAE (0.1416). Both tree-based models performed worse in point prediction. Current synchronicity and VIX conditions were important predictors, while performance varied across volatility regimes and sectors. The random forest nevertheless separated stocks with relatively high and low future synchronicity. Overall, simple linear methods were more reliable for precise forecasting, whereas machine learning offered complementary ranking insights.</jats:p>
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld37894.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

doi:10.54254/2753-8818/2026.pu37983.title: Comparison of Machine Learning Models under the Background of the 2013 University of California, Irvine Wholesale Customers Dataset
doi:10.54254/2753-8818/2026.pu37983.abstract: <jats:p>Customer spending patterns can provide useful information for identifying the channels of wholesale customers, supporting customer management and marketing decisions. This study examines whether six annual spending categories can be used to classify customers by sales channels. Using the University of California, Irvine (UCI) Wholesale Customers dataset, which contains 440 customers, four classification models, including Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting, were compared using Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-score, and Receiver Operating Characteristic - Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC). Stratified five-fold cross-validation was used to report mean and standard deviation. Feature subsets, Channel and Region prediction, and K-Means clustering were also compared. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting showed similar performance, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) performed worse. Using two or three important features produced performance close to that of all six features. Channel was easier to predict than Region, and K-Means showed moderate agreement with the true Channel labels (ARI = 0.5135). These findings show that a small number of spending features can provide useful information for customer channel classification.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8069-8.ch010.title: From Styles to Strategies
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8069-8.ch010.abstract: <jats:p>Immersive virtual reality (IVR) learning environments have the potential to support embodiment, engagement, and experiential problem-solving approaches, enhancing the performance and engagement of diverse learners. Existing research has drawn on cognitive and learning style frameworks to account for these distinctions. Findings based on frameworks are often inconsistent and offer limited explanatory value in immersive settings. This chapter argues for inconsistencies, offering a framework for the interaction design. Taking a human-technology interaction perspective, it reframes individual differences in IVR learning by shifting attention from cognitive and learning styles. It focuses on behavioural strategies, emotional regulation, and technological adaptation as key processes. The chapter addresses methodological implications, pointing to the value of process-oriented, longitudinal, and mixed-method approaches to study immersive learning. It takes a strategy-oriented approach to IVR design to clarify theory and provide practical insights for researchers, educators, and designers.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-3373-8069-8.ch010.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld38022.title: Data Quality Challenges in Artificial Intelligence: Impacts of Missing, Mislabeled and Biased Data on Machine Learning
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld38022.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is developing at a high speed and is now used in many places. AI models need a large amount of data to some extent; therefore, problems in the data can lead to errors in the model. The three main types of harmful data that are the subject of this study are biased, mislabelled and missing data. If a large part of the data set is missing, it will result in information loss and a lower-performing model. In addition, the model may be incorrectly trained due to mislabelled data and thus unreliable. If the data are biased, then there will be discrimination against some groups. Some possible countermeasures have also been mentioned in the discussion. Imputation or Deletion Methods are used to address missing values. Data cleaning, label verification and noise-robust learning can all reduce mislabelled data. Bias in the data can be addressed before, during and after model training. Generally speaking, there is no single way to handle all the data problems. Different datasets and problems have different solutions, so they will be different.</jats:p>
doi:10.54254/2754-1169/2026.ld38022.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

doi:10.26599/frict.2026.9441239.title: Generative deep learning for hydrodynamic lubrication prediction by a deconvolutional neural network
doi:10.26599/frict.2026.9441239.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Classical hydrodynamic lubrication simulation solves the Reynolds equation to unveil the lubrication pressure and film thickness distributions, yet it overlooks the latent high-level representations buried beneath the lubrication data. While deep learning has illustrated that the mining of high-level representations helps to generate desired outputs from input prompts, lubrication research has not fully exploited generative deep learning in lubrication prediction and generation. Here, we propose adopting a deconvolutional neural network to learn the latent representations in hydrodynamic lubrication data and directly generate a two-dimensional (2D) lubrication scenario from the given working conditions without solving any governing equation. Compared with the classical method, our approach can output the distribution of lubrication pressure and film thickness in less than 0.1 s on a personal computer and be extended to more complicated scenarios, including cavitation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.31464/jlere.1944527.title: Concept Teaching in B1-Level Foreign Language Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study
doi:10.31464/jlere.1944527.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">In teaching Turkish as a foreign language, learners’ ability to acquire concepts meaningfully and effectively, to establish relationships among concepts, and to concretise abstract notions is crucial to conceptual learning. Especially at the B1 proficiency level, where abstract concepts become more prevalent, conceptual instruction needs to be systematically addressed to enable learners to use the target language effectively. However, studies conducted in the field of teaching Turkish as a foreign language indicate that instructional materials and classroom practices predominantly focus on vocabulary teaching. Moreover, the absence of a comprehensive instructional model specifically designed for concept teaching negatively affects the quality of the concept learning process. Given this gap in the literature, the present study aims to examine the effect of the Holistic Concept Development Model (HCDM) on learners of Turkish as a foreign language's concept learning outcomes. The study was designed according to a mixed-methods research approach and conducted during the 2024–2025 academic year at the Gaziantep University Turkish Language Teaching Implementation and Research Centre, involving 34 volunteer students: 21 in the experimental group and 13 in the control group. In the experimental group, concepts were structured according to the stages of the HCDM and taught through activities utilising concept teaching tools and Web 2.0 tools. In contrast, instruction in the control group was conducted solely through textbook-based activities, without the use of concept-teaching tools or Web 2.0 applications. Overall, the findings suggest that the HCDM strengthens the learning process and effectively supports meaningful concept learning in teaching Turkish as a foreign language.</jats:p>

arxiv:2610.28250.title: Physics-constrained graph closures and working-point conditioning for a fast surrogate of linac beam dynamics
arxiv:2610.28250.abstract: When a graph neural network estimates a physical quantity, its frame, edge direction, aggregation and feature normalization decide which laws it can break. Wrong choices leave systematic errors the loss never registers. We build a linac beam-dynamics surrogate on this observation. Space charge, short-range wakefields and coherent synchrotron radiation enter as bounded closures on analytic kernels, on graphs whose frame and direction follow the interaction and whose symmetry makes the net space-charge self-force vanish for any weights. Verified without training, with randomized weights, the invariants break by five to eight orders of magnitude once the responsible feature is inverted. Per-working-point models constrained by the rms envelope equation are distilled into one model conditioned on 15 machine settings. On the 18.4~m L0+L1 section of the Shanghai soft x-ray free-electron laser linac, this model predicts the transverse beam envelope at 50 unseen settings to about $7\%$, with the centroid trajectory and emittance, in 0.38~s on a single Quadro RTX 6000 GPU. Training is instead dominated by a normalization choice, a data-derived output range for the beam size: at all 16 working points it lowers the starting error 2.2- to 8.5-fold and fixes the convergence speed. The remaining accuracy differences between hybrid and data-driven architectures vary with the working point and with the density of observation. The held-out error scales roughly as $N^{-0.6}$ with the corpus size $N$. Whether the physics pays off where collective effects are strong, as in a magnetic bunch compressor, is in the next phase of our study.

arxiv:2610.28619.title: Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction: How far should we go?
arxiv:2610.28619.abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival, the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner's prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft-target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%.

arxiv:2610.28591.title: PaPi: Parallel Picard-Duhamel Integration for Fast Neuro-Spectral Architectures
arxiv:2610.28591.abstract: Neuro-spectral architectures (NeuSA) are a class of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that have proven effective for solving time-dependent PDEs in the frequency domain. However, training and inference often rely on costly numerical integration of the learned vector field, typically using sequential Runge-Kutta time stepping, which limits temporal parallelism. We introduce PaPi, an integration scheme inspired by weakly nonlinear flows that enables time-Parallel inference through exponential integration and a Duhamel-Picard scheme. We show that the Duhamel-Picard iteration converges exponentially for all flows, and provide explicit error bounds that depend on how close the flow is to linear. Experiments show that PaPi accelerates training and inference by up to two orders of magnitude, achieving training times of under one second for low-dimensional PDE learning problems, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.

arxiv:2610.28559.title: Large Flow Language Models
arxiv:2610.28559.abstract: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.

arxiv:2610.28500.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
arxiv:2610.28500.abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP

arxiv:2610.28441.title: Stratified Sparse Attention: Reducing the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity
arxiv:2610.28441.abstract: Large Language Model inference over long contexts is increasingly bottlenecked by the cost of attending to a growing Key-Value (KV) cache. Sparse attention reduces this cost by accessing only a fraction of the cache, but existing methods face a trade-off between deterministic retrieval, which captures high-scoring tokens but discards residual attention mass, and sampling, which improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combine top-$k$ retrieval with uniform sampling, yet still exhibit a substantial gap from dense attention at aggressive sparsity. We introduce \emph{Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA)}, a unified framework combining deterministic retrieval with score-guided sampling. SSA deterministically attends to high-scoring tokens while sampling the residual using proxy attention scores and correcting for their inclusion probabilities, thereby recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set. SSA encompasses top-$k$, top-$p$, and hybrid top-$k$+sampling as special cases. Across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME, and five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters, SSA consistently improves over the baselines at matched sparsity. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B, SSA improves accuracy over the strongest practical baseline from 81.8\% to 84.2\% at 32K and from 63.8\% to 69.3\% at 128K under $50\times$ attention sparsity, recovering 94\% and 85\% of dense-attention performance, respectively. With optimized CUDA kernels, SSA achieves up to $2.96\times$ decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context, demonstrating that its accuracy gains translate into practical long-context inference acceleration. We open-source our code at https://github.com/skylight-org/SSA-Paper-Code.

arxiv:2610.28351.title: RayCo4D: Ray-Conditioned Continuous Motion Model for Monocular 4D Dynamic Reconstruction
arxiv:2610.28351.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video requires inferring motion from noisy and intermittently visible observations. Long-range tracks provide valuable geometric constraints, but integrating their fragmented temporal coverage into shared, continuous motion remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{RayCo4D}, a ray-conditioned continuous motion model for monocular 4D reconstruction that explicitly separates visual measurements from latent 3D motion states. Each track is associated with a reference-time 3D query constrained to its camera ray, and its image and depth observations constrain shared latent motion nodes through local many-to-many associations. Each node maintains an $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ pose and body-frame velocity at sparse support times. A white-noise-on-acceleration process prior couples neighboring states and defines continuous-time interpolation, allowing observations across visibility intervals to jointly constrain the same latent state sequence.The inferred shared motion is transferred to Gaussian primitives through dual-quaternion blending, while reference-anchored local $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ residuals capture fine-scale non-rigid deformation beyond the shared scaffold. Experiments on diverse monocular dynamic scenes show that RayCo4D achieves competitive novel-view synthesis quality, improves structural and temporal consistency under rapid motion and incomplete tracks, and supports continuous-time rendering.

arxiv:2610.28173.title: Africa-Papers: A 10-Billion-Token Multi-Domain Academic Corpus for African Foundation Language Models
arxiv:2610.28173.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) depend fundamentally on the diversity, depth, and factual rigor of their pre-training corpora. However, contemporary foundational pre-training datasets (such as The Pile, S2ORC, and Dolma) exhibit a severe structural omission: African scientific, medical, legal, and agricultural scholarship constitutes less than 0.5% of global pre-training tokens. Consequently, state-of-the-art models suffer from systematic failure modes when reasoning about tropical epidemiology, localized smallholder agro-ecologies, regional economic governance, and indigenous linguistic structures. To resolve this representation deficit and advance African intellectual sovereignty in artificial intelligence, we introduce Africa-Papers, the largest curated multi-domain Pan-African academic pre-training corpus to date. Comprising over 844,807 full-text papers spanning 10.15 billion tokens across 879 Parquet shards, Africa-Papers unifies four primary scientific streams: (1) continental peer-reviewed journals indexed in DOAJ across 31 African nations, (2) the CGIAR CGSpace agricultural repository, (3) African-authored and African-focused STEM/AI preprints on arXiv, and (4) open-access international publications by scholars affiliated with African institutions indexed via OpenAlex. The entire corpus is processed into layout-aware, clean Markdown preserving section hierarchies, mathematical equations, and tabular data, accompanied by exact BPE token counts and a standardized 8-domain taxonomy. We release Africa-Papers openly on the Hugging Face Hub under the AfriSpeech organization to accelerate continual pre-training and domain evaluation for foundation models globally.

arxiv:2610.28107.title: Weak-$L^α$ Noise, Strong Guarantees: Gradient Clipping under Affine Heavy Tails
arxiv:2610.28107.abstract: Gradient clipping is a key tool for obtaining high-probability convergence guarantees for stochastic first-order methods under heavy-tailed noise. Existing analyses typically assume a bounded central moment of order $α\in(1,2]$, which excludes distributions with tails of order $u^{-α}$ at the critical exponent. In this paper, we consider smooth convex optimization under affine heavy-tailed noise, whose scale may grow with the gradient norm. We derive high-probability convergence guarantees for clipped SGD (Clip-SGD) and its accelerated variant Clip-SSTM under a weak-$L^α$ tail condition, which is strictly weaker than the corresponding moment bound. For $1<α<2$, the clipping bounds have the same powers of the clipping level as in the moment case, and both methods attain the additive stochastic rate $K^{-(α-1)/α}$. The gradient-dependent noise contributes a faster-decaying term of order $K^{-2(α-1)/α}$, up to logarithmic factors. At $α=2$, we characterize the additional logarithmic factor on the Lorentz scale and establish its necessity for the additive error at fixed confidence. We also analyze Clip-SGD with prescribed clipping levels and derive finite-horizon guarantees for reaching a neighborhood determined by the clipping bias. For additive noise, matching lower bounds show that this neighborhood is unavoidable, up to constants and the natural error cap. Numerical experiments with Pareto noise illustrate the theoretical results.

arxiv:2610.27895.title: The Shape of the DPO Hyperparameter Landscape: What to Measure, How It Moves with Scale, and When Not to Transfer It
arxiv:2610.27895.abstract: Direct preference optimisation (DPO) is widely used for language model post-training, but its performance depends strongly on the choice of its hyperparameters, such as the learning rate and the reference-policy regularisation parameter $β$. To better understand the DPO hyperparameter landscape, we conduct extensive experiments using a dense hyperparameter grid across different model scales from the same family. This allows us to analyse how the optimal DPO hyperparameters evolve with model size and the number of update steps, with intermediate checkpoints providing an inexpensive signal to accelerate the hyperparameter optimisation process. Furthermore, by evaluating our models on both static and dynamic benchmarks, we identify which benchmarks provide the strongest signal for hyperparameter selection. Finally, we investigate how different state-of-the-art hyperparameter optimisation strategies perform in this setting. Our experiments show that the optimal learning rate varies with model size and that hyperparameters are not transferable across training datasets. We also find that validation loss is a poor proxy for hyperparameter optimisation, as hyperparameters that minimize validation loss only weakly correlate with optimal hyperparameters for downstream benchmarks. Therefore, DPO hyperparameters need to be tuned specifically for the target model, dataset, and evaluation objective. We also show that short candidate training runs can substantially reduce the cost of this selection. We release all our training configurations and evaluation results to support reproducible analysis of selection quality and training cost.

arxiv:2610.27888.title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems
arxiv:2610.27888.abstract: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.

arxiv:2610.27815.title: ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding
arxiv:2610.27815.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive (AR) language models by letting a small model draft tokens serially and a large model verify them in parallel. We reverse these roles. Starting from a standard AR checkpoint, we fine-tune the large model into a proposer that predicts a block of future tokens in a single forward pass, then use one additional forward pass to verify the proposed block. This gives ProVe, Proposer-Verifier decoding. The verifier can be a smaller AR model or the proposer itself; the latter gives ProVe-lossless, which reproduces the proposer's greedy AR decoding. Block proposals already provide substantial room for acceleration: with a block size of 16, the proposed block has an average AR-matching prefix of 6.6 tokens on GSM8K. Across six benchmarks with a 32B proposer, ProVe-lossless reaches 2.5x average AR throughput without training a separate draft head. With a small 3B verifier, ProVe reaches 2.7x average throughput at 2.6 accuracy points below AR on the six-task average, providing a controllable tradeoff between speed and accuracy.

arxiv:2610.27813.title: LatBridge: Efficient and Stable Model Replacement in Latent-Communication Multi-Agent Systems
arxiv:2610.27813.abstract: Multi-agent systems rely on communication to complete tasks, and latent communication passes continuous representations to reduce text generation and re-encoding. However, multi-agent systems must reconfigure agent models, whereas existing latent-communication methods are built for fixed model combinations, so their interfaces may fail after replacement. Our pilot study confirms this interface failure and identifies the requirement for interface reuse after model replacement. We present LatBridge, which connects agent models through a shared Bridge and separate interfaces under a shared latent-communication protocol. After agent model replacement, LatBridge reuses unchanged interfaces, selects matching low-rank interfaces, and combines them through the Bridge, training only missing ones with all models frozen. The Bridge processes source representations in the basic mode and constructs target input without autoregressive generation in the accelerated mode. Experiments support effective communication after model replacement, with mean basic-mode accuracies of 14.8% on MATH and 27.3% on ALFWorld next-action prediction across eight small-model configurations. Analyses examine the factors supporting task accuracy and communication efficiency.

arxiv:2610.27621.title: A Radiation-Hardened, Fault-Aware Quantized Neural Network That Self-Heals
arxiv:2610.27621.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly being deployed into radiation-challenging environments in spacecraft, particle accelerators, and, soon, space-based data centers. Instantiated as a learned orchestration of numbers stored in persistent memory, models are susceptible to continual degradation as high-energy particles corrupt data. At inference time, new data passed through the network fundamentally break the off-line assumptions and guarantees of a static model determined during training. To preserve the quality and efficacy of the models, fault tolerance against bit flips is a clear objective. In this work we developed a runtime method for repairing the quantized weights of neural networks (NNs) after bit flips on commodity, commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware, without storing extra replicas. Our work extends the well-established Fault-Aware Training (FAT) paradigm by adding an alignment penalty to concentrate undamaged activations and weights into a low-rank subspace, and we then reconstruct flagged corrupted coordinates from the uncorrupted survivors. We call this method {\it Projection Healing} and apply it to six regression benchmarks on quantized NNs. Holding a FAT checkpoint fixed and toggling only the runtime heal gives a further ${\sim}23\%$ reduction in the native-unit excess integral. Across those datasets the method extends the operational scrub interval by a median of $2.04\times$ at a $+5\%$ RMSE degradation and $1.96\times$ at $+50\%$, compared with $1.62\times$ and $1.07\times$ for classical Single Error Correction, Double Error Detection (SECDED). This introduces a new path towards designing resilient data-driven models, complementing established hardware redundancy, ECC, and FAT-based techniques.

arxiv:2610.27588.title: Beyond Experience: Knowledge-Guided Evolution for NPU Kernel Generation
arxiv:2610.27588.abstract: LLM agents have become capable kernel engineers on mainstream GPU stacks, but they struggle on emerging accelerators such as Ascend NPUs, whose programming model is barely represented in pretraining data. Recent NPU agents address this gap largely through experience: they accumulate memory from their own generation and optimization trials and reuse it on later tasks. We argue that experience alone is not enough for kernel generation. An agent can only remember what it has tried, and it rarely tries a mechanism it does not know. As a result, such memory offers little help when a new operator calls for a different mechanism, and even familiar operators raise unseen situations as optimization proceeds. We present ASCENDEVOLVE, which grounds every step of an evolutionary kernel search in a large external knowledge base built from platform documentation, toolkit headers, and operator repositories. Because this corpus far exceeds any context window, ASCENDEVOLVE indexes it and routes each agent to a small, task-specific slice of evidence instead of the corpus itself. The retrieved knowledge seeds diverse implementation strategies, guides repair when a candidate fails, and constrains how strong candidates are recombined. On 53 Ascend C operators from CANN-Bench spanning four difficulty levels, ASCENDEVOLVE achieves an overall score of 71.39, improving over Reflexion and OpenEvolve by 11.6% and 17.2%.

arxiv:2610.27379.title: DStill: Trajectory Consistency Distillation for Accelerated One-Step Drafting in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
arxiv:2610.27379.abstract: Block-diffusion speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel. However, one-step drafting in discrete diffusion is limited by token factorization error: each token is predicted from the same masked block, without conditioning on the tokens selected at other positions in that step. This can produce inconsistent drafts and reduce acceptance length. Iterative refinement mitigates this limitation by conditioning later predictions on previously committed tokens, though additional passes increase drafting cost. To address this trade-off between draft fidelity and inference latency, we introduce DStill, a two-stage framework that distills a target-conditioned drafter's own multi-step refinement into one-step drafting. We first train the drafter to complete partially revealed blocks, then use its refinement trajectories to train a student to predict the final completion in one pass. Using a curriculum that gradually transitions from partial to fully masked inputs, we successfully transfer the multi-step refinement capabilities into one step. Across reasoning, math, code benchmarks on three model families DStill improves acceptance length by up to 28% and speedup by up to 25% over one-step DFlash, achieving up to 6.45x speedup over auto-regressive decoding.

arxiv:2610.27296.title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
arxiv:2610.27296.abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. Across 36 years of computer science, we analyze 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers and their topic shifts. The field expanded while its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer. Over half of topic-shifting researchers moved into AI, especially mid-career ones, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each successive breakthrough, from AlexNet to large language models, raised the field's carrying capacity for ideas but was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas. Bigger breakthroughs capture attention more completely, depleting the diversity their successors may draw upon. Structural biology shows the same cycle after cryo-EM and AlphaFold. Simulations show how well-intentioned and widely used policies such as reciprocal reviewing empower prolific authors and further narrow what the field accepts. We call for institutions that protect diverse attention in artificial intelligence rather than reward concentration on the winning paradigm.

arxiv:2610.27230.title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
arxiv:2610.27230.abstract: Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

arxiv:2610.26992.title: CoASFL: Coupled Consistency Optimization for Asynchronous Split Federated Learning
arxiv:2610.26992.abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training large-scale deep models on resource-constrained edge devices. Although asynchronous SFL alleviates the straggler bottleneck caused by system heterogeneity, it inevitably introduces two coupled dimensions of inconsistency: horizontal inconsistency across clients and vertical inconsistency between clients and the server. These inconsistencies, further exacerbated by statistical heterogeneity, result in biased activation representations, model divergence, and severe client drift. To address these challenges, we propose CoASFL, an inconsistency-aware asynchronous SFL framework that incorporates a dynamic activation merging mechanism and a consistency-aware model aggregation mechanism. Specifically, CoASFL constructs more consistent activation sequences from heterogeneous clients to alleviate horizontal inconsistency, and dynamically adjusts aggregation weights according to client participation frequencies and progress gaps to mitigate vertical inconsistency. By jointly coordinating activation-level and model-level consistency, CoASFL effectively suppresses inconsistency propagation during asynchronous training. Extensive experiments on an 80-device heterogeneous edge testbed demonstrate that CoASFL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SFL approaches, accelerating training by 1.61$\times$ to 3.74$\times$ and improving final model accuracy by up to 3.26\% under heterogeneous scenarios.

arxiv:2610.24806.title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
arxiv:2610.24806.abstract:
Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven.
  Here we use protein-binding aptamer design as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, \$1-\$3 per candidate) to demonstrate a wet lab in a closed loop with AI systems. We tasked agentic pipelines with developing aptamer binders against $α$-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles ($\sim$1,000 candidates per round; $\sim$4,400 constructs). Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose across rounds from 0.0% in Round 1 to 26.0% in Round 2 and 42.1% in Round 3 on $α$-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% in Round 1 to 3.7% in Round 2 and 33.5% in Round 3 on myoglobin. Single-clone bead-binding titrations of eight full-length $α$-thrombin candidates confirmed concordance with pooled sequencing enrichment (Pearson $r = 0.90$). In these assays, literature-derived motifs engineered by the agents to reduce off-target reactivity in the pooled screen reached apparent affinities of $K_D = 24.6$--$133$ nM, whereas de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding ($K_D > 1\ μ$M).
  We also report how our pipelines used myoglobin binding data to exploit the G-quadruplex binder space, diagnose cross-reactivity as on-target specificity dropped from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recover by developing strategies that restored specificity to 72.4%. We demonstrate that empirical lab data is more valuable than existing computational proxies, showing how iterative experimental feedback enables AI agents to diagnose assay artifacts and refine molecular designs across rounds.

arxiv:2610.27366.title: Trail-Weighted Influence Scores for Approximate Outcome Prediction in Bayesian Networks
arxiv:2610.27366.abstract: We study trail-weighted pruning of evidence for Bayesian-network prediction. A traversal enumerates the active trails from each evidence node to the outcome, scores each trail by the product of its edge strengths, and drops evidence whose score falls below a threshold. For collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables, we show that the trail score equals the exact correlation between a trail's endpoints, that a chain and a fork with equal edge strengths have identical joint distributions, and that the pruned posterior is within a computable sum of per-trail terms of the exact posterior when each dropped trail lies in its own branch of the outcome node. We prove this bound, check it exhaustively on all small trees, and show that it fails when dropped trails share a branch. In simulations on random trees, thresholding trail scores gives 1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning of the same size. We also apply the score, as an unproven heuristic, to seven bnlearn networks with colliders and loops. Keeping the top half of the active evidence by trail score gives lower error than random pruning on all seven, but it is not clearly better than a mutual-information ranking, and scoring costs more than the inference it saves on six of the seven, so we show no speedup. Models trained on trail, graph and information features and tested on networks they never saw do not beat the trail score or mutual information, but trail features carry most of what they use and clearly outperform generic graph features. A bound for general networks is left to future work.

arxiv:2610.27106.title: This is SParTA: A modular, efficient and scalable transformer architecture for jet-tagging
arxiv:2610.27106.abstract: We present the Sparse Particle-interaction Transformer Architecture (SParTA), a modular, scalable, and efficient transformer for jet tagging at high-energy colliders. Exploiting the steeply falling transverse-momentum ($p_T$) spectrum of jet constituents, SParTA factorizes constituent processing into two topological regimes. Ordered by descending $p_T$, only the $N$ hardest constituents (the hard core) participate in quadratic $O(N^2)$ differential interaction attention driven by pairwise physical and learned relational features. The remaining soft constituents are integrated via linear $O(lN)$ cross-attention to the hard core, preserving soft-radiation and color-flow information while avoiding the $O(l^2)$ memory bottleneck of full self-attention over all $l$ constituents. Pairwise interaction features are computed dynamically in-network from constituent four-momenta and conditioned on global jet-level substructure observables. On the quark-gluon tagging benchmark, a 300K-parameter SParTA model achieves an AUC of 92.02% and accuracy of 85.06%, matching the 2.14M-parameter Particle Transformer (ParT) at one-seventh the parameter count and outperforming IAFormer by 21% in background rejection at 30% signal efficiency. On the boosted top-tagging benchmark, SParTA outperforms ParT and ParticleNet with 511K parameters, while we analyze the architectural trade-offs relative to fully dense multi-layer interaction networks.

arxiv:2610.27983.title: Annealed correlation and quenched noise sensitivity in biased deep neural networks
arxiv:2610.27983.abstract: In earlier work by Jonasson, Steif and Zetterqvist (2023), fully connected deep neural networks with layers of width $n$, i.i.d.\ standard Gaussian weights, sign activations and no bias terms were shown to be annealed and quenched noise sensitive with respect to any joint probability distribution $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}$ on the input $\boldsymbolω$ and its perturbation $\boldsymbolη$ satisfying a mild positive-correlation condition and $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbolη \in \{\boldsymbolω,-\boldsymbolω\}) \to 0$. Here we add independent Gaussian biases of the natural order and show that quenched noise sensitivity is retained over a broad range of depths, indeed under the slightly weaker assumption that $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbolω = \boldsymbolη) \to 0$. Thus, subject to the positive-correlation condition, quenched noise sensitivity holds under the minimal requirement that the perturbed input is asymptotically unlikely to coincide with the original input. At the same time, the annealed covariance remains bounded away from zero and is entirely accounted for by fluctuations in the network-dependent output means.

arxiv:2610.28411.title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
arxiv:2610.28411.abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.

arxiv:2610.27586.title: Sensitivity-Orthogonal Residual Learning for Adaptive Sideslip and Cornering Stiffness Estimation
arxiv:2610.27586.abstract: Online adaptation of the cornering stiffness keeps a model-based sideslip estimator valid as tires change, but competes with learned model correction for the same filter innovation. A corrector with enough parameters can absorb the innovation pattern that a stiffness change produces, and adaptation is suppressed while the fit improves. We propagate the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted measurements through the vehicle states and construct a corrector orthogonal to them. A null-space parameterization enforces the constraint without a penalty coefficient and preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each identification segment. In full-vehicle simulation, the stiffness response of the unconstrained corrector declines as its parameter count grows, whereas the orthogonal corrector responds at least as fully as the uncorrected filter at all sizes and lowers sideslip error by 12.7% to 22.0%. In a simulated drive with a stiffness step, the orthogonal corrector adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter and lowers sideslip error during and after the transient. On public real-vehicle data, the 430-parameter unconstrained corrector loses most of its response to deliberate offsets of the filter's nominal stiffness, whereas the orthogonal corrector of the same size retains most of it, with a sideslip error slightly above the uncorrected filter's.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.09005.title: When Double Rounding is Correct
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.09005.abstract: Number libraries, which implement number formats and their arithmetic in software, are used to simulate hardware, making hardware behavior reproducible and thus verifiable and easier to design. However, modern machine learning accelerators are difficult to simulate, as they increasingly use specialized number formats that existing number libraries do not support. It is costly to extend these libraries using traditional methods: each combination of operation, format, and rounding mode typically requires a bespoke implementation. An easier way is to double round---compute at higher precision, then re-round---so that one high-precision kernel serves many formats, but double rounding is only known to be correct in select cases. We give a precise, efficiently checkable characterization of when double rounding is correct across many formats and rounding modes. Our result rests on a novel abstract number format that unifies fixed- and floating-point representations, reducing the correctness of double rounding to format containment: whether every value of one format is representable in another. We mechanized these results in Lean 4. In addition, we introduce a format inference algorithm that, given a sequence of operations, bounds each expression by a number format guaranteed to contain its result. We apply these insights in two ways. First, we present MPFX, a correctly-rounded, multi-precision number library that exploits correct double rounding to efficiently simulate many number formats. MPFX's correctly-rounded operations are up to 11x (mean: 6.05x) faster than MPFR's, and competitive with SoftFloat's---between 0.46x and 1.63x as fast (mean: 0.94x)---at the same precision. Second, in a case study, we implement a software simulation of a hardware specification using both SoftFloat and MPFX's primitives; the MPFX version is up to 13.5x faster.

doi:10.15662/ijeetr.2026.0805007.title: AI in Cloud-Native Architecture: Rethinking Software Design for Data-Intensive and Machine Learning Systems
doi:10.15662/ijeetr.2026.0805007.abstract: The migration of computing workloads from on-premises data centers to elastic cloud platforms has changed how data is collected, processed, and turned into intelligence. Cloud-native architecture, which treats elasticity, distribution, automation, and failure as first-class design inputs, has become the default foundation for modern data platforms and machine learning systems. Yet AI and data workloads differ in important ways from the web and transactional applications for which cloud-native practice was first developed. They move and transform large volumes of data, depend on long-running training jobs and scarce accelerators, serve models whose behavior is determined by data rather than code alone, and can degrade silently as the world changes. This paper examines cloud-native design from the perspective of AI and data systems and makes four contributions. First, it reinterprets the foundational principles of the approach, including statelessness, loose coupling, and designing for failure, for data pipelines, feature management, and model lifecycles. Second, it surveys the recurring patterns used to build distributed data and AI systems, from logs and feature stores to streaming pipelines, online inference, and resilience strategies for model serving. Third, it examines how training, inference, and continuous data pipelines reshape assumptions about state, consistency, and resource elasticity. Fourth, it analyzes the trade-offs that architects of AI and data platforms must reconcile, since no single design optimizes for scalability, data correctness, model quality, cost, and operational simplicity at once. The central argument is that building AI on the cloud is not a matter of deploying models on cloud infrastructure. It requires treating data, features, and models as first-class architectural concerns, governed by the same principles of decoupling, versioning, and resilience that cloud-native design applies to services.
doi:10.15662/ijeetr.2026.0805007.venue: International Journal of Engineering & Extended Technologies Research

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.478.title: <b>Analysis of the Understanding of Straight-Line Equation Concepts Based on Action, Process, Object, Schema Theory</b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.478.abstract:
<jats:p>Understanding the concept of straight-line equations is essential as a prerequisite for advanced mathematics. Observations at SMP Negeri 5 Jayapura indicated that eighth-grade students still encountered difficulties, particularly in determining the gradients of parallel and perpendicular lines. This study aimed to describe students' conceptual understanding profiles of straight-line equations based on APOS Theory (Action, Process, Object, and Schema) across high-, medium-, and low-ability categories. The research employed a descriptive qualitative method. Subjects were purposively selected from 27 students based on their MID scores, categorized as high (≥90), medium (80–89), and low (<80), with one student representing each category. The instruments consisted of two essay-type test questions incorporating Papuan cultural contexts and a semi-structured interview guide. The findings revealed that the high-ability student achieved all four APOS stages, the medium-ability student achieved the Action, Process, and Object stages, whereas the low-ability student achieved only the Action stage. Although performance across the Action to Object stages varied, the collective failure of all three subjects in graphical representation indicated cognitive obstacles during the encapsulation process at the Schema stage. These findings recommend the implementation of the APOS-based ACE cycle and special attention to graphical aspects in learning straight-line equations.




 </jats:p>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.478.venue: Journal of Education and Teaching Learning

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.476.title: The Effectiveness of Learning Institution Management on Students’ Learning Interest and Satisfaction
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.476.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to analyze the effect of the management effectiveness of a tutoring institution on students’ learning interest and learning satisfaction at Esensi Tutoring Center. The study employed a mixed-methods approach using an explanatory sequential design, which integrates quantitative and qualitative analyses sequentially. The research subjects consisted of 25 respondents, including one tutoring center manager, four tutors, and 20 students. Quantitative data were collected through questionnaires, while qualitative data were obtained through interviews and observations. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and simple linear regression, whereas qualitative data were analyzed through data reduction, data presentation, and conclusion drawing. The results indicate that the management effectiveness of the institution has a positive and significant effect on students’ learning interest, with a correlation coefficient (R) of 0.765 and a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.586, indicating a contribution of 58.6%. Management effectiveness also has a positive and significant effect on students’ learning satisfaction, with a correlation coefficient (R) of 0.835 and a coefficient of determination (R²) of 0.698, indicating a contribution of 69.8%. The qualitative findings further support these results, demonstrating that systematic instructional planning, effective coordination, engaging teaching methods, responsive services, and a conducive learning environment contribute to enhancing students’ learning interest and learning satisfaction.</jats:p>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.476.venue: Journal of Education and Teaching Learning

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.475.title: <b>Teachers’ Lived Experiences Implementing GASING in Mathematics Learning: A Phenomenological Study at SMPN 9 Jayapura</b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.475.abstract:
<jats:p>This study aimed to explore the subjective experiences of a mathematics teacher at SMPN 9 Jayapura in implementing the GASING (Gampang, Asyik, dan Menyenangkan) learning method using a qualitative phenomenological approach. The main problem underlying the application of this method was the students' difficulty in understanding abstractly taught mathematical concepts and their low basic numeracy skills, such as multiplication and division. Data were collected through in-depth interviews with a teacher who had practiced the method. The results showed that the GASING method successfully changed the teacher's teaching paradigm to start learning from concrete to abstract stages. The approach using real objects proved to significantly increase students' interest, active participation, and quick calculation skills, including in students who previously had very low basic abilities. However, the teacher faced several challenges in its implementation, including the lack of comprehensive training time support from the school, passive student characteristics at home, and low student literacy levels that hindered the resolution of word problems. In conclusion, the GASING method was highly effective in creating deep and meaningful mathematics learning, but it required high commitment from teachers and systemic collaboration within the school environment.




 </jats:p>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.475.venue: Journal of Education and Teaching Learning

doi:10.58602/itsecs.v4i4.388.title: Analysis of Land Cover Change Using Support Vector Machine Algorithm on Satellite Imagery (Case Study: Mining Area of IWIP).
doi:10.58602/itsecs.v4i4.388.abstract: <jats:p>Unsupervised mining activities and the lack of proper management of the environment can bring very serious ecological effects. One of the worst is large-scale land cover change. This paper investigates the land cover changes in the mining area of PT Indonesia Weda Bay Industrial Park (IWIP), Weda Bay Nickel (WBN) area, and measures the performance of the Support Vector Machine technique of land cover classification using satellite imagery. This research is a quantitative study based on a remote sensing technique and spatial analysis in a GIS environment. Multi-temporal satellite images, Landsat-7 (2010), Landsat-8 (2014), and Sentinel-2 (2019 and 2025) were processed to land cover classes (vegetation, open land, cloud) based on the spectral indices NDVI, NDBI, and BSI. Through the post-classification comparison method, land cover changes were detected. The overall change from 2010 to 2025 is quite significant. The vegetation cover decreased from 91.2% to 84.3%, while open land increased from less than 1% to 11.4%. The greatest changes were observed in 2019 and 2025, suggesting that mining activities and related industry development have speed up A lot. The Support Vector Machine algorithm reached excellent classification accuracy over the different periods (97.47%, 96.67%, 89.52%, 95.12% in the cases of 2010 2014 2019 and 2025 respectively), and the results were supported by the high Kappa agreement scores (ranging from 0.84 to 0.96). The low difference between training and testing accuracy indicates a strong generalization without any sign of the model getting overfitted to the training data. The work highlights that Support Vector Machine algorithm, is a very good and reliable method for detecting land cover change in mining areas, where patterns are both complex as well as dynamic.</jats:p>
doi:10.58602/itsecs.v4i4.388.venue: Journal of Information Technology,  Software Engineering and Computer Science (ITSECS)

doi:10.22488/okstate.26.000081.title: Literature Review Adventures
doi:10.22488/okstate.26.000081.abstract: <jats:p>The challenge of writing a literature review often feels daunting, but the application of processes and technology tools can make it an exciting adventure. This book is intended to guide graduate students along the quest of finding, knowing, synthesizing and communicating published scholarship on a topic of interest.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73549-w.title: Spatial metabolomics-guided deep learning framework for dissecting immune evasion mechanisms in fungal infection microenvironments
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-73549-w.abstract: Invasive fungal infections cause high mortality in immunocompromised patients, yet the spatially organized metabolic circuits that enable pathogens to evade host immunity remain poorly understood. Here we present an integrated computational–experimental framework coupling high-resolution spatial metabolomics with attention-enhanced deep learning to dissect immune evasion mechanisms within fungal infection microenvironments. We constructed a spatial metabolic atlas from MALDI-MSI and DESI-MSI data acquired on murine invasive pulmonary aspergillosis tissue sections, identifying 1,847 reproducible metabolite features across histologically distinct tissue compartments. A multi-scale convolutional network with fused channel and spatial attention modules was designed for automated segmentation of infection core, immune infiltration zone, and a transitional boundary zone, not previously resolved spatially in this infection model, that is enriched in immunosuppressive metabolites including kynurenine, prostaglandin E₂, and gliotoxin, achieving a mean Dice coefficient of 0.887 against expert pathologist annotations. To reconstruct the dynamic regulatory wiring underlying immune evasion, we developed a variational graph autoencoder coupled with neural ordinary differential equations, which inferred temporally evolving metabolite–immune interaction networks across 24, 48, and 72 h post-infection with an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.782 against KEGG and Reactome benchmarks. Network analysis ranked kynurenine as the highest-centrality hub metabolite at 48–72 h, and Neural ODE interpolation placed a putative metabolic tipping point between 36 and 48 h, marked by abrupt activation of tryptophan catabolism edges and a concurrent loss of Th1-associated signaling connectivity. Ablation experiments showed that the dual attention mechanism contributed the largest gain in segmentation and the second-largest in network inference, after the Neural ODE temporal coupling. This framework offers a hypothesis-generating, data-driven paradigm that recasts immune evasion as a spatially encoded and temporally dynamic process, and it yields prioritised candidate targets and therapeutic windows that remain to be tested by perturbation experiments before any antifungal intervention strategy can be built on them.

doi:10.3389/fcvm.2026.1927124.title: Explainable machine learning for predicting in-hospital mortality in acute heart failure: a prospective single-center cohort study from Vietnam
doi:10.3389/fcvm.2026.1927124.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Accurate risk stratification is essential in acute heart failure (AHF), which carries substantial in-hospital mortality. The Get With The Guidelines–Heart Failure (GWTG-HF) score is widely used, but its performance may vary across populations, and prospective data from Southeast Asia are scarce. We developed and internally validated explainable machine-learning (ML) models for in-hospital mortality in a Vietnamese AHF cohort and compared them with the GWTG-HF score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We prospectively enrolled 572 consecutive patients admitted with AHF (October 2024–June 2025). Missing data were imputed with a random forest–based algorithm, and class imbalance handled with SMOTE within training folds. Six algorithms (logistic regression, elastic net, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) were trained with stratified cross-validation, with optimism correction, and evaluated on an independent 25% test set. We assessed discrimination (ROC-AUC, PR-AUC), calibration (calibration slope/intercept, Brier and scaled Brier scores), classification, and clinical utility (decision-curve analysis); thresholds were derived from training data only. Pairwise AUC comparisons used the DeLong test, and interpretation used SHAP. Reporting followed TRIPOD + AI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Fifty-three patients (9.3%) died in hospital. Random forest had the highest discrimination (AUC 0.846, 95% CI 0.757–0.922), followed by the GWTG-HF score (0.817), logistic regression (0.795), elastic net (0.794), CatBoost (0.786), XGBoost (0.763), and LightGBM (0.694). No ML model significantly outperformed the GWTG-HF score (all DeLong
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       &gt; 0.05), a comparison limited by only 13 test-set events. Although CatBoost had the numerically lowest Brier score (0.085), scaled Brier scores were low for all models and calibration intercepts were uniformly negative, indicating over-estimation of risk from aggressive imbalance correction; predicted probabilities therefore require recalibration. SHAP identified respiratory failure, NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity troponin I (risk-increasing) and an ADHF phenotype and left ventricular dilation (associated with lower predicted risk) as the most influential features.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
