                    <jats:p>Explainable ML, led by random forest, achieved good discrimination but did not significantly outperform the GWTG-HF score, most plausibly reflecting limited statistical power rather than true equivalence. With miscalibrated probabilities requiring recalibration, explainable ML is best viewed as a complementary risk-ranking tool; external, multicenter, and temporal validation are required before clinical use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1186/s12982-026-03102-7.title: Machine learning analysis of the association between fertility and under five mortality in Bangladesh using BDHS 2022 data
doi:10.1186/s12982-026-03102-7.abstract: Under-five mortality is a key indicator of child health, reflecting healthcare quality, nutrition, and socio-economic conditions. In Bangladesh, under-five mortality remains a public health concern despite substantial declines, with fertility-related factors potentially contributing to child survival. Traditional logistic regression may not adequately capture complex and nonlinear relationships, whereas machine learning methods can capture such patterns and provide complementary predictive insights. This study examined the association between fertility-related factors and under-five mortality using traditional logistic regression and machine learning approaches with nationally representative BDHS 2022 data. Data were obtained from the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) 2022. Ten machine learning models Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, Random Forest, Decision Tree, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, Neural Network, XGBoost, and LightGBM were implemented in Python, while complex-sample logistic regression was conducted using SPSS Version 25. Model interpretability was assessed using SHAP values and partial dependence plots (PDPs). Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC), Cohen’s Kappa, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Decision Tree demonstrated the best overall performance for identifying under-5 mortality, achieving a mortality precision of 15.25%, recall of 52.94%, F1-score of 0.2368, MCC of 0.2424, Cohen’s Kappa of 0.1973, and AUROC of 0.8045. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest mortality recall (55.88%). Key predictors included household size, total children ever born, currently breastfeeding status, and parental education. SHAP and PDP analyses identified important contributions from fertility-related, household, and socio-economic factors to model predictions. Higher parity, measured by the total number of children ever born, was significantly associated with increased odds of under-five mortality. Current breastfeeding status was inversely associated with mortality; however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because of potential temporal ambiguity. Machine learning models complemented complex-sample logistic regression by identifying important fertility-related, household, and socioeconomic predictors and capturing potentially nonlinear patterns in the data. These findings provide evidence to inform further research and public health planning aimed at reducing under-five mortality in Bangladesh.

doi:10.1186/s11671-026-05024-4.title: Machine learning algorithm of thermo-diffusion effects on 10W40 engine oil hybrid nanomaterial for automotive engine cooling
doi:10.1186/s11671-026-05024-4.abstract: This machine learning model can improve automotive engine cooling by properly predicting the heat transfer performance of 10W40 engine oil hybrid nanomaterials under thermo-diffusion conditions. It also helps to develop energy-efficient lubricating systems, which reduce friction, improve fuel efficiency, and increase engine durability. This article provides a short analysis of the thermos-diffusion influence on a hybrid nanofluid based on 10W40 motor oil with LTNE (local thermal non-equilibrium effects). The neural network with the Levenberg-Marquardt method (NN-LMA) is the foundation of an integrated numerical computing system. In order to improve people’s intellect and abilities in daily work, this field of study is especially eager to investigate and develop innovative (AI) techniques in the fields of technology and engineering. The LTE (local thermal equilibrium) model (one equation) and the LTNE model (two equations) are two fundamental models that can be used to explain convective heat transfer in porous media. The LTNE model takes into account the heat differential between the liquid and solid phases. If there is a heat disparity between the two phases, the LTE assumption may not be valid. It is now necessary to use the LTNE model and provide an extra thermal boundary condition at the one another. The liquid phase’s thermal field increases as the inter-phase heat transmission characteristic upsurges, while the solid phase’s temperature field declines. Clinical trial: This study is not a clinical trial.

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.474.title: <b>STUDENTS’ PERCEPTIONS TOWARD THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TOOLS FOR GRAMMAR LEARNING IN ENGLISH EDUCATION PROGRAM</b><b></b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.474.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed educational practices by providing new opportunities for personalized learning, automated feedback, and independent learning support. In English language education, AI-based tools have emerged as potential learning assistants, particularly in grammar learning, which remains challenging for many English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. This study aims to investigate students’ perceptions toward the use of Artificial Intelligence tools for grammar learning among English Education students at STKIP Insan Madani Airmolek. This study employed a descriptive quantitative research design involving 97 students selected through a total sampling technique. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) developed by Davis (1989), consisting of four dimensions: perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, attitude toward AI utilization, and perceived challenges. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistical analysis, including frequency, percentage, and mean score analysis. The findings revealed that students demonstrated a high level of acceptance toward AI-based grammar learning tools, with an overall mean score of 4.07. The highest perception was found in the attitude toward AI utilization dimension (M = 4.25), followed by perceived usefulness (M = 4.21) and perceived ease of use (M = 4.18). Although students recognized the benefits of AI in providing immediate feedback, improving grammar understanding, and supporting independent learning, they also expressed concerns regarding AI dependency, accuracy of AI-generated feedback, and academic integrity. The study concludes that AI tools have significant potential to support grammar learning among English Education students; however, effective implementation requires appropriate guidance to ensure critical, ethical, and responsible use of AI technology.</jats:p>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.474.venue: Journal of Education and Teaching Learning

doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-229-620261006.title: Adaptive Practices and Local Realities: Reflections on a Regional Learning Recovery Programme in the Caribbean
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-229-620261006.abstract: <jats:p>The United Nations Education 2030 agenda affirms the global aspiration for inclusive, equitable, and high-quality education and lifelong learning for all. Yet, the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the fragility of education systems, particularly in the Caribbean, where entrenched inequalities were intensified and progress towards Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) was sharply disrupted. This chapter reflects on the initial implementation of a regionally coordinated learning recovery initiative in the Caribbean, developed to not only respond to the aftermath of the pandemic's educational shock but also to accelerate equitable learning outcomes. Drawing on qualitative insights from national focal points for the programme, it explores how the initiative was interpreted, negotiated, and adapted within varied school and system contexts. Using the Theory of Practice Architectures (TPA) as a guiding framework, the discussion highlights how cultural-discursive, material-economic, and social-political arrangements enabled or constrained changes in educational practices. The analysis foregrounds how adaptive practices emerged in context – often driven by local leadership, communities of practice (COPs), and context-sensitive decision-making. This chapter signals that educational reform efforts are most effective when grounded in the everyday realities of school life and when supported by enabling practice architectures which condition the emergence of adaptive practice. Insights shared offer implications for policymakers, practitioners, and researchers seeking to design and evaluate education initiatives that are responsive, sustainable, and equity driven.</jats:p>
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-229-620261006.venue: Enhancing Inclusive Practices, Teacher Development and Institutional Capacities in the Caribbean

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.424.title: <b>THE EFFECT OF VISUAL, AUDITORY, AND KINESTHETIC (VAK) LEARNING MODELS ON PPKN LEARNING OUTCOMES IN ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS</b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.424.abstract:
<jats:p>Learning outcomes of fourth-grade students in Civics education (PPKn) at SD Negeri 1 Watubelah were still below the minimum mastery criterion, largely because instruction remained teacher-centered and did not accommodate students' varied learning styles. This study examined the effect of the Visual, Auditory, Kinesthetic (VAK) learning model on the learning outcomes of fourth-grade students in the topic of Indonesia's cultural diversity. A quantitative quasi-experimental design with a nonequivalent control group was used, involving 33 students in the experimental class (IV B) and 36 in the control class (IV A), selected through cluster sampling. Data were collected through a 15-item multiple-choice test (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.892) and observation sheets, then analyzed using the Shapiro-Wilk normality test, Levene's homogeneity test, an independent-samples t-test, and the N-Gain test. The results showed the average posttest score of the experimental class (85.55) was higher than that of the control class (71.03), with a significant difference (t = 11.573; Sig. = 0.000 < 0.05), so H0 was rejected. The average N-Gain of the experimental class (69.35%) fell into the "fairly effective" category, while the control class (36.69%) fell into the "ineffective" category. It is concluded that the VAK learning model has a significant positive effect on students' PPKn learning outcomes.




 </jats:p>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.424.venue: Journal of Education and Teaching Learning

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.468.title: Toward AI-Assisted Islamic Reproductive Health Education: ChatGPT-Supported FiqhTaharah Learning for Adolescent Health Literacy
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.468.abstract: <jats:p>Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Islamic education requires a pedagogical model that preserves teachers’ epistemic authority while addressing adolescents’ health needs. This study examines the implementation, pedagogical affordances, and limitations of ChatGPT-assisted Fiqh al-Ṭahārah learning and develops a model for strengthening Islamic value-based reproductive health literacy. Employing a qualitative single-case study design, the research was conducted at MA Al Ishlah Banjarejo Blora. Data were collected through observations, semi-structured interviews, documentation, and analysis of students’ interactions with ChatGPT, and were analyzed using the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña. The findings revealed three stages of implementation: preparation, inquiry-based interaction, and reflection and verification. ChatGPT provided a psychologically safer space for sensitive questions, flexible access to explanations, contextualized Fiqh learning, increased engagement, and critical AI literacy. However, its use was constrained by potential inaccuracies, oversimplification of differences among Islamic legal schools, prompt quality, unequal access, and privacy and ethical concerns. The resulting AI-Assisted Thaharah Learning Model integrates AI-assisted inquiry, teacher facilitation, source verification, and Islamic value internalization while maintaining teachers’ pedagogical, epistemic, and moral authority.</jats:p>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.468.venue: Journal of Education and Teaching Learning

doi:10.52366/edusoshum.v6i3.675.title: Digital Ethics Integration in Akidah Akhlak Learning to Prevent Hoaxes and Hate Speech Among Students at Madrasah Tsanawiyah Negeri
doi:10.52366/edusoshum.v6i3.675.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid spread of hoaxes and hate speech through social media has become a serious moral concern for adolescents in Indonesian madrasahs. This study examines how digital ethics is integrated into Akidah Akhlak learning as a preventive measure against hoaxes and hate speech, how students respond to such content, and which factors support or hinder this integration. It adopts a qualitative field design with a phenomenological approach and was conducted at MTsN 1 and MTsN 2 Padangsidimpuan between March and May 2026. Data were gathered through observation, interviews, and documentation involving thirteen informants: two headmasters, three Akidah Akhlak teachers, two vice principals for student affairs, and six students. Analysis proceeded from open coding and focused coding to the extraction of themes, supported by source, technique, and time triangulation. Three findings emerge. First, teachers translate tabayyun, muraqabah, and the prohibition of ghibah and fitnah into seven practical forms of integration, ranging from daily advice and the discussion of viral screenshots to briefings delivered by the police and the prosecutor's office. Second, most students can define hoaxes and hate speech and report checking information before sharing it, yet the practice weakens when students are unsupervised, particularly in grade 7. Third, integration rests on six supporting factors, the most decisive being the relevance of the material and the competence of teachers, and is constrained by students' dispositions and by family and community environments. The study therefore offers classroom-level evidence of a process that earlier research has described mainly as a normative proposal or as a relationship between variables, and it shows that students' knowledge of digital ethics develops faster than their conduct outside the classroom.</jats:p>
doi:10.52366/edusoshum.v6i3.675.venue: Edusoshum : Journal of Islamic Education and Social Humanities

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10998937/v1.title: Identification and Validation of Disulfidptosis‑Related Genes in DKD via Integrative Machine Learning and Single‑Cell Transcriptomics
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10998937/v1.abstract: Background The global occurrence of diabetes is steadily increasing, with DKD representing a major and severe complication arising from this condition. Disulfidptosis is a recently identified form of programmed cell death strongly associated with various diseases. The objective of this investigation was to identify hub genes related to disulfide in DKD and to reveal their potential functions via integrative bioinformatic analyses. Method To screen for DEGs that are related to DKD, we obtained transcriptomic profile data from GEO. GO, KEGG, and GSEA functional enrichment analyses revealed that the DEGs were associated with cellular immunity, cytoskeletal organization, and ferroptosis. Through the joint application of WGCNA, differential expression, PPI network, and machine learning algorithms, we pinpointed hub genes that exhibit strong diagnostic capability. The diagnostic performance and predictive accuracy of these genes were evaluated using ROC curves, a nomogram model, and the Nephroseq database. Immune infiltration analysis and single‑cell RNA sequencing were employed to investigate the effects of hub genes on immune and renal cells involved in DKD progression. The protein and mRNA expression of the hub genes were subsequently corroborated through Western blotting and quantitative real‑time PCR assays. The functional role of PDLIM1 in disease pathogenesis was assessed through CCK‑8 viability assays, siRNA‑mediated knockdown, and DTT‑based rescue experiments. Results Four hub genes were ultimately identified via the combined use of differential expression analysis, WGCNA, PPI network analysis, and machine learning: DSTN, RAC1, ACTB, and PDLIM1. AUC for each of the four genes exceeded 0.60, and calibration curves showed a high degree of agreement between predicted and observed risks, indicating robust diagnostic performance. Inverse correlations with GFR were found for all four genes through correlation analysis, PDLIM1 was positively correlated with serum creatinine. Significant correlations between these genes and diverse immune cell subsets were observed via immune infiltration analysis. Cell‑type‑specific expression profiles in proximal tubular cells and macrophages were uncovered through single‑cell analysis, with enhanced signaling between macrophages and neutrophils. Experimental validation confirmed the association of the four hub genes with DKD severity. Conclusion These findings identify four hub genes as promising DKD biomarkers. Notably, PDLIM1 may contribute to DKD pathogenesis by modulating SLC7A11‑mediated disulfide stress, and its upregulation appears to represent a pathogenic driver rather than a compensatory protective response.

doi:10.5194/tc-20-6045-2026.title: GlaUnTI: a hybrid physics–machine learning model enables transferable glacier surface mass balance estimation
doi:10.5194/tc-20-6045-2026.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Glacier surface mass balance (SMB) is a key climate indicator and a central driver of glacier change. Direct SMB observations remain sparse and unevenly distributed. Hence, transferable SMB models are essential for large-scale assessments and projections. Here, we propose the GLAcier-UNiversal Temperature Index model (GlaUnTI) for this purpose. This hybrid physics–machine learning model modifies a fully differentiable temperature index (TI) SMB model by introducing a shallow convolutional neural corrector. It learns spatially and temporally varying adjustments to a small set of physically interpretable TI parameters, using glacier geometry and aggregated climate information. We calibrate four models – a basic TI model, a purely data-driven recurrent neural network with no physical inductive bias and two GlaUnTI variants, with and without glacier facies maps as predictors – using a dataset of 65 European glaciers spanning 1995–2024 and covering the Alps, Scandinavia, Iceland, Svalbard and the Pyrenees. Their spatial transferability is evaluated on a held-out, spatially independent test subset of 13 glaciers across climatically and geometrically contrasting European regions. The evaluation uses 793/756/314 (annual/winter/summer) point SMB measurements and 312/235/233 glacier-wide SMB estimates. On the test glaciers, the baseline TI model achieves annual point-level performance with
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                    =0.854 and an RMSE equal to 1.707 m w.e. With GlaUnTI,
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                    increases to 0.940 and the RMSE reduces to 1.068 m w.e. At the glacier-wide scale, the baseline TI model attains an
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                    equal to 0.606 and an RMSE of 0.805 m w.e. With GlaUnTI,
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                    increases to 0.700 and the RMSE reduces to 0.627 m w.e. Including glacier facies maps from the end of the ablation season to the corrector yields moderate benefits in glacier-wide summer (11.0 %) and annual (12.2 %) SMB estimates. In contrast, the purely data-driven baseline model overall shows the weakest spatial transferability. Beyond modelling accuracy, end-to-end differentiability enables efficient gradient-based calibration, transfer learning, inverse optimisation of effective forcing perturbations, formal model explainability and propagation of forcing-driven aleatoric uncertainty through long SMB trajectories. These results demonstrate that parameter-corrected hybrid models improve SMB transferability across diverse climate regimes while preserving a physically grounded structure, suitable for integration into broader glacier evolution workflows and for informing climate-related policies.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.17148/ijarcce.2026.151071.title: SentinelML: Behavioral Machine-Learning-Based Ransomware Detection with Decoupled AI Security Analysis
doi:10.17148/ijarcce.2026.151071.abstract: Ransomware remains a critical threat to modern enterprise and personal computing infrastructure.Traditional signature-based detection mechanisms exhibit operational degradation when confronted with previously unobserved polymorphic or zero-day variants.This paper presents SentinelML, an autonomous endpoint detection architecture that identifies ransomware activity through 19 dynamic behavioral indicators collected entirely in user space without requiring kernel-level filter drivers.By sampling filesystem Shannon entropy, process concurrency anomalies, shadow copy deletion commands, and cryptographic module bindings, SentinelML trains a local Random Forest classifier that operates as an unprivileged host daemon.To address operational triage transparency, the local classifier is coupled with an architecturally decoupled Large Language Model (LLM) advisory explainer operating via an isolated HTTPS interface.We conduct an exhaustive technical audit of the production system: confirming that Shannon entropy accounts for 41.31% of aggregate Gini importance, documenting the operational tradeoffs of heuristic user-space proxies, analyzing platform asymmetry between Windows and Linux deployments, and evaluating the system strictly as an Intrusion Detection System (IDS).Finally, we disclose that previously reported internal metrics (0.9567 accuracy across candidate algorithms) could not be independently reproduced due to unpreserved training artifacts, and establish an open empirical evaluation protocol for reproducible validation.

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.518.title: <b>Developing an Android-Based Digital Snakes and Ladders Media on Life Cycles to Enhance Science Literacy in Fourth-Grade Elementary Students</b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.518.abstract:
<jats:p>This study was motivated by the relatively low scientific literacy of elementary school students, particularly in explaining scientific phenomena, interpreting information, and relating scientific concepts to everyday life. In addition, science and social studies (IPAS) instruction was still dominated by conventional teaching methods, while the use of Android-based digital learning media remained limited. This study aimed to develop Android-based digital Snakes and Ladders learning media on the topic of the life cycle of living things and to analyze its validity, practicality, and effectiveness in improving elementary school students’ scientific literacy. The study employed a Research and Development (R&D) method using the 4D development model, consisting of Define, Design, Develop, and Disseminate stages, combined with a mixed-methods approach. The research subjects involved 47 fourth-grade students from SDN 17 Tilamuta, SDN 11 Tilamuta, and SDN 05 Tilamuta. The research instruments consisted of validation sheets for media, subject-matter, and learning experts, teacher and student response questionnaires, observation sheets, and scientific literacy tests administered as pretests and posttests. The data were analyzed using quantitative and qualitative descriptive techniques, while N-Gain analysis was employed to determine the improvement in students’ scientific literacy. The results showed that the developed media obtained validity scores of 92.5% from the media expert, 92.5% from the subject-matter expert, and 89% from the learning expert, with an overall average of 91.33%, categorized as highly valid. The practicality assessment showed a student response score of 92.61% and a teacher response score of 97.22%, both categorized as highly practical. The effectiveness of the media was indicated by an increase in the mean scientific literacy score from 58.50 on the pretest to 89.80 on the posttest, with an N-Gain score of 0.75, categorized as high. Therefore, the developed Android-based digital Snakes and Ladders media was determined to be highly valid, highly practical, and effective in improving elementary school students’ scientific literacy on the topic of the life cycle of living things.




 </jats:p>

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.426.title: <b>INDIVIDUAL COUNSELING USING THE REALITY APPROACH WITH THE WDEP TECHNIQUE TO IMPROVE STUDENTS' LEARNING CONCENTRATION: A SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW</b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.426.abstract: <jats:p>Learning concentration is one of the important abilities that supports students’ academic engagement and success. Low concentration can be indicated by being easily distracted, having difficulty sustaining attention, being less able to follow instructions, and showing low engagement in academic tasks. This study aims to analyze empirical evidence regarding reality therapy, individual counseling, learning concentration, attention, self-regulation, and academic behavior as a conceptual basis for developing an individual counseling guide based on the reality approach for junior high school students. This study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with reporting guided by PRISMA 2020. The literature focuses on publications from 2021 to 2026. The analysis was conducted through identification, screening, eligibility assessment, data extraction, coding, and thematic synthesis. The review findings indicate that the reality approach and WDEP technique have the potential to support responsibility, motivation, self-efficacy, academic resilience, academic adjustment, and learning behavior control. The literature on attention highlights the importance of self-monitoring, self-regulation, distraction control, and engagement in maintaining focus. Based on this synthesis, the counseling guide can be developed through the stages of Wants, Doing, Evaluation, and Planning, specifically directed toward learning concentration behaviors.</jats:p>

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.520.title: Improving Student Learning Outcomes Through the MORDISCVEIN Learning Model Assisted by Animated Video Media in Science and Social Studies (IPAS) Instruction for Fourth-Grade Students at SDN 6 Tapa, Bone Bolango
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.520.abstract:
<jats:p>This study is Classroom Action Research (CAR) with the research question of whether student learning outcomes can be improved through the Mordiscvein learning model assisted by animated video media in Science and Social Studies (IPAS) learning for Class IV students at SDN 6 Tapa Bone Bolango. The objective of this study is to improve student learning outcomes through the Mordiscvein learning model assisted by animated video media in IPAS learning for Class IV students at SDN 6 Tapa Bone Bolango. This research was conducted in two cycles, where each cycle consisted of two meetings with four stages: planning, acting, observing, and reflecting. The research subjects consisted of 18 students, comprising 9 male students and 9 female students. The results showed that in Cycle I, out of 18 students, only 6 students achieved the Learning Objective Completion Criteria (KKTP $\ge$ 75) with a percentage of 33%, while 12 students or 67% had not achieved mastery. After learning improvements were made in Cycle II, student learning outcomes increased: 16 students or 89% achieved mastery, while 2 students or 11% had not yet achieved the Learning Objective Completion Criteria (KKTP < 75). Thus, it can be concluded that the application of the Mordiscvein learning model assisted by animated video media can improve the learning outcomes of Class IV students in IPAS at SDN 6 Tapa Bone Bolango.




 </jats:p>

doi:10.14324/lre.24.1.20.title: Towards the learning estate: from digital–physical to experience orchestration
doi:10.14324/lre.24.1.20.abstract: <jats:p>Universities increasingly orchestrate teaching and learning through compound configurations that span spaces, devices, timetables and roles. As digital content and workflows increasingly shape physical estates, and vice versa, alignment frames overlook the compound, cross-host configurations already in motion. In this article we ask whether estate-level orchestration, rather than digital–physical alignment alone, should be the operative unit of design for planning and delivering student experiences across and beyond campus. We draw on three exemplars at a research-intensive university: (1) a theatre-scale interactive three-dimensional system, which streams or web-delivers interactive three-dimension into traditional lecture theatres and learners’ devices; (2) a high-fidelity virtual reality digital twin of a chemistry lab for pre-lab rehearsal; and (3) space-planning web apps for co-design and decision support. From these, we sketch a purpose-orientated, configuration-first stance and situate it within work on cyber-/smart-campus estates, learning ecologies, TPACK and postdigital perspectives. Beyond education, digital-first space planning is already operational at scale, including in automotive manufacturing (BMW Group), cultural architecture (Dubai Museum of the Future) and national infrastructure (National Grid’s Triton platform). Higher education has both the conceptual case and, in several respects, the enabling conditions to follow. Hence, we argue that the convergence of immersive, computational and spatial technologies is expanding what institutions can compose and deliver, making device-label categories less useful for both learning and space design. This configuration-first stance is also directly applicable to the governance of artificial intelligence in higher education: as with earlier technology labels, institutions risk misallocating attention and resource if ‘artificial intelligence’ is treated as a discrete category rather than as a family of capabilities, from generative code or audiovisual models to computer vision and wearable ‘artificial intelligence’, some of which already permeate the configurations described here. We conclude with operational implications and a call for institutions to transcend their siloed functions and budgets, by elevating orchestration (not devices, spaces or platforms) as the primary unit of design.</jats:p>

doi:10.1098/rspa.2026.0073.title: Dynamics-informed deep learning for predicting extreme events
doi:10.1098/rspa.2026.0073.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Predicting extreme events in high-dimensional chaotic dynamical systems remains a fundamental challenge because these events are rare, intermittent and often driven by transient dynamical mechanisms that are difficult to identify from limited observations. We propose a fully data-driven framework for real-time forecasting of extreme events based on an interpretable, mechanism-aware precursor that tracks the transient instabilities preceding event onset. Specifically, we use the finite-time Lyapunov exponent (FTLE) as the precursor, computed directly from state snapshots through a reduced-order, equation-agnostic formulation. By restricting the instability dynamics to an adaptively evolving subspace spanned by optimal time-dependent (OTD) modes, the method substantially reduces the computational cost of classical FTLE evaluation while retaining the dominant transiently amplifying directions. The resulting FTLE sequence serves as input to a transformer-based model that forecasts the system observable at future lead times, enabling long-lead prediction of extreme events. We demonstrate the framework on Kolmogorov flow, a canonical model of intermittent turbulence. The results show that explicitly encoding transient instability mechanisms substantially extends extreme-event prediction horizons compared to baseline observable-based approaches.</jats:p>
doi:10.1098/rspa.2026.0073.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society A Mathematical Physical and Engineering Science

doi:10.26740/jpus.v10n2.p280-290.title: Improving Student Achievement in Ecosystem Learning through Environment-Based Culturally Responsive Teaching
doi:10.26740/jpus.v10n2.p280-290.abstract: <jats:p>Biology learning becomes more meaningful when scientific concepts are linked to students’ cultural backgrounds and everyday environments. This classroom action research investigated the impact of Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT), integrated with local cultural contexts, on students’ Biology learning outcomes in ecosystem instruction. The study was conducted in two cycles, each consisting of planning, action, observation, and reflection. Data were collected through learning outcome tests and classroom observations, and were analysed descriptively by comparing student achievement across the pre-cycle, Cycle I, and Cycle II. Results demonstrated progressive improvements in learning outcomes. The average score increased from 43.44 in the pre-cycle to 59.68 in Cycle I and 72.16 in Cycle II. The proportion of students meeting the predetermined mastery criterion rose from 12% to 44% and 84%, respectively. This study contributes by examining CRT implementation in ecosystem learning by connecting biological concepts to students’ local cultural experiences and environments. The findings indicate that CRT-based instruction, combined with iterative instructional adjustments, was associated with improved learning outcomes. However, these improvements cannot be attributed solely to CRT, as other instructional changes across cycles may have contributed. This study underscores the potential of context-sensitive Biology instruction to make ecosystem concepts more relevant to students’ lived experiences and provides a foundation for further research on CRT implementation in similar educational contexts.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1947608.title: Beyond technical training: teacher collaboration and informal learning in digital continuing professional development for business studies
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1947608.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Teachers' continuous professional development (CPD) is critical for effective digital technology integration in teaching and learning. This study explored how professional development initiatives support Grade 12 Business Studies teachers in integrating digital technologies in resource-constrained rural schools in South Africa.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study adopted a qualitative case study design within the interpretivist paradigm. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews with six purposively sampled Grade 12 Business Studies teachers and analysed thematically.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study findings revealed that teachers participated in formal continuous professional development initiatives, including departmental workshops and cluster meetings, as well as informal opportunities such as peer collaboration and self-directed online learning. However, most formal initiatives focused predominantly on technical skills rather than the pedagogical application of digital technologies. Consequently, teachers relied heavily on peer collaboration, professional learning communities and informal digital networks to address gaps in formal training.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study further highlights the need for sustained and contextually responsive professional development that aligns digital technologies with pedagogical practice. The study recommends evidence-based district support systems that integrate technical assistance with pedagogical mentorship to strengthen teachers' capacity to integrate digital technologies effectively in resource-constrained rural schools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1962474.title: Quality assurance 5.0: reframing quality management in higher education through artificial intelligence and continuous institutional learning
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1962474.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies is fundamentally reshaping higher education, exposing the limitations of conventional quality assurance systems that are often compliance-driven, periodic, and insufficiently responsive to dynamic institutional demands. This conceptual paper introduces Quality Assurance 5.0 (QA 5.0) as a proposed conceptual framework intended to reframe quality management by integrating artificial intelligence, continuous institutional learning, and evidence-informed governance. Drawing on Organisational Learning Theory, Total Quality Management, and Continuous Improvement Theory, the paper synthesises emerging scholarship to propose an adaptive quality ecosystem that is theorised to shift quality assurance from retrospective evaluation to predictive, real-time, and continuous institutional enhancement. The framework conceptualises AI as an enabler of intelligent quality monitoring, predictive analytics, automated feedback systems, and data-driven decision-making. At the same time, institutional learning serves as the mechanism through which universities continuously generate, share, and apply knowledge to improve academic, administrative, and student outcomes. By integrating technological intelligence with organisational learning capabilities, QA 5.0 is theorised to foster institutional agility, innovation, accountability, and resilience within increasingly complex higher education environments. The paper further presents a conceptual model illustrating the interrelationships among AI-enabled quality systems, learning-oriented organisational culture, strategic leadership, and sustainable institutional performance, specified as a set of testable propositions rather than as established, empirically confirmed relationships. Beyond extending existing quality assurance paradigms, the proposed framework offers a forward-looking perspective for policymakers, university leaders, accreditation agencies, and researchers seeking to modernise quality governance in the era of digital transformation. The study concludes that Quality Assurance 5.0 is proposed as an internally coherent and testable conceptual framework for moving quality management from static compliance toward intelligent, adaptive, and continuously evolving practice; its practical value for diverse higher education contexts remains to be established through the empirical validation identified as a priority for future research.</jats:p>

doi:10.33546/bnj.4656.title: Predictors of nursing students’ satisfaction with the clinical learning environment in Kosovo: A multivariate analysis using the Clinical Learning Environment, Supervision and Nurse Teacher framework
doi:10.33546/bnj.4656.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: A supportive clinical learning environment is essential in nursing education; however, evidence regarding predictors of student satisfaction in Southeast European higher education contexts remains limited.
Objective: To identify demographic and item-level CLES+T predictors of nursing students’ overall satisfaction with the clinical learning environment in Kosovo.
Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted between April and May 2025 among 300 undergraduate nursing students. Data were collected using the Clinical Learning Environment, Supervision and Nurse Teacher (CLES+T) scale, while overall student satisfaction was assessed using a separate single-item measure. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, non-parametric tests, and multiple linear regression analyses. The primary demographic model included sex, year of study, and economic status, while a second model included all 34 CLES+T items simultaneously.
Results: The demographic model was statistically significant, F(4, 295) = 35.894, p < 0.001, explaining 32.7% of the variance in satisfaction (R² = 0.327; adjusted R² = 0.318). Compared with first-year students, second- and third-year students reported significantly lower satisfaction, while sex and Economic Status were not significant predictors. The CLES+T item-level model was statistically significant, F(34, 265) = 18.319, p < 0.001, explaining 70.2% of the variance (R² = 0.702; adjusted R² = 0.663). The strongest positive predictors were positive joint meetings with the mentor and nurse teacher (β = 0.415), feeling comfortable going to the ward at the start of the shift (β = 0.335), and sufficient meaningful learning situations (β = 0.249). Because several item-level predictors showed elevated multicollinearity, individual coefficients, particularly negative coefficients, should be interpreted cautiously.
Conclusion: Nursing students’ satisfaction was associated with both academic year and specific relational, supervisory, and pedagogical characteristics of the clinical learning environment. Supportive mentorship, meaningful learning opportunities, and effective integration of theory and practice remain important components of positive clinical learning experiences.</jats:p>

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.432.title: Improving Geometric Visualization and 3D Modeling of SMK Students through Reverse Engineering-Based CAD and Loft
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.432.abstract:
<jats:p>The geometric visualization skills and 3D modeling accuracy of vocational high school (SMK) students in Computer Aided Design (CAD) instruction were previously relatively low, as evidenced by difficulty in understanding relationships between geometric profiles, visualizing shape changes, and producing accurate three-dimensional models. This study aimed to improve students' geometric visualization skills and 3D modeling accuracy through reverse engineering-based CAD instruction utilizing the Loft feature. The method employed was Classroom Action Research (CAR), conducted in two cycles—each comprising planning, implementation, observation, and reflection—involving tenth-grade SMK students enrolled in a CAD course. Data were collected through observation, questionnaires, and practical tests. In the pre-cycle stage, instruction without reverse engineering resulted in an average score of
86.33 with a mastery rate of 77.78%. Cycle I increased the average score to 88.74 (mastery rate 86.42%), while Cycle II, using more complex objects and intensive guidance, raised it to
91.47 (mastery rate 93.83%). Observation and questionnaire results also showed improved student precision in geometric and three-dimensional modeling. This study concluded that reverse engineering-based CAD instruction using the Loft feature effectively improved SMK students' geometric visualization and modeling accuracy.</jats:p>

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.465.title: <b>A Microgenetic Analysis of Students’ Statistical Thinking Processes in Solving Grouped Data Decile Problems</b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.465.abstract:
<jats:p>This study aims to analyze the development of students’ statistical thinking processes in solving grouped-data decile problems through a taks-based microgenetic study approach. The study was motivated by students’ difficulties in determining decile positions, using cumulative frequency, and understanding the relationship between decile position and decil values. A qualitative method with a task-based microgenetic study approach was employed at SMA Negeri 4 Jayapura during the second semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. The participants were there Grade 11 students purposively selected from 30 students based on diagnostic pretest results, representing high, medium, and low ability categories. The instruments consisted of a diagnostic pretest, microgenetic task sheets, think-aloud guidelines, structured interview guidelines. The findings indicate that students’ statistical thinking developed gradually through six phases, culminating in an understanding of deciles as measures of data position. The most prominent change occurred when students began using cumulative frequency as a reference for determining the decile class, which constituted a critical moment in the development of their thinking strategies. The study concludes that the task-based microgenetic study approach is affective for revealing changes in students’ strategies and the development of their statistical thinking processes during task completion. 




 </jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s13007-026-01603-9.title: A 3D grain-level phenotypic extraction framework for rice using contour-guided NeRF reconstruction and mamba-based point cloud segmentation
doi:10.1186/s13007-026-01603-9.abstract: Grain-level three-dimensional phenotyping of rice provides quantitative traits for breeding and yield assessment, but remains challenging because dense panicles exhibit severe organ adhesion, boundary ambiguity, and large-scale point-cloud complexity. We developed PRSNeRF, a grain-level phenotyping workflow that combines contour-guided neural radiance field reconstruction with point cloud instance segmentation, and evaluated it on rice grown in controlled indoor environments. PRSNeRF integrates CoNeRF for reconstruction and PRSNet for segmentation. CoNeRF combines image deblurring, contour-guided sampling, and rendering-projection consistency to improve geometric fidelity and suppress floating artifacts. PRSNet uses a Mamba-based encoder, adaptive Gaussian detail enhancement, multi-scale feature fusion, and three-dimensional dynamic anchor boxes to separate densely adjacent grains. Under a fixed 5,000-iteration budget on the Blur Rice benchmark, CoNeRF reduced the scaled NeRF-space Chamfer distance from 10.61 to 7.81. Relative to the 30,000-iteration NeRFacto baseline, it shortened training time from 368 s to 77 s and point cloud export time from 120 s to 10 s. On the RiceNeRF-IS dataset, plant-level five-fold cross-validation showed that PRSNet achieved an overall AP of 87.31%, outperforming OneFormer3D by 22.30 percentage points. The reconstructed point clouds enabled automated estimation of grain count, grain dimensions, and voxel-based occupancy traits. Together, these results connect reconstruction, instance separation, and trait extraction within one workflow. PRSNeRF supports grain-level rice panicle phenotyping from multi-view images under controlled indoor acquisition. It improves reconstruction fidelity, separates densely adhered organs, and supports downstream trait extraction within an end-to-end processing time of about 3.3 min per plant.

doi:10.33546/bnj.4736.title: Self-directed learning readiness and its associated factors among undergraduate nursing students in Maldives: A cross-sectional correlational study
doi:10.33546/bnj.4736.abstract:
<jats:p>Background: Self-Directed Learning (SDL) readiness is a critical competence in nursing education, as it provides students with the characteristics needed for lifelong learning in complex healthcare contexts. With the evolving healthcare landscape, cultivating SDL readiness is essential for preparing competent nursing professionals.
Objective: This study aimed to determine the level of self-directed learning readiness and its related factors among undergraduate nursing students.
Methods: A cross-sectional correlational design was conducted from April to December 2024. Data were collected from 182 undergraduate nursing students in the Maldives, recruited using proportionate stratified random sampling techniques. A structured questionnaire with five instruments, including the Fisher’s Self-Directed Learning Readiness Scale, Kolb’s Learning Style Inventory, Academic Motivation Scale, Dundee Ready Education Environment Measure (DREEM), and Revised two-factor version of the Study Process Questionnaire (R-SPQ-2F), was used. Descriptive statistics and Pearson’s correlation coefficient were employed to analyze the data.
Results: The results revealed that nursing students exhibited SDL readiness at a high level. As for the factors related to SDL readiness, significant positive correlations were found for learning environment (r = 0.457, p < 0.01), deep learning approach (r = 0.442, p < 0.01), and academic motivation (r = 0.350, p < 0.01). In contrast, a surface learning approach was negatively correlated with SDL readiness (r = -0.201, p < 0.01). In addition, no significant correlations were observed between learning style and SDL readiness. However, abstract conceptualization demonstrated a weak positive correlation with self-management (r = 0.171, p = 0.021), while reflective observation showed a weak negative correlation with desire for learning (r = -0.165, p = 0.026).
Conclusions: This study adds contextual evidence from the Maldivian undergraduate nursing education setting regarding factors related to SDL readiness. The findings support the broader body of evidence emphasizing the importance of educational environments, learning approach, and academic motivation in fostering SDL readiness in nursing education.</jats:p>

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.466.title: <b>microgenetic Analysis of Students’ Strategy Changes in Determining Grouped Data Quartiles</b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.466.abstract:
<jats:p>Students often experience difficulties in understanding grouped data quartiles because they tend to apply procedures without comprehending the relationships among quartile positions, cumulative frequencies, and quartile formulas. This study aimed to analyze students’ strategy changes in determining grouped data quartiles through a microgenetic approach. This research employed a qualitative method using a task-based microgenetic study approach. The study was conducted at SMA Negeri 4 Jayapura during the second semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. A total of 41 students participated in a pretest to identify their initial abilities, from which three students representing high (S1), medium (S2), and low (S3) ability levels were selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected through a diagnostic pretest, graded microgenetic tasks, observations, and semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed microgenetically by identifying problem-solving episodes, strategies, strategy changes, and critical moments. The findings revealed that students’ strategies developed through four stages: understanding quartile positions, using cumulative frequencies, determining quartile classes, and applying quartile formulas conceptually. Strategy changes occurred when students understood the role of cumulative frequencies in determining quartile positions and classes. It can be concluded that understanding cumulative frequencies served as a critical moment that promoted strategy changes from procedural use toward conceptual understanding in determining grouped data quartiles.




 </jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s43020-026-00221-z.title: Pan-Tropical Land Surface Modulation of CYGNSS GNSS-R DDM Coherence Based on Explainable Machine Learning
doi:10.1186/s43020-026-00221-z.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantifying how land surface properties modulate Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) coherence is essential for assessing the performance and limitations of GNSS-R land applications. However, these modulations remain poorly characterized at the pan-tropical scale. We develop an explainable machine-learning framework to quantify the pan-tropical land surface modulation of GNSS-R delay–Doppler map (DDM) coherence, including topography, surface water, soil moisture, and vegetation. We represent the coherence with a proxy derived from Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) observations and model it with a Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM). Under spatial cross-validation, the model explains about 60% of the spatial variance in the coherence proxy and demonstrates reasonable generalization performance under spatial and regional holdout validation. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and accumulated local effects (ALE) show that GNSS-R DDM coherence is enhanced over smooth, wet, and moderately vegetated surfaces, but reduced over rough, steep, and densely vegetated terrain. Topographic factors, particularly terrain roughness, emerge as the dominant controls, while surface water occurrence and soil moisture are associated with enhanced coherence across identifiable empirical transition ranges. A dominant-control analysis further reveals distinct regional patterns in which topography, surface water, soil moisture, or vegetation serves as the leading control. Topography dominates about 68% of land, surface water and vegetation each about 14%, and soil moisture about 4%. These results provide a physically meaningful account of where and why land DDM coherence varies, together with an interpretable empirical basis for understanding how land-surface conditions influence DDM coherence and for informing the design of future GNSS-R land applications.</jats:p>

doi:10.51878/educator.v6i4.16156.title: PEMETAAN PERKEMBANGAN PENELITIAN SELF-REGULATED LEARNING DAN PROBLEM SOLVING: SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE REVIEW DAN ANALISIS BIBLIOMETRIK 2020–2026
doi:10.51878/educator.v6i4.16156.abstract:
<jats:p>Research on self-regulated learning (SRL) and problem solving has expanded because students’ ability to regulate learning processes is important when addressing complex tasks. However, research development remains dispersed across different contexts, requiring systematic mapping to identify the structure and direction of the field. This study aims to map research on SRL and problem solving from 2020 to 2026 using a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) and bibliometric analysis. Data were obtained from Scopus using the search string ("self-regulated learning" OR "self-regulation") AND ("problem solving" OR "problem-solving"). From 730 initial documents, 198 English-language journal articles were retained after screening. VOSviewer and Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny were used to analyze publication development, keyword relationships, collaboration, and thematic evolution. The results show an increase in publications from 21 articles in 2020 to 53 articles as of September 28, 2026. Self-regulated learning, problem solving, and metacognition were the dominant keywords, with strong connections to self-efficacy, motivation, game-based learning, learning analytics, and artificial intelligence. Artificial intelligence and generative artificial intelligence emerged as recent research directions. These findings indicate that SRL and problem solving research is increasingly integrating cognitive, motivational, social, and technological dimensions.
ABSTRAK
Penelitian self-regulated learning (SRL) dan problem solving berkembang karena kemampuan mengatur proses belajar penting dalam penyelesaian tugas kompleks. Namun, perkembangannya masih tersebar pada berbagai konteks sehingga diperlukan pemetaan sistematis untuk mengidentifikasi struktur dan arah penelitian. Penelitian ini bertujuan memetakan perkembangan penelitian SRL dan problem solving periode 2020–2026 melalui Systematic Literature Review (SLR) dan analisis bibliometrik. Data diperoleh dari Scopus menggunakan kata kunci ("self-regulated learning" OR "self-regulation") AND ("problem solving" OR "problem-solving"). Dari 730 dokumen awal, diperoleh 198 artikel jurnal berbahasa Inggris setelah proses penyaringan. Analisis dilakukan menggunakan VOSviewer dan Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny untuk memetakan perkembangan publikasi, hubungan keyword, kolaborasi, dan evolusi tema. Hasil menunjukkan peningkatan publikasi dari 21 artikel pada 2020 menjadi 53 artikel hingga 28 September 2026. Self-regulated learning, problem solving, dan metacognition menjadi keyword dominan, dengan keterkaitan kuat pada self-efficacy, motivation, game-based learning, learning analytics, dan artificial intelligence. Tema AI dan generative artificial intelligence muncul sebagai arah penelitian terbaru. Penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa kajian SRL dan problem solving berkembang menuju integrasi kognitif, motivasional, sosial, dan teknologi.</jats:p>
doi:10.51878/educator.v6i4.16156.venue: EDUCATOR : Jurnal Inovasi Tenaga Pendidik dan Kependidikan

doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1939077.title: Incorporating natural language processing-derived features from pathology reports into machine learning models to predict differentiated thyroid cancer recurrence
doi:10.3389/fendo.2026.1939077.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the performance of machine learning (ML) models tasked with predicting thyroid cancer recurrence using natural language processing (NLP) and large language model (LLM) derived features.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Patients and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This was a retrospective study of adult thyroid cancer patients treated at an academic medical center between January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2022. Patients were classified as having cancer recurrence or no recurrence. Novel NLP features were extracted from cytopathology and surgical pathology reports using Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), and a zero-shot large language model (LLM) classification. Five learning algorithms (Decision Tree, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) were trained to predict cancer recurrence utilizing a combination of NLP-derived features and structured electronic medical record (EMR) variables. All models were evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using F1 score and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). The top performing model was hyperparameter-tuned, and feature importance was evaluated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values and gain-based importance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>310 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer diagnosed on final surgical pathology were included in this study. The optimized XGBoost model incorporating EMR variables and LDA-derived features achieved the best performance, with a cross-validated F1 score of 0.647 on the training set and a held-out test F1-score of 0.631 (95% CI 0.509–0.758) and ROC-AUC of 0.741 (95% CI 0.572-0.892). SHAP analysis and gain-based feature importance identified surgical pathology topic—cervical and lateral neck lymph node dissection—as the dominant predictor of cancer recurrence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Various classifiers including machine learning models utilizing novel NLP features derived from unstructured pathology reports may enable improved prediction of recurrence in patients with differentiated thyroid cancer.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1186/s12903-026-10063-5.title: A systematic literature review of convolutional neural network and transfer learning approaches for smoker’s melanosis classification on intraoral images: methods, evidence quality, and readiness for clinical decision support
doi:10.1186/s12903-026-10063-5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Smoker’s melanosis is a benign melanin hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa, common in smokers and clinically useful both as a marker of tobacco exposure and as a lesion requiring differential diagnosis. Its severity is still graded by subjective visual indices, motivating objective, image-based approaches using deep learning. This review maps how convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, and the EfficientNet family have been applied to smoker’s melanosis and related oral mucosal lesions on intraoral images, appraises the quality of that evidence, and assesses its readiness for clinical decision support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The review followed the PRISMA 2020 statement and the Kitchenham and Charters guidelines, addressing five research questions on architectures, transfer learning strategy, class imbalance and acquisition variability, evaluation protocols, and interpretability and clinical integration. Six databases (IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, PubMed/Medline, SpringerLink, Scopus, Google Scholar) were searched for 2019 to 2025 with additional citation searching; the last search was run on 28 March 2026. Risk of bias was appraised with PROBAST and reporting completeness against the CLAIM checklist; certainty per research question was rated using a GRADE-CERQual style scheme with pre-specified downgrading rules. The protocol was not registered in PROSPERO or any other prospective registry; eligibility criteria were fixed in writing before screening.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>From 440 identified records, 21 studies were included. Seven address the target condition directly, but only two develop a computational model; the remaining five are clinical observational studies. Transfer learning was the dominant strategy. Four of the five appraised primary studies were at high risk of bias in the analysis domain, reflecting small samples, reliance on overall accuracy, and absent calibration. Subject-wise, patient-level data splitting was applied in only one study, and none reported external cross-device validation. No published EfficientNet study has used intraoral images of smoker’s melanosis; the sole EfficientNet study identified used non-intraoral photographs of smoking scenes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>EfficientNet-based transfer learning is a promising but unproven direction for smoker’s melanosis. Progress requires a graded intraoral dataset with standardised acquisition, imbalance handling as a design constraint, clinically oriented evaluation with subject-wise splitting and calibration, and interpretability. We also set out image acquisition standards clinicians can adopt now.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.509.title: THE EFFECT OF WELCOME DRINK AND FRONT OFFICE SERVICE QUALITY ON GUEST COMFORT DURING REGISTRATION
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.509.abstract: <jats:p>This study was motivated by guest waiting time during the registration (check-in) process, particularly during periods of high hotel occupancy, which may affect guest comfort. The Balcone Suites & Resort provides welcome drinks and Front Office services as part of its initial service while guests wait. This study aims to determine the effect of welcome drinks and Front Office service quality on guest comfort while waiting for the registration (check-in) process, both partially and simultaneously. This study employed a quantitative approach with a causal associative design. The sample consisted of 120 respondents selected using purposive sampling. Data were collected through a Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive analysis, classical assumption tests, and multiple linear regression with SPSS. The results showed that all variables were in the good category. Partially, welcome drinks did not have a significant effect (sig. = 0.079), while Front Office service quality had a significant effect (sig. = 0.010). Simultaneously, both variables had a significant effect (sig. = 0.002), with an R² of 0.105.</jats:p>

doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.435.title: <b>Implementation of the Project-Based Learning (PjBL) Model to Improve Student Creativity in Grade I of SDN 3 Setu Wetan, Weru District, Cirebon Regency</b>
doi:10.59211/mjpjetl.v4i2.435.abstract:
<jats:p>This study was motivated by the limited opportunities given to students to think creatively and develop their potential, which ultimately resulted in low levels of creativity. Of the 25 students, only 5 students (20%) demonstrated creativity and mastered the Pancasila learning material, while the remaining 20 students (80%) had not yet mastered the material. This study aimed to (1) determine the planning of the Project Based Learning (PjBL) model, (2) describe the implementation of the PjBL model, and (3) examine the improvement of students' creativity through the implementation of the PjBL model in Pancasila learning. The subjects of this study were first-grade students of SDN 3 Setu Wetan. This research employed Classroom Action Research (CAR) based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, conducted in two cycles. Data were collected using qualitative and quantitative approaches through observation, tests, project assessments, and field notes. The results showed that (1) the planning of the PjBL model was implemented well in Cycle II, with achievement increasing from 67% to 88%; (2) the implementation of the PjBL model improved by 22%, from 72% in Cycle I to 94% in Cycle II; and (3) students' creativity increased by 28%, from 64% in Cycle I to 92% in Cycle II. Therefore, it can be concluded that the implementation of the Project Based Learning (PjBL) model effectively improved the creativity of first-grade students at SDN 3 Setu Wetan.




 </jats:p>

doi:10.31234/osf.io/vb9u6_v2.title: The Role of Working Memory in Reward-based Learning over Long Timeframes: Opponent Bootstrapping and Interference Effects of Working Memory on Incremental Learning
doi:10.31234/osf.io/vb9u6_v2.abstract: Learning from feedback is essential for effective decision-making in daily life. Previous experiments have indicated that feedback-based learning involves multiple processes, such as slower reinforcement learning (RL) and fast working memory (WM). However, most of these studies focused on the dynamics of RL and WM in short timeframes, ranging from a few seconds to minutes, whereas real-life learning may occur over hours, days, or weeks. This study aimed to investigate the interplay between RL and WM in long-term feedback-based learning. Instead of learning back-to-back iterations in quick succession, participants learned one or two iterations per day for 24 days. In this scenario, initial trials each day should isolate non WM decision processes, and WM should primarily assist in subsequent trials, and in low load conditions, for example when a given item was repeated in short succession.There were four key findings. First, WM contributed broadly to learning in trials 2-n of each day, especially in low load conditions, while trial 1 isolated non WM contributions. Second, when WM was available, it produced both immediate and long-term benefits. WM steered choices toward correct responses, allowing more immediate rewards, but also supporting the training of correct stimulus-action associations over time (a bootstrapping effect). Third, both test-phase performance and computational modeling revealed that using WM had an additional deleterious interference effect; trials during which WM was available produced slower RL updating and worse test-phase performance. Fourth, the long-term training benefits of WM overshadowed its interference effect, such that the overall effect of WM on long-term learning remained positive.

doi:10.64807/bf8r1998.title: Effectiveness of Game-Based Learning Quizzes in Enhancing the Academic Performance of Araling Panlipunan 8 Learners
doi:10.64807/bf8r1998.abstract: <jats:p>Araling Panlipunan 8 requires learners to understand interconnected historical and sociopolitical concepts; however, lecture-centered instruction may provide limited opportunities for active retrieval, immediate feedback, and repeated practice. This study examined the effectiveness of Game-Based Learning Quizzes (GBLQs) in improving the formative assessment, posttest, and gain-score performance of Grade 8 learners compared with conventional lecture-discussion instruction. It employed a quantitative quasi-experimental pretest-posttest non-equivalent group design involving 74 learners from two intact sections of San Jose Integrated High School, San Pablo City, Laguna, during School Year 2025-2026. The experimental group (n = 37) received curriculum-aligned GBLQs through Kahoot!, Wayground, Wordwall, and researcher-made quiz games, while the comparison group (n = 37) received conventional lecture-discussion instruction. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, independent-samples and paired-samples t-tests, and Cohen’s d. Both groups had identical pretest means (M = 8.76, SD = 3.91), indicating comparable measured baseline performance. The experimental group obtained significantly higher total formative assessment scores (M = 66.13, SD = 4.70) than the comparison group (M = 57.03, SD = 7.22), t(72) = 6.425, p < .01, d = 1.49. It also achieved significantly higher posttest scores (M = 17.73, SD = 2.10) than the comparison group (M = 13.46, SD = 2.85), t(72) = 7.340, p < .01, d = 1.71. Although both groups improved significantly, the experimental group attained a significantly greater mean gain (M = 8.97, SD = 4.82) than the comparison group (M = 4.70, SD = 5.06), t(72) = 3.72, p < .001, d = 0.86. These findings demonstrate that curriculum-aligned GBLQs produced a statistically significant and educationally meaningful advantage in the measured academic performance of Grade 8 learners in Araling Panlipunan. Therefore, GBLQs may serve as structured formative assessment, review, and concept-reinforcement tools when quiz items align with curriculum competencies and are followed by explanatory feedback and teacher-guided discussion.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/ffgc.2026.1996868.title: Apparent thermal thresholds of carbon sink weakening in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area revealed by remote sensing and spatial machine learning
doi:10.3389/ffgc.2026.1996868.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Extreme summer heat poses a growing threat to terrestrial carbon sequestration, particularly in the forest and mountainous ecosystems of rapidly urbanizing subtropical regions, yet the spatial variability of heat-induced carbon-cycle responses and associated thermal threshold-like behavior remain insufficiently quantified. This study examined the effects of extreme summer heat on carbon cycling in the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) during summer 2023 using multi-source remote sensing and ERA5 reanalysis data processed through Google Earth Engine. A total of 4,158 spatially representative samples covering urban cores, suburban transition zones, and peripheral forested ecological areas were analyzed using an integrated framework combining geographically weighted regression (GWR), GW-XGBoost nonlinear prediction, SHAP explainability, and Q
                    <jats:sub>10</jats:sub>
                    -based carbon budget accounting. Land surface temperature (LST) was identified as one of the key factors associated with reduced net primary productivity (NPP), showing a strong negative correlation with NPP (
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                    = −0.68,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     &lt; 0.001), whereas NDVI exhibited a strong positive association (
                    <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                     = 0.72). The LST–NPP relationship was nonlinear, with a SHAP-identified transition interval near 27 °C –28 °C marking the onset of accelerated NPP decline, which progresses to substantially larger reductions at higher temperatures. Q10-based carbon budget estimates indicate that NPP falls below soil respiration—an indicator of source-like behavior—as surface temperature approaches 32 °C (estimated switch temperature, B
                    <jats:sub>switch</jats:sub>
                     = 32.05 °C). Across the sampled locations, 93.6% were estimated to be carbon sinks and 6.4% carbon sources, with the latter concentrated primarily in urban heat island areas along the Pearl River estuary. Strong sinks were concentrated in the northern mountainous forest belt, indicating that forest carbon-sink stability along urban–forest gradients is a key determinant of regional carbon balance. These findings highlight spatially uneven carbon vulnerability and support targeted heat mitigation, forest conservation, and adaptive-management strategies in subtropical megacity regions.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.5397/cise.2026.00395.title: Deep learning assessment of visualization in rotator cuff repair: a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial comparing epinephrine irrigation and intravenous tranexamic acid
doi:10.5397/cise.2026.00395.abstract: <jats:p>Background: This study aimed to compare intraoperative visualization between diluted epinephrine (EPN) irrigation and preoperative intravenous tranexamic acid (TXA) during the glenohumeral and subacromial phases of rotator cuff repair. Methods: Eighty-two patients with rotator cuff tears were prospectively randomized (1:1) to receive either 0.33 mg/L EPN irrigation without TXA (EPN group) or preoperative intravenous TXA (15 mg/kg) without EPN irrigation (TXA group). Visual clarity was evaluated using a pretrained deep learning model with a 3-point grading scale across three stages: intra-articular assessment, subacromial debridement, and rotator cuff repair. Irrigation pump pressure was recorded at each stage. Hypotensive bradycardic events (HBEs) and postoperative adverse events were monitored. Results: Overall visual clarity was significantly greater in the EPN group than in the TXA group (mean difference [MD], 0.07; 95% CI, 0.03–0.10; P<0.001). Visualization was superior with EPN during subacromial debridement (MD, 0.08; 95% CI, 0.03–0.13; P=0.001) and rotator cuff repair (MD, 0.03; 95% CI, 0.004–0.06; P=0.02). The EPN group required lower pump pressures and fewer increases in pressure. No significant differences in HBEs or adverse events were observed. Conclusions: Diluted EPN irrigation improved intraoperative visualization compared with TXA, particularly during the subacromial phases, without increasing perioperative risk. Deep learning provided objective support for its clinical use. Level of evidence: II.</jats:p>

doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-229-620261005.title: Examining Students' Attitudes Towards School and Learning in Five Countries in the Eastern Caribbean
doi:10.1108/978-1-83742-229-620261005.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the findings of a study conducted in 2017 among 1,477 secondary students, across five Caribbean countries – Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Grenada, St Kitts, and St Vincent and the Grenadines. Guided by the Tripartite Model of Attitudes (Ajzen, 1993) which conceptualises attitude as comprising three interrelated components, affective (emotional reactions), behavioural (actions or tendencies to act), and cognitive (beliefs or thoughts), the study utilised a multidimensional approach to examine students’ attitudes towards school and learning, capturing how they feel, what they believe, and how they behave in academic contexts as a result of their attitudes. The research used Gray's (1983) 24-item attitude scale and explored the differences in attitudes by gender and form level and identified specific aspects of schooling eliciting positive and negative responses. The findings indicated that overall, Caribbean students’ attitudes towards school and learning were moderately positive. No statistically significant difference was found across gender or form level. Additionally, while students understood the educational and developmental value of school, nuanced differences were found in their emotional responses to school. These results highlight the need for instructional practices that stimulate student interest and for ongoing teacher professional development that emphasises inclusive approaches to teaching. Furthermore, it emphasises the need for improving the affective climate of schools.</jats:p>
