doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02565-6.title: Machine learning based assessment of meditation for teen anger management
doi:10.1007/s44163-026-02565-6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Anger dysregulation during adolescence can negatively affect emotional well-being, interpersonal relationships, and academic functioning. Although meditation and yoga-based practices have been studied for emotional regulation, predictive machine-learning approaches remain comparatively limited. This study evaluates the feasibility of predicting self-reported improvement in anger management using behavioral, lifestyle, meditation, and yoga-related characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A publicly available survey dataset of 400 observations is analyzed. The prediction target is the response to
                      <jats:italic>“Do you feel an improvement in anger management?”</jats:italic>
                      , with 331 “Yes” and 69 “No” responses. Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and XGBoost are evaluated using a stratified 60:40 train-test split and five-fold stratified cross-validation. Preprocessing included imputation, categorical encoding, feature selection, scaling where required, and SMOTE within the modelling pipeline. Hyperparameters are optimized using RandomizedSearchCV with weighted F1-score.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Random Forest achieved the highest independent-test accuracy with Hold-out approach 86.25% and the highest mean five-fold accuracy 83.00 ± 1.90%. SVM and XGBoost achieved 83.75% test accuracy, while XGBoost obtained the highest mean Macro ROC-AUC 0.8447 ± 0.0489 and mean F1-score 83.01 ± 2.70% in cross-validation. Feature-importance and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses highlighted social activity/confidence, concentration/focus, and mindfulness/presence as influential predictors. No statistically significant differences are observed between models.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Machine learning can feasibly predict self-reported improvement in anger management from meditation-, behavioral-, and lifestyle-related characteristics. RF showed the strongest overall accuracy and stability, while XGBoost demonstrated stronger cross-validated discrimination. These findings represent predictive associations rather than causal effects and require validation using larger, longitudinal, independently collected datasets.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1186/s40359-026-05253-3.title: The impact of physical activity on self-esteem among Yi ethnic group secondary school students: the moderating role of authoritarian parenting
doi:10.1186/s40359-026-05253-3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Self-esteem is a key predictor of adolescent mental health, yet few studies have examined how family parenting styles moderate the relationship between physical activity and self-esteem among ethnic minority adolescents in China. This study investigated the association between physical activity and self-esteem among Yi junior high school students and tested whether authoritarian parenting attenuated this association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional survey of 712 Yi junior high school students (grades 7–9) from 10 middle schools in Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Sichuan Province was conducted using cluster convenience sampling. Physical activity was assessed using the Chinese version of the IPAQ short form; self-esteem was measured with the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale; authoritarian parenting was assessed using the harshness dimension of the Parenting Style Questionnaire. Moderation analysis was performed using Hayes' PROCESS macro (Model 1) with 5,000 bootstrap samples, controlling for gender and grade.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Physical activity was positively correlated with self-esteem (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                       = 0.196,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.01). Authoritarian parenting significantly moderated this relationship (interaction term B = -0.152,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.008). Simple slope analysis revealed that physical activity significantly predicted self-esteem when parental strictness was low (B = 2.322,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.008) but this association was attenuated and became non-significant when parental strictness was high (B = -0.401,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.233).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The beneficial effect of physical activity on self-esteem among Yi junior high school students is contingent upon the family rearing environment. Physical activity interventions targeting adolescent mental health should incorporate family-based components, particularly in contexts characterized by authoritarian parenting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

arxiv:2610.31600.title: SympFormer: Inertial Attention Blocks from Damped Hamiltonian Dynamics on Spaces of Probability Measures
arxiv:2610.31600.abstract: The attention mechanism underpins modern large language models, yet their dynamics remain only partially understood. Recent perspectives interpret attention blocks as interacting particle systems, whose mean-field limits correspond to gradient flows of energy functionals on spaces of probability densities on $\mathbb R^d$ equipped with Wasserstein-type metrics. We extend this viewpoint by deriving accelerated attention blocks from inertial, Nesterov-type damped Hamiltonian dynamics on these density spaces, developing the geometry and differential calculus needed to make the construction rigorous. In particular, we introduce a local-mobility geometry for the Otto-Wasserstein and softmax-Wasserstein settings, and a quotient Stein geometry that resolves the degeneracy of the linear-attention kernel to yield a well-defined metric and differential calculus. We provide rigorous foundations when softmax attention admits a gradient-flow formulation and when its inertial counterpart admits a damped Hamiltonian on explicitly characterized domains. For linear attention, we obtain a finite-dimensional solution theory with sharp conditions for global existence versus finite-time second-moment blow-up. We further prove a quantitative link between continuous moment blow-up and the discrete-layer depth at which token norms cross a prescribed threshold. Finally, motivated by the finite-token geometry, we propose geometric corrections to token and momentum updates. In decoder-only, nanoGPT-style experiments on TinyStories and OpenWebText, these corrections lower validation negative log-likelihood on next-token prediction relative to momentum-only controls.

arxiv:2610.31478.title: MoG-VLM: Efficient Video Anomaly Detection through Motion-Guided Vision-Language Models
arxiv:2610.31478.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong potential for video anomaly detection, but dense frame-level inference makes them impractical for real-time deployment. Existing acceleration commonly relies on uniform sampling, which ignores content dynamics and can either waste computation on static segments or miss localized anomalies. We propose MoG-VLM a motion-adaptive anomaly detection framework that leverages motion purely as a lightweight control signal to decide when VLM inference is necessary. To this end, we introduce Temporal Gradient Magnitude (TGM) which performs content-aware sampling to concentrate computation on informative regions while avoiding redundant processing. We further introduce a hierarchical dual-stream design in which dense multi-frame VLM reasoning is activated only around frames with elevated anomaly likelihood, via anchor-triggered context-window expansion with early termination. A fusion module then reconciles these instantaneous semantic cues with temporal action dynamics. Across four benchmarks, our method achieves 91.91%, 84.30%, 87.88%, and 78.96% AUC-ROC on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, MSAD, and ShanghaiTech, respectively, establishing new state of the art on three benchmarks under the zero-shot, training-free setting. On XD-Violence, we improve over the previous best result by +0.57% while delivering a 1.31x inference speedup. These results demonstrate that content-aware allocation of VLM capacity, processing fewer frames more intelligently rather than all frames uniformly, is a more effective axis of progress than uniformly densifying VLM inference across frames. Code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kdawoud91/MoG-VLM.

arxiv:2610.31338.title: ValuSpec: Plug-and-Play Candidate Valuation before Target Verification for Tree-Based Speculative Decoding
arxiv:2610.31338.abstract: Tree-based speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by verifying multiple candidate branches in parallel. However, in practical serving scenarios, similar requests repeatedly induce overlapping candidate branches. While retrieval-based methods mitigate this by reusing historical drafts, the resulting candidate trees often contain many low-quality branches as the candidate tree grows, which reduces verification efficiency and wastes target-side computation. To address this, we propose ValuSpec, a plug-and-play candidate valuation mechanism that filters low-quality branches from a supplied candidate tree before expensive target-side verification. ValuSpec introduces transfer-based supervision to align filtering with the target model's behavior. A filtering threshold is estimated from the target model's greedy trajectories on a calibration split, without any parameter training. The target model then verifies the filtered tree under the output-identical greedy rule, so accepted tokens are guaranteed to match standard autoregressive decoding exactly. Experimental results on HumanEval, GSM8K, Dolly, and SpecBench show that, in our main evaluation, ValuSpec achieves up to 2.38x end-to-end speedup in retrieval-based tree settings. Furthermore, integrating ValuSpec into the EAGLE-3 dynamic tree framework yields up to 2.78x end-to-end speedup without modifying its tree construction strategy, demonstrating that ValuSpec serves as a generally applicable and plug-and-play candidate valuation module.

arxiv:2610.31322.title: Hyperreduction accelerates finite element model updating for the discovery of neural materials
arxiv:2610.31322.abstract: Finite element model updating is among the most general approaches to discover constitutive models from structural experiments: since the displacement field is computed rather than measured, it accommodates arbitrary geometries, boundary conditions, and sparse or noisy data. However, every loss evaluation requires a nonlinear finite element solve per load step, and training neural materials requires many such evaluations. Intrusive model order reduction lowers this cost while retaining boundary conditions and variational structure. How can a reduced model remain accurate while the network weights change at every training step? We combine proper orthogonal decomposition and energy-conserving sampling and weighting with adjoint sensitivities of the reduced model, and adapt both the trial space and the sampled elements along the optimization path. The constitutive law is a polyconvex neural network: a logarithmic normalization term, together with a zero-anchored input convex architecture and a growth term, renders the energy polyconvex, coercive, and non-negative by construction, independent of the trained weights. We demonstrate the approach on two experimental datasets and one synthetic three-dimensional example. For a two-phase specimen, training time decreases from nine hours to 41 minutes compared with a full-order identification, without loss of accuracy. In the three-dimensional example, six modes replace 48 672 degrees of freedom, 116 of 15 625 elements suffice to evaluate the internal forces, and training takes 13 minutes. In all cases, the identified material reproduces the measured reaction force and predicts the displacement field from the force alone. Hyperreduction makes the discovery of neural materials from structural data affordable while retaining the advantages of finite element model updating.

arxiv:2610.31089.title: Transformers with CoT Discover Heavy-Ball Acceleration Through Training
arxiv:2610.31089.abstract: Modern transformers often solve complex tasks by generating and refining intermediate reasoning steps. To develop a theoretical understanding of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, a notable recent study by Huang et al. (2025) viewed transformers as algorithm executors, and showed that when transformers' CoT steps are supervised by a gradient-descent teacher, they can learn to implement gradient descent for in-context weight prediction in linear regression. In this paper, we study the same in-context weight prediction task but ask whether CoT reasoning can go beyond merely imitating the teacher algorithm. We show that, after initial supervision from a gradient-descent teacher, further trajectory-level supervision using the true regression weights leads the model to implement the Heavy-Ball method, thereby achieving acceleration over the original teacher. Notably, this accelerated algorithm emerges without supervision from any Heavy-Ball teacher. Our results provide a concrete theoretical example in which transformer reasoning can discover new algorithms through training, rather than merely imitate the algorithm used for supervision.

arxiv:2610.31024.title: NN-Based Transistor Modeling for Ultra-Fast SPICE Simulation and Standard Cell Library Characterization
arxiv:2610.31024.abstract: Neural network (NN)-based transistor models have proven to be a promising solution to accelerate device modeling. Although these models demonstrated remarkable speedup in circuit simulations, they were not rigorously tested in complex tasks within standard EDA tool flows for chip design, which require very high transistor model precision to provide accurate results and converge properly. To investigate their full potential and promise, we develop NN-based transistor models that accurately predict the drain current and various charges for a 3nm nanosheet, and employ the models for a standard cell library characterization. This enables us to evaluate the accuracy and speedup under a very wide range of SPICE simulations, benchmarking our models against an industry-standard implementation. Since standard cell library characterization involves thousands of SPICE simulations, it serves as a great benchmark for transistor model quality and consistency. To further evaluate model accuracy, we also perform analog- and digital-level simulations for various complex circuits. Our experiments reveal that NN-based models are a valid alternative to existing transistor compact models, capable of producing accurate delay and power estimates with a much higher speed and convergence time compared to the conventional Verilog-A-based industry-standard (BSIM-CMG) transistor compact model. Our NNs achieve sub-0.11% and 0.76% errors for delay and total power evaluation on a wide range of circuits, while taking up to 8 times less time during the standard cell library characterization. Additionally, we provide comprehensive information and guidance on NN accuracy, unveiling the relationship between NN size and its effect on circuit simulation precision.

arxiv:2610.30923.title: Low-Latency MoE Inference in Space Data Centers: A Wireless-Power-Transfer Perspective
arxiv:2610.30923.abstract: Space data centers (SpaceDCs) are emerging as platforms for large language models (LLMs), supported by continuous solar-energy harvesting and high-speed interconnections. The mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture supports distributed LLM inference by deploying experts across satellites. However, skewed expert activation creates uneven computation power demands despite uniform solar-power supply at the dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit (SSO). Consequently, active experts remain power-constrained while harvested power at idle experts is underused. These reduce inference efficiency and increase latency. To address this supply-demand mismatch, we propose the SpaceWPT framework, which uses inter-satellite laser-based wireless power transfer (WPT) to redistribute harvested power. The key design challenge is to balance the computation demands of power-donating and power-receiving satellites under WPT losses: transferring more power accelerates computation at the receiver but leaves less power for the donor. After deriving design principles that simplify WPT control, we characterize the resulting latency tradeoff through a tractable surrogate of average inference latency. Minimizing the surrogate yields a novel two-sided water-filling strategy that determines whether each active expert donates, retains, or receives power according to the water level and its WPT link efficiency. Simulations with Mixtral-8x7B and Phi-3.5-MoE show up to 29.25% lower inference latency than without WPT, with larger gains under more compact formations and higher transfer efficiencies.

arxiv:2610.30858.title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
arxiv:2610.30858.abstract: An AI system can produce more economically valuable work while delivering less value for the energy it consumes. We therefore ask: How much economic value does an AI system create per unit of energy consumed? We formalize economic value in two ways: (1) net dollar value, the output's dollar value minus AI-system execution cost, and (2) time saving, the expert's completion time minus the AI system's completion time. Dividing each by measured end-to-end energy yields Net Value per Joule (NVJ) and Time Saving per Joule (TSJ), reported in USD/MJ and hours/MJ. We study 220 public GDPval tasks across 44 occupations, serving five open-weight models locally and evaluating four accelerator types. First, the occupation groups where AI systems succeed most often, deliver the greatest dollar value, or save the most time do not necessarily provide the greatest economic return per joule. For example, among the tested tasks, engineering work delivers about 10% more net dollar value per task than software development. Yet software development delivers about 27% more net value per joule. Second, GLM 5.2 delivers the highest average net dollar value, at $72.27 per task using 0.430 MJ, equivalent in energy to about four hours of active laptop use. By contrast, Gemma 4 31B delivers 56% of that net dollar value using just 23% of the energy, achieving approximately 2.5 times the NVJ and 2.8 times the TSJ. Third, across four single-accelerator deployments, Qwen3.6-27B's NVJ varies by a factor of 4.32 and TSJ by 9.27, with B200 leading both. Additionally, one and eight H100s deliver similar net dollar value, but eight reduce completion time by 22% at 3.24 times the energy. Our framework makes output value and expert time saving under an energy budget explicit objectives for improving models, accelerators, and software, while offering a new basis for assessing AI's potential economic effect on occupational work.

arxiv:2610.30599.title: Impacts of generative AI skill development on academic adaptation and learning outcomes among university students
arxiv:2610.30599.abstract: Understanding how university students perceive the development of their generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) skills over time can clarify how GenAI use relates to learning and academic outcomes. This study examined perceived skill-development trajectories, changes in learning practices, and associated academic gains using a retrospective questionnaire with 313 analyzed responses and interviews with 18 students across subject areas. Descriptive and comparative analyses and exploratory structural equation modeling (SEM) were integrated with thematic analysis. Perceived developmental trajectories were heterogeneous: 34.2% of students reported rapid early improvement followed by a plateau, 28.4% steady improvement, and 21.1% delayed acceleration. Development was also uneven across skills, with improvement in evaluating GenAI outputs perceived as more challenging; assignments were the most frequently selected driver of skill growth. Interviews further indicated increasingly specific prompting, tailored verification, and selective delegation, although some students reported stable routines, dependence, skipped reasoning, or improvements attributable partly to better GenAI tools. Academic gains were reported more often for assignments than for examinations. The SEM indicated a positive indirect association between perceived skill growth and academic gains through adaptation of assignment processes, whereas academic gains did not clearly differ across developmental trajectory groups after multiplicity correction. The findings suggest that perceived GenAI skill development varies in both trajectory and skill domain and is associated with changes in learning practices and differentiated academic benefits.

arxiv:2610.30500.title: PhysibleMDM: Enforcing Inference-Time Physical Feasibility Constraints on Motion Diffusion Models via Noise Optimization
arxiv:2610.30500.abstract: Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model. We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.

arxiv:2610.30480.title: FIGFLEX: A Mixed-Precision FP-INT GEMM Accelerator Co-Designed with Low-Bit LLM Quantization
arxiv:2610.30480.abstract: Weight-only quantization keeps LLM activations in floating point and stores weights as low-bit integers, turning the dominant workload into floating-point-integer (FP-INT) general matrix multiplication. Recent quantizers reach a 2-3-bit average with mixed precision, but hardware has not kept pace: GPUs dequantize weights to FP16 before the tensor-core multiply-accumulate, and bit-parallel FP-INT accelerators run at a single weight precision, so fewer bits save memory but not computation. In this paper, we present FIGFLEX, an algorithm-hardware co-designed mixed-precision accelerator whose bit-parallel datapath scales throughput as precision falls. FIGFLEX contributes (1) a shift-add, radix-4 reformulation of FP-INT multiplication that fuses the multiply-accumulate into a unified, precision-flexible partial-product reduction and roughly halves the partial products, together with a novel INT3 optimization that reclaims the idle datapath radix-4 leaves at that precision; and (2) a mixed-precision quantizer that assigns each channel group its bit-width according to the error GPTQ cannot compensate, with a per-input-channel column scaling whose power-of-two normalization keeps the scaled activations out of the FP16 subnormal range, so that the quantized model maps directly onto FIGFLEX's datapath with the same accuracy as on a GPU. On LLaMA-2-7B, FIGFLEX attains 5.85 and 8.77 WikiText-2 perplexity at 3- and 2-bit average precision, lower than GPTQ, AWQ, SliM-LLM, AMQ, and QuIP# (without fine-tuning), while delivering 1.56x and 1.42x higher whole-chip throughput per area on the linear GEMMs of a 3-bit mixed-precision model than AxCore and FIGLUT, respectively.

arxiv:2610.30334.title: MPBRS: Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Unified Reward Configuration in Humanoid Locomotion
arxiv:2610.30334.abstract: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.

arxiv:2610.30293.title: EgoHand: Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
arxiv:2610.30293.abstract: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.69 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.

arxiv:2610.30170.title: Accelerating Wildfire Hazard Mapping Across Canada with an AI Surrogate Modelling Framework
arxiv:2610.30170.abstract: Canada's increasing wildfire activity requires frequent national hazard mapping to guide proactive mitigation, including fuel management, land-use planning, infrastructure protection, and evacuation routing. However, process-based wildfire simulation frameworks (e.g., BurnP3 and BurnP3+) rely on computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations to model burn probability, fire intensity, and rate of spread. These workflows can take days to weeks to process a single regional modelling unit. To overcome these computational bottlenecks, we present three contributions developed through collaboration between AI researchers and wildfire modelling experts: (a) a standardized framework for training, fine-tuning, and evaluating AI surrogate models against process-based wildfire simulators; (b) a multi-task deep learning surrogate trained on national-scale data to emulate burn probability, mean fire intensity, and mean rate of spread at a fraction of the computational cost (seconds); and (c) domain-specific metrics and counterfactual evaluation protocols to probe out-of-distribution generalization. Integrating geospatial data (fuel, terrain, ignition likelihood) and regional weather, our model approximates BurnP3+ simulation outputs, achieving strong performance across agreement, rank-correlation, error, and spatial-overlap metrics. It preserves downstream hazard classifications and produces physically plausible responses to expert-informed counterfactual interventions. On a representative region, the surrogate achieves 806-fold end-to-end CPU acceleration and uses 13% of BurnP3+'s host memory, facilitating rapid scenario analysis.

arxiv:2610.30688.title: An Agent Architecture with Tools and Memory for Selective Correction of Wrist PPG Heart Rate Estimates
arxiv:2610.30688.abstract: Wrist photoplethysmography (PPG) heart rate estimates are vulnerable to motion artifacts, and corrections that reduce mean error can worsen individual windows. We propose an agent architecture with tools and memory around a fixed heart rate estimator. Pulse, motion, and limited historical evidence generate candidate estimates, whose predicted benefits and harms guide selection. An independent risk gate determines whether to retain, correct, or reject each output. We trained the architecture on PPG-DaLiA and tested it on Wrist Exercise, GalaxyPPG, and WildPPG with frozen weights. Across these four public datasets, mean absolute error (MAE), macro-averaged over ten estimators, decreased by up to 44.5%, with the largest reduction on GalaxyPPG. Beneficial and harmful corrections decreased and increased absolute error by more than 1 bpm, respectively. Their ten-estimator macro-averaged proportions ranged from 16.06% to 36.64% and from 1.68% to 6.77%, respectively, across the four datasets. At 60% and 80% target coverage, numerical correction on the same accepted windows contributed more to total error reduction than window selection. We implemented real-time wearable acquisition, Bluetooth reception, and smartphone deployment of a selected estimator and the framework. In backend analysis of four prototype recordings from one participant, ten-estimator macro-averaged MAE decreased from 9.09 to 4.45 bpm without additional rejection. Under the evaluated conditions, the architecture improved average accuracy while quantifying correction benefits and harms, supporting wearable heart rate analysis that considers error, correction risk, and coverage.

arxiv:2610.31180.title: Track finding and particle identification performance with particle physics foundation models
arxiv:2610.31180.abstract: Modern high energy nuclear and particle physics experiments produce large amounts of sparse data that must be reduced significantly in size before performing physics analysis. Recently, there has been an effort to evaluate Foundation Models as a potential tool for performing data analysis. These models have been shown to learn features in high dimensional datasets based on the multi-modal data they are trained on. To show their effectiveness at performing complex pattern recognition tasks, such as reconstructing charged particles in a magnetic field, we evaluated the performance of a Foundation Model based reconstruction on several downstream tasks with a dataset composed of spacepoints in a Time Projection Chamber. We show that the performance of the Foundation Model based data analysis significantly improves upon that of traditional methods, and furthermore can be adapted to learn additional tasks that are not necessarily related to the initial training objective.

arxiv:2610.31108.title: DRAFT: Decoding and Reconstructing 3D Room Layouts from fMRI and Camera Trajectories
arxiv:2610.31108.abstract: While functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) decoders reconstruct images and 3D objects, recovering the metric geometry of rooms from a moving viewpoint remains an open challenge. We introduce, to our knowledge for the first time, the task of reconstructing 3D layouts of held-out scenes using only the known camera trajectories and the fMRI signals of participants watching indoor walkthroughs, without any visual frames. The task is hard because of the temporal mismatch between rapid visual changes and blurred fMRI signals. Our method, DRAFT (Decoding and Reconstructing 3D room lAyouts from fMRI and Trajectories), extracts a compact layout representation from the early visual cortex and fuses this neural code with the geometric free space derived from camera motion. To evaluate it, we propose layout r, the Pearson correlation between predicted and ray-cast log depths. On ten held-out scenes (20 participants), DRAFT reaches a layout r of 0.480, outperforming the camera path alone (0.446) and seven fMRI decoders (at most 0.429). DRAFT also works as a plug-in that improves all seven decoders without retraining, raising their layout r from 0.171-0.429 to 0.487-0.493. Brain activity and camera motion can thus recover the metric layout of unseen rooms, a first step toward reconstructing the 3D spaces people see.

arxiv:2610.30528.title: Decision Making and Ride Comfort Evaluation Based on Lane-Change Prediction for Autonomous Vehicles
arxiv:2610.30528.abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicles' lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle's lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.

arxiv:2610.30338.title: Machine Learning Neutrino-Nucleus Cross Sections II: More Leptons
arxiv:2610.30338.abstract: Neutrino-nucleus cross sections are essential inputs for long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments, yet remain challenging to model with high precision. Recent work demonstrated that fully black-box data-driven cross-section models cannot accurately generalize between near- and far-detector fluxes, but imposing Standard-Model symmetries via structure-function parameterizations provides a well-posed learning problem in a simplified DUNE-inspired muon-neutrino disappearance analysis. Here, we extend this framework to multiple lepton flavors and both neutrino and antineutrino beam modes, incorporating the electron appearance channel and enabling a simultaneous determination of $\sin^2θ_{23}$, $Δm^2_{31}$, and the CP-violating phase $δ_{\rm CP}$. We find that the learned cross section model recovers the injected oscillation parameters without significant bias, with constraints comparable to those obtained using the exact underlying cross section. Flux uncertainties have more significant effects in the multi-channel case, and incorporating flux nuisance parameters into the learning problem is required for accurate results. Our results demonstrate that this data-driven approach can be extended to the multi-channel measurements needed for long-baseline neutrino oscillation analyses.

doi:10.1103/49ns-fryv.title: Real-time reinforcement learning on coupling correction
doi:10.1103/49ns-fryv.abstract: The stability of vertical emittance is a critical performance metric for modern high-brightness synchrotron light sources. This paper presents a real-time, reinforcement learning (RL)-based correction framework based on deep reinforcement learning by employing dueling deep Q-network with a discrete action space to dynamically adjust skew quadrupole magnets. To ensure operational safety and accelerate convergence, we introduce a curriculum learning strategy and leverage a high-fidelity simulation of the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility for systematic hyperparameter optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that the agent, trained in situ on the real machine, successfully achieves stabilization of the beam-size readback at the submicrometer fluctuation level and exhibits rapid adaptability to target changes. This work validates the feasibility of using RL for robust, online accelerator optimization during user beam delivery.

doi:10.1103/ktbp-csd3.title: Search for single production of a vectorlike <math display="inline"><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> quark decaying to a top quark and a <math display="inline"><mi>W</mi></math> boson in the single-lepton final state in proton-proton collisions at <math display="inline"><msqrt><mi>s</mi></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mtext> </mtext><mtext> </mtext><mi>TeV</mi></math>
authors: Torres Da Silva De Araujo, F.
Silva, C. Beirão Da Cruz E.
Calderon De La Barca Sanchez, M.
doi:10.1103/ktbp-csd3.abstract: A search is presented for the production of a single narrow-width vectorlike <math display="inline"><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> quark that decays to a <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> quark and a <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> boson. This search targets a single-lepton final state, where a muon or electron originates either from the semileptonic decay of the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> quark or from the leptonic decay of the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> boson, with the other particle decaying hadronically. The (semi)leptonic portion of the event is reconstructed from an electron or muon, missing transverse momentum, and a small-radius jet identified as a <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> quark jet if the muon or electron originates from the <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> quark. The hadronic portion of the event is reconstructed as a single large-radius jet. The originating particle of the large-radius jet is identified using a neural-network-based tagger, and the dominant background contributions are modeled from data using a neural autoregressive flow network. The data were collected from 2016 to 2018 by the CMS experiment at the LHC in proton-proton collisions at <math display="inline"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn><mtext> </mtext><mtext> </mtext><mi>TeV</mi></mrow></math>, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of <math display="inline"><mrow><mn>138</mn><mtext> </mtext><mtext> </mtext><msup><mrow><mi>fb</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. This search is the most sensitive to date to the production of single narrow-width <math display="inline"><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> quarks. It excludes electroweak-singlet <math display="inline"><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> quarks with <math display="inline"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Γ</mi><mo>/</mo><msub><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mi>B</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>′</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> for masses between 0.8 and 1.23 TeV. Limits are also placed on the production cross section of single <math display="inline"><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> quarks produced in association with <math display="inline"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> quarks, and on the coupling factor of the <math display="inline"><msup><mi>B</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></math> quark to electroweak bosons.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.27530.title: ZKPU: Zero-Knowledge Processing Unit for Heterogeneous Workloads
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.27530.abstract: Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) have become a fundamental building block for privacy-preserving computation, blockchain systems, and verifiable machine learning. Modern ZKP protocols span two distinct families: curve-based protocols, which rely on large finite-field arithmetic, and hash-based protocols, which operate over native 64-bit fields. Existing hardware accelerators are specialized for one protocol family because they are built on operand-scanning Montgomery multiplication, resulting in fixed-width datapaths, poor utilization across heterogeneous operand widths, and limited scalability. This paper presents \emph{ZKPU}, a Zero-Knowledge Processing Unit for heterogeneous ZKP workloads. ZKPU introduces a new compute paradigm by co-designing finely integrated product scanning (FIPS) Montgomery multiplication with a reconfigurable Twin Systolic Fabric (TSF), enabling modular multiplication at arbitrary widths in 64-bit increments. Combined with a fine-grained Deque buffer, on-chip twiddle-factor generator, and memory-efficient MSM preprocessing strategy, ZKPU provides a unified architecture for both curve-based and hash-based protocols. Evaluation using Groth16 and Plonky2 shows that ZKPU achieves up to $144\times$ speedup for NTT, $13.6\times$ for MSM, and approximately $7.2\times$ end-to-end application speedup over state-of-the-art accelerators, while being the first architecture to efficiently support both protocol families on a single reconfigurable hardware platform.

doi:10.47389/41.4.51.title: How Australian fire and rescue service personnel would like to improve their decision-making learning and training programs
doi:10.47389/41.4.51.abstract: <jats:p>Effective management of the response to an incident or emergency event is critically dependent on the decision-making skills of incident and emergency management (IEM) personnel. In a series of workshops conducted in 2022 by Natural Hazards Research Australia, priorities were identified that specified future needs for the practice and training of IEM decision-making. The research in this paper contributes to the understanding of how to address these priorities by considering the views of a sample of fire and rescue service personnel about their agency’s current decision-making training program and aspects to improve. This paper provides findings from 34 semi-structured interviews with fire and rescue services personnel in Australia. The sample comprised 29 men and 5 women. Participants worked in rural fire services (n=17), urban fire services (n=9) and State Emergency Services (n=8). The findings suggest that there is need for greater training focus on emergency management decision-making, greater use of exercise-based training activities, a formal approach to mentoring and coaching staff development programs and mandatory refresher courses and review exercises to maintain incident management skills. Australian fire and rescue services agencies need to ensure they are taking a strategic and holistic approach to emergency management learning and development programs.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4599-2.ch009.title: Automated Detection of Ventricular Flutter and Ventricular Hypertrophy From ECG Using Deep Learning
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4599-2.ch009.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate automated detection of ventricular arrhythmias and structural cardiac abnormalities remains a major clinical challenge. This paper presents an ECG-based framework to identify acute life-threatening arrhythmias and detect chronic structural changes. For ventricular flutter, the detection module achieved 99.28% accuracy (95% CI: 99.11–99.43%), with 94.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity using classical machine learning on 32 engineered time-, frequency-, and entropy-based features extracted from 3–5 second ECG windows and classified using an SVM with RBF kernel. Bilateral ventricular hypertrophy detection used a CNN-LSTM model processing 10-second 12-lead ECG recordings, achieving ROC-AUC values of 0.918 for LVH and 0.938 for RVH. The LVH module achieved 88.2% sensitivity and 84.7% specificity, while RVH detection reached 91.7% sensitivity and 88.6% specificity. Evaluation used the MIT-BIH Malignant Ventricular Ectopy, Creighton University, and PTB-XL echocardiography-validated databases, demonstrating strong cross-database performance and real-time clinical applicability.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch007.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter discusses ways decentralized metaverse classrooms promote inclusive, collaborative and learner-centered education at the same time bringing out challenges of accessibility, privacy, governance and equity. Based on contemporary literature on immersive learning, digital transformation and decentralized educational governance, the chapter interrogates the potential of metaverse environments to develop social interaction, experiential learning and participation among geographically dispersed, marginalized and differently abled learners. The chapter is premised on the assumption that the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), blockchain technologies, federated learning and metaverse ecosystems is transforming educational systems worldwide. The chapter proposes an integrated conceptual framework comprising immersive metaverse learning spaces, blockchain governance systems, federated intelligence architectures and inclusive educational practices.</jats:p>

doi:10.68012/shem.v2i2.313.title: <b>Designing a Hybrid CNN-Transformer Architecture for Robust Medical Image Diagnosis</b>
doi:10.68012/shem.v2i2.313.abstract: <jats:p>Medical image diagnosis increasingly relies on deep learning against a background where convolutional neural networks capture local texture well but miss long-range spatial relationships, while transformer models need large labeled datasets and heavy computation that clinical settings rarely have. This study pursues the objective of designing a hybrid CNN-Transformer architecture that fuses convolutional feature extraction with self-attention to raise diagnostic accuracy on X-rays, MRI scans, and histopathology slides without exceeding the computational budget of real-world deployment. The proposed method pairs a lightweight convolutional backbone, which extracts local texture and edge features, with a transformer encoder that models global relationships across image regions, merging the two branches through a cross-attention fusion module before a classification head outputs the diagnosis. Training the architecture on publicly available medical imaging datasets and evaluating it against standalone CNN and transformer baselines using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score, the result reveals that the hybrid architecture beats both baselines, raising accuracy and sensitivity on cases with subtle abnormalities that need local texture recognition and broader spatial reasoning together, while inference time stays within a practical range for clinical workflows. These findings lead to the conclusion that the hybrid CNN-Transformer design gives clinicians a computationally feasible path to more robust medical image diagnosis, and the paper releases the architecture and source code to support reproducibility and further research toward accessible, trustworthy AI-assisted healthcare.</jats:p>

doi:10.62762/tmi.2026.633155.title: The Medieval Text and the Modern Question: AI for Multilingual Semantic Retrieval across Centuries
doi:10.62762/tmi.2026.633155.abstract: <jats:p>Multilingual access to medieval literature requires retrieval systems to bridge historical and cross-lingual semantic variation. This article introduces HistRAG, a language-aware framework combining lexical retrieval, multilingual dense representations, historical adaptation, hybrid fusion, and cross-encoder reranking. HistRAG separates the effects of document modernization, query adaptation, and retrieval architecture within a unified experimental setting. The framework is evaluated on a heterogeneous collection of Medieval Catalan literature using equivalent queries in three contemporary languages. Results show that lexical retrieval is highly sensitive to query language, while multilingual dense representations provide more robust cross-lingual access. Fixed hybrid fusion offers no systematic advantage over dense retrieval, and historical adaptations produce heterogeneous, non-additive effects. Cross-encoder reranking achieves the strongest average effectiveness, although its contribution varies across languages and evaluation subsets. These findings support an architecture- and language-sensitive approach to semantic retrieval from historically distant collections and provide a reproducible basis for extending AI-enabled access to other medieval textual traditions.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4599-2.ch012.title: Causal Machine Learning and Explainable AI for Understanding the Impact of Technology Use on Obesity in Healthcare
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4599-2.ch012.abstract: <jats:p>Obesity is one of the most significant public health problems of our time due to its multifaceted causes and increasing prevalence. The integration of digital technologies into daily life has increased interest in the effects of technology use on obesity. However, most current studies focus on predicting obesity or examining relationships between variables at the correlation level. In this chapter, the effect of technology use intensity on obesity is evaluated using a combination of explanatory artificial intelligence and causal machine learning approaches. For this purpose, predictive and explanatory analyses were performed using XGBoost and SHAP methods; mean and heterogeneous causal effects were examined using Double Machine Learning and Causal Forest methods. The findings show that the effect of technology use on obesity may not be linear and unidirectional, but may differ according to individual characteristics. This chapter presents a causal perspective on the effects of digital lifestyle on health.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1925423.title: Diagnostic performance of deep learning models using ultrasound for preoperative axillary nodal status in breast cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1925423.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deep-learning (DL) models may extract nodal-risk information from breast or axillary ultrasound, but the relevant studies differ in anatomical input, preprocessing, reference standard, and validation design.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We updated PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and Cochrane CENTRAL, with supplementary OpenAlex and Crossref searches and repeated backward and forward citation searching through 24 August 2026. Eligible studies evaluated a deep-learning model using ultrasound as the sole imaging modality for pretreatment binary axillary or sentinel nodal status in breast cancer, used surgical pathology as the reference standard, and reported an independent patient-level validation cohort with an exact or uniquely reconstructable 2 × 2 table. One cohort per study was selected using a prespecified hierarchy. Sensitivity and specificity were synthesized with a bivariate random-effects model and an HSROC curve.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eleven studies comprising 1,027 validation patients were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.75 (95% CI 0.66–0.81; 95% prediction interval 0.50–0.90) and pooled specificity was 0.89 (95% CI 0.83–0.93; prediction interval 0.66–0.97). The summary HSROC area was 0.81. The positive likelihood ratio was 6.60 (95% CI 4.29–10.42), the negative likelihood ratio was 0.29 (0.21–0.38), and the diagnostic odds ratio was 23.12 (12.89–41.50). Descriptive univariate I² values were 64.2% for sensitivity and 73.8% for specificity. Deeks’ test did not indicate funnel-plot asymmetry (P = 0.677).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ultrasound-based DL models showed moderate sensitivity and high specificity in selected validation cohorts. Wide prediction intervals, heterogeneous anatomical inputs and preprocessing, incompletely reported definitions of nodal positivity, and the geographic concentration of studies limit immediate clinical transportability. These models should be evaluated as adjuncts to, rather than replacements for, pathological axillary staging.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Systematic review registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>

                      , identifier CRD42024589342.

doi:10.3389/fenvs.2026.1937303.title: Comparison and spatial heterogeneity of eco-efficiency in two major river basins of China: nonlinear mechanism analysis based on spatial machine learning
doi:10.3389/fenvs.2026.1937303.abstract: <jats:p>Achieving a synergy between economic expansion and environmental conservation across major watersheds is vital for China’s sustainable trajectory. This study proposes a unified cross-basin framework, using a three-stage super-efficiency Slack-Based Measure (SE-SBM) and Global Malmquist-Luenberger (GML) index to assess the static and dynamic eco-efficiency (EE) of the Yellow River Basin (YRB) and the Yangtze River Economic Belt (YREB). For the analysis of spatiotemporal evolution, kernel density estimation (KDE) and the Dagum Gini coefficient (DGC) are implemented. A Geographically Weighted Random Forest (GWRF) model is introduced to characterize nonlinear associations and spatial heterogeneity among the factors associated with EE. Results reveal that: (1) The adjusted EE of the YRB declined, but it remained superior overall compared to the slightly rising YREB. In terms of space, the YRB shows a stepwise decline, while the YREB presents a concave shape with a lower center. (2) The technical progress (TC) is the primary contributor to GML-based EE growth in the two major river basins. The GWRF model uncovers significant nonlinear threshold effects (e.g., urbanization and environmental regulations) and U-shaped evolutionary characteristics (e.g., industrial structure and financial development). Local feature-importance patterns further indicate distinct spatial structures: a regulation-oriented constraint pattern in the YRB and a market-oriented radiation pattern in the YREB. This multi-method integration provides a novel theoretical perspective and a solid basis for decision-making in formulating cross-basin collaborative policies.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1960677.title: How is leader-member exchange related to teachers’ instructional practices in Türkiye? The mediating role of collective teacher innovativeness and learning effectiveness
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1960677.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>How leadership processes that support teacher motivation are related to effective instructional practices remains a relevant topic in educational research. However, how leader-member exchange in schools is related to instructional practices is not yet well understood. Furthermore, there remains uncertainty in the literature regarding how the relationship between leader-member interaction and teachers’ instructional practices shapes collective innovation and learning effectiveness. In this respect, the aim of the study is to examine the mediating role of perceived collective teacher innovativeness and learning effectiveness in the association between leader-member exchange and teachers’ instructional practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample consisted of 1185 teachers recruited from all 12 NUTS-1 regions of Türkiye through proportional regional stratification with voluntary participation within schools. Moreover, the study was conducted using quantitative and cross-sectional design, the study data were collected with structured scales, and Structural Equation Modeling was used in the analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis showed positive associations among all four constructs. Leader-member exchange had a small direct association with instructional practices (β = 0.10) and larger associations with perceived collective innovativeness (β = 0.34) and learning effectiveness (β = 0.25); the two mediators together carried about 63% of the total association (total indirect β = 0.17), with the learning pathway (β = 0.10) somewhat larger than the collective pathway (β = 0.07). The model explained 28.8% of the variance in instructional practices. Because the design is cross-sectional and all measures were self-reported, these results describe associations consistent with the proposed model rather than causal effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>They suggest that relational leadership is related to instructional practice mainly through teachers’ perceptions of collegial innovativeness and their beliefs about their own professional learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1108/heswbl-05-2026-0347.title: How coachability shapes entrepreneurial learning in venture acceleration programs
doi:10.1108/heswbl-05-2026-0347.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study develops a process-oriented understanding of how entrepreneurs enact entrepreneurial learning when engaging with coaching feedback in venture accelerators. Conceptually, we link the active use of feedback to research on coachability. The research question is formulated as follows: How do entrepreneurs enact coachability in ways that condition entrepreneurial learning in venture acceleration programs?</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We adopt an inductive, informant-centric research design to explore the processual dynamics surrounding how entrepreneurs enact entrepreneurial learning in venture acceleration programs. Empirically, we employ a longitudinal study of a ten-month venture accelerator program in Sweden. The core of our analysis centres on interviews with business coaches and lead entrepreneurs who took part in coaching sessions during the program.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings highlight coachability as a conditioning capacity enacted through learning processes and shaped by situational orientations. We identify four key themes that condition entrepreneurial learning from coaching feedback: ownership of learning, openness to change, preference for tangible outcomes, and a short term learning preference. In all, our findings suggest that coachability is not a stable trait but a dynamic learning capacity that unfolds under the temporal and emotional conditions characteristic of venture acceleration contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our findings provide a qualitative, process-focused framework of how coachability is enacted in ways that condition entrepreneurial learning. Rather than assuming complete learning cycles, our framework depicts entrepreneurial learning as shaped by situational orientations that may accelerate, distort, or truncate entrepreneurial learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.47667/ijppr.v7i3.492.title: The Influence of Digital Systems on Public Asset Management Practices in Tanzania: A Case of Selected Public Higher Learning Institutions
doi:10.47667/ijppr.v7i3.492.abstract:
<jats:p>The rapid advancement of digital technologies and systems has fundamentally reshaped how public sector organizations operate and deliver services, although the influence of digital systems on public asset management practice is yet to be explored. The study assessed the influence of digital systems on public asset management practice in selected public higher learning institutions such as the College of Business Education and Dar es Salaam Institute of Technology. Specifically, it examined the influence of e-procurement system on public asset management practice. The study adopted a pragmatist research philosophy and a mixed methods approach, operationalized through a convergent mixed methods design. A sample size of 63 respondents was selected using purposive (10) and random sampling techniques (53). Respondents were administered with questionnaires and in-depth interviews. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data were analysed using content analysis. The results reveal that e-procurement systems positively influence public asset management practice in Tanzanian higher learning institutions. This positive influence heavily dependents on overcoming significant infrastructure, capacity and system reliability challenges. Similarly, the findings reveal an R2 of 0.634, indicating that the model explains 63.4% of the variation in public asset management practices, which represents a stronger model fit. The remaining 36.6% of the variation can be explained by other unmeasured factors, such as localized macroeconomic conditions, organizational culture and specific public sector policies. It is concluded that, higher learning institutions need to ensure that assets are acquired optimally, tracked transparently and maintained to maximize institutional value. The study recommends aligning digital procurement (NeST), asset registries and management information systems with capacity building on staff and IT infrastructures.
 </jats:p>

doi:10.1021/acs.jchemed.6c00247.title: Organic Compound Hunters: An Educational Game Supporting the Learning of Organic Compound Formulas and Nomenclature
doi:10.1021/acs.jchemed.6c00247.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The educational game titled “Organic Compound Hunters” was designed to reinforce preservice teachers’ learning regarding the naming and formula determination of organic compounds within the scope of chemistry education. The game is based on matching the chemical names of organic compounds─including alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, aromatics, and those containing functional groups (alcohols, ethers, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, amines, and amides)─with their structural, bond-line, and molecular formulas; it aims to teach a total of 104 different organic compounds. The game set consists of 104 task cards, nine fixed cards, and a checklist. Five to eight students can play, with one student checking the accuracy of the matches in each round. The study found that the Organic Compound Hunters game offers an interactive learning environment that can help preservice teachers to understand the relationships between organic compound nomenclature and their structural, bond-line, and molecular formulas.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/math14213866.title: A Mathematical Modeling Framework for Semantic–Temporal Graph Learning in Log Anomaly Detection
doi:10.3390/math14213866.abstract: <jats:p>System logs provide valuable information for monitoring system states, identifying failures, and detecting anomalous behaviour in large-scale distributed computing systems. However, their unstructured text, complex semantic dependencies, temporal variation, and severe class imbalance limit conventional methods based on event templates, sequence statistics, or shallow features. To address these challenges, this study proposes a unified mathematical modelling framework for log anomaly detection, instantiated as the Conditional Graph Attention Transformer for Log Analysis (CGATLog). The framework represents temporally ordered log observations as a weighted attributed graph and jointly models semantic representations, event dependencies, temporal associations, and minority-class distributions. A BERT-Transformer encoder first extracts contextual semantic representations from log entries. A weighted log graph is then constructed from event-transition relationships, semantic similarity, and temporal proximity. To alleviate anomaly scarcity, anomalous node representations are generated in the graph embedding space and connected to the original graph through a learnable edge-relation predictor. A semantic–temporal gated graph attention mechanism further regulates the contributions of semantic and temporal associations during neighbourhood aggregation. Experiments on HDFS, BGL, and Thunderbird show that CGATLog achieves competitive log anomaly detection performance. The results also confirm that semantic–temporal graph modelling and anomaly sample augmentation improve robustness, particularly under severe class imbalance.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4599-2.ch011.abstract: <jats:p>Information and communication technologies (ICT) have become essential for delivering healthcare services in a faster, more accessible, and data-driven manner. At the same time, the growing scale of digital health data has raised concerns about privacy, security, and the effective use of distributed data sources. In this chapter, federated learning is presented as a privacy-preserving and scalable approach for collaborative model training in healthcare. A skin cancer classification case study was conducted. Centralized learning achieved the highest accuracy of 87.27%, while FedBN-based personalized federated learning reached an average accuracy of about 86% in a two-client setting, showing performance close to centralized learning and clearly outperforming client-based local learning. Overall, the findings indicate that personalized federated learning is a promising solution for privacy-sensitive healthcare applications by combining strong predictive performance with data protection and scalability advantages.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1976588.title: How does community of inquiry matter? Mediating effects and configurational pathways linking project-based learning design to learning engagement
doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1976588.abstract: <jats:p>The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) has reshaped animation students’ skill profiles and the conditions of instructional design in project-based learning (PBL) studios. We examine whether and how perceptions of PBL design are associated with Learning Engagement (LE), treating AIGC-assisted PBL studios as the research context rather than testing generative AI as a model variable. Drawing on Community of Inquiry (CoI) theory, we examine Problem Driven (PD), Project Design (PDe), Project Implementation (PI), and Project Evaluation (PE) as antecedents; Cognitive Presence (CP), Social Presence (SP), and Teaching Presence (TP) as statistical mediators; and LE as the outcome. We analyzed two-wave survey data from 490 upper-year animation students using PLS-SEM and fsQCA. PBL and CoI were measured concurrently at T1, and LE at T2; indirect effects therefore represent indirect statistical associations rather than mediation with a fully established temporal sequence. PD, PDe, and PI showed significant positive direct associations with LE. PE’s zero-order and single-predictor associations were positive, but its direct path coefficient became significantly negative after controlling for the other PBL dimensions and CoI mediators. The coefficient was sensitive to model specification, suggesting possible statistical suppression; it should not be interpreted as evidence that evaluation itself inherently inhibits engagement. The three CoI dimensions showed significant statistical mediation associations across all 12 indirect paths. TP and SP had relatively higher point estimates of indirect statistical associations, but differences between indirect effects were not formally tested; no dimension is claimed to be optimal. PE’s positive indirect associations through CoI partially offset its negative net direct association without reversing the total association after adjustment. The extent of this offset may depend on the degree to which CoI-related experiences are concurrently reported. fsQCA identified seven high-engagement configurations. No individual PBL dimension was indispensable. CoI dimensions appeared as core or peripheral conditions, although not every configuration included all three. These findings clarify the dual pathways linking evaluation and engagement through indirect statistical associations and configurational conditions, and provide guidance for optimizing PBL under different resource constraints. Conclusions are limited to AIGC-assisted PBL studios and do not establish the instructional effects of generative AI.</jats:p>

doi:10.61233/zijed.v4i2.51.title: Education Management in Islamic-Based Holistic Learning Challenges for Madrasa
doi:10.61233/zijed.v4i2.51.abstract: <jats:p>This study explores the development and implementation of Islamic‑based holistic learning management in madrasas, focusing on Jambi Province. Its purpose is to examine how Islamic education can integrate academic achievement with moral and spiritual values, preparing students to face global challenges while preserving their Islamic identity. Using a qualitative case study approach, data were collected through interviews, classroom observations, and curriculum analysis, with triangulation applied to ensure validity.  Findings reveal the need for curriculum reform that balances intellectual growth with character and spiritual development. However, challenges include limited infrastructure and resistance to change among educators.  The study recommends investment in modern technology, continuous teacher training, and collaboration with local communities and international institutions to bridge resource gaps. Its originality lies in offering a comprehensive model of holistic Islamic learning management tailored to Jambi’s private madrasas. The contribution of this research is providing a framework that integrates Islamic principles with contemporary educational demands, ensuring relevance and quality in today’s globalized era</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fcimb.2026.1927286.title: Differential diagnosis of pulmonary Talaromyces marneffei infection and pulmonary tuberculosis in HIV/AIDS patients using a CT-based multimodal 2.5D deep learning approach
doi:10.3389/fcimb.2026.1927286.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To investigate the diagnostic value of a computed tomography (CT)-based multimodal 2.5-dimensional (2.5D) deep learning model for differentiating Talaromyces marneffei (TSM) from pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) in patients with human immunodeficiency virus infection/acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (HIV/AIDS).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 380 HIV/AIDS patients with pulmonary infections who were admitted to the Fourth People’s Hospital of Nanning from January 2018 to August 2025 were retrospectively enrolled, including 203 patients with PTB, 177 with TSM. The cohort was randomly divided into a training set and a test set at a ratio of 7:3. A clinical model, a radiomics model, and a 2.5D deep learning model were constructed separately.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the clinical feature model, Random Forest achieved the optimal performance, with a test set AUC of 0.856. In the radiomics model, XGBoost attained the highest AUC of 0.866. In the 2.5D deep learning model, ResNet18 performed best at the slice level with an AUC of 0.865, and the patient-level support vector machine (SVM) model based on MIL achieved an AUC of 0.885. The multimodal combined model integrating clinical, radiomics, and deep learning features achieved the highest AUC of 0.931 and a specificity of 0.981. It significantly outperformed the clinical model (P = 0.020) and the radiomics model (P = 0.008), but the improvement over DL25D was not statistically significant (ΔAUC = 0.046; P = 0.116). The high specificity of the combined model should be interpreted alongside its sensitivity (0.717) and the selected decision threshold.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The CT-based multimodal 2.5D deep learning model effectively integrates clinical indicators, radiomics features, and deep learning representations, and substantially improves the differentiation of TSM from PTB in HIV/AIDS patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1145/3772063.3841667.title: Communication Design for Cohort-based Professional Learning Programs
doi:10.1145/3772063.3841667.abstract: Cohort-based professional learning programs are common in both higher education and the broader nonprofit sector. These programs are complex communicative contexts: heterogeneous yet capable of developing a shared identity, goal-oriented yet focused on goals that are often of secondary concern to their members, and highly scripted by their designers yet also open to the innovation and agency of their members. Drawing on the author's experiences as both a researcher and designer of cohort-based professional learning programs, this experience report describes cohort programs as a communicative context and examines the texts and textual practices that have been important in one program, a cohort-based fellowship for university faculty and community partners.

doi:10.65168/bs.226-14.abstract: <jats:p>It is essential to identify students’ diverse needs and provide timely, appropriate support. Visual–motor integration plays an important role in children’s learning, and weaknesses in this ability may contribute to learning difficulties. This study examined visual–motor integration among primary school students with diverse needs in relation to cognitive indicators and emotional states. For a small number of students, the findings were also compared with information from parents, caregivers, and teachers using an ICF-based questionnaire.Recall drawing performance was significantly and positively associated with attention and short-term visual memory, suggesting the importance of attending to, retaining, and recalling visual information. In contrast, copy drawing performance was not significantly associated with these cognitive indicators. Recall drawing performance also differed according to emotional state. Parent and teacher observations were consistent with children’s cognitive assessment results on some indicators but differed on others. These findings highlight the importance of using multiple sources of information, rather than a single assessment, to identify children’s learning needs.</jats:p>

doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c01181.title: Blood–Brain Barrier Permeability Prediction by Integrating Deep Learning Representations with Chemical Compound Knowledge
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c01181.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Predicting blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability is essential for central nervous system drug discovery, but traditional descriptor-based methods of predicting BBB permeability lack structural context, and deep learning-based methods struggle with overfitting. We introduce a multimodel framework that integrates both transformer-derived molecular embeddings with physicochemical descriptors using a late-stage ensemble fusion strategy. Trained on both the B3DB and NeuTox data sets and evaluated on the benchmark BBBP, our model showed strong predictive performance, with data set-dependent performance. Feature fusion improved performance relative to embedding-only models in several settings, whereas descriptor-based models achieved comparable or higher performance in some settings. These results suggest that combining learned structural embeddings with chemical descriptors provides complementary predictive information, while the benefit of their integration may depend on the data distribution or classifier used.</jats:p>
