doi:10.21274/jtm.2026.9.2.261-282.title: Penerapan model Focus, Explore, Reflect and Apply berbantuan aplikasi Baamboozle untuk meningkatkan representasi matematis dan self-regulated learning siswa
doi:10.21274/jtm.2026.9.2.261-282.abstract: <jats:p>This study was motivated by the need to improve students’ mathematical representation ability and the importance of self-regulated learning in mathematics learning. It aimed to examine the implementation of the FERA learning model assisted by the Baamboozle application, determine whether students’ mathematical representation ability improved better than through conventional learning, and describe students’ self-regulated learning in the implementation of the FERA learning model. This study employed a quasi-experimental method with a Nonequivalent Control Group Design. The research was conducted at a senior high school in Sukabumi using purposive sampling, involving 30 students in the experimental class X-2 and 30 students in the control class X-1. The study was conducted on the Statistics topic over three meetings. Data were collected using a mathematical representation test, a self-regulated learning questionnaire, and observation sheets, and analyzed using the Ngain test, normality test, homogeneity test, and an independent-samples t-test. The results showed average implementation scores of 90.93% for the teacher and 87.50% for the students, the experimental class obtained a higher mean Ngain 0.756 than the control class 0.556, with a significant difference t(58) = 4.95, p <0,001 and a large effect size Cohen’s d = 1.278 and students’ self-regulated learning obtained a mean score of 3.48, which was categorized as good.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s12917-026-06021-6.title: Deep learning-based differentiation of FLASH ultrasound windows
doi:10.1186/s12917-026-06021-6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Equine colic emergencies present highly stressful, time-critical scenarios for both clinicians and patients, thus rapid and accurate diagnostic triage is paramount. To support veterinarians under these high-pressure conditions, deep learning tools can be leveraged for automated image recognition to assist in localizing abdominal organs and interpreting FLASH (Fast Localized Abdominal Sonography of Horses) ultrasound windows.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A software tool was developed to identify FLASH-specific ultrasound windows on the equine abdomen and to recognize ultrasonographic organ patterns.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Study design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Retrospective-prospective comparison of software and clinical examination, model development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A deep learning approach for image classification was used to train software to assign ultrasound images to FLASH windows.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Strongest software performance was observed for the duodenal window, with all test images correctly classified, corresponding to a recall of 1.00. Nephrosplenic window demonstrated high classification accuracy, but 23% of images were misclassified as gastric window. While 84% of ventral images were correctly classified, 16% were predicted as duodenal window. Most pronounced confusion was observed between ventral and thoracic windows, with only 55% of thoracic images correctly identified. Left and right middle third FLASH windows 4 and 6 were substantially underrepresented and were therefore excluded from further analyses. In addition, these windows exhibited high anatomical similarity, which further complicated their differentiation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Main limitations</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sources of selection bias was interpretation of windows and the definition of normal physiological ultrasound images by the examiners. The specific FLASH windows were not homogeneously dispersed in the dataset (e.g., FLASH windows 4 and 6 were underrepresented).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The developed deep learning tool demonstrates the feasibility of automated recognition of standardized equine FLASH windows and may support ultrasound training as an educational aid for first-day competencies. Future incorporation of organ-level annotations and probe position information may improve discrimination between anatomically similar windows and enhance model performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch004.title: Decentralized Credential Ecosystems
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch004.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter discusses how blockchain-based verifiable credentialing, federated learning, and immersive metaverse environments converge as a single architectural solution to three structural failures in modern digital education: centralised credential vulnerability, privacy personalisation trade-off, and lack of experiential learning environments in remote environments. The proposed Decentralized Credential Ecosystem (DCE) combines an Ethereum-compatible smart contract layer of immutable credential issuance and on-chain verification, a cross-institutional federated learning layer of privacy-preserving personalised assessment, and a WebXR-based metaverse classroom layer where credentials are represented as verifiable non-fungible token (NFT) badges attached to learner avatars. The chapter features a formal three-layer architecture, component-level specifications, a smart contract credential state machine, a federated learning topology, with differential privacy guarantees, an adversarial threat model and mitigation matrix.</jats:p>

doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c09949.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Transport Properties in Amorphous Polymer Electrolytes Using Chemically Informed Structural Descriptors
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c09949.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Amorphous polymer electrolytes are promising candidates for next-generation lithium batteries. They offer improved safety and mechanical stability compared to conventional liquid electrolytes. However, predicting their transport performance remains challenging. Ionic conductivity and diffusivity depend on complex, coupled interactions between polymer structure, chemistry, and ion dynamics. This work leverages machine learning to predict four key transport properties in amorphous polymer electrolytes using a molecular dynamics data set of more than 6,000 polymer electrolyte systems. These are ionic conductivity, bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI) diffusivity, lithium-ion diffusivity, and polymer diffusivity. To enhance predictive capability and preserve mechanistic interpretability, we engineered chemically and structurally meaningful features from Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES) representations. Selected features include elemental composition, functional group densities, polarity descriptors, and polymer flexibility metrics. Three modeling frameworks were trained and evaluated under 5-fold cross-validation, including random forest, gradient boosting, and neural networks. The neural network achieved the highest predictive performance across all four targets and exceeded prior benchmarks on three of them. It also exhibited substantially greater robustness to data partitioning than the tree-based baselines. Feature importance analysis was performed using both impurity-based rankings and Shapley additive explanations. Polymer backbone flexibility, polarity, and ionic environment were found to dominate transport behavior. Directional attribution further identified primary and secondary amines and carboxylate groups as specific negative contributors to lithium-ion mobility. The results of this work demonstrate that chemically informed structural descriptors can effectively predict electrolyte performance while yielding mechanistic insight. This enables accelerated screening and design of high-efficiency polymer electrolytes for future energy storage applications.</jats:p>

doi:10.55578/fepr.2610.016.title: The Lived Experience of Professional Learning of Teachers in the North of Scotland
doi:10.55578/fepr.2610.016.abstract:
<jats:p>In Scotland, as elsewhere, it is widely recognised that the quality of teaching is the most important factor in children’s learning, and therefore on education system outcomes. The quality of teaching can be improved through high-quality teacher professional learning. However, there is a lack of empirical research on how teachers experience professional learning.  
This paper describes the experiences of professional learning of twelve physics teachers in secondary schools across the north of Scotland. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews and by teachers completing professional learning career roadmaps and year-long reflective diary-logs. These experiences are compared with their contractual requirements and analysed against a theoretical framework based on Timperley’s principles of effective of professional learning, and Kennedy’s models professional learning. This aims to achieve an understanding of professional learning practices for teachers in Scotland.
The study finds that most of the teacher professional learning is transmissive rather than transformative with little evidence of enquiry as stance or collaborative enquiry-based approaches. This neither serves the macro-level desire for transformative change nor the micro-level and nano-level desire for improved instruction and is unlikely to result in improvements in pupil outcomes or system performance.</jats:p>

doi:10.33369/pendipa.10.4.1321-1327.title: Implementasi Model Pembelajaran Problem Based Learning Berbasis E-Newspaper Terhadap Pemahaman Konsep Struktur Atom Kelas X
doi:10.33369/pendipa.10.4.1321-1327.abstract: <jats:p>Pemahaman konsep struktur atom yang masih rendah akibat sifatnya yang abstrak menuntut adanya inovasi model dan media pembelajaran. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui pengaruh yang signifikan dari implementasi model Problem Based Learning (PBL) berbasis E-Newspaper terhadap pemahaman konsep struktur atom peserta didik kelas X SMA YP HKBP 1 Pematangsiantar. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan metode kuasi eksperimen dan desain Nonequivalent Control Group Design. Sampel ditentukan dengan teknik purposive sampling, yaitu kelas X-3 (31 peserta didik) sebagai kelas eksperimen yang belajar menggunakan model PBL berbasis E-Newspaper dan kelas X-4 (29 peserta didik) sebagai kelas kontrol yang belajar menggunakan pembelajaran konvensional. Data pemahaman konsep dikumpulkan melalui pretest dan posttest berupa 20 soal pilihan ganda yang valid, kemudian dianalisis menggunakan uji normalitas Shapiro-Wilk, uji homogenitas Levene, uji Mann-Whitney U, dan uji N-Gain. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan rata-rata posttest kelas eksperimen (90,48) lebih tinggi daripada kelas kontrol (83,97), dengan N-Gain sebesar 0,81 (kategori tinggi) dibandingkan 0,68 (kategori sedang). Uji Mann-Whitney U menghasilkan nilai Sig. 0,004 (< 0,05) sehingga H0 ditolak. Dengan demikian, terdapat pengaruh yang signifikan dari implementasi model PBL berbasis E-Newspaper terhadap pemahaman konsep struktur atom peserta didik kelas X.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11464247/v1.title: Deep Learning and Computational Modeling for Epitope-Focused Immunogen Design Targeting Monkeypox
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11464247/v1.abstract: Monkeypox (MPX), now widely called mpox, is a zoonotic orthopoxvirus infection that has moved from a neglected tropical disease to a global public health concern. Live-attenuated smallpox vaccines offer cross-protection, but they are produced in limited quantities, are unevenly distributed, and are not suited to every recipient. These constraints motivate the search for rationally designed, epitope-focused immunogens that can be produced at scale and tailored to emerging viral variants. This article describes an in silico framework that combines amino acid feature engineering, classical machine learning (ML) benchmarking, and a deep neural network (DNN) to predict potential T-cell and B-cell epitopes from the MPX virus proteome (VP). Epitope and non-epitope sequences, together with antigen information, were collected from public immunology and virology databases, encoded numerically, and described by a panel of 84 amino acid features. Hierarchical heat-map clustering based on Pearson correlation identified 44 of the 84 features as redundant, and these were removed before modeling. Twenty-eight ML algorithms were then screened; the five best performers, namely Random Forest, Label Spreading, Decision Tree, Label Propagation and Extra Trees, were compared using accuracy, F1 score and the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), the last two being appropriate for imbalanced data. A DNN with fully connected dense layers, trained by back-propagation with the Adam optimizer, was evaluated with two and four hidden layers. The four-layer network converged faster in terms of loss, while accuracy did not differ significantly between architectures across training epochs. According to the held-out test data, the DNN outperformed the traditional ML models and other deep learning approaches. Because the framework is not specific to one pathogen, it can in principle be retrained to support vaccine design against other emerging infectious diseases. We discuss the biological rationale, methodological choices, limitations, and the experimental validation steps required to move from computational candidates to a multivalent MPX immunogen.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11464247/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.5430/ijhe.v15n5p73.title: Student Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse-Enabled Remote Learning in New Zealand Tertiary Education
doi:10.5430/ijhe.v15n5p73.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing development of emerging digital technologies is creating new possibilities for remote tertiary education. Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse technologies offer potential for personalised learning, intelligent support, immersive interaction, and collaboration; however, their educational value depends partly on how students perceive their usefulness, accessibility, supporting conditions, and motivational potential. This study examined New Zealand tertiary students’ perceptions of prospective Artificial Intelligence- and Metaverse-enabled remote learning environments and investigated whether selected technology-acceptance and motivational factors were associated with perceived learning engagement. A mono-method quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected through an online questionnaire comprising 20 Likert-scale items representing six constructs: performance expectancy, facilitating conditions, motivation, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and perceived learning engagement. A total of 356 responses were retained for analysis. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, exploratory chi-square analysis, and multiple linear regression were conducted. The regression model was statistically significant and explained 33.8% of the variance in perceived learning engagement (R² = .338; adjusted R² = .329; F = 35.773, p < .001). Perceived usefulness (β = .279, p < .001), motivation (β = .218, p < .001), and facilitating conditions (β = .179, p < .001) were statistically significant predictors of perceived learning engagement. Performance expectancy (β = .065, p = .223) and perceived ease of use (β = .089, p = .058) were not statistically significant predictors. An exploratory chi-square analysis also identified a statistically significant association between age and perceptions of virtual teamwork (p = .001). The findings provide preliminary evidence that perceived usefulness, motivation, and facilitating conditions are important considerations in understanding student engagement with prospective advanced remote learning environments. Given the cross-sectional design and purposive non-probability sampling, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal effects and should be interpreted within the study sample.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s41239-026-00632-7.title: Effects of question-chain prompting on self-regulated learning, metacognition, and achievement in a generative AI environment
doi:10.1186/s41239-026-00632-7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.</jats:p>

doi:10.1186/s43093-026-01003-4.title: Evaluating machine learning and econometric models for inflation forecasting: evidence from a Sub-Saharan African panel
doi:10.1186/s43093-026-01003-4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Policymakers in Sub-Saharan Africa increasingly face decisions regarding the adoption of machine learning methods for inflation forecasting, yet these approaches are rarely benchmarked against simple persistence models. This study constructs a reproducible, annual panel of macroeconomic indicators for eight Sub-Saharan African economies (1972–2024, 
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                    = 424) to compare eight forecasting approaches: a naive random-walk benchmark, two linear econometric models (pooled OLS and country fixed effects), three machine learning models (Elastic Net, Random Forest, and XGBoost), and a recurrent neural network (LSTM) evaluated with and without early stopping. Using a chronological train/validation/test split and pairwise Diebold–Mariano tests, we evaluate out-of-sample predictive accuracy. The empirical results indicate that no estimated model statistically outperforms the naive persistence baseline. While Random Forest, XGBoost, Elastic Net, and the early-stopped LSTM show no statistically significant difference from the random walk, traditional linear models and the uncorrected LSTM are significantly dominated by it. Although implementing early stopping substantially improves LSTM performance, it does not yield a competitive advantage over simpler tree-based ensembles. These findings align with the well-documented random-walk puzzle in global inflation forecasting, suggesting that structural breaks, high volatility, and modest sample sizes pose substantial challenges for highly parameterized forecasting architectures. Consequently, these results suggest that regional central banks and finance ministries should maintain simple persistence models as active baselines when evaluating investments in complex forecasting infrastructure. These conclusions are robust to a battery of additional checks: HAC-Newey–West/Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold-corrected and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted Diebold–Mariano tests, a strictly lagged-only predictor respecification, expanding-window recursive re-estimation, per-country and subperiod decomposition, LSTM input-sequence-length sensitivity analysis, a pooled AR(1) benchmark, a five-seed LSTM replication, and a country-clustered block-bootstrap Diebold–Mariano test.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4664-7.ch004.title: Integrating Prompt Literacy Into Learning Management Systems for Effective Use of Generative AI in Education
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4664-7.ch004.abstract: <jats:p>Prompt literacy is a term introduced in this chapter that refers to designing, evaluating, refining, and reflecting on prompts for artificial intelligence systems. With the growing popularity of generative AI in education and K-12 settings, students may interact with generative AI systems without developing necessary communication skills. Thus, integrating prompt literacy as a digital competency within learning management systems can address the issue by providing a scaffolded approach to teaching the skill. In this regard, drawing on constructivist and socio-cultural theories, the author suggests a multi-level model for integrating prompt literacy within an LMS. The chapter analyzes existing LMSs such as Canvas, Moodle, Blackboard, and Google Classroom, focusing on their strengths and weaknesses. Moreover, the chapter offers some guidelines for implementing prompt literacy within the mentioned platforms and provides current evidence from research studies that support this idea.</jats:p>

doi:10.3390/geohazards7050127.title: VSTAR-G: Cloud-Based Tool for Global Detection and Quantification of Volcanic SO2 Plumes Using TROPOMI and Machine Learning Approach
doi:10.3390/geohazards7050127.abstract: <jats:p>SO2 emissions are among the primary indicators of magmatic activity and play a fundamental role both in local-scale risk management, including air quality and aviation safety, and in regional-to-global climate processes through the formation of sulfate aerosols capable of altering the Earth’s radiative balance. In recent years, satellite observations have revolutionized the monitoring of volcanic emissions. In particular, the Sentinel-5P satellite, part of the Copernicus programme, carries the TROPOMI spectrometer, which provides high-resolution observations for monitoring of atmospheric trace gases (e.g., SO2). Here, we present VSTAR-G, a Google Earth Engine (GEE) application that operationalizes an algorithm previously developed. The application is able to visualize and analyse, using an algorithm previously developed, the automatic detection of volcanic SO2 plumes and their mass quantification according to plume altitude. Through an intuitive interface, users can interactively explore SO2 emissions from more than 200 volcanoes worldwide, define spatial and temporal regions of interest (ROIs), and compare different dates or plume-height products using a synchronized split-window visualization. The application also generates time series of the SO2 mass within the selected area, supports the simultaneous analysis of multiple plumes, and allows users to export plume-detection maps in GeoTIFF format and the associated satellite data as CSV files. The developed application transforms an existing detection algorithm into an accessible operational tool, combining satellite observations, machine learning, and cloud computing to support scalable and near-real-time monitoring of volcanic SO2 emissions.</jats:p>

doi:10.1007/s00572-026-01323-x.title: MycorrhizaFinder: a user-friendly machine-learning tool to quantify endomycorrhizal colonisation of nursery and field roots
doi:10.1007/s00572-026-01323-x.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Root colonisation by endomycorrhizal fungi has long been a widely used metric in mycorrhizal studies. However, due to the significant time required to assess colonisation using traditional microscopy techniques, studies of colonisation at large scales are impractical. Machine-learning-based approaches may increase output and facilitate ecosystem assessments. We trained a machine-learning-based tool (MycorrhizaFinder) on 42 field roots (132 unique 1 cm sections, with > 100,000 tiles) and validated on a further 37 sections from grasslands and heathlands hosting common Northern European plants with arbuscular (AM) and ericoid mycorrhizal (ErM) fungal structures, and dark septate endophytes (DSE), also common in field-sourced roots. We incorporated a user-customized confidence threshold to encourage engagement with morphological ambiguities, in e.g. ErM and DSE. A Macro F
                    <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                    statistic was used to assess the tool’s development performance. We provide a sample workflow from root processing and microscope slide scanning to semi-automated model training and performance evaluation. Our model performance combining all classes, the Macro F
                    <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                    , is conservatively 66% for arbuscular and 57% for ericoid mycorrhizal colonisation assessment. MycorrhizaFinder is user-friendly, requires no programming skills and offers flexibility for advanced agronomists or ecologists to train the tool using their own labelled mycorrhizal root datasets, including images acquired from different instruments or staining protocols. This adaptability allows users to customize the model for specific ecosystems or experimental designs. Leveraged with molecular identification and/or functional traits of fungi (e.g. arbuscules), MycorrhizaFinder supports scalable and repeatable nursery experiments and monitoring across ecosystems to assess mycorrhizal status and track land-use changes over time.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.1108/jhti-03-2026-0470.title: Oops! I did it again: learning modes and innovation novelty in a small island destination
doi:10.1108/jhti-03-2026-0470.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Learning is often positioned as a precondition for innovation in tourism; however, it is frequently treated as a broad construct. This study examines how different modes of learning shape innovation in boutique hotels in Valletta, Malta and it investigates whether these modes of learning stimulate novelty or imitation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study adopts a qualitative design based on semi-structured interviews with 25 respondents, including nine boutique hotel owners and 16 managers from 14 boutique hotels in Valletta, Malta.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cumulative, vicarious, exploitative and experiential learning were found to support adaptation, problem solving, operational refinement and incremental improvement. However, the reliance of respondents on prior experience, visible market practices and established routines, constrained novelty by reinforcing imitation and reactive adaptation. Exploratory and creative learning were less prevalent; however, they were more closely associated with differentiation and novelty. Covid-19 further intensified adaptive and crisis-driven learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hoteliers seeking distinctiveness should look beyond local competitors and routines, and encourage staff generated ideas. Destination stakeholders should promote ideational diversity by broadening hotel knowledge sources.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study advances a granular understanding of the relationship between learning and innovation by illustrating the impacts of different modes of learning on novelty. It also demonstrates how vicarious learning amplifies knowledge circulation while constraining distinctiveness in a small island destination.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202662651.title: A deep learning algorithm for black hole spin estimation using hot spot secondary images
doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202662651.abstract:
<jats:p>Sagittarius A* exhibits frequent flaring activity across the electromagnetic spectrum that is often associated with a localized region of strong emission known as a hot spot.
Our study is aimed at training a deep learning model to provide a link between key parameters of this phenomenon (hot spot emission radius and the black hole inclination and spin) to the observed angle difference between the primary and secondary image (Δ PA) that could potentially be resolved by present and future interferometric arrays.
Using the general relativistic radiative transfer code we generated a library of sim100000 models with varying system parameters and computed the position angle difference on the image plane between the primary and secondary images of the hot spot. We explored the equatorial and non-equatorial circular orbits and evaluate our models against approximate observational constraints, including partial-orbit visibility and observational errors.
Our algorithm ̊amiland shows remarkable accuracy in calculating spin and inclination from the majority of the observational tests we perform (σ_ α_* ̧irc ), even in extreme conditions where only half of the orbit is visible. The off-equatorial estimation provides softer constraints in the absence of prior information.
Our results demonstrate the importance of hot spot observations for spacetime estimations. Given the increasing efforts to detect the photon-ring, our framework could prove valuable in interpreting the first observations of lensed emission.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11188693/v1.title: A Review of Deep-learning-based Seismic Data Denoising and Its Promising Paradigm Shift to Foundation Models
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11188693/v1.abstract: Denoising is a long-standing and widely-concerned topic in seismic data processing, for it can significantly increase the signal-to-noise ratio of seismic data. Numerous deep learning (DL) methods have shown promising denoising performance, but most of them are task-specific and focus on a certain type of seismic background noise. The real condition that seismic datasets are often contaminated by various types of noises motivates us to explore a well-generalized and versatile DL model for seismic data denoising. Recently, in the fields of computer vision and natural language processing, foundation models (FMs) pre-trained on vast datasets demonstrate outstanding adaptability and generality across diverse downstream tasks. This paradigm offers a promising path to address the challenges faced by task-specific DL denoising models, such as poor generalization, retraining from scratch for different noise, and the lack of labeled data. We first provide a brief review of traditional seismic denoising methods, followed by a comprehensive review of existing DL-based denoising methods categorized by noise type. Furthermore, we conduct a case study on a dedicated seismic denoising foundation model termed SeisDeFM. This is the first study in geophysical research to develop and validate a seismic denoising foundation model on pre-stack gathers with diverse noise conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with task-specific DL baselines, SeisDeFM achieves superior denoising performance and cross-noise generalization by the advantages of sufficient pre-training and appropriate downstream adaptation, and it effectively preserves weak reflection events while suppressing complex noise in pre-stack seismic data.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11188693/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10639-3.title: Evaluation of undergraduate medical students’ experiences, perceptions and learning from a deaf insights and British Sign Language course: a qualitative study
doi:10.1186/s12909-026-10639-3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deaf people experience healthcare inequities driven in part by limited deaf insights and specialist communication skills training in medical education. Evidence suggests deaf insights training and exposure to deaf culture and communication styles can improve students’ communication skills and understanding of deaf culture, yet it remains uncommon in undergraduate curricula.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We co-developed a Deaf Insights and British Sign Language student-selected component (SSC) for Year 3 medical students at Imperial College London with a deaf awareness trainer, and deaf insights advocate, who is also a deaf doctor, who shared their expertise and lived experiences of deaf culture, healthcare and patient journeys. The SSC comprised three weekly sessions (three hours each) focusing on health equity, communication, and reflective practice.</jats:p>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated the SSC using an interpretivist qualitative approach with a dyadic interview and online survey. Data was analysed thematically using transformative learning theory as a sensitising lens.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across three cohorts in 2025-2026, forty students completed the SSC. Students described learning from the SSC that appeared to be aligned with the initial steps of transformative learning theory. Students discussed their assumptions being challenged and perspectives changing. This included a new understanding of deaf culture alongside a recognition of healthcare barriers and inequities faced by deaf people, and a perceived increase in their confidence in communicating with deaf people. This learning appears to have been facilitated by the co-design, co-delivery and opportunity to interact directly with deaf trainers and advocates. Students reflected upon their learning during group discussions and described intentions to act upon these new insights by changing their own practice and educating others regarding their new learning, hoping to act as advocates for deaf people in future.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Co-creation and co-delivery of an SSC in deaf insights training with deaf trainers and advocates shows features consistent with the initial stages of transformative learning occurring in undergraduate medical students. Our approach and findings may be of interest to other institutions developing similar training. Wider adoption of this model could help improve students’ confidence and understanding of how to meet the needs of deaf people which may in turn contribute to improving health equity for deaf individuals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

doi:10.1145/3772063.3841666.abstract: Within the technical and professional communication classroom, students need opportunities to engage in complex situations to explore ethical decision-making, genre conventions, and workplace dynamics. Within the practice of user experience (UX), students can gain these experiences with community-engaged projects and experiences. However, students also need experiences that can precede and scaffold working with community partners. We argue that case studies, which have a long history in the TPC classroom, can be helpful ways to explore ethical issues and design concerns. In this experience report, we share and reflect on two case studies that can be used to help students explore ethical and methodological issues in design.

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch003.title: Decentralized Education Ecosystems Integrating Blockchain, AI, and the Metaverse for Next-Generation Learning
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch003.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines decentralized education ecosystems by integrating blockchain, artificial intelligence, and the metaverse for next-generation learning. It explains how blockchain can provide trust, secure credentials, learner-owned records, and verifiable micro-certifications, while AI supports personalization, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, analytics, and competency-based assessment. The metaverse adds immersive classrooms, simulations, digital campuses, and experiential skill development. The chapter argues that these technologies can transform education from institution-centered systems to learner-centered, portable, flexible, and lifelong learning ecosystems. It also discusses challenges such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, credential fraud, platform control, metaverse safety, and quality assurance.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4664-7.ch001.title: Investigating Students' Agency During AI-Assisted Learning
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4664-7.ch001.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates students' agency during AI-assisted learning, focusing on how they interact with AI tools and exercise independent thinking. It examines how students create and use prompts, as well as how they modify or adapt AI-generated solutions to apply their own problem-solving strategies. Using qualitative analysis of student interactions with AI, the study reveals patterns of agency, including initiative, critical evaluation, and strategic adaptation of AI output. Findings suggest that students actively shape their learning by combining AI support with personal reasoning, highlighting AI's potential as a tool that complements, rather than replaces, independent thinking. Implications underscore the importance of designing AI-assisted learning environments that foster student autonomy, creativity, and reflective problem-solving.</jats:p>

doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1937336.title: Learning from drops: AI-guided integration of liquid biopsy features in cancer studies
doi:10.3389/frai.2026.1937336.abstract: <jats:p>Cancer is a major global health issue with rising incidence and mortality. Early detection, tumor characterization, and disease surveillance are crucial for timely, effective treatment and ultimately reduce mortality. Liquid biopsy (LB) has emerged as a valuable detection tool, offering a non-invasive method to detect tumor-derived biomarkers in body fluids and demonstrating translational potential. To increase biomarker sensitivity, high-throughput sequencing platforms deliver massive volumes of data. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is pivotal to enabling large-scale, complex data integration. This contribution assesses the current state of integrative AI-based research in the LB field and provides methodological guidance. First, we conducted a PubMed search and found that the literature is sparse in studies integrating LB features, particularly by applying AI. When adopting this approach, defining study objectives is crucial to guide subsequent methodological decisions, including study design, patient selection criteria, sample size, the nature of the LB features, and the metadata to collect. Specifically, we propose strategies and tools for data preprocessing, including normalization and batch-effect correction, as well as for handling outliers and missing data. Furthermore, we recommend various Machine/Deep Learning approaches for feature selection techniques to ensure model robustness, and we highlight the importance of undergoing rigorous internal and external validation of the selected models. Assessing clinical utility and interpretability is often overlooked but fundamental for real-world implementation. In conclusion, we provide the LB scientific community with AI-based methodological guidance to bridge the two fields and enhance the integrative analysis of LB features.</jats:p>

doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11193544/v1.title: Net carbon benefit of CO₂ curing of cement from coupled machine learning and process carbon accounting
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11193544/v1.abstract: Carbonation curing can store CO₂ in cementitious materials, but its net carbon benefit depends on the emissions associated with CO₂ supply and curing. We manually compiled and curated a literature database, harmonised uptake to an original-material mass basis including aggregates, and coupled machine learning with process carbon accounting. Using 461 records and eight material and curing descriptors, we compared eight regressors and evaluated uptake responses alongside supply, transport and curing emissions. This framework connects experimental uptake data to the conditions under which the assessed process yields a net carbon benefit. At an illustrative predicted uptake of 0.231 kg CO₂/kg original material and an assumed material mass of 2400 kg/m³, all five supply scenarios yield net benefits of 0.189–0.219 kg CO₂/kg original material with electricity at 0.05 kg CO₂/kWh. Two scenarios become net emitters at 0.40 kg CO₂/kWh. Calculated break-even electricity intensities range from 0.314 to 2.047 kg CO₂/kWh, demonstrating how supply assumptions change the conditions for a positive balance. The curated database and coupled analysis provide a basis for comparing these conditions; limited cross-study predictive performance confines the numerical results to conditional scenarios.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11193544/v1.venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC

doi:10.21274/jtm.2026.9.2.241-260.title: Perbandingan kemampuan berpikir kreatif dan kritis matematis mahasiswa setelah pembelajaran inkuiri dan problem-based learning: Analisis mancova
doi:10.21274/jtm.2026.9.2.241-260.abstract: <jats:p>Mathematical creative and critical thinking are essential competencies that need to be developed among prospective mathematics teachers. However, studies directly comparing inquiry learning and problem-based learning (PBL) in terms of these two competencies simultaneously, while accounting for prior mathematical ability (PMA), remain limited. This study aimed to compare students’ mathematical creative and critical thinking outcomes between inquiry learning and PBL groups after adjustment for PMA. A quasi-experimental design was employed involving 50 second-semester mathematics education students from two intact classes, with 25 students in each group. PMA was measured before the intervention and treated as a covariate, whereas mathematical creative and critical thinking were assessed after three instructional sessions. Data were analyzed using multivariate analysis of covariance (MANCOVA). The results showed that, after adjusting for PMA, no statistically significant simultaneous difference was found between the inquiry learning and PBL groups in the two outcomes, Pillai’s Trace = 0.017, F(2,46) = 0.388, p = 0.680, partial η² = 0.017. The follow-up univariate analyses likewise indicated no significant differences in either mathematical creative thinking or mathematical critical thinking. Thus, within the context and duration of this study, inquiry learning and PBL did not produce statistically distinguishable outcomes after adjustment for PMA.</jats:p>

doi:10.1017/s0265051726101090.title: Who mentors the mentors? Early childhood music educators as mentors and the professional learning and development of generalist practitioners
doi:10.1017/s0265051726101090.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The majority of early childhood practitioners in England receive little or no initial training in how to work in music with young children. To remedy this deficit, mentoring schemes place expert early childhood music educators to work alongside generalist practitioners. A review of literature revealed that little attention has been given to the processes of mentoring in early childhood music education. We invited a team of specialist music educators who had been involved in mentoring to participate in focus group discussions and found that, while they recognised the importance of interpersonal skills for music mentoring, they were less able to elucidate the content and processes of mentoring.</jats:p>

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh9320.title: In-memory phononic learning toward cognitive mechanical intelligence
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh9320.abstract: <jats:p>Mechanical intelligence seeks autonomous materials that embody memory, perception, learning, and decision-making within the mechanical domain. A fundamental challenge is to integrate memory with information processing in an efficient, scalable, and interpretable way that supports cognitive learning and decision-making. Here, we introduce in-memory phononic learning, a framework that unifies non-volatile mechanical memory with wave-based perception in a phononic metastructure. Spatial information is stored as structural states that program elastic-wave responses, allowing probing waves to act as queries that retrieve informative features through parallel, physically transparent localization modes. Learning is achieved by offline optimization of input waveforms to selectively combine these features for multitask memory-pattern recognition without hardware redesign, with decisions inferred directly from output-energy responses. We experimentally and numerically demonstrate high-accuracy classification across tasks from geometric shapes to handwritten digits. Overall, this work elevates “materials that compute” toward “cognitive matter” that can interpret, reason, and learn through wave physics, laying a foundation for scalable and robust autonomous material systems.</jats:p>

doi:10.1038/s41598-026-76357-4.title: Two-stage synthetic-to-real transfer learning for automated mammography report generation using vision-language models
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-76357-4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    We present a two-stage synthetic-to-real training pipeline for automated mammography report generation, together with a controlled, preregistered evaluation of whether its synthetic pretraining stage contributes to final report quality. Automated mammography report generation is constrained by the scarcity of paired mammogram-report data: public collections such as VinDr-Mammo and CBIS-DDSM provide structured annotations but no free-text reports. The pipeline converts BI-RADS annotations into synthetic reports (400 generated, 390 retained) to pretrain MedGemma-4B with multimodal LoRA, then fine-tunes on 407 real DMID reports. On the leak-free DMID test subset (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$n = 49$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ) it reaches ROUGE-L 0.656, METEOR 0.666, CIDEr 0.649 and BERTScore 0.917, exceeding every external baseline, including the published state of the art. The evaluation then shows that synthetic pretraining does not produce these numbers: the apparent advantage was measured between models of unequal adapter capacity, and at matched capacity the two schemes are equivalent. Across 60 training runs over three corpus sizes, three capacities and five initialisations, against a margin fixed in advance, no configuration favours two-stage training; capacity alone reproduces the gap. Two findings bear on evaluation. Under an assertion-level criterion no model fabricates findings on normal studies; the failure mode is omission. Textual and clinical quality diverge within one model: where two-stage training gains 0.058 ROUGE-L, BI-RADS agreement and sensitivity both fall. With agreement never exceeding
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\kappa = 0.14$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    , the obstacle to clinically useful reporting is diagnostic accuracy, not fluency.
                  </jats:p>

doi:10.3389/fpls.2026.1981493.title: From seed centres to tray cells: a geometry-aware machine vision framework for full-tray sowing quality assessment in maize plug trays
doi:10.3389/fpls.2026.1981493.abstract: <jats:p>Accurate sowing-quality assessment of maize seedling trays requires both reliable seed localisation and correct correspondence between detected seeds and physical tray cells. This study presents a semi-automated machine-vision framework combining heatmap-based seed-centre localisation, sliding-window inference, global non-maximum suppression (NMS), and four-corner-calibrated adaptive grid assignment. Each assessable cell was classified as empty, single-seeded, or multi-seeded according to the number of assigned seed centres. On source-image-independent subsets, the framework achieved an accuracy of 0.9821 and a macro F1-score of 0.9040 for 27 complete-tray images (3,456 cells), and 0.9798 and 0.9344, respectively, for 9 visible-cell images (1,140 assessable cells). Separately, the larger evaluation sets yielded accuracy/macro F1 values of 0.9783/0.9145 for 44 complete trays and 0.9782/0.9368 for 30 visible-cell images. These results support cell-level sowing-quality assessment under the evaluated acquisition conditions and within manually assessable regions. The source-image-independent subsets control direct source overlap but remain within the same acquisition domain; external generalisation across production sites, imaging devices, tray specifications, and acquisition conditions has not yet been established.</jats:p>

doi:10.1364/opticaopen.34729989.v1.title: Machine Learning Assisted Optimization of Lead-Free Dual Perovskite (Cs2SnBr6 and RbGeBr3) / ACIGS Tandem Solar Cells Using SCAPS-1D Simulation
doi:10.1364/opticaopen.34729989.v1.abstract: <jats:p>This Study focuses on the design, simulation, and performance prediction of a novel photovoltaic device using SCAPS-1D combined with machine learning techniques. A dual perovskite absorber (Cs2SnBr6 and RbGeBr3) layered solar cell structure has been proposed, where different ETL (CdS, TiO2, SnO2) and HTL (CBTS, CuO, P3HT) layers have been systematically analyzed. Device performance has also been optimized by varying absorber thickness, defect density, doping concentration, and operating temperature. After a comparative study, CdS and CBTS are the most effective ETL and HTL, respectively. So, Al / FTO / CdS /Cs2SnBr6 /RbGeBr3 / CBTS is the proposed top-sub cell architecture of the studied tandem cell. Then, the top sub-cell is combined with the FTO / ZnO: Al/i -ZnO / CdS /ACIGS / Au bottom sub-cell, which combinedly provided 31% PCE, 19.14 mA/cm2 JSC, 1.76 VOC, and 78.32% FF. To predict and validate the simulated photovoltaic performance, four machine learning regression algorithms- Linear Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Decision Tree Regression (DTR) have been employed. Comparatively, random forest has shown better accuracy than the other models in predicting JSC, VOC, FF, and PCE. Feature importance analysis considered RbGeBr3 as the most influential absorber layer and its thickness as the most significant parameter for improving PCE. The top and bottom sub-cells showed good agreement with previously reported results, with deviations of less than 5%. The proposed architecture demonstrates the potential of lead-free tandem solar cells and provides useful insights for developing efficient, low-cost, and environmentally friendly tandem devices.</jats:p>

doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202661648.title: Data-driven characterisation of variable source light curves with multimodal representation learning
doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202661648.abstract:
<jats:p>Large-scale photometric surveys such as the Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) are producing light curves for hundreds of millions of variable sources. Characterising these sources has traditionally relied on supervised classifiers trained with hand-crafted features and curated label sets, limiting their applicability to predefined taxonomies and individual surveys. Zwicky Vera C. Rubin
We present a general, survey-agnostic framework for the characterisation of variable sources from photometric time series that operates entirely without labelled training data and produces low-dimensional representations capturing light curve properties such as amplitude, periodicity, and asymmetry directly from the observations.
Our method combines two complementary views of each light curve in a multimodal architecture. Raw time-domain observations are processed by a Transformer encoder, and a generalised Lomb--Scargle (GLS) periodogram is processed by a convolutional neural network. Training uses a split-half augmentation strategy, where each light curve is randomly divided into two temporal halves that serve as independent views of the same underlying variability. The two branches are trained jointly using the Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularisation (VICReg) objective to produce embeddings that are invariant across the two halves while maintaining high information content per dimension. No labels enter the training procedure at any stage.
We evaluate the framework on 37,006 ZTF sources spanning 14 variable star classes across four broad physical categories. A linear classifier trained on the frozen 64-dimensional embeddings achieves 77.1% balanced accuracy at the individual class level and 90.5% at the broad category level. Combining the light curve and periodogram branches improves balanced accuracy by up to 14.9 percentage points over the best single modality for individual classes, confirming that the two branches capture complementary information. The embedding encodes interpretable light curve properties on distinct embedding dimensions, and within-class analysis reveals physically interpretable substructure that the reference labels do not resolve. Retraining on ZTF g and i bands without modification reproduces the main results, and concatenating multi-band embeddings improves balanced accuracy to 86.1%, demonstrating complementary wavelength-dependent information capture.
The self-supervised framework produces physically interpretable representations without requiring labelled training data, phase folding, or survey-specific pre-processing. The framework is survey-agnostic by design and directly applicable to other ground-based and space-based photometric surveys with different cadences and wavelength coverage. The trained model and the source code with tutorials are publicly released.</jats:p>

doi:10.29130/dubited.1907458.title: A Hybrid Model Combining Neural Learning and Uncertainty Modeling for Estimating the Average Phase Voltage in Three-Phase IGBT Inverters
doi:10.29130/dubited.1907458.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">Accurate modeling of power electronics-based inverter systems is very important in the analysis of electric drive systems, as well as in the development of sophisticated control systems and condition monitoring systems. Nevertheless, the non-linear nature of inverter systems, owing to their switching characteristics, and the variability in system parameters make it difficult to accurately model average phase voltages using analytical models. In this study, a hybrid data-driven model is presented, which combines residual learning with heteroscedastic uncertainty modeling in the estimation of average phase voltages using the pulse width modulation (PWM) period in two-level three-phase insulated gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) inverters. In this study, the reference voltage is estimated using the physical operating principle of the inverter system, and this is combined with the use of an artificial neural network in the development of the residual learning model. In addition, probabilistic voltage estimation is performed in this study to assess the reliability of the model outputs. The framework is validated using an open-access three-phase inverter dataset. The results show that the physics-guided residual model substantially improves the standalone physical reference and direct MLP estimation, achieving RMSE values in the range of 1.05–1.11 V, MAE values in the range of 0.59–0.62 V, and (R2≈ 0.99990) for three-phase voltage estimation. The uncertainty-aware extension provides reliability-related uncertainty indicators that may be useful for monitoring, diagnostic, and supervisory-level applications; however, these uncertainty estimates should be interpreted as practical reliability indicators rather than perfectly calibrated probabilities.</jats:p>

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch006.title: Reimagining Education Through the Metaverse
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch006.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter delineates the evolution of educational technology from conventional online learning platforms to sophisticated immersive systems, including Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, and XR, culminating in metaverse-enabled 3D virtual environments that enhance learning experiences in disciplines such as STEM education, medical studies, and cross-cultural education. The chapter describes technological foundations such as headsets, haptic systems, 3D audio systems, and AI-driven adaptive systems; theoretical foundations such as constructivist learning, situational learning, and embodied cognition; application dimensions such as distance learning systems, simulation learning systems, and online learning systems. Overall, this paper views met adverse learning systems as a technology revolution waiting to transform Education 4.0 by overcoming all space and time constraints while attempting to address a maze of other issues, including but not limited to accessibility and ethics, in order to promote a far more personalized learning revolution.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch006.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch005.title: Metaverse-Based Immersive Learning Environments
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch005.abstract: <jats:p>Immersive Learning environments that are designed using metaverse are a revolutionary change in contemporary education by introducing Virtual Reality, Augmented Reality, and smart interaction systems into single digital ecosystems. These spaces allow learners to be active in terms of simulation, avatars, and real-time collaboration, which facilitates experiential and personalized learning. The chapter introduces a conceptual framework that unites architecture, interaction design, and AI-based personalization, which is backed by the case-based analysis that shows quantifiable gains in engagement, retention, and learning performance. Findings show that there are huge improvements in participation, knowledge retention, and development of skills in comparison to the traditional systems. The chapter further addresses issues of scalability, interoperability, accessibility, and ethical issues and provides directions for future research and managerial implications of successful institutional adoption of Immersive Learning technologies.</jats:p>
doi:10.4018/979-8-2600-4649-4.ch005.venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

doi:10.26877/jipmat.v11i2.4143.title: PENGEMBANGAN LEMBAR KERJA PESERTA DIDIK BERBASIS PROBLEM BASED LEARNING DENGAN KONTEKS BUDAYA LOKAL UNTUK MENINGKATKAN KEMAMPUAN REPRESENTASI MATEMATIS SISWA SMP
doi:10.26877/jipmat.v11i2.4143.abstract: <jats:p>Penelitian ini bertujuan mengembangkan LKPD berbasis Problem Based Learning (PBL) dengan konteks budaya lokal yang valid, efektif, dan praktis dalam meningkatkan kemampuan representasi matematis siswa SMP pada pembelajaran matematika kelas VII. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode penelitian dan pengembangan dengan model ADDIE meliputi tahap Analysis, tahap Design, tahap Development, tahap Implementation, dan tahap Evaluation. Subjek penelitian adalah siswa kelas VII SMP Negeri 1 Kalinyamatan tahun ajaran 2025/2026. Penelitian menggunakan dua kelas yaitu VII H sebagai kelas eksperimen dan VII G sebagai kelas kontrol. Instrumen yang digunakan untuk mengukur kualitas LKPD yaitu angket lembar validasi untuk mengukur kevalidan, tes kemampuan representasi matematis untuk mengukur keefektifan, dan angket respon guru dan siswa untuk mengukur kepraktisan. Hasil analisis validasi meliputi validasi isi dan validasi konstruk menunjukkan nilai validitas berturut-turut sebesar 0,811 dan 0,828 sehingga LKPD tergolong sangat valid. Kualitas LKPD memenuhi kriteria efektif  ditunjukkan dengan hasil N-Gain sebesar 0,569 yang berkategori sedang, kemudian ketuntasan belajar siswa kelas eksperimen memiliki persentase 84% siswa mendapatkan nilai di atas KKM. Berdasarkan uji t data posttest didapatkan bahwa kemampuan representasi matematis kelas eksperimen lebih tinggi dibandingkan kelas kontrol. Serta analisis angket respon siswa menghasilkan nilai kepraktisan sebesar 77,74% yang berkategori “Baik” dan angket respon guru menghasilkan nilai kepraktisan sebesar 84,28% yang berkategori “Sangat Baik”. Dengan demikian, disimpulkan bahwa LKPD berbasis Problem Based Learning (PBL) dengan konteks budaya lokal yang dikembangkan terbukti valid, efektif, dan praktis untuk meningkatkan kemampuan representasi matematis siswa pada pembelajaran matematika SMP.</jats:p>

doi:10.25082/amler.2026.02.006.title: Expected Performance, Habit, and Enjoyment as Key Factors Influencing Teachers' Intentions to Use Personal Learning Environments for Educational Purposes
doi:10.25082/amler.2026.02.006.abstract: <jats:p>Recent research emphasizes the importance of Personal Learning Environments (PLEs) in the educational process. However, before their integration into school classrooms, it is important to investigate the extent to which teachers accept PLEs for educational purposes---an area that has received limited attention in the existing literature. To this end, this study empirically investigates teachers' intention to use and Use Behavior of PLEs. Drawing on the UTAUT2 model, data from 540 Greek primary and secondary school teachers were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings showed that Performance Expectancy, Habit, and Hedonic Motivation were significantly associated with Behavioral Intention, while Behavioral Intention, Habit, and Facilitating Conditions were significantly associated with Use Behavior. Mediation analysis further showed significant indirect effects of Performance Expectancy, Hedonic Motivation, and Habit on Use Behavior through Behavioral Intention. Behavioral Intention partially mediated the relationship between Habit and Use Behavior, indicating complementary partial mediation. No significant moderating effects of gender, age, or classroom technology-integration experience were found. The findings offer further insight into the mechanisms underlying teachers' use of PLEs and inform their integration into educational practice.</jats:p>
doi:10.25082/amler.2026.02.006.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research

doi:10.33369/pendipa.10.4.1301-1305.title: Pengaruh Model Pembelajaran Problem Based Learning Berbantuan Media Poster Terhadap Hasil Belajar Siswa Pada Materi Struktur Atom Kelas X SMA
doi:10.33369/pendipa.10.4.1301-1305.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to determine the effect of implementing a poster-based problem based learning (PBL) model on student learning outcomes in the topic of atomic structure among X student at Pematangsiantar state high school 4. The study employed a quasi-experimental design with a pretest-posttest control group. The research subjects consisted of two classes: an experimental class that received instruction using the poster-based PBL model and a control class that received conventional instruction. The research instrument consisted of learning outcome tests administered before and after the intervention. Data were analyzed using nonparametric tests and N-Gain calculations. The results showed that the average pretest scores for both classes were relatively similar. After instruction, the average posttest score for the experimental class increased to a higher level than that of the control class. The N-Gain test yielded an N-Gain score of 0.64 > 0.30, falling into the “moderate” category, and an N-Gain percentage of 64% > 56%, falling into the “fairly effective” category. Thus, it can be concluded that the poster-based PBL learning model has a positive effect on students’ learning outcomes regarding atomic structure material in X grade high school.</jats:p>
